Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more data, rows, or time than functionally required.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine runtime settings for memory, logging, parallelism, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware, workload mix, or version defaults.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, making access paths and stored rows unreliable.

When all three conditions coexist, the system exhibits a tangled set of symptoms: long-running statements and transactions that repeatedly hit slow-query thresholds; erratic latency where the same query alternates between slow execution, errors, or silent mis-reads; spikes in I/O, CPU spin, or log-write waits that do not match actual hardware utilization; surges of checkpoint, auto-vacuum, or page-verification activity; duplicate or missing rows returned by heavy scans; sudden fallback to full table scans despite available indexes; repeated application retries that amplify load; and intermittent corruption errors or crash-recovery events that escalate under peak workload periods.

Causally, inefficient SQL drives excessive scans, joins, and long transactions, multiplying the physical touch-rate on pages that already contain latent corruption. Misaligned configuration—such as undersized buffer pools, over-aggressive checkpoint intervals, or disabled verification settings—both magnifies the performance cost of the bloated workload and increases churn on the compromised storage blocks. The heavier I/O and checkpoint storms induced by poor SQL and bad parameters accelerate exposure of damaged pages, which in turn trigger retries, error handling paths, and emergency maintenance workers; these extra activities further inflate resource contention created by the original workload logic. Meanwhile, corruption-induced plan instability forces the optimizer to abandon indexes, deepening the performance penalty of the already inefficient queries. The feedback loop among inefficient SQL, misconfiguration, and structural corruption therefore degrades throughput, inflates tail latency, and jeopardizes data correctness across both transactional and analytical usage.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Critical optimizer metadata (row counts, histograms, correlation data) is stale or incomplete, producing systematic cardinality errors and sub-optimal execution plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : The replication channel cannot ship, write, or apply change-stream records as fast as the primary generates them, causing widening log gaps and replay lag.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport paths, listeners, sockets, or authentication slots are saturated or unstable, throttling client traffic and any database communication that relies on the same network.

When all three root causes strike together, the database exhibits a blended symptom set:  • Queries on the primary and on read replicas show severe plan drift, long runtimes, and explosive I/O because misestimated cardinalities choose inefficient join orders or missing indexes. • These bloated queries emit outsized result sets and hold transactions open longer, enlarging write-ahead logs. • Replication views show rapidly increasing send/receive/replay lag, while primary log segments accumulate and disk usage grows because they cannot be recycled. • Concurrently, client sessions and replication transport report connection stalls, timeouts, retransmissions, or "too many connections" errors as the network and listener queues saturate. • On read replicas, both stale data (because of lag) and stale statistics (never refreshed due to catch-up backlog) yield even poorer plans, making troubleshooting signals hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causal interaction: Inaccurate statistics produce heavyweight queries that inflate log volume and prolong transaction lifetimes; the surge in redo must traverse the replication channel, stressing apply workers. Network congestion and exhausted connection resources throttle that channel, amplifying replication lag. The growing lag forces the primary to retain more log files, increasing storage pressure and further slowing I/O for already inefficient queries. On replicas, delayed replay postpones statistics refresh jobs, perpetuating optimizer inaccuracy and compounding bad plan generation. The feedback loop between poor plans (from stale statistics), network-induced replication slowdown, and replication-induced resource retention drives a cascading degradation that impacts both OLTP and analytical workloads across the cluster.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though the statistics fed to the costing model are reasonably accurate.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine parameters (memory, checkpoint, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics, causing avoidable pressure on internal subsystems.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The network layer, listener, or connection slots cannot sustain the offered session or data-transfer rate, introducing transport-level latency and throttling.

When these three root causes coincide, symptoms layer on top of each other: 1) plan flips or plan skew inflate CPU time, I/O volume, and row counts; 2) mis-sized memory pools or overly aggressive checkpoint and parallelism settings amplify the resource demand created by the bad plans, producing bursty log flushes, buffer churn, and background-worker backlog; 3) the inflated execution times keep back-end sessions open longer, increasing concurrent connection counts and result-set sizes, which further saturate listener queues and network throughput. Clients experience sporadic latency spikes, mixed SQL wait events (plan-related CPU/iowait, configuration-driven buffer and log waits, plus client-read/write waits), and occasional connection timeouts or refusals that are hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causal chain: a sub-optimal plan detonates resource usage; the mis-configured memory/checkpoint/parallelism parameters prevent the engine from absorbing this surge efficiently, leading to page-flush storms, log-write stalls, or worker exhaustion; the prolonged queries then hold sockets, backlog authentication, and push the connection pool over its limits, making the network layer itself a visible bottleneck. Conversely, network slowdowns lengthen query durations, giving the optimizer more chances to cache or reuse poor plans under skewed bind values, while configuration pressure keeps invalidating or recompiling plans. Together these feedback loops magnify each anomaly’s impact, dragging overall throughput and predictability far below what any single issue would cause alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table layouts, data types, indexes, and partitioning do not match access patterns, forcing every statement through intrinsically inefficient access paths.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, and I/O slots, stalling while competing for low-level memory structures rather than logical locks.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume most available CPU cycles, driving run-queue pressure and system-wide latency once cores saturate.

When all three issues occur together, the workload shows a mix of plan scans and lookup amplification that flood the buffer pool, triggering excessive page replacements and dirty-page flushes. Sessions pile up on buffer-busy and page-latch waits, while at the same time CPUs peg near 100 % due to constant buffer pin spinning, latch polling, and over-executed, non-selective query plans. Performance views report simultaneous spikes in logical I/O, latch wait time, and CPU time per transaction; response-time variance grows unpredictably, and even simple queries intermittently stall behind internal contention rather than explicit user locks.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design inflates the number of pages each statement must touch, rapidly churning the limited buffer cache. The heightened churn forces frequent page evictions and flushes, concentrating accesses on a small set of root or hotspot pages that all sessions must repeatedly pin, thereby escalating buffer-latch contention. The resulting spin-loops and retry logic, combined with the already bloated execution work, drive CPU utilization to saturation. High CPU load then prolongs latch holding times and slows background flusher threads, which in turn exacerbates buffer pressure and contention, creating a reinforcing feedback loop that magnifies latency and erodes overall throughput.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level queries or transaction patterns demand more data processing, scanning, and logging than the business case requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The optimizer relies on stale or incomplete statistics, causing systematic cardinality errors and sub-optimal execution plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot ingest or apply primary log records fast enough, creating widening replication lag and retained log segments.

When these three root causes coincide, the database experiences an amplified feedback loop of stress: poorly written or chatty application logic generates heavyweight scans and bloated transactions; stale statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing even more I/O-intensive plans, further inflating CPU, memory, and log volume; the surge of redo and larger result sets saturates the replication pipeline, causing log-position gaps, replica staleness, and prolonged retention of primary log files. End-users see erratic and long-tail response times, timeouts, and inconsistent read results between primary and replicas, while administrators observe ballooning disk usage from un-recycled logs, frequent plan recompilations, and replica apply backlogs.

Causally, excessive scans and updates from the workload anomaly quickly invalidate existing statistics, yet high data-change velocity may still not trigger or complete automatic statistics refreshes, locking the optimizer into bad estimates. The resulting mis-estimated plans magnify resource consumption and redo generation, accelerating the growth of the transaction log. The swollen log stream overwhelms replication bandwidth or apply throughput, and the resulting lag prevents log truncation on the primary, further aggravating I/O pressure. Meanwhile, replicas starved of up-to-date data can no longer serve read traffic effectively, pushing more load back to the primary and deepening contention. Each anomaly thus reinforces the others, producing a compound performance and availability degradation that is far more severe than any individual issue in isolation.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same objects, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress. 
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data or index pages causes unreliable access-paths and errors during reads or writes. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Allocated data, log, or temporary space is exhausted, preventing further page splits, allocations, or log growth. 

When these three root causes coincide, the database experiences a multifaceted failure mode. Applications observe surging lock-wait times and deadlock rollbacks while simultaneously hitting "out of space" or "cannot allocate extent" errors. Corrupted pages or mis-linked index nodes can force the optimizer to abandon efficient index probes and fall back to full scans that touch far more rows, sharply increasing lock footprints, temp-space consumption, and log volume. As space dwindles, auto-extension failures block data-file or log growth, which in turn prolongs open transactions waiting on space, lengthening lock hold times. Corruption-induced retries and recovery attempts inflate transaction counts, amplifying contention, while background integrity checks or rebuilds required to fix corruption compete for the same scarce space and locks. Monitoring shows an interleaving of lock-wait spikes, corruption errors, and space-exhaustion alerts, making it difficult to isolate a single culprit. 

Causally, page or index corruption can trigger unexpected lock escalation or long-running consistency checks that monopolize high-level locks, setting the stage for severe contention. The additional I/O and logging generated by repeated scan retries and rollbacks accelerate space consumption in data, temp, and log areas, pushing the system toward capacity limits. Once space exhaustion occurs, allocation failures prevent lock-holding transactions from completing and releasing resources, further deepening the contention spiral. Conversely, near-full data or log files can impede corruption-repair operations, allowing structural damage to persist and propagate. The feedback loop among locking delays, structural corruption handling, and space shortages culminates in widespread throughput collapse, elevated error rates, and heightened risk of systemic outage.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level query or transaction design forces the engine to process far more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : The cross-node log shipping and apply path falls behind, creating widening gaps between primary and replica positions.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are internally inconsistent, leading to corrupt or unreliable access paths.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: expensive or chatty statements generate voluminous redo that must be shipped to replicas; the overwhelmed replication pipeline accumulates unapplied log segments whose contents include corrupt pages or malformed index changes; replicas show rapidly growing apply lag, intermittent apply failures, repeated retry loops, and may abruptly switch to full table scans because their local indexes are flagged unusable. On the primary, the same heavyweight statements suffer from inconsistent execution plans and erratic runtimes as corrupted indexes intermittently omit or duplicate rows, triggering application-level retries that further inflate workload volume. Monitoring dashboards simultaneously report chronic slow queries, soaring replication delay, rising disk space consumption from unrecycled logs, page-checksum errors on both primary and replica, and divergent result sets between nodes, making diagnosis difficult.

Causally, inefficient SQL inflates data change volume and transaction size, amplifying the byte rate the primary emits and extending transaction lifetimes so that unrecycled log segments pile up. The swollen log stream increases replica I/O and CPU pressure, lengthening the window during which any latent page or index corruption can surface during apply or query execution. Corrupt data blocks encountered by the replica can stall or abort replay, which in turn exacerbates replication lag and forces the primary to retain even more log data. Meanwhile, corruption on the primary can propagate downstream, causing replay errors that cascade into replica downtime. The resulting feedback loop—inefficient workload producing excess log traffic, replication backlog magnifying the impact of corruption, and corruption causing further replication failures—drives escalating latency, data divergence risks, and potential loss of high-availability guarantees.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers (1) intense page-level latch and buffer-cache contention, (2) replication pipelines that are unable to keep pace with the primary’s log generation, and (3) underlying on-disk data or index corruptions. The coexistence of these three root causes creates a feedback loop where local access serialization, cross-node log back-pressure, and structural corruption all interact to degrade throughput, inflate latency, and jeopardize data availability and correctness.

Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot or churned buffer pages force sessions to queue or spin on latches, pins, or page-content locks, stalling CPU cores and delaying I/O.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or replay the primary’s WAL/redo stream at production speed, causing growing replica lag and retention of log segments on the primary.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical page faults, checksum mismatches, or broken index structures make on-disk data unreliable, provoking verification errors, failed probes, or forced full scans.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Severe and uneven response-time spikes as foreground queries wait on contested buffer latches while simultaneously encountering checksum or key-order failures that trigger re-reads or error handling. • Escalating replication lag and ballooning retained log files because corrupted pages or invalid index changes repeatedly fail during apply or trigger error-induced rollbacks, further throttling the replication receiver and apply threads. • CPU saturation from spin-locks on the primary, paired with high I/O and checkpoint pressure as unrecycled log segments accumulate. • On replicas, apply workers loop on retry logic or halt on corruption detection, leading to divergent data sets and loss of fail-over readiness.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Corrupted pages or indexes force additional buffer fetches, page retries, and error-handling logic, amplifying latch contention on already hot pages. The same corrupt blocks propagate into the write-ahead log; when replicas attempt to fetch or apply these records, they stall or error, slowing acknowledgment and widening replication lag. The primary, unable to recycle log segments due to replica lag, retains extra dirty buffers and log pages, inflating memory pressure and intensifying buffer churn. Heightened page churn and larger dirty sets extend flush cycles, keeping buffer latches locked longer and feeding back into contention. Meanwhile, replication apply retries repeatedly touch the same corrupt pages, further loading buffer latches and I/O paths. This vicious circle degrades both local transaction latency and distributed consistency, risking cascading failures and potential loss of data durability across the cluster.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of statistics or plan-choice quality.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records that outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and adding visibility-check overhead in high-churn transactional systems.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside heap or index pages that breaks key ordering, page links, or heap-to-index mappings, making stored structures unreliable.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a blended failure signature: queries that are already forced into full scans by poor indexing now traverse massively bloated bitemporal heaps and indexes, causing steep latency spikes and memory pressure; bloated or corrupted index pages yield divergent row counts, duplicate or missing rows, and sudden plan flips to table scans. Autovacuum/cleanup workers run constantly yet fail to reclaim space because corruption aborts passes or because schema design (e.g., missing partitioning) forces them to process huge ranges. Checksum or page-verification errors appear intermittently, sometimes only during long-running maintenance, making it hard to discern whether slowness stems from design, version bloat, or structural damage. Statistics drift rapidly due to both bloat and silent row loss, so the optimizer oscillates between bad plans, further masking the underlying integrity faults.

Causally, the absence of appropriate indexes or partitioning drives the engine to perform large update/delete operations via full scans, generating a flood of row versions that stress the MVCC cleanup subsystem. As version store and table size swell, I/O pressure rises and page churn increases, elevating the likelihood of torn pages, incomplete writes, or failed online index rebuilds that introduce physical corruption. Conversely, corrupted pages or broken index links can cause cleanup workers to loop, abort, or skip ranges, allowing even more dead versions to accumulate. The growing heap and corrupted index entries in turn invalidate remaining noncovering indexes, magnifying the original design flaw. This feedback loop rapidly degrades both read and write performance, compromises data correctness, and complicates recovery efforts, producing a severe, self-reinforcing composite anomaly.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer statements or transaction patterns that unnecessarily scan, join, or retain more data or longer transactions than the business logic requires.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records that outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and visibility-check costs.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Mis-tuned engine parameters governing memory, background workers, checkpoints, and parallelism that are misaligned with workload characteristics and hardware capacity.

When all three conditions coincide, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: 1) a growing population of slow and timing-out queries whose latency is dominated by both excessive data access and ever-larger version chains; 2) rapid bloat of tables, indexes, and version stores causing drastic drops in cache hit ratios and longer sequential scans; 3) cleanup workers and checkpoints alternately starving or overrunning I/O, leading to bursty disk activity, checkpoint storms, and erratic throughput; 4) inflated lock and snapshot lifetimes that cascade into higher memory footprint and transaction-ID wraparound warnings; 5) monitoring views show paradoxical resource utilization—CPU under-utilized during I/O stalls, or vice versa—because mis-set parameters throttle some subsystems while others are saturated.

Causally, chatty or long-lived application transactions (SQL Workload Logic Anomaly) generate large volumes of updates and deletes, creating an abundant supply of dead tuples. MVCC cleanup must work harder, but its effectiveness is hampered both by the lingering snapshots held open by those same long transactions and by conservative maintenance thresholds or memory/I/O caps imposed by sub-optimal configuration parameters. As version bloat increases, query plans degrade and force even wider scans, further amplifying the workload logic inefficiency. Simultaneously, poorly sized buffer pools, work memories, and checkpoint intervals intensify I/O pressure, slowing both user queries and vacuum/garbage-collection workers. The feedback loop of bloated storage, sluggish cleanup, and ever-costlier queries drives the system into chronic performance instability, particularly under high-concurrency OLTP conditions.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan selection.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing is slowed by saturated log buffers, undersized or poorly placed log files, or sluggish archiving/replication, making the log path the dominant bottleneck for writes.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical devices or storage fabric cannot deliver the required read/write bandwidth or IOPS, so data-file, temp, or log I/O requests queue up and incur excessive latency.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database exhibits a mixture of severe plan inefficiencies, persistent log-related stalls, and generalized I/O saturation. Queries may choose nested-loop or hash joins that spill to disk because of cardinality errors, multiplying read and temp I/O. The extra I/O load collides with an already throttled storage layer, inflating data-file and temp-space latency, while every write must still traverse the overloaded transaction-log path, driving up commit times and causing "log write", "log flush", and device wait events to dominate. Checkpoints and log-archive operations extend their duration, leading to frequent log-full conditions, blocked DML, and application timeouts. Performance counters oscillate between CPU under-utilization (waiting on I/O) and sudden CPU spikes when I/O briefly clears, making diagnosis difficult as symptoms appear to migrate across layers.

Causally, stale or missing statistics can cause the optimizer to choose plans that amplify page reads, temp spills, and row-by-row processing, inflating both data I/O and redo generation. The inflated redo rate accelerates log growth, forcing more frequent log flushes, switches, and archives exactly when the shared storage subsystem is already throughput-bound. In turn, the saturated log device holds commit processing hostage, prolonging transaction duration and keeping locks active, which causes additional contention and may prevent automatic statistics refresh, perpetuating the statistics staleness. The competition for limited I/O bandwidth between data reads/writes and log flushes forms a positive feedback loop, driving systemic slowdown and making each individual anomaly harder to isolate without considering their mutual reinforcement.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data items, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress until waiters are released or victims are aborted.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and undo/rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating tables and indexes and adding visibility-check overhead.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Data, index, log, or temp areas approach or reach their physical or logical size limits, causing allocation failures, halted writes, and system-wide back-pressure.

When all three conditions arise together, the database exhibits compound symptoms: lock-wait queues lengthen while table and index sizes balloon, buffer-pool hit ratios fall as bloated pages evict hot ones, and checkpoint or log-flush operations stall when storage space runs out. Applications experience timeouts and frequent deadlock or "out of space" errors, throughput collapses, and background vacuum/garbage-collection workers spin but make little progress because they themselves are blocked or cannot allocate additional work space. Monitoring shows soaring lock-wait time, rapidly shrinking free bytes in data and log volumes, expanding version stores, and a surge of log and temp-space allocation failures.

Causally, heavy lock contention tends to prolong transaction lifetimes, delaying commit/rollback and preventing cleanup workers from advancing the MVCC horizon; this accelerates version bloat. The swelling version store expands data files and rollback segments, consuming additional disk space, while extended lock holds also keep undo and redo logs active, slowing log recycling. As storage fills, auto-extension failures and throttled write paths further lengthen commit latency, which in turn exacerbates lock queues and deadlock frequency. The feedback loop between blocked transactions, unreclaimed versions, and dwindling storage amplifies each individual anomaly, driving the system toward a space-exhaustion and availability crisis that is more severe than any single root cause alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model and indexing choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of plan selection quality.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or misleading statistics feed wrong cardinality estimates to the optimizer, causing sub-optimal plan choices even when the schema is adequate.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot ingest or apply primary redo fast enough, producing sustained replication lag and retention of transaction logs on the primary.

When all three root causes coincide, the database displays a blend of local performance pathologies and distributed-consistency issues. Queries on the primary show erratic and often escalating latency: some statements fall back to full scans because needed indexes are missing, while others pick inefficient join orders due to severe cardinality misestimates. These heavier plans inflate CPU, I/O, and lock footprints, lengthening transaction commit times. The enlarged transactions generate larger redo bursts, which replicas—already throughput-constrained—cannot replay promptly. Monitoring tools simultaneously report growing execution times, inflated actual-vs-estimated row count gaps, chronic automatic statistics refreshes that never catch up, and steadily widening replication delay with mounting log storage at both primary and replica sites. Stale read-only replicas deliver increasingly outdated data, and failovers risk data loss.

Causally, poor schema and index design magnifies the impact of bad statistics: missing or non-covering indexes force the optimizer to rely on table or index scans whose cost is underestimated when statistics are stale or skewed, leading to heavyweight execution plans. The resultant surge in I/O and longer-running transactions produce larger, more bursty WAL/redo streams. Replicas, already limited by apply inefficiencies or network constraints, fall behind faster as they must process the bloated redo generated by inefficient plans and possible full-table modifications (e.g., bulk updates without proper indexing). Conversely, replication lag can delay statistics refresh jobs that run on replicas or offload maintenance traffic, further extending statistics staleness on the primary. The intertwined feedback loop—design flaws causing heavier workload, statistics errors choosing worse plans, and replication lag preventing timely relief—drives systemic degradation across both transactional and analytical operations.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible locks on the same data items, resulting in blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort sessions.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings such as buffer-pool size, checkpoint frequency, work-memory limits, or parallelism are mis-tuned, so performance degrades even though raw hardware resources are not fully utilized.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions repeatedly collide on hot buffer pages, page pins, or internal latches, causing excessive wait or spin time inside the buffer manager.

When all three root causes surface together, the workload experiences a cascading slowdown: lock-wait and deadlock events coincide with surges in page-latch and buffer-busy waits, while system-wide performance counters show CPU saturation alternating with idle gaps and erratic I/O bursts. Transactions queue in the application layer, connection pools fill, and user-visible response times spike unpredictably. Deadlock reports, lock-timeout errors, and long semaphore/latch hold times appear in close temporal proximity, making it hard to attribute the primary bottleneck. Checkpoints or background writers may trigger sudden storms of dirty-page flushes that amplify both lock and latch durations, further depressing throughput.

Causally, mis-sized or mis-timed configuration parameters (e.g., undersized buffer pool, aggressive checkpoint intervals, or excessive per-session work memory) force hot pages to be evicted and reloaded, inflating latch acquisition and I/O latency. Longer page-level contention extends the time locks are held, heightening the probability of blocking chains and deadlocks. In turn, lock contention prolongs transaction lifetimes, keeping pages pinned and latches occupied, which feeds back into buffer-cache contention. The intertwined feedback loops between poor configuration, latch pressure, and lock waits reinforce each other, producing a severe concurrency bottleneck characteristic of this composite anomaly.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging pipeline—covering in-memory log buffers, log file groups, flushing, switching, archiving, and replication retention—cannot keep pace with commit generation, making the log subsystem the primary bottleneck on the write path.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : One or more storage areas (data, log, archive, temp, backup, diagnostic) reach or approach physical or logical space exhaustion, causing allocation failures and stalling operations that require additional space.

When both anomalies are active, the database experiences compounding symptoms: commit latency and log-flush waits rise while free space in the online redo or archive destinations simultaneously plummets; log switches become abnormally frequent yet stall because the next log segment cannot be created; archiver or replication processes back up, filling remaining disk quickly; checkpoints and background writers thrash to reclaim space; DML sessions encounter "cannot allocate log", "out of space", or "archive destination full" errors; temporary-space and data-file growth operations may also fail, leading to widespread transaction timeouts, lock contention, and potential instance-wide freeze.

Causally, an overloaded log subsystem emits log data faster than it can be flushed or archived, accelerating space consumption in the log and archive areas. As space dwindles, the storage capacity anomaly prevents new log segments or archives from being created, which in turn blocks log switches and commit processing, amplifying log-write latency. The stalled log pipeline then prolongs transaction hold times, increases in-memory pressure, and may force emergency checkpoints that further inflate I/O and space demand. Thus each root cause feeds the other: slow or stuck log handling hastens space exhaustion, while space exhaustion further degrades log throughput, spiraling the database into a hard stop unless both logging performance and free-space availability are simultaneously remediated.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Simultaneous transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks on the same data items, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks inside the lock-manager layer and stalling statement execution. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process or its children hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other OS-level objects, preventing creation of new backends, workers, or I/O contexts. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Server- or network-side constraints on sockets, listener backlogs, authentication threads, or transport capacity limit the establishment and servicing of client connections.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blended failure pattern: existing sessions become trapped in prolonged lock waits or cyclical deadlocks while new clients experience connection refusals, timeouts, or prolonged authentication delays. Lock-bound backends that cannot complete free their locks slowly or hold them indefinitely if OS limits block their ability to write to WAL, open extra files, or spawn background workers; this prolongs blocking chains and inflates wait-event and deadlock counters. Concurrently, exhausted file-handle or thread quotas reduce the pool of accept()able sockets, so the listener queues overflow, causing TCP resets and application-level connection storms that repeatedly retry and further raise incoming connection pressure. Monitoring shows runaway lock-wait times, rising deadlock victim counts, sharp drops in completed transactions per second, escalating OS error messages about "too many open files" or "cannot create thread", and surges in half-open sockets and retransmissions.

Causally, heavy lock contention increases backend counts and prolongs session lifetimes, accelerating consumption of OS resources (descriptors, semaphores, threads). Once kernel limits are hit, the database cannot create additional server processes or worker threads, which in turn prevents deadlock detectors, autovacuum workers, or I/O helpers from starting, delaying lock resolution and log flushing and deepening the backlog. Simultaneously, socket and backlog exhaustion triggered by the same OS limits or by retry storms prevents blocked applications from reconnecting to roll back or retry, leaving their orphaned transactions and locks in limbo. The feedback loop between in-engine lock stalls, OS-level exhaustion, and network-layer connection failures amplifies service degradation, potentially leading to a full outage even though each individual anomaly might have been survivable on its own.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible locks and block or deadlock each other, stalling progress at the lock-manager layer. 
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions compete for hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots, forcing serialization below the lock layer. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process exhausts kernel-enforced limits such as file handles, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or thread quotas, preventing new allocations.

When all three root causes arise together, the system exhibits compound symptoms: long lock-wait chains mixed with high buffer-busy/latch wait events, CPU spin with no throughput gain, spikes of deadlock victim rollbacks, and surging connection-pool backlogs. Simultaneously, the engine begins to log failures to create threads, allocate shared memory, or open files; new sessions, background workers, or parallel tasks are intermittently rejected even as existing ones hang on locks or latches. Latency becomes unpredictable, throughput collapses, and monitoring views show ballooning lock queues, latch waits, and kernel-level allocation errors, making it difficult to isolate any single bottleneck.

Causal chain: intense lock contention leaves transactions open longer, multiplying the number of concurrent sessions and pinned buffer pages. The enlarged session count and page churn amplify hot-page and latch competition inside the buffer manager. As workers spin or wait, they consume additional kernel objects—threads, file descriptors, async-I/O contexts—which pushes the process toward or beyond operating-system limits. Once limits are hit, the engine fails to spawn the very background tasks (e.g., deadlock detectors, checkpointers, flushers) needed to relieve lock and buffer pressure, further prolonging locks and latches and causing positive feedback that rapidly degrades the entire workload.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The primary’s write-ahead log files, buffers, or archiver processes become the bottleneck for commit processing, inflating log-flush and log-sync latency and triggering frequent log-file switches or checkpoint storms.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or change-data consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply log records quickly enough, causing widening log-position gaps, replay lag, and retained log segments on the primary.

When both root causes manifest together the database exhibits a feedback loop of write-path stress and replication backlog. Observable symptoms include: 
• Spiking commit latency, "log file sync/log flush" and "log file write" waits on the primary, accompanied by rising "replication send/receive" waits.
• Rapid log-file growth, repeated log rotation or archiver stalls, and exhaustion of log or archive storage because replicas hold old segments open.
• Steadily increasing replication delay metrics (lag in bytes, seconds, or LSNs), stale read-only replicas, and degraded failover readiness.
• Periodic write stalls or throttling when the primary cannot obtain a free log segment, coinciding with network congestion or apply slowdowns on replicas.
• Amplified recovery-time objectives (RTO) as both local crash-recovery checkpoints and remote apply queues grow.

Causal interaction: A saturated transaction-log subsystem lengthens commit cycles, inflating the volume and duration of outstanding redo that must be shipped. The slower and bulkier the local logging becomes, the more bursty and voluminous the traffic a replica must ingest and replay. Conversely, replication lag prevents timely log-segment reuse, forcing the primary to keep and continuously allocate additional log files. This enlarges the on-disk log footprint, increases file-switch frequency, and intensifies flushing pressure, further degrading log I/O performance. The two anomalies thus reinforce each other, creating a vicious cycle where log congestion on the primary and apply lag on replicas mutually aggravate, potentially culminating in write outages, replica desynchronization, or uncontrolled storage growth.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) is mis-aligned with workload access patterns, forcing plans into full scans, non-covering lookups, and other inefficient paths.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, causing prolonged buffer-busy and page-latch waits and CPU spin without throughput gain.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing is throttled by log buffer, log file, or archiver saturation, elevating log-flush and log-sync waits and stalling write workloads.

Composite anomaly definition: All three root causes are active at the same time in an OLTP system: sub-optimal schema/index design amplifies logical I/O and redo generation, the resulting surge of page accesses leads to acute buffer-cache and latch contention, and the elevated redo stream overwhelms the transaction-log subsystem, forming a multi-layer bottleneck that spans from SQL access path to memory management to durable logging.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Queries show full scans or non-covering index probes with many logical reads; 2) wait-event views report simultaneous spikes in buffer_busy/page_latch, log_flush/log_sync, and physical I/O; 3) CPU usage oscillates between spin loops and idle while commit latency climbs; 4) hotspot pages such as index roots, monotonically growing tables, or sequence blocks exhibit latch contention and rapid dirtying, while log files switch frequently and archivers fall behind; 5) adding extra buffer cache reduces but does not eliminate symptoms, and adding an index or enlarging log files alone yields only partial relief, signaling intertwined root causes.

Causal chain and interaction: Poor schema and indexing force each transaction to touch more pages, inflate row versioning, and emit excessive redo. The enlarged working set churns through a limited buffer pool, so the same root or data pages become hot, intensifying latch competition. Dirty hot pages in turn prolong checkpoint and flush activity, keeping latches held longer and enlarging the log buffer. The heightened redo rate pushes the log writer to its throughput limits; when log flushes slow, transactions hold locks and keep pages pinned even longer, exacerbating buffer contention. Meanwhile, the latch stalls lengthen critical sections that hold the log mutex or generate redo records, further reducing log throughput. This positive feedback loop causes cascading slowdowns across the access path, buffer manager, and logging layers, leading to severe, workload-wide performance degradation that is difficult to attribute to any single layer in isolation.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The system concurrently suffers from (1) Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly—physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk data and index pages, (2) CPU Resource Anomaly—sustained saturation of host CPU by database processes, and (3) Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly—exhaustion of kernel-enforced objects such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or thread quotas. The coexistence of all three faults means storage structures are untrustworthy while the compute layer is overloaded and the operating system is actively denying additional resources.

Combined observable phenomena: Queries may intermittently return wrong or duplicated rows, abruptly fall back from index scans to full table scans, or raise corruption errors. At the same time overall response times climb as CPU usage pins at or near 100 %, with long run-queues and pervasive scheduler/runnable wait events. Concurrently, new sessions, parallel workers, or file opens may fail, and engine or kernel logs will show "too many open files", ENOMEM, semaphore, or AIO context errors. Integrity-check or recovery tasks invoked to repair corruption intensify CPU demand, while their file and memory requests frequently hit OS limits, causing retries, hangs, or crashes. The overlapping symptoms blur boundaries—performance slow-downs, data errors, and resource-exhaustion messages appear interleaved, making root-cause identification difficult.

Causal interaction: Corrupted pages often trigger repeated read-retry, checksum verification, and full-table rescans, markedly increasing CPU consumption; this extra load accelerates CPU saturation. To bypass corruption, the engine and clients may spawn additional worker processes, enlarge sort/hash areas, or open replacement files—quickly exhausting kernel object limits. Conversely, when OS limits on file handles, shared memory, or threads are reached, I/O or allocation failures during write-ahead logging, checkpointing, or index rebuilds can interrupt atomic operations and propagate new page or index corruptions. Persistent CPU saturation further prolongs critical sections and recovery windows, heightening the probability of torn pages during power events. Thus each anomaly intensifies the others, driving a feedback loop that degrades throughput, jeopardizes data integrity, and risks partial or total service outage.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive and uncontrolled growth of database memory structures (buffer/plan caches, work areas, parallel buffers, leaks) that pushes the host into sustained memory pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical or logical corruption inside data pages or index structures that invalidates checksums, key ordering, or page links and causes unreliable query results and recovery errors.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Persistent oversubscription of host CPU where database processes monopolize cores, producing high run-queue depth, context-switch thrashing, and system-wide latency.

When these three anomalies occur together, the system is hit by a triple-failure mode in which (1) aggressive memory consumption drives the OS into swap storms and stalls, (2) corrupted pages or indexes provoke repeated retries, verification scans, or full-table fallbacks, and (3) the resulting surge of re-execution, error handling, and background recovery floods the CPUs. Observable symptoms include: oscillating resident-set size with simultaneous paging and CPU saturation, erratic query latencies with some returning wrong or duplicate rows, frequent checksum or logical-consistency errors in engine logs followed by crash-recovery cycles, escalated I/O from forced page flushes and integrity-check utilities, and a noisy mixture of memory pressure waits, corruption-related errors, and CPU run-queue waits in performance views. Administrators may find it difficult to attribute slowdowns to any single layer because each anomaly masks and inflates the others.

Causally, runaway memory allocation can starve buffer pools, forcing the engine to evict and reread pages, increasing the chance of encountering latent corrupt blocks; memory pressure may also interfere with checkpoint or background scrubber threads, leaving pages only partially written and thus propagating corruption. Once corruption is detected, the engine often initiates page rereads, integrity checks, or index rebuilds—operations that are CPU‐intensive and allocate additional memory, further amplifying the initial memory shortfall. Concurrently, elevated CPU usage delays critical recovery and checkpoint tasks, extending the window during which pages remain dirty and vulnerable to incomplete writes, while CPU starvation impedes timely detection and repair of corruption. The feedback loop among memory exhaustion, integrity faults, and compute saturation can cascade into repeated crash-recovery cycles, degraded throughput, and potential data loss unless all three root causes are addressed in concert.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer relies on stale, incomplete, or inaccurate statistics, producing systematic cardinality misestimates that drive poor plan choices.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level memory, I/O, parallelism, and background-worker parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, introducing artificial resource pressure or throttling that is unrelated to true capacity limits.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical table or index pages contain corruption or logical inconsistencies, making access paths unreliable and causing incorrect or missing data to surface at execution time.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms multiply and blur: queries may oscillate between unexpectedly slow full scans (from misestimation) and erroneous, partial, or duplicated result sets (from corrupted indexes or pages). Repeated plan changes, sudden plan regressions after data loads, and frequent statement or transaction aborts appear alongside unusual wait-event patterns—e.g., excessive buffer-busy or log-write waits—even when CPU and I/O utilization remain low due to mis-set memory pools, checkpoint intervals, or parallelism caps. Integrity checkers may intermittently report page or key-order errors, yet operators may misinterpret them as fallout from the performance issues, delaying corrective action. Overall, troubleshooting becomes difficult because each symptom (poor plans, resource imbalance, data errors) can masquerade as the sole culprit while actually stemming from their interaction.

Causally, stale or missing statistics push the optimizer toward plans (such as narrow-range index probes or large hash joins) whose effectiveness depends on healthy index structures and adequate memory. If indexes are internally corrupt, these plans return wrong results or trigger run-time error handling that forces full scans, amplifying the cost of the original misestimation. Simultaneously, misconfigured memory or checkpoint parameters can starve the buffer cache, inflate I/O latency, and induce frequent background flushes, magnifying the performance penalty of the unexpected scans and heightening the likelihood of torn pages or incomplete writes that deepen existing corruption. Conversely, corruption-induced retries and long-running error-handling paths inflate workload variability, thwarting auto-tuning heuristics and preventing statistics refresh jobs or autovacuum-style maintenance from completing. The feedback loop between bad statistics, harmful configuration, and structural corruption accelerates degradation of both performance and data correctness, threatening overall system stability.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or poorly governed growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, and other in-memory structures pushes the database process and host beyond safe physical- or virtual-memory limits.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot or rapidly churning buffer pages provoke intense latch, pin, or buffer-busy waits, causing CPU spin and latency spikes as sessions serialize on page access rather than on logical row locks.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Data files, temp areas, or log/archival destinations approach or reach full allocation, halting further writes, auto-extension, or log recycling and thereby stalling foreground activity.

When these three conditions arise together, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: memory pressure drives frequent page evictions while latch contention inflates CPU usage and response-time variance; escalated dirty-page churn collides with shrinking free disk space, triggering aggressive checkpointing, prolonged flush cycles, and "out-of-space" or "cannot extend" errors. Concurrently, cache blow-out and swap activity magnify latch hold times, while blocked writes caused by full data, temp, or log areas propagate back to buffer flushers and user sessions, producing a mixture of memory OOM events, page-latch stalls, checkpoint storms, and transaction timeouts that are difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, runaway memory allocation shrinks effective buffer-pool headroom, forcing hotter pages to be recycled more often and increasing latch pressure on the remaining working set. Heightened latch contention keeps pages pinned longer, decelerating flush threads; the resulting backlog inflates dirty-page counts, accelerating file growth and temp/log consumption. As storage capacity tightens, checkpoints lengthen, extension or log-archive failures freeze buffer write-out, causing even more resident-set growth (as dirty pages cannot be freed) and further latch congestion. Each anomaly thus reinforces the others—memory bloat fuels contention, contention inflates dirty buffers, and space exhaustion blocks relief paths—culminating in system-wide stalls, crashes, or node evictions.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, density, and correlation metadata no longer match the actual data, causing systematic cardinality misestimation.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The cost model or plan-cache logic chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistical inputs are nominally adequate.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, so the storage layer can no longer guarantee that index lookups or heap scans return the correct rows.

When all three root causes coexist, the database can exhibit mutually reinforcing symptoms: estimates in execution plans are wildly inaccurate, but even repeated statistics refreshes fail to correct them; identical SQL statements oscillate between very different plans, some of which rely on damaged index structures and therefore return wrong or fluctuating result sets; operators that the optimizer expected to be inexpensive explode in runtime because they read chains of corrupt pages or because the true row counts are far higher than estimated; integrity-check utilities, plan re-compilations, and excessive statement retries appear together in logs, while performance swings and correctness errors grow harder to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, stale or missing statistics can mislead the optimizer into selecting access paths that rely heavily on particular indexes; if those indexes are partially corrupted, the resulting runtime faults amplify execution cost and may trigger emergency plan invalidations, pushing the optimizer toward alternative but still sub-optimal plans. Conversely, corruption that silently drops or duplicates keys distorts sampling during automatic statistics collection, further degrading cardinality accuracy. The optimizer, deprived of reliable metadata and forced to choose among degraded structures, produces erratic plans whose poor execution characteristics impose additional I/O and recovery stress, potentially aggravating latent corruption. The intertwined feedback loop between bad statistics, bad plans, and bad pages intensifies both performance degradation and data-quality risk.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or missing optimizer statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimates that lead the cost-based optimizer to choose sub-optimal execution plans.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, log files, flushing, switching, or archiving—cannot keep pace with redo generation, making commit processing and write activity I/O-bound.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared-memory segments, AIO contexts, threads, or cgroup quotas throttle database processes independently of internal engine settings.

When these three root causes occur simultaneously, workloads—especially high-concurrency OLTP systems—exhibit extreme and erratic latency on write statements and commits, sudden pauses during peak periods, multiplication of "log flush" or "commit" wait events, inflated CPU yet low throughput, and bursts of engine errors such as "cannot allocate shared memory" or "too many open files." Execution plans show large disparities between estimated and actual row counts, while alert logs report rapid log switches, archiver backlogs, and background-process failures to obtain operating-system resources. Automatic statistics refresh may be disabled by the prolonged log switch backlog, and new sessions or parallel workers intermittently fail to start as kernel object limits are reached.

Causal interaction: poor statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing plan shapes that generate excessive redo—e.g., row-by-row updates, fragmented index maintenance, or unnecessary logging of intermediate results—dramatically increasing pressure on the transaction-log subsystem. As log files and buffers saturate, commit delays lengthen, causing sessions to stay active longer and inflate the population of open file handles, threads, and AIO requests. This accelerated consumption of kernel resources pushes the system toward operating-system limits; once those ceilings are reached, log archiving, checkpoint helpers, and statistics-collection workers fail to start or allocate resources, perpetuating stale statistics and further plan degradation. The feedback loop between misestimated plans, log saturation, and OS-level exhaustion amplifies each anomaly, producing a compounded degradation that is more severe and harder to isolate than any single issue alone.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures on disk no longer match their logical contents, leading to corrupted or inconsistent data blocks, page links, or key order. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database exhausts or approaches exhaustion of allocated disk or filesystem space for data, logs, temp, or backup areas, resulting in allocation failures and stalled write-ahead activities. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other OS-managed objects, preventing new allocations or worker creation.

When these three conditions arise concurrently, symptoms overlap and amplify: corruption verification errors and checksum failures appear at the same time as data-file growth, redo, or temp writes are being refused because disks are full; error logs alternate between "out of space" messages and OS denials to open additional files or map pages; background recovery, checkpoint, or index-rebuild tasks loop or crash for lack of both disk blocks and kernel resources, causing repeated instance restarts; queries that fall back to full table scans due to broken indexes now also fail on temporary-space exhaustion, and new client connections intermittently fail when the engine cannot obtain file handles or shared memory—creating a mixed pattern of logical errors, I/O failures, and session drops that is difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, storage exhaustion and OS resource saturation can precipitate or magnify physical corruption: when space is scarce, data and log writes contend for the last free extents; interrupted or partial writes (e.g., due to ENOSPC or inability to extend files) leave pages half-written, producing integrity faults. Simultaneously, hitting file-descriptor or I/O context limits prevents the engine from opening replacement files, completing checkpoints, or flushing dirty buffers, increasing the window during which torn or inconsistent pages persist. Conversely, corruption inflates error logging and forces emergency reorganization or repair jobs that allocate temp space and extra file handles, accelerating both space consumption and kernel-resource depletion. The intertwined feedback loop degrades availability and risks unrecoverable data loss unless all three underlying constraints—on-disk integrity, free capacity, and OS limits—are addressed together.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions block or deadlock each other while waiting for incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata resources.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions stall on hot buffer pages or the latches that protect them, causing CPU spin or wait time and slowing page access.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing and redo generation are throttled by saturated log buffers, slow log writes, or delayed archive/replication, inflating commit latency.

When all three conditions arise together, the database experiences a compound bottleneck in which logical row-level blocking, physical buffer-page serialization, and log-flush back-pressure converge. Symptoms include extreme and erratic transaction latency, long blocker–waiter chains that do not clear after deadlock resolution, surging page-latch and log-write waits, CPU spikes from spin-locks, stalled checkpoints, and cascading application timeouts. Standard diagnostic views show simultaneous growth in ungranted locks, latch wait events, and pending log-flush queues, making it hard to attribute the slowdown to any single layer.

Causally, hot rows or pages drive up lock conflicts; blocked transactions then hold buffer pages and latches longer, increasing buffer contention. Prolonged critical-section occupancy inflates redo generation bursts when blockers finally commit, which overwhelms the log buffer and stretches log-flush times. In turn, the sluggish log subsystem delays commit completion, extending lock hold times and keeping pages pinned, which feeds back into both lock and latch queues. The intertwined feedback loops between lock duration, latch residency, and log-flush latency amplify each other, creating a severe, self-reinforcing degradation of OLTP throughput.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing is throttled because log-buffer flush, log-file switching, archiving, or retention stalls the write-ahead logging path.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical devices or virtualization layers cannot sustain the required read/write throughput or latency budget for data, temp, or log files.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client-to-server transport, listener, authentication, or socket resources are saturated, causing connection establishment or data transfer delays.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a multi-layer bottleneck: commits queue behind slow log flushes, those flushes in turn wait on an overloaded storage subsystem, and inflight application sessions accumulate because network handshakes, result shipping, or keep-alive traffic are throttled. Observable symptoms include prolonged commit and transaction response times, surging log-related wait events alongside high device queue depths and elevated read/write latency, growing redo and archive backlogs, connection timeouts, rising counts of half-open sockets, and sessions stuck in client I/O waits. System-wide throughput collapses even though server CPU may remain under-utilised, and performance troubleshooting becomes difficult as wait-event profiles oscillate between log, I/O, and network categories.

Causally, restricted storage bandwidth slows every log-buffer flush; this inflates commit latency and prolongs transaction lifetimes, increasing the number of concurrent connections and the volume of network traffic each must sustain. The swelling session pool and larger in-flight result sets then overrun listener backlogs and socket buffers, introducing additional delays that further defer application ACKs needed for synchronous commits. These extra delays, in turn, keep transactions open longer, extending redo generation intervals and swelling log segments, which worsens the already saturated storage channel and pushes archive and replication pipelines further behind. The intertwined feedback loops between log pressure, storage saturation, and network congestion therefore amplify each other, rapidly degrading OLTP workload performance and raising the risk of service outage or data-loss scenarios if durability SLAs are violated.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously limited by a saturated transaction-log subsystem, suffering from on-disk data/index corruption, while the underlying storage layer is unable to supply adequate read/write throughput. All three conditions are active at the same time, forming a multi-layer fault that degrades durability, consistency, and performance, and greatly complicates recovery and diagnosis.

Observed phenomena: 1) Commit operations stall behind escalating log-flush, log-write, and log-sync waits; archive or replication pipelines fall behind and trigger checkpoint storms. 2) Queries intermittently return missing or duplicate rows, integrity-check utilities report page-checksum, key-order, or pointer errors, and execution plans degrade to full scans. 3) Device metrics show queue depths pegged, soaring read/write latencies, and prolonged data-file, temp-file, and log-file I/O waits. When these symptoms overlap, end-user sessions may see timeouts, deadlocks on allocation pages, repeated crash-recovery cycles, or sudden read-only failovers as the engine attempts to protect itself from further corruption.

Causal interaction: Sustained storage I/O saturation throttles both data-page and redo-log traffic, directly slowing log flushes and amplifying the transaction-log bottleneck. The resulting backlog forces larger checkpoints and keeps dirty pages and un-archived log segments on disk longer, increasing the window in which any latent media error can corrupt data or index pages. In turn, corrupted pages provoke repeated read retries, verification scans, and failed recovery attempts that generate additional I/O and log activity, pushing the already overloaded storage further past its limits. This feedback loop deepens commit latency, broadens corruption scope, and can ultimately exhaust log space or crash the instance, making the three anomalies mutually reinforcing and highly disruptive to OLTP workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, join, or lock far more data and for longer durations than business requirements dictate.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Engine and session memory structures grow beyond safe host limits, leading to pressure, paging, and cache churn that slow execution and risk OOM failures.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging layer cannot absorb or persist redo fast enough, causing commit stalls, backlog in log archival/replication, and write-path throttling.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a blend of severe and mutually amplifying symptoms: end-user statements run with extreme and highly variable latency; commits pause on log-flush waits that lengthen as memory pressure forces dirty buffers to be flushed and log buffers to shrink; slow queries and prolonged transactions monopolize buffer pages and work memory, driving resident-set growth, OS paging, and plan-cache bloat; concurrent long-running writes generate surges of redo that outpace log device throughput and fill log segments, triggering checkpoint storms and cascading stalls. Administrators may observe simultaneous slow-query spikes, escalating memory usage or OOM events, and commit latency alerts, making it difficult to attribute performance collapse to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL inflates row scans, sorts, and joins, expanding per-query work areas and dirty-page generation. This heightened memory demand collides with already stressed buffer, sort, and cache regions, accelerating memory pressure and evictions. As memory tightens, the engine may shrink log buffers or stall background flushers, further slowing commit throughput. Meanwhile, the bloated and long-running transactions from the workload anomaly emit excessive redo, saturating the undersized or contended transaction-log subsystem. Log flush delays prolong transaction lifetimes, which in turn hold memory and locks even longer, feeding back into memory exhaustion and elevated concurrency waits. The intertwined effects of heavy logical workload, memory overcommit, and log bottlenecks thus create a reinforcing loop that degrades both throughput and stability in write-intensive OLTP environments.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from excessive accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions and uncontrolled growth of memory-resident structures, causing both storage-level bloat and host-level memory pressure at the same time.

MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, undo/rollback records, and dead index entries pile up faster than background cleanup processes can purge them, inflating on-disk objects and lengthening visibility checks.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other memory heaps expand beyond the safe limits of physical RAM, leading to paging, OOM kills, and degraded cache efficiency.

Combined symptoms: • Rapid growth of both on-disk relation size and in-memory buffers devoted to stale row versions and undo, driving the database process’s RSS steadily upward. • Cleanup workers that are chronically scheduled yet starved for RAM, showing frequent restarts or throttling under OS memory pressure. • Elevated I/O due to double handling of data: bloated tables require longer scans while reduced cache effectiveness forces more disk reads; simultaneous swapping further slows I/O paths. • Query latencies become highly variable: readers traverse ever-larger version chains while also stalling on memory allocation, and writers may experience checkpoint or WAL backpressure. • Nodes in clustered/VM environments may be evicted or reboot due to exceeded memory cgroups, with recovery complicated by large undo/redo segments.

Causal interaction: The surge of obsolete versions expands both the persistent heap and the in-memory buffer pool, directly increasing memory consumption. As the memory envelope is exceeded, the operating system begins paging or terminates processes, which in turn slows or interrupts background vacuum/garbage-collection workers, allowing even more dead versions to accumulate—a positive feedback loop. Memory pressure also reduces effective work memory per query, causing hash/sort spills that further inflate temporary files and prolong transactions, keeping old snapshots open and preventing version pruning. Conversely, long-running or memory-hungry queries spawned during memory bloat delay transaction-ID advancement, deepening the MVCC horizon problem. The intertwined effects amplify each other, degrading throughput, increasing crash risk, and making root-cause isolation harder because symptoms of storage bloat and memory exhaustion appear concurrently.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly inefficient execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request conflicting locks, leading to prolonged blocking or deadlocks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions compete for hot buffer-cache pages and latches, stalling on low-level synchronization primitives.

When all three conditions co-exist, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: an ill-chosen execution plan triggers large scans or explosive join fan-outs that touch many more rows and pages than necessary; these bloated data accesses demand numerous locks and repeated buffer pin/latch operations. As a result, lock-wait queues grow, deadlock reports surge, CPU time is consumed by latch spin/sleep cycles, and overall response times and throughput degrade erratically. Performance counters may simultaneously show optimizer plan churn, escalating lock-wait and deadlock statistics, plus spikes in buffer busy or page-latch waits, making single-root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, the sub-optimal plan is the spark: by scanning or joining far more rows, it expands the lock footprint and lengthens transaction duration, increasing the window for conflicting lock requests. These prolonged holds, in turn, keep buffer pages pinned and their associated latches occupied, propagating latch contention to other sessions that need the same pages. The resulting latch stalls slow query execution even further, extending lock lifetimes and intensifying lock contention—a feedback loop that can culminate in systemic throughput collapse, widespread deadlocks, and severe latency spikes for transactional workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database concurrently suffers from stale or incomplete optimizer statistics, a replication pipeline that cannot keep up with primary redo generation, and impending or actual exhaustion of allocated storage space. The intersection of these three root causes causes a compound failure mode where poor cardinality estimates drive inefficient execution plans that inflate write-amplification, which in turn overwhelms both replication apply capacity and on-disk free space, precipitating log-retention and allocation failures across the cluster.

Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Critical metadata about row counts, value distributions, and correlations is outdated or missing, leading the optimizer to systematically misestimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes lag in receiving or applying WAL/redo, widening log position gaps and preventing timely log recycling on the primary.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space in data, temp, or log areas approaches exhaustion, threatening allocation failures and halting workload progress.

Combined Phenomena:  • Query plans suddenly shift to full scans, large hash joins, or bloated sort/hash spill operations, driving up data-file growth, temp usage, and redo volume.  • Replication lag accelerates; relay logs or retained primary log segments balloon because space-starved replicas replay changes ever more slowly.  • Free space drops in multiple segments (data, temp, WAL, archive) leading to auto-extend failures, checkpoint stalls, and "disk full" errors that propagate to both primary and replicas.  • Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in buffer cache churn, background statistics auto-update retries, replication retransmissions, and space-management alarms, making it hard to pinpoint a single culprit.

Causal Chain: Stale or absent statistics trigger inefficient, I/O-heavy execution plans that inflate the volume of modified pages and generated redo.
