The surge in redo must traverse the replication channel; limited apply throughput on replicas widens lag windows and forces the primary to retain log segments longer, consuming additional disk space. As data and log files grow, storage free space dwindles; once thresholds are crossed, auto-stats jobs may be skipped, temp spills fail to allocate space, and replication may halt when it cannot write relay or archive logs—each feedback loop worsening the others. Ultimately, the trio of misestimation, replication backlog, and space exhaustion creates a self-amplifying degradation that threatens both performance and availability across the database ecosystem.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same objects, forming blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress until a victim is chosen or the blocking clears.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database processes collectively consume more RAM than the host can safely supply, provoking paging, OOM terminations, or cache churn that slows every operation.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Growth of data, log, temp, or backup areas exhausts allotted disk space, leading to allocation failures, halted checkpoints, or inability to persist new data.

When all three root causes strike together, the system exhibits a layered failure pattern: long-running lock waits accumulate sessions that continue to hold memory grants; the pinned buffers, work areas, and unreleased cursor state inflate physical memory usage, pushing the host into swap. As memory pressure rises, sort and hash operations spill to TEMP, and frozen transactions prevent log truncation, rapidly consuming remaining disk space. The resulting space exhaustion then blocks further writes and checkpoints, which in turn prolongs lock retention and forces even more sessions into wait queues. Observable symptoms include explosive growth of lock-wait time, escalating resident-set size, heavy paging, TEMP and log files auto-extending until full, aborted transactions due to deadlock, OOM, or "no space left" errors, and cluster failover or crash-recovery storms that make diagnosis difficult.

Causally, initial lock contention lengthens transaction lifetimes, keeping their memory allocations and unflushed log segments open. This sustained resource hold amplifies memory pressure and temp-space use. As RAM becomes scarce, the engine spills work to disk, accelerating space consumption; once disk fills, checkpoints and log archiving stall, so lock-holding transactions cannot commit or roll back, deepening the contention. Each anomaly therefore feeds the others in a reinforcing loop that can drive the database into a cascading outage if not interrupted.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application SQL and transaction design compel the engine to scan or manipulate far more data and hold resources longer than functionally required.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data files, logs, and temporary areas is exhausted or cannot grow, causing allocation failures.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, processes, or related objects are reached, blocking further resource acquisition by the database.

When these three root causes manifest together, the system experiences compound symptoms: long-running or repetitive statements consume excessive CPU and memory, inflate redo and undo logs, and generate large temporary segments. The surging I/O and spill-to-disk activity accelerate space consumption until tablespaces, logs, and temp areas hit hard limits, at which point DML, queries, index builds, and checkpoint operations stall with "no space" or "cannot extend" errors. Simultaneously, the same bloat drives a spike in open files, shared memory segments, and background worker creation; as kernel quotas are met, new sessions fail to connect, parallel workers abort, and existing tasks receive OS-level "too many open files" or "cannot allocate memory" errors. The overlap of storage exhaustion and OS-resource exhaustion leaves the engine partially frozen: some sessions hang on I/O or log writes, others on kernel denials, producing a confusing mosaic of timeouts, lock contention, and crash-recovery events.

Causally, poorly written SQL amplifies data churn, flooding redo, undo, and temp space and forcing the engine to open additional data files, sort runs, and temporary objects—each requiring file handles and shared memory. Rapid space depletion causes frequent auto-extension or archive operations, further multiplying file opens and background processes until kernel limits are breached. Conversely, once OS limits are reached, the database cannot allocate the very handles and shared segments it needs to recycle space or archive logs, so space remains unreclaimed and fills even faster. The intertwined feedback loop between inefficient workload, space exhaustion, and OS resource starvation escalates into a systemic outage far more severe than any of the individual anomalies alone.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, often due to flawed costing logic or unstable plan reuse.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpoint, logging, etc.) are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, so performance bottlenecks arise from the settings themselves rather than true resource exhaustion.

When both root causes manifest concurrently, workloads can display erratic and highly unpredictable behavior: the same query text flips between multiple poor plans, each suffering from exaggerated latency spikes whenever mis-configured memory, I/O, or parallelism thresholds are crossed. For example, a nested-loop plan mistakenly preferred by the optimizer may thrash in buffer cache because work-memory or buffer-pool sizes were reduced, leading to sudden spills, excessive log-write stalls, and surges in CPU wait events even though system-wide utilization appears low. Observers may see alternating patterns of unused hardware capacity and short bursts of saturation, growing plan cache churn, frequent checkpoint storms following heavy scans, and performance regressions that defy single-factor explanations.

Causally, misaligned configuration parameters distort the runtime feedback loop the optimizer relies on—e.g., underestimated I/O costs after an overly small buffer pool, or skewed parallelism decisions when max worker threads are capped—raising the likelihood of sub-optimal plan selection. Once an inefficient plan is chosen, the stress it places on memory, I/O, or logging can quickly collide with the already tight engine limits, amplifying waits and triggering further plan invalidations or re-compilations. This feedback cycle deepens the performance degradation: bad plans magnify pressure on mis-configured resources, while the resulting resource contention influences the optimizer to continue choosing or retaining poor plans, ultimately destabilizing both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions hold or request mutually incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall forward progress. 
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Database components (buffer/cache, work areas, background heaps) collectively grow beyond safe physical limits, provoking host-level memory pressure and paging. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database process exhausts kernel-enforced quotas for objects such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or process IDs, preventing new allocations.

When these three root causes coincide, symptoms overlap and magnify: lock-wait time and deadlock frequency surge while overall throughput and connection acceptance plunge; meanwhile the database’s resident-set size climbs until the kernel begins paging or refuses further memory, leading to sporadic "cannot allocate memory" or "too many open files" errors. Stalled or killed transactions repeatedly reconnect and retry, inflating connection bursts that generate more processes/threads and file handles, which in turn collide with OS limits. Administrators observe alternating lock-wait spikes, sudden session failures, escalating swap usage, growing wait queues in the connection pool, and flurries of engine and kernel log messages about lock timeouts, out-of-memory kills, and resource-limit denials—all without a single clear chokepoint.

Causally, intensive lock contention lengthens transaction lifetimes, inflating the number of concurrent sessions that stay resident and each one’s memory/work-area footprint. The bloated memory demand brings the host to the brink of physical exhaustion; once paging starts, transaction execution slows further, prolonging locks and amplifying contention—a feedback loop. Simultaneously, the surge in waiting sessions and frequent reconnection attempts multiply process/thread and file-descriptor usage, quickly breaching OS quotas. Hitting those limits causes some sessions or background workers to crash, which roll back their locks and force other transactions to restart, re-enter queues, and allocate fresh memory, perpetuating the instability. Thus, the interplay of lock contention, runaway memory growth, and kernel resource exhaustion creates a self-reinforcing spiral that can culminate in partial or total service outage.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Remote replicas or subscribers cannot ingest or apply transaction-log records as fast as the primary emits them, creating widening replay lag and retention of log segments.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database host CPUs are saturated by sustained, abnormal compute demand, starving other activities of processor cycles and inflating latencies across the stack.

When both conditions exist together, replication delay and CPU exhaustion compound. Observables include rapidly growing replica apply lag, swelling on-disk WAL/relay logs, prolonged commit latency on the primary as recyclable log files accumulate, near-100 % CPU utilization on either the primary or replicas, spikes in run-queue wait events, and system-wide query slow-downs. Catch-up workers on replicas may show extreme CPU times, while primary back-pressure mechanisms (throttled senders, longer commit waits) manifest concurrently. Failover readiness degrades as replicas drift further behind, and administrative queries to inspect replication or CPU state also slow, making diagnosis harder.

Causally, CPU saturation can both cause and be exacerbated by replication lag: overworked replicas lack CPU to replay incoming WAL, which increases backlog size; the resulting surge of deferred apply work then drives even higher CPU usage when capacity briefly becomes available. Conversely, large replication backlogs force the primary to retain and occasionally re-transmit log segments, adding encoding and network CPU overhead that pushes the primary toward saturation. The feedback loop between compute starvation and log-shipping delay amplifies resource pressure on all nodes, risking transaction latency spikes, storage exhaustion from un-recycled logs, and potential replication collapse.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating data structures and visibility-check cost.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log generation, flushing, switching, or archiving path becomes saturated, lengthening commit latency and stalling write activity.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, leading to allocation failures and cascading stalls.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: data files and indexes bloat with dead tuples while log directories balloon with unarchived segments, rapidly depleting overall storage. Commit operations slow first due to log-flush and switch waits; long-running queries encounter escalating visibility checks over swollen version stores; autovacuum or purge workers run continuously yet fall further behind; checkpoints and archive processes thrash the same saturated devices; eventually tablespace and log destinations hit hard size limits, triggering allocation errors, frozen transaction horizons, forced read-only mode, or total outage. Symptoms appear interleaved—space-related errors may surface as log sync stalls, while query slowdowns may be misattributed to normal load rather than hidden storage exhaustion.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn produces both abundant MVCC debris and a surge in redo generation. The inflated version store expands heap and index footprints, directly accelerating space consumption and increasing the bytes that must be logged. The swollen log stream, in turn, overwhelms log files and archive pipelines; as archives lag, old segments cannot be recycled, locking down yet more disk space. Dwindling free space then throttles or halts autovacuum/purge activity, preventing dead-row reclamation and further inflating tables and logs—a positive feedback loop that rapidly degrades performance and risks database unavailability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing scans or non-covering look-ups that inflate I/O and lock footprints.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or tables, resulting in blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger rollbacks or timeouts.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage devices are saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, so each physical read or write stalls, independent of database configuration.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compounded symptoms: queries that already perform full scans or many non-selective index probes generate large volumes of physical I/O against an over-subscribed storage layer, pushing device queues to their limits and inflating I/O latency. Slower I/O prolongs statement execution, leaving locks held open longer and expanding the window for conflicting transactions to collide. This magnifies lock-wait chains, deadlock frequency, connection-pool exhaustion, and application timeouts. Meanwhile, blocked sessions accumulate, creating bursty "thundering-herd" releases that further spike I/O demand when locks are freed, perpetuating the saturation cycle. Overall, CPU usage remains uneven, with threads oscillating between runnable yet waiting on I/O and lock events, while business throughput degrades sharply and variability in response times escalates.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and missing or non-optimal indexes force the engine to touch far more data than necessary, increasing both the number of pages locked and the volume of read/write requests. The bloated lock scope raises the probability of conflicts, while the excess I/O pushes the storage subsystem into sustained saturation. Elevated I/O latency slows down every lock-protected operation, keeping locks active longer and intensifying contention; heightened contention in turn clusters wake-ups and retries, generating I/O bursts that exacerbate storage overload. Thus, each root cause amplifies the others, driving a feedback loop that degrades transactional performance far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model and indexing choices mismatch workload access paths, forcing otherwise correct SQL to read or write far more data than necessary.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores become saturated by database processes, throttling all sessions regardless of their individual efficiency.

When these root causes strike together, the system displays a blend of I/O-heavy access paths and persistent CPU saturation. Execution plans show full scans, large hash or sort operations, and repeated key lookups, while OS metrics report high run-queue depth, elevated context switches, and spikes in CPU time for the most frequent statements. Latency escalates non-linearly: queries slowed by scan-heavy plans also wait longer in CPU run queues, causing lock hold times, connection pool exhaustion, and sporadic timeouts. Maintenance tasks (auto-vacuum, statistics refresh, checkpoint, log flushing) compete for already scarce CPU, so short stalls ripple into user-visible slowdowns and variance in response times.

Causally, sub-optimal schema and missing or misaligned indexes compel the optimizer to choose resource-hungry plans that read and process excess rows; this inflates per-query CPU demand. The aggregate effect of many such inefficient executions drives CPU Resource Anomaly. Once cores are saturated, the scheduler elongates every CPU quantum, further magnifying the cost of each scan, join, and sort. High CPU pressure delays background tasks that might otherwise mitigate bloat or refresh statistics, locking the system into a feedback loop where degraded physical design and compute starvation reinforce one another, ultimately depressing throughput and threatening stability under both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonable statistics, leading to unnecessarily expensive operator choices, poor join orders, or inappropriate degrees of parallelism.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine and its sessions over-allocate buffer, work, and cache memory, pushing the host into paging, swap, or OOM situations and causing frequent memory-pressure stalls.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server communication paths and connection slots are saturated or unstable, producing connection timeouts, socket backlog growth, and prolonged data-transfer waits.

When these three root causes arise together, symptoms interleave and intensify: expensive plans inflate working-set sizes and per-query work memory, accelerating buffer-cache churn and hash/sort spillover while bloating the plan cache; the resulting memory pressure triggers paging and CPU stalls that elongate statement runtimes. Longer runtimes hold server back-end processes and sockets open, inflating connection counts and transmit queues just as the network layer is already bandwidth- or handshake-constrained. Clients observe erratic response times, intermittent authentication failures, and frequent connection drops, while the database shows oscillating cache hit ratios, skyrocketing memory consumption, rapid plan churn with alternating good and bad plans, and an explosion of wait events related to both memory management and client I/O.

Causally, a vicious cycle forms: 1) poor plans demand excessive memory for scans, joins, and sorts; 2) this over-consumption collides with unbounded work areas and plan-cache growth, exhausting physical RAM and provoking paging, which throttles CPU and I/O throughput; 3) degraded execution speeds stretch transaction lifetimes, thereby increasing the number of concurrently active sessions and the volume of result data in transit; 4) the already congested network and limited listener or process pools cannot absorb the surge, causing connection stalls and retries; 5) retry storms and session churn further pollute the plan cache and allocate additional memory, feeding back into steps 1 and 2. The intertwined nature of these issues obscures single-factor diagnosis and can rapidly destabilize both the database host and its client ecosystem.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions stall while competing for hot buffer-cache pages, page pins, or latches, leading to spin or sleep delays during page access.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database engine or its worker processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for objects such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or I/O contexts, preventing further resource acquisition.

When both root causes manifest together, the system shows a mixture of intense page-level contention and sporadic kernel allocation failures. Symptom patterns include surging buffer-busy and page-latch waits intertwined with error messages about exhausted file handles, semaphore limits, or thread creation failures. Throughput oscillates as some sessions spin on latch acquisition while others are aborted or blocked by the OS, leading to sharp latency spikes, uneven CPU utilisation (alternating between spin storms and idle time), partial loss of parallel workers, and a rapid drop in cache hit ratios as pages are evicted or cannot be pinned. Monitoring views may show rising I/O due to reduced cache residency, yet background writers and checkpoint threads fail intermittently, amplifying dirty-page backlogs and prolonging flush-related holds.

Causally, OS-level resource exhaustion reduces the number of buffer-pool frames, background processes, or I/O contexts available, forcing more aggressive page replacement and enlarging the set of hot pages contended by surviving sessions—thereby aggravating latch contention. Conversely, severe latch spin or sleep loops inflate thread counts and open-file usage as sessions retry I/O and spawn additional workers, accelerating consumption of kernel objects until limits are breached. The two anomalies thus form a feedback loop: OS limits constrict the buffer manager’s operating headroom, heightening page-level serialization, while the resulting contention multiplies kernel object requests, hastening limit exhaustion and driving the database into cascading stalls or partial outages.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or page pins, stalling CPU threads while they wait to read, modify, or flush pages. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage subsystem cannot deliver the required read/write bandwidth or IOPS, so physical I/O latency and queue depths surge and database I/O waits dominate. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The network path, listener, or connection slots are saturated or unstable, causing slow or failed connection establishment and prolonged client read/write waits. 

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences a layered slowdown: 1) internal workers spin or block on buffer-latch waits, 2) outstanding I/O requests pile up because the storage layer is already at its throughput ceiling, and 3) client sessions struggle to connect or to consume results across an overloaded network. Observable symptoms blend and amplify—buffer-busy and page-latch waits coexist with soaring read/write latencies, while active session counts, socket queues, and retry storms grow. Application response times fluctuate wildly; some statements hang inside the engine, others time out on the wire, making the true bottleneck difficult to pinpoint. 

Causally, saturated storage keeps dirty or requested pages in flight longer, extending latch hold times and magnifying buffer contention. Prolonged execution increases session lifetime and concurrency, swelling the number of open connections and the volume of result data, which in turn stresses network and listener resources. Conversely, network stalls delay acknowledgement of commits and fetches, holding transactions open and keeping their locked and latched pages active, which further inflates buffer pressure. The compounded effect is a feedback loop: storage slowness fuels latch contention, latch contention lengthens transactions, and protracted transactions multiply network usage—all three reinforcing each other and driving the database into a severe, multi-layer performance collapse.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more rows, columns, or time than the business case requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, indexes, partitions, and constraints are structured in a way that does not support the workload’s access patterns, pushing even well-written statements toward inefficient data access.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, or correlation metadata is stale or absent, causing the optimizer to mis-estimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal plans.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits extreme and erratic latency spikes, runaway I/O, and CPU saturation. Queries already bloated by poor SQL logic devolve into repeated full-table or non-covering index scans because useful indexes are missing or mis-designed; simultaneously, outdated statistics convince the optimizer that these heavy plans are cheap, so it avoids better alternatives or fails to consider them. Symptoms include: the same statements dominating slow-query and lock-wait logs, sudden plan regressions after data changes, high variance between estimated and actual rows, excessive temp-space usage from mis-sized hash or sort operations, lock escalation due to long-running transactions, and dramatic performance improvements only when all three layers (SQL, schema, and statistics) are corrected together.

Causally, ill-formed SQL amplifies pressure on the physical design: wide scans and Cartesian joins become catastrophic when no suitable indexes exist. The deficient physical design, in turn, inflates the cost of every superfluous access the workload demands. Stale or inaccurate statistics mask these deficiencies from the optimizer, preventing it from selecting whatever limited indexing aids do exist and discouraging DBAs from recognizing design gaps, because estimated costs appear acceptable. Each layer therefore reinforces the others: bad SQL drives demand, bad design blocks efficient supply, and bad statistics obstruct corrective planning, jointly degrading both OLTP responsiveness and OLAP throughput.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime settings are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database memory structures grow beyond safe physical limits, provoking OS memory pressure and instability.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high share of CPU, driving the host toward sustained core saturation.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: rapidly rising resident-set size, frequent or continuous paging, and escalating CPU utilisation that remains high even while I/O devices are under-used. Checkpoints, log flushes, or parallel workers may spike suddenly after parameter changes, intensifying run-queue waits and context switching. Cache-hit ratios oscillate as buffer churn collides with swap activity, and query latency becomes erratic—sometimes bound by CPU, other times by stalls on memory allocation or page-in operations. Clustered or virtualised deployments may suffer node eviction or failover storms because watchdog timers expire under the combined memory and CPU stress, making the individual anomalies hard to isolate.

Causally, mis-set configuration parameters (e.g., oversized buffer pools, uncapped work-mem, aggressive parallelism, or overly frequent checkpoints) initiate uncontrolled memory consumption. As physical RAM is exhausted, the operating system starts paging; this not only slows memory access but also forces the database scheduler and background writers to perform extra work, driving CPU utilisation upward. The elevated CPU demand lengthens critical code paths—checkpoint processing, buffer eviction, and memory reclamation—feeding back into both memory pressure and parameter-driven worker proliferation. The positive feedback loop between bad configuration, runaway memory growth, and CPU saturation magnifies each condition, rapidly degrading throughput and stability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries because vacuum/cleanup workers cannot keep pace with update-delete churn or long-running snapshots.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Severe competition among sessions for buffer frames, page pins, and lightweight latches, leading to stalls, CPU spin, and inflated wait-event counters on hot pages.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Saturation of the physical storage layer’s bandwidth or IOPS budget, causing elevated read/write latency, deep I/O queues, and database waits dominated by file-I/O events.

Composite behaviour: When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits runaway bloat of heap and index pages, soaring buffer-busy and page-latch waits, and steadily rising device-level latency. Cleanup processes remain permanently backlogged, checkpoint and background-writer activity increase, and active queries suffer from both latch spin and prolonged I/O waits. Autovacuum or purge workers contend with foreground sessions for the same hot pages, amplifying latch contention, while their flush traffic keeps the storage queue saturated. Administrators observe shrinking buffer-hit ratios despite high memory usage, drastic variance in statement latency, frequent snapshot-too-old or transaction-ID wraparound warnings, and overall throughput collapse even though CPU utilisation appears moderate.

Causal chain: Heavy update/delete workloads create large volumes of dead tuples, inflating page counts and forcing more pages into the buffer pool. This expansion raises the probability that many sessions touch the same root or index pages, intensifying latch contention. The extra dirty pages generated by version churn must eventually be flushed, pushing sustained write rates toward or beyond the storage subsystem’s limits; once the I/O path saturates, checkpoints lengthen and dirty pages remain in cache longer, holding latches and pinning buffer slots. Prolonged I/O waits slow cleanup workers further, allowing even more version buildup. The resulting feedback loop—version bloat → latch pressure → I/O saturation → impaired cleanup—drives a self-reinforcing degradation that can cripple OLTP workloads unless all three layers (vacuuming, buffer management, and storage bandwidth) are addressed together.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a static physical-schema/index design that mismatches workload access patterns, relies on stale or insufficient optimizer statistics that distort cost estimates, and is further constrained by saturated or unreliable network/connection resources. Together these three root causes drive inefficient execution paths and unpredictable end-to-end latency that cannot be alleviated by addressing only one layer.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Queries that already scan large tables or perform excessive row fetches because of missing or inappropriate indexes receive plans based on badly misestimated cardinalities, amplifying plan inefficiency (e.g., choosing nested-loop joins with millions of actual rows or avoiding desirable indexes assumed to be non-selective). The bloated I/O and CPU generated by these misguided plans elongate server processing time, which in turn prolongs result streaming across an overloaded network layer. Meanwhile, clients experience longer connection establishment, higher query latency, intermittent timeouts, and sporadic "too many connections" or socket reset errors. Monitoring shows a mixture of symptoms: chronic full-table scans, high logical and physical I/O, optimizer estimated-vs-actual row count ratios far from one, frequent statistics refresh or dynamic sampling events, growing server-side session queues, client-read/client-write waits, retransmissions, and surges in aborted connections during workload spikes.

Causal interaction: Poor schema/index design forces heavier data access, making execution cost and row-count estimates more sensitive to statistics accuracy; when those statistics are stale or lack correlation data, the optimizer consistently selects sub-optimal plans that magnify I/O and CPU demand. The inflated resource usage increases query response time and stretches transaction duration, holding server processes and network sockets open longer. This higher concurrency exacerbates listener queue saturation, connection pool exhaustion, and packet congestion, which feeds back additional latency into application tiers. The ensuing retries or prolonged sessions further raise database load, masking the underlying design and statistics issues and complicating diagnosis. Thus, the three anomalies reinforce each other, creating a feedback loop that degrades both compute efficiency and network-level service quality across OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently selects sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are adequate, leading to inefficient operator choices, wrong join orders, or loss of parallelism.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path (buffer, file group, archiver, or replica shipping) becomes the primary bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling write activity.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network transport, listener, socket, or authentication resources are saturated or unstable, limiting connection throughput and inflating client-side latency.

When all three root causes strike together, the database experiences a multilayer performance collapse: 1) poorly chosen plans amplify the volume and burstiness of redo generation; 2) the overloaded log subsystem lengthens commit and flush times, causing sessions to queue on log-related waits; 3) prolonged execution and commit phases keep server processes busy and network sockets open, driving up concurrent connection counts, which in turn suffer from network backlog, retransmissions, and timeout storms. Observable symptoms blend: sudden plan flips to full scans coincide with surging redo size per transaction; commit duration, "log write" and "log sync" waits skyrocket; at the same time, clients report connection timeouts, authentication stalls, or sluggish result streaming. Monitoring may show high CPU from sub-optimal plans, disk I/O saturation isolated to log devices, growing archive or replica lag, plus an explosion of ESTABLISHED and TIME_WAIT sockets and listener backlog overflows.

Causally, sub-optimal plans inflate I/O and row-level change volume, directly increasing redo generation and frequency of log flushes. The stressed log path elongates transaction completion, holding locks and backend processes longer, which multiplies concurrent session counts and socket occupancy. Network saturation further delays acknowledgement of commit replies and result sets, causing application retries that re-enter the optimizer, generating yet more inefficient plans and additional redo. This feedback loop causes each anomaly to reinforce the others, degrading throughput, inflating latency across tiers, and making isolated diagnosis difficult because symptoms of one layer (e.g., network timeouts) are in fact rooted in the compounded failures of all three subsystems.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction flows demand more data, rows, or time than the business case requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table structures, partitioning, and index choices are mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even for well-written queries.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine runtime parameters (memory, logging, parallelism, checkpoints, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.

When all three conditions coexist, the database is simultaneously stressed by excessive logical work, sub-optimal physical access paths, and ill-sized runtime resources. Observable symptoms include: 
• Extremely long and erratic statement latencies, with the same queries dominating slow-query logs and holding locks far beyond normal durations.
• Execution plans showing table or index scans, repeated key lookups, and spilled sorts/hash operations, accompanied by high physical I/O despite low buffer-pool hit ratios.
• Wait-event patterns that oscillate between I/O starvation and artificial throttling (e.g., small dirty-page checkpoints, excessive log flush waits, memory pressure evictions) even though hardware metrics show unused capacity.
• Sudden throughput collapses or timeouts under peak load as bloated transactions interact with write-amplified indexes and mis-sized memory/worker limits, causing lock escalation, checkpoint storms, and cache thrashing.

Causal chain: Inefficient SQL logic expands the data that must be read, joined, sorted, or updated. Because the schema lacks appropriate indexes or partitions, those inflated requests translate into large sequential or random scans, excessive row fetches, and heavier undo/redo generation. The escalated I/O, memory, and concurrency demands collide with poorly chosen configuration parameters—such as undersized buffer pools, over-aggressive work-memory, or misaligned checkpoint intervals—preventing the engine from absorbing the extra load. The configuration shortfalls amplify the latency introduced by design flaws, while the workload’s bloated access patterns hinder background maintenance tasks tuned for lower volumes, creating feedback loops of backlog, contention, and unpredictable performance degradation. Together, the three root causes reinforce one another, masking individual symptoms and driving the database into chronic instability until each layer is addressed in concert.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer consistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are credible, leading to excessive CPU, I/O, or memory consumption per statement.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server transport, listener, or session resources are saturated or unstable, producing connection delays, socket backlogs, and data-transfer stalls.

When both root causes are present, the database shows a mixture of intra-engine and external latency signals: queries oscillate between different plans or stick to an inefficient plan that produces large intermediate result sets; those result sets linger in memory and on the wire while network throughput is constrained, causing back-end sessions to accumulate in client-read waits. Application servers observe longer connect times, sporadic authentication failures, and wide variability in statement latency, with some executions timing out during planning, others during result shipping. Plan changes may appear random because plan recompilations coincide with bursts of connection retries, while connection pool exhaustion masks whether the slowness originates in the optimizer or the network.

The causal chain often starts with a poor plan that executes for much longer and returns far more rows than necessary, inflating payload size and holding server processes and sockets open. The extended lifespan of each session amplifies pressure on the listener backlog and OS socket queues, pushing the network layer into congestion and raising round-trip times. Elevated network latency, in turn, delays completion feedback to the optimizer and exacerbates bind-sensitive plan instability; frequent reconnect attempts triggered by client timeouts further churn the plan cache, encouraging additional sub-optimal plan compilations. The two anomalies thus reinforce each other, multiplying concurrency, skewing resource estimates, and degrading overall throughput far beyond what either issue would cause in isolation.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table structure, partitioning, and indexing do not match workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans and lookups independent of statistics freshness.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas approaches exhaustion, leading to allocation failures and stalled writes.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode: poorly indexed statements fan out to many rows or pages, inflating the lock footprint of every transaction; the resulting long-lived locks generate extensive blocker–waiter chains that back up connection pools. At the same time, bloated table and index structures plus un-ended transactions prevent space reuse, pushing data files, transaction logs, and temp areas toward their capacity limits. Operators may observe a mixture of symptoms—escalating lock-wait time, sudden spikes in full-table scan I/O, deadlock victim errors, autogrow failures, and "out of space" messages—all intertwined and therefore difficult to attribute to a single root cause.

Causally, the design flaw is the first domino: missing or non-covering indexes make each query touch more rows, holding more locks for longer. The enlarged lock scope amplifies contention; blocked or rolled-back transactions remain open, keeping undo and redo segments active and preventing space reclamation. As log files cannot be truncated and tablespaces swell with untouched but still-locked pages, the storage subsystem fills up. Near-full disks slow auto-extension, which in turn lengthens commit processing and prolongs lock duration, further intensifying contention. Thus, deficient physical design, lock manager stress, and dwindling free space form a self-reinforcing loop that rapidly degrades transactional performance and risks outright service interruption.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are accurate, inflating logical I/O, work-set size, and concurrency demand.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Multiple sessions compete for hot buffer pages, latches, or page-pin resources, stalling on shared memory structures below the lock manager.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem is saturated so that physical read/write latency, IOPS, or throughput no longer meet the database engine’s demand.

When these three root causes strike together, the workload experiences runaway response times and throughput collapse. Poorly chosen plans generate excessive and often non-sequential page access, rapidly rotating working sets through an already stressed buffer pool. As the same hot index or data pages are repeatedly loaded and evicted, latch and buffer-busy waits spike, while the engine simultaneously floods the storage layer with redundant physical I/O that it cannot sustain. Observable symptoms include: frequent plan flips coinciding with bursts of PAGE-LATCH or BUFFER_BUSY waits, CPU cores spinning while others idle in I/O wait, oscillating throughput, dramatic variance between executions of the same statement, inflated physical I/O counts despite a high logical read footprint, and sustained device queue depths with increasing storage latency. Monitoring views will show intertwined wait classes—optimizer-induced re-compilations, buffer latch stalls, and disk I/O waits—making single-root attribution difficult.

Causal chain: a sub-optimal plan widens scans or drives high-fan-out nested loops, multiplying page requests. The surge in page fetches thrashes an undersized or already hot buffer cache, forcing frequent page replacements and intensifying latch acquisition on root and leaf pages. Each latch stall lengthens statement duration, keeping pages pinned longer and raising concurrency on the same hot structures. The inflated physical read/write demand then overruns storage throughput limits, elongating I/O service times; the slower I/O further extends page residency in the buffer and prolongs latch holds, feeding back into even more contention and reinforcing the optimizer’s incentive to keep or regenerate bad plans. The intertwined feedback loops between inefficient plans, memory-level contention, and storage saturation magnify latency and can lead to systemic slowdown or near-stall conditions under both OLTP and hybrid analytical workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the database to scan, lock, or return more data than business logic requires, inflating execution time, resource demand, and result-set size.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file handles, shared memory, threads, or other per-process / cgroup quotas, leading to failures in allocating required operating-system resources.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport paths, listener sockets, authentication handshakes, or connection slots become saturated or throttled, causing delays, refusals, and dropped or stalled client connections.

When all three anomalies are present, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: long-running or chatty SQL inflates the number and lifetime of sessions, each retaining open files, sockets, and memory segments until OS limits are exhausted. As limits are reached, the database intermittently fails to create back-end threads, accept new connections, or perform I/O, producing kernel “too many open files,” “cannot allocate memory,” or “cannot create thread” errors while simultaneous client-side timeouts, handshake failures, and rising retransmissions appear. Slow, data-heavy queries hold network sockets open for extended periods, clogging listener backlogs and leading to a surge of half-open or idle sockets. Application retries, triggered by connection failures, further lengthen transaction queues and exacerbate slow-query tails, making symptoms difficult to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies resource consumption per session—larger scans demand more file descriptors and shared memory, while bulky result sets and extended transaction windows monopolize sockets and keep network buffers full. This elevated baseline drives the system toward kernel limits; once those limits are crossed, the OS blocks new threads or I/O, which in turn forces the database to reject or stall additional work. Rejected or slow connections provoke client-side retry storms that inflate connection counts, magnify socket and authentication pressure, and deepen OS resource exhaustion. The feedback loop of heavy SQL, kernel-level denials, and network congestion accelerates degradation, potentially progressing from sporadic slowdowns to partial outages and, ultimately, complete service unavailability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or page-pin slots inside the buffer manager, stalling logical access to data despite available rows and indexes.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical volumes that hold data, temp, or log files are saturated for bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, throttling every read and write the database issues.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database and background processes drive host CPU usage to sustained saturation, exhausting runnable-queue capacity and elongating scheduling latency.

When all three root causes strike together the system exhibits an extreme "triple choke" pattern: 1) Page-level latch waits and buffer-busy waits climb, often accompanied by high spin counts that burn CPU while real work stalls. 2) Physical read/write latency from the storage subsystem stretches far beyond normal, filling I/O queues and inflating data-file, log-write, and buffer-I/O wait events. 3) Overall CPU utilisation sits at or near 100 %, with elevated context switches and scheduler delays, yet throughput and commit rates fall, giving the appearance of a CPU bottleneck that does not improve even when additional cores are provisioned. Application sessions may pile up in a mixture of latch, buffer I/O, and CPU run-queue waits, making the dominant symptom oscillate from CPU saturation to I/O wait spikes, complicating troubleshooting efforts.

Causal chain: Storage saturation slows every buffer read, write, and checkpoint flush, forcing pages to stay pinned and latches to remain held longer; this inflates latch-contention windows and drives more sessions into spin-waits, which in turn consume extra CPU. The extra CPU burn crowds the scheduler, delaying the submission and completion of asynchronous I/Os, which further deepens the storage backlog. Meanwhile, prolonged dirty-page residency and frequent eviction caused by the constrained buffer pool amplify the need for physical I/O, feeding additional load into an already saturated storage layer. The feedback loop between slow I/O, extended latch holds, and runaway CPU consumption can cascade rapidly, crippling both transactional and analytical workloads until one or more resources are relieved.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, producing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall statement execution until locks are granted or victims are aborted.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, logs, temp, or backup destinations is exhausted or cannot grow, causing allocation failures and halting write-ahead logging, sorting, or DDL.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server transport, listener, authentication, or socket resources become saturated or unstable, yielding connection refusals, timeouts, and stalled result transmission.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a multilayered slowdown: blocked or deadlocked transactions accumulate while their sessions hold locks and remain connected; meanwhile log writes, temp spills, or data-file extensions fail as space runs out, turning brief lock waits into indefinite hangs. Clients experience both long-running statements waiting on locks and sporadic connection failures or broken sockets; retry storms amplify the active session count, deepening the lock queues and further taxing limited network endpoints. Engine and OS monitoring show soaring lock-wait time, growing wait-for graphs, space-allocation errors, suspended checkpoints, and spikes in refused or half-open connections. Application tiers face cascading timeouts, backlog growth, and possible data-consistency anomalies due to repeated transaction aborts.

Causally, lock contention keeps transactions open longer, inflating UNDO, REDO, and temp usage and accelerating space consumption; once space boundaries are hit, log writes or temp allocations stall, freezing transactions mid-commit and holding locks even longer. These prolonged stalls tie up server processes and sockets, exhausting connection pools and listener backlogs; clients retry, increasing connection churn and network load, which in turn raises authentication and handshake latency, delaying the release or acquisition of new locks. The positive feedback loop between lock retention, space exhaustion, and connection saturation drives the database into a state where progress halts across multiple resource planes until at least one constraint is relieved.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, leading to blocking chains or deadlocks managed by the lock manager.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings for memory, logging, checkpointing, parallelism, or session limits are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, creating artificial resource pressure or background-worker imbalance.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: The client-to-server communication path or connection-handling layer cannot accept, authenticate, or stream data at the offered rate, causing connection stalls, socket backlog growth, and retransmissions.

When all three root causes coincide, the database exhibits a multi-faceted performance collapse:  • Connection establishment and query submission slow down or time out while authenticated sessions pile up in client-read/write waits.  • Sessions that do reach execution quickly encounter long lock-waits or deadlocks, driving retries that further inflate connection churn and lock pressure.  • Wait-event histograms show a confusing blend of network I/O waits, lock waits, and apparently contradictory idle CPU or idle I/O periods that do not align with hardware utilisation because mis-set parameters throttle buffer flush, background workers, or concurrency slots.  • Application-side symptoms escalate from sporadic latency spikes to wholesale service degradation as thread pools are exhausted by hanging connections and retry storms.

Causal chain: sub-optimal configuration (e.g., too many allowed backends, undersized work-memory, or aggressive checkpoint intervals) increases session count and I/O bursts, inflating both lock footprints and connection-handling load. Heightened concurrency amplifies the likelihood of hot-row conflicts; mis-sized memory or checkpoint storms prolong critical-section hold times, deepening lock queues. Blocked or deadlocked transactions trigger client-side timeouts and automatic retries, multiplying connection attempts and result-set replays that saturate listener sockets and network bandwidth. In turn, network stalls leave server backends waiting on client reads, holding locks even longer and feeding back into contention. The intertwined effects of poor configuration, lock contention, and connectivity saturation therefore reinforce each other, producing a severe OLTP outage that is harder to diagnose because each symptom masks and intensifies the others.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions block or deadlock because they request incompatible locks on the same database resources.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database and related processes drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, starving other work of compute cycles.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server communication or connection-handling infrastructure becomes a bottleneck, producing slow or failed connects and stalled socket I/O.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database experiences compound distress: lock wait chains and deadlocks lengthen application response times; at the same time, CPU cores are fully subscribed by spin-loops, deadlock detection, and repeated statement retries; meanwhile, clients struggle to obtain or keep connections as the listener and socket queues overflow. Observable symptoms include: exploding lock-wait and deadlock counters, soaring host load averages and context-switch rates, widespread "CPU busy" or scheduler wait events, surging connection-attempt failures, elevated network retransmissions, and application timeouts that cannot easily be attributed to a single layer.

Causal interaction: Network slowdowns or connection slot exhaustion increase transaction round-trip latency, keeping transactions open longer and extending the interval during which they hold locks—thereby intensifying lock contention. Prolonged blocking chains induce repeated client retries and server-side deadlock detection, each consuming additional CPU and spawning more connection activity that further stresses the network stack. In parallel, near-maxed CPU resources lengthen lock acquisition and deadlock-resolution cycles, causing locks to persist even longer and amplifying contention. The escalating feedback loop among delayed network I/O, prolonged locks, and CPU saturation can quickly propagate through the workload, degrading throughput, inflating latency, and precipitating widespread application failures.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite having reasonably accurate statistics, causing unnecessary work or wrong join/scan strategies.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database and related processes saturate host CPU, driving run-queue and context-switch pressure and inflating response times across the workload.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes exhaust kernel-enforced limits (file descriptors, threads, shared-memory segments, AIO contexts, cgroup quotas, etc.), preventing creation or use of required OS resources.

When these three issues coincide, the system shows a tangled symptom set: plans suddenly oscillate between different shapes, often favoring CPU-hungry scans or over-parallelized executions; overall CPU utilization sticks at or near 100 %, with long scheduler waits and rising load averages; at peak times new worker threads, parallel execution servers, or file handles fail to allocate, triggering engine errors, session drops, or silent plan de-parallelization. Latency spikes and throughput collapse propagate across both transactional and analytical statements, and troubleshooting is complicated because each layer (optimizer, database engine, kernel) reports its own errors that appear unrelated but stem from the same intertwined crisis.

Causally, a poor plan may multiply CPU instructions per row, immediately driving processor saturation. As CPUs max out, thread scheduling delays lengthen, which stretches query runtimes, prolongs lock holds, and amplifies the impact of the bad plan. The prolonged high concurrency keeps spawning or retaining additional workers, consuming file handles, threads, and AIO slots until kernel limits are breached. Once those limits are hit, the engine cannot create new execution or I/O contexts, forcing further plan changes (e.g., abandoning parallelism or spilling to disk) that again increase CPU demand. Conversely, initial OS-level denials of resources can cause the optimizer to discard preferred plans, selecting fallback plans that are far more CPU intensive. The feedback loop between sub-optimal plans, CPU exhaustion, and kernel limit violations rapidly degrades performance and can escalate to partial or full service outages.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible locks on the same objects, producing long blocker-waiter chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, logging, checkpointing, parallelism, and worker pools are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, creating artificial pressure or throttling where no physical limit is yet reached.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, pushing run-queue lengths and context-switch rates high enough to inflate latency for all work.

When these three root causes overlap, the system exhibits a compound failure mode in which lock wait time, deadlock frequency, and overall latency soar while throughput collapses. Long lock holds slow every subsequent transaction, amplifying connection-pool exhaustion and user‐visible timeouts. Mis-sized memory pools, checkpoint cadence, or parallelism knobs exacerbate the problem by forcing extra I/O, aggressive flushing, or excessive worker spawning, which in turn drives CPU usage to 100 %. The saturated CPU then starves the lock manager and background cleaners, lengthening lock-grant times and delaying deadlock detection. Monitoring views show simultaneous spikes in lock waits, scheduler or run-queue waits, and configuration-driven waits (e.g., excessive checkpoint or work-memory spills), making single-factor diagnosis difficult.

Causally, sub-optimal configuration settings can increase the number and duration of lock acquisitions—for example, small buffer pools cause more page faults that extend critical sections, while overly high max parallelism or per-query work memory spawns many worker threads that compete for CPU. The extra CPU demand both from the application and from background tasks (checkpoint, vacuum, log flush) pushes the host into sustained compute saturation. Once CPU headroom disappears, lock acquisition and deadlock detection algorithms run more slowly, so blocked sessions wait longer, keep locks held, and propagate contention further. The resulting positive feedback loop between lock contention, configuration-induced resource churn, and CPU saturation quickly drives the database into a severe throughput collapse typical of high-concurrency OLTP systems.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of engine and session memory areas pushes the database process and host beyond safe physical- or virtual-memory limits.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot ingest and apply primary-generated log records fast enough, producing widening replay lag and preventing log truncation.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical devices or storage layer are unable to sustain the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency demanded by data, temp, and log traffic.

When all three conditions materialize together, the system exhibits compound symptoms: rapid growth of cache and work-area memory inflates the working-set size, driving the OS into paging just as storage devices are already saturated, so read/write latencies soar. Swapping and frequent buffer eviction lower cache hit ratios, forcing more physical I/O against an already throttled storage path. The primary’s inability to recycle transaction logs—because replicas lag in receiving or replaying them—causes log volumes to expand, further loading the storage subsystem. Replicas show steeply rising receive, flush, and replay lag; users observe stale read-only replicas, blocked failovers, and escalating disk consumption on both primary and standby nodes. End-user workloads experience elongated response times, elevated I/O wait ratios, intermittent out-of-memory terminations, and possible cluster node evictions.

Causally, aggressive memory allocation on the primary and/or replicas diminishes available RAM, triggering OS paging that redirects pressure onto the storage layer. The resultant surge in random I/O competes with foreground data access and the steady stream of WAL/redo writes needed for replication, pushing the storage subsystem past its throughput ceiling. Elevated storage latency decelerates both local commit processing and remote log shipping, which inflates replication backlogs. Those backlogs, in turn, prevent log file recycling, swelling on-disk log footprints and increasing write load, which further intensifies storage contention and prolongs memory residency of dirty buffers. This feedback loop between memory overcommit, storage exhaustion, and replication lag magnifies each individual anomaly, threatening overall database availability and recovery objectives.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, or other in-engine heaps drives the database server’s physical memory and swap consumption beyond the safe capacity of the host.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or saturated network, listener, authentication, or socket resources prevent timely creation, maintenance, or teardown of client connections and data streams.

When both root causes are active, the system exhibits intermixed memory-pressure and connectivity symptoms: rapid RSS growth and paging coincide with surging connection-establishment latency, sporadic authentication failures, and rising counts of orphaned or half-open sockets. Background OOM killings or node evictions interrupt sessions, prompting client retry storms that flood the listener. Simultaneously, stalled result transmissions caused by congested NIC queues keep back-end processes idle yet resident in memory, inflating per-session buffers and further degrading cache hit ratios. Overall query latency becomes erratic, with spikes tied to both memory-induced CPU stalls and retransmission-driven waits, making single-cause diagnosis difficult.

Causally, the two anomalies reinforce one another: memory bloat increases each server process’s footprint, so every additional or leaked connection disproportionately consumes RAM, hastening memory exhaustion and triggering kernel swapping that slows packet processing. Conversely, network slowdowns and connection pool thrashing inflate the number and lifetime of backend processes, amplifying aggregate memory demand. Large result sets transferred slowly over a congested network keep per-query work areas and sort buffers allocated longer, compounding allocation pressure. The feedback loop between rising memory use and deteriorating connectivity can cascade into widespread session drops, automatic restarts, or cluster node fencing, severely impairing overall database availability and throughput.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: concurrent transactions block or deadlock each other while competing for incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata. 
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: obsolete row versions and undo records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating on-disk/ in-memory version stores and slowing visibility checks. 
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: sessions stall on buffer-pool page pins, latches, or I/O slots when many workers hammer the same hot pages or when dirty-page flushes back up.

Composite definition: The system simultaneously suffers from excessive lock conflicts, runaway MVCC version buildup, and intense buffer-pool/latch contention. Blocking and deadlocked transactions hold locks for long periods; their uncommitted updates leave large trails of undo/row versions that must be tracked in a crowded buffer cache whose pages are themselves hotly contested. 

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Steep increases in lock-wait time, deadlock victim errors, and cascading application retries; 2) Rapid growth of undo segments or version stores, falling live-row density, and autovacuum/cleaner processes perpetually active yet ineffective; 3) Surging buffer_busy, page_latch_x/sh waits, high CPU spin, and prolonged checkpoint or flush cycles; 4) Multiplicative slowdown where blocked or rolled-back transactions re-execute, further flooding the buffer cache and version store, while latch waits mask underlying lock wait statistics, making diagnosis harder.

Causal reinforcement: Long-lived or repeatedly aborted transactions caused by lock contention delay the advancement of the MVCC vacuum horizon, preventing cleanup and letting obsolete versions balloon. The bloated relation size and heavier visibility map scans increase buffer-pool pressure, forcing frequent page replacements and dirty flushes that intensify latch contention. Conversely, latch and I/O stalls lengthen the time each transaction holds its locks, deepening blocking chains and raising deadlock probability. The swollen version store also forces additional page reads and writes, amplifying buffer contention. Together, these feedback loops degrade throughput, exhaust memory and I/O bandwidth, and can precipitate systemic thrashing or emergency shutdown due to space exhaustion or wraparound risk.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other in-process memory regions pushes the database host beyond its physical RAM and swap limits, provoking paging, OOM kills, and cache-churn inefficiencies.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The generation, buffering, flushing, or archiving of write-ahead log (WAL) records cannot keep pace with commit throughput, making the log file group, log buffer, or archiver the primary bottleneck on the write path.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream standbys or subscribers are unable to receive, persist, or apply WAL data at the rate produced by the primary, causing growing log-position lag and preventing log-segment recycling.

When these three root causes occur together, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: commit latency and user-visible stalls rise sharply as log buffers back up behind a saturated log device while memory pressure simultaneously forces buffer eviction, swap storms, and CPU stalls. The primary accumulates large, unrecycled log segments because replicas lag, inflating on-disk log space; meanwhile, over-allocated in-memory caches and work areas bloat the resident set, further constraining I/O cache effectiveness. Administrators may observe oscillating throughput, frequent checkpoint storms, and emergency restarts triggered by out-of-memory or full-log conditions, along with widening replication delay and inconsistent read freshness on replicas. The overlapping waits (log flush, log sync, memory latch, page-in I/O) make it difficult to isolate any single culprit.

Causally, aggressive memory allocation reduces effective filesystem cache and amplifies paging, slowing physical log writes and elevating commit latency. Prolonged log flush times expand the log tail that replicas must ship and apply; replica lag in turn prevents log recycling, causing the primary to retain ever-growing log files that consume additional disk and may prompt larger in-memory directory and metadata caches—exacerbating memory pressure. Conversely, as replicas fall behind, the primary must hold more WAL in memory and on disk, inflating both log buffer residency and archive queues, which collide with already scarce memory resources. The feedback loop between memory exhaustion, log-subsystem saturation, and replication backlog thus intensifies each anomaly, pushing the OLTP system toward throughput collapse or forced failover.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log files, archiver/replication pipeline) becomes the primary bottleneck, throttling commit throughput and forcing sessions to wait on log-related events.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database executable and worker threads saturate available CPU cores, driving run-queue growth and inflating response times across the workload.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings on objects such as file descriptors, threads, shared-memory segments, or AIO contexts, preventing further resource acquisition.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set: commit latency and log-flush waits spike while overall query latency rises in lock-step with host CPU saturation; OS logs show ‘too many open files’, inability to create threads, or exhausted AIO slots, and the database reports both log write stalls and scheduler/runqueues waits. Archiver or replication lag grows because CPU-starved and file-handle-starved background processes cannot keep up, causing log directories to bloat, more log file switches, and periodic freezes where new transactions or worker threads cannot start. The mixture of symptoms makes it difficult to isolate any single layer—log, CPU, or kernel limits—because each amplifies the others, producing a system-wide slowdown that can culminate in partial or full service outage.

Causally, heavy write workloads generate high redo volume that drives both log I/O activity and CPU consumption. As CPU headroom disappears, log-related background tasks (flush, archive, replication) are delayed, lengthening log occupancy time. The prolonged presence of many active log segments inflates the number of open files, AIO contexts, and background threads, quickly breaching conservative OS limits. Once those limits are hit, further log file creation, thread spawning, or I/O submission fails, which in turn blocks commits and forces even more foreground sessions to spin on CPU waiting for log space. This feedback loop—log congestion raising CPU demand, CPU saturation slowing log handling, and OS limits choking both—drives the database into a compounded degraded state that is significantly worse than any single anomaly acting alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between data model structures (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns forces queries into full scans, non-covering index lookups, and other inefficient access paths.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine heaps drives the database process beyond the physical memory envelope, triggering paging, swap-thrashing, or out-of-memory events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-managed resources (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, process/thread counts, AIO contexts, cgroup quotas, etc.) prevents the database from allocating additional system objects, despite internal demand.

When these three root causes surface simultaneously, the workload experiences compounding symptoms:  
• Queries that already scan large tables or perform multi-stage joins spill massive intermediate results into memory, inflating per-query work areas and bloating buffer caches.  
• The ballooning memory footprint pushes the host into constant reclamation, page cache eviction, and swap I/O; once kernel limits are reached, new buffer allocations, shared-memory extensions, temp-segment mappings, or parallel worker spawns fail with OS-level errors.  
• Sessions intermittently abort with "cannot allocate memory", "too many open files", or "cannot attach to shared memory" messages; surviving sessions throttle as they contend for depleted memory and file handles, while checkpoint, logging, and background threads may be killed or hang.  
• Performance becomes erratic: some queries stall during hash or sort phases, others fall back to disk-based temp I/O, and overall throughput collapses.  

Causal interaction: Poor schema and indexing force the optimizer to choose wide scans, large hash joins, and repeated non-covering lookups, inflating buffer and work-area demand. This surge in memory consumption accelerates the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly, driving the engine to request additional caches, work buffers, and temporary segments. As the process RSS climbs, it collides with host-level caps on address space, shared memory, file descriptors, and swap, triggering the Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly. OS denials feed back into the database: failed allocations invalidate plans, cause worker starvation, and force spill-to-disk strategies that further amplify I/O and memory churn. The intertwined effects create a vicious cycle where inefficient access paths continually demand more resources that the engine and OS can no longer provide, leading to progressive degradation and potential service outages.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, write, or lock more data than the business logic truly requires.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine runtime parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capabilities and workload characteristics, leading to inefficient memory, logging, checkpoint, or parallelism behavior.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is unable to sustain the read/write volume demanded, causing elevated latency and saturated I/O queues.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits pronounced and wide-ranging distress: individual statements and whole transactions linger in slow-query logs, while wait-event histograms show a mix of buffer-IO, log-write, checkpoint, and CPU spin waits that do not correlate with actual CPU saturation.
