Memory pools may thrash, causing frequent page evictions and a surge of physical reads; meanwhile, undersized log or checkpoint settings trigger aggressive flushing that collides with already maxed-out storage bandwidth. Users observe erratic response times, timeouts, and long recovery or maintenance windows. Monitoring tools report simultaneously high logical work (scans, joins, large result sets), sub-optimal cache hit ratios due to constrained buffers, and steep rises in device-level latency and queue depth. Distinguishing which layer is primary becomes difficult because symptoms propagate across SQL, engine, and hardware boundaries.

Causally, inefficient SQL patterns inflate data access demands, multiplying buffer misses and redo generation. Misaligned configuration—such as an undersized buffer pool, low work-memory, or aggressive checkpoint interval—prevents the engine from absorbing this excess demand in memory, forcing even more traffic to disk and more frequent log flushes. The compounded I/O volume then overwhelms storage throughput, further slowing page and log writes. In turn, the elevated I/O latency prolongs transaction lifetimes and amplifies lock holding introduced by the chatty or bulk SQL, while the engine’s reactive background tasks (auto-checkpoint, cleaner, autovacuum, etc.) intensify their efforts and compete for the same scarce I/O bandwidth. The feedback loop between poor workload design, misconfiguration, and storage saturation drives a self-reinforcing degradation that can stall both OLTP and analytical workloads until all contributing layers are addressed together.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency limits of the underlying storage stack are saturated, making the device—not the DB engine—the performance bottleneck.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space on data, log, temp, or backup volumes falls to-or below-minimum thresholds, triggering allocation failures or growth stalls.

When both anomalies surface together, the database experiences prolonged and highly variable I/O latencies, escalating wait events, and near-continuous auto-extend or checkpoint activity while simultaneously running out of space. Back-end devices show long queue depths and service-time inflation, while foreground sessions report slow response, "out of space" or "cannot allocate extent" errors, log switch hangs, paused DML, aborted ETL/loads, and backup failures. Space-reclamation tasks, log archiving, and purge jobs slow or halt due to the I/O bottleneck, further accelerating space depletion. Maintenance windows and recovery time objectives are breached as both performance and availability degrade in tandem.

Causally, space exhaustion and throughput saturation reinforce one another: 1) As free space dwindles, the engine issues more frequent auto-extend, file growth, and log switch operations, spiking random and sequential I/O that pushes already-constrained storage beyond its throughput limits. 2) The elevated I/O latency slows background tasks such as log archiving, snapshot merges, purges, and index rebuilds, delaying space release and causing the free-space curve to fall even faster. 3) Checkpoint and flush operations contend with emergency space-management writes on the same saturated devices, risking dead-end stalls where neither throughput nor space can recover without external intervention (adding capacity, throttling workload, or moving data). The intertwined failures therefore create a feedback loop that magnifies both response-time slowdowns and the probability of hard allocation outages.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Execution-plan costing relies on stale, missing, or inaccurate catalog statistics, producing systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal plans.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, causing allocation failures and blocking new work.

When both root causes strike concurrently, the workload exhibits a mix of logical and infrastructural pathologies: queries choose wrong join orders or degrees of parallelism and then abruptly abort with system-level errors such as “cannot create shared memory segment,” “too many open files,” or “failed to start worker.” Batch jobs may swing between severe under-estimation (tiny memory grants leading to spills) and over-estimation (requests for memory or workers that the OS refuses), resulting in thrashing, frequent plan recompilations, intermittent session failures, and oscillating performance. Because failures appear in both the execution plan (row-count gaps, excessive I/O, temp spills) and the system log (resource exhaustion messages), symptoms can seem unrelated, elongating triage time.

Causal interplay: stale statistics can inflate optimizer estimates, prompting the engine to ask the OS for large memory areas, high parallel-worker counts, extra temp files, or additional file handles; if kernel quotas are tight, those requests are denied, turning a performance issue into hard errors and session drops. Conversely, once OS limits are hit, automatic statistics jobs and parallel scan workers cannot start, preventing statistics refreshes and locking the system into an ever more outdated cost model. This feedback loop escalates misestimation and resource starvation, degrading throughput and reliability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings for memory, logging, checkpoints, parallelism, and other runtime limits are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload profile, or version defaults, causing artificial contention or idle resources.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical table or index pages are corrupted or internally inconsistent, leading to unreliable access paths, checksum failures, and mismatched row counts.

When these two root causes strike simultaneously, the system experiences a dual-layer failure: poorly chosen configuration parameters mask or magnify the effects of underlying page or index corruption. Symptoms include erratic and non-reproducible performance dips, alternating bursts of CPU spin and I/O stalls, repeated plan flips between index and full scans, phantom or missing rows, unexpectedly aggressive checkpoint or autovacuum activity, and a flood of disparate log messages ranging from wait-event warnings to corruption alerts. Recovery operations such as index rebuilds, crash recovery, or replication re-sync may thrash or stall because mis-sized memory pools and log files choke throughput while the engine struggles to read or rewrite damaged pages.

Causally, sub-optimal configuration amplifies the impact of corruption: undersized buffer pools force more frequent page evictions, increasing touch-points with damaged blocks; over-aggressive checkpoint or flush policies surface latent checksum errors sooner and more often; insufficient work-memory or mis-set parallelism slows integrity-check and rebuild tasks, prolonging exposure to bad data. Conversely, the presence of corrupted pages can mislead tuning efforts—skewed statistics and unpredictable plans prompt administrators to adjust parameters in ways that further destabilize workload behavior. The feedback loop between configuration misalignment and structural corruption degrades performance, complicates diagnosis, and heightens risk of data loss across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot or frequently churned buffer-cache pages and their associated latches, causing CPU spin, buffer-busy waits, and page-level access stalls.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing and redo persistence are throttled by saturated log buffers, files, or archiver components, inflating log-write and log-sync latencies and delaying transactional progress.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client/server communication or connection-handling resources are exhausted or unstable, inflating connection setup time, socket waits, and data-transfer latencies.

When these three root causes co-exist, end-to-end response times deteriorate sharply and symptoms overlap:  
• Application threads pile up in buffer-busy, page-latch, log-flush, and client-write waits simultaneously; CPU usage oscillates between spin-loops on latches and idle periods forced by log-sync or socket back-pressure.  
• Commit latency becomes highly variable; some transactions hang in prepare/commit while others stall earlier on page access, making it hard to isolate a single choke point.  
• Connection pools see rising time-to-connect and intermittent "too many clients" or timeout errors, while established sessions intermittently report network write waits due to slower commit acknowledgements and prolonged page-latch holding.  
• Monitoring shows runaway log growth, elevated checkpoint frequency, and surging network retransmissions; yet storage I/O and CPU may appear under-utilized because concurrency collapses behind the compounded bottlenecks.

Causal interaction: Heavy concurrent writes concentrate on a few index or hot-row pages, elevating latch contention and delaying buffer eviction. These stalls stretch transaction lifetimes, inflating in-memory redo that must be flushed at commit time. The already strained transaction-log subsystem now encounters larger, burstier flush requests, exacerbating log-write congestion and prolonging commit latency. Extended commit cycles in turn keep latches held longer and increase the number of active back-end processes waiting for log sync, swelling the pool of connected sessions. As requests queue up, client drivers retry or open new connections, saturating listener backlogs and socket descriptors, which inject additional network waits into the critical path. The network slowdown further delays commit acknowledgements, feeding back into longer latch hold times and higher redo accumulation. The reinforcing loop among hot-page contention, log bottlenecks, and network saturation drives a systemic throughput collapse characteristic of this composite anomaly.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Multiple concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same objects, creating blocking chains or deadlocks that force sessions to wait or be aborted.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions compete for access to hot buffer-pool pages, latches, or I/O slots, stalling while they spin or sleep for low-level synchronization resources.

Composite anomaly definition: The database concurrently suffers from high-level transaction lock contention and low-level buffer/latch contention, so statements are serialized twice—first at the lock manager and again inside the buffer manager—causing severe throughput collapse and runaway latency.

Combined observable phenomena: In addition to long lock-wait queues, deadlock victim errors, and rising application timeouts, the instance also exhibits surges in buffer-busy/page-latch wait events, elevated CPU spin time, and slow physical I/O completions. Wait graphs may show the same sessions alternating between "lock" and "latch/buffer busy" wait states; lock-wait durations appear longer because latch stalls delay lock acquisition and release, while latch contention metrics spike because blocked transactions hold buffer pins longer. Connection pools exhaust, checkpoint and autovacuum tasks fall behind, and overall throughput degrades non-linearly.

Causal interaction: Hot rows or index keys draw many concurrent updates, creating lock hot spots. While blocked, holders keep buffer pages pinned, shrinking the effective buffer-pool supply and funnelling more threads toward the same hot pages, which in turn amplifies latch contention. Conversely, heavy latch or buffer-busy waits slow down the execution and commit phases of transactions, prolonging their lock tenure and enlarging blocker chains or deadlock windows. The two feedback loops reinforce each other: prolonged locks worsen buffer pressure; buffer/latch stalls lengthen lock lifetimes, producing a compounding congestion spiral that can culminate in systemic throughput collapse and widespread query timeouts.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) sub-optimal application SQL that touches and changes more data than necessary, (2) intense lock-manager conflicts among concurrent transactions, and (3) saturation of the write-ahead logging path. Together these three root causes form a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades throughput and inflates response times in write-heavy, concurrent workloads.

Combined Observable Phenomena: End-user requests exhibit long and highly variable latencies, with frequent time-outs and retries. Engine instrumentation shows the same fat or repetitively executed statements dominating the slow-query and statement-statistics views; meanwhile, lock tables reveal deep blocking chains and recurrent deadlocks, and wait-event histograms are dominated by log-flush, log-sync, and lock-wait classes. Commit operations linger, causing transactions to retain row/page/table locks far beyond normal duration. Connection pools back up, replication or archive processes lag, and checkpoint frequency rises as log files fill rapidly. Because waiting can be attributed either to lock contention or to synchronous log I/O, the two signals become entangled and hard to disentangle during triage.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Inefficient workload logic increases the number of scanned and modified rows per transaction, inflating lock footprints and prolonging transaction execution time. The expanded work set raises the probability that multiple sessions contend for the same hot rows or ranges, creating longer blocking queues and more deadlock cycles. At the same time, the surplus data modifications amplify redo generation; every enlarged transaction emits more log bytes and must wait for log flush on commit. The overloaded log subsystem lengthens commit latency, causing transactions to hold locks even after finishing their in-memory work. These extended lock holds, in turn, intensify contention for subsequent transactions, which further escalate redo volume as they retry or time out, thereby pushing the log subsystem deeper into saturation. The mutual reinforcement between bloated SQL, lock contention, and log-write bottlenecks can precipitate a cascade that stalls the entire OLTP workload unless all three contributing layers are addressed in concert.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: A simultaneous condition where on-disk data or index structures are physically corrupted while the underlying storage subsystem is also approaching or has reached its space limits, causing the database engine to contend with both structural inconsistency and space-allocation failures at the same time.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Administrators may see checksum or page-verification errors interleaved with "no space left" or "cannot extend datafile" messages. Index scans can intermittently miss rows, yet forced full-table scans may also fail when the engine cannot allocate new extents or spill areas. Crash-recovery or DBCC/ANALYZE utilities invoked to repair corruption may themselves abort due to insufficient free space for scratch areas, redo, or snapshot copies. Log archives can back up, freezing write activity, while corruption in the same datafiles magnifies the urgency because standard online rebuilds or CTAS operations cannot proceed. Overall, query performance becomes erratic, with sudden fallbacks, blocking, and engine-level retry storms that are difficult to attribute to either space or integrity issues in isolation.

Causal Interaction: Space exhaustion can exacerbate latent or emerging block and index corruption by interrupting in-flight writes, online rebuilds, and checkpoint cycles, leaving partially written pages that violate structural invariants. Conversely, corruption inflates space pressure: orphaned pages, endlessly cycling crash-recovery attempts, and repeated error logging consume additional disk space, accelerating capacity depletion. The two root causes therefore create a reinforcing loop—corruption drives space consumption, space scarcity hinders corrective maintenance—pushing the database into a degraded state that is harder to recover without immediate administrative intervention.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to scan or manipulate more data than necessary, inflating execution time and resource footprint.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Engine and session memory segments expand beyond safe host limits, provoking paging, cache churn, or OOM-related terminations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client–server communication paths or connection slots become saturated or unstable, causing slow or failed connection establishment and data transfer.

When all three anomalies arise concurrently, the database exhibits extreme and erratic latency: long-running, chatty, or over-fetching SQL drives large in-memory work areas and swollen buffer/plan caches, which in turn intensify OS memory pressure and trigger swapping or OOM kills. At the same time, bloated result sets and prolonged transaction lifetimes monopolize network sockets and listener threads, increasing connection queue depths, client-side timeouts, retransmissions, and a surge in aborted or half-open sessions. Monitoring views show simultaneous spikes in memory consumption, cache churn, statement and transaction wait times, and network wait events, making it difficult to attribute delays to any single layer.

Causally, inefficient workload logic amplifies memory demand (e.g., wide scans, large sorts, oversized batches), accelerating the onset of memory exhaustion. Memory pressure then slows processing and may force result spilling, lengthening data-transfer windows and holding connections open longer. Prolonged or stalled transfers consume additional network buffers and connection slots, which feed back into the application layer as retries that spawn even more SQL statements and sessions. These cascaded effects create a feedback loop where bad SQL inflates memory use, memory contention throttles throughput, and constrained connectivity magnifies latency and retry storms, jointly degrading overall database stability and performance.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Simultaneous transactions acquire mutually incompatible locks on shared rows, pages, or metadata, creating long blocker–waiter chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and undo records pile up faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, bloating storage and slowing visibility checks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory, checkpointing, worker limits, etc.) leave critical subsystems over- or under-provisioned relative to the workload and hardware.

When all three conditions coexist, workloads suffer a compounded failure mode: lock wait times and deadlock frequency escalate while the heap and indexes swell with unreclaimed versions, and configuration mis-settings prevent the buffer pool, cleanup workers, and lock-manager from recovering. Symptoms include: 1) exploding lock-wait and deadlock logs paired with rising application timeouts; 2) rapidly growing table and version-store size that degrades cache hit ratios and forces more physical I/O; 3) nonstop or thrashing background processes (autovacuum, purge, checkpoint, lock-deadlock detectors) consuming CPU yet failing to make headway; 4) paradoxical hardware metrics—disks idle during log-write stalls or CPUs under-utilised while sessions spin on locks—because memory, worker, or checkpoint parameters throttle true resource use; and 5) planner misestimates from bloat and outdated stats, leading to scans that further extend lock hold times and version churn.

Causally, sub-optimal configuration settings (e.g., undersized buffer pool, too few cleanup workers, aggressive checkpoint timeout) slow version reclamation and increase physical I/O, lengthening transaction runtimes and the duration locks are held. The resulting longer lock lifetimes raise the probability of collisions and deadlocks, which in turn cause rollbacks that create yet more undo records and garbage. Meanwhile, the same mis-configurations may starve both the lock manager (e.g., limited lock table memory) and MVCC cleaners of resources, so neither contention nor bloat can self-resolve. The feedback loop—bloat inflating I/O and lock duration, contention spawning additional deadlocks, and ill-sized parameters limiting recovery throughput—drives a severe throughput collapse and instability in OLTP workloads.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model and indexing choices do not match workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of statistics or plan quality.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime settings for memory, parallelism, logging, and background workers are mis-tuned for hardware resources and workload characteristics, causing artificial contention or under-utilisation.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced caps on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas prevent the database from allocating required OS resources, provoking errors and throttling.

When these three root causes coincide, the workload experiences a multi-layer performance collapse: badly designed tables and missing or bloated indexes inflate I/O and CPU demand; mis-sized buffer pools, work-memory, and checkpoint / parallelism settings fail to absorb that excess demand, leading to erratic cache hit ratios, aggressive eviction, checkpoint storms, or runaway sort/spill activity; concurrently, low OS limits choke the additional file handles, shared memory, or worker threads that the engine now attempts to obtain, generating kernel allocation failures, session drops, stalled parallel workers, and sudden latency spikes. Symptoms may appear contradictory—high logical I/O but low physical I/O due to throttled handles, CPU threads spinning while actual CPU utilisation stays moderate because OS thread quotas block scheduling, or alternating bursts of full-table scans and idle periods as the engine repeatedly hits OS ceilings and retreats.

Causally, the poor schema/index design raises the baseline resource footprint of each query, inflating memory, I/O, and parallel worker needs. Misconfigured database parameters then misallocate the already strained resources—either overcommitting memory so the engine requests segments larger than kernel limits allow, or under-allocating caches so every inefficient scan amplifies disk traffic. The inflated and misdirected demand accelerates exhaustion of OS-level objects (file descriptors, shared memory, threads), which in turn triggers allocation failures and forces the database to throttle or abort operations. The resulting stop-and-go execution further degrades cache effectiveness and intensifies checkpoint and recovery work, closing the vicious loop and magnifying performance instability, error rates, and risk of partial outages.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Costing metadata (row counts, histograms, correlation stats) is stale, missing, or inaccurate, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan choices.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Critical engine parameters for memory, parallelism, checkpoints, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware, workload, or version defaults, leading to resource imbalance and atypical wait profiles.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Host CPUs become saturated by database processes, driving high run-queue pressure, context switching, and widespread latency inflation.

When all three root causes coexist, workloads exhibit extreme and volatile performance degradation: queries abruptly switch to grossly inefficient plans that explode CPU seconds consumed per execution; parallel workers proliferate or starve depending on mis-set parallel-degree limits; system-wide CPU utilisation hovers near or at 100 %, yet individual statements still show large estimated-vs-actual row disparities. Checkpoint or log-flush storms may intermittently pre-empt CPU, amplifying latency spikes. Wait-event views report a confusing mix of CPU-related waits (RUNNABLE, SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD, CPU_QC) alongside configuration-induced stalls (CHECKPOINT_QUEUE, LOG_BUFFER) and frequent plan recompilations triggered by statistics updates. Performance may nosedive immediately after bulk loads, parameter changes, or version upgrades, and recovers only briefly after manual intervention before regressing again under load.

Causal chain: stale or absent statistics push the optimizer toward plans with underestimated costs that choose small hash tables, serial scans, or overly aggressive parallelism; mis-configured memory/parallelism parameters then fail to supply sufficient work memory or spawn excessive worker threads, inflating CPU demand through spills, rescans, and context switches. The resultant CPU saturation feeds back negatively: throttled background workers delay automatic statistics refresh and checkpoint processing, further aging statistics and triggering emergency checkpoints that hold critical latches on hot CPUs. Together, these feedback loops entrench poor plan quality, resource thrashing, and sustained compute exhaustion, creating a self-reinforcing composite anomaly that is far more severe than each issue in isolation.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite having reasonably accurate statistics.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback data accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network, listener, socket, or authentication resources become saturated, slowing or preventing client connections and data transfer.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits extreme and hard-to-pinpoint performance degradation. Poorly chosen plans trigger long-running scans or nested-loop explosions that touch far more rows than expected; the excess I/O and CPU prolong transaction lifetimes, causing snapshots to remain open and preventing version cleanup. The resulting table and index bloat further pollute statistics and widen the gap between estimated and actual costs, encouraging the optimizer to continue selecting bad plans. Meanwhile, the oversized result sets and elongated execution times keep back-end processes and sockets busy, filling connection pools, exhausting listener backlogs, and amplifying network queuing delays, retransmissions, and connection-establishment failures. Observability signals therefore include rapidly growing table sizes and version-store length, erratic plan changes with soaring execution costs, rising client-side timeouts, half-open connections, and a mix of in-database (buffer-read, MVCC visibility check) waits and network I/O waits.

Causally, a feedback loop emerges: (1) Sub-optimal plans inflate row access counts and execution duration. (2) Prolonged transactions retain old snapshots, blocking vacuum/cleanup and accelerating MVCC version bloat. (3) The swollen heap and misestimated cardinalities drive the optimizer toward even worse plans, perpetuating step 1. (4) Larger result sets and longer server think-time keep connections occupied, pushing the network and listener layer to saturation, which in turn delays new sessions and retries, increasing concurrency spikes. (5) Connection stalls further lengthen transaction lifetimes, intensifying MVCC retention and plan misestimation. Together, these intertwined effects degrade throughput, inflate latency, and threaten availability in high-churn transactional environments.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine runtime settings are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload intensity, or version defaults, causing artificial pressure or idle gaps in internal subsystems.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical or virtual storage layer is saturated for bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, becoming the dominant bottleneck for data, temp, or log files.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host processors are driven to sustained saturation, producing scheduler back-pressure and broad latency inflation across the workload.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database shows a tangled symptom set: chronic log-write, buffer-I/O, and scheduler waits coexist with high CPU utilisation, long run-queues, and soaring device queue depths. Checkpoint or flush storms triggered by mis-sized memory or aggressive durability settings rapidly fill the storage queues; as write latency increases, foreground sessions stall, yet CPU remains pegged by spin-waits, retry loops, and inflated parallelism. Performance counters may misleadingly suggest that either CPU or I/O alone explains the slowdown, while misconfigured parameters (e.g., tiny shared buffers, oversized work memory, excessive max_parallelism, or aggressive checkpoint_timeout) obscure the true dual-resource crisis. Batch windows elongate, OLTP transactions time out, analytics spill to disk, and background maintenance never catches up, creating an all-round degradation that is hard to attribute to a single tier.

Causally, poor configuration choices can provoke both CPU and I/O stress: undersized cache or too-frequent checkpoints amplify physical reads/writes, driving the storage layer into throughput saturation; in turn, the heightened I/O latency causes the engine to hold latches and spin longer, inflating CPU consumption. Simultaneously, mis-set parallelism or memory parameters increase CPU demand and plan concurrency, further intensifying I/O issuance rates. The saturated storage responds with even longer latencies, which stall worker threads and trigger additional background activity (e.g., checkpoints, log flushes), creating a feedback loop that deepens both CPU and I/O contention. The intertwined effects of misconfiguration, device saturation, and compute exhaustion therefore reinforce one another, dragging overall database performance into a severe, multi-resource bottleneck state.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine’s buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and auxiliary heaps grow beyond the safe physical- or virtual-memory envelope of the host, provoking paging, OOM kills, and cache-churn side effects.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical read/write demand of data, log, temp, or backup volumes exceeds the throughput, IOPS, or latency budget of the storage subsystem, driving up wait times and stalling database tasks.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other process quotas are reached, preventing the database from acquiring essential OS-managed resources.

When these three conditions strike together, the database shows a layered degradation: inflated memory footprints push the host into swap while I/O paths are already saturated, causing each page fault, checkpoint, or temp spill to endure extreme latency. Concurrently, exhausted kernel limits hamper the engine’s ability to open additional files, grow shared memory, dispatch background or parallel workers, and allocate asynchronous I/O contexts. The observable outcome is a system oscillating between CPU stalls, runaway I/O waits, and hard resource denials—sessions hang during buffer reads, checkpoints linger, log flushes miss service-level objectives, new connections or workers fail with OS errors, and cluster nodes risk eviction as watchdog timers expire.

Causally, aggressive memory allocation elevates pressure on swap and amplifies page churn, inflating physical I/O demand exactly when the storage layer is already throughput-bound. The prolonged I/O queues, in turn, delay buffer recycling, encouraging the engine to request even more memory for new work areas and to hold on to dirty pages longer, further swelling resident sets. As the process footprint and I/O concurrency climb, the database consumes additional file handles, AIO contexts, and threads, quickly breaching OS resource ceilings. Once those limits are hit, critical operations such as log file growth, sort spills, or recovery worker spawns fail, cascading into lock contention, hung transactions, and possible crash-recovery cycles. Thus, memory over-commitment, storage saturation, and kernel quota exhaustion form a self-reinforcing loop that severely degrades throughput and availability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload profile, or version defaults, causing artificial pressure on memory, logging, background workers, parallelism, and checkpoints.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, processes/threads, or other OS objects are reached, preventing the database from allocating the resources it requests.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport, listener, socket, or authentication layers cannot sustain the incoming connection or data-transfer rate, leading to backlog growth, refusals, and stalled client I/O.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits a mosaic of symptoms: connection attempts time out or are rejected even when the instance appears up; established sessions suffer erratic latency with alternating client-read/client-write waits, punctuated by spikes of log-write or checkpoint waits that do not correlate with disk utilization; background workers and parallel executors intermittently fail to start, producing engine errors about thread creation, file-descriptor exhaustion, or shared-memory allocation; monitoring shows low CPU or I/O utilization despite severe throughput collapse, while OS socket queues and semaphore tables are saturated and network retransmission rates climb. Administrators may observe sudden surges of aborted connections after configuration changes, followed by partial outages where only pre-existing sessions continue processing slowly.

Causally, aggressive or ill-suited database parameter settings (e.g., too many max connections, oversized work-memory, or excessive parallel-worker limits) drive the engine to request more kernel objects and network sockets than the host’s hard limits allow. Once OS quotas are hit, new backends, files, or AIO contexts cannot be created, which in turn starves internal executors and amplifies the mis-tuned engine behaviors—checkpoints bunch up, log buffers fill, and memory pressure grows. Simultaneously, the throttled listener and congested network stack delay or drop connection attempts, prompting client retries that further inflate connection counts and resource requests, accelerating exhaustion of both OS and engine quotas. The interlocking feedback loops between misconfiguration, kernel denials, and network contention thus reinforce each other, yielding a compound degradation that is harder to diagnose than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data or metadata objects, causing prolonged blocking chains or deadlocks that the lock manager must resolve.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Critical engine parameters (memory sizes, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, so bottlenecks arise even when physical resources are not yet exhausted.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database process hits kernel-enforced ceilings for files, memory segments, threads, or other OS objects, preventing new allocations and stalling activity.

When all three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: lock-wait and deadlock frequency soar while overall throughput and connection availability plummet; sessions pile up waiting not only on locks but also on artificially throttled I/O, CPU, or background workers; deadlock detectors or autovacuum/cleanup tasks fail to start because the process has exhausted file descriptors or thread quotas; error logs show a mix of lock-timeout/victim-abort messages, parameter-driven warnings about buffer, log, or worker shortages, and kernel errors for resource denial. Recovery spikes (checkpoints, flush storms) can coincide with massive blocking, making performance swings sudden and severe and obscuring which layer is primary.

Causally, mis-tuned database parameters can lengthen transaction lifetimes (e.g., small work_mem causing extra sorts, aggressive checkpoints inducing I/O stalls), so locks are held longer and contention intensifies. The attempt to compensate—by opening more connections or parallel workers—consumes additional file handles, threads, and shared memory, pushing the process toward OS limits. Once those limits are breached, new backend or auxiliary processes cannot start, deadlock detectors or background writers stall, and waiting transactions remain blocked indefinitely, further deepening lock queues. Conversely, OS denials of resources can thwart parameter settings (e.g., requested shared_buffers exceeds kernel SHMMAX), forcing the engine into degraded fall-back configurations that amplify the original mis-tuning. The interlocking feedback among lock contention, poor configuration, and OS resource exhaustion creates a vicious cycle that severely degrades OLTP responsiveness and can culminate in partial or full outage.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Critical metadata about row counts, data distribution, and correlations is stale, missing, or inaccurate, causing systematic cardinality misestimation by the optimizer.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Despite acceptable or refreshed statistics, the optimizer’s plan–choice logic (cost model, parameter sniffing, cache reuse, hinting, etc.) selects execution plans that are substantially sub-optimal for the current runtime context.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas or subscribers cannot receive, write, or apply redo at the rate the primary generates it, producing widening log-position gaps, replay lag, and retention of excessive log files on the primary.

When these three root causes manifest simultaneously, a workload may show oscillating or chronically poor query performance on the primary, skyrocketing redo generation, and rapidly growing replication lag. Stale or incomplete statistics combine with an already fragile plan-selection process to create highly variable, often bloated execution plans—e.g., hash joins degraded to nested loops or full-table scans materializing large intermediate results. The resultant surge in I/O, CPU, and log volume prolongs transaction durations and inflates redo streams. Replicas struggle to keep pace, leading to seconds-to-hours of apply lag, swollen relay/WAL files, stale read-only query results, and reduced failover readiness. Because replicas replay long-running, poorly planned transactions serially, their apply workers may become backlogged or blocked by lock contention, further compounding lag.

Causally, inaccurate statistics seed cardinality errors that steer the optimizer toward fragile plans; even if statistics are corrected, plan-selection anomalies (e.g., parameter sniffing or cost-model quirks) may continue to favor inefficient strategies. These inefficient plans inflate resource consumption and transaction sizes, multiplying redo output. The heavier the write volume and transaction duration, the more pressure is placed on the replication pipeline. Conversely, replication lag prevents timely feedback such as replicated statistics refreshes or plan–stability hint deployments on replicas, allowing bad plans to persist there as well. The intertwined feedback loop—bad stats ⇒ bad plans ⇒ high redo ⇒ replication backlog ⇒ delayed metadata convergence—drives a self-reinforcing degradation that affects both primary performance and replica consistency.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries that outpaces background cleanup, inflating on-disk and in-memory data footprints and enlarging visibility-check work. 
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, and I/O slots, producing CPU spin and wait time instead of useful work. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client/server communication and connection-handling resources saturate, causing slow or failed connection attempts and stalled socket I/O.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a multilayer slowdown: queries spend extra CPU cycles scanning bloated heaps, then block on latch and buffer-busy waits while seeking or modifying the same hot pages already inflated by version bloat. Prolonged statement execution holds network sockets, authentication slots, and result streams open, so new client sessions pile up behind an overworked listener, and existing backends linger in client-write or client-read waits. System views show simultaneously rising dead-tuple ratios, surging buffer/latch wait counters, growing dirty-page queues, and spikes in connection-queue depth, with application timeouts and sporadic throughput collapses that are hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, long-running or stalled client sessions (due to network congestion or throttled consumers) keep transactions open, advancing the vacuum horizon slowly and preventing removal of obsolete versions; the ensuing table and index bloat multiplies the number of buffer pages that must be touched and pinned, amplifying latch contention. In parallel, the enlarged working set strains an already pressured buffer pool, increasing page churn and dirty-page flushes that further extend latch hold times. These longer critical sections propagate up the stack as slower queries, which in turn prolong connection lifetimes and raise the likelihood of hitting socket, process, or authentication limits—feeding back into the network/connectivity bottleneck. The intertwined feedback loops between version bloat, buffer contention, and connection saturation thus reinforce each other, degrading OLTP responsiveness and risking cascading outages.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excess accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update/delete churn.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical read/write demand exceeds the bandwidth, IOPS, or latency capacity of the underlying storage subsystem.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources (file descriptors, async-I/O contexts, threads, shared memory, etc.) needed by the database engine and its workers.

When all three conditions coincide, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: tables and indexes balloon in size, causing every scan, vacuum, checkpoint, or log flush to issue more physical I/O against devices that are already saturated. Read and write latencies rise sharply, buffer-pool hit ratios plunge, and wait profiles fill with both I/O waits and kernel-level "resource temporarily unavailable" errors. Autovacuum or garbage-collection workers start and stop erratically as they hit OS limits on file handles or AIO contexts, further delaying cleanup. Administrators observe runaway disk-space usage, near-continuous storage queues, intermittent inability to start new backend or maintenance processes, and a mix of MVCC horizon warnings, I/O stall messages, and kernel denials in system logs. Planner misestimates and timeout-driven query cancellations become frequent, and parts of the workload may hang while existing sessions cling to old snapshots that prevent reclamation of space.

Causal chain: heavy OLTP churn creates surplus row versions, inflating on-disk structures and multiplying physical pages that must be read, written, and eventually vacuumed. This extra traffic pushes the storage subsystem to (or beyond) its throughput limits, lengthening I/O completion times. Prolonged I/O stretches the window during which cleanup workers must hold resources, so they consume more file descriptors, AIO slots, and threads; meanwhile other sessions also queue additional I/O, driving kernel resource counts higher. Once OS ceilings are reached, new workers or I/O submissions are rejected, which stalls or aborts garbage collection and checkpoints, causing even faster version buildup and still more I/O. The feedback loop—version bloat → higher I/O demand → storage saturation → kernel resource exhaustion → stalled cleanup—amplifies both performance degradation and risk of outage until manual intervention or configuration changes break the cycle.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and the workload’s access patterns forces otherwise well-formed SQL to scan or probe data inefficiently.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Insufficient or unstable network, listener, authentication, or socket resources limit the rate at which client sessions can connect or exchange result data with the database.

Composite anomaly definition – simultaneous impact: The database is concurrently burdened by sub-optimal physical schema design AND by constrained network/connection resources, so each logical request encounters both inefficient data access inside the engine and delays while entering or leaving the system. Performance degradation is therefore driven by a dual bottleneck: slow server-side execution paths plus impaired client/server data transfer and session management.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Queries exhibit long total response times that fluctuate widely, with execution plans showing full scans, excessive row fetches, and heavy I/O, followed by prolonged client-read or client-write waits. • Connection pools reach their maximum size as sessions linger in network I/O states, causing new connection attempts to time out or be refused; at the same time, existing sessions consume CPU and I/O on repeated, poorly indexed lookups. • Monitoring shows high logical I/O, segment scans, and index maintenance overhead alongside growing listener backlogs, rising TCP retransmissions, and an accumulation of idle-in-transaction or socket WAITs. • Application retries amplify load, further stressing both the mis-indexed tables and the limited connection slots, leading to cascading slowdowns or outages.

Causal chain and mutual amplification: Poor schema/index design lengthens statement runtimes, which in turn prolongs the lifespan of each client session and the volume of data transmitted. Longer-lived sessions consume more network buffers and keep sockets open, accelerating exhaustion of connection slots and listener queues. Conversely, network congestion or handshake delay stretches the end-to-end time of every query, magnifying the impact of inefficient access paths by extending their blocking window on locks, latches, and cache structures. The feedback loop—slow execution inflating session counts and network waits, while network stalls inflate per-query wall-clock time—produces a compound performance collapse that is more severe and harder to diagnose than either anomaly in isolation.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, and correlation statistics are stale or missing, causing systematic cardinality misestimation during plan compilation.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages are physically or logically corrupted, breaking key ordering, page links, or heap-to-index consistency.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The client/server communication layer is saturated or unstable, leading to connection churn, socket exhaustion, and elevated network waits.

When all three root causes occur together, the database exhibits a multidimensional failure signature: queries may choose grossly sub-optimal plans because of bad statistics, then hit corrupted indexes that return wrong or duplicate rows, forcing fall-back full scans whose bloated result sets travel slowly across a congested network. Clients experience timeouts, authentication retries, and intermittent data inconsistencies; the server shows alternating spikes of CPU (from mischosen join methods), I/O (from full table scans after corruption detection), and network wait time. Integrity-check utilities and error logs report page or checksum failures at the same time that monitoring dashboards show widening gaps between estimated versus actual rows and rising counts of refused or aborted connections, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal interaction: (1) Corrupted pages or mis-linked indexes invalidate existing statistics and prevent automatic statistics refresh, seeding cardinality errors. (2) These errors drive the optimizer toward plans that amplify touch patterns on damaged structures, triggering more corruption detections and expensive fall-back scans. (3) The resulting surge in data volume and latency stretches network bandwidth and connection pools; retransmissions and stalled sessions accumulate, leading to further connection churn that can starve maintenance tasks needed to repair corruption or update statistics. Conversely, network instability prolongs bulk data-load or rebuild operations, increasing the window during which pages can be partially written and become corrupt, and delays statistics-collection jobs, thus tightening the feedback loop that reinforces all three anomalies and exacerbates overall database degradation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from poorly written or overly heavy application SQL (SQL Workload Logic Anomaly), inaccurate or stale optimizer statistics (Optimizer Statistics Anomaly), and an excess buildup of obsolete MVCC row versions (MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly). Acting together, these three root causes drive the execution engine to read and process far more data than necessary, choose sub-optimal plans, and wade through bloated storage, all while background cleanup lags behind.  

Combined Observable Phenomena:  
• End-user transactions and reports show extreme and highly variable latency; many statements linger in slow-query logs with widening long-tail response times.  
• Execution plans reveal severe cardinality misestimates alongside scan-heavy or plan-flip behaviour; re-optimizations occur frequently yet fail to converge on efficient plans.  
• Buffer-pool hit ratios drop and I/O spikes as wide scans traverse pages full of dead or irrelevant rows; physical table and index sizes grow rapidly.  
• Locking is minimal, but snapshot/visibility checks escalate CPU usage; cleanup workers remain continuously active, and alerts about transaction-ID or version-store pressure appear.  
• Application-side retries and timeouts increase, sometimes masking as network or service failures, while DBA monitoring shows both statistics staleness warnings and vacuum/autovacuum backlog.  

Causal Interaction: Inefficient SQL causes large scans, large result sets, and long-running transactions that delay version reclamation, accelerating MVCC bloat. The expanding dead tuples, in turn, distort data distribution and row-count statistics, worsening the Optimizer Statistics Anomaly and leading the planner toward even poorer plans. Stale statistics further misguide the optimizer into full-table scans or wrong join orders, magnifying the overhead imposed by bloated heaps and indexes. The feedback loop between bad SQL logic, outdated statistics, and unchecked version buildup produces a self-reinforcing degradation cycle where each anomaly amplifies the others, rapidly eroding OLTP performance and stability.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or un-bounded growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine heaps drives the database process beyond the safe physical or virtual memory envelope. 
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing is throttled because log buffering, flushing, segment switching, or archiving cannot keep pace with the rate of redo generation. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas falls to zero or below auto-extend thresholds, causing allocation failures and write stalls.

When these three root causes arise together, the instance exhibits a compound failure pattern: commit latencies and log-flush waits lengthen while overall memory consumption surges and physical free space dwindles. Checkpoints and log switches fire in rapid succession, yet archived-log backlogs and full destinations prevent reuse, so active log files balloon until the underlying volume is exhausted. As space tightens, the engine is forced to retain extra dirty buffers in memory because checkpoints cannot persist pages, amplifying memory pressure, paging, and OOM risks. Concurrently, background archiver and cleanup processes contend for both memory and I/O, further delaying log rotation and consuming the last bytes of available space. Application sessions observe timeouts, "cannot allocate extent / no space left on device" errors, and eventual instance or node eviction when the operating system can no longer satisfy memory or disk requests.

Causally, aggressive memory allocation (e.g., un-capped per-query work areas or plan-cache bloat) increases the rate and size of redo records as large in-memory operations generate heavy transactional metadata. The swollen redo stream pushes the transaction-log subsystem past its flush and switch capacity; because archives are slow or space-constrained, log segments cannot be recycled, causing on-disk log growth that quickly consumes the same storage pool where data and temp files reside. As the device fills, checkpoints stall, forcing dirty pages to remain resident and inflating memory use even further. The positive feedback loop—memory bloat → higher redo volume → log bottleneck → storage exhaustion → blocked checkpoints → more memory bloat—drives the system into a state where neither memory, log throughput, nor space can recover without external intervention.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer selects or reuses an execution plan that is materially sub-optimal even though statistics are adequate.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings such as file-handle, shared-memory, or thread quotas, causing allocation failures outside the engine’s direct control.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server communication or connection-handling resources (sockets, listener queues, authentication slots) become saturated, leading to refused, stalled, or aborted connections.

When all three conditions manifest together, the workload exhibits a mix of erratic query latencies, intermittent connection failures, and partial service stalls. Poor plans drive excessive I/O, memory, and CPU consumption, lengthening query execution times and keeping back-end sessions open longer. The prolonged sessions inflate the number of simultaneously active worker processes and file descriptors, hastening exhaustion of kernel resource limits. As resource ceilings are hit, new back-end or parallel worker creation fails, prompting connection rejections and spikes in client timeouts. The backlog of half-open sockets and retries further stresses the network stack, while existing sessions running bad plans accumulate large result sets that trickle over congested or throttled network paths, amplifying TCP retransmissions and client-wait events. Observers may see oscillating plan flips, sudden drops in parallelism, error messages about failing to fork or open files, and surges in "too many connections" or "could not accept connection" errors, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to any single layer.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan (e.g., unexpected full table scan) magnifies resource consumption per query, pushing the database toward OS limits on memory areas, file handles, and worker threads. Hitting those limits prevents new sessions or parallel workers, which in turn causes connection backlog growth at the listener and an increase in half-open sockets—triggering the network/connectivity anomaly. Conversely, network saturation or authentication stalls prolong session lifetimes, inflating active back-end counts and accelerating exhaustion of OS resources, which feeds back into the optimizer by forcing plan re-compilations without available workers, increasing the likelihood of unstable or downgraded plans. The intertwined feedback loops between inefficient plans, kernel resource exhaustion, and connectivity constraints can degrade both throughput and availability, creating a complex, self-reinforcing performance collapse.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements and transaction flows are written so inefficiently that they compel the engine to scan or manipulate far more data than the business case requires.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Database memory regions—buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, and session heaps—expand beyond safe host limits, provoking paging, swap thrashing, or allocator failures.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume a persistently high share of CPU cycles, driving run-queue lengths and pre-emption latency to damaging levels.

When all three root causes coexist, the system experiences a compound anomaly in which bloated, poorly filtered SQL drives excessive logical I/O and large in-memory work sets; these work sets fight for limited RAM, triggering allocation churn, paging, and NUMA or swap overhead, while the same wasteful access patterns and memory pressure push CPU utilization to saturation. Observable symptoms include:
• Extreme and widely varying statement and transaction latencies, with many operations timing out or stalling during memory allocation or CPU scheduling waits.
• Simultaneous spikes in buffer cache misses, sort/hash spill events, and OS swap-in/out as the engine evicts pages to satisfy new, ever-growing work areas.
• Run-queue and context-switch explosions that amplify CPU wait events (e.g., "CPU run queue", "OS scheduler delay"), accompanied by soaring slow-query counts and application-level retries.
• Intermittent out-of-memory terminations or instance/node evictions that cascade into availability incidents.

Causal chain: Inefficient SQL inflates row scans, intermediate result sizes, and transaction lifetimes, inflating both per-query work memory and shared buffer demand. The memory subsystem attempts to honor these allocations, displacing useful cache pages and initiating paging, which in turn increases CPU overhead for memory management. Elevated CPU consumption slows query execution, keeping transactions open longer and further enlarging their in-flight memory footprint, which feeds back into memory pressure. The vicious cycle of heavy logic-driven resource demand, memory exhaustion, and CPU saturation mutually reinforce each other, rapidly degrading throughput, expanding tail latency, and threatening overall system stability.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction demarcations force the engine to read, scan, or hold more data and locks than the business logic really requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, column, partition, or indexing choices do not align with access patterns, obliging otherwise correct queries to traverse large data regions or touch non-covering paths.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions request mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, tables, or metadata, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall OLTP throughput.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits an interwoven symptom set: statements appear persistently in slow-query and deadlock logs; execution plans show table or index scans and wide lock footprints; lock-wait time, deadlock frequency, and transaction latency climb together; connection pools back up while CPU and I/O fluctuate between under-utilization during waits and sudden spikes when blocks clear; end-user requests time out or retry, and even modest workload spikes can trigger cascading stalls.

Causally, poorly written workload logic (e.g., missing predicates, oversized batches, or long user-think-time transactions) magnifies the surface area of data each statement touches, multiplying the number and duration of locks it acquires. Because the underlying schema lacks appropriate, selective, and covering indexes, these bloated statements escalate to full scans, further enlarging lock scopes (row → page → table) and prolonging critical-section hold times. The extended locks then collide with other concurrent transactions, and the lock manager becomes a bottleneck, producing wait chains and deadlocks. In turn, these waits lengthen transaction lifetimes, making long-running statements even more susceptible to being blocked and to blocking others, creating a feedback loop in which inefficient logic, poor physical design, and lock contention reinforce each other and dramatically degrade OLTP performance.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution metadata are stale, missing, or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan selection.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot buffer pages and their protecting latches become serialization points, forcing sessions to spin or sleep while competing for page access or I/O slots.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log file, flush, switch, or archive) cannot keep up with redo generation, lengthening commit latency and back-pressuring writers.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits intertwined symptoms: queries choose inefficient plans that inadvertently hammer a small set of index or data pages, sharply increasing buffer hit traffic and latch waits; the resulting page churn produces a surge of dirty buffers whose flushes queue behind an already saturated transaction log, inflating log-flush and checkpoint waits. End users observe erratic response times, spikes in CPU spin, blocked commits, and sudden throughput collapses after data-modification bursts or bulk-load events. Execution-plan explain outputs show severe cardinality errors, while performance views simultaneously record high buffer busy/latch contention and log-related waits, making the dominant bottleneck difficult to isolate.

Causally, stale or missing statistics drive the optimizer toward plans that concentrate reads or inserts on a few root/leaf pages or hot ranges, amplifying latch contention in the buffer pool. The repeated retries and page splits from this contention generate excess redo, which in turn overwhelms the transaction-log subsystem and delays buffer flush completion. The slowed log flush prolongs page-write hold times, further intensifying latch pressure and starving the buffer cache of free pages, which increases page eviction and reload cycles. This feedback loop magnifies latency and stalls across the stack, turning three individually manageable issues into a cascading performance collapse during write-intensive OLTP workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction scopes are written in a way that forces the engine to process and persist more changes than business logic really requires.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The generation, buffering, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log records becomes the bottleneck on the primary node’s commit path.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or subscribers cannot receive or apply the primary’s log stream at the rate it is produced, causing growing replication lag.

When all three conditions coexist, the database experiences a compounded failure mode in which chatty, long-running, or excessively bulk-modifying transactions inflate redo volume, saturating the primary’s log buffer, log device, and archiver. Commit latency spikes and back-pressure propagates to the application layer, while replicas fall progressively behind, evidenced by rapidly expanding log files, stalled log recycling, escalating log-flush and log-sync waits, widening replica replay lag, and a surge of application timeouts and retried statements. Monitoring views may simultaneously show the same heavyweight SQL statements in slow-query logs, high log write times on the primary, and growing apply delay on replicas, making it difficult to attribute blame to any single layer.

Causally, inefficient workload semantics generate unnecessary DML volume and long transactions; this amplifies redo generation and forces the transaction-log subsystem to operate at or beyond its physical limits. As the log device and archiver struggle, commit stalls lengthen, further extending transaction lifetimes and exacerbating lock retention and row version buildup. The swollen and slower log stream must then be shipped to replicas, which, already constrained by network, I/O, or apply throughput, cannot keep pace. Their mounting lag prevents the primary from recycling old log segments, inflating on-disk log usage and adding even more pressure to the log subsystem. The feedback loop—heavy workload ➝ log saturation ➝ replication backlog ➝ log retention—creates a self-reinforcing performance degradation that can culminate in write stalls, replica desynchronization, and risk of availability loss.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer SQL or transactional design forces the engine to scan or manipulate far more data than the business logic really needs, resulting in excessive row touch, long-running statements, and bloated transactions.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, so index look-ups, page links, or key orders no longer reliably reflect the true contents of the tables.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded by the database, driving queue depths and latency beyond acceptable thresholds.

When all three conditions coexist, the system exhibits extreme and erratic slowdown: heavy, non-selective queries and long transactions repeatedly fall back from damaged indexes to full table scans, flooding the I/O subsystem with random and sequential reads that it is already unable to serve. Checksum or page-verification errors intermingle with surging I/O wait events, slow-query logs balloon, retry storms appear at the application tier, and recovery or consistency checks become protracted or fail outright. Administrators observe widening latency variance, unexplained row discrepancies between index and heap probes, sporadic corruption errors, and storage devices stuck at 100 % utilization even when CPU usage is modest.

Causally, poorly written SQL magnifies the read and write pressure on both indexes and data pages, accelerating wear on suspect blocks and increasing the likelihood of surfaces interactions with latent corruptions. Each corruption encountered can force the optimizer to abandon otherwise efficient access paths, switching to full scans that multiply I/O volume. The resulting surge of physical I/O exacerbates an already saturated storage layer, further lengthening service times and inflating in-flight I/O queues. Prolonged latency keeps transactions open longer, intensifying contention and the window during which additional corruptions or write-back failures may occur. In turn, extended storage stalls heighten the risk of incomplete writes or torn pages, feeding back into the integrity problem and creating a self-reinforcing spiral of degradation that is difficult to isolate to any single layer.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint, log, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to workload and hardware, creating artificial pressure or idle gaps even when raw resources are available.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying disks, array, or cloud volume have reached or exceeded their physical IOPS/MB-per-s/latency budget, so read and write requests queue and stall.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated space for data, log, temp, or backup areas is nearly or completely exhausted, provoking allocation failures, auto-extend stalls, and log/archive rollover blockage.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database is simultaneously governed by counter-productive engine settings, starved for I/O bandwidth, and pressed against hard space limits. Operators observe a confusing mix of symptoms: erratic checkpoint or log-flush storms that generate surges of writes against storage already at throughput saturation; rapidly rising I/O queues and latency coupled with non-linear slowdowns in query and batch completion; frequent "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors interleaved with long write-wait times; CPU may oscillate between spin-waiting on I/O and under-utilisation due to blocked sessions; background maintenance (vacuum, defrag, compression) falls irrecoverably behind, further inflating space usage while failing to reclaim it; monitoring may show paradoxical metrics such as high log-write waits while disks appear busy and free-space alarms firing in quick succession.

Causally, poor configuration choices—such as undersized log files, aggressive checkpoint intervals, disabled async I/O, or oversized per-session work areas—inflate I/O demand and write amplification. The swollen I/O workload pushes the storage layer to its throughput ceiling, inflating latency and prolonging unit I/O operations. Prolonged I/O times slow log archiving and space reclamation, causing log segments, temp areas, and data files to accumulate and consume remaining capacity. As free space dwindles, the storage subsystem may introduce additional throttling or garbage-collection overhead, further reducing effective throughput. The cyclic feedback between mis-tuned parameters (which create bursty or excessive I/O), physical bandwidth exhaustion, and mounting space pressure quickly escalates into pervasive stalls, allocation failures, and potential service outage.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write demand exceeds the throughput, IOPS, or latency capacity of the underlying storage volumes, making the storage layer the immediate performance bottleneck.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high share of host CPU cycles, driving the CPU subsystem into sustained saturation.

When both anomalies strike simultaneously, the database shows a blended symptom set: device-level queues are full while OS run queues are equally backed up; read, write, and durability wait events climb together with scheduler and spin waits; statement response times and batch windows expand non-linearly; CPU-bound sessions may stall waiting on I/O completions, yet once I/O returns they compete for already exhausted CPU, causing saw-tooth latency patterns. Monitoring dashboards reveal near-100 % CPU utilization alongside storage latency spikes, but it becomes difficult to attribute delays to a single layer because every execution phase—parsing, execution, logging, checkpointing—encounters both CPU and I/O contention.

Causally, the two root causes reinforce each other: slow storage elevates CPU demand by extending every I/O-bound code path, keeping worker threads active longer, increasing context switches, and driving up spin and latch activity. Conversely, CPU saturation lengthens I/O submission and completion processing, inflates interrupt handling time, and can starve the I/O scheduler of CPU, which further degrades effective throughput. Maintenance tasks or poorly tuned queries may first saturate CPU, pushing checkpoints and log flushes into backlog, which then overruns the storage bandwidth; or a storage degradation event may prolong synchronous I/Os, causing threads to pile up and flood the CPU once data finally arrives. The vicious feedback loop magnifies individual impacts, ultimately crippling both compute and storage subsystems and making traditional single-bottleneck tuning ineffective.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The system is concurrently suffering from lock-manager contention, saturation of physical I/O throughput on the underlying storage, and dwindling or exhausted storage space. All three root causes are active at the same time, so sessions are blocked both by lock waits and by slow or failed I/O operations that themselves stem from bandwidth exhaustion and near-full devices. 

Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress and force rollbacks.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical read/write demand exceeds the bandwidth, IOPS, or latency capacity of the disks or storage layer, inflating I/O wait time and slowing buffer flushes, checkpoint writes, and log appends.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space on data, log, temp, or archive volumes falls to critical levels or is exhausted, causing allocation failures, auto-extend errors, and stalled background tasks that depend on space availability.

Combined phenomena: Users observe sharply rising response times, frequent timeouts, and sporadic deadlock or "out of space" errors. Lock-wait graphs show blockers whose own progress is impeded by slow or failed disk writes; buffer pools accumulate dirty pages because checkpoints and log flushes crawl, extending lock hold times. Log file growth pauses when volumes fill, causing transactions to freeze in the COMMIT phase while holding locks. Monitoring dashboards reveal CPU under-utilization, I/O wait percentages spiking, device queue depths at maximum, escalating lock-wait seconds, and rapidly declining free-space alarms. Batch jobs, index maintenance, and purge tasks slow or abort, further extending space and lock pressure.

Causal interaction: Saturated or failing storage throughput prolongs page reads, log flushes, and checkpoint writes, stretching the duration that transactions retain locks and thus magnifying lock contention. Prolonged transactions increase the rate of concurrent lock requests and exacerbate deadlock probability. In parallel, near-exhausted disk space blocks file growth and log archiving, which can force the engine to halt checkpoints or suspend transactions while still holding locks, freezing other sessions in wait queues. The stall cascades: blocked transactions keep undo and redo space allocated, accelerating space exhaustion; full disks prevent I/O operations that could relieve lock pressure; and ongoing lock contention prevents housekeeping tasks (e.g., purges, truncations) from reclaiming space. The mutual reinforcement of these three bottlenecks drives the database into a degraded or unrecoverable state unless all contributing layers—concurrency control, I/O bandwidth, and capacity—are jointly remediated.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot or frequently churned buffer-cache pages and their associated latches, causing CPU spin, buffer-busy/page-latch waits, and stalled logical I/O despite adequate total memory.
