Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The client–server communication path or connection-handling layer cannot accept, authenticate, or move data at the offered rate, producing connection timeouts, socket backlog growth, and elevated client-read/client-write waits.

When both anomalies strike together, users see erratic but severe end-to-end slowdowns: connection attempts hang or are rejected, established sessions pause on network I/O waits, and those that do reach the executor frequently block on page latches. CPU utilisation oscillates between spin-loops inside the engine and kernel time in network interrupts, while transaction latency and abort rates surge. Monitoring views show simultaneous spikes in buffer busy/page latch waits and client-read/client-write waits, with an inflated count of active back-end processes holding latches yet unable to flush or return result sets because network throughput is impaired. Application servers exhaust connection pools, triggering retry storms that further amplify both latch pressure and network congestion.

Causal interaction: Impaired network throughput lengthens the time each backend spends streaming result sets, prolonging the interval during which it keeps buffer pages pinned or dirty-flush slots allocated, thereby heightening latch contention for other sessions. In the opposite direction, heavy buffer contention slows query completion, so sessions occupy network connections longer and increase concurrent socket demand, which pushes the listener and OS queues toward their limits and raises the probability of connection errors. The feedback loop between prolonged in-engine critical-section holding and saturated network resources escalates queuing at both layers, degrading overall throughput and making the individual root causes harder to isolate.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design causes the engine to process more data or keep transactions open longer than business logic requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks on the same resources, producing blocking chains or deadlocks in the lock manager.

Combined phenomena: Inefficient, long-running statements hold extensive row, page, or table locks while other sessions attempt conflicting operations. The system exhibits extreme and erratic statement latencies, soaring lock-wait time, frequent deadlock victim errors, swelling connection-pool queues, and application timeouts. Monitoring views show the same heavyweight SQL text both in slow-query logs and at the head of long blocker trees; lock-wait graphs grow deeper, and throughput collapses despite low CPU utilization as sessions idle in lock waits.

Causal chain: Over-broad scans, missing predicates, or transactions stretched across user think-time enlarge the lock footprint and duration of each unit of work. This increases the probability that concurrent requests target already-held rows or keys, triggering lock waits. The resulting contention further prolongs the problematic transactions, which in turn extends their lock hold times—a positive feedback loop that intensifies blocking and deadlocks. Thus, flawed workload logic and lock contention reinforce each other, jointly degrading OLTP performance far more severely than either issue alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing the optimizer into sub-optimal, scan-heavy plans and inflating maintenance work on writes. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Saturation of the underlying storage subsystem’s bandwidth, IOPS, or latency budget, causing elevated I/O wait times even when the database engine is issuing requests efficiently. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion or near-exhaustion of allocated disk or file-system space for data, temp, or log areas, leading to allocation failures, halted growth, and stalled background maintenance.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compounding symptoms: 1) poorly indexed or non-partitioned tables trigger large table and index scans, dramatically inflating read and write volumes; 2) the excess I/O quickly pushes the storage array to its throughput limits, producing long device queues, rising read/write latencies, and session wait events; 3) the bloated access patterns and excessive spill-to-disk operations consume free space rapidly, filling data, temp, or log areas, which in turn causes auto-extend failures, out-of-space errors, and stalled checkpoints or archive writes. Performance degradation becomes erratic—queries oscillate between slow and failing outright—while maintenance tasks such as index rebuilds, backups, or purge jobs cannot complete due to both bandwidth starvation and lack of space.

Causally, an inefficient schema design inflates I/O volume, accelerating both throughput consumption and space usage. As the storage subsystem hits its throughput ceiling, operations slow, lengthening the time that temporary segments, inflated redo, and intermediate work areas remain on disk, which further depletes available space. Conversely, dwindling free space forces more frequent file-growth and log-switch events, amplifying write bursts and exacerbating the existing I/O bottleneck. The resulting feedback loop—poor design generating excess I/O, saturating bandwidth, which prolongs disk residency and hastens space exhaustion—creates a severe, self-reinforcing degradation of overall database performance and stability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale, absent, or overly coarse, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and misleading the cost model.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer’s decision logic or plan-reuse mechanism selects a sub-optimal execution plan even when statistical inputs are acceptable, leading to inefficient access paths, join orders, or degrees of parallelism.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared memory, threads, or other OS-managed objects, preventing the allocation of additional resources despite apparent database availability.

When all three anomalies coexist, the workload exhibits a volatile mix of wrong estimates, erratic plan flips, and hard OS-level allocation failures. Symptoms may include: 
• Extreme divergence between estimated and actual row counts followed by sudden switches between radically different plans.
• Queries that oscillate between sluggish full scans and explosive nested-loop iterations, creating bursts of temporary objects, file handles, or worker threads until OS limits are hit.
• Intermittent errors such as "cannot allocate shared memory" or "too many open files" appearing in tandem with frequent plan recompilations and statistics refresh attempts.
• Degradation that is hard to triage because poor plans inflate resource consumption, which in turn triggers kernel denials, causing further plan invalidations or forced serial execution.

Causal chain: Stale or incomplete statistics mislead the cost model, increasing the search space of viable plans. The plan-selection anomaly may then lock in an inefficient plan (e.g., parallel hash join with excessive workers or a nested loop with underestimated outer rows). The bloated plan drives higher memory, file-handle, and thread demands, quickly exhausting conservative OS quotas. Once these limits are reached, parallel worker launches, temporary-file creation, or I/O contexts fail, prompting the optimizer to recompile statements or fall back to even less efficient serial plans that run longer and generate more data modifications—further invalidating already stale statistics. This feedback loop intensifies contention, widens the gap between estimated and actual costs, and produces a cascading performance crisis that is more severe than any single anomaly would cause in isolation.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer relies on stale, incomplete, or missing statistics, producing cardinality misestimates that lead to systematically poor execution-plan choices.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical or virtual storage layer is saturated, so read/write latency and queue depths rise sharply, throttling database operations regardless of CPU availability.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Logical or physical free space on data, temp, or log destinations is nearly exhausted, causing allocation failures, write stalls, and related errors.

When these three conditions coincide, workloads can exhibit extreme and erratic slowdowns: queries may shift to full-table scans or spill to disk because of bad cardinality estimates, immediately overwhelming an already bandwidth-starved storage subsystem. Elevated I/O latency and deep queues amplify statement runtimes, inflating undo, redo, and temp space consumption until remaining free space collapses. Users observe escalating I/O wait times, exploding temp and log files, repeated plan re-compilations with wild estimate-to-actual divergences, sudden "out of space" or "cannot extend segment" errors, and prolonged recovery or checkpoint durations.

Causally, stale statistics can drive the optimizer to select scan-heavy or hash-intensive plans that issue far more physical reads and generate larger spills than necessary, directly aggravating storage throughput saturation. The ensuing longer execution windows and heightened write volumes accelerate space consumption in data, temp, and log areas, pushing the system toward capacity limits. As space dwindles, auto-extension failures and log-archive backpressure further inflate I/O latency, which in turn prolongs query execution and hampers automatic statistics refresh jobs, keeping statistics stale and closing a vicious feedback loop that degrades overall database performance and stability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing metadata is stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan choices.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot pages or undersized cache force heavy latch and pin competition, stalling sessions at the buffer-manager layer.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Data, log, or temp areas run out of free space, leading to allocation failures, forced checkpoints, and I/O back-pressure.

When all three root causes strike together, the workload exhibits a confusing mix of symptoms: execution plans flip unpredictably after every load or purge, yet even "good" plans run slowly because they spin on buffer latches; wait-event dashboards show a tug-of-war between PAGE-LATCH and space-allocation waits; sudden space-full errors, long-running auto-extend operations, or emergency checkpoints magnify latency spikes; CPU usage oscillates between idle (sessions sleeping on space waits) and near-100 % (sessions spinning on latches), while query elapsed times balloon and throughput collapses.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing access paths that hammer a small subset of pages (e.g., full table scans on narrow but very hot tables or nested-loop joins against skewed predicates). These hot pages saturate the buffer cache and amplify latch contention. The extra physical reads and dirty-page churn accelerate growth of data files, temp segments, and redo logs. Because free space is already low—or grows low due to the inflated I/O volume—auto-extends, checkpoints, or archive operations pause foreground work, further stretching execution times. The prolonged runtimes, in turn, keep the same hot pages busy longer, intensifying latch pressure and generating even more redo, which consumes the remaining space faster. The three anomalies therefore form a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades performance, exhausts storage, and obscures root-cause diagnosis.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously constrained by (1) the internal transaction-log subsystem, (2) the physical I/O bandwidth of the storage stack, and (3) exhaustion of available storage space. All three bottlenecks are active at the same time, so any write-ahead logging, data-file activity, or archive operation is slowed or blocked both by log-layer limits, by device-level throughput saturation, and by the lack of free capacity. 

Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The log buffer, log files, or archive/replication pipeline cannot accept or flush redo fast enough, inflating commit-path waits and stalling writers.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying volumes hit their IOPS/MB-per-sec ceiling, causing long I/O service times for data, temp, and log requests even when CPU is idle.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space on data, temp, log, or archive destinations falls to zero, triggering allocation failures, auto-extension aborts, and blocked background writers.

Combined phenomena:  • Exponential growth in commit latency as log flushes queue behind saturated devices whose queues are already deep.  • Bursts of log-file switches, checkpoints, and archiver warnings, quickly followed by "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors when remaining capacity is consumed.  • Mixed wait-event profiles showing both log-related waits (log file sync, log buffer space) and generic storage waits (db file sequential/scattered read, write complete), often accompanied by repeated retry loops from background processes trying to allocate or archive space they cannot get.  • Throughput collapses for both transactional and maintenance workloads; batch windows elongate while foreground OLTP sessions experience timeouts or deadlocks due to stalled commits.  • Monitoring may show paradoxical metrics: high I/O queue depth with near-zero write progress and a flat-lining archive-log position.

Causal chain and interaction: The undersized or slow log subsystem forces frequent flushes and switches, which in turn drive additional write traffic to the already saturated storage, deepening I/O queues and increasing latency. As throughput drops, the log archives and datafile checkpoints slow, preventing timely reuse of log segments and accelerating space consumption. When remaining capacity is exhausted, new log segments and auto-extending datafiles can no longer be allocated, freezing further writes. Conversely, space exhaustion can push the engine into aggressive checkpointing and log switching, amplifying log-subsystem pressure. The intertwined feedback loops among log pressure, bandwidth saturation, and capacity depletion produce a self-reinforcing stall that is far more severe than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The system concurrently exhibits on-disk data/index corruption and depletion or instability of network and connection-handling resources, so that storage-layer integrity faults coexist with transport-layer bottlenecks while the same workload is executing.

Combined Anomalous Phenomena: Users may observe intermittent or persistent query failures in the form of checksum or logical-corruption errors interleaved with connection-establishment timeouts and sudden session drops. Index probes can miss or duplicate rows, forcing the optimizer to fall back to full scans that inflate result-set sizes; these larger result streams exacerbate already congested network paths, leading to prolonged client-read waits, retransmissions, and spikes in application latency. Monitoring may show mismatches between heap and index row counts, rising physical-corruption alerts, simultaneous surges in refused or half-open sockets, and database backends stalled in client I/O while error logs report page verification failures.

Causal Interaction: Storage corruption can elongate or repeatedly restart query execution, amplifying the number of concurrent sessions and the volume of data sent over the network, thereby exhausting listener backlogs, socket buffers, or connection pool limits. Conversely, chronic network stalls, abrupt disconnects, and retry storms can interrupt write-ahead flushes or crash ongoing index rebuilds, increasing the likelihood of torn pages and orphaned index entries. Together, these feedback loops degrade both the physical integrity of data structures and the reliability of client connectivity, making recovery and diagnosis significantly more complex and prolonging overall service disruption.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of engine memory regions (buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, session heaps, etc.) pushes the database process beyond the safe memory envelope of the host, causing paging, OOM kills, and cache-churn stalls.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging pipeline (log buffer, log file, archiver, replication retention) cannot flush or recycle redo fast enough, inflating commit latency and stalling writers.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The path between clients and the database (listener, authentication, socket I/O, physical network) cannot sustain connection or data-transfer demand, leading to refusals, retransmissions, and idle backends waiting on client reads or writes.

When all three anomalies co-exist, symptoms overlap and amplify: commit operations stretch far beyond SLA because they wait first on log flushes and then on congested network handshakes or result delivery; backend processes pile up, each holding large private working sets, inflating overall memory consumption and pushing the host into swap, which in turn elongates log-writer and network-I/O scheduling. Engine wait events show a mixture of LOG_FLUSH, CLIENT_WRITE, and memory-stall states, while OS metrics report paging spikes, elevated disk writes on swap, saturated log devices, rising TCP retransmissions, and a flood of connection-pool retries. Alert logs may alternate between "log switch incomplete", "cannot spawn backend", and "out of memory" messages, making the dominant bottleneck hard to pin down.

Causal chain: slow or blocked log flushes lengthen transaction duration, increasing the number of simultaneously active sessions. Each session retains its work and buffer allocations, driving memory pressure. Memory pressure causes kernel paging that further slows the log writer, worsening commit queues. Prolonged commits leave client threads blocked, which, together with retry logic, inflates connection counts and saturates listener and socket queues. Network congestion or handshake delays then hold backend processes in CLIENT_WRITE waits, keeping their memory allocations live even longer and allowing plan and buffer caches to grow unchecked. The mutually reinforcing feedback loop among memory exhaustion, log-flush delay, and network back-pressure can push the database into a cascading failure where it can no longer accept new connections, flush logs, or reclaim memory without intervention.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction patterns that retrieve, scan, or update far more data than business logic requires, prolonging statement and transaction execution times.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records because background cleaners cannot reclaim space as fast as new versions are created, inflating table/index size and visibility-check cost.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas or subscribers fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply primary-generated log records at production speed, causing log-position gaps and retention of old segments.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits an amplified mix of symptoms:  
• Individual queries and batches run long, appear repeatedly in slow-query logs, and generate outsized undo/redo volume.  
• Heap and index bloat rise rapidly, dragging down cache efficiency and lengthening sequential scans and visibility checks; autovacuum or purge workers stay saturated yet never catch up.  
• Primary-side transaction logs grow quickly while replica replay lag widens; checkpoints stall waiting for log recycling, and disk-space alarms fire on both primary and standby.  
• Replica read consistency degrades because larger version stores must be traversed during snapshot creation; long-running replica queries further delay vacuum on the primary, increasing bloat.  
• End-users see highly variable latency, timeouts, and stale read results, and failover readiness deteriorates as replicas fall ever further behind.

Causally, chatty or poorly filtered application workloads (SQL Workload Logic Anomaly) drive excessive updates, deletes, and wide scans, inflating the volume of row versions produced per transaction. This surge overwhelms MVCC cleanup processes, leading to persistent version bloat that slows both foreground queries and background maintenance. The same write amplification balloons the transaction log, which must be shipped and replayed on replicas; their apply threads struggle with the heavier redo stream and the expanded tables they must update, creating Replication Synchronization Anomaly. Replica lag prevents the primary from recycling log segments, prolongs the global transaction-id horizon, and holds back vacuum from pruning old versions—thereby worsening MVCC bloat. In turn, the bloated storage multiplies the cost of the already inefficient application queries, further escalating change volume and log generation. The feedback loop among chatty workload, version accumulation, and replication lag compounds resource exhaustion and performance instability in OLTP environments.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonably accurate statistics, often because of flawed cost comparisons, plan reuse issues, or version/configuration changes.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : The on-disk heap or index pages have become physically or logically inconsistent, causing look-ups or scans to return incorrect or unpredictable results.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes monopolise host CPU, driving sustained saturation and system-wide latency inflation.

When all three root causes surface together, the engine must execute poor plans against corrupted or internally inconsistent structures while the server is already starved for CPU. Observable effects include:  • Frequent plan flips between index and full scans as the optimizer struggles to evaluate damaged indexes, leading to erratic and ever-changing plan caches.  • Corruption-induced logical I/O retries, checksum validations, or forced page reads magnifying CPU usage so that run-queue lengths spike and scheduler waits dominate wait-class statistics.  • Queries that should return quickly instead loop through large row sets or perform repeated look-ups that either miss rows (due to bad indexes) or re-read the same pages, producing both correctness anomalies (missing/duplicated rows) and severe latency variability.  • Emergency fail-over, corruption-check jobs, or auto-rebuild operations launching under CPU pressure, causing further contention and making it difficult to pin blame on a single layer.  • Error logs may show alternating entries of "corrupt page detected" and "plan removed from cache due to recompile", coinciding with CPU spikes and throughput collapse.

Causally, damaged data or index pages can mislead the optimizer: page-level inconsistencies prompt the engine to distrust indexes, leading to sudden plan changes that favour full table scans. These broader scans, in turn, inflate CPU consumption. The resulting CPU saturation slows background validation and recovery threads, delaying page-repair tasks and allowing corruption to persist longer. High CPU pressure also accelerates plan cache churn, increasing the likelihood that the optimizer will pick different—and often worse—plans on each execution. The vicious circle of corrupt structures provoking bad plans, which then explode CPU usage, which in turn hinders corruption remediation and plan stability, amplifies both performance degradation and data-integrity risk.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database cluster concurrently suffers (1) a replication pipeline that cannot ship or apply WAL/redo as fast as it is generated, (2) a saturated storage subsystem whose physical read/write throughput and latency budgets are exceeded, and (3) constrained network and connection-handling capacity between nodes and client endpoints. The triple condition means log generation, log shipping, log replay, and client traffic are all bottlenecked at once.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Log-position gaps and replay lag widen far beyond normal as primary and replica disks exhibit long queue depths, elevated service times, and stalled durability flushes. Retained WAL segments and relay logs grow rapidly, consuming space on overworked volumes. Primary and standby sessions accumulate on commit, buffer-I/O, client-read, and client-write waits while CPU remains under-utilised. Clients observe intermittent connection refusals, prolonged authentication, query timeouts, and erratic latency spikes correlated with surges in packet loss and retransmissions. Maintenance windows, backups, and analytical reporting jobs elongate or fail, and failover readiness degrades as replicas become too stale to promote.

Causal interaction: Disk saturation slows WAL flush on the primary, lengthening commit paths and forcing larger bursts of log data once writes succeed; these bursts collide with limited replication bandwidth and network congestion, inflating transport queues and aggravating replica lag. The swollen backlog prevents WAL recycling, which in turn inflates I/O pressure on already constrained storage. On the replica side, poor disk throughput and delayed network delivery hamper redo apply, further postponing feedback to the primary and perpetuating retention growth. Meanwhile, client connection stalls and retries increase session counts and write amplification, adding more log traffic and random I/O to the stressed storage layer. Each anomaly reinforces the others, forming a feedback loop that degrades throughput, increases latency, and threatens data-durability and availability guarantees across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The optimizer’s metadata (row-count estimates, histograms, correlations) is out of date or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality errors and poor plan choices.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions request incompatible locks on the same resource, resulting in long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger rollbacks.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, breaking key order, page links, or heap-to-index mappings and causing read errors or wrong results.

When all three faults coexist, the database exhibits an intertwined failure pattern. Queries may choose full scans or inefficient nested-loop plans because stale statistics misrepresent row counts; these bloated scans touch many damaged pages and acquire far more locks, stretching their execution time and lock scope. Corruption-induced retries, consistency check scans, or forced fallbacks to heap scans further lengthen lock hold times, amplifying lock queues and deadlock frequency. Simultaneously, widespread blocking delays automatic statistics refresh jobs and index-rebuild attempts, so inaccurate statistics persist. Corruption can also cause phantom duplicates or missing keys that mislead the optimizer and expand lock footprints, while repeated rollbacks from deadlocks or corruption errors leave tables in high-churn states that quickly age statistics. The feedback loop of bad plans → extended locking → inhibited maintenance → worsening stats, combined with structural corruption that undermines access paths, degrades both performance and data correctness, making root-cause isolation extremely difficult and risking cascading outages.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The log-writer, flush, and archiver pipeline cannot keep pace with redo generation, driving up commit-path latency.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, preventing further allocations and recycling.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network transport or connection-handling resources are saturated or unstable, delaying client traffic and any log shipping or archival flows.

When these three root causes strike at once, the database faces a compound failure on its primary write-commit path, on-disk capacity, and on the network channels that move log and archive data. Observable symptoms intertwine: commits and checkpoints stall while log flush waits soar; log switches trigger but hang because the next segment cannot be created on a full device; archiver or replication processes report timeouts or disconnections as congested networks throttle log shipping; free space in both active and archive log destinations plummets, producing "cannot allocate log" or "out of space" errors; meanwhile clients experience connection establishment delays, query timeouts, and sudden disconnects as socket queues overflow and retransmissions spike. The administrator may see a rapidly growing queue of unarchived log files, a surge in retry storms from application tiers, and an overall degradation that is hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, heavy transactional activity first drives up log-write volume. Because archival throughput is limited by network congestion, completed log segments linger, consuming space in the log/ archive area. As capacity is consumed, the storage subsystem rejects further extensions, blocking new log switches and forcing foreground transactions to wait for space. The prolonged commit latency keeps connections open longer, increasing session counts and network load, which further stresses already constrained listener and socket resources. The feedback loop—log saturation → space exhaustion → blocked archiving → network retries → additional log growth—amplifies itself until the database enters a near-hang or shutdown condition. Only coordinated remediation of log tuning, space reclamation/expansion, and network bandwidth or connection-handling limits can break the cycle.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures (tables, partitions, indexes, constraints, data types) are misaligned with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of query logic.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer metadata (row counts, histograms, correlation statistics) is stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and poor plan choices.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions contend for buffer-cache pages and internal latches, leading to page-level serialization, CPU spin, and wait events that slow down all concurrent work.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits a blended symptom set: 1) execution plans show full scans or deeply nested loops on non-covering indexes with grossly wrong row-count estimates, 2) the bad plans funnel many sessions toward the same small set of hot pages (index roots, sequence pages, or narrowly partitioned tables), 3) buffer busy, latch, and page I/O wait events skyrocket, masking their origin behind apparent "contention" rather than plan inefficiency, and 4) performance may oscillate after statistics refreshes or index rebuilds, yet never stabilize because each fix only partially alleviates the intertwined problems.

Causal chain: a mismatched schema or missing/oversized indexes inflate the logical I/O footprint of otherwise selective queries. Stale or low-quality statistics hide this inflation from the optimizer, leading it to choose plans that touch even more pages or drive high fan-out join orders. The inflated demand converges on a subset of pages—root blocks of remaining indexes, small dimension tables, or last pages of monotonically inserted heaps—creating hotspots. As more sessions queue on latches for those pages, overall throughput drops, I/O stalls lengthen dirty-page retention, and latch contention further delays plan operations, which in turn keeps pages pinned longer and intensifies buffer pressure. Thus each anomaly amplifies the others, forming a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades both transactional and analytical workloads until the underlying schema, statistics, and cache contention issues are jointly resolved.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : A static physical-model mismatch that forces queries and DML to use inefficient access paths because tables, indexes, or partitions are not aligned with workload access patterns.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) that make the runtime environment unsuitable for the hardware and workload, creating throttling or storms despite adequate raw resources.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Page-level serialization inside the buffer manager where many sessions compete for the same cache pages, latches, or I/O slots, stalling while buffers are pinned, dirtied, or flushed.

Composite anomaly definition: The system simultaneously suffers from a poor physical schema/index design, sub-optimal instance configuration, and intensified buffer-cache/latch contention. Ill-suited data structures generate excessive or hotspot-focused page activity; misconfigured memory, checkpoint, or parallelism settings prevent the engine from absorbing that activity smoothly; together they create severe page-level contention and resource thrashing.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Queries that should be selective degrade into full scans, inflating logical and physical I/O. 2) Undersized or over-committed buffer pools, work memory, or checkpoint parameters cause constant cache eviction or flush storms, visible as alternating periods of I/O idleness and bursty write spikes. 3) Buffer-busy/latch waits and CPU spin events surge on hot index root pages or monotonically growing tables; at the same time, storage and CPU utilization appear paradoxically low or oscillatory because sessions are stalled on synchronization rather than raw resource limits. 4) Adding an index or changing a parameter in isolation yields only marginal or short-lived relief, and the interplay of symptoms makes plan analysis, wait-event interpretation, and conventional tuning misleading.

Causal chain and mutual reinforcement: Sub-optimal schema/index design amplifies page reuse on a small set of blocks (e.g., a missing composite index funnels all lookups through one non-covering index), creating hot pages. Misconfigured memory or checkpoint cadence reduces the residence time of those pages, forcing frequent re-latching and dirty-page flushes. Each flush evicts useful pages and triggers additional I/O and latch acquisition, lengthening critical sections and spreading contention to other objects. Conversely, excessive latch waits elongate statement runtimes, increasing concurrent session counts, which in turn exceed the memory or worker limits set by faulty parameters, triggering even more cache churn and background activity. The feedback loop between design flaws, configuration mis-sizing, and buffer-manager choke points culminates in unpredictable throughput, erratic latency, and difficulty isolating the primary performance inhibitor.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously burdened by inefficient or over-broad SQL logic, runaway memory consumption inside the engine, and lagging downstream replicas that cannot keep pace with the primary’s write-ahead log stream.

Combined anomalous phenomena: End-user requests show highly variable and often excessive latency; some stall while waiting for memory or lock release, others time out due to stale replica reads or failovers that take longer than expected. On the primary, statement and transaction statistics expose wide table scans, oversized result sets, and long-lived transactions that hold buffer pages and transaction IDs. Memory graphs reveal rising resident-set size, frequent swapping, and oscillating buffer-cache hit ratios caused by churn in work areas and plan cache. In parallel, replication monitoring views show widening write/flush/replay lags, growing retained WAL segments or relay logs, and periodic cascading back-pressure where the primary blocks log recycling. Cluster managers may detect node heart-beat stalls or trigger failover because memory pressure and replication backlog jointly lengthen recovery point objectives.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient SQL constructs inflate result sets and prolong transactions, inflating per-query work memory, sort/hash buffers, and plan-cache entries. This accelerates overall memory allocation growth; once physical RAM is saturated, the OS begins paging, slowing local I/O and CPU scheduling. The same heavy queries generate larger and more numerous log records, which must traverse the replication channel. Memory pressure on both primary and replicas throttles apply workers and can evict useful cache lines, diminishing replay throughput. As replicas fall behind, the primary is forced to retain additional log segments, further consuming memory and storage and exacerbating the allocation anomaly. Conversely, memory stalls on the primary delay log generation and transmission bursts, producing uneven flow control and amplifying replication lag. The intertwined feedback loop between bloated workload semantics, memory exhaustion, and impaired replication escalates resource contention, degrades performance for both OLTP requests and analytical queries, and erodes high-availability guarantees.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism limits, etc.) create artificial pressure or idle gaps that do not reflect the true hardware capacity.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures on disk become internally inconsistent or corrupted, making stored data and access paths unreliable.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally large share of CPU cycles, driving the host to sustained compute saturation.

Combined phenomena: The instance shows near-100 % CPU utilisation, long run-queues, and pervasive scheduler waits while I/O devices oscillate between bursts and idle periods. Queries that once used indexes fall back to full scans or repeatedly re-read pages after failed checksum validations, inflating CPU usage and causing erratic latency spikes. Frequent checkpoints or aggressive background verification jobs—triggered by tight configuration thresholds—collide with corruption-induced page rereads, producing log-flush storms and lock contention. Monitoring highlights mismatches between hardware utilisation (CPU pegged, disks underused) and wait-event mixes that include CPU spin waits, page verification failures, and redo-flush pressure. Application symptoms range from sporadic “page corruption” or “could not read block” errors to global slow-downs as the engine burns CPU retrying failed I/O and running mis-sized maintenance tasks.

Causal chain: 1) Misconfigured memory and checkpoint parameters shrink buffer pools or force excessively frequent flushes, magnifying I/O churn and the probability that latent page or index corruption is touched. 2) Encountering corrupted structures causes the optimizer to abandon indexes or to invoke page-verification and error-recovery code paths that are markedly CPU-intensive. 3) The unexpected CPU demand pushes the host into saturation; with parallelism caps set too high, additional worker threads compete for already scarce cycles, further amplifying CPU waits. 4) High CPU load slows checkpoint completion and recovery threads, extending the window in which partially flushed or torn pages can propagate, potentially worsening corruption. Thus, mis-tuned configuration, latent storage corruption, and compute exhaustion create a self-reinforcing loop that degrades performance, increases error rates, and jeopardizes data integrity across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback data that outpaces background cleanup, inflating data structures and visibility-check overhead.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion of physical or logical free space for data, indexes, logs, or temp areas, leading to allocation failures and stalled database operations.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Sustained saturation of host CPUs by database processes, producing long run-queue waits and broad latency spikes across workloads.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from runaway MVCC version bloat, dwindling available storage, and CPU saturation. Cleanup workers cannot reclaim dead tuples quickly enough, data and log files swell toward their size limits, and the extra housekeeping load drives CPU utilization to or above capacity.

Combined phenomena: Administrators observe an accelerating drop in free disk space as bloated tables and indexes expand; auto-extend or allocation failures begin to surface alongside growing transaction logs that cannot be recycled because long-running snapshots persist. Concurrently, background vacuum/garbage-collection workers run continuously, yet application queries and maintenance tasks experience rising latency due to CPU queuing (high run-queue depth, scheduler wait events) and longer table scans through sparsely populated pages. Planner cardinality errors increase, temporary-space requests for sorts or index builds fail, and once storage reaches critical thresholds, write operations stall, compounding transaction backlogs and further inflating CPU demand.

Causal interaction: MVCC version bloat rapidly consumes disk space, pushing the system toward storage exhaustion; as free space shrinks, auto-extension retries and log/archive retention work generate additional I/O and CPU load. At the same time, limited CPU capacity slows vacuum and log-archive workers, allowing obsolete versions and unrecycled logs to accumulate even faster. Storage near capacity forces more aggressive cleanup and checkpoint activity, which competes for already scarce CPU cycles. The feedback loop—bloat → space pressure → intensified cleanup → CPU saturation → slower reclamation—drives the database into a vicious spiral culminating in halted writes, transaction timeouts, and potential downtime.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model and indexing choices do not align with access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer decisions.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and read-path costs in update-heavy workloads.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes drive sustained CPU saturation that throttles overall throughput and inflates latency across the workload.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits compound symptoms: queries already forced into full-table scans or non-covering index probes run against bloated heaps and indexes swollen by dead versions, dramatically enlarging I/O and CPU demand. Sequential scans traverse many more pages than contain live data, while point lookups suffer both from missing/inefficient indexes and from extra visibility checks through long version chains. Background vacuum/cleaner tasks contend for CPU with foreground queries yet still fail to stem version-store growth, so table and index files expand rapidly, statistics drift, and the optimizer’s cost estimates become increasingly inaccurate. Host metrics show near-continuous CPU saturation, rising context-switch and run-queue depths, and a gradual degradation of transaction latency and throughput that standard tuning of isolation levels or hardware alone cannot fix.

Causally, the poor schema and index design amplifies the impact of MVCC bloat: lack of proper indexing or partitioning magnifies the number of pages touched per statement, spreading obsolete versions across a wider footprint and slowing cleanup processes that must scan these structures. As cleanup falls behind, each query must traverse longer version chains and ever-larger relations, further increasing CPU cycles per row and keeping cores busy. The resulting CPU exhaustion slows both user queries and maintenance workers, allowing even more dead tuples to accumulate and inducing a feedback loop that accelerates storage growth and performance collapse. Thus, sub-optimal physical design, unchecked MVCC debris, and compute saturation form a mutually reinforcing triad that can cripple OLTP systems unless all three dimensions are addressed together.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The engine allocates more RAM or swap for buffer caches, work areas, plan cache, background heaps, and other regions than the host can safely supply, triggering paging, OOM events, and cache churn.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical read/write demand on the underlying storage subsystem reaches or exceeds its sustained bandwidth, IOPS, or latency limits, producing long device queues and high wait times.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: The free physical or logical capacity of data, temp, log, or backup volumes falls to critical levels, provoking allocation failures, halted extensions, or log-archive stalls.

When all three anomalies co-exist, the database is under-provisioned in every core resource dimension—memory, bandwidth, and capacity—causing a reinforcing spiral of resource contention. Symptoms include: relentless growth of the database process RSS followed by operating-system paging that floods the storage layer; soaring read/write latency with queues pegged as memory shortfalls force more buffer evictions, re-reads, and large temp spills; sudden or intermittent "out of space" errors as emergency temp and redo growth consume the last free blocks; erratic query performance, prolonged checkpoints, stalled commits, and unplanned node reboots that complicate diagnosis because wait events for memory, I/O, and space failure interleave in monitoring snapshots.

Causally, excessive memory allocation fills RAM, causing the OS to swap, which multiplies I/O traffic and immediately stresses storage throughput. The overwhelmed storage layer slows page-in operations, lengthening memory stalls and encouraging the engine to evict clean buffers more aggressively, which in turn amplifies read churn. Simultaneously, temp spills from under-sized work memory and prolonged log flushes inflate data and log files, accelerating consumption of already scarce disk space. As space dwindles, auto-extension or archive operations may hang, holding locks and freezing writers, which further prolongs transactions and retains even more memory. The mutual amplification among memory pressure, I/O saturation, and space exhaustion can culminate in system-wide deadlocks, forced shutdowns, or data-loss situations if not promptly mitigated.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Anomaly Definition: The database concurrently suffers from stale or insufficient optimizer statistics, runaway internal memory consumption, and exhaustion of critical operating-system resource limits. Together these three root causes create a feedback loop in which poor cardinality estimates drive memory-hungry plan choices that in turn collide with both engine-level memory ceilings and kernel-enforced quotas, provoking severe instability and performance collapse.

Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count and distribution statistics no longer reflect actual data, forcing the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and select sub-optimal execution plans.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Buffer caches, work areas, and other engine heaps grow beyond the host’s safe memory envelope, triggering paging, swapping, or OOM terminations.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes hit kernel limits on virtual memory, shared memory, file descriptors, or thread counts, leading to failed allocations and partial outages even while the database remains nominally online.

Combined Phenomena: Queries may oscillate between unexpectedly large hash joins and nested loops, each consuming excessive work memory; sudden surges in parallel workers or spilled sorts drive resident-set size upward until the kernel begins to swap or deny new allocations. Execution plans show huge gaps between estimated and actual rows, while system logs simultaneously record memory-pressure stalls and "cannot allocate shared memory / cannot fork" errors. Automatic statistics jobs or plan recompilations may fail due to missing resources, making statistics staleness persistent. Application sessions encounter intermittent timeouts, plan regressions after data loads, and sporadic crashes as the database alternates between memory thrashing and kernel-level denials.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Stale statistics underestimate result set sizes, causing the optimizer to prefer in-memory hash joins, large sorts, or wide parallelism that request generous work buffers. These inflated allocations accelerate the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly, pushing the engine toward or beyond physical memory and swap limits. As memory pressure intensifies, the operating system enforces hard ceilings on shared memory, address space, or thread creation, which prevents new backends or parallel workers from starting and may abort ongoing queries. Failed allocations interrupt statistics maintenance and query execution, leaving statistics even more outdated and prompting further misestimation. The three anomalies thus reinforce one another—misestimation fuels memory over-commitment, over-commitment exhausts kernel resources, and kernel denials impede the corrective mechanisms—culminating in cascading slowdowns, aborted queries, and potential instance restarts.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, index, and partition design does not fit actual access patterns, forcing even well-written SQL to use inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, often because of cost-model or plan-cache quirks.

Composite definition: Both a static mismatch in the physical schema and a dynamic mis-selection of execution plans coexist. Poor or missing indexes, oversized or redundant structures, and ill-suited partitions leave only a small set of viable access paths, while the optimizer still fails to pick the best among those, compounding inefficiency.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Workload exhibits frequent full table or non-covering index scans, but even when suitable indexes are present the same statements sometimes flip between different bad plans. You may observe extreme variance in response times, sudden CPU or I/O spikes, bloated buffer-pool churn, and lock contention as long-running scans block short OLTP lookups. Adding or modifying an index may help one statement yet unexpectedly slow another because the optimizer latches onto the new structure with an ill-costed plan. Performance improvements gained by manual hinting or index tuning are fragile, disappearing after plan cache invalidations, statistics refreshes, or version upgrades.

Causal interaction: The deficient physical design narrows the pool of efficient plans, increasing the likelihood that any costing inaccuracy or plan-cache quirk will land on a pathological path. Conversely, when the optimizer does stumble upon a partly efficient plan, the absence of covering or selective indexes forces additional key lookups or broad range scans that negate the benefit. Repeated plan flips driven by parameter sensitivity or cache pollution obscure the root schema issue, while the schema flaw magnifies the cost gaps between good and bad plans, making performance instability more severe and harder to diagnose. Together, the two anomalies reinforce each other and degrade both transactional and analytical workloads far beyond the impact each would have in isolation.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Pages in the buffer pool become hot bottlenecks; sessions spend excessive time spinning or waiting on latches, buffer-busy events, or page-pin contention rather than doing useful work.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical data-file or index structures are corrupted—checksums fail, page links are broken, or key ordering is incorrect—so the storage layer can no longer be trusted.

Composite anomaly definition:
Both anomalies are present simultaneously: the system must serialize access to a small set of buffer-cache pages while some of those very pages (or others they reference) are physically or logically corrupted. The engine therefore contends for buffers that may be unreadable, fail verification, or require rebuild/repair logic, coupling heavy latch pressure with integrity faults.

Combined observable phenomena:
• Extremely high buffer-busy, page-latch, and pin waits mixed with bursts of physical I/O retries, checksum failures, or corruption error messages.
• Queries alternately hang (due to latch spin or waits) and abort (due to corruption detection), causing erratic latency and throughput collapse.
• Repeated automatic page rereads, forced checkpoints, or background verification tasks intensify buffer churn, while failing index lookups trigger fall-back full scans that further stress the buffer pool.
• Recovery or consistency-checker utilities run longer than usual, holding latches while rereading or rebuilding corrupted pages, which starves foreground workloads.

Causal interaction and amplification:
Corrupted pages often force extra I/O, checksum validation, or reconstruction work, keeping the corresponding buffer frames pinned and latches held far longer than normal; this multiplies latch wait times and propagates hot-page contention across sessions. Conversely, severe latch contention slows dirty-page flushing and recovery operations, increasing the window during which corrupted or partially written pages remain in play, raising the likelihood of additional integrity errors. The intertwined feedback loop of prolonged latch holds and recurring corruption checks can eventually exhaust worker pools, trigger automatic fail-safe shutdowns, or lead to cascading query failures, making rapid identification and coordinated remediation essential.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys and downstream consumers fall behind because they cannot receive or apply WAL/redo traffic as fast as the primary generates it.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network paths, listeners, or session slots saturate or flap, delaying or aborting client and replica connections as well as log streaming.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a multi-layered slowdown: tables and indexes bloat, full-table scans and index probes lengthen, and primary commit latency rises as replication send queues back up. Replication lag metrics climb while replica read staleness grows; simultaneously, clients and replication workers suffer connection timeouts, increased round-trip times, and frequent reconnect storms that exhaust server connection slots. Log-segment retention balloons because lagging replicas and disconnected receivers prevent recycling, which in turn increases disk-space pressure and prolongs crash-recovery and backup windows. Planner misestimates due to MVCC bloat further amplify load on the primary, and the resulting higher write throughput aggravates both network saturation and replica replay deficits.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn creates rapid version buildup, enlarging the write-ahead log volume that must be shipped over the network. The swollen WAL stream competes with application traffic on constrained or unstable network links, elevating packet loss and retransmissions and causing receiver backends to stall or drop. Each disconnect forces replication to restart log streaming, multiplying network handshakes and further delaying apply. The sustained replica lag holds old transaction snapshots open, slowing vacuum/cleaner progress and locking in even more dead rows on the primary, which inflates table size and write rates—a feedback loop that perpetuates version bloat, network congestion, and replication backlog until storage or connection capacity is exhausted.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Excessive or poorly-formed statements and transaction scopes at the application layer force the engine to process more rows, pages, or time than the true business need demands.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot buffer-pool pages and their protective latches become serialization points, making sessions wait or spin while competing for access to the same memory frames.

When these two root causes coincide, the database executes bloated, scan-heavy, long-running statements that touch large swaths of data while simultaneously funneling many concurrent sessions through a small set of buffer pages (e.g., index roots, sequence blocks, hotspot tables). Observable symptoms include:  
• A surge of slow-query log entries for the ill-written statements.  
• Dramatic rises in buffer busy, page-latch, and latch-free wait events, often accompanied by CPU spin and elevated system load.  
• Prolonged transaction lifetimes that keep locks and latches held, magnifying queueing delays for otherwise short operations.  
• Fluctuating buffer hit ratios and rapid page churn, with checkpoint or background writer spikes as the engine struggles to maintain dirty-page targets.  
• Application-level timeouts, retry storms, and cascading latency across seemingly unrelated requests due to depleted worker threads stuck on latches.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies buffer traffic: wide scans, Cartesian joins, and over-fetched result sets read or dirty far more pages than necessary, injecting them into an already constrained buffer pool. The resulting churn and concentration on a subset of frequently referenced pages (e.g., root or allocation pages) escalates latch pressure. Each latch wait prolongs statement execution, keeping transactions open longer, which in turn sustains their grip on the same hot pages and perpetuates contention. The feedback loop between bloated workload logic (demand side) and buffer/latch serialization (supply side) drives systemic throughput collapse and tail-latency spikes across both transactional and analytical activities.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging pipeline—log buffer, log file groups, flush/sync path, archival, or replication retention—cannot keep pace with redo generation, throttling commit throughput.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database and host processes saturate available CPU cores, driving up run-queue depth and causing wide-spread latency inflation regardless of statement type.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: The transport and connection-handling layer (listeners, sockets, authentication, wire encryption, network path) becomes a bottleneck, delaying or dropping client requests and server responses.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database exhibits a multi-layer performance collapse: 1) commits stall behind slow log flushes, 2) CPU utilisation stays pinned at or near 100 %, with elevated context switches and scheduler waits, and 3) connection establishment and data-transfer latencies spike, leading to client timeouts, increased retransmissions, and an explosion of idle-in-transaction or socket-wait sessions. Observable symptoms overlap and mask each other—e.g., high commit latency may be misattributed to network RTT, while excessive CPU spin on log-writer and listener threads inflates both wait metrics and OS load. Monitoring dashboards show simultaneous saturation of CPU, log-write waits, and connection backlog queues; alert logs may display frequent log switches, archiver lag, and too-many-connections errors occurring in the same timeframe.

Causally, a feedback loop develops: network slow-downs and connection retries extend transaction lifetimes, inflating the volume of unflushed redo and holding log segments active for longer; the overgrown log and heavier context management load force the log writer, checkpointer, and listener processes to consume more CPU, driving the host toward compute exhaustion. In turn, CPU saturation delays log flushing and socket processing, deepening both the log bottleneck and network backlog. As commits queue behind log I/O and CPU-bound background tasks, application threads remain active longer, further amplifying connection counts and CPU demand. The intertwined contention across log I/O, CPU scheduling, and network endpoints accelerates queue build-ups, risks cluster-wide replica lag or failover, and can precipitate a full write stall or loss of client connectivity unless all three layers are relieved in concert.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between table structures, indexes, partitioning, data types, or constraints and the workload’s access patterns, driving the optimizer to choose intrinsically inefficient paths.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency of data or index pages that causes missing, duplicated, or mis-ordered rows and undermines the reliability of persisted structures.

When both root causes coexist, the database exhibits a blended symptom set: queries already slowed by non-optimal or non-covering indexes may further suffer from random outliers where corrupted pages force full scans, unpredictable re-scans, or sudden plan fallbacks. Operators may observe alternating performance between runs, discrepancies between index and table row counts, integrity-check failures on the very objects whose design is already sub-optimal, lock escalation or blocking during emergency page-level repairs, and erratic plan stability as the optimizer oscillates between flawed indexes and expensive full-object access. Maintenance operations such as index rebuilds or statistics updates can fail or prolong unexpectedly because design issues inflate object size while corruption triggers extra verification and page-level retries.

Causally, an inefficient or excessive indexing strategy elevates I/O and churn, amplifying stress on storage subsystems and increasing the window for write-path failures that introduce physical corruption. Conversely, latent page or index-link corruption masks or distorts optimizer feedback (e.g., misleading cardinality estimates or partial scans), making it harder to detect that the underlying design lacks proper selectivity or coverage. Together, poor design continuously re-touches vulnerable structures, while corruption conceals or worsens performance defects, accelerating performance degradation, complicating diagnosis, and raising the risk of data loss or prolonged downtime.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are acceptable.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions acquire incompatible locks, causing long waits, blocking chains, or deadlocks.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Critical data, log, or temp areas run out of free space, preventing new allocations and stalling work.

When these three root causes strike at once, the database experiences a compound failure pattern. A poor plan (e.g., full-table scan instead of an index seek) inflates I/O, CPU, and row touch counts, lengthening statement execution and transaction duration. The prolonged transactions keep locks active far longer, expanding blocker–waiter chains, increasing deadlock frequency, and raising lock-wait timeouts. Simultaneously, the bloated I/O from the bad plans and the pile-up of uncommitted work accelerate growth of data files, undo segments, and especially transaction logs and temp space. As lock queues deepen, many sessions remain open and idle in wait states, preventing log truncation or space reclamation; the swollen logs and temp segments then drive the system into space exhaustion. Once space limits are reached, new page, extent, or log-file allocations fail, which in turn forces even trivial statements to error out, widens lock hold times further, and forces additional plan recompilations that may again select sub-optimal plans, completing a vicious reinforcing loop.

Causally, the sub-optimal plans initiate the chain by amplifying resource consumption and execution time. Longer-running transactions elevate lock contention, which both blocks other sessions and prevents log cleanup. The resulting backlog accelerates space consumption; when space becomes scarce, allocation stalls further delay or abort running statements, propagating more lock waits and forcing the optimizer to recompile queries under degraded conditions (e.g., reduced temp space, emergency plan changes). Thus each anomaly feeds the others: bad plans create lock and space pressure, contention prevents space reclamation, and space exhaustion magnifies planning and execution instability, producing a severe, self-reinforcing degradation of OLTP throughput and availability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot or rapidly churning pages force sessions to serialize on buffer-cache latches or pins, inflating latch wait time and CPU spin without delivering useful work.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical devices or virtualization layers reach their IOPS / bandwidth limits, causing read- and write-latencies to climb and driving database I/O waits while CPU is under-utilized.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Allocated disk or file-system space for data, temp, or log areas is exhausted, halting extensions, allocations, or log archiving and provoking "no space" errors.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits an interlocking failure pattern: 1) foreground sessions queue on hot buffer pages and latches, 2) their eventual I/O requests pile up behind saturated storage controllers, and 3) once space ceilings are hit, new page allocations, log writes, and checkpoints stall completely. Observable symptoms include extreme and oscillating wait profiles that alternate between buffer-busy/latch waits, storage read/write/io_wait events, and space-allocation or log-switch pauses; runaway CPU spin and yet low useful throughput; sudden spikes in response time for both random OLTP queries and large batch jobs; and a flood of error messages about failed extensions, full log/archive destinations, and timeouts on page reads or dirty-page flushes.

Causal chain: Hotspot pages generate high churn in the buffer pool, which drives more physical I/O as pages are repeatedly read and flushed. This heightened I/O demand collides with an already saturated storage subsystem, lengthening flush cycles and prolonging buffer pin holding times, thereby intensifying latch contention. Simultaneously, sustained write pressure and prolonged checkpoints accelerate space consumption; once free space is depleted, data-file growth, temp usage, or log archiving fail, freezing further writes and forcing even more sessions to spin on latches waiting for buffers that can never be written out. The shortage of throughput prevents timely space-reclamation tasks (e.g., log archiver, cleaner, or auto-vacuum) from completing, while the space exhaustion prevents buffer eviction and I/O queues from draining, creating a feedback loop that degrades the database to near standstill.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions acquire mutually incompatible locks that block or deadlock each other, stalling task execution at the lock-manager layer.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path (buffer, flush, file, archiver, or replication retention) becomes the bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling further modifications.

When both root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences intertwined blocking and durability delays: sessions queue for locks that cannot be granted, yet even once a lock holder reaches commit, it remains stuck on slow log flushes, prolonging its lock tenure and expanding blocking or deadlock windows. Observable symptoms therefore include exploding lock-wait chains with victims rolled back, surges in both lock and log-write wait events, escalating transaction response times, shrinking throughput, connection pool exhaustion, and application timeouts. Monitoring will show growing numbers of ungranted locks, repeated deadlock detections, high log flush/sync latency, log file switch storms, and possibly archiver or replication backlog—all occurring together, making diagnosis non-trivial.

Causally, log subsystem saturation lengthens commit processing, so transactions hold critical locks far longer, amplifying contention and elevating the probability of deep blocker trees and deadlocks. In turn, the resulting lock waits inflate the volume of concurrent open transactions, accelerating redo generation (due to rollbacks, retries, and longer-lived transactions) and further pressuring the log subsystem. This positive feedback loop can push the system into a severe throughput collapse, where neither additional log capacity nor lock tuning alone resolves the issue; both dimensions must be addressed concurrently.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback data because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update-/delete-driven churn.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply the primary’s WAL/redo stream at its production rate.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated, driving up read/write latency and queue depth for data, log, and temporary files.

When all three faults are active, the system exhibits a compound symptom set: version stores, rollback segments, and table bloat expand rapidly while replica lag grows and primary log segments pile up, inflating disk-space usage. Autovacuum or purge workers and replica apply threads contend for the same over-burdened I/O subsystem, so both visibility-map scans and redo replays slow sharply. Checkpoints, sequential scans, and large deletes stretch far longer; replica read freshness degrades from seconds to minutes or hours; failovers risk data loss because the replica’s recovery point trails the primary’s transaction-ID horizon; meanwhile the primary warns of imminent wraparound yet cannot recycle WAL because lagging replicas still need it. Global performance shows high I/O wait, moderate CPU, swollen disk queues, and an accelerating feedback loop of bloat → more I/O → deeper lag.

Causally, heavy update/delete activity inflates the version store, forcing more page writes and generating extra WAL. The surge in log volume must traverse the replication channel, but limited network, CPU, or single-threaded apply logic on the replica slows consumption, so WAL accumulates on the primary. Retention of these log segments and the growing on-disk tables/indexes both expand the storage footprint, pushing the underlying disk array to its throughput limit. Elevated I/O latency then throttles autovacuum/purge and replica apply even further, allowing yet more dead tuples and WAL to gather. This positive feedback loop ties together MVCC cleanup debt, replication backlog, and storage saturation, creating a self-reinforcing degradation that can culminate in transaction-ID exhaustion, replica desynchronization, and service-level breaches.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to inefficient access paths, excessive I/O, or wrong join methods.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, creating long blocker–waiter chains or deadlocks that stall throughput.

When both root causes strike together, an ill-chosen plan dramatically enlarges the lock footprint and execution time of critical statements while the lock manager simultaneously becomes saturated with incompatible requests. Observable symptoms include: sudden shifts from index seeks to full table scans that acquire thousands of row, page, or even table locks; explosive growth of lock queues, deadlock frequency, and victim rollbacks; erratic query runtimes where identical statements alternate between fast, parallel index access and slow, blocking scans; rising CPU and I/O due to the bad plan coupled with application-level timeouts as sessions wait on locks; and volatile throughput with alternating bursts of progress and stalls.

Causally, the optimizer’s poor plan increases both the number and duration of locks it holds—e.g., a hash join that spills or a nested-loop on the wrong join order—thereby lengthening critical-section time and magnifying the probability of conflicts. Conversely, the resulting lock waits and deadlocks prolong transaction lifetimes and inflate table cardinalities seen by later optimizer invocations, which can bias plan selection further toward full scans or conservative join orders. This feedback loop between sub-optimal plan reuse and escalating lock contention amplifies performance degradation, making it difficult to attribute slowness to either component in isolation and potentially driving the database into sustained throughput collapse under transactional workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is simultaneously burdened by inefficient application-level SQL logic, a mis-chosen optimizer execution plan, and an overwhelmed replication pipeline. Together, these three root causes inflate data access and modification volume, execute them with an overly expensive physical plan, and then replicate the excessive redo more quickly than replicas can receive or apply it.

SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-issued statements or transaction scopes process far more rows, columns, or time than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects a markedly sub-optimal plan even though statistics are adequate, producing needless scans, joins, or memory usage.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or downstream replicas cannot consume, write, or replay the primary’s log stream at the rate it is generated, leading to lag and log-retention growth on the primary.

Combined Symptoms: • Individual statements show extreme and highly variable latency, with the same SQL text occasionally exploding into multi-second or multi-minute runtimes. • Primary nodes exhibit CPU spikes, inflated logical and physical I/O, and rapid transaction-log growth. • Replicas report widening receive/replay lag, accumulate large relay logs, serve increasingly stale reads, and may fall out of synchronous commit windows. • Application tiers observe both foreground timeouts (from slow queries) and eventual consistency anomalies (stale replica reads). • Monitoring tools reveal erratic plan-cache behavior, large gaps between estimated and actual costs, and replication performance alerts, making isolation of any single culprit difficult.

Causal Chain and Reinforcement: Inefficient SQL statements (workload logic anomaly) generate large scans, wide result sets, or unnecessarily long transactions. When the optimizer compounds this by choosing a poor plan (plan selection anomaly), resource usage and redo generation surge.
