The bloated and prolonged transactions emit voluminous and bursty log streams that must be shipped and applied downstream. Replicas, already limited by network bandwidth, single-threaded apply, or hardware constraints, fall behind (replication synchronization anomaly). The growing replica lag prevents timely log truncation on the primary, expanding storage pressure and lengthening recovery time objectives. Meanwhile, lagging replication can starve read-only workloads of fresh data, prompting additional load on the primary and further worsening the optimizer’s plan quality through changing cache and memory pressure. Thus the three anomalies form a feedback loop that degrades both primary performance and replication health in OLTP and mixed analytical scenarios.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Inaccurate, stale, or missing statistics distort the optimizer’s view of data distribution and cardinalities.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer, even when given acceptable statistics, may pick or reuse a sub-optimal plan because of cost-model or plan-cache issues.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Highly contended buffer pages or latches force sessions to stall or spin, causing severe throughput and latency degradation.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compounding symptoms: queries oscillate between wildly different plans, some suddenly regressing to full-table scans or explosive nested-loop joins that read or update the same hot pages. Estimated vs. actual row counts diverge sharply, execution plans fluctuate across executions, and wait-event dashboards show simultaneous spikes in page-latch, buffer-busy, and CPU-spin waits. Bulk loads or skewed parameter runs can trigger immediate plan flips followed by a surge in latch contention as many sessions converge on a small set of blocks or index root pages. Overall response times become erratic, with occasional stalls that resemble deadlocks but are actually latch storms aggravated by poor plan choices.

Causally, stale statistics mislead the optimizer into misestimating cardinalities; this misestimation either pushes the optimizer toward sub-optimal join orders or causes it to rely on previously cached plans that are no longer appropriate. The resulting plans often concentrate I/O on a narrow working set (e.g., single-root index lookups, hotspot ranges, or repeated table rescans). This access pattern heats up a small subset of buffer pages, driving up contention for buffer pins and latches. Conversely, the latch congestion slows data access and prolongs query execution, delaying automatic statistics refresh operations and keeping the statistics stale, which perpetuates the misestimation and plan instability loop. Together, inaccurate statistics, poor plan selection, and buffer-level contention reinforce each other, producing a self-sustaining performance spiral that is harder to diagnose than any individual anomaly alone.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The log-write, flush, switch, or archive path on the primary instance cannot sustain the redo generation rate, so commit processing stalls on log-related waits and space shortages.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys or downstream consumers fall behind because they cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing growing send/receive/replay lag and preventing log recycling on the source.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures are corrupt or mutually inconsistent, producing checksum failures, wrong-result reads, and apply/redo errors.

When all three faults are present simultaneously, the system exhibits an intertwined symptom set:  
• End-user transactions see sharply rising commit latency, intermittent "log full" or "cannot allocate new log segment" errors, and sudden throughput cliffs.  
• Replication monitoring shows ballooning send-, write-, and replay-lag; relay logs and retained primary log segments grow unchecked; failover readiness drops to zero.  
• Integrity checkers and query workloads report checksum failures, duplicate/missing rows, and replication apply errors such as "redo/row for missing page" or "index inconsistent with heap".  
• The primary’s log directory and the replica’s relay/redo directories expand simultaneously, checkpoint frequency spikes, and background archiver or apply processes cycle between idle, retry, and crash-restart states.  
• Because the same retained log segments are needed both for crash-recovery of corrupt objects and for lagging replicas, storage fills faster, further throttling log writes and widening replication gaps.

Causal chain: Corruption inside data blocks or index pages can cause the replica’s apply thread to halt or repeatedly retry the same failing redo, instantly creating a replication backlog. That backlog forces the primary to retain old log files, which consumes log-device space and intensifies the existing log-subsystem bottleneck; the resulting commit stalls generate even more drastic checkpoint and log-switch pressure, raising the chance of additional corruption during stressed I/O. Meanwhile, the saturated log path slows delivery of fixes (e.g., repairs, index rebuilds) to replicas, so corruption-induced apply failures persist and continue blocking log recycling. The feedback loop between log saturation, replication lag, and corruption-triggered apply errors amplifies each individual anomaly, degrading both write availability and read consistency across the cluster and leaving the entire estate vulnerable to data loss or extended outage.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, background heaps, or leaked allocations causes the DBMS processes to exhaust physical memory and swap, leading to OS-level paging and memory-pressure stalls.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes are unable to receive, persist, or apply the primary’s transaction-log stream fast enough, so log-position gaps widen, replay lag grows, and log segments accumulate on the primary.

When both root causes surface together, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: memory pressure on the primary and/or replicas throttles log-sender and receiver threads, increases context-switch latency, and starves apply workers of cache, while the growing replication backlog forces the primary to retain additional in-memory log buffers and metadata. Observable symptoms therefore include rapidly rising resident-set size, sustained paging, swelling unflushed or retained WAL segments, escalating replication delay, stale read replicas, and possible node eviction or crash loops on memory-starved standbys. Administrators may see contradicting metrics—high memory usage suggesting local workload stress while replication dashboards show widening lag—making isolation difficult.

Causally, excessive memory allocation on the primary can slow checkpointing and background writer activity, lengthening commit cycles and enlarging the log stream the replicas must consume. The resulting surge in outbound WAL intensifies CPU and memory demand on replica apply processes, which, under their own memory saturation, replay even more slowly, further expanding the backlog. Conversely, a replication slowdown keeps log buffers and metadata alive on the primary for longer, inflating its memory footprint and aggravating the existing allocation anomaly. This positive feedback loop amplifies both issues, risking cascading failures such as forced process termination, out-of-sync replicas, and prolonged recovery times after crash or failover.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction logic oblige the engine to process and keep more rows, data, or transactional state than business requirements dictate.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Engine memory structures—buffer pools, work areas, caches, and session heaps—grow beyond the host’s safe physical limits, provoking paging, OOM terminations, or cache churn.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages and associated latches, suffering wait-time spikes, CPU spin, and stalled I/O while vying for page access or flush slots.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the system exhibits extreme and erratic latency, with the same costly statements flooding slow-query logs while overall throughput collapses. Over-wide scans and long transactions inflate the working-set size, which in turn bloats buffer and work memory, driving the process resident set to the edge of physical RAM. Sustained memory pressure triggers paging, shrinking effective cache size and forcing constant page eviction. The resulting churn elevates buffer-busy and page-latch waits, causing CPU spin loops, queueing on hot pages, checkpoint stalls, and eventually OOM kills or node eviction. From the application perspective, users see timeouts, sporadic retries, and unpredictable performance cliffs that are difficult to attribute to a single layer because SQL, memory, and latch waits interleave in AWR/STATISTICS views.

Causal chain: Inefficient SQL enlarges data touches and keeps transactions open longer, inflating per-query work areas and populating the buffer cache with more pages than hardware can comfortably hold. The excess allocations intensify memory pressure; once the OS begins reclaiming pages, cache turnover accelerates. Frequent evictions force the same hot root or sequence pages to be reloaded repeatedly, concentrating traffic and amplifying latch contention. Meanwhile, latch waits prolong each statement, stretching transaction lifetimes and further increasing the volume of in-memory state, which circles back to exacerbate memory exhaustion. Thus, the semantic inefficiencies of the workload ignite a feedback loop with memory over-commitment and buffer-latch hot spots, producing a severe, multifaceted performance degradation that persists until all underlying causes are addressed together.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal physical schema/index design, uncontrolled accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions, and impending or actual exhaustion of available storage space. Each individual defect is problematic on its own, but their coexistence creates a feedback loop that severely degrades performance, threatens data availability, and complicates recovery or maintenance operations.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Queries that should be index-efficient devolve into full-table or full-index scans across massively bloated heaps and indexes. Execution plans show both missing/ineffective indexes and misestimates caused by inflated table statistics. DML workloads experience escalating latency due to heavier page splits, visibility checks, and cache churn. Background cleanup workers (vacuum, purge, garbage collection) run nearly continuously yet fail to reclaim space fast enough; they also contend with poorly designed indexes that prolong every page visit. Meanwhile, data files, index segments, undo/rollback areas, and archive or log destinations grow rapidly, pushing the system toward auto-extend limits, out-of-space errors, or emergency read-only mode. Administrators may observe cyclic spikes of I/O, checkpoint stalls, and failed maintenance tasks that themselves need additional temporary space.

Causal Interaction: Poor schema and indexing force queries—especially UPDATE and DELETE statements common in OLTP—to touch far more rows and pages than necessary, inflating the number and size of versioned tuples produced by MVCC. The surge in obsolete versions overwhelms cleanup workers; because indexes are non-covering or redundant, those workers must scan and rewrite extra pages, consuming CPU, I/O, and generating further versions. The resulting table and index bloat accelerates storage consumption, edging the system toward capacity limits. As free space dwindles, auto-extension failures and log-recycling stalls slow or block both application traffic and background maintenance, allowing even more version debris to accumulate. Conversely, space exhaustion prevents full vacuuming or index rebuilds that could mitigate bloat, locking the system into a vicious spiral of growing size, falling performance, and increasing risk of downtime.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to touch far more data and keep transactions open longer than the business case requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses an execution plan that is materially worse than the available alternatives even though statistics are adequate.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback information accumulate because background cleaners cannot reclaim them fast enough.

When all three root causes surface together, the database exhibits extreme and erratic response times: the same statement alternates between different and generally poor plans, appears constantly in slow-query logs, and holds locks or snapshots for extended periods. Heap and index sizes grow rapidly, sequential scans become longer, and the optimizer’s cost estimates diverge further from reality, resulting in a vicious circle of plan instability. Autovacuum or equivalent cleaners run almost continuously yet still fall behind, while application sessions experience timeouts, increased dead tuples, and occasional transaction-ID wraparound warnings. Diagnostics simultaneously show bloated tables, exploding version stores, and wide row scans triggered by inefficient application SQL.

Causal chain: overly broad or poorly filtered SQL drives high row churn and large result sets. Because the workload is already heavy, even a minor mis-estimated predicate or missing index causes the optimizer to pick plans that devolve into full scans or nested-loop explosions, inflating execution time and the number of modified rows per statement. Longer-running transactions and higher update/delete volume generate vast numbers of MVCC versions. As cleaners lag, table bloat skews statistics and page density, which feeds back into the optimizer and increases the probability of future bad plans. The growing version store also slows visibility checks, compounding the latency induced by both the workload logic flaw and the sub-optimal plans, ultimately degrading OLTP performance across the system.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Inefficient or over-broad application SQL and transaction design that forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic truly requires.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpoint, etc.) that are out of line with hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults, independently of actual resource limits.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Aggregate in-engine memory areas grow beyond the safe operating envelope, causing OS pressure, paging, or OOM events.

When these three root causes coexist, the workload issues, the engine settings, and the host-level memory footprint all collide. Inefficient statements run in larger, longer transactions, each granted overly generous work or sort buffers by mis-configured parameters; as concurrency rises, aggregate memory skyrockets past physical limits. The system then shows a mixed symptom pattern: explosive resident-set growth, sudden paging or cgroup kills, erratic spikes of CPU spin on memory reconciliation, checkpoint and log-flush storms that do not align with I/O utilization, long-tail query latencies, application timeouts, and a flood of slow-query and out-of-memory entries in logs. Observability is clouded because waits oscillate between memory pressure, log I/O, and lock contention, making any single diagnostic view appear inconsistent or misleading.

Causally, the sub-optimal SQL drives high intermediate result volumes and longer transaction lifetimes. Mis-sized configuration parameters—such as excessive per-query work memory, inflated parallel-worker counts, or an oversized buffer pool—allocate disproportionately large chunks of RAM to each bloated operation. The cumulative effect breaches physical memory, triggering OS paging or OOM killers that evict useful pages and terminate processes. Memory pressure, in turn, forces aggressive background flushing and checkpoint activity, amplifying I/O waits and extending the runtime of the already inefficient statements. The feedback loop between chatty or data-heavy SQL, over-generous configuration settings, and runaway memory allocation magnifies performance instability and obscures the primary culprit, leading to systemic slowdown or even node failure across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks a sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, leading to excessive CPU, memory, or I/O work per statement.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, temp, log, or backup areas is exhausted or critically low, provoking allocation failures, halted growth, or stalled background maintenance.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network pathways or connection-handling facilities (listeners, sockets, authentication slots) become saturated or unstable, delaying or preventing session establishment and data transfer.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a multi-layered degradation pattern: poorly chosen plans inflate I/O and temp-space consumption, quickly driving already tight storage to full exhaustion; as space runs out, sorts, hash spills, log growth, and segment extensions fail, causing sessions to hang. Stalled or killed statements hold server processes and TCP sockets open, so connection pools back up, listener queues overflow, and clients experience mounting time-outs and retransmits. Administrators may observe wildly oscillating execution plans, sudden surges in disk-space usage, a spike in temp-space and redo allocation errors, coupled with escalating counts of refused or half-open connections. The overlap of plan instability, space shortages, and network contention obscures clear attribution—symptoms such as long response times or session drops can originate from any layer, making conventional single-axis diagnostics misleading.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan (e.g., full table scan instead of index access) magnifies I/O volume and temp usage, accelerating space depletion in datafiles and temp segments. Once space alarms trigger, background extensions pause or fail, causing active DML and sort operations to stall; these blocked back-end processes keep network sockets occupied, exhausting connection concurrency limits and increasing client wait times. Conversely, network slowdowns elongate statement runtimes, keeping temp segments and uncommitted redo active for longer periods, which further delays space reclamation and pushes the system toward capacity exhaustion. The vicious circle culminates in a systemic slowdown where optimizer mis-plans, storage full conditions, and network congestion perpetuate and amplify each other, jeopardizing both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer bases its cost estimates on stale or incomplete metadata, causing systematic misestimation of cardinalities and ultimately poor plan choices.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating table and index size and increasing visibility-check costs.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical devices that store data, temp, or log files become throughput- or latency-bound, so every read or write waits behind saturated queues.

When all three root causes appear together, symptoms overlap and magnify: execution plans chosen from incorrect statistics are forced to scan or join vastly larger on-disk structures bloated by version buildup; these larger scans, in turn, drive far more physical I/O against disks that are already maxed out, pushing latency higher and keeping buffer-pool hit ratios low. Administrators observe wildly inaccurate row-count estimates, sudden plan flips after data-change bursts, soaring table and index sizes, nonstop autovacuum or purge activity, steep growth in I/O wait events, and long-running queries that stall during large sequential reads or log flushes. Cleanup workers and statistics refresh jobs may run continuously but still fall behind because every page read or written is throttled by the saturated storage layer, while critical OLTP transactions suffer from both plan inefficiency and I/O backlog.

Causally, MVCC version bloat first enlarges the physical footprint of hot tables and indexes. This footprint inflation invalidates previously correct statistics and raises the volume of data the optimizer must consider, seeding the Optimizer Statistics Anomaly. Misestimated plans often select full scans or sub-optimal join orders that touch even more pages, amplifying storage traffic. The extra I/O exacerbates the Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly, slowing both foreground queries and the background cleaners that would otherwise shrink the version store and trigger statistics refreshes. The stalled cleaners allow even more bloat to accumulate, which further skews statistics and perpetuates a feedback loop of increasing workload cost and diminishing throughput.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries pile up faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and bloating table and index pages.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions fight for access to hot buffer-cache pages and their associated latches, causing buffer-busy waits, CPU spin, and stalled I/O.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive or apply the primary’s redo stream at the rate it is produced, resulting in widening log gaps and retention of old log segments on the primary.

When all three root causes strike together, the database shows a compound failure signature: 1) rapidly expanding on-disk heaps and indexes, 2) soaring buffer-busy and page-latch wait times concentrated on hot, bloated pages, 3) continuously rising replication receive/write/replay lag, 4) primary-side WAL segments and replica relay logs accumulating well beyond normal retention windows, and 5) cleanup and checkpoint workers running constantly yet failing to shrink either the version store or the WAL backlog. End users observe erratic response times, pronounced latency spikes, and increasingly stale reads on replicas, while administrators see warnings about transaction-ID or log-cycle exhaustion alongside replication-lag alarms.

Causal chain: Heavy OLTP update/delete traffic first inflates the MVCC version store. The extra dead tuples enlarge every data block, so more pages must be fetched and dirtied, intensifying buffer-pool turnover and putting hot root and free-space-map pages under severe latch pressure. Prolonged latch waits slow foreground commit throughput but still generate WAL at a steady pace; the larger, more fragmented pages also produce more WAL per transaction. Replicas already running near capacity fall further behind, and their delayed replay keeps old snapshot horizons open, preventing the primary’s vacuum from reclaiming obsolete versions. This feedback loop—version bloat → latch contention → replication lag → vacuum inhibition—locks the system into a self-reinforcing degradation spiral that exhausts I/O, memory, and disk space while eroding both primary and replica performance.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses and/or re-uses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though basic statistics are accurate, leading to inefficient access paths, wrong join methods, or inappropriate degrees of parallelism.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, undo records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating table size and visibility-check cost in high-churn transactional workloads.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings governing memory, logging, checkpointing, background workers, and parallelism are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, causing indirect performance pathologies that are not tied to any true resource exhaustion.

When all three conditions coexist, the system exhibits compounding symptoms: query execution times become wildly erratic as the optimizer alternates between cached sub-optimal plans and newly generated plans that must plow through a heavily bloated heap. Sequential scans and nested-loop joins suddenly dominate the profile, generating surges of I/O and undo that further enlarge the version store. Autovacuum or equivalent cleaners run constantly yet never catch up, while poorly sized maintenance workers, buffer pools, and checkpoint intervals exacerbate I/O storms and lock out useful work. Wait-event histograms show a mix of CPU spin on plan compilation, buffer-pin waits during visibility checks, and log-flush stalls even though hardware utilization appears uneven.

Causally, misaligned configuration parameters (e.g., too small autovacuum memory, aggressive plan_cache_size, sub-optimal cost constants, or undersized buffer pool) first create fertile ground for MVCC debris to build up and for the optimizer to receive distorted cost signals. The swelling of dead tuples skews table statistics and increases true I/O costs, widening the gap between estimated and actual costs and prompting the optimizer to pick or reuse plans that look cheap but perform poorly. Those bad plans—such as table scans over bloated relations or explosive nested loops—generate additional undo and redo, accelerating version-store growth. Meanwhile, throttled or starved cleanup workers cannot reclaim space because conservative maintenance cost limits or checkpoint settings delay page recycling. Thus, each root cause amplifies the others: configuration mis-tuning enables version bloat, version bloat misguides plan selection, and poor plans in turn intensify the workload on an already lagging maintenance subsystem, leading to cascading degradation of transactional throughput and stability.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The log-writing, flushing, switching, or archiving path on the primary instance becomes the bottleneck, throttling commit progress and preventing timely log recycling.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or subscribers cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing widening apply and retention lags.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes collectively oversubscribe host CPU cycles, driving sustained saturation and scheduler contention.

When all three root causes strike together the system exhibits compound symptoms: commit latency and log-flush wait times rise sharply; log file switches and checkpoints pile up but archive and replication queues keep growing because replicas fall further behind; monitoring shows ballooning retained WAL/redo segments on the primary, swollen relay logs on replicas, and replication apply delay measured in minutes or hours. Meanwhile, hosts on both primary and replicas run at or near 100 % CPU, with long run queues and frequent context switches. Application threads stall behind log-sync and scheduler wait events, while read-only replicas deliver increasingly stale data and may become unavailable for failover due to excessive replay lag.

Causally, a saturated CPU starves critical background threads—log flusher, archiver, and replication sender/receiver—reducing their throughput and amplifying the inherent bottleneck in the transaction-log subsystem. Slower log writes lengthen commit paths and defer log file recycling, which in turn forces the primary to retain more segments for lagging replicas. The replication backlog grows because replicas, themselves CPU-constrained, cannot parse and apply incoming redo quickly enough, further delaying acknowledgment to the primary. This feedback loop increases disk pressure in the log area, heightens checkpoint frequency, and propagates latency spikes across all transactional workloads, ultimately risking forced shutdowns or failovers when log space is exhausted.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more rows, data, or time than business logic requires.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or page pins, throttling access despite sufficient overall memory.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, write, or replay the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing widening log-position and apply lag.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database exhibits extreme and wide-ranging distress: individual statements and whole transactions run long, saturating the buffer pool and generating spikes of buffer-busy and page-latch waits. CPU usage climbs yet throughput stalls as sessions spin on latches. Simultaneously, the primary’s write-ahead log grows rapidly and is retained because replicas fall behind; replica read staleness increases, failover readiness degrades, and log-shipping queues balloon. Monitoring views show the same costly SQL repeatedly in slow-query lists, elevated latch wait classes, and ever-increasing replication delay. These symptoms intertwine, making it difficult to attribute slow response times, memory pressure, or log growth to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies logical I/O volume and concentrates access on a small working set (e.g., hot index root pages), driving buffer churn and latch contention. The stalled foreground sessions extend transaction lifetimes, yielding larger and burstier log batches that must traverse the replication pipeline. At the same time, latch contention and buffer thrashing on the primary slow log generation checkpoints, while replicas—already stressed by reapplying the same inefficient SQL—struggle to read hot pages fast enough, further widening replay lag. The growing log backlog prevents space reclamation on the primary, inflating the buffer cache footprint and intensifying contention. Thus, inefficient workload logic, internal buffer-manager contention, and replication apply bottlenecks form a reinforcing loop that degrades both primary performance and downstream consistency.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transactional design that requests or touches more data, rows, or time than business logic really requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonable, causing avoidable work or poor access paths.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions repeatedly serialize on hot buffer-cache pages or latches, stalling while acquiring or holding low-level synchronization primitives.

When all three root causes are present, the database experiences a cascading performance failure: overly greedy SQL statements trigger large or long-running executions; the optimizer, already inclined to pick inefficient plans, may lock in full scans, wide nested loops, or non-parallel plans; the resulting surge of page reads, writes, and hotspot accesses concentrates traffic on a small set of buffer pages or index roots, driving extreme latch and buffer-busy waits. Observable phenomena include: slow-query logs filled with the same heavy statements, oscillating plan shapes for identical SQL, sharp spikes in page-latch or buffer-busy wait events, CPU spin without throughput gain, erratic application timeouts, and sudden plan flips that coincide with latency or contention spikes.

Causal chain and reinforcement: Excessive data access from poor workload logic inflates the search space the optimizer must cost; if it then selects a bad plan, row counts and I/O amplify further, funneling many concurrent sessions toward the same data blocks. The resulting hot pages increase latch hold times, elongating each physical or logical I/O and feeding misleading runtime feedback (e.g., longer observed I/O latencies) that can prompt additional plan invalidations or re-optimizations, perpetuating plan instability. Meanwhile, latch contention throttles throughput, prolongs transaction lifetimes, and keeps locks open longer, which in turn widens the concurrency window in which the same inefficient SQL keeps hammering the same pages. The mutual amplification of bloated workload logic, poor plan choice, and low-level buffer contention drives a feedback loop that severely degrades overall database responsiveness and scalability.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion of physical or logical free space for data files, logs, temp areas, backups, or diagnostic outputs, leading to allocation failures and write stalls.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Hitting kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, preventing the database from opening files, spawning workers, or attaching shared memory.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Saturation or exhaustion of listener, socket, authentication, or network bandwidth resources that blocks new client connections or slows data transfer.

When all three anomalies manifest together, symptoms overlap and amplify: connection attempts pile up while the listener’s socket queues are full and kernel file-descriptor limits are reached; existing sessions hang in client I/O or log-file-write waits because archive, redo, or temp spaces are full; background processes fail to allocate shared memory or threads, yet errors cannot be written because diagnostic log files and destinations lack space. Administrators observe surging connection timeouts, "too many open files" or "cannot allocate memory" errors, sudden inability to create new sessions, and critical write failures for data, temp, or log files. Performance degrades erratically—some transactions block on space, others on OS resource denials, while still others stall on network retransmissions—making the outage pattern appear intermittent and hard to pinpoint.

Causal chain: space exhaustion in logs or datafiles forces the database to issue additional file-open, extend, and archive operations, rapidly consuming file handles and shared memory descriptors, thereby triggering OS resource limit breaches. Once kernel limits are hit, the listener and background writers cannot open new sockets or files, which in turn causes connection queues to back up and network sockets to linger in half-open states, aggravating the network resource bottleneck. Simultaneously, clients retry failed connections, inflating the socket and process counts and accelerating OS limit exhaustion, while prolonged result streaming holds disk space and network buffers longer, further delaying log archival and space reclamation. The intertwined feedback loops among dwindling storage, depleted kernel resources, and choked connectivity quickly cascade into a full system outage that is more severe and harder to remediate than any single anomaly alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design that forces the engine to scan, update, or hold more data and longer transactions than business semantics require.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request conflicting locks on the same resources, causing prolonged waits or deadlocks in the lock-manager layer.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and undo/rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.

When these three root causes coincide, the database experiences an amplified failure mode in which overloaded statements generate large update/delete footprints, each holding locks for extended durations while simultaneously churning out massive version chains. The oversized transactions and wide scans increase lock footprints and hold times, lengthening blocker-waiter chains and raising the probability of deadlocks. Meanwhile, the same long-running or blocked transactions keep old snapshots alive, preventing garbage-collection workers from pruning obsolete versions. The swelling version store enlarges table and index sizes, slows down scans, and drives up buffer churn, which further prolongs statement execution and exacerbates lock hold times. The feedback loop—inefficient SQL inflating work, which intensifies lock contention, which in turn prolongs transactions and stalls cleanup, which then bloats storage and slows access paths—leads to cascading performance degradation, rising latency variance, throughput collapse, and frequent application timeouts or rollbacks.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level knobs (memory, checkpoint, log, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, causing avoidable pressure on subsystems even when raw resources are available.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical or virtual storage layer cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded by the database, resulting in persistently high I/O latency, deep device queues, and long database I/O waits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server transport, listener, or socket resources are saturated or unstable, producing connection errors, socket backlogs, and prolonged data-transfer waits.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set:  • Sudden surges in checkpoint, page-flush, or log-write waits elongate transaction commit paths while storage latency and queue depth remain elevated.  • Back-end workers stall on I/O, hold locks, and accumulate in client-write or client-read waits, inflating active session counts and exhausting connection slots.  • Application servers observe both slow statement execution and sporadic connection refusals; retry storms further inflate throughput demand, amplifying storage and CPU spikes that appear inconsistent with overall hardware utilization.  • Monitoring shows oscillating CPU usage (from spin waits on mis-set parameters) co-occurring with storage wait domination and rising TCP retransmissions or listener backlog overflows, making single-layer diagnosis misleading.

Causal chain: Sub-optimal configuration parameters—such as an undersized buffer pool or overly aggressive checkpoint interval—drive excessive physical I/O, pushing the storage subsystem to (or beyond) its throughput limits. The resulting I/O stalls propagate back into the engine, holding back-end processes longer and inflating connection lifetimes. As active back-ends linger, listener and socket resources saturate, and network round-trip delays grow; this, in turn, slows client consumption of result sets, prolonging hold times on server buffers and causing even more dirty pages to accumulate. The feedback loop between misconfiguration-induced I/O amplification, storage saturation, and network congestion reinforces each anomaly, degrading overall throughput and making the database appear resource-starved across multiple layers simultaneously.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical table, index, partition, datatype, and constraint layout does not match workload access patterns, forcing queries into broad or row-by-row access paths independent of statistics or plan choice.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on overlapping data or metadata, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall throughput and trigger rollbacks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level memory, checkpoint, log, parallelism, and worker settings are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, so internal subsystems operate with sub-optimal capacity or cadence.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compound symptom set: queries already slowed by table scans or non-covering index probes hold locks longer, magnifying blocking chains; lock waits accumulate inside connections whose work memories, lock-hash buckets, or log buffers are under-sized by configuration, causing CPU spin or flush storms even while hardware is under-utilised; deadlock victims trigger retries that re-enter the same poorly indexed code paths, amplifying I/O and lock traffic; checkpoints or background writers start unexpectedly because mis-sized log or buffer pools fill quickly after each retried modification burst, adding more I/O latency that further prolongs lock holding time.

Causally, a bad schema and index design inflates the row set any modification must touch, expanding the lock footprint and extending the duration each lock is held; this enlarged contention surface raises the probability and depth of blocking chains. Simultaneously, mis-set configuration parameters (e.g., too small lock memory, aggressive checkpoint frequency, inadequate work memory) throttle the lock manager’s ability to grant or clean up locks and push additional latency into every statement. The added delays feed back into even longer hold times on the already bloated locks coming from the design flaw, while the surging lock queues trigger further background work (flush, checkpoint, deadlock detection) that contends for CPU and I/O, creating a positive feedback loop that degrades OLTP throughput sharply.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, ranges, pages, or metadata, causing blocking chains or deadlocks managed by the lock manager.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read- or write-request volume saturates the bandwidth, IOPS, or latency budget of the underlying storage devices that hold data, log, or temp files.

When both anomalies strike together, sessions pile up behind conflicting locks while the storage layer is simultaneously unable to service the flood of buffer-pool misses, log flushes, and page writes quickly enough. Observable effects include lock-wait and I/O-wait events interleaved in wait-profiling views, runaway transaction response times, elevated deadlock frequency, growing lock queues whose wait durations rise in step with disk latency spikes, stalled checkpoint or redo flush activity prolonging lock holds, and an overall collapse in throughput even though CPU may appear only moderately loaded.

Causally, heavy lock contention prolongs transaction lifetimes, which in turn extends the window during which each transaction issues reads, dirty-page writes, and mandatory log flushes—pushing the storage subsystem toward saturation. Conversely, storage saturation slows every page fetch, undo read, and commit flush, keeping locks held far longer than normal and creating longer blocking chains and more opportunities for deadlocks. The two resource bottlenecks therefore form a positive feedback loop: slow I/O extends lock duration, extended locks increase concurrency pressure and I/O volume, and the compound effect degrades the database far more severely than either anomaly in isolation.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical data model lacks the indexes, partitions, or correct data types required by the workload, forcing otherwise well-written statements into wide scans and row-by-row lookups.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or tables and are blocked or dead-locked while the lock manager resolves the conflict.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: The transport path between clients and the database is saturated or connection slots are exhausted, slowing or aborting session establishment and data transfer.

When these three root causes strike at once, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set: full-table or non-covering index scans take longer and touch more rows, magnifying the number and duration of row and page locks they hold. Those prolonged locks create deeper blocker-waiter chains and more frequent deadlocks, which in turn keep backend sessions open and idle while they wait on locks or perform rollbacks. The inflated session count pushes the listener or process pool toward its limit; new client connections stall in handshake or are refused, and existing sessions pile up in client-read/client-write waits as network queues back up. Application layers experience a mix of slow query responses, lock-timeout or deadlock errors, and connection-establishment failures that are hard to attribute to a single layer because they surface concurrently.

Causally, the missing or mis-shaped indexes expand the lock footprint and execution time of each statement, directly increasing the probability of lock contention. Blocked transactions then occupy server processes and hold TCP sockets open longer, consuming connection slots and filling the listener backlog. As the connection pool reaches its ceiling and network latency grows, clients retry and open additional sessions, further pressuring the listener and leaving even more idle sessions that still retain locks. This feedback loop amplifies both lock contention and network exhaustion, degrading throughput and making recovery difficult until all three design, concurrency, and connectivity issues are addressed together.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements or transaction boundaries are written in a way that forces the engine to process more data or hold resources longer than the business logic actually requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer relies on stale, incomplete, or misleading statistics, causing systematic misestimation of cardinalities and selection of sub-optimal execution plans.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-level quotas on file handles, shared memory, threads, or similar objects are exhausted, preventing the database from allocating the OS resources it needs.

When these three root causes occur together, the database exhibits amplified performance degradation and intermittent failures:  • Queries already bloated by poor workload design are further misplanned because of bad statistics, resulting in massive full scans, spill-to-disk sorts, and runaway parallelism.  • The excessive I/O, memory, and worker-thread demand drives the process toward OS-enforced ceilings; once limits are hit, new sessions, parallel workers, or I/O contexts fail to start, causing sudden spikes of errors, timeouts, and transaction rollbacks.  • Monitoring shows chronic long-tail latency, repeated slow-query entries, wide gaps between estimated and actual rows, frequent plan recompiles, and concurrent kernel messages about resource-allocation failures.  • Symptoms can be mistaken for pure workload, optimizer, or system issues in isolation, obscuring the intertwined nature of the problem.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL logic inflates data volume and resource consumption, magnifying the impact of any cardinality misestimates produced by stale or inadequate statistics. The misestimates lead the optimizer to pick plans that consume even more CPU, memory, and I/O than the inflated workload already demands. This burst of resource pressure accelerates exhaustion of kernel-level quotas; once OS limits are reached, the database can no longer grow its worker or I/O pools, which in turn feeds back into longer queue times and more application retries, keeping transactions open even longer and compounding the statistics staleness. Thus each root cause reinforces the others, creating a self-amplifying loop that degrades performance and availability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index tuples accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and slowing visibility checks.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures become physically or logically corrupt, so index/heap mappings and page links no longer match the true data contents.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport and connection layer cannot supply or sustain enough sockets, bandwidth, or handshake capacity, leading to refused or stalled connections and prolonged client/server waits.

When these three root causes strike at once, symptoms mingle and reinforce each other:  • Sequential scans grow dramatically because corruption forces the optimizer to abandon damaged indexes while MVCC bloat expands table size; the vastly larger result sets sit in network send buffers, holding back-end processes in client-write waits.  • Clients observe alternating query-timeout, corruption, and connection-exceeded errors; retries amplify connection churn so listener backlogs and OS socket queues fill, producing cascades of "too many connections" or half-open sockets.  • Engine logs show a mixture of vacuum/autovacuum lag warnings, corruption or checksum errors, and spikes in aborted or reset connections; snapshot horizons advance slowly because long-running or stalled sessions (waiting on network I/O) pin old row versions, further hindering cleanup.  • Integrity-check and vacuum operations both demand heavy I/O on already swollen heaps, increasing latency that the constrained network path exposes directly to users.

Causal chain: network slow-downs prolong transaction lifetimes, keeping snapshots open that block version reclamation and accelerate MVCC bloat. The enlarged version store magnifies the I/O footprint of any integrity-verification or recovery pass, making it more likely that those passes hit damaged pages and raise further corruption flags. Corruption in turn forces plan changes to full scans and larger result sets, which must traverse the already congested network and occupy scarce connection slots even longer. Aborted or retried rebuilds caused by network disconnects can leave indexes half-written, worsening structural corruption. Thus each anomaly feeds the next—network stalls preserve snapshots, snapshots prevent cleanup, the bloated and possibly corrupt data set increases network load—forming a reinforcing loop that degrades OLTP performance and stability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The static physical data model and index layout do not fit workload access patterns, forcing queries into sub-optimal, scan-heavy plans and inflating maintenance work on every modification.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages and latches, producing buffer-busy waits, spin-loop CPU burn, and checkpoint-related stalls even though total memory may be sufficient.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, so page checksums fail, index keys are out of order, and the optimizer reluctantly falls back to full scans or throws corruption errors.

When all three conditions co-exist, the database shows a compound failure signature: queries that already favor full-table or non-covering index scans (because of poor schema and index design) pour traffic onto a small set of hot pages, amplifying latch and buffer-pin waits. The same pages may intermittently raise checksum or key-order errors, causing query retries, plan fallbacks to even broader scans, and emergency page repairs. Observable symptoms include oscillating CPU spikes from latch spin followed by I/O bursts from corruption-triggered page rereads, sudden drops in plan stability, mismatch between index and heap row counts, and erratic latency that improves only after both index redesign and corruption repair.

Causally, inefficient schema design drives high page churn and repeated access to specific root or leaf pages, which intensifies buffer contention. Prolonged contention keeps pages locked or dirty longer, stretching checkpoint windows and increasing the chance that an unexpected shutdown or storage glitch leaves those frequently written pages in an inconsistent state—thus seeding or aggravating block and index corruption. In turn, corruption forces the optimizer to abandon damaged indexes, magnifying the original design flaw by routing even more traffic through full scans, which further heats the buffer cache and latches. The feedback loop among design mismatch, hot-page contention, and structural corruption rapidly degrades throughput and threatens data integrity unless all three layers are addressed together.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Exhaustion of physical or logical free space for data, logs, or temporary areas, causing allocation failures and write stalls.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Saturation of host CPU cycles by database processes, driving high run-queue waits and global latency.

Composite phenomena: When space is running out while CPUs are already saturated, the database may exhibit a cascade of symptoms—DML, index builds, and temp-space operations first slow because the scheduler is starved, then fail outright with "no space" or "cannot extend" errors. Log writer, checkpoint, and archive processes contend for CPU at the same moment they are blocked on space, inflating commit latency and replica lag. Auto-extend attempts or space-reclaim jobs invoke additional background workers, spiking CPU even higher. From the client side the system appears intermittently hung, with query response times oscillating between CPU wait events and space-allocation errors, making the primary bottleneck hard to isolate.

Causal chain and interaction: Space exhaustion forces the database to perform emergency tasks—auto-extension, space-reclamation, aggressive checkpointing, or archival moves—that themselves consume CPU. Conversely, heavy CPU saturation can delay or starve regular purge, compression, or backup jobs that would normally free space, allowing unused segments and logs to accumulate until the capacity threshold is hit. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other: lack of CPU prevents space cleanup, while lack of space spawns more CPU-intensive exception handling, ultimately degrading throughput and raising the probability of a full outage.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Persisted data- or index-page contents, linkages, or checksums are damaged so that on-disk structures no longer faithfully represent the logical rows and keys.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database, log, temporary, or backup storage reaches hard capacity limits, preventing further allocation or auto-extension operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Listener, socket, or network-path resources are exhausted or unstable, limiting the rate at which clients can establish sessions or transfer result sets.

When the three root causes act at the same time, symptoms overlap and reinforce each other: 1) corrupted indexes force query plans to abandon selective access paths and fall back to heap scans or full index rebuild attempts; 2) those heavier scans and emergency rebuilds explode data-file growth, temporary-segment usage, and redo/undo volume, rapidly consuming the remaining storage headroom; 3) as space depletion triggers allocation failures, affected statements hang in space-wait states, and log archival or checkpoint progress stalls, cascading more sessions into backlog; 4) the increasing execution latency, coupled with connection-slot exhaustion and retransmissions caused by the network anomaly, produces a spike of connection timeouts, half-open sockets, and client retries; 5) monitoring shows an apparently erratic mixture of corruption errors, out-of-space errors, and connection refusals that are difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, page or index corruption can initiate large-scale table scans, online repairs, or forced rebuilds that accelerate space consumption. The resulting space scarcity, in turn, amplifies the corruption impact because failed allocations abort in-place rebuilds and leave structures only partially repaired, deepening logical inconsistency. Both the corruption-induced long-running operations and the space-related stalls hold server back-end processes longer, inflating concurrent session counts. The saturated connection layer then drops or throttles new sessions, causing clients to retry and pile additional load on an already resource-starved and logically inconsistent engine. Each anomaly thus feeds the others: corruption drives space growth, space limits stall recovery and normal processing, and network saturation hides or delays error feedback while multiplying connection pressure, jointly degrading availability and increasing the risk of further corruption through incomplete I/O or abort sequences.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction design force the engine to scan, join, or hold more data than the business case actually requires.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or change-data consumers fall behind because they cannot receive, persist, or apply log records at the rate the primary generates them.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, leaving insufficient compute cycles for the rest of the workload.

When these three root causes manifest together, the primary node executes inefficient queries that drive high CPU usage while simultaneously emitting an oversized, bursty stream of redo that replicas struggle to consume. Observable symptoms converge across layers: 1) primary-side CPU consistently runs near 100 %, with run-queue wait events dominating wait-class views; 2) statement and transaction latency on the primary shows long tails, accompanied by frequent slow-query log entries for the same application patterns; 3) replication monitoring reports widening receive, write, and replay lag, growing retained log segments, and increasingly stale read-only traffic; 4) failover readiness degrades as replicas fall further behind, and 5) both primary and replica hosts exhibit load-average spikes, context-switch storms, and apply-side lock conflicts, making it difficult to distinguish whether performance pain originates at the application, engine, or replication tier.

Causal chain: inefficient workload logic inflates row counts, intermediate result sets, and transaction size, which directly amplifies CPU consumption on the primary. The elevated CPU load lengthens commit paths and enlarges each transaction’s redo payload. The replication subsystem must now ship and apply a hotter, heavier log stream, but the replicas are already CPU-constrained from replaying previous backlog; as lag grows, their own apply threads run more intensely, further saturating their CPUs and slowing them down even more. High CPU on both sides increases scheduling latency for network and I/O threads, worsening throughput and inducing exponential replica delay. In turn, the primary cannot recycle log segments because replicas hold retention pointers, inflating disk usage and causing additional I/O and CPU overhead for checkpoint and log-management tasks. The three anomalies thus reinforce one another in a feedback loop that degrades overall database performance and resiliency.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer repeatedly chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite accurate statistics, yielding excessive logical work, wrong join methods, or missing index usage.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging path—generation, buffering, flushing, or archiving—becomes the primary bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling writers even though general storage I/O may appear adequate.

When both root causes manifest concurrently, statements may oscillate between poor plans that create unusually large modification workloads and a log layer unable to absorb the resulting redo volume. Symptoms include: 1) sharp, unpredictable spikes in transaction latency where CPU time, logical I/O, and log-flush waits all surge in the same timeframe; 2) frequent plan changes from efficient index probes to wide table or hash scans that multiply row touches and redo generation, exhausting log buffer space; 3) bursts of log-related wait events (LOG_FLUSH, LOG_WRITE, commit waits) coinciding with dramatic increases in physical I/O and buffer churn driven by the bad plans; 4) checkpoint storms, rapid log-file switches, and archiver backlog triggered immediately after plan regressions; 5) erratic throughput where some executions sail through on good plans while others stall behind saturated log flushes, complicating performance diagnosis.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan that amplifies row updates or causes large sort/insert loops escalates redo generation, directly stressing an already constrained log subsystem. The swollen write volume fills the log buffer faster than it can be flushed or archived, extending commit latency and forcing user sessions to wait. The prolonged transaction durations increase row and log contention, which in turn can influence the optimizer’s adaptive decisions, fostering further plan instability—a feedback loop that compounds both anomalies. Conversely, elevated commit latency from log saturation can delay statistics updates and cause plan cache invalidations, provoking additional plan recompilations and increasing the likelihood of selecting poor plans. The intertwined effects magnify resource contention, leading to severe and erratic slowdowns in high-write OLTP workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously experiencing severe lock-manager contention that blocks or deadlocks foreground transactions and a replication pipeline that is unable to receive, persist, or apply write-ahead log records at the pace they are produced.

Combined phenomena: On the primary, lock-wait queues, growing deadlock reports, rising transaction latency, and connection-pool back-pressure are observed at the same time that monitoring shows widening log-position gaps, increasing apply lag, and expanding retained WAL or relay logs on replicas. Users may see time-outs and retry storms, while read replicas deliver ever-staler data and lose fail-over currency. Disk consumption for unrecycled logs escalates, CPU on replicas spikes as single-threaded apply workers fall behind, and replica error logs may contain lock-conflict messages when replay encounters the same hot rows currently contended on the primary.

Causal interaction: Prolonged or blocked transactions keep exclusive locks and their corresponding commit LSNs open, preventing log recycling and enlarging the volume of WAL that must be shipped downstream. When the locks finally release, large bursts of accumulated WAL can saturate network or I/O on replicas, deepening lag. Conversely, if synchronous or semi-synchronous replication is in use, a slowed or stalled replica lengthens commit acknowledgment times on the primary, forcing locks to be held even longer and intensifying contention. Apply-side lock conflicts on the replica can further delay replay and feed back into the commit path if the primary waits for replica confirmation, creating a mutually reinforcing loop that rapidly degrades both transactional throughput and replication freshness.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model and indexing strategy do not match workload access patterns, forcing queries into sub-optimal, page-hungry access paths.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates or leaks more memory than the host can safely provide, causing OS pressure, paging, and cache eviction.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages and internal latches, stalling while waiting for page pins, I/O slots, or flush slots.

When all three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a blended failure signature: massive full-table/partial-index scans and large in-memory sorts inflate per-session work areas; the swollen memory footprint forces the OS to reclaim pages, shrinking the effective buffer cache just as demand for it peaks. Shrink-and-churn drives dirty-page flushing and buffer replacement, which in turn amplifies latch waits on hot root and data pages. Users observe steep and erratic query latencies, periodic freezes during swap storms, CPU cores lost to latch spinning, and dramatic throughput collapse that rebounds only after both design and memory settings are corrected.

Causal chain: poor schema and index design expands the volume of pages each query must touch, driving up both buffer-cache residency and per-query work memory. This heightened memory appetite accelerates exhaustion of the global memory budget, triggering OS paging and aggressive buffer evictions. Frequent eviction means the same small set of hot pages is repeatedly read, dirtied, and flushed, intensifying latch and buffer-busy contention. In parallel, memory pressure slows background flushers, lengthening the time pages stay dirty and prolonging latch hold duration, which further blocks already inefficient queries. The three root causes therefore reinforce one another in a vicious cycle: design inefficiency → memory overuse → cache churn → latch contention → more concurrency and memory usage, ultimately destabilizing both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive growth of buffer caches, work areas, or other engine heaps drives the host into sustained memory pressure.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Stand-by or downstream replicas cannot receive or apply the primary’s transaction log fast enough, causing widening replication lag.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume most or all available CPU cycles, saturating the host scheduler.

When all three root causes occur together the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: memory pressure triggers paging and stalls, while CPU saturation lengthens every critical path—foreground queries, background check-pointers, and replica receiver / applier threads alike. Replica apply lag widens rapidly, retaining ever-larger log segments on the primary; these segments increase both disk and in-memory metadata footprints, aggravating the already tight memory envelope. Operators may observe "run-queue" and "memory-pressure" wait events simultaneously, soaring context-switch rates, growing WAL/redo queues, expanding plan and buffer eviction churn, and replicas drifting so far behind that read scalability and fail-over readiness collapse.

Causal chain: (1) Heavy workload or run-away operations inflate per-session work areas and caches, pushing the engine beyond safe RAM limits and causing OS paging; (2) paging and cache churn escalate CPU demand as the engine repeatedly faults and re-loads pages; (3) with CPU now saturated, replication receiver and applier threads are de-scheduled more frequently and replay throughput drops; (4) falling replay throughput forces the primary to retain more log segments and in-memory replication state, further swelling memory usage and intensifying pressure; (5) this positive feedback loop amplifies latency across the whole workload and risks OOM kills, primary node eviction, or replica divergence. The mutual reinforcement of memory exhaustion, CPU starvation, and replication backlog makes the composite anomaly harder to diagnose than any single component defect.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures (tables, partitions, indexes, constraints, data types) are mis-aligned with workload access patterns, forcing the optimizer to consider inherently inefficient access paths even when good statistics are available.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale or incomplete, leading the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal plans even when adequate physical structures exist.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from poor physical schema/index design and inaccurate optimizer statistics, so both the set of access paths considered and the cost estimates for those paths are systematically wrong. The optimizer is therefore trapped between a limited set of inefficient structures and misleading metadata about those structures, resulting in chronically bad execution plans.

Combined anomalous phenomena:  • Queries show extreme and unstable latency, with some executions scanning huge volumes of data while others spill to disk due to underestimated memory needs.  • Execution plans contain full table scans, unselective index range scans, repeated key lookups, or partition elimination failures, and the estimated versus actual row counts differ by several orders of magnitude.  • Plan performance oscillates after data loads or index rebuilds but never stabilizes, and automatic statistics refreshes or index hints give only temporary relief.  • DML operations experience high blocking and log growth because oversized or redundant indexes are maintained unnecessarily, yet the optimizer still ignores them due to bad statistics.  • Monitoring tools show both high physical I/O from design issues and excessive re-compilations or plan cache churn from statistics issues, making the root cause appear ambiguous.

Causal chain: The absence of well-targeted or covering indexes forces the optimizer to rely on broad scans; stale statistics then exaggerate or underplay the cost of those scans, causing it to pick even worse plans such as nested loops against massive row sets or hash joins spilling to temp space. Conversely, redundant or poorly chosen indexes inflate maintenance cost, but because statistics on them are outdated, the optimizer cannot recognize when they would actually be beneficial, leaving them unused yet still expensive to maintain. Stale global statistics on mis-partitioned tables hide hot partitions that suffer from skew, amplifying latch contention and I/O hotspots already introduced by the flawed schema design. Thus, each anomaly masks and reinforces the other, degrading both read and write performance across OLTP and OLAP workloads while complicating diagnosis.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive growth of buffer caches, work areas, or background heaps drives the database process beyond the safe physical-memory envelope of the host.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: The replication pipeline cannot receive, persist, or apply transaction-log records at the pace the primary produces them, causing widening log-position gaps and retained log segments.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database or its auxiliary processes exhaust kernel-enforced quotas such as file handles, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or thread counts, leading to allocation denials and partial outages.

When all three root causes surface together, the system exhibits an interwoven symptom set: sustained host memory pressure and paging; abrupt failures to spawn new sessions, background, or replication apply workers due to kernel quota exhaustion; accelerating replication lag accompanied by ballooning retained WAL/relay logs; growing resident-set sizes on both primary and replicas; intermittent "cannot allocate shared memory/file descriptor" errors in engine and system logs; and, in clustered deployments, heightened risk of node eviction or unviable failover targets because replicas fall ever further behind.

Causal interaction: Runaway in-memory structures on the primary inflate its RSS, pushing the process toward kernel limits (e.g., shmmax, memlock, thread count). Allocation denials stall or kill parallel and replication sender processes, immediately throttling the log-shipping rate. The resulting backlog forces the primary to retain additional log segments, which in turn grow memory and file-descriptor usage, amplifying both the memory bloat and OS-limit pressure. On replicas, the same retention enlarges apply queues; added work must be handled by workers that may already be starved for shared memory or threads, deepening lag. The feedback loop—memory over-consumption → OS limit breaches → replication slowdown → further memory and handle accumulation—quickly degrades overall throughput and jeopardizes data-protection objectives.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, resulting in excessive CPU, I/O, and elapsed time per statement.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or downstream replicas cannot receive and/or apply WAL / redo at the rate the primary generates it, creating ever-growing replication lag.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from inefficient query plans on the primary and an overloaded replication pipeline. The primary produces an abnormally large volume of work per transaction, while the replicas are already behind and unable to keep pace, so both latency-sensitive query processing and replication consistency degrade in tandem.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Sudden plan changes or plan instability on the primary coincide with steep spikes in WAL generation, I/O, and CPU utilisation. 2) Replication monitoring shows log-position gaps widening much faster than normal, relay / retained log files accumulating, and replica read-only sessions returning increasingly stale data. 3) Failover RPO/RTO metrics deteriorate, yet the primary’s plan cache, CPU run queues, and I/O queues are also saturated, making it difficult to attribute slowdown solely to either optimisation or replication. 4) Lock contention and long-running transactions caused by bad plans further delay log recycling, amplifying disk pressure on both primary and replicas.

Causal chain and interaction: A poor plan (e.g., full table scan instead of index probe or a nested-loop with underestimated outer cardinality) inflates row touches, generates more undo/redo, extends transaction duration, and locks data longer. This escalates WAL volume and commit latency, pushing more data into the replication stream just as each transaction finishes. The replication subsystem, already limited by network, disk, or single-threaded apply, falls further behind, causing additional log retention on the primary. Retained logs consume disk and may trigger aggressive checkpointing or Autovacuum/auto-purge activity that invalidates plans, leading to even more plan recompilations and potential selection of yet another sub-optimal plan. Thus, each anomaly feeds the other: bad plans bloat the workload the replicas must process, while replication lag prolongs log retention and resource pressure on the primary, increasing the likelihood of plan cache eviction and unstable plan selection. The feedback loop magnifies overall throughput loss, latency spikes, and disaster-recovery risk.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model elements (table structure, indexes, partitioning, data types) are not aligned with workload access patterns, forcing otherwise correct SQL to scan or probe data inefficiently.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.

When both root causes coexist, the database experiences a mix of I/O-heavy access paths and intense lock manager pressure. Full-table or broad range scans caused by missing or non-covering indexes hold larger lock footprints and keep locks for longer durations, inflating wait queues. Escalated page- or table-level locks acquired during the scans block OLTP writers and downstream readers, while repeated deadlocks trigger rollbacks and application retries.
