Observed symptoms therefore include: 1) soaring lock-wait and deadlock counts, 2) sudden spikes in buffer pool churn and disk I/O, 3) execution plans dominated by full scans despite selective predicates, 4) erratic transaction latencies in connection pools, and 5) throughput collapse that recovers only after both indexing fixes and blocking relief.

Causal chain: poor schema/index design forces wide scans that touch many rows or partitions, expanding the set of locked resources. The longer scan duration and larger lock scope magnify the probability of collisions with update or delete statements common in OLTP workloads. In turn, the resulting blocking delays prolong transaction lifetimes, increasing the window during which additional queries rely on suboptimal plans and further compound contention. Automatic lock escalation from row to page or table can be triggered by the excessive scan footprint, reinforcing the blockage cycle. Thus, each anomaly amplifies the other—structural inefficiency spawns lock contention, while prolonged contention hides the root schema weakness and encourages more concurrent retries—driving the database into a self-reinforcing performance spiral.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of database memory regions (buffer caches, work areas, plan cache, etc.) pushes the host beyond its safe physical- or virtual-memory envelope.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot buffer pages and their protecting latches become serialization points, forcing sessions to wait, spin, or stall while competing for page access rather than for higher-level locks.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database engine or its worker processes exhaust kernel-enforced limits such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or thread quotas, preventing new allocations or spawns.

When all three root causes arise concurrently, the system exhibits a blended failure pattern: 1) memory-pressure symptoms such as paging, rising RSS, or OOM kills; 2) escalating buffer-busy and latch wait events accompanied by CPU spin and latency spikes; and 3) intermittent "cannot allocate resource" errors, failed connection attempts, or stalled background workers as kernel limits are hit. Swapping amplifies latch hold times, making contention metrics surge, while blocked or crashed auxiliary processes (e.g., check-pointers, log writers, or parallel workers) further starve the buffer pool and inflate both wait and memory footprints. The overall effect is sharp throughput collapse, erratic response times, and partial outages that can be difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain: unbounded memory allocation enlarges the buffer cache and per-session work areas, increasing the absolute number of dirty pages and active latches; longer flush cycles and greater page churn intensify latch contention. The prolonged waits keep transactions open and memory pinned, which in turn accelerates memory consumption. As memory pressure mounts, the kernel begins paging and elevates the likelihood of hitting process limits for address space, file handles, or worker threads. Once OS limits are breached, essential database helpers fail to start or crash, reducing the system’s ability to recycle or flush buffers and releasing latches even more slowly. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another in a positive feedback loop—memory bloat fuels contention, contention prolongs memory residency, and both drive the engine into kernel resource exhaustion—culminating in severe, workload-agnostic instability.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database system simultaneously suffers from delayed or stalled replication apply pipelines (Replication Synchronization Anomaly) while also hitting host-level kernel or container resource ceilings that prevent the database processes from obtaining additional file descriptors, shared-memory segments, threads, or other kernel objects (Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly).

Combined anomalous phenomena: Replica lag metrics rise sharply and remain stuck; relay logs, retained WAL/redo segments, or primary-side pg_wal/* archives accumulate faster than they can be recycled.  At the same time, error logs show "could not open file", "too many open files", "failed to allocate shared memory", or "cannot fork thread" messages.  New replication workers, logical decoding slots, or parallel apply processes fail to start, and primary sessions that try to commit large transactions may block waiting for replication-confirmation feedback that never arrives.  Existing sessions continue to run but VACUUM, CHECKPOINT, or background writer processes intermittently abort, making disk usage and replica delay grow in lockstep.  Monitoring may show CPU and I/O under-utilized even though throughput collapses, because the bottleneck is hidden in the kernel limit layer.

Causal chain and interaction: Replication lag forces the engine to keep more WAL segments open, more file descriptors in use, and more background apply workers alive on both the primary and replicas.  This surge in kernel-object demand pushes the database up against fixed per-process or cgroup limits; once those limits are reached, new apply workers or WAL sender processes cannot be spawned, causing replication to fall even further behind.  Conversely, the resource-limit anomaly can independently block the creation of parallel replay or logical decoding workers, immediately throttling the replica’s ability to catch up.  Each condition therefore amplifies the other: replication delay increases kernel object pressure, while kernel denials exacerbate replication delay, eventually leading to a feedback loop that endangers failover readiness, increases primary disk consumption, and risks service outage if the primary runs out of space or the replicas time out.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are sound, leading to excessive or misplaced resource demand.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying disk subsystem is saturated, introducing high read/write latency and stretched I/O queues regardless of how the engine issues requests.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPUs run near saturation because database processes consume most cycles, leaving little headroom for additional work.

Combined anomalous phenomena: The workload exhibits erratic performance spikes in which some executions of the same SQL text swing between moderate and extreme latency. Execution plans that should have been light are chosen yet become painfully slow because they issue a flood of physical reads to an already throttled storage layer; other plans that switch to full scans or excessive parallelism try to mask the I/O stall but instead drive CPU utilization to 100 %, filling OS run queues and producing both I/O and CPU wait events in diagnostic views. Batch windows expand unpredictably, log flushes stall, and end-user response times degrade across the board, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single tier.

Causal interaction: A sub-optimal plan may demand far more random I/O than necessary, quickly pushing the storage subsystem past its throughput ceiling and lengthening every subsequent I/O. The rising latency extends statement execution time, so worker threads remain active longer and aggregate CPU consumption climbs. Conversely, once CPUs are saturated—especially by plans that rely on excessive parallelism—the engine issues I/O requests in larger bursts and with deeper queues, further congesting storage paths. The two resource-level bottlenecks therefore reinforce each other: poor plans inflate demand, storage saturation inflates latency, longer execution keeps cores busy, and limited CPU makes the optimizer less able to recompile or adapt, locking the system into a vicious cycle that amplifies both anomalies and degrades overall database stability.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or unbounded allocation of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, temporary structures, and background heaps drives the database process beyond the host’s safe memory envelope.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space for data files, logs, temporary areas, backups, or diagnostics is exhausted, preventing further allocations, extensions, or writes.

When these two root causes occur together, the system experiences simultaneous memory pressure and space exhaustion. Observable effects include: rapid growth of process RSS alongside increasing swap activity; sorts, hashes, and parallel operations that first overrun work memory then attempt to spill to temp areas that are already near full; checkpoints and log flushes that stall because archive or data spaces cannot accept more blocks, leaving dirty buffers pinned in memory; cascading "out of memory" and "no space left" errors, session terminations, and node eviction events; and monitoring dashboards that oscillate between memory and storage alerts, obscuring the primary trigger.

Causally, each anomaly reinforces the other. Runaway in-memory structures and high concurrency inflate RAM demand; once memory thresholds are crossed, the engine spills intermediate data to disk, rapidly consuming remaining temp or datafile space. Conversely, as free space diminishes, writers are throttled and checkpoints back up, forcing more dirty pages to linger in buffer cache and expanding memory usage. Archive-log saturation blocks log reuse, further prolonging cache retention and increasing memory footprints. This feedback loop accelerates exhaustion of both resources, narrows the recovery window, and heightens the risk of sudden, hard-to-diagnose outages.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, absent, or insufficient optimizer statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimation that misguides the cost-based optimizer.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or supporting filesystems run out of allocatable free space, leading to allocation failures for data, logs, or temporary work areas.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced quotas on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or related objects are exhausted, preventing the database from obtaining required OS resources.

When all three root causes coexist, symptoms overlap and amplify: execution plans already mis-estimated by stale statistics choose hash joins, large sorts, or spill-to-temp operations that inflate temporary segments and redo volume, accelerating space consumption. As free space dwindles, auto-extension or archive-log operations fail, producing "cannot allocate extent", "out of space", or "archiving paused" messages alongside severe performance drops. Concurrently, the engine attempts more re-compilations and worker spawns to find alternative plans or perform emergency space management, but hits kernel limits on file descriptors, shared memory, or threads. The cluster therefore exhibits erratic slowdowns, frequent plan invalidations, aborted DML, failed new connections, and a mixture of database-level and OS-level errors that are hard to disentangle.

Causal chain: Stale statistics first generate bloated or spill-heavy plans that create excess temporary I/O and log output, rapidly consuming free space. Imminent space exhaustion forces the engine into frequent file opens, auto-extend attempts, and log switches, multiplying the demand for file handles and other kernel objects. Simultaneously, failed space allocations block normal maintenance tasks such as statistics refresh jobs, further prolonging statistics staleness and reinforcing poor plan choices. As space and temp usage surge, each additional session or background process needed for recovery or parallelism contends for shrinking OS quotas, eventually breaching per-process or cgroup limits. The three anomalies thus form a feedback loop: bad statistics → space pressure → OS resource pressure → inability to gather new statistics or free space, culminating in widespread contention, partial outages, and unpredictable query behavior.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, data types, constraints) and workload access patterns, forcing sub-optimal access paths and excessive I/O. 
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Overcommitment or fragmentation of engine memory (buffer caches, work areas, plan cache, session heaps) that pushes the host into pressure, paging, or OOM scenarios. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or saturated network and connection-handling resources that delay or abort session establishment and data transfer between clients and the database. 

When all three root causes are present, the workload experiences a multi-layered degradation: poorly indexed queries trigger large full-table scans and non-covering index probes that flood buffer caches and inflate per-query sort/hash areas, accelerating memory growth and eviction churn. Memory pressure induces paging and stalls, elongating query response times and holding backend processes in client-read/client-write waits. As these sluggish backends occupy connection slots longer and transmit voluminous result sets slowly, listener queues and TCP socket buffers saturate, amplifying packet retransmissions and connection timeouts. From the application side this manifests as intermittent connection failures, sharp latency spikes, and erratic throughput even under moderate load, while the database side shows concurrent surges in physical reads, memory allocation failures, and network I/O wait events that are hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, sub-optimal schema and index design is the first domino: it inflates data touched per query, driving up buffer and work-area demand. The swollen memory footprint competes for limited physical RAM; once the engine begins paging or trimming caches, each repeat execution re-reads data, multiplying I/O and CPU work. Prolonged execution times keep sessions open, increasing the simultaneous connection count and the volume of data that must be shipped over the network. The congested network, in turn, slows result delivery, forcing server backends to linger in send/receive waits and retain their private memory longer, further aggravating memory exhaustion. This feedback loop—inefficient access paths → memory pressure → slower execution → extended connections → network saturation → additional memory retention—creates a self-reinforcing cycle that can culminate in system-wide slowdown, connection storms, or even node eviction.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions contend for mutually incompatible locks, forming blocking chains or deadlocks that stall statement progress until waits time out or a victim is aborted.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine and its sessions collectively allocate more memory than the host can safely supply, provoking paging, OOM kills, or cache-churn stalls.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network paths, listener slots, sockets, or authentication workers become saturated, delaying connection establishment and slowing result transfer between clients and the server.

When all three root causes strike at once, symptoms overlap and amplify: lock-wait time rises while overall query latency balloons; back-end processes linger in a blocked or idle-in-transaction state, yet their resident sets keep growing under memory pressure; swapping exacerbates CPU stalls and prolongs critical sections, so locks are held even longer. Clients experience intermittent connection refusals, SSL handshake timeouts, or slow result streaming, which in turn keeps transactions open on the server side, deepening lock queues and consuming more memory for retained result buffers and session state. Monitoring dashboards show simultaneous spikes in lock-wait events, OS page-in/out rates, backend counts near the max-connections limit, rising retransmission and round-trip times, and a steep drop in completed TPS.

Causally, any one factor can trigger the others: network slowness stretches query duration, so locks remain held longer and more worker memory stays allocated; swelling lock queues force new sessions to wait, increasing the number of connected backends and their aggregate memory footprint; global memory pressure induces CPU stalls and garbage collection that further slow protocol I/O, aggravating network backlog. The positive feedback loop—slower I/O → longer lock hold → more memory retained → heavier paging → even slower I/O—can rapidly push the system into cascading timeouts, deadlock retries, or ultimately node eviction, making the composite anomaly more severe than the sum of its parts.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition:
The database is simultaneously suffering from MVCC version-store bloat, exhaustion of kernel-level resource limits, and saturation of network/connection handling capacity. Together these three root causes form a feedback loop in which the engine must manage an ever-growing number of row versions and background maintenance tasks while the host operating system can no longer provide sufficient file handles, shared-memory, or threads, and client endpoints experience connection backlogs, retransmissions, and authentication stalls.

Combined Observable Phenomena:
• Rapid growth of table and index size, high dead-to-live row ratios, and autovacuum or cleanup workers reported as permanently behind schedule.
• Intermittent "too many open files", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "could not create thread" errors in database logs, often coinciding with peaks in autovacuum or check-point activity.
• Rising counts of refused or timed-out client connections, half-open sockets in the OS WAIT/LISTEN queues, and sessions blocked on client-read/client-write waits even though the database itself is lightly loaded on CPU.
• Sudden drops in parallel-worker availability, inability to start new background workers, and cascading plan misestimates because bloated tables inflate statistics yet maintenance cannot catch up.
• End-user perception of a worsening but uneven slowdown: queries that complete run progressively slower, while new sessions sporadically fail to establish or hang during authentication.

Causal Chain and Interaction:
1. Heavy OLTP update/delete churn creates large numbers of obsolete row versions. Cleanup workers try to reclaim them, but the additional tables and indexes they must touch inflate the number of open file descriptors and worker threads required.
2. The surge in background activity pushes the database process toward kernel limits on files, shared memory segments, and threads; once reached, new maintenance workers fail to spawn and version cleanup falls even further behind, accelerating heap bloat.
3. Bloated tables lengthen query execution and result-set transfer times. Sessions stay open longer, increasing the total number of concurrent sockets and backend processes, which in turn consume even more kernel resources (FDs, stack, address space) and move the system deeper into limit exhaustion.
4. Extended session lifetimes keep old snapshots alive, preventing MVCC garbage collection and directly reinforcing the version-maintenance problem.
5. As OS limits tighten, the listener cannot accept new sockets fast enough; SYN backlog overflows and packet retransmissions appear. Connection retries from the application layer create burst traffic that further stretches both network queues and process/thread quotas, producing visible outages even though the engine has CPU and memory headroom.
6. The three issues therefore reinforce one another: version bloat triggers more workers and file usage; OS limit exhaustion blocks those workers and new sessions; blocked or slow connections keep transactions open, freezing the undo horizon and compounding version bloat—leading to a spiraling degradation of throughput and availability.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data objects, forcing wait queues or deadlocks inside the lock manager and stalling execution paths.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, flush, file switch, or archiving—becomes a throughput or latency bottleneck, slowing commits and blocking further redo generation.

When both root causes surface together, the database exhibits a compound slowdown: lock-wait and deadlock reports appear at the same time that commit and log-flush latencies climb. Transactions remain idle while waiting for locks, yet even after becoming unblocked they may pause again on log-related waits before completing, stretching overall response times. Application threads pile up in connection pools, autovacuum or purge processes fall behind, deadlock frequency rises because long-held locks increase cycle probability, and checkpoint or archive storms coincide with surges of lock timeouts and retry storms. The overlapping symptoms can obscure diagnosis because every blocked session shows both lock and log wait states in alternating patterns.

Causally, a slow log subsystem prolongs the commit phase of each transaction, extending the lifetime of every lock it holds. The longer locks stay active, the higher the chance that other sessions collide on the same resources, amplifying lock contention. In the opposite direction, severe lock queues delay transactions, causing sudden bursts of commits once the queue frees; these commit spikes push more redo to the already saturated log devices, worsening log flush congestion. The two feedback loops reinforce each other, driving a self-sustaining performance collapse unless both the lock hot spots and the log throughput constraint are addressed together.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data files, logs, or temp areas is exhausted, blocking further allocations and persistence operations.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database and host processes saturate available CPU cores, driving run-queue growth and broadly inflating statement latency.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network bandwidth, latency, packet loss, or server-side connection slots become limiting, producing connection failures, socket backlogs, and slow client I/O.

When all three conditions arise concurrently, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: connection attempts time out or are refused; active sessions that do connect experience erratic response times as both CPU run-queues and network socket queues lengthen; DML statements and bulk loads stall on "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors; commits hang waiting for log flushes that themselves are delayed by full archive destinations; background processes repeatedly retry space-management and network send operations, further consuming CPU; monitoring agents may also fail to report due to network saturation, obscuring real-time visibility.

Causally, each root cause amplifies the others. Space exhaustion triggers aggressive checkpointing, log switching, and catalog cleanup cycles that spike CPU consumption; the resulting CPU saturation slows those very housekeeping tasks, prolonging space shortages. Full data or archive destinations force the database to wait on external copy or purge jobs, which, if they traverse congested networks, are delayed, extending log file occupancy and stalling write activity. Simultaneously, network congestion and connection storms increase process counts and context switches, intensifying CPU pressure. As CPU becomes scarce, connection authentication and I/O threads are starved, inflating socket queues and client wait times, which encourages application-level retries that inflate connection counts and generate additional logs, hastening space depletion. The intertwined feedback loops can rapidly cascade into widespread service unavailability unless all three resource domains are relieved together.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, causing secondary performance pathologies even though the physical resources are not inherently exhausted.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots inside the buffer manager, producing buffer-busy waits, CPU spin, and latency spikes driven by page-level contention rather than total memory shortage.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply redo at the rate generated on the primary, leading to widening log gaps, replay lag, and retention of un-recycled log segments.

Composite behaviour: When mis-tuned configuration parameters simultaneously foster buffer-cache/latch hot spots and accelerate redo generation, the primary instance experiences both severe page-level contention and a surge in transaction-log traffic that replicas fail to keep up with. Observable symptoms include: 1) mixed wait-event spikes—buffer-busy, page-latch, log-flush, and replication-sender waits—cycling in unpredictable patterns; 2) CPU utilisation that oscillates between spin-loops on latches and idle periods while replication back-pressure throttles commit throughput; 3) bloating of the primary’s transaction log because replication prevents recycling while aggressive checkpoints keep forcing additional flushes; 4) replica-side apply workers falling further behind, showing elevated lock conflicts on the same hotspot pages once they finally replay, and 5) end-user latency outliers that are hard to attribute to a single tier because stalls propagate from buffer manager to commit path to replication pipeline.

Causal chain: Poor configuration—for example an undersized buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint interval, or improper work-memory/granule sizing—magnifies page churn and concentrates traffic on a limited set of cache lines. This intensifies latch contention, which lengthens commit time and inflates the volume and burstiness of redo writes. The heavier, more bursty log stream in turn overwhelms replicas, introducing apply lag that blocks log truncation on the primary. Retained log segments consume more cache and I/O bandwidth, further shrinking effective buffer space and prolonging dirty-page residence, which feeds back into even higher latch contention cycles. Thus, each anomaly amplifies the others: mis-tuned parameters create the hot pages, latch contention slows commit, slow commits inflate log backlog, and replication drag prevents cleanup, together degrading both primary and replica performance far beyond what any single issue would cause.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: This anomaly represents the concurrent occurrence of a sub-optimal execution plan chosen by the optimizer (Query Plan Selection Anomaly) together with saturation or mis-configuration of the write-ahead log infrastructure (Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly). Both root causes are active at the same time, so the workload suffers from inefficient SQL execution paths while every data-modification operation is additionally throttled by log I/O delays.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Highly variant and often degraded response times: some statements suddenly switch to full scans or row-by-row nested loops, inflating CPU and I/O, while commits stall on log-flush waits. • Dramatic spikes in redo generation, frequent log file switches, and enlarged archive backlogs driven by the extra work performed by sub-optimal plans (e.g., unnecessary wide-range updates or large sort/merge spill redo). • Plan instability that coincides with rising log-related wait events, making it difficult to attribute performance drops to either the optimizer or logging alone. • Elevated contention on buffer cache and temp space caused by poor plans, further increasing the volume of dirty pages that must be flushed at checkpoint, which in turn competes with log writes for the same I/O channels. • Application-level symptoms include timeouts, deadlock-like stalls at commit boundaries, erratic throughput, and exponential latency under peak write load.

Causal Interaction: Poor plan selection can magnify the rate and burstiness of data modifications—e.g., choosing a table scan plus large hash aggregation that spills to disk may touch and dirty far more pages than a selective index access, thereby generating excessive redo. This surge stresses the log buffer, amplifies log file switch frequency, and exposes any sizing or device-placement weaknesses in the transaction-log subsystem. Conversely, when log-flush latency rises, transactions stay open longer, holding locks and keeping their execution contexts alive. This inflates the working set and can prompt the optimizer to evict or recompile plans, increasing the probability of unstable or downgraded plan choices. The feedback loop between growing redo pressure and deteriorating plan quality accelerates resource exhaustion, leading to severe throughput collapse in write-intensive OLTP workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing inputs such as row counts, histograms, and correlation statistics are stale, absent, or misleading.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses or reuses a sub-optimal execution plan even though acceptable alternative plans exist.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine allocates or retains more memory than the host can safely supply, causing pressure, paging, or OOM events.

When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the workload experiences a multi-layer performance collapse. Poor or missing statistics drive large cardinality errors; the cost model, already skewed, may still pick an ill-suited plan or inappropriately reuse one, amplifying misestimation damage. The selected plans often request exaggerated memory for sorts, hashes, or parallel workers, while the engine’s global memory governance is already over-committed. Observable symptoms therefore include wildly inaccurate estimated vs. actual rows, sudden switches between access paths, exploding join buffers, runaway temp-space and swap usage, erratic query runtimes that worsen with each recompile, frequent plan-cache flushes, and ultimately operating-system level paging storms or database process terminations. Because memory pressure feeds back into the optimizer (e.g., spilling to disk changes cost dynamics) and plan invalidations trigger fresh miscompiled plans, troubleshooting becomes noisy and non-deterministic.

Causal chain: stale or incomplete statistics mislead the cost model, increasing the probability of a poor plan choice. Sub-optimal plans often require more memory—larger hash tables, broader scans, or excessive parallelism—which inflates per-query and global memory footprints. The resulting memory strain provokes paging and forces the engine to evict buffers or flush plan cache entries, causing more recompilations that again consult bad statistics and repeat the cycle. In extreme cases, memory exhaustion triggers OS-level intervention, aborting queries or crashing instances, while the root misestimations and plan churn remain unresolved. This feedback loop between faulty statistics, misguided plan selection, and unchecked memory growth magnifies latency, throughput variability, and stability risks across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Inaccurate, stale, or incomplete optimizer statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimates that mis-guide plan selection and operator choices.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Excessive competition for hot buffer pages, latches, and I/O slots forces sessions to spin or wait, throttling throughput even when adequate memory exists overall.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive, write, or apply WAL/redo changes as fast as the primary generates them, producing widening log-position lag and blocking log recycling.

When all three conditions occur together, the database exhibits a compound performance crisis: the primary produces sub-optimal, latch-heavy execution plans that hammer a small set of pages; these hot-page storms inflate buffer latch waits and CPU spin on the primary while simultaneously generating large, bursty transaction logs. The bloated and write-amplified redo stream overwhelms network or replica apply capacity, causing replication lag and retention of unsent or unapplied log segments. End-users observe erratic query latencies, periodic throughput collapses, and stale or unavailable read replicas; administrators see ballooning primary log storage, chronic buffer_busy/latch contention, and extreme estimated-vs-actual row count divergence in plan diagnostics.

Causally, stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing access paths—such as nested loops into hot index root pages or overly selective filters—that concentrate traffic on very few buffers. This localized I/O and latch pressure increases CPU spin and stretches commit times, enlarging individual transactions and the volume of redo emitted. The intensified log generation then widens replication lag; replicas that already struggle to replay suffer further because inefficient plans are re-executed during apply, compounding their CPU and I/O deficit. Conversely, replication delay prevents log recycling, lengthening checkpoint cycles and keeping more dirty pages in memory, which raises buffer flush pressure and prolongs latch hold times on the primary, completing a reinforcing negative feedback loop that degrades both primary and replica performance.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction patterns force the engine to touch more rows, hold locks longer, or perform excessive round-trips beyond actual business need.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or page-pin structures, causing CPU spinning and wait events rather than true resource shortage.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas prevent the database from allocating new low-level resources.

When these three root causes manifest together, the workload generates oversized scans and long-running transactions that hammer a limited buffer pool, creating hot pages and latch hotspots. At the same time, the database process periodically fails to obtain additional kernel objects, intensifying stalls. Observable symptoms include: explosive growth of slow-query log entries, buffer-busy and latch wait events spiking in lockstep with application timeouts, CPU cores saturated by spin loops yet low transactional throughput, sudden "cannot allocate shared memory / file handle / thread" errors, aborted background workers, and severe variance in response times. Monitoring may show buffer cache hit ratios oscillating as pages churn, while OS metrics reveal descriptor or memory namespace exhaustion exactly when latch waits peak.

Causally, chatty or bulk-scan SQL inflates the rate and duration of page accesses, concentrating pressure on a subset of data blocks. This amplifies latch contention in the buffer manager; each stall extends transaction lifetimes, which in turn holds resources longer and issues more I/O, deepening the hotspot. Prolonged contention causes threads to linger and proliferate, quickly consuming kernel file handles, shared-memory segments, or thread slots. Once OS limits are hit, the engine cannot create new worker threads or allocate additional shared buffers, so latch contention can no longer be alleviated by scaling concurrency, and blocked sessions accumulate. The feedback loop—inefficient SQL driving latch storms that balloon process counts and exhaust kernel quotas—leads to cascading slowdowns, partial outages, and ultimately systemic unavailability unless both the workload logic and the underlying resource ceilings are corrected.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between physical table / index layout and workload access patterns that forces inefficient full-object operations and excessive write amplification.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries because background cleanup workers cannot keep up with update/delete churn.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-managed objects (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, threads, etc.) that prevents the database from allocating additional resources even though engine-level quotas are not reached.

When all three root causes are present, the database exhibits a blended failure mode: queries that should be selective devolve into wide scans across bloated heaps and non-covering indexes, each scan having to wade through layers of dead tuples. Cleanup workers try to reclaim space but can neither keep pace with the churn nor obtain the extra worker processes, file handles, or shared-memory slices they need because OS-level limits have been hit. Administrators observe rapidly growing table and index sizes, misestimated row counts, escalating I/O per query, chronic checkpoint and autovacuum backlogs, and intermittent "cannot open file" or "cannot spawn worker" errors. Performance degrades non-linearly—latency spikes on both reads and writes, maintenance jobs are canceled or throttled, and partial outages occur when new sessions or parallel workers are refused despite apparent headroom inside the database.

Causal chain: missing or sub-optimal indexes force queries and batch modifications to touch far more pages than necessary, dramatically increasing update/delete traffic and hence MVCC version creation. The resulting version bloat inflates on-disk structures, further slowing already inefficient scans and generating even more cleanup work. To catch up, the engine attempts to launch additional autovacuum, compaction, or parallel I/O workers, but these requests collide with tight kernel limits on file handles, threads, or shared memory that may already be strained by the enlarged object set. The OS denials stall maintenance tasks, letting version bloat grow unchecked, which in turn amplifies the workload on the poorly designed schema. This positive feedback loop between design inefficiency, version accumulation, and resource exhaustion pushes the system toward steady-state overload or cascading failure.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Inefficient or incorrect application-level SQL and transaction design that causes the engine to process, move, or lock more data than business logic truly requires.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk data pages or index structures that makes storage structures unreliable and forces corrective or fallback behaviour.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Insufficient or unstable network, listener, authentication, or socket resources that throttle connection establishment and data transfer between client and server.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blended fault pattern: expensive statements generate very large scans and result sets that traverse damaged pages or mis-linked indexes, triggering error conditions, retries, or full table scans. These bloated operations keep transactions and server backends open for longer, inflating memory use and holding locks while the engine re-reads or re-checks suspect pages. The oversized result sets then contend for limited network bandwidth and connection slots, causing client-side timeouts, increased round-trip latency, rising counts of aborted or half-open sessions, and retry storms. Concurrently, corruption-induced plan fallbacks replace index probes with full scans, further multiplying data volume sent across an already constrained network. Monitoring may therefore show an interleaving of slow-query log explosions, integrity check failures, connection queue buildup, and oscillating throughput that can be mis-attributed to any single layer.

Causally, inefficient workload design amplifies the impact of underlying corruption by touching more pages and indices, increasing the likelihood of encountering bad blocks and forcing expensive recovery or verification paths. Each corruption-triggered retry or full scan magnifies the data transferred, which, in turn, saturates network and connection resources. Network congestion then prolongs transaction lifetimes, raising the window during which further corrupt pages can be read and additional retries spawned. Extended sessions also increase the probability of abrupt client disconnects, and these ungraceful terminations—especially under heavy load—can interrupt in-flight writes, potentially deepening physical corruption. The feedback loop among excessive workload demand, structural corruption, and network exhaustion degrades overall database availability and complicates diagnosis because symptoms at one layer mask or imitate failures in the others.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model and indexing choices are mis-aligned with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient data access regardless of statistics freshness.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are adequate, often due to cost-model or plan-cache issues.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or replay log records as fast as the primary generates them.

When all three root causes are present, the system suffers a compound performance and availability degradation. Queries on the primary exhibit excessive full scans, non-covering index lookups, or poorly chosen join methods, inflating CPU and I/O. These bloated executions enlarge transaction logs and generate more redo, while inefficient plans may also hold locks longer and bundle more row changes per statement. The oversized and plan-inflated redo stream then overwhelms replicas whose apply threads are already struggling, causing rapidly widening replication lag, persistent replica read staleness, and a rising backlog of retained log segments on the primary. Meanwhile, sporadic plan flips further vary redo volume and execution latency, making lag patterns erratic and troubleshooting harder.

Causally, poor schema/index design creates wide scans and row fetch amplification. The optimizer, already faced with ill-suited structures, may still pick sub-optimal plans, multiplying the work per transaction. This extra work translates directly into larger and burstier redo generation. Replication pipelines must ship and apply every changed row; therefore, the inflated and uneven log traffic stresses network, disk, and apply CPU on replicas, triggering or worsening synchronization slowdowns. As replicas lag, they retain older log segments, preventing log recycling on the primary and increasing primary storage pressure, which in turn can slow production queries even more. The intertwined feedback loop—inefficient data access, bad plan choices, and stalled replication—magnifies latency, resource consumption, and risk of failover gaps beyond what any single anomaly would cause alone.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine’s internal caches, work areas, and background heaps grow beyond the safe physical- or swap-memory envelope of the host, provoking sustained OS memory pressure and allocation stalls.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Persisted data pages and index structures become physically or logically inconsistent with their expected state, leading to corruption errors and unreliable access paths.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process exhausts kernel-enforced limits on objects such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or address space, causing allocation failures outside the engine’s own quota system.

When all three root causes co-exist, symptoms overlap and intensify: frequent OOM killer events or heavy paging coincide with sporadic "cannot allocate descriptor" or "unable to map shared memory" errors, while corruption alerts or checksum failures begin to appear in engine logs. Recovery attempts or integrity-check utilities may hang or crash because they cannot acquire the required OS handles or memory, and repeated retries inflate memory use further. Queries may oscillate between full scans (forced by corrupted or unusable indexes) and aborted executions (blocked by OS limits), producing erratic performance, duplicated or missing rows, and intermittent node evictions in clustered deployments. Administrators observe a system that alternates between memory thrashing, resource-limit denials, and corruption warnings, making it difficult to isolate any single culprit.

Causally, excessive memory allocation drives the process closer to both physical exhaustion and configured OS object limits—for example, each new work area or parallel worker consumes additional file handles, shared-memory segments, and address-space mappings. As the kernel begins to deny allocations or invokes the OOM killer, abrupt termination of checkpoints, log flushes, or background writers can leave pages half-written, seeding data-block and index corruption. Conversely, once corruption emerges, the engine may abandon efficient index paths and fall back to wide scans that allocate larger buffers and temporary structures, further exacerbating memory pressure. Any restart or recovery cycle triggered by corruption or OOM events must reopen files and recreate IPC structures, pushing the process back against the same OS limits. Thus, each anomaly feeds the others in a reinforcing loop, rapidly degrading stability and data integrity across both OLTP and analytic workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, density, or correlation metadata no longer matches the real data distribution, so the optimizer bases plan costing on inaccurate cardinality estimates.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database host CPUs are persistently saturated, creating a compute bottleneck that slows both query execution and supporting background tasks.

When both root causes are active, the database exhibits a blend of tell-tale symptoms: execution plans show extreme under- or over-estimates alongside very high per-statement and system-wide CPU time; run-queue and OS load averages spike during and immediately after plan compilations; statement latency and variance rise sharply even for previously fast queries; automatic statistics jobs, parallel execution crews, and user queries all contend for CPU, causing statistics refreshes to miss maintenance windows and reinforcing stale metadata; retry storms or connection pool timeouts may appear as response times lengthen.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing CPU-heavy access paths such as wide nested loops, full scans, or over-parallelized plans. These plans drive sustained CPU demand that saturates cores, raising compile and execution times and monopolizing scheduler resources. The resulting CPU pressure delays or cancels automatic statistics collection and hinders manual refresh attempts, so statistics remain stale and misestimation persists. The two anomalies thus reinforce one another in a feedback loop that degrades throughput and increases latency across the entire workload.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload intensity, or version defaults, creating artificial bottlenecks that do not reflect true resource exhaustion.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database memory structures (buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, background heaps, etc.) grow beyond the safe physical or virtual memory envelope, leading to OS pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging pipeline (log buffer, log files, archiver, replication retention) becomes the throughput or latency bottleneck on the write path, stalling commits and checkpoints.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blended symptom pattern that is louder and harder to attribute:  • Commit latency and log-flush waits rise while CPUs and disks oscillate between idle and 100 % utilization;  • Memory pressure causes buffer eviction and plan-cache churn, inflating redo generation and checkpoint frequency, which in turn amplifies log-write peaks;  • Sudden log-file switches, archive backlogs, or replication gaps coincide with kernel swap bursts, background autovacuum/cleaner backlog, and sharp drops in cache hit ratio;  • Instance restarts or node evictions may occur when OOM killers intervene during a prolonged log-flush stall;  • Wait-event histograms show an unusual mix of memory-allocation stalls, log-sync waits, and configuration-driven spin loops, masking the primary culprit.

Causal chain: Mis-set parameters (e.g., oversized per-session work memory, undersized log buffer, aggressive checkpoint timeout) trigger excessive allocation that pushes the host into swap. Memory pressure elongates dirty-buffer flush times and forces more frequent checkpoints, driving up redo volume. The swollen redo stream overwhelms the already under-provisioned log subsystem, further delaying commits and causing the checkpointer to fall behind. Each delay prolongs the lifetime of in-memory modified pages and private work areas, escalating memory consumption even more. The vicious cycle—mis-tuned settings → runaway memory usage → heavier log workload → log subsystem saturation → further memory retention—results in a self-reinforcing feedback loop that degrades OLTP throughput and stability far beyond what any single anomaly would produce alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction logic forces the engine to touch, scan, or move more data than the business task truly requires.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical storage devices or virtualization layers are unable to supply the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency the database engine requests.

When both root causes are active, the database simultaneously issues an excessive volume of I/O operations and the storage subsystem cannot service them at the necessary speed. Observable effects include: runaway statement and transaction latency that increases non-linearly under load; buffer-cache miss rates and physical read counts spiking while device queue depths stay fully saturated; prolonged lock and latch hold times because sessions wait for pages to arrive from disk; log-flush, temp-spill, and checkpoint waits stretching far beyond normal windows; application timeouts and retry storms that further multiply I/O pressure; and monitoring dashboards showing high logical I/O inside the engine coupled with high physical wait percentages outside it.

Causally, inefficient workload logic multiplies the number of pages that must be fetched, dirtied, and flushed. This inflates the I/O demand to a level that exhausts the storage throughput budget, driving up device latency. The elevated latency feeds back into the workload: long scans and large result sets stay open longer, holding locks, extending transaction lifetimes, and causing even more redo and undo to accumulate. As the storage layer falls further behind, the optimizer may switch to even more I/O-heavy plans (e.g., table scans instead of index probes) due to skewed statistics, aggravating the situation. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other in a vicious cycle, turning what would be tolerable inefficiency or marginal storage saturation into a severe, system-wide performance degradation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records outpaces background cleanup, inflating the version store and enlarging physical data structures.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path—generation, flushing, switching, or archiving—cannot keep up with the redo rate, driving up commit latency and stalling writers.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages, index structures, or heap–index mappings become internally inconsistent, causing logical corruption and unreliable access paths.

When all three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits a mix of space bloat, rising commit and checkpoint delays, and intermittent data-integrity errors. Bloated tables and indexes lengthen scans and enlarge checkpoint footprints just as the log subsystem is already saturated, so checkpoints and log switches occur more often and take longer. Corrupted pages or mis-linked index nodes encountered during cleanup, vacuum, or recovery processes surface as checksum failures, failed autovacuum passes, or crash-recovery loops. Applications observe sporadic timeouts on writes, escalating snapshot-too-old or serialization failures, incorrect query results from damaged indexes, and sudden crash-restores that replay very large, backlog-laden logs.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn first drives MVCC bloat, inflating both the data files and the volume of redo that must be logged. The swollen log stream stresses the transaction-log subsystem; when log flushing or archiving lags, checkpoints are delayed, holding dirty pages longer and extending the window during which an unexpected crash can leave partially written, corrupt pages. Simultaneously, overfilled version stores force longer vacuum cycles that touch more pages; if those pages reside on hardware already strained by sustained log I/O, the probability of torn-page or write-ordering violations rises, seeding data-block and index corruption. Once corruption appears, cleanup and recovery processes generate even more redo and may repeatedly visit the same damaged pages, amplifying both the MVCC maintenance backlog and log-write pressure. The feedback loop among unchecked version buildup, log saturation, and physical corruption rapidly degrades performance and reliability until all three layers—visibility management, durability path, and on-disk structures—need immediate remediation.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) a static mismatch between the physical schema/index design and the workload’s access patterns, (2) intense contention on buffer-cache pages and their associated latches, and (3) saturation of network or connection-handling resources between clients and the database server. The three conditions coexist and interact, causing cascading slow-downs that span the storage engine, memory subsystem, and client/server communication path.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Queries that should be selective devolve into full-table or non-covering index scans, inflating logical and physical I/O. • Buffer-busy waits, page-latch or buffer-pin waits, and CPU spin time rise sharply as many sessions fight for a small set of hot pages (e.g., root or leaf blocks of sub-optimal indexes). • Checkpoints and dirty-page flushes lengthen, further holding latches. • End-user response times are erratic; spikes propagate outside the server as clients experience longer socket read/write waits, connection-establishment delays, and intermittent "too many connections" or timeout errors. • Network interfaces and listener backlogs show elevated retransmits and queued connections because slow queries keep back-end sessions busy and tied to open sockets, while application pools repeatedly retry.

Causal Chain and Mutual Reinforcement: Inefficient schema and missing/ill-chosen indexes force large scans and concentrate inserts/updates on a few pages, rapidly cycling pages through a limited buffer pool. The resulting churn and hot-page concentration escalate buffer cache and latch contention, stalling worker threads and extending query runtimes. Prolonged execution keeps transactions and result sets open longer, inflating the number and lifetime of network connections. As network buffers fill and authentication slots or socket queues become saturated, new sessions wait or fail, prompting client retries that further increase concurrency inside the engine. The surge of concurrent, long-running scans worsens latch pressure and buffer churn, while stalled network I/O delays page clean-outs and checkpoint completion, creating a feedback loop that amplifies latency and throughput collapse across all three layers.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) and workload access patterns forces inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : Optimizer chooses a sub-optimal execution strategy despite reasonably accurate statistics, yielding plans that diverge from the cost-efficient options available.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space in data files, logs, temp areas, or backups approaches hard limits, risking allocation failures and blocking DML or query processing.

When all three root causes co-exist, the workload may exhibit runaway I/O and CPU consumption from full-table scans or non-covering index probes, frequent plan flip-flops, explosive temporary-space usage for sorts and hash joins, and accelerated growth of tables, indexes, and redo/undo logs. Operators may observe simultaneous query slowdowns, spike-shaped latency patterns, sudden "out of space" or "cannot allocate extent" errors, aborted batch jobs, and cascaded stalls as log files, temp segments, or archive destinations saturate. The overlapping symptoms make it difficult to isolate any single culprit because design flaws, bad plans, and space exhaustion each manifest in similar performance degradations.

Causally, missing or sub-optimal indexes and inappropriate partitioning inflate table and index sizes and force the optimizer to pick heavier plans (e.g., full scans or large hash joins). Even when selective paths exist, the plan-selection anomaly can disregard them, compounding the I/O footprint generated by the design flaw. The enlarged working set and higher redo/undo generation accelerate space consumption in data, temp, and log areas; once space becomes scarce, auto-extension failures or log-archive back-pressure further degrade plan performance by disabling parallelism, spilling to disk sooner, or triggering statement aborts. Conversely, near-full tablespaces may cause extent fragmentation that degrades index efficiency and influences the optimizer’s cost model, increasing the likelihood of sub-optimal plans. Thus, each root cause perpetuates the others, leading to a feedback loop of worsening performance, erratic plan behavior, and eventual space-related outages.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data objects, forcing other sessions to wait or be aborted by the deadlock detector.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine and connected sessions collectively consume more physical memory than the host can safely supply, triggering paging, allocation stalls, or OOM events.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The sustained rate of physical reads and writes reaches or exceeds the throughput and latency limits of the underlying storage subsystem, causing long device-level wait times.

When these three root causes strike at once, blocking chains and deadlocks lengthen because each locked statement is slowed by memory-pressure stalls and storage latency. Queries wait not only on locks but also on buffer-cache misses, swap-in delays, and overloaded I/O queues, inflating lock-wait timers, application response times, and retry storms. OS paging and I/O saturation keep CPU utilisation deceptively moderate while connection pools back up, cache-hit ratios collapse, and lock-manager tables fill with ever-growing blocker–waiter graphs. Deadlock reports, OOM terminations, and storage wait spikes may appear interleaved in logs, making the true scope of the incident hard to discern.

Causally, acute memory overcommit forces the engine to evict hot buffers and spill work areas, which increases physical I/O. The surge in disk traffic pushes the storage layer to its throughput ceiling, lengthening every read and write. These I/O delays prolong the lifetime of row and metadata locks held by active transactions, thus magnifying lock contention and the likelihood of deadlocks. In turn, sessions waiting on locks remain connected longer and continue to reserve memory for cursors and work buffers, worsening the memory shortfall. The positive feedback loop—memory pressure ➝ more I/O ➝ longer lock holds ➝ more waiting sessions ➝ higher memory usage—amplifies all three anomalies and can drive the database into a cascading slowdown or crash unless one of the underlying resource constraints is relieved.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction design force the engine to read, write, or hold more data than the business requirement actually needs.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine settings such as memory, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, and parallelism are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space for data, logs, temp, or backup areas runs up against hard physical or logical limits, leading to allocation failures.

When these three root causes coincide, the database experiences an avalanche of mutually reinforcing symptoms: statement and transaction latency lengthens; slow-query logs and wait-event views show heavy page reads, log writes, and checkpoint activity; free-space monitors drop precipitously, with auto-extend or log-archive failures appearing alongside application timeouts and retries. Mis-sized memory pools or aggressive checkpoint parameters amplify write-amplification produced by inefficient SQL, filling datafiles and transaction logs faster than housekeeping processes can recycle them. Conversely, space exhaustion forces frequent checkpoints, log switches, and temp-space purges, further stalling already bloated queries and long-running transactions. Operators may observe idle CPU or I/O gaps alternating with sudden spikes, making the performance pattern erratic and hard to correlate with a single layer.

Causal chain: chatty or wide-scan SQL generates excess data modifications and temporary spill that inflate datafiles and redo volumes. Because configuration parameters are set without regard to this inflated workload, buffer pools and work-memory segments flush and spill sooner, triggering more writes and checkpoint storms. The accelerated write rate rapidly consumes free space; once tablespaces, logs, or temp areas approach capacity, the engine issues frequent space-management operations and may block transactions waiting for space, further lengthening locks and holds initiated by the inefficient SQL. Each layer therefore tightens the pressure loop: poor SQL drives volume, mis-tuning magnifies volume into churn, and capacity ceilings turn churn into outright stalls, leading to a compound degradation far worse than any single anomaly would cause.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions compete for incompatible locks on the same data or metadata resources, causing waits, blocking chains, and potential deadlocks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, logging, checkpointing, parallelism, or worker limits are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload demands, leading to secondary bottlenecks despite apparently idle resources.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Data files, log segments, temp areas, or archive destinations run out of free space, producing allocation failures and halting write activity.

When all three root causes surface simultaneously, the system exhibits intertwined symptoms: lock wait time and deadlock frequency rise sharply while transaction commit latency unpredictably spikes; background checkpoints or log flushes thrash yet disks show uneven utilization; sudden "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors abort long-held transactions, leaving other sessions blocked behind locks that cannot be released; connection pools back up as new requests wait both for locks and for space-related retries; monitoring shows memory pools oscillating because mis-sized buffers amplify checkpoint storms that collide with lock-held pages, and automatic retry storms enlarge temp and log usage until capacity thresholds are breached.

Causally, misconfigured parameters can lengthen transaction lifetimes (e.g., too-slow checkpoints or oversized work_mem prompting large spills), thereby keeping locks active longer and intensifying contention. Prolonged blocking inflates undo and redo growth, accelerating consumption of data-file, log, and temp space. As free space dwindles, allocation failures trigger rollbacks or force log-flush pauses, which in turn hold critical locks even longer and push more sessions into the wait queues, feeding back into lock contention. Each anomaly thus magnifies the others: poor configuration creates the conditions for lock buildup; lock buildup drives explosive space usage; space exhaustion stalls writes and rollbacks, freezing locks in place and deepening the overall performance crisis.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) a physical-schema and indexing design that is misaligned with workload access patterns, (2) low-level corruption or inconsistency of data pages and index structures on disk, and (3) exhaustion of critical operating-system resources such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or process/thread quotas. Together these conditions force even well-written queries onto inefficient paths, operate on unreliable physical structures, and contend with kernel-level hard limits, creating a multi-layer failure state that degrades performance, correctness, and availability.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Queries expected to use selective, covering indexes instead perform full scans or revert to table scans after detecting corrupted index pages. • Result sets show missing or duplicated rows, while concurrent integrity-check utilities or background workers intermittently fail to start because the engine cannot obtain additional processes, semaphores, or AIO contexts. • Rebuild or reindex commands abort with both corruption messages and "cannot open file" / "cannot allocate shared memory" errors. • Latency is erratic: some sessions hang during I/O retries, others are denied connection; meanwhile write workloads slow dramatically due to bloated or redundant indexes that the optimizer cannot safely ignore because of suspected corruption. • Engine and kernel logs interleave checksum or key-order errors with ENFILE/EMFILE, ENOMEM, or EAGAIN denials, making the original root causes hard to isolate.

Causal Interaction: The poor schema and indexing strategy amplifies I/O volume and maintenance traffic, expanding the number of active files, index pages, and background workers the engine must handle; this drives the process toward operating-system limits. Once those limits are reached, critical maintenance tasks such as index rebuilds, auto-vacuum, or corruption-repair threads fail to start or complete, allowing latent on-disk inconsistencies to persist and spread. Conversely, existing corruption forces the optimizer to discard damaged indexes, further exposing the inefficiencies of the design anomaly and increasing load on heap scans and temporary files, which in turn consumes even more OS resources. The mutual reinforcement of heavy, poorly targeted I/O, unreliable physical structures, and kernel-level resource starvation accelerates degradation, leading to cascading performance collapse, data-consistency risks, and partial or total service outage.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition:
The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal execution-plan choices, unchecked accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions, and saturation of the underlying storage throughput budget. The three conditions reinforce each other, producing symptoms that are broader and more severe than any single anomaly alone.

Combined Observable Phenomena:
• Identical statements oscillate between different or obviously poor plans while response times keep rising.
• Sequential scans, hash builds, or nested-loop outer scans read far more pages than expected because tables and indexes are bloated with dead tuples.
• Device-level metrics show queue depths pegged, read and write latency multiples higher than normal, and log-flush or buffer-I/O waits dominating the wait profile even when CPU is idle.
• Autovacuum/cleanup workers run constantly yet fail to shrink the version store; catalog views report high dead-tuples-to-live-tuples ratios and growing on-disk size.
• Planner misestimates become more frequent as statistics lag behind the rapidly changing and bloated heap, leading to further plan instability.
• Business transactions time out, batch windows stretch, and analytic queries executed on the same system observe inconsistent runtimes depending on whether they hit a cached or newly compiled plan.

Causal Chain and Interaction:
1. MVCC bloat inflates table and index size, distorting cardinality statistics and making cost estimates less reliable.
2. The optimizer, already prone to plan-selection mistakes, is now working with misleading size estimates, increasing the probability of choosing plans that trigger large table scans, spill to temp, or lose beneficial parallelism.
3. These poorly chosen plans generate excess physical I/O; the swollen objects mean each scan or index probe touches more pages, quickly saturating the storage subsystem.
4. Once storage throughput is maxed out, I/O latency rises. Long-running queries hold snapshots open longer, which prevents cleanup workers from advancing the MVCC horizon, so dead versions accumulate even faster.
5. The growing version store further enlarges the data footprint, feeding back into even worse cost estimates and heavier I/O, creating a self-reinforcing degradation loop that is difficult to attribute to any single layer without holistic analysis.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The local write-ahead logging path on the primary instance is saturated or stalled while generating, flushing, switching, or archiving redo. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas or change-data consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing replication lag and retention of log segments. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage volumes for data, temp, and log files are bandwidth- or IOPS-constrained, creating elevated read/write latency and long device queues.

When all three root causes co-exist, the database experiences a compound slow-commit and replication-backpressure scenario. Commit latency rises sharply as the log buffer waits both for slow physical flushes and for replication–safe acknowledgement. Log-write, log-sync, and durability wait events dominate, while storage wait events for data and log files simultaneously surge. Checkpoints and log-file switches occur more frequently yet clear space slowly, archive and relay log directories grow unchecked, and replica replay lag widens. The primary’s disk usage escalates because retained log segments cannot be recycled, further increasing I/O pressure. Application symptoms include stalled write transactions, timeouts, and degraded read-only replica freshness; maintenance windows and analytic reporting that touch large data ranges also slow because they compete for the already saturated storage bandwidth.

Causally, limited storage throughput lengthens every physical write, throttling the log subsystem first; the bloated log path then compounds storage pressure by generating large sequential writes that the device cannot serve promptly. Because log recycling waits on downstream replay, any delay in replication— itself hampered by the same storage or network bottlenecks—forces the primary to retain additional log segments, inflating I/O volume and metadata churn. In turn, the growing backlog keeps replicas further behind, reinforcing retention pressure on the primary and amplifying the storage bottleneck. This positive feedback loop between slow device I/O, log-flush stalls, and replication lag escalates until the system exhausts commit latency budgets or runs out of disk space, producing a severe OLTP availability and performance crisis.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Memory regions owned by the database engine grow beyond the safe limits of the host, driving paging, swapping, or OOM events.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage volumes are unable to deliver the required read/write bandwidth or IOPS, resulting in persistently elevated latency and long device queues.

Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously exhausts server memory while the storage subsystem is already throughput-bound. The memory allocator keeps demanding pages that the storage layer cannot supply or flush fast enough, and the storage layer cannot keep pace with the extra traffic induced by memory pressure.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Dramatic oscillation between memory and I/O waits—buffer-cache eviction storms lead to surges of physical reads, while swap activity inflates write traffic. 2) CPU utilization appears sporadic: worker threads stall on both page-in/page-out operations and storage waits, masking the true root causes. 3) Cache-hit ratios plunge despite large cache sizes, checkpoint and log-flush latency spikes, batch windows stretch, and clustered or virtualized nodes face eviction due to compounded memory and I/O SLA violations. 4) Diagnostic views show ballooning resident-set size, high page-fault rates, deep storage queues, and mixed wait events (buffer I/O, memory latch sleep, page flushes) that are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain and interaction: Excessive memory allocation evicts hot pages prematurely, forcing the engine to issue more physical reads; the already saturated storage cannot satisfy these reads quickly, causing sessions to remain active longer and hold even more memory, which further heightens memory pressure. Conversely, slow storage flushes delay the release of dirty buffers and temp segments, obliging the engine to allocate additional memory to continue processing, inching the system closer to swapping. Each anomaly amplifies the other, creating a feedback loop that degrades throughput, increases latency, and threatens instance stability far more severely than either issue in isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transactions are written in ways that process or touch far more data, rows, or time than business logic actually requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions request incompatible locks on the same resources, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks inside the lock manager.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The engine’s cumulative buffer, cache, work-area, and session allocations outgrow safe physical limits, causing memory pressure, paging, or OOM events.

When these three root causes manifest together, the system experiences prolonged statement runtimes, expanding lock-wait trees, rising deadlock and timeout errors, and simultaneous memory pressure. Bulky, poorly filtered queries and transactions hold row or table locks for extended periods, stalling other sessions. While they wait, blocked sessions keep their work areas, sort/hash buffers, and transaction state pinned in memory, inflating overall RAM consumption. Elevated memory usage intensifies OS paging or swap storms, which in turn slows lock acquisition and release, drives up lock-wait durations, and triggers more application-level retries.
