Monitoring views show spikes in both lock-related wait events and memory-related stalls; slow-query and deadlock logs reference the same heavyweight statements; the database process’s RSS grows continuously while transaction throughput collapses and connection pools back up.

Causally, inefficient workload logic initiates large scans, huge intermediate result sets, and overlong transactions. These operations acquire broad or numerous locks that persist for their extended execution window, seeding hot-spot contention. The same bloated operations consume excessive work memory and expand buffer-cache footprints; as concurrency rises, each blocked session retains its allocations, pushing the node toward memory exhaustion. Memory pressure degrades I/O and CPU scheduling, elongating transaction runtimes and further prolonging lock holding times—thereby aggravating the contention spiral. Conversely, lock waits keep transactions active longer, preventing memory from being released and escalating pressure. The mutually reinforcing feedback loop between inefficient workload design, persistent locking, and runaway memory growth can rapidly degrade OLTP service levels and precipitate crashes or widespread timeouts.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Sustained reads or writes saturate the physical storage subsystem, driving up latency, queue depth, and I/O-related wait events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other per-process quotas prevent the database from allocating required operating-system objects.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, socket, or authentication resources between clients and the server are exhausted or slowed, impeding connection establishment and data transfer.

When all three root causes occur concurrently, the database exhibits a multi-layer resource gridlock: I/O wait times surge while sessions already connected cannot read from or write to disk promptly; at the same time, new or parallel sessions may fail to spawn because the kernel refuses additional threads, file descriptors, or AIO contexts, and clients attempting to connect face timeouts or refusals as listener backlogs and socket queues overflow. Observable metrics become noisy and intertwined—CPU appears idle, yet transaction latency climbs; wait profiles show a mixture of storage waits, client I/O waits, and internal latch or semaphore allocation failures; system logs alternate between kernel "out of resources" messages and network stack "connection reset" or "cannot allocate socket" errors. Batch windows stretch, OLTP response times spike, and connection-pool retry storms amplify both network and storage pressure, making it difficult to attribute symptoms to a single layer.

Causally, saturated storage bandwidth forces background writers and log flushers to hold file descriptors and AIO contexts for longer periods, rapidly consuming the limited kernel resources governed by per-process limits. As these limits are reached, new I/O contexts and threads cannot be created, causing further backlog in the I/O submission path and lengthening storage queues. Simultaneously, exhausted file handles and listener socket quotas prevent timely acceptance of new TCP connections, which causes clients to retry aggressively, inflating the connection rate and deepening the socket backlog. The compounded effect is a feedback loop in which storage stalls increase kernel resource retention, depleted kernel resources hinder both I/O and connection handling, and network retries multiply the load, jointly degrading overall database availability and performance far more severely than any single anomaly would alone.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine settings (memory, logging, parallelism, checkpoint cadence, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload needs.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive or apply WAL/redo at the rate the primary produces it, causing ever-growing replication lag.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced quotas on file descriptors, shared memory, processes, or other OS objects throttle the database independently of its own internal resource management.

When all three faults coexist, the system exhibits a blended failure signature: replication slots stall and retain large volumes of primary WAL, checkpoint frequency spikes yet log recycling is blocked, background workers or apply processes fail to start due to exhausted OS handles, and wait-event statistics show both idle hardware and intense spin or log-write waits. End-users observe increasing replica staleness, sudden session or worker creation errors, erratic latency on the primary, and rapid disk-space consumption from unrecycled logs. Troubleshooting is complicated because each layer (engine parameters, replication, kernel) shows partial symptoms that mask or mimic the others.

Causally, an undersized checkpoint or work-memory setting can inflate WAL generation and stall autovacuum, pushing more redo toward replicas. If OS limits simultaneously cap network sockets, async-I/O contexts, or background threads, the apply side or even the primary’s replication sender processes cannot keep pace, amplifying lag. The growing log backlog prevents log truncation, which in turn triggers aggressive checkpoints per the misconfigured parameters, intensifying I/O surges and memory pressure. Each layer’s throttling therefore compounds the next: mis-tuned engine parameters accelerate load, OS limits restrict the threads and kernel objects needed to digest that load, and replication becomes the visible bottleneck while the primary itself edges toward resource exhaustion. Together they create a self-reinforcing loop that degrades throughput, threatens availability, and obscures root-cause isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written such that they touch or return far more data than the business case requires.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The database engine allocates or leaks memory past the safe capacity of the host, triggering paging, swapping, or OOM events.

Composite definition: The workload simultaneously contains inefficient SQL that inflates data-processing volume AND the engine is already operating beyond its safe memory envelope, so both logical and physical resource excesses coexist.

Combined phenomena: 1) Statement latency and variance grow dramatically as bulky scans, joins, and wide result sets contend for shrinking buffer cache and work memory. 2) Sudden spikes of per-query hash/sort buffers, parallel workers, or in-memory constructs drive the operating system into swap, causing stalls, plan cache eviction, and background process throttling. 3) Applications report timeouts, retries, or dead-session backlog while the host shows sustained memory pressure, high page-fault rates, and occasional OOM kills or node evictions.

Causal chain: Inefficient SQL multiplies the amount of data each query must read, join, sort, or hold, which inflates per-statement work areas and buffer requirements. The over-allocation of memory, in turn, reduces cache efficiency, forces spills to disk, and may evict useful pages, causing the same bloated queries to reread data and further extend their execution time. Longer-running transactions hold latches, cursors, and session heaps even longer, increasing the resident-set size and magnifying global memory pressure. As the engine starts swapping or terminating workers, queues build up, retries are issued, and concurrency climbs, feeding back into even more memory consumption—creating a vicious circle that degrades both throughput and stability.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The log-generation, buffering, flushing, or archival pipeline is throttled, making commit processing the primary performance bottleneck.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk data pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupt, causing unreliable access paths and consistency errors.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Usable free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas is exhausted or about to be, provoking allocation failures and write stalls.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database experiences a cascade of amplified symptoms: commit latency and log-flush waits climb while log switches stall because archive destinations are full; corruption-related retries or full-table scans inflate redo generation and temporary space usage; integrity-check or recovery operations emit additional diagnostic output that quickly consumes the dwindling free space; page-checksum failures, "no space left on device" errors, and timeout-driven rollbacks appear interleaved in the logs; instance restarts or crash-recovery attempts may loop or hang as corrupted pages force repeated redo application while log files cannot be written or archived.

Causal chain: data and index corruption often stimulates heavy redo production through forced page clean-ups, index rebuilds, or full scans, which in turn pressures the already constrained transaction-log subsystem. The higher redo volume quickly fills log files and their archive destinations; once those locations reach capacity, log flushing stalls, freezing new transactions and preventing checkpoint progress. Because space exhaustion also blocks archiver and backup jobs, corrupted pages cannot be repaired or exported, prolonging exposure. Repeated aborts or crash recoveries invoked to address corruption must replay ever-growing, possibly damaged log streams, further stressing both the log subsystem and the limited storage. The three anomalies therefore reinforce each other, rapidly degrading throughput, threatening data durability, and complicating root-cause isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transactional logic that processes more data, rows, or time than business semantics require.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : Optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics.

When both root causes strike simultaneously, the database exhibits pronounced and erratic performance degradation: statements already bloated by poor SQL logic are executed with inefficient access paths, causing extreme elongation of response times, frequent appearance in slow-query and lock-wait logs, sudden shifts between fast and very slow executions, CPU spikes from unnecessary scans or nested-loop explosions, and inflated I/O and memory footprints that ripple through the buffer cache and temp space. As transactions stay open longer, secondary effects such as lock retention, queue buildup in connection pools, and application-level timeouts become common, obscuring which layer is primarily responsible.

Causally, verbose or improperly filtered SQL inflates row counts and widens intermediate result sets. The optimizer, already prone to picking fragile or non-robust plans, now evaluates inflated cardinality estimates and may favor full scans, Cartesian joins, or non-parallel plans that magnify the workload’s excess. Conversely, a mischosen plan that scans or joins large tables amplifies the cost of the workload logic’s unnecessary columns, predicates, or batch size, turning what would have been a minor inefficiency into a severe bottleneck. The feedback loop—sub-optimal logic feeding a sub-optimal plan—exacerbates resource consumption, stretches transaction length, and masks the individual contribution of each root cause, making diagnosis and remediation more difficult than if either anomaly occurred in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating the version store and bloating data pages.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, checkpointing, worker throttles, and parallelism are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload demands, creating artificial bottlenecks.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage subsystem reaches or nears its physical I/O bandwidth or IOPS limits, driving up read/write latency and queue depth.

When all three root causes strike together, the database experiences a feedback loop in which version churn rapidly enlarges tables and indexes, mis-calibrated parameters prevent aggressive vacuuming and amplify checkpoint bursts, and the swollen data plus write-heavy cleanup tasks saturate an already over-stressed storage layer. Observable symptoms converge: the version store and rollback segments grow without bound; autovacuum or purge workers stay perpetually active yet make little progress; checkpoint and log-flush waits spike even while CPU cores are idle; device-level latency soars, causing statement execution times and replication lag to lengthen; query plans degrade because optimizer statistics lag behind the bloated heap; and monitoring shows conflicting signals of low CPU but high wait ratios on buffer-I/O, log write, and vacuum-related events.

Causally, heavy UPDATE/DELETE workloads generate large numbers of dead tuples (MVCC anomaly). Because memory, autovacuum cost limits, and checkpoint intervals are misconfigured (configuration anomaly), the engine cannot reclaim space promptly and instead accumulates ever-larger dirty pages and WAL. The enlarged working set and prolonged checkpoints push sustained random and sequential I/O beyond what the disk subsystem can deliver (storage throughput anomaly). Elevated I/O latency further slows cleanup workers, lengthening the visibility horizon and accelerating version buildup. This vicious cycle intensifies page bloat, inflates WAL, and keeps the system trapped in a deteriorating state where each anomaly reinforces the others, ultimately threatening transaction-ID wraparound or instance unavailability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Simultaneous hot-page access forces sessions to serialize on buffer-cache latches, page pins, or I/O slots, stalling execution at the storage-engine layer.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database and ancillary processes drive host CPU utilisation to saturation, exhausting compute cycles and lengthening run-queue and scheduler waits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client ↔ server transport, listener, socket, or authentication resources become bottlenecked, delaying connection setup and data transfer.

When these three root causes strike together the system exhibits a multilayer bottleneck: 1) intra-engine waits such as buffer-busy and page-latch spikes, 2) host-level symptoms of CPU exhaustion—high load averages, context-switch storms, runaway spin polling in latch code, and 3) external indicators of connectivity stress—rising connection-establishment latency, backlog overflow, and client-side timeouts. Because each tier is impaired, end-to-end response times degrade non-linearly, with seemingly random query slowdowns, erratic throughput, and bursts of failed or abandoned client sessions that mask the true root causes.

Causal interaction: Hotspot pages force sessions into latch spin loops that chew CPU; the inflated CPU demand pushes the host to saturation, lengthening the time threads hold latches and further intensifying buffer contention. The overwhelmed schedulers also delay kernel-space network interrupts and socket processing, which inflates round-trip times and backs up the database listener. Conversely, stalled or retried client connections keep backend processes in a suspended or half-active state while still owning buffer pins, extending the lifetime of page locks and exacerbating latch queues. The feedback loop among latch spin, CPU starvation, and network backlog can cascade quickly, turning localized hot-page contention into cluster-wide performance collapse.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete MVCC versions and index entries because background vacuum/clean-up can’t keep pace with update/delete churn.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine settings (memory pools, checkpoints, parallelism, cleanup thresholds, etc.) that are out of line with hardware capacity or workload demands.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Run-time memory consumption by caches, work areas, and background workers that exceeds safe physical limits, leading to OS pressure or OOM events.

When these three root causes strike at the same time, the system exhibits a super-imposed fault pattern: version stores and rollback segments balloon rapidly while vacuum or purge workers are hamstrung by overly conservative parameter limits; meanwhile, memory granted to buffer pools, workspaces, or parallel workers keeps expanding until the host experiences swap storms or OOM kills. Operators observe
• explosive growth of table and index size with falling live-row density,
• vacuum/cleanup processes constantly active yet failing to shrink bloat,
• checkpoint and background writer bursts that coincide with memory pressure, paging, or sudden restarts,
• erratic planner estimates due to stale statistics and cache churn, causing sub-optimal plans that further increase work-memory usage,
• wait-event mixes that contradict hardware metrics (e.g., log write stalls while disks and CPUs are under-utilised), and
• sharp throughput collapses whenever the OS reclaims memory or the database throttles activity to protect its version store.

Causally, mis-aligned configuration parameters (e.g., undersized autovacuum workers, small maintenance_work_mem, overly large shared buffers, excessive per-query work_mem, or aggressive parallelism) throttle the very processes required to prune dead tuples while simultaneously inflating memory footprints. The unreclaimed MVCC versions bloat tables and indexes, forcing the buffer manager to cache more pages and the planner to choose heavier hash/sort paths, which in turn demands additional work memory. As memory pressure mounts, the OS starts paging; swap latency slows both cleanup and foreground queries, allowing even more version build-up. Any emergency vacuum, checkpoint storm, or crash recovery triggered by OOM then restarts the cycle, making the intertwined anomalies mutually reinforcing and progressively degrading OLTP performance and stability.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures are corrupted or inconsistent with logical row sets, leading to unreliable data retrieval and integrity-check failures.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem is saturated or degraded, driving up read/write latency, queue depths, and I/O waits for data, temp, or log files.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client–server traffic is constrained by exhausted connection slots, socket backlog, or congested network paths, producing connection errors and prolonged data-transfer waits.

When these three root causes coexist, the database may exhibit a confusing mix of symptoms: queries intermittently return wrong, duplicated, or missing rows, yet reported I/O and network latencies are simultaneously high. Integrity-check errors and checksum failures may appear alongside surging I/O wait events, slow commit acknowledgements, and a spike in client connection timeouts or retransmissions. Batch loads and backups can stall on disk queues, while application servers experience cascading connection retries. Because corruption can force the engine to abandon indexes and fall back to full table scans, the extra physical reads inflate disk traffic, which in turn exacerbates the already-saturated storage layer. Larger result sets flowing over degraded network paths further extend transaction lifetimes, keeping locks and resources held longer and amplifying contention.

Causally, corruption in data or index pages may trigger inefficient scan patterns that multiply I/O volume; the inflated I/O demand then collides with storage throughput limits, lengthening latency and delaying page delivery to the engine. Prolonged statement execution extends the duration of result streaming to clients, swelling network usage and keeping connection slots occupied. Conversely, network slowdowns cause back-pressure on the server’s send buffers, preventing worker threads from completing and releasing pages, which prolongs lock holding and increases the window in which corrupted blocks are reread. Together, the three anomalies form a feedback loop—corruption forces heavier I/O, I/O saturation delays processing, and network congestion prolongs resource occupation—culminating in severe, multidimensional performance degradation and a heightened risk of permanent data loss or extended downtime.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Stale, missing, or insufficiently detailed optimizer statistics misrepresent actual data distribution, causing systematic cardinality errors and mis-costed plan choices.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level parameters (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, distorting internal behaviors without any true resource exhaustion.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions contend for shared buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots inside the buffer manager, leading to wait-state storms and CPU spin that serialize access at the page level.

When all three root causes coexist, the symptoms overlap and intensify: queries chosen by a misinformed optimizer funnel excessive traffic onto a small set of index or heap pages, while an undersized or aggressively flushed buffer pool (the result of bad configuration parameters) keeps those pages hot, repeatedly evicting and reloading them. The amplified page churn widens the gap between estimated and actual row counts, triggers frequent plan recompilations, and pushes latch and buffer-busy waits to the top of the wait-event profile. Observables include wildly inaccurate cardinality estimates in plans, sudden spikes in page-latch and buffer-busy waits despite low overall CPU or I/O utilization, checkpoint or flush storms immediately after DML bursts, and erratic throughput that worsens after configuration or data-loading events.

Causally, stale or incomplete statistics misdirect the optimizer toward plan shapes (e.g., nested loops or single-threaded index probes) that hammer a narrow set of pages. Misconfigured parameters—such as an undersized buffer cache, overly frequent checkpoints, or excessive per-session work memory—reduce the cache residency of those hot pages and increase dirty-page pressure, provoking more latch acquisitions and longer retention times. The resulting latch contention inflates query runtimes, holding locks and pins longer, which in turn delays background processes that would otherwise refresh statistics or advance checkpoints. This feedback loop deepens cardinality inaccuracy, aggravates configuration stress points, and drives the system into a persistent high-latency, low-throughput state.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible locks on the same data or metadata objects, forming blocking chains or deadlocks that stall statement execution until a waiter is granted, times out, or is chosen as a deadlock victim.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating storage, lengthening visibility checks, and slowing scans and look-ups.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server network links, listener sockets, or backend connection slots are saturated or slow, causing connection establishment delays, data-transfer stalls, and session-level wait events.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set: long transaction latencies and timeouts surface first as network-side slow query or connection errors, while backend diagnostics simultaneously show deep lock-wait queues, deadlock rollbacks, bloated heaps and indexes, and cleaners permanently at 100 % duty cycle. Transactions that finally obtain a lock still spend extra CPU cycles traversing oversized version chains, prolonging their critical sections and locking window, which in turn lengthens blocking chains and keeps sockets open longer. Clients perceive sporadic connection refusals or abrupt resets as the server exhausts connection slots held by lock-blocked backends that are further delayed by MVCC bloat. Monitoring tools show a self-reinforcing rise in lock-wait time, version-store size, listener backlog depth, and end-to-end RTT, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to any single subsystem.

Causally, heavy lock contention increases the lifetime of in-flight snapshots because waiting transactions hold older transaction IDs open, throttling vacuum/cleaner progress and aggravating MVCC version accumulation. In turn, the larger version store stretches the duration of read and write statements, widening the timeframe in which they hold locks and intensifying contention. Both factors keep backend processes active yet unproductive, consuming connection slots and keeping TCP sockets open; this swells the listener queue and pushes the system toward network-level saturation. Conversely, network stalls slow down result delivery, extending transaction completion time and further delaying lock release and version cleanup. The feedback loop across concurrency control, version maintenance, and connectivity layers ultimately drives a compounded degradation that is more severe than any individual anomaly acting alone.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are acceptable, leading to inefficient data access patterns and resource over-consumption.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log files, flushing, switching, archiving, replication retention) becomes the primary bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling write activity.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database approaches or reaches hard space limits in data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas, causing allocation failures and cascading stalls.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a compound failure signature: • Queries that once used selective index access flip to wide scans or Cartesian joins, exploding row touches, temporary‐space usage, and change volume. • The bloated change sets generate surges of redo that saturate the log buffer and log devices, driving up log flush and commit waits and triggering rapid log-file switches. • Accelerated log and data growth quickly exhausts remaining free space; auto-extension failures, archive-destinations running full, and temp-space errors appear together. • End-user symptoms include sharp spikes in response times, intermittent "cannot allocate extent" or "log file switch timeout" errors, and sudden session terminations when space limits are hit.

Causal interaction: The sub-optimal plans inflate I/O and modify more rows than necessary, dramatically increasing redo generation and data growth. This additional pressure magnifies any latent weakness in the transaction-log subsystem, so log flush waits and checkpoint storms lengthen transaction duration and hold locks longer, creating more contention and further workload skew. Because the log subsystem struggles, archive and recycle operations slow, preventing space reclamation and hastening exhaustion of both log and data areas. As free space dwindles, auto-extension failures and emergency space-management actions fragment files and may trigger additional plan invalidations, perpetuating the optimizer mis-choices. The three anomalies therefore reinforce each other, turning what might have been isolated inefficiencies or capacity alerts into a cascading OLTP outage.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, or other in-process heaps pushes the database process and host into sustained memory pressure, paging, or OOM risk.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes drive host CPU utilization to saturation, producing long run queues and broad latency elevation independent of any single query plan.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient network bandwidth, socket capacity, or listener/connection-handling resources prevents timely establishment and servicing of client sessions and data transfer.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits intertwined symptoms: (1) memory pressure provokes paging and frequent garbage or cache churn, inflating CPU cycles spent on memory management; (2) the resulting CPU saturation lengthens every critical code path, including connection authentication, encryption handshakes, and packet serialization; (3) slower connection setup and data streaming cause sessions to remain open longer, inflating the count of backend processes/threads, each holding its own memory allocations and keeping network sockets half-open; (4) clients observe rising connect and query latency, sporadic timeouts, connection refusals, and erratic throughput, while administrators see escalating resident-set size, load average, run-queue waits, TCP retransmits, and listener backlog overflows.

Causally, any of the three factors can ignite the chain: a burst of memory-hungry queries may trigger swapping, which increases CPU demand and slows packet processing; or a network slowdown can stall result delivery, causing backends to accumulate and retain their work areas, swelling memory use and spawning more worker threads that contend for CPU. Likewise, CPU saturation—whether from inefficient plans or swap storms—degrades network I/O and prolongs connection life, which in turn hoards memory buffers. The mutual reinforcement among memory exhaustion, compute starvation, and network congestion amplifies each symptom, rapidly degrading overall database availability and making it difficult to attribute blame to a single layer.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) the optimizer selecting sub-optimal execution plans, (2) the transaction-log subsystem becoming a write-path bottleneck, and (3) downstream replicas unable to receive or apply the generated log stream at the primary’s production rate. The three root causes coexist and interact, producing a compound failure that degrades both primary OLTP throughput and replica freshness.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Statements whose text is constant are intermittently re-optimized into expensive plans, causing explosive row scans, large sort or hash work-tables, and bursts of write activity. • Commit latency, log flush and sync waits, and checkpoint frequency spike as the bloated plans generate excessive redo, saturating the undersized or contended log files. • Replication monitoring shows rapidly widening send/receive and replay lags; relay or archive logs accumulate, replicas fall behind, and primary log space cannot be recycled, leading to log-file exhaustion warnings. • Operationally, users observe erratic response times, stalled write transactions during log switches, and stale or unavailable read replicas, making failover risky and maintenance windows unpredictable.

Causal chain and interaction: A poor optimizer decision (e.g., full-table scan instead of index seek, or a nested-loop with mis-estimated outer rows) dramatically inflates the volume and duration of data modifications and row versioning, which amplifies redo generation. The surge of log records overwhelms a marginal log subsystem, lengthening commit cycles and increasing the backlog of un-archived or un-flushed segments. Because replication relies on timely shipping and application of the same log stream, any slowdown in log I/O instantly throttles replica catch-up; conversely, replica lag prevents log truncation and forces the primary to retain more segments, further stressing the log disks. The prolonged commits also raise the likelihood of plan invalidations and recompilations, encouraging the optimizer to keep exploring alternative (often still sub-optimal) plans, perpetuating the high-redo pattern. Together, the three anomalies reinforce each other, producing a feedback loop that degrades write throughput, destabilizes plan selection, and jeopardizes replication SLAs.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Optimizer metadata (row counts, histograms, correlations) is stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and poor plan selection.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Under-provisioned or degraded storage devices saturate throughput, IOPS, or latency budgets, inflating physical read/write wait time.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Network transport or connection-handling resources are exhausted or unstable, delaying session establishment and result transfer.

When all three root causes are present, the database may exhibit amplified and intertwined symptoms: execution plans chosen on bad statistics drive excessive random or large-volume I/O, which immediately collides with an already saturated storage layer, inflating physical I/O latency and enlarging buffer cache churn. At the same time, client sessions experience long connection handshakes and slow data streaming; result sets linger in network queues, holding server backends in client-wait states that obscure and interleave with storage waits. Overall response times fluctuate unpredictably, AWR/monitoring views show simultaneous spikes in optimizer re-parse/recompile counts, storage-level wait events, and client/network wait events, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single subsystem.

Causal interaction: stale or missing statistics can select plans that read far more pages than necessary or force non-selective full scans; this inflated I/O demand pushes the storage system beyond its throughput ceiling, further extending statement runtimes and keeping server processes busy. The prolonged runtimes in turn hold open network sockets for longer periods and generate larger in-flight result sets, increasing connection pool occupancy and consuming listener backlog slots, which aggravates the Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly. Conversely, network stalls delay completion of queries and DML that would trigger automatic statistics refreshes, allowing statistics staleness to persist. The feedback loop between misestimated plans, storage saturation, and network congestion compounds resource contention across all three layers, severely degrading both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, forcing wait queues or deadlocks that stall or abort user work.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records pile up because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update/delete churn, causing table and index bloat and extra visibility-check overhead.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying disks or storage fabric reach their bandwidth, IOPS, or latency limits, so reads, writes, and durability flushes queue and slow down.

When all three conditions arise together, the database exhibits a compound slowdown: lock-wait events and deadlock retries spike, autovacuum or purge workers run constantly yet fall further behind, data and index files balloon, sequential scans become longer, and I/O wait dominates response-time profiles while CPU remains underutilized. Application sessions time out waiting for locks, checkpoints linger, replication falls behind, and emergency disk-space alerts appear as bloated tables consume the saturated storage.

Causally, heavy lock contention often leaves transactions open for extended periods; their old snapshots prevent MVCC cleanup from reclaiming dead versions, so the version store and table size grow. The ensuing bloat forces all readers and writers—including the very transactions holding locks—to touch more pages, inflating the volume of physical I/O. This extra traffic pushes the storage subsystem toward or past its throughput ceiling, raising read/write latencies. Elevated I/O latency prolongs lock-holding statement runtimes and further delays cleanup workers, which in turn accelerates bloat growth and perpetuates the lock backlog. The feedback loop among prolonged locks, stalled version reclamation, and saturated storage amplifies each individual anomaly, degrading overall OLTP performance far beyond their isolated effects.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or page pins, stalling while they wait for access to shared in-memory blocks.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database runs out of free physical or logical space for data files, logs, or temp areas, leading to allocation failures and write stoppages.

When these two root causes strike at the same time, the system exhibits a hybrid failure pattern: extreme buffer-busy and page-latch waits coexist with space-related allocation, extend, and redo/archive stalls. Checkpoints, background writers, and user processes spin or block on latches while dirty pages accumulate, yet they cannot be flushed because data files, temp segments, or log destinations have no room to grow. Symptoms include skyrocketing latch wait time, CPU spin without progress, repeated "no space left" or "cannot extend" errors, log switch holdups that freeze commits, and abrupt latency spikes on all I/O paths. Monitoring may show the buffer pool nearly full of dirty or pinned pages, IO throughput plummeting despite high device activity, and free-space gauges dropping to zero.

Causal chain: space exhaustion throttles or outright blocks background flushes and log writes, forcing dirty pages to remain in the buffer longer; those pages stay latched, amplifying buffer contention for every session that needs them. Simultaneously, the prolonged latch holds slow transaction throughput, so log segments remain active and cannot be recycled, accelerating space depletion in both data and log areas. Failed auto-extension attempts further increase latch hold times as processes repeatedly retry buffer flushes and metadata updates. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other: space shortages prevent relieving buffer pressure, while buffer contention slows down the very maintenance actions (flush, archive, cleanup) required to free space, driving the database into a self-sustaining spiral of stalls and eventual service outage.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table structure, partitioning, and index choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths that inflate logical and physical I/O.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is unable to deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required, so I/O queues back up and wait times dominate execution.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores are saturated by database processes, leaving insufficient compute capacity for the workload and elongating run-queue waits.

When all three root causes manifest together the database simultaneously suffers from excessive data access, stalled disk subsystems, and maxed-out CPU. Execution plans show full-table scans or non-covering index probes that issue huge I/O volumes; storage latency and queue depth spike, producing long data-file, log-write, and buffer-I/O waits; meanwhile CPU usage remains near 100 %, with high context-switch rates and scheduler waits. Application response times lengthen unpredictably, batch jobs overrun maintenance windows, and even lightweight queries experience both I/O and CPU contention, making symptoms appear systemic rather than query-specific.

Causally, the physical design mismatch is the primer: missing or ineffective indexes force scans that flood the buffer cache and drive large, random and sequential I/O. The extra traffic pushes the storage array beyond its throughput envelope, so each read or write takes longer, further prolonging query execution. Longer runtimes keep worker threads active and multiply the number of concurrent sessions, which in turn intensifies CPU consumption for predicate evaluation, sorting, and context switching. The saturated CPU then slows the I/O submission threads and background flusher processes, amplifying the storage backlog. This feedback loop between poor schema design, storage saturation, and CPU exhaustion rapidly degrades overall database performance and obscures the original design flaw behind cascading resource bottlenecks.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions block or deadlock each other while waiting on mutually incompatible locks managed by the lock manager.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots inside the buffer manager, stalling logical I/O even when row-level locks are free.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, driving long run queues and scheduler waits regardless of which logical layer issues the work.

When all three anomalies arise together, the system experiences intertwined blocking at multiple layers: row/table locks queue transactions; those waiting transactions continue to hold buffer pins and latches, inflating internal contention; meanwhile the accumulation of spin-loops, latch retries, deadlock detectors, and repeated application retries drives CPU utilization to saturation. Observable effects include explosive wait-event diversity (lock waits, buffer-busy waits, latch spins, and CPU run-queue waits), steep increases in end-to-end latency, throughput collapse, escalating deadlock victim counts, and connection pools that exhaust while CPUs remain pegged at or near 100 percent.

Causal chain: a small set of hot rows or pages first triggers lock contention; blocked sessions keep their buffer pages pinned and repeatedly wake to recheck lock status, amplifying buffer-cache and latch contention. The extra spin/wakeup activity multiplies CPU demand, and the over-utilized CPUs delay the lock manager, latch acquisition, and I/O completion, lengthening critical sections and further widening lock and latch queues. The feedback loop between lock holding, buffer/latch hot spots, and CPU saturation creates a self-reinforcing spiral that rapidly degrades overall database performance until one or more pressure points are relieved.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite adequate statistics, yielding unexpected access paths, join orders, or parallelism settings.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on shared resources, causing prolonged blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume most available CPU cycles, driving the host into sustained compute saturation.

When these three root causes strike together, the system experiences a feedback loop of performance degradation. Sub-optimal plans inflate statement runtimes, touch more rows or pages, and often escalate lock scope, greatly increasing the number and duration of locks held. The enlarged lock footprint causes extensive blocking and deadlocks, which in turn stall sessions and prompt repeated retries or rollbacks that further elevate CPU usage. Meanwhile, the excessive CPU demand produced by the inefficient plans and by the lock manager’s heightened deadlock detection intensifies scheduler run-queue pressure, slowing the progress of already blocked or victimized transactions. Observable symptoms therefore overlap and amplify: frequent plan flip-flops, full-table scans or wide nested loops appearing in execution plans; growing lock-wait and deadlock counts alongside application timeouts; and host CPU utilization pegged near 100 %, with lock-manager and user sessions topping the CPU list. Latency balloons across both read and write paths, connection pools back up, and overall throughput collapses.

Causally, a single plan regression can trigger the entire cascade: the poor plan prolongs execution and holds locks longer, which raises contention. The ensuing blocking stretches transaction lifetimes, magnifying lock footprints and spawning deadlocks. Every retry or victim rollback feeds additional optimizer compilations and execution attempts, compounding CPU demand. In parallel, CPU saturation slows the lock-granting and deadlock-detection threads, lengthening wait times even further. The intertwined effects create a self-reinforcing spiral in which each anomaly deepens the others, dramatically worsening the database’s operational state until one of the root causes is resolved.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Cardinality and cost inputs fed to the optimizer are stale, incomplete, or misleading, systematically skewing plan selection away from what the actual data distribution would require.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates or retains more memory than the host can supply, resulting in sustained memory pressure, paging, and frequent work-area spills.

When both anomalies manifest simultaneously, the workload exhibits compounded symptoms: queries whose row-count estimates are far below reality may choose memory-hungry hash joins or large in-memory sorts that instantly overrun the already stressed memory envelope; conversely, gross over-estimates may inflate work-area reservations, accelerating buffer-cache eviction and swap activity. Operators that spill to disk because memory is exhausted can generate long execution times, burst I/O, and additional temp-space consumption, while concurrent sessions experience erratic performance and higher CPU wait-for-memory stalls. Monitoring shows a mix of extreme estimate-vs-actual divergences, rapid growth of per-query memory allocations, resident-set inflation, and frequent re-optimization or cursor reloading as memory pressure forces plan cache purges.

Causal interaction: stale or absent statistics mislead the optimizer into selecting plans whose memory footprint is either unintentionally huge or cannot be honored under current load. Those oversized allocations accelerate the memory-allocation anomaly, pushing the engine into aggressive paging or global memory pressure states. In turn, memory pressure triggers more spills and longer runtimes, delaying or canceling automatic statistics refresh jobs and keeping statistics stale, thereby reinforcing the optimizer error. The feedback loop magnifies both root causes, degrading throughput and threatening node stability across OLTP and analytical workloads alike.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model objects (tables, partitions, indexes, constraints, data types) are misaligned with workload access patterns, forcing even well-written SQL to use inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer, despite having reasonably fresh statistics, picks a noticeably sub-optimal execution plan because of cost-model errors, plan reuse quirks, or context-dependent decisions.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a static physical design mismatch and an optimizer that frequently selects poor plans. Together they create an environment where sub-optimal plans are not only likely but also have no viable physical structures to fall back on, leading to extreme and unpredictable performance degradation.

Combined anomalous phenomena:  • Rampant full-table or full-index scans, some caused by missing or non-covering indexes and others by bad plan choices, making it difficult to attribute blame to a single layer.  • Wild plan variability between executions: one run may scan an entire unpartitioned table, another may attempt an index access that still requires many random I/Os because the index lacks needed columns.  • Sudden latency spikes after plan-cache invalidation, statistics refresh, or workload shifts, where a new but still poor plan amplifies the cost of an already inefficient physical design.  • Excessive CPU and I/O on both read and write paths—writes suffer from bloated or redundant indexes while reads suffer from mis-chosen join orders and scan methods.  • Performance only stabilizes when both an index is added/restructured AND plan guidance (hints, baselines) is applied, indicating the interplay of the two root causes.

Causal chain and interaction: Poor physical design supplies the optimizer with limited efficient choices; at the same time, plan-selection anomalies make the optimizer pick from those limited choices poorly. The absence of well-targeted or covering indexes inflates the estimated cost of index access, biasing the cost model toward full scans; conversely, an inaccurate cost model may underestimate the benefit of the few useful indexes that do exist, leaving them unused and masking the design flaw from simple index-usage reports. Plan reuse with skewed parameters can lock the system into a bad plan that is especially harmful given the table and index shortcomings. Together, the anomalies reinforce each other: inadequate structures magnify the impact of bad plans, while bad plans discourage investment in better structures by hiding or misrepresenting their benefit, leading to a feedback loop of degraded performance across both OLTP and OLAP workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements or transaction boundaries are written in a way that forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions request mutually incompatible locks on the same resource, causing queues, blocking chains, or deadlocks in the lock manager.

When both root causes are present, the oversized or poorly filtered statements produced by the SQL Workload Logic Anomaly inflate the number of rows scanned, updated, or held open in a transaction. This broad lock footprint collides with other concurrent transactions, leading to prolonged blocking chains, frequent deadlocks, rising lock-wait times, and sharply deteriorating throughput. Symptoms include the same slow or long-running statements repeatedly appearing in both slow-query and lock-diagnostic logs, lock-wait metrics climbing in parallel with query execution time, application timeouts that coincide with deadlock victim rollbacks, and connection pools backing up even when hardware resources are not saturated.

Causally, inefficient workload logic extends transaction duration and expands the set of locked resources, thereby amplifying the probability and severity of lock contention. In turn, lock waits stall the inflated statements even longer, further lengthening transaction lifetimes and broadening their lock scopes. This positive feedback loop magnifies performance degradation, makes individual root causes harder to isolate, and can push the database into a persistent low-throughput, high-latency state until either the workload logic is corrected or lock pressure is relieved.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or missing optimizer metadata causes systematic cardinality misestimation and drives the optimizer toward sub-optimal plans.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level parameters (memory pools, parallelism, checkpoint cadence, etc.) are mis-tuned so that runtime behavior diverges from hardware capacity and workload demands.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, or temporary areas reaches hard limits, producing allocation failures and stalls.

When all three anomalies coexist, symptoms overlap and amplify: plans chosen on the basis of wrong statistics request excessive parallel workers or memory, but mis-set parameters cap usable resources, forcing large intermediate results to spill to TEMP. Repeated spills, enlarged by the same misestimates, quickly consume remaining tempfiles or tablespace quota, producing “no space left” errors, session aborts, or sudden query slowdowns. Simultaneously, undersized redo/log areas configured by poor parameters fill faster because mis-planned queries generate bloated undo and redo; once full, checkpoints and log switches stall foreground activity, appearing as log-write or buffer-busy waits even though I/O bandwidth is idle. Automatic statistics refresh jobs may fail to run or to persist results when catalog tablespaces are full, freezing bad statistics in place and masking the original cause. Monitoring will show a confusing mix of cardinality skew, memory-related spills, unexpected parallel downgrade, and space-exhaustion alerts, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing resource-hungry execution strategies (e.g., multi-way hash joins, wide index scans) that inflate memory and temp usage. Misconfigured parameters—such as low work-memory, aggressive checkpoint intervals, or small temp/log file size caps—prevent the engine from absorbing these demands, forcing spills and frequent checkpoints that intensify I/O and space consumption. The resulting surge in temp and log growth accelerates storage exhaustion. Once space becomes scarce, mandatory operations like statistics persistence, temp allocation, or log archival begin to fail, which in turn blocks auto-statistics refresh and increases plan staleness, creating a positive feedback loop that rapidly degrades overall performance and availability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (table layout, indexes, partitioning, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of statistics freshness.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Replication pipeline cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo at the rate generated by the primary, leading to widening log-position gaps and retention of log files.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database or replication processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, I/O contexts, or cgroup quotas, causing allocation failures at the OS level.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, symptoms intertwine: 1) primary queries and background writers suffer high latency from full scans and non-covering index probes; 2) the heavier I/O and CPU load generated by those inefficient plans inflates the volume and velocity of transaction-log output; 3) replicas already starved for apply bandwidth fall further behind, exhibiting rapidly growing receive, write, flush, and replay lag; 4) as backlog accumulates, both primary and replica retain more WAL segments and relay files, increasing file-descriptor consumption and exacerbating kernel-level limits; 5) once per-process or cgroup caps for file handles, shared memory, or asynchronous I/O are exhausted, new client sessions, parallel workers, or replication threads fail to start, producing intermittent errors even for previously healthy operations; 6) monitoring shows simultaneous query slowdowns, replication delay spikes, and OS messages about ENFILE/EMFILE, out-of-shared-memory, or semaphore-allocation failures, making diagnosis difficult because each symptom can mask or mimic the others.

Causal chain: A poor schema/index design forces the engine to scan more pages and generate larger undo/redo records per transaction. The inflated WAL stream stresses the replication subsystem; apply threads on replicas must process more data per commit, which magnifies any existing network or CPU bottlenecks. As replicas lag, the primary is prevented from recycling old log segments, increasing on-disk log retention and the number of open file descriptors. The larger working-set and lingering logs require additional shared memory and kernel I/O contexts. Simultaneously, the extra CPU threads spawned for long-running queries and delayed replication apply workers drive process/thread counts upward. These cumulative pressures collide with conservative OS limits, causing resource-allocation failures that in turn throttle query execution and replication even further. The feedback loop—inefficient access paths → higher WAL volume → replication backlog → elevated kernel object usage → OS denials → further slowdown—creates a severe, multi-layer outage that is harder to resolve than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database engine is simultaneously mis-configured at the internal parameter level while also experiencing scarcity or instability in the network / connection-handling layer. The first root cause compromises how the server allocates memory, workers, checkpoints, and connection slots; the second restricts or delays the flow of client traffic to those same resources. Together they form a compound bottleneck that can manifest even when underlying CPU, memory, and storage hardware are not fully utilized.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Sudden surges of "too many connections" or authentication timeouts followed by log-write or buffer-pin waits inside already connected sessions. • Listener backlog overflows that coincide with background writers or checkpointers awakening more frequently than expected. • In-flight transactions stalling on client-read/client-write events while the server side simultaneously shows idle CPU yet elevated spin or latch contention because work-memory, parallelism, or buffer-pool sizes were tuned for a higher throughput than the unstable network can deliver. • Rapid oscillation between under-utilization (due to absent clients) and burst saturation (due to retry storms) that triggers checkpoint storms, aggressive WAL flushing, or worker exhaustion dictated by the mis-set parameters. • OS socket tables and database backend counts both hitting their respective limits, producing a mixture of connection-refused errors and internal "resource busy" wait events that are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain: Poorly calibrated configuration parameters (e.g., oversized connection limit, undersized work-memory, aggressive checkpoint cadence) raise the sensitivity of the engine to fluctuations in connection rate and traffic volume. When the network layer concurrently suffers congestion, packet loss, or listener queue exhaustion, clients perform retries or leave half-open sockets that consume the very connection slots the engine over-allocated. This inflates backend processes/threads, increases per-session memory pressure, and forces more frequent checkpoints or log flushes. These engine-level side effects, in turn, lengthen transaction latency, causing yet more client-side timeouts and retransmissions that further stress network and socket resources. The feedback loop between parameter misconfiguration and network resource exhaustion amplifies both problems, obscures the true root causes, and can degrade throughput and stability well beyond what either anomaly would cause in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously suffers from unchecked growth of obsolete MVCC row versions and rollback records while also exhausting critical kernel-level resources (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, threads, etc.) enforced by the operating system. The two root causes coexist and interact, producing a compound failure mode that is more severe than either anomaly on its own.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Administrators observe rapidly increasing dead-tuple ratios, bloated tables and indexes, and cleanup workers that are unable to keep pace; at the same time the engine begins to emit errors about failing to open files, create background or parallel workers, or attach to shared memory. Autovacuum/VACUUM jobs may start and immediately abort due to inability to acquire additional file handles or shared-memory slots, causing the version store to grow even faster. Long-running queries and replication slots hold old snapshots, while new sessions intermittently fail to connect. Query latencies rise because of swollen page scans, and partial outages emerge where existing back-ends remain active but maintenance and new work cannot proceed.

Causal interaction: MVCC bloat drives increased I/O, additional temporary files, more background vacuum workers, and larger shared-memory requests—directly inflating consumption of kernel resources such as file descriptors and shm segments. Simultaneously, hitting OS limits throttles or terminates the very maintenance workers needed to reclaim dead versions, so version accumulation accelerates. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the other: MVCC churn pushes the system toward OS ceilings, and the OS ceilings prevent cleanup, creating a feedback loop that rapidly degrades performance, threatens transaction-ID wraparound, and can culminate in a service-level outage.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between table structures / indexes and the workload forces queries into wide scans, non-covering lookups, and write hot-spots.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine parameters for memory, parallelism, checkpoints, and workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload mix.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate memory consumed by caches, work areas, and sessions exceeds the safe limit of the host, provoking OS-level pressure or OOM events.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: 1) full-table or full-index scans initiated by poor schema design allocate large work-memory regions that grow unchecked because per-query and per-session limits are misconfigured; 2) the bloated memory footprint collides with an undersized or overgrown buffer pool, causing rapid eviction, cache-hit volatility, and emergency flushes; 3) checkpoint storms, log-write stalls, or background-worker backlogs appear while CPU and I/O devices remain paradoxically under-utilised; 4) the host shows paging, swap thrashing, or abrupt process termination, after which execution plans may oscillate unpredictably as statistics, caches, and parameter adaptive features struggle to stabilise.

Causal chain: Inefficient access paths produced by the schema/index mismatch dramatically increase the volume of rows read, sorted, and hashed. Because configuration parameters such as work-memory, temp-space thresholds, buffer-pool size, and parallel-worker caps are mis-set, each inflated operation reserves more memory than the host can realistically supply. The resulting ballooning of session and cache memory triggers the memory-allocation anomaly, pushing the operating system into paging and forcing the database to flush or evict useful buffers prematurely. These evictions, in turn, magnify the original design flaw by making every repeated table or index scan re-read pages from disk. Meanwhile, mis-tuned checkpoint and background housekeeping parameters amplify I/O bursts caused by the additional dirty pages. The feedback loop between bad access paths, misallocated resources, and systemic memory pressure leads to cascading slowdowns, erratic throughput, and, in extreme cases, service instability or crashes.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages or latches, causing page-level stalls despite adequate overall memory size.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Underlying disks or storage fabric reach their throughput/IOPS ceiling, stretching read- and write-service times well beyond the engine’s expectations.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced quotas on file descriptors, shared memory, async-I/O contexts, or threads are exhausted, blocking further resource acquisition by the database process.

When all three conditions arise together, the wait profile is dominated by a chaotic mix of buffer-busy/latch waits, abnormally long I/O latencies, and intermittent "cannot allocate <kernel object>" errors. Checkpoint, buffer flush, and log-flush events stay in flight far longer than usual, keeping dirty pages pinned and intensifying latch contention. CPU usage oscillates between spin-waiting on latches and idle periods while sessions sleep on I/O or kernel resource waits. Connection spikes, bulk loads, or index maintenance can suddenly tip the system into a state where new back-end or parallel workers fail to start, even as existing sessions hang on buffer pins.

Causal chain: Saturated storage slows every page read and dirty-page write, lengthening the window during which pages remain pinned and latches are held. Extended latch hold times magnify buffer-cache contention, increasing the number of concurrent sessions stalled in spin loops or waiting queues. To compensate, the engine issues more outstanding I/O and spawns additional background workers, pushing file handles, async-I/O rings, and thread counts toward their OS limits. Once those limits are hit, further I/O submission or worker creation is denied by the kernel, creating a feedback loop where buffers cannot be flushed or read, latches remain locked, and the transaction and query workload deteriorates rapidly.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements and transaction scopes are written in a way that forces the engine to process, lock, or return more data than the business logic actually requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer’s metadata is stale or incomplete, leading to systematic cardinality misestimation and poor plan choices.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures are corrupted or internally inconsistent, making on-disk data no longer fully trustworthy.

When these three root causes coexist, the database can exhibit an unusually wide spectrum of symptoms: extreme and highly variable statement latency, repeated slow-query log entries, sudden switches from index seeks to full table scans, estimator-vs-actual row count gaps that grow with each plan execution, unexpected duplicate or missing rows in result sets, CRC or page-checksum errors surfacing only on certain access paths, frequent plan recompilations, and cascading application timeouts or deadlocks as long-running transactions collide with corruption-triggered lock escalations or error retries. Because each anomaly can mask or amplify the others, the operational picture becomes noisy—making it difficult to tell whether performance, correctness, or physical health is the primary issue on any given statement.

Causal interaction: poorly written workload patterns generate oversized scans, floods of singleton lookups, and long-lived transactions that churn large portions of the data set. This high change rate prevents automatic statistics thresholds from firing in time and accelerates divergence between real and recorded data distributions, which in turn pushes the optimizer toward plans that touch even more pages. The broadened I/O surface area increases the likelihood of hitting latent corrupt pages or split-brain index chains. Once corruption is encountered, the engine may invalidate or bypass indexes, forcing further full scans that magnify both the workload stress and the statistical drift. The feedback loop—inefficient workload causing stale statistics, stale statistics producing expansionary plans, and those plans exposing corruption that then eliminates efficient access paths—rapidly degrades overall performance and reliability, while making root-cause isolation far more complex.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution statistics are stale, absent, or incomplete, causing the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal access paths and join orders.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort user work.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates more working memory than the host can safely supply, triggering paging, OOM events, and cache-turnover stalls.

When all three root causes strike together, the system exhibits a mixed pattern of symptoms: queries generate poor plans that scan far more rows than expected, inflating their lock footprint and holding locks for longer; the resulting lock queues lengthen response-time tails, while sessions that are blocked still retain work buffers, plan cache entries, and pinned pages, accelerating memory growth. Under continued pressure, the host begins swapping, which in turn extends lock-hold durations and widens the gap between estimated and actual execution times. Administrators may observe exploding waits on both locks and memory pressure, frequent deadlock reports interleaved with out-of-memory terminations, erratic query throughput, and plan re-compilations that repeatedly pick inefficient paths because statistics remain stale.

Causal interaction: stale or missing statistics push the optimizer toward full scans, broad range scans, or unordered join strategies, greatly increasing the number of rows touched and thus the number and duration of locks acquired. The enlarged lock footprint heightens the probability of contention and deadlocks in a highly concurrent OLTP workload. While sessions wait, they keep their allocated work buffers, pinned cache pages, and partially filled hash/sort areas, inflating overall memory consumption. Rising memory pressure forces the OS to page or the engine to trim caches, prolonging I/O latency, which further lengthens transaction execution and lock holding periods—a positive feedback loop that reinforces both lock contention and memory exhaustion. Because blocking prevents timely data changes from committing, statistics refresh jobs may be delayed, perpetuating the optimizer-statistics inaccuracy and deepening the cycle.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite accurate statistics, leading to excessive I/O, CPU, or row versions.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, log file, flushing, or archiving—cannot keep pace with redo generation, inflating commit latency and stalling writers.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, I/O contexts, threads, or shared memory are reached, preventing the database from allocating the low-level resources it needs.

When these three root causes arise together, workloads experience a perfect storm of symptoms: queries unexpectedly switch from efficient indexed access to scan-heavy or nested-loop plans that emit far more redo, causing explosive growth in transaction-log volume. The log device shows sustained 100 % utilization, with surging log flush and commit wait times. Simultaneously, the database and archiver processes begin reporting "too many open files," "cannot allocate shared memory," or "AIO context limit reached," further throttling log writes and causing checkpoints, replication catch-up, or crash-recovery to stall. Applications observe erratic response times—some statements hang on plan compilation or commit, others fail outright with OS-level resource errors—while existing sessions linger in lock-held states, amplifying contention.

Causally, a bad plan that scans or loops excessively multiplies the volume of row modifications and undo/redo records, driving the log subsystem toward saturation. As log flush latency rises, transactions take longer to commit, leading to a backlog of database processes waiting on log space or syncs. This surge in concurrent waiting sessions grows the number of open files, I/O requests, threads, and shared-memory attachments, quickly consuming the host’s kernel quotas. Once OS limits are hit, the database can no longer create additional log write contexts, archiver threads, or temporary files, which further slows or blocks both query compilation and log flushing. The feedback loop between poor plan-induced write amplification, an overtaxed log path, and hard OS ceilings escalates into widespread slowdown or partial outage, making each individual anomaly harder to diagnose and resolve in isolation.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, log buffer size, parallelism, connection limits, etc.) are mis-calibrated with respect to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path—generation, buffering, flushing, switching, or archiving—cannot sustain the redo rate and therefore becomes the primary bottleneck on commits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, authentication, or socket resources between clients and the database server are saturated or unreliable, throttling request flow and result delivery.

When all three faults manifest together, the instance exhibits a dense mix of wait events: sessions stall on LOG FLUSH/LOG WRITE while socket queues simultaneously back up with CLIENT WRITE or CLIENT READ waits; transaction commit latency and connection-establishment timeouts rise in tandem; checkpoint storms and rapid log-file switches coincide with surges of half-open or aborted TCP sessions; archive-lag alarms and replication backlog grow while network retransmissions and round-trip times spike. Performance counters may misleadingly show low CPU and storage utilization because throttling moves upstream to the configuration-limited log buffer and the saturated network layer.

Causal chain: Mis-tuned configuration parameters (e.g., undersized log buffer, aggressive checkpoint interval, synchronous-commit mode, or excessively high connection cap) increase the frequency and volume of log flushes. The already stressed transaction-log subsystem cannot clear buffers fast enough, lengthening commit critical paths. Prolonged commit waits hold backend processes in a socket-write state, inflating the number of active connections and consuming the listener backlog. The congested network further delays replication or archiver shipping, which in turn prevents log file reuse and forces even more frequent log switches and checkpoints. Each layer’s slowdown feeds the next: bad parameters amplify log pressure, log pressure amplifies network queuing, and network lag prevents log archival, starving the log subsystem of free segments and cascading into a full-system throughput collapse.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrency hotspots inside the buffer manager force sessions to serialize on page-latch or pin operations, inflating CPU spin time and I/O churn.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, threads, shared memory, or other per-process/host objects prevent the database from acquiring the resources it needs to run new work.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Server-side listener, socket, or authentication capacity is exhausted or slow, producing connection errors, half-open sockets, and client-side timeouts.

When these three root causes manifest together, the instance experiences a compound performance collapse: hot pages already gating throughput hold back worker threads that are themselves scarce because the OS will not create more. Existing backends spend longer in latch wait or spin loops while new clients repeatedly retry connections, swelling the inbound socket backlog. System views show simultaneous surges in page-latch waits, failures to fork or create threads, and connection refusals.
