This sustained pressure forces the storage layer into throughput saturation, prolonging every I/O and keeping queue depths persistently high. The prolonged queues, in turn, require more kernel objects—threads, async-I/O contexts, file descriptors—which quickly consume the OS resource quotas. Once these limits are breached, the database engine can neither launch relief workers nor open additional files, so the mis-configuration and storage congestion self-reinforce, driving the system into a cascading slowdown that is far more severe than any of the three anomalies would cause in isolation.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer repeatedly chooses sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are sound, leading to excessive I/O, CPU, or parallel-execution misuse.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot buffer pages and their protecting latches become points of serialization, stalling sessions that compete for page access or page-state changes.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys cannot receive, write, or apply primary log records fast enough, producing widening replication lag and preventing log recycling.

When these three root causes manifest together, the database shows an explosive mix of symptoms: single statements oscillate between fast and extremely slow runtimes, while system-wide wait profiles are dominated by buffer-busy and page-latch waits. Concurrently, replication dashboards report growing receive/write/replay lag, swollen relay or retained log segments, and stale read-only replicas. Primary nodes exhibit CPU spin and erratic throughput as queries hammer hot pages; replicas inherit both the sub-optimal plans (through statement shipping or view routing) and the same latch hotspots during redo-apply or read traffic, amplifying their own delay. Checkpoints lengthen, dirty-page queues build up, and storage I/O saturates, further inflating query latency and replica catch-up times.

Causally, a bad plan that favors full scans or high-fan-out nested loops generates a flood of logical reads, concentrating activity on a narrow set of root or data pages. This magnifies latch contention in the buffer manager, slowing every session—including the background processes that flush dirty buffers and ship or apply WAL/redo. The prolonged execution times inflate transaction size and log volume, causing the primary to outpace replica apply rates. The ensuing replication lag prevents log-segment recycling, keeping more pages dirty for longer and extending checkpoint cycles, which in turn deepens buffer churn and latch pressure. The feedback loop between poor plan choice, buffer-cache contention, and replication backlog progressively degrades both primary and replica performance until all tiers are simultaneously bottlenecked.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from uncontrolled growth and pressure in engine memory structures while the transaction-log subsystem becomes a bottleneck for commit processing and log maintenance, causing intertwined resource exhaustion on both memory and log-write paths.

Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or ungoverned consumption of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other in-process heaps that pushes the host beyond its safe physical or virtual memory limits.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Saturation or stall of the write-ahead logging pipeline—generation, buffering, flushing, switching, or archiving—so that commit latency and log-related waits dominate foreground response times.

Combined Phenomena: When these root causes coincide, users observe sharp and erratic increases in transaction commit latency, sporadic hangs during checkpoints or log switches, and surges in memory-related wait events (e.g., latch or spin contention on shared buffers). The database process RSS balloons while the operating system begins paging, which further slows log-buffer flushes. Checkpoint storms, log-archive backlogs, and replication lag expand alongside dropping cache hit ratios, frequent worker memory spills, and OOM terminations. Performance metrics show intertwined CPU stalls on memory pressure and log-sync waits, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single layer. Clustered or virtualized nodes may be evicted as both memory starvation and prolonged I/O times violate health thresholds.

Causal Interaction: Excessive in-memory allocations inflate the log-buffer contents (larger hash/sort results, bigger undo segments, expanded cache metadata), generating a higher redo rate that intensifies pressure on already constrained log files. Conversely, log-flush slowdowns lengthen transaction lifetimes, holding work and session memory for longer and preventing allocations from being released, which amplifies overall memory consumption. Paging triggered by memory overcommit further degrades log-write throughput, while blocked commits keep more sessions active, snowballing both anomalies. This positive feedback loop quickly degrades throughput and stability, making remediation of either layer alone insufficient until both memory governance and log subsystem capacity are addressed.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The system simultaneously experiences a Query Plan Selection Anomaly, in which the optimizer reuses or chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite accurate statistics, and a Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly, in which sessions block or spin while fighting for access to hot buffer pages, page pins, or latches inside the buffer manager.

Combined phenomena: The workload shows erratic plan flips, sudden shifts to full table scans or explosive nested-loop joins that dramatically raise page touches per statement. Concurrently, wait-event dashboards light up with buffer busy waits, page-latch or spinlock stalls, and CPU burn without matching throughput. I/O volumes surge because poorly chosen plans thrash the buffer pool, while latch contention lengthens critical sections, making individual statements slower and widening latency variance. Execution plans appear to deteriorate further under heavy concurrency, and end-to-end response times fluctuate unpredictably, obscuring whether the bottleneck is in execution logic or memory access.

Causal chain: Inefficient plans inflate logical I/O, repeatedly hammering a small set of root pages, index leaves, or temporary work tables, concentrating traffic on a handful of buffers and amplifying latch contention. The resulting stalls prolong statement runtimes and delay completion of data-modifying operations, which keeps those same hot pages pinned even longer, further escalating contention. Extended latch waits can, in turn, trigger automatic recompiles, plan cache evictions, or adaptive plan changes that pick yet another sub-optimal plan, creating a feedback loop. Together, the two root causes reinforce each other, driving up CPU spin, blocking time, and I/O pressure, and making the overall performance degradation deeper and harder to diagnose than either anomaly in isolation.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : A static mismatch between table structure, partitioning, and indexing versus actual access patterns, forcing scans and non-covering lookups that bloat I/O and touch far more rows or pages than necessary.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger rollbacks or timeouts.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path—buffer, files, flushing, or archiving—cannot absorb the redo volume, so commits stall on log-write, switch, or archive waits.

When these three root causes are present simultaneously, the database experiences a cascade of compounding symptoms: inefficient queries read or modify large row sets, acquiring wider or higher-level locks; those locks are held longer because each commit must wait for a slow log flush; prolonged lock holding inflates blocking queues, raises deadlock frequency, and pushes more sessions into retry loops. Meanwhile, the same lock contention and repeated rollbacks intensify redo generation, further saturating the log subsystem. Observable metrics therefore show a mixture of full-scan plans, skyrocketing buffer and physical reads, lock and deadlock wait events, steadily rising log-write and log-sync waits, checkpoint storms, and sudden collapses in transaction throughput that recover only after both indexing/design fixes and log-path relief are applied.

Causally, missing or poorly chosen indexes inflate the data footprint of each statement, so even simple lookups convert to large scans or range updates that require broad row/page locks. The greater the locked footprint, the higher the probability that concurrent sessions collide, escalating to page or table locks. Each blocked or deadlocked transaction must later redo its work, doubling log traffic. Simultaneously, the oversized DML operations and additional rollbacks swell redo volume per transaction, quickly overrunning an already undersized or slow log subsystem. Log flush delays lengthen transaction lifetimes, keeping locks active and propagating contention to other sessions. The feedback loop—poor design → bigger locks → slower commits → longer lock retention → more contention and redo → worse log pressure—drives the system into a self-reinforcing performance spiral until both the schema/index issues and log throughput bottleneck are resolved.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions, rollback records, and deleted index entries because background cleaners cannot keep up.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk data pages or index structures become physically or logically corrupt, breaking key order, page links, or heap–index mappings.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer is saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, causing prolonged waits on reads, writes, and durability flushes.

When all three root causes are present, the database exhibits a blended symptom set: version stores and rollback segments expand rapidly while VACUUM or purge workers are throttled by slow I/O, causing autovacuum backlogs and rising transaction-ID age. Concurrently, corruption in indexes or data pages yields mismatches between index and heap counts, checksum errors, and sudden plan shifts to sequential scans. The shift to full scans and repeated page re-reads inflate I/O demand, further overwhelming an already saturated storage subsystem; meanwhile corruption-induced retries, double-reads for verification, or forced page repairs increase latency variability and queue depth. Administrators observe a vicious cycle of longer query response times, high I/O wait, bloated tables, integrity-check failures, and relentless engine warnings about wraparound, corruption, and I/O stalls—making it difficult to distinguish which subsystem is primarily at fault.

Causally, saturated storage slows the purge and vacuum processes needed to reclaim obsolete versions, allowing version bloat to escalate. The larger heaps and indexes produced by this bloat in turn require more pages to be read and written, amplifying I/O pressure. Simultaneously, any latent corruption—perhaps triggered by prior I/O errors or abrupt shutdowns—causes index lookups to fail and the planner to fall back to heap scans, dramatically multiplying I/O volume and exposing additional corrupt pages. Each corrupt-page encounter can force re-reads or page-level recovery writes, further congesting the storage path. The compounded effect is a reinforcing feedback loop where I/O saturation, version bloat, and structural corruption mutually aggravate one another, accelerating performance degradation and threatening data availability.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are sound, yielding overly expensive operators or inappropriate join methods.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Database components (buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, etc.) collectively consume more physical memory than the host can sustain, driving paging, OOM events, and cache churn.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Data files, temp areas, or log/backup destinations run out of free space, leading to allocation failures and stalled workload progress.

When these three root causes strike together, the workload may oscillate between memory and storage crises: bad plans inflate work-area demand and fragment the buffer-pool, which in turn forces large sorts, hashes, or spill files into already constrained temporary or log spaces. Operators may start in memory, then spill to disk, rapidly depleting free space; once space is exhausted, the same statements abort with "out of space" or "cannot allocate” errors, while concurrent sessions experience severe latency from swapping, frequent plan cache evictions, and erratic plan flips. Background processes struggle to extend datafiles or recycle logs, leading to checkpoint stalls, replication lag, and even instance terminations.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan (1) amplifies memory consumption (e.g., choosing hash joins over indexed lookups, or requesting large sort buffers). The inflated work areas push the engine beyond physical RAM, activating the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly; paging and memory pressure then force operators to dump intermediate results to temporary storage. Those spills, plus bloated logs from long-running, poorly planned queries, quickly exhaust tablespace, temp, and archive destinations, triggering the Storage Space Capacity Anomaly. Conversely, once space fills, the optimizer may reject optimal index or parallel plans that require additional scratch or log space, defaulting to even heavier full scans or serial plans, further prolonging memory residency and perpetuating the vicious cycle. The intertwined feedback loops between bad plans, runaway memory growth, and space exhaustion dramatically degrade both transactional and analytical workloads and can culminate in service outages.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing costly access paths regardless of optimizer or statistics quality.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Oversubscription or mis-sizing of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine heaps that pushes the host into paging, swapping, or OOM situations, degrading cache efficiency and stability.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk pages and index structures, leading to incorrect or unpredictable data retrieval and engine error conditions.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blended failure signature: 1) queries repeatedly fall back from expected index seeks to full scans because damaged or ill-chosen indexes cannot be trusted or do not satisfy predicates; 2) the resulting large I/O and memory-hungry hash/sort operations inflate buffer and work memory usage, driving the engine past safe memory limits and provoking sustained OS paging, swap storms, or forced process terminations; 3) memory pressure amplifies corruption symptoms as dirty buffers are flushed and re-read, causing sporadic checksum failures, latch contention, and plan cache evictions; 4) application sessions observe erratic latency spikes, intermittent wrong-result sets, and sudden node restarts that are hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causal chain: a poor schema/index design expands I/O footprints and work-area sizes, directly increasing memory consumption. The inflated memory demand collides with already aggressive or uncapped allocations, tipping the system into memory pressure that magnifies every access inefficiency. Under stress, the engine touches more pages, including already corrupted ones; repeated reads of damaged pages trigger additional retries, checksum validations, or forced full-table scans, which further bloat memory and I/O load. Conversely, memory exhaustion can lead to incomplete writes, interrupted index rebuilds, or crash-recovery gaps, injecting fresh corruption into data blocks and indexes. The corruption then erodes optimizer trust in existing indexes, pushing even more queries onto the pathologically designed fallback scans and perpetuating a vicious cycle of design inefficiency, memory depletion, and structural corruption.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing inputs (row counts, histograms, correlations) are stale or absent, driving systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan selection.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Access to popular buffer pages is serialized by heavy latch or pin waits, causing sessions to stall or spin while competing for the same in-memory blocks.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, exhausting scheduler capacity and inflating run-queue and context-switch overhead regardless of the logical origin of the demand.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the workload exhibits a mixture of misleading estimates, acute page-level hot spots, and full CPU saturation. Queries whose plans were already risky because of wrong statistics may choose nested-loop joins on underestimated result sets or full scans on underestimated large tables; both inflate logical I/O, repeatedly touch a small set of root or bitmap pages, and amplify latch waits. Sessions spin on buffer latches, inflating CPU consumption without progressing work, driving overall host utilization to 100 %. As CPU headroom disappears, latency balloons across the instance, autovacuum or automatic-statistics jobs fall further behind, and wait-event dashboards show alternating bursts of “latch: buffer busy”, “CPU run queue”, and “cardinality feedback” events, making the true culprit hard to pinpoint.

Causally, stale or missing statistics (1) misdirect the optimizer into plans that concentrate reads or writes on a few pages. This creates artificial hot pages that (2) trigger buffer-cache latch contention; the spin-loop behavior of those latches (3) burns CPU cycles, escalating the CPU Resource Anomaly. In turn, CPU starvation delays background I/O writers and statistics jobs, allowing statistics to grow even staler and hot pages to stay longer in cache, which perpetuates the latch conflict. Thus all three anomalies form a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades throughput far more severely than any single anomaly in isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer statement or transaction design that forces the engine to read or write more data, rows, or time than business logic actually requires.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Mis-tuned engine parameters governing memory, logging, checkpointing, parallelism, or connection limits that are out of line with hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Saturation, misconfiguration, or instability in the network or listener layer that restricts the rate at which clients can establish or sustain database connections and move result bytes.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, observable symptoms spread across every tier: statement execution times become highly variable, slow-query logs fill with the same chatty or wide-scan SQL, while server metrics show erratic buffer-pool hit ratios, bursty checkpoint or log-write waits even though CPU or I/O may appear underutilized. Concurrently, clients experience intermittent connection timeouts, increased authentication latency, and stalled result streaming, leading to retry storms that inflate transaction concurrency. Internal views may show innocent-looking wait events alternating between client-read/client-write, configuration-induced stalls (e.g., small log buffers or aggressive checkpoints), and long-running scans triggered by unfocused predicates—all blending into a hard-to-separate symptom set.

Causal chain: chatty or bloated SQL overwhelms memory and I/O; if configuration parameters such as work-memory, buffer-pool size, max connections, or checkpoint cadence are set too low or too aggressive, the engine thrashes—evicting hot pages, flushing dirty buffers, and throttling background writers. These stalls lengthen transaction lifetimes, keeping sockets open longer and pushing more bytes over the wire. The stressed network layer, already constrained by queue, TLS, or process limits, now becomes a second bottleneck, delaying packet exchange and authentication cycles. Those network delays in turn hold server backends in client-I/O waits, further consuming connection slots and worker threads governed by the same mis-tuned parameters, which widens the resource gap for every subsequent bloated statement. The feedback loop—inefficient SQL creating load spikes, poor configuration amplifying internal contention, and network saturation magnifying end-to-end latency—drives a compound degradation that is more severe and harder to diagnose than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers fall behind because they cannot ingest, persist, or apply WAL/redo records as fast as the primary generates them.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical volumes servicing data, log, and temp files reach or exceed their read-write throughput limits, sharply increasing I/O latency and queue depth.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes saturate host CPU cycles, driving run-queue pressure and elevating CPU wait events across the workload.

When all three root causes occur together, the database exhibits a compound failure surface: replicas show rapidly widening log-position gaps while both primary and replica servers report soaring I/O latency and near-full CPU utilization. Check-point and log-flush operations slow down, causing the primary to retain ever-growing segments, which in turn inflate storage usage and further stress disk throughput. Queries on both primary and replicas experience multi-facet waits—first on CPU scheduling, then on disk service, and finally on replication consistency—causing erratic response-time spikes, missed SLAs, and compromised failover readiness. Monitoring views may alternate between I/O, CPU, and replication wait states, masking which layer is dominant at any given moment and making single-symptom diagnosis unreliable.

Causal chain: Saturated storage extends write-flush times; longer fsync or write-batch completion forces the primary to hold WAL segments open, inflating the volume of data that replicas must eventually consume. Because storage limits also slow replica redo reads, apply lag grows even faster. Simultaneously, high CPU usage—whether driven by heavy user workload, redo apply threads, or I/O polling—steals cycles from both the log-writer and replication receiver, elongating commit paths and apply loops. The CPU bottleneck aggravates storage saturation by limiting the dispatch rate of async I/O, while prolonged I/O waits keep worker threads runnable and spinning, compounding CPU load. The intertwined feedback loops of CPU starvation, disk congestion, and replication backlog amplify each other, producing a severe, self-reinforcing degradation that impacts both primary and replica nodes across transactional and analytical activity.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating the version store and visibility-check cost.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive host CPU utilization toward saturation, lengthening run-queue waits and inflating per-statement CPU time.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network transport, listener, or connection-slot capacity becomes a bottleneck, delaying connection setup or data transfer between clients and the database.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: bloated tables and indexes increase the CPU needed for visibility checks, just as cores are already saturated; long-running or stalled client sessions held up by network latency keep old snapshots open, preventing vacuum/cleaner progress and driving further version buildup; backend processes linger in client-read/client-write or run-queue waits, inflating process counts and CPU context switches. Overall throughput collapses, statement latency shows both CPU and network wait components, connection timeouts rise, and storage footprints and host load graphs climb together, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to any single layer.

Causally, network slowdowns extend transaction lifetimes, so obsolete row versions cannot be reclaimed, swelling the MVCC store. The enlarged heap forces every subsequent statement to scan more versions, consuming additional CPU cycles and pushing the host into saturation. CPU pressure, in turn, slows both background cleaners and packet processing, exacerbating network queuing and further prolonging client sessions. This positive feedback loop links MVCC backlog, compute exhaustion, and network congestion, each reinforcing the others and jointly degrading database performance under OLTP workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions block or deadlock each other by requesting incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, stalling foreground work on the primary. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Stand-by or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply the primary’s change stream at the pace it is generated. 
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages become corrupt or internally inconsistent, breaking the logical mapping between physical storage and relational contents.

When all three anomalies co-exist, the database exhibits a compound symptom set: long-running or hung foreground transactions accumulate lock-wait time, while replication lag grows uncontrollably; replicas may repeatedly stop applying or go into error due to checksum or key-order failures encountered in the corrupted pages they read from the primary’s log stream. On the primary, blocked or victim-aborted transactions exaggerate log generation bursts (due to rollbacks and retries) that widen the replica’s delay. Application observers see timeouts, duplicate or missing rows across read replicas, and sudden failover incapability because secondaries are both far behind and possibly carrying physical corruption. Administrators find bloated transaction logs retained for replay, deadlock reports, extended lock-wait graphs, and integrity-check failures on both primary and replicas, making it hard to attribute errors to a single layer.

Causally, page or index corruption can initiate lock contention by forcing query plans to devolve into full scans or by causing index rebuilds that hold long-lived locks; these long locks block other writers, inflating lock chains and deadlock probability. The resulting transactional back-pressure amplifies write-volume spikes (commits, rollbacks, and retries), which pushes more redo into the replication pipeline just as replicas are already struggling to apply corrupted pages, compounding replay lag. Conversely, a heavily backlogged replica may request missing segments or restart apply loops, increasing I/O load on the primary’s storage layer and lengthening the time locks are held during crash-safe page rewrites, thereby feeding further contention. Thus, corruption, lock contention, and replication lag form a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades both data integrity and availability in an OLTP environment.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures and index layout do not match workload access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written SQL to take inherently inefficient access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Catalog statistics describing row counts, distribution, and correlation are stale or incomplete, causing the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal plans.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating on-disk structures and adding visibility-check overhead.

When all three anomalies appear together, the system exhibits blended and mutually reinforcing symptoms: queries gravitate toward full-table or full-index scans not only because useful indexes are missing but also because bloated heaps and skewed statistics hide the selectivity of remaining indexes; estimated-vs-actual row counts diverge by orders of magnitude, leading to plan oscillation, excessive memory grants, and spill events; table and index sizes grow rapidly, lengthening I/O for any scan and delaying auto-vacuum or purge tasks, while DML latency rises due to both index-maintenance overhead and version-store pressure. Administrators may observe constantly busy cleanup workers, escalating table bloat and checkpoint sizes, rising write-amplification, and query plans that improve only temporarily after manual statistics refreshes or ad-hoc index creation.

Causally, poor schema and index design increases the amount of data each statement must touch; that extra I/O bandwidth is further amplified by MVCC bloat, which multiplies physical page counts. The inflated structures corrupt the accuracy of existing statistics more quickly, while stale or low-quality statistics, in turn, mask the usefulness of any remaining selective indexes and stop the optimizer from preferring them, making the design flaw appear worse. Because inefficient plans prolong statement execution, long-running transactions hold old snapshots open, slowing version reclamation and deepening MVCC bloat. The version bloat then enlarges sample space for statistics collection, making automatic refreshes slower and less frequent, perpetuating the stale-statistics condition. The three root causes therefore reinforce one another in a feedback loop that degrades throughput and predictability on write-intensive workloads.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Persisted heap and index pages contain physical or logical corruptions that render on-disk structures internally inconsistent with the logical data model.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database engine, causing sustained I/O queuing and stalls.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space on data, log, temp, or backup volumes falls to or below hard limits, preventing successful allocation, extension, or recycling operations.

When these three conditions coexist, the database may exhibit a tangled symptom set: index and table scans intermittently miss or duplicate rows; integrity-check utilities report checksum or key-order errors; meanwhile foreground sessions and background tasks accrue extreme I/O wait times, and log flush, buffer-I/O, and allocation waits dominate wait profiles. Space-related allocation failures, auto-extend errors, or frozen transaction logs further stall change processing and exacerbate I/O queue depths. Checkpoint and recovery operations lengthen, and corruption-detection mechanisms may be delayed or starved, causing sudden bursts of corruption errors when space is finally freed or I/O resumes. Administrators may observe a cascade: first space alerts, then throughput saturation, followed by corruption reports, making the root causes appear intertwined and difficult to isolate.

Causally, sustained I/O saturation slows down page writes and checkpoints, increasing the window in which torn, partially written, or out-of-order pages can arise—heightening the likelihood of data-block and index corruption, especially after forced restarts. Simultaneously, dwindling storage space limits the ability of the engine to allocate new pages, perform online rebuilds, or write full redo and archive logs, forcing aggressive reuse of existing space. This pressure can interrupt in-flight I/O, amplify fragmentation, and impede verification or repair utilities that themselves require both throughput and space. The resulting feedback loop—corruption that demands I/O to repair, throttled I/O that cannot keep up, and no free space to reallocate or rebuild—drives the database into an increasingly unstable and performance-degraded state.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and logically-deleted index entries pile up faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating data structures and lengthening visibility checks.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical read/write capacity of the underlying storage subsystem is saturated, driving up latency and queue depth for data-, temp-, and log-file operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Network paths, listener sockets, or connection slots are exhausted, producing connection errors and stalling back-end processes while they await client I/O.

When all three root causes strike at once, the database exhibits a multi-layer performance collapse: bloated tables and indexes demand more I/O per statement, yet the storage layer is already throughput-bound, so buffer flushes, checkpoints, and VACUUM/garbage-collection work are throttled by long device waits. Concurrently, back-end sessions become stuck in client-read or client-write waits because network congestion and socket exhaustion delay result transmission and acknowledgement. Application servers observe both longer query runtimes and sporadic connection failures; inside the database, wait-event profiles oscillate between buffer-cache I/O, VACUUM or purge workers, durability flushes, and client I/O waits. Monitoring shows rapidly expanding on-disk size, rising version-store counters, soaring storage latency, growing replication or WAL sender backlogs, and an increasing count of half-open or timed-out connections. These overlapping symptoms can mask each other: for example, slow query completion caused by storage stalls keeps MVCC snapshots open longer, which in turn inflates version buildup metrics, while network retransmissions can make storage waits appear intermittently idle.

Causally, the three anomalies reinforce one another in a feedback loop. High update/delete churn creates version bloat that forces more page reads and dirty-page writes; this extra traffic pushes the storage subsystem further past its throughput ceiling, lengthening every I/O. Prolonged I/O extends transaction lifetimes and keeps old snapshots alive, preventing MVCC cleanup and amplifying version accumulation. Meanwhile, the elongated statement and commit times hold server processes in active or idle-in-transaction states, swelling the concurrent connection count and filling socket queues. Network slowdowns and retries then stretch transaction durations even more, exacerbating both snapshot retention and I/O pressure. The interlocked resource starvation across MVCC bookkeeping, storage bandwidth, and network connectivity drives the database into a degraded steady state that is far worse than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Runtime settings such as buffer-pool size, log buffer, checkpoint cadence, and parallelism are mis-aligned with hardware capacity or workload characteristics.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path—generation, flushing, switching, or archiving of log records—becomes the principal bottleneck for commits and data-change activity.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, archive, or temporary areas approaches or reaches exhaustion, causing allocation failures and stalls.

When all three root causes strike together, the database experiences a feedback loop of space-related and log-related stalls amplified by maladjusted parameters. Observable symptoms include:  
• Sharp spikes in commit latency with simultaneous "log flush", "log file switch", and "space allocation" wait events.  
• Repeated checkpoint storms and rapid cycling of small log files that quickly fill the remaining device space.  
• Engine alerts reporting "cannot allocate log", "no space left on device", or "archive destination full" immediately after configuration changes.  
• CPU spin or idle gaps while user sessions wait for log space, despite overall I/O devices showing intermittent idleness.  
• Sudden throughput collapse in write-intensive OLTP workloads, followed by cascading read slowdowns as dirty-page back-pressure rises and background cleanup falls behind.

Causal interaction: mis-tuned configuration parameters (e.g., undersized log buffer, aggressive checkpoint interval, or small max log size) elevate the transaction-log generation and switching frequency. This overstresses an already fragile log subsystem, which must flush and archive segments more often. Because log files and archives share limited storage that is near capacity, every extra switch consumes scarce free blocks, hastening space exhaustion. Once space is full, the log subsystem cannot obtain the next segment; commit paths stall, dirty pages cannot be flushed, and checkpoints pile up—conditions that further magnify wait events and accentuate the performance cliff. In turn, elevated waits mislead auto-tuning heuristics or administrators into further parameter tweaks (e.g., shortening checkpoints), unintentionally reinforcing the vicious cycle and deepening the outage.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Page-level serialization inside the buffer manager where sessions spin or block on latches, pins, or page-content locks while trying to access a small set of hot buffers.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive or apply WAL/redo at the rate the primary generates it, producing widening log-position gaps and retaining log segments on the primary.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Transport-layer or listener resources between nodes and clients are saturated, lossy, or starved, leading to slow or failed connection establishment and high socket-level waits.

When all three conditions occur together, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: 1) front-end clients see intermittent connection timeouts, elevated latency, and sporadic "too many connections" or authentication failures; 2) active back-end sessions show surging buffer-busy and page-latch waits, high CPU spin, and sharp response-time spikes on hot tables or index roots; 3) replication dashboards report rapidly growing send, write, and replay lags, expanding retained-WAL or relay-log storage, and replicas fall out of synchronous commit windows; 4) storage pressure from unrecycled WAL files triggers aggressive checkpoints that evict useful pages, amplifying buffer churn and extending latch hold times; 5) system-level network metrics reveal retransmissions and queue overflows exactly when database wait events and replication gaps worsen, making the root causes hard to distinguish in isolation.

Causal chain: Network congestion or listener overload throttles the primary’s ability to stream WAL, immediately slowing replica catch-up. The primary therefore retains additional log segments, inflating disk usage and forcing more frequent checkpoints or background flushes. These writes compete for buffer-pool space, evicting pages that active OLTP sessions soon re-read, which elevates buffer cache churn and concentrates access on hot root or sequence pages—intensifying latch contention. Heightened latch waits elongate transaction execution times, keeping connections open longer and increasing the number of concurrent sockets the listener must juggle, which in turn aggravates network/connection saturation. The intertwined feedback loop between network backlog, replication stalling, retained-WAL pressure, and hot-page latch contention drives a severe, self-reinforcing degradation that is much harder to remediate than any of the individual anomalies alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths irrespective of optimizer statistics.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records that background vacuum/cleanup workers cannot reclaim quickly enough, inflating table size and visibility-check cost.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log pipeline (generation, flushing, switching, archiving, retention) is saturated, elongating commit latency and stalling further DML.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: queries read far more pages because poorly designed or missing indexes push them into full scans over bloat-inflated heaps and indexes; each scan must traverse long version chains, increasing CPU and buffer-pool pressure. Concurrently, the excessive DML generated by design flaws (e.g., unneeded secondary-index maintenance, hot-spot primary keys) and by MVCC cleanup work produces a surge in redo that overwhelms the log buffer and log file subsystem, manifesting as rising commit times, frequent log flush waits, and delayed checkpoints. Background vacuum or garbage-collection workers stay perpetually active yet fall further behind because their own delete and prune operations add additional redo and contend for the same clogged log and I/O channels. End-user sessions experience a mix of slow queries, unpredictable latency spikes, and occasional write stalls when log space or transaction-ID horizons are exhausted.

Causally, the poor schema and index design increases the volume and cost of both reads and writes—more non-covering index lookups, more page splits, and heavier update/delete churn—thereby accelerating row-version creation. The surging version count bloats table and index pages, worsening scan performance and causing still more I/O that must be logged. Simultaneously, every extra page modification and every MVCC cleanup action emits additional log records, pushing the transaction-log subsystem past its throughput budget. The saturated log path then slows commit acknowledgment, lengthening transaction lifetimes, which in turn widens the snapshot horizon and delays version reclamation. This feedback loop reinforces each anomaly, quickly degrading overall OLTP performance and stability.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from poorly written or chatty SQL workload logic, a physical schema and indexing layout that does not match access patterns, and operating-system level resource ceilings that throttle the database process. The three layers—application logic, physical data model, and kernel resource governance—create a stack of mutually reinforcing inefficiencies and hard limits.

SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-issued statements and transaction boundaries force the engine to process more data, rows, or time than the true business requirement demands.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Tables, partitions, and indexes are laid out in ways that prevent the optimizer from choosing selective, low-cost access paths even for otherwise well-formulated queries.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, threads, or other OS objects cap the database’s ability to allocate the resources it needs for query execution and background work.

Combined Phenomena: Long-running queries dominate statement statistics and repeatedly hit slow-query logs, but their execution plans also show full scans, excessive random I/O, or many extra lookups because of missing or non-covering indexes. Concurrently, the database starts emitting intermittent errors such as "too many open files", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "failed to create worker thread", causing some sessions to abort or retry. Connection pools see timeouts; parallel workers fail to start, leading to serial execution and even longer runtimes. Check-pointing, vacuum, or redo flushing is delayed because background processes cannot obtain OS resources, amplifying lock hold times of the already slow transactions. Monitoring shows both high logical I/O and CPU from inefficient query patterns and sudden hard caps on throughput or worker counts unrelated to internal configuration.

Causal Chain: Inefficient SQL statements inflate row counts and I/O volume, which are further exacerbated by sub-optimal schema and index design that forces wide scans and extra lookups. The bloated execution demand multiplies the number of file handles, buffer pins, temporary files, sort runs, and worker threads required. This surge drives the database engine closer to the host’s per-process limits; once those OS ceilings are reached, allocation failures begin to surface. Each allocation failure in turn prevents the optimizer from using parallelism, increases queuing, and lengthens transaction lifetimes, which keeps locks, temp files, and memory segments alive even longer. The feedback loop—heavy workload logic, schema inefficiency, and OS resource exhaustion—creates a compounded performance cliff and sporadic outages that are far more severe than any single anomaly would have produced in isolation.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing metadata no longer matches the real data distribution, producing systematic cardinality errors and sub-optimal execution plans.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, log file, archiver, or replication retention—cannot persist or recycle redo fast enough, throttling commit throughput.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU cycles, keeping runnable queues permanently full and inflating latency across all operations.

When these three root causes strike together, the system shows a confused mixture of symptoms: queries exhibit wildly inaccurate cardinality estimates and choose plan shapes that scan or join far more rows than intended; the excessive row processing amplifies redo generation, quickly filling log buffers and exhausting log file bandwidth. As log flush and sync waits climb, user transactions stall at commit time, while foreground sessions already burdened by poor plans consume ever more CPU in longer execution paths. Log-writer and archiver processes compete for the same CPU cores now saturated by query workers, so both data processing and log persistence slow further. The database reports simultaneous spikes in CPU-bound wait events, log write-related waits, and optimizer recompile events, making isolation of any single culprit difficult.

Causally, stale or incomplete statistics produce execution plans that scan and update large data volumes, inflating CPU demand and redo generation. The surge of log records overwhelms an already constrained transaction-log subsystem, lengthening commit times and forcing foreground processes to linger in log-related waits where they still hold latches and locks. These blocked or looping sessions keep consuming scheduler time slices, pushing CPU utilization toward saturation. In turn, CPU saturation starves the log-writer and statistics-gathering tasks, preventing timely statistics refresh and slowing log flushes, which feeds back into even poorer plans and deeper commit stalls. The intertwined feedback loop of bad plans → high CPU & redo → log bottleneck → more CPU pressure → deferred statistics refresh creates a self-reinforcing degradation spiral that can cripple OLTP throughput and inflate end-to-end response times.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, page pins, and latches, stalling logical I/O even when physical memory is available.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing is throttled by log buffer flush, log file write, or archiver activity, making the log path the critical choke point.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive host CPU to sustained saturation, starving all threads—including internal background workers—of scheduler time.

When all three root causes strike together, the system exhibits an intertwined symptom set:  • End-to-end transaction latency and commit latency rise sharply, with wait-event views showing a mix of LOG-WRITE, LOG-FLUSH, BUFFER-BUSY, and PAGE-LATCH waits.  • CPU usage stays at or near 100 %, yet throughput plateaus or declines; spin loops on buffer latches crowd the run queue while log writer and archiver threads contend for CPU slices to perform synchronous writes.  • Checkpoint storms and rapid log-file switches amplify dirty-buffer pressure, so foreground sessions alternately wait for latch access to hot pages and for log space to be freed.  • Monitoring tools may mis-attribute the slowdown because the dominant symptom—CPU saturation—masks the underlying dual I/O bottlenecks on buffers and the redo log.

Causal interaction: Hot pages and frequent page churn inflate latch acquisition attempts; many of those attempts spin rather than sleep, inflating CPU consumption. The elevated CPU load delays log writer, archiver, and buffer-flush threads, stretching commit latency and prolonging the time dirty pages remain pinned. Those pinned or dirty buffers, in turn, intensify latch contention because they cannot be evicted or reused until the log is persisted, further increasing spin and CPU pressure. Meanwhile, slow log advancement forces aggressive checkpoints, which flush more dirty pages and request additional latches, closing a feedback loop that binds buffer contention, log backlog, and CPU starvation into a self-reinforcing performance collapse.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction design force the engine to scan, join, or return far more data than business logic requires.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database process allocates buffer cache, work memory, plan cache, and other heaps beyond the safe physical memory envelope, provoking OS-level pressure.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data files, logs, or temporary areas drops to a hard boundary, risking allocation failures and stalled writes.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database experiences a compound failure mode: chatty or over-broad SQL rapidly fills buffer caches and per-query work areas, driving resident-set size to the limit. As memory pressure mounts, the engine begins spilling sort, hash, and intermediate result sets to temporary segments, which in turn accelerates consumption of data-file, temp, and log space. The already space-starved storage layer struggles to extend or recycle files, causing write stalls, "out of space" errors, aborted transactions, and repeated retries from the application layer. Performance telemetry shows a mix of long-tail statement latency, swapping or OOM events, and sudden allocation failures in temporary or archive areas—symptoms that, when observed in isolation, are difficult to attribute to any single layer.

Causal chain: overly expensive SQL (1) inflates memory demand, inflating caches and per-operation work buffers; (2) this pushes the instance into heavy paging or triggers aggressive spill-to-disk behavior; (3) the resulting temporary and log growth rapidly depletes remaining storage capacity; (4) once space is exhausted, memory-relief spills fail, forcing even more memory retention and amplifying OOM risk. Each anomaly therefore feeds the next: inefficient workload begets memory saturation, memory saturation begets disk spills, and disk spills exhaust space, which in turn prevents the memory layer from offloading work, creating a feedback loop that can cascade into node eviction, service outage, or data-load failure.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction semantics force the engine to touch more data or hold locks longer than the business requirement really needs.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, or partition design is mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing otherwise reasonable SQL into inefficient scans, lookups, or maintenance overhead.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, or connection-handling resources between client and database are saturated or unreliable, throttling session establishment and data transfer.

When these three root causes are active at the same time, their symptoms overlap and amplify one another. Chatty or bloated SQL generated by the application produces large result sets and long-running transactions; the poor schema and index design prevents the optimizer from finding selective access paths, inflating execution time and result size even further; the oversized data streams then traverse a congested or connection-starved network layer, causing additional round-trip latency, retransmissions, and connection pool exhaustion. Observable phenomena therefore include: a surge of slow-query log entries that also exhibit client-read waits; execution plans dominated by full scans combined with long application think-times; spikes in network RTT, retransmits, or socket queue depth exactly when large, non-covering queries run; prolonged transactions holding locks while waiting for network I/O; exponential growth in active sessions due to retry storms following connection timeouts; and erratic application response times that do not improve when only server-side tuning is attempted in isolation.

Causally, chatty or over-broad SQL increases both the volume and duration of data access. Because the underlying schema lacks the right indexes or partitions, each statement consumes more CPU and I/O, elongating execution and enlarging result sets. These heavier payloads must then traverse an already constrained network, which slows completion of result delivery and keeps server back-ends and locks open far longer than planned. The extended hold time further increases concurrency pressure, triggering additional retries and connection churn that worsen network congestion—creating a feedback loop in which logical workload inefficiencies, physical design gaps, and transport bottlenecks mutually reinforce, driving systemic performance collapse under both OLTP and analytical mixed workloads.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently selects sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are adequate, leading to disproportionate resource consumption per statement.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer cannot deliver the read/write throughput, IOPS, or latency required by the workload, producing device-level wait inflation.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client–server transport or connection-handling capacity is exhausted, causing connection establishment delays, socket backlog growth, and stalled data transfer.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: queries flip to full-table scans or poorly chosen join orders that inflate page reads; the surge in random and sequential I/O collides with an already saturated storage subsystem, driving disk queues and read/write latencies even higher. Prolonged statement runtimes hold server processes and sockets open, so listener backlogs, half-open TCP sessions, and client-side timeouts escalate. End-to-end response times swing wildly, and performance graphs show intertwined peaks of I/O waits, client-read/client-write waits, and hard-parse or plan-change events. Administrators may mis-attribute slowdowns to a single layer because each bottleneck masks and amplifies the others.

Causally, a bad plan is the spark: it multiplies physical I/O demand, pushing the storage layer past its throughput ceiling. The resulting I/O stalls extend query execution and result-set streaming time, which ties up server worker threads and keeps network sockets active longer. As active connections swell and data trickles slowly over the congested network, handshake retries and backlog overflows appear, feeding further delays that lengthen query runtimes and increase optimizer re-parses, perpetuating the selection of the same poor plan. This feedback loop between plan inefficiency, storage saturation, and network congestion degrades overall capacity far more severely than any single anomaly acting alone.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk data or index pages have become physically or logically corrupt, making structural metadata and row contents unreliable.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: The database, log, temp, or backup areas have run out of free bytes, causing allocation failures and write stalls.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate host CPU, leaving too few compute cycles for normal query execution and background tasks.

When all three root causes are active, symptoms overlap and intensify: corruption-induced full-table scans or rebuild attempts run while CPUs are already pegged, making every statement—whether touching damaged pages or not—incur high run-queue delays. Space exhaustion prevents the engine from creating new index leaves, spill files, or corruption-repair copies, so error logging shows alternating "page checksum failure," "cannot extend segment," and "CPU scheduler wait" events. Autovacuum, consistency-check, or backup jobs start but hang halfway because they hit both space and CPU limits, producing a rising backlog of un-checkpointed dirty pages. Clients observe erratic latency spikes, time-outs, and result set mismatches as some queries fail with corruption errors, others with "no space left on device," and the rest slow under CPU starvation, making troubleshooting ambiguous.

Causal chain: damaged blocks often trigger emergency index rebuilds, full scans, or forced consistency checks that demand extra CPU and temporary space; if the underlying storage is already near capacity, these repair operations quickly exhaust the remaining bytes, turning intermittent corruption into hard allocation failures. Conversely, space exhaustion can interrupt write-ahead logging or unfinished index rebuilds, leaving pages partially written and thereby introducing new corrupt blocks. Both conditions escalate CPU consumption as the engine retries failed writes, spins on corruption handling routines, or falls back to compute-heavy table scans. The feedback loop—corruption causes heavier CPU and space use, space failures introduce further corruption, and CPU saturation slows recovery—locks the system into a progressively worsening state until one or more resources are freed or the instance is taken offline for repair.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or missing optimizer statistics misrepresent actual data distribution and drive systematic cardinality misestimation.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume or request more CPU cycles than the host can provide, leading to sustained CPU saturation and broad latency inflation.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes exceed kernel-enforced quotas for threads, file handles, shared-memory segments, or similar objects, causing allocation failures outside the engine’s direct control.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: execution plans generated from bad statistics choose CPU-intensive operators (e.g., hash joins, large sort/aggregate, over-parallelized scans) that flood all cores. The surge of threads, processes, and I/O descriptors needed to execute those plans pushes the database past OS limits, producing sporadic errors such as "cannot create thread", "too many open files", or "failed to allocate shared memory". Meanwhile, CPU saturation lengthens query runtimes, further extending the interval during which OS quotas remain exhausted. Users observe a mix of symptoms—wildly inaccurate plan estimates, skyrocketing CPU wait and run-queue times, sudden session or worker spawn failures, and cascading slowdowns across unrelated queries.

Causal chain: stale or absent statistics misguide the optimizer into selecting plans that require excessive CPU and high degrees of parallelism; this overconsumption pushes the host into CPU saturation. The inflated worker and descriptor counts generated by those plans rapidly consume kernel-limited resources, which in turn block new sessions, background statistics refresh jobs, and parallel workers—preventing automatic statistics collection and perpetuating the original misestimation. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others, producing a feedback loop that degrades throughput, increases error rates, and risks partial or complete service outage.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to scan or change more data than business logic really requires.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log files, flush, archive, replication retention) becomes the primary bottleneck for commits.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high share of CPU, saturating host cores and slowing all work.

When these three root causes are active together the system exhibits extreme and unpredictable latency spikes: statements linger in the slow-query log while commit calls block behind log-flush waits; CPU utilisation stays near 100 %, with long run-queues and scheduler waits; log files grow and switch rapidly yet archiver or replication threads fall behind, triggering "log file full" or "cannot allocate next log" conditions; application timeouts, deadlocks, and recovery-driven crashes become more frequent because transactions remain open for extended periods and hold locks longer than expected. Diagnostic views simultaneously show top SQL by CPU time, high redo generation rates, and dominant log-related wait events, making single-factor analysis inconclusive.

Causally, inefficient workload logic produces oversized scans, updates, and long-lived transactions that explode redo volume and CPU demand. The surge in redo overwhelms the transaction-log subsystem; flush and archive stalls delay commits, which in turn keep transactions—and their locks—open even longer. While sessions wait for log space, they continue to consume CPU in spin-loops, context switching, or retry logic, driving further CPU saturation. The oversubscribed CPU then slows both query execution and the log writer/archiver threads, deepening log congestion. This feedback loop between bad SQL semantics, log pressure, and CPU exhaustion amplifies each individual anomaly, rapidly degrading overall OLTP throughput and stability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, page pins, or latches, stalling logical I/O without exhausting physical memory.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Replicas fall behind because they cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL / redo as fast as the primary generates it.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes monopolize host CPU, driving utilization to sustained saturation and elongating every code path.

When all three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a mingled symptom set: CPU usage stays pegged while throughput drops; wait-event dashboards alternate between page-latch waits, replication sender/receiver backlog waits, and scheduler run-queue waits. Standbys show rapidly widening replay lag, yet the primary’s log recycling stalls, inflating on-disk log volume. Hot index root pages and monotonic insert pages on the primary incur heavy latch spin, amplifying CPU burn and exposing latency spikes for both foreground queries and background writer/checkpointer threads. The same CPU saturation slows the replica’s single-threaded apply workers, so relay logs accumulate and feedback pressure to the primary intensifies. Administrators may mis-attribute the issue to any one layer because the symptoms overlap and mask each other.

Causal interaction: page-level contention on the primary forces processes into tight spin loops, inflating CPU demand; the inflated CPU demand lengthens log generation intervals and stretches commit latency. High commit latency and spin burning delay the shipping of finished log segments, so replication lag widens. As replicas fall behind, the primary must retain more unrecycled log files, filling buffer cache with log-writer pages and further choking the same latch paths already under pressure. The sustained spin-loop activity keeps CPU saturated on both primary and replica, slowing latch release and apply threads alike, thereby reinforcing buffer contention and replication backlog in a positive feedback loop that degrades the entire cluster’s resilience and performance.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count and data-distribution metadata are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal plan choices.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The generation, flushing, or archival pipeline of the write-ahead log is saturated, so commit processing becomes a bottleneck.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: One or more database storage areas—data files, log files, archive locations, temp or backup areas—approach or reach space exhaustion.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the system exhibits a mixture of misestimated execution plans, escalating log-related waits, and sudden space-related allocation failures. Bad statistics may produce plans that generate excessive redo (e.g., full-table updates instead of targeted index lookups), amplifying log-flush latency. Long commit waits elongate transaction duration, keeping undo, temp, and log segments active, so free space shrinks faster. As space dwindles, automatic growth, log switching, or statistics refreshes can fail, causing a feedback loop of plan invalidations, repeated recompilations, and further log pressure. Symptoms therefore include wildly inaccurate cardinality estimates on plan output, spikes in LOG_WRITE or LOG_SYNC waits, checkpoints that cannot complete because the next log file is full, auto-extend errors on both data and log files, aborted statistics-gather jobs due to lack of temp space, and application time-outs triggered by cascaded stalls.

Causal chain: Stale or missing statistics drive execution plans that touch far more rows than expected, inflating redo volume and filling log files quickly. The log subsystem, already undersized or placed on the same device, struggles to flush and archive those larger log streams; commit latency rises and transactions stay open longer. Extended transaction lifetimes pin space in undo/rollback and temp segments, accelerating overall space consumption. As free space approaches zero, log files cannot switch or extend, preventing commits and blocking the statistics-refresh operations required to correct the original misestimates. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others, producing a compounded degradation that is more severe and harder to diagnose than any single issue alone.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: This anomaly occurs when the optimizer persistently selects sub-optimal execution plans (Query Plan Selection Anomaly) while the engine simultaneously over-allocates and exhausts host memory (Database Memory Allocation Anomaly) and the database processes drive the CPUs into sustained saturation (CPU Resource Anomaly). All three root causes are active at the same time, creating a multi-layer failure that degrades throughput and predictability across the entire workload.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Statements flip between radically different plans, some exploding into full table scans or multi-way nested loops. • Memory usage of buffer cache, work areas, and plan cache grows without bound, pushing the operating system into paging or OOM kills; after each memory reclaim, new plans are recompiled, further inflating the plan cache. • CPU utilization remains near 100 %, run-queue length spikes, and wait events shift from I/O or lock waits to scheduler waits and spin-locks inside memory allocators. • Latency outliers become extreme; short OLTP requests time out while long analytical queries stall in memory pressure throttling. • Node failures or automatic failovers may be triggered by combined memory and CPU stress, masking the underlying plan instability.

Causal Interaction: Sub-optimal plans often require larger hash/sort areas or read far more pages, inflating both per-query work memory and buffer-cache churn. The bloated memory footprint accelerates overall memory exhaustion; when the engine or OS begins paging, CPU cycles are wasted on page-fault handling and plan recompilations, further heating CPU. In turn, CPU saturation slows the optimizer and memory managers, lengthening critical sections and increasing contention on shared allocation latches, which feeds back into even poorer plan choices (e.g., time-outs in adaptive optimization) and larger memory grants issued as guard bands. The positive feedback loop between bad plans, runaway memory growth, and CPU starvation rapidly amplifies resource pressure, causing a system-wide degradation that is much worse than any single anomaly would produce in isolation.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a severely sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are acceptable.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical data pages or index structures are corrupted or inconsistent with their logical contents.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage layer is saturated, creating high latency and constrained read/write bandwidth.

When all three root causes are present, the database may exhibit an erratic mixture of symptoms: plans may flip between index and full-table scans or force parallelism yet still deliver poor performance; index scans can silently miss or duplicate rows, prompting the optimizer to distrust indexes and fall back to heavy full scans that flood the already-saturated storage subsystem; corruption-triggered retries, page re-reads, or forced consistency checks magnify I/O waits, while excessive physical reads caused by bad plans further deepen the storage bottleneck. Administrators may observe soaring logical and physical I/O counts, plan cache churn, frequent checksum or page-link errors in the error log, growing queue depths on the storage array, and wildly fluctuating query latencies that are difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, corrupted index or data pages undermine the optimizer’s cardinality assumptions, increasing the likelihood of a poor plan choice. A sub-optimal plan in turn generates higher I/O volumes (e.g., full scans, random lookups) that push the storage system beyond its throughput budget. The saturated storage prolongs every page access, which amplifies the runtime cost gap between the chosen plan and an ideal plan, and may expose additional latent corrupt pages as more blocks are touched. Feedback loops such as automatic plan re-compilation after error detection or repeated I/O retries can cause plan thrashing and further I/O escalation, creating a self-reinforcing degradation that impacts both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and logically-deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating on-disk and in-memory structures and lengthening visibility checks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions repeatedly fight for hot buffer pages, page pins, and latches, causing stalls, CPU spin, and prolonged waits in the buffer manager.

When both root causes strike at once, the system experiences a compound failure mode in which bloated MVCC metadata increases the number and churn rate of buffer pages while those same pages become hotspots contended for by many sessions. Observable symptoms include: 1) rapidly growing table and index size that pushes the working set beyond the ideal buffer-pool footprint, 2) sharp rises in buffer-busy/latch wait events coinciding with background vacuum/cleaner activity, 3) CPU usage dominated by spin-loops and visibility scans rather than useful work, 4) escalating I/O as the cache thrashes between old and freshly dirtied versions, and 5) unstable query plans as the optimizer misjudges bloat-inflated statistics and fluctuating cache hit ratios.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn generates excess MVCC garbage, swelling the number of distinct physical pages that must stay resident or be repeatedly fetched. This expansion dilutes buffer-pool effectiveness and forces more sessions to converge on the remaining truly hot root, index, and free-space pages, intensifying latch contention. At the same time, cleaners that try to prune dead versions issue additional reads and writes, further saturating the buffer manager and extending latch hold times. The longer latches are held, the more they delay other sessions, allowing even more obsolete versions to pile up. The feedback loop between version-store bloat and latch congestion accelerates resource exhaustion, leading to severe throughput degradation and potentially catastrophic wraparound or emergency autovacuum scenarios.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Overall engine memory consumption grows beyond the safe capacity of the host, triggering OS or engine-level memory pressure.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages and their associated latches, stalling on low-level synchronization primitives.

When all three anomalies surface together, operators observe a volatile mix of plan instability, memory stress, and internal buffer contention. A single statement may oscillate between index probes and full scans; after each plan flip, rows flood the buffer cache, inflating working-set size, evicting other pages, and expanding per-query work areas. Resident-set bloat pushes the host into paging or swap storms, while the shrinking effective cache intensifies latch waits on the remaining hot pages. Execution latency becomes highly jittery: some executions terminate quickly, others stall on page-latch or memory-pressure waits, and overall throughput collapses with CPUs either spin-locking or blocked by the OS memory manager.

Causal chain: poor plan selection can inflate I/O and memory demand (e.g., hash joins that spill or table scans that load large objects), accelerating buffer-pool turnover and forcing the engine to allocate additional work memory. The enlarged footprint worsens host memory pressure, provoking aggressive page evictions and dirty-page flush cycles. These churns create a handful of survivor pages that every session must repeatedly acquire, amplifying latch competition. Conversely, severe latch contention extends query runtimes, keeping sub-optimal plans resident longer and holding work areas open, which further inflates memory usage. The feedback loop between plan mis-choice, memory exhaustion, and hot-page serialization drives the database into a degraded state that is deeper than any of the single anomalies would have caused on their own.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persists or selects markedly sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are accurate, causing excessive I/O, CPU, or row explosion.
