Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Instance-level settings for memory, parallelism, checkpoints, and worker pools are mis-aligned with hardware capacity or workload demands, so the engine behaves inefficiently even though physical resources are not exhausted.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path—buffer, flush, file rotation, or archiving—cannot sustain the redo rate, making commits stall and triggering log-related wait events.

When all three root causes co-exist, the workload exhibits a compound failure signature: 1) sudden plan flips to full table scans or fat hash joins inflate row touches and redo volume; 2) mis-sized shared buffers and per-session work memory force extra page reads, bloated sort/Hash spills, and more frequent checkpoints; 3) log-flush and log-write waits skyrocket, driving up commit latency, which in turn elongates lock holding times and dampens throughput; 4) CPU and I/O utilization appear paradoxically low or skewed—cores spin on latch contention while storage idles between bursty checkpoint or log-switch storms; 5) performance degradation often starts immediately after an upgrade or parameter change that invalidates cached plans and simultaneously alters memory or checkpoint defaults, making the symptoms hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, a poor plan (1) multiplies data-modification and redo generation, pushing the transaction-log subsystem toward saturation. In parallel, sub-optimal configuration parameters (2)—for example, an undersized log buffer, aggressive checkpoint timeout, or insufficient shared pool—reduce the margin for absorbing the extra redo and amplify log flush frequency. The overloaded log path (3) then feeds back into the optimizer and configuration layers: high commit latency delays statistics refreshes and prolongs locks, which can further skew plan selection and provoke more ad-hoc compilations, while emergency checkpoints invalidate additional plans and consume memory that is already mis-configured. The intertwined feedback loops between wrong plans, ill-tuned parameters, and a choking log path produce a runaway degradation that is more severe than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions continuously request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, forcing sessions to wait in blocking chains or enter deadlock cycles managed by the lock manager.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively consume almost all available CPU cycles on the host, driving the operating-system run queue high and leaving too few compute resources for timely execution of the workload.

When these two root causes strike together, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: 1) elevated lock-wait time, deadlock victim errors, and growing client time-outs; 2) sustained near-100 % CPU utilization with long scheduler run queues; 3) lock-manager and scheduler wait events appearing side-by-side, making it unclear whether waits or CPU starvation is primary; 4) throughput collapse in bursts as transactions alternate between spinning on CPU while attempting to acquire locks and then blocking once pre-empted; and 5) monitoring tools showing both a spike in CPU-bound statements and a backlog of sessions waiting on locks, giving the impression of mutually conflicting bottleneck signals.

The causal chain can be self-reinforcing: heavy lock contention forces the lock manager and waiting sessions to spin or wake frequently, inflating CPU demand. The resulting CPU saturation slows query execution and lengthens the time each transaction holds its locks, which further extends blocking chains and deadlock windows. As lock waits grow longer, more client retries or timeouts spawn additional sessions, adding background work (logging, deadlock detection, retry logic) that consumes still more CPU. This feedback loop rapidly degrades both concurrency control and compute availability, driving a severe OLTP-focused performance crisis.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata objects, resulting in wait queues or deadlock cycles that stall statement progress until a lock is granted or a victim is aborted.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log buffer, log file group, or archive/redo shipping mechanism cannot flush or switch log segments at the rate commits generate redo, turning the log subsystem itself into the bottleneck for every commit.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing replay lag and forcing the primary to retain log segments beyond its normal recycling window.

When all three root causes appear together, the database shows a compound "grid-lock": commit latency rises sharply, session wait graphs display interleaved LOCK_* and LOG_* waits, deadlock detectors frequently kill victims that must be replayed after application retries, replication lag numbers climb, and disk space consumed by live log files and retained relay/redo logs balloons. Read replicas fall ever further behind, stale reads mislead applications, and failover windows lengthen. Monitoring dashboards may alternately attribute the slowdown to lock waits, log I/O, or replication lag, making the primary bottleneck hard to pinpoint.

Causal chain: lock contention lengthens transaction lifetimes, so locks are held while more redo accumulates; this increases log flush pressure. A saturated log subsystem further delays commits, extending the time locks are held and enlarging blocking chains. At the same time, replicas already struggling to keep up with redo now face bursts of large, long-running transactions flushed in clumps, widening replication gaps. Because replicas hold retention pins on un-replayed segments, the primary cannot recycle log files, forcing additional log switches that intensify log-device pressure. The enlarged log backlog inflates commit latency even more, creating a feedback loop that magnifies both lock contention and log saturation, while replication lag continues to grow and threatens disk exhaustion on both primary and replicas.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, leading to wait chains or deadlocks that stall or abort user work. 
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine’s aggregate memory footprint grows beyond safe limits, provoking host-level pressure, paging, or OOM terminations as caches, work areas, and background heaps expand uncontrollably. 
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots, producing high latch and buffer-busy waits and CPU spin without useful progress. 

When all three anomalies coincide, the system experiences compounding symptoms: lock wait times and deadlock rates surge while CPU usage oscillates between spin-looping on latches and kernel scheduling delays caused by memory pressure. Throughput collapses as transactions queue behind both lock owners and latch holders, while memory overcommitment forces buffer evictions and paging, further inflating latch durations and lengthening lock hold times. Users observe erratic response times, frequent query cancellations or victim rollbacks, intermittent "out of memory" or node-eviction events, and sharp drops in cache hit ratios that aggravate I/O latency and extend blocking intervals.

Causal interaction: excessive memory allocation shrinks true free memory, increasing buffer churn and forcing more frequent page replacement and flush activity; this elevates buffer-latch contention as many sessions compete for the same hot pages. Longer latch acquisition extends the time transactions keep logical locks, intensifying lock contention and enlarging blocker-waiter chains. Conversely, lock queues slow statement completion, allowing work areas, sort buffers, and session heaps to stay resident longer and inflate memory pressure. The resulting paging amplifies latch hold times, forming a positive feedback loop that escalates all three anomalies and can ultimately trigger deadlocks, OOM terminations, or engine restarts.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction patterns are written so that they process far more rows, data, or time than business logic actually requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress until a victim is rolled back.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively drive host CPU utilization to saturation, starving runnable tasks of compute cycles.

When these three root causes surface together, the database experiences prolonged statement runtimes, widespread blocking and deadlock storms, and system-wide latency spikes amplified by CPU exhaustion. Slow or looping SQL generated by the application touches excessive rows; each over-sized operation acquires larger and longer-held locks, expanding the duration and scope of lock queues. As blocked sessions spin on the scheduler or are repeatedly aborted and retried by the application, runnable threads accumulate, driving host CPU to sustained 90-100 % utilization. High CPU, in turn, lengthens context-switch and lock acquisition times, so even moderately contended resources become severe choke points. Monitoring views show simultaneous surges in slow-query counts, lock-wait time, deadlock reports, and CPU run-queue depth; application layers observe timeouts, cascading retries, and throughput collapse.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL patterns (wide scans, large batches, open-ended transactions) dramatically increase the number of rows touched and the lifetime of locks. The enlarged lock footprint raises the probability and duration of conflicting lock requests, producing blocking trees and deadlocks. Blocked or killed transactions are commonly retried by application logic, further inflating concurrency pressure. Meanwhile each bloated statement consumes more CPU per execution; the retries, lock-manager housekeeping, and victim rollbacks add still more CPU load. CPU saturation slows down every thread, including those that could otherwise release locks quickly, thereby feeding a feedback loop: prolonged execution keeps locks held, extended locks intensify contention, contention causes retries, and retries plus heavy scanning drive CPU to its limits. The intertwined effects of inefficient workload design, lock contention, and compute starvation thus reinforce one another, creating a severe performance degradation scenario typical of high-throughput OLTP systems.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) is mis-aligned with workload access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written queries into systematically inefficient access paths.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table and index pages are internally corrupted or mutually inconsistent, so logical rows can be missing, duplicated, or inaccessible even when the optimizer selects the right access path.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport layer between clients and the DBMS cannot sustain offered load because of link congestion, packet loss, handshake/ authentication limits, or exhausted connection slots, causing frequent connect and I/O stalls.

When these three root causes coexist, the system exhibits compound symptoms across all tiers: 1) query plans already slowed by poor or absent indexing fall back to full scans, which in turn traverse corrupted pages and trigger corruption errors, retries, or silent data mismatches; 2) corruption-induced retries, error logging, or engine failovers amplify session churn, driving up connection establishment rates until listener backlogs overflow, producing client timeouts and half-open sockets; 3) network stalls elongate transaction times, so more concurrent sessions hold locks while simultaneously performing scan-heavy I/O against damaged structures, inflating buffer-pool churn, latch contention, and recovery events; 4) monitoring shows a mix of slow logical query metrics, sporadic "row not found" or "checksum failure" messages, and rising connection-related wait events, making root-cause isolation difficult because each layer’s symptoms obscure the others.

Causally, the misdesigned schema initiates excessive full-table/ index activity that increases physical page touch-rate, heightening the probability of encountering latent block or index corruption; once such corruption manifests, queries repeatedly fail or fall back to even more expensive scans, magnifying load. The resultant latency and retry storms overload client connection pools and database listener resources, feeding a feedback loop where network congestion and authentication bottlenecks prolong transactions, further stressing the flawed schema and exposing additional corrupt pages. Together, the structural inefficiency, physical corruption, and connectivity saturation reinforce each other, rapidly degrading both throughput and data correctness across transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Runtime engine parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload profile, or version defaults, creating artificial bottlenecks or idle resources.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, making storage contents inconsistent with logical expectations.

When both root causes exist, the database exhibits a confusing blend of resource-misuse and data-corruption symptoms: skewed wait-event distributions (e.g., sustained log-write or page-flush waits despite idle I/O devices) coincide with query results that are missing, duplicated, or trigger checksum and page-verification errors. Checkpoint storms or aggressive background flushes spawned by misconfigured parameters repeatedly touch the same corrupted pages, flooding the log with page-level errors, while inconsistent indexes force the optimizer to abandon index scans and fall back to full table scans that overrun the undersized buffer pool. After upgrades or instance resizing, runtime settings that silently changed may amplify corruption visibility—integrity-check utilities start during low-checkpoint intervals, or recovery attempts loop because truncated logs cannot replay damaged pages. As a result, performance degrades unpredictably, correctness alarms rise, and the signals of the two issues mask each other, complicating triage.

Causal chain: Mis-calibrated parameters (e.g., too-frequent checkpoints, undersized WAL, disabled page checksums, or over-aggressive parallel write-back) increase I/O churn and recovery pressure, heightening the chance of uncovering latent corruption or even causing it during crash-recovery edge cases. Once corruption exists, it forces plan fallbacks and larger data scans, which in turn stress the poorly sized memory and I/O settings, generating further flush storms and log pressure. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other—parameter misconfiguration can precipitate corruption, and corruption-triggered workload shifts magnify the impact of the bad configuration—creating a feedback loop that degrades both performance and data integrity.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table, index, partition, and data-type choices do not match workload access patterns, forcing queries into inefficient and excessively large data access paths.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Cumulative buffer cache, work-area, plan cache, and background allocations grow beyond the host’s physical memory envelope, triggering paging, allocation churn, and OOM events.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Generation, flush, switching, or archival of write-ahead logs cannot keep pace with redo production, inflating commit latency and stalling write activity.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compounded failure pattern: 1) poorly indexed tables drive full-table scans, wide nested-loop lookups, and large batch modifications that explode redo volume; 2) the oversized intermediate result sets and hash/sort operations inflate per-session work memory and thrash the buffer cache, pushing the server into sustained memory pressure; 3) under pressure, the log buffer flushes more frequently yet still backs up behind a saturated log device or slow archiver, so commits stall and sessions linger while still hoarding memory and latches. Observable symptoms include dramatic and erratic response times, simultaneous spikes in physical I/O, paging, and log-flush waits, sudden drops in cache hit ratios, frequent checkpoint storms, and cascaded connection timeouts or node evictions.

Causal chain: Inefficient schema and indexing multiply the amount of data each write or read touches, inflating both memory demand and redo generation. The bloated working set competes for limited RAM, causing cache churn and forcing dirty buffers to be flushed more aggressively—actions that funnel yet more traffic into the already stressed transaction-log subsystem. As log flushes lag, commit latency rises; longer-running transactions accumulate and hold even more memory, further intensifying allocation pressure. Meanwhile, memory pressure can shrink log buffers and increase write fragmentation, worsening log I/O throughput. The feedback loop between design-induced workload amplification, runaway memory usage, and log subsystem saturation quickly degrades overall system stability and throughput in write-intensive OLTP workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall forward progress.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, so read or write operations encounter checksum, linkage, or key-order errors.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume nearly all available CPU cycles, leaving little headroom for other sessions or background tasks.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a multi-layer crisis: 1) sessions accumulate in lock wait queues and deadlock detectors fire; 2) queries that finally obtain a lock may fail with corruption or page-verification errors, triggering repeated retries and rollbacks; 3) the surge of retries, deadlock detection sweeps, and corruption checks drives sustained CPU saturation. Observable symptoms therefore span long transaction latency, victim-abort errors, corruption messages in logs, spikes in lock-wait and CPU wait events, runaway run-queue length at the OS level, and rapidly shrinking throughput despite high thread activity.

Causal chain: corrupted pages or mis-linked index nodes can force the optimizer or storage engine to abandon efficient index probes and fall back to broader scans or page-level recovery logic, greatly extending the time each transaction holds locks. Prolonged lock tenure intensifies blocking, deadlocks, and exponential retry storms. Every retry, deadlock cycle, or corruption re-read translates into additional CPU work—deadlock detection graph walks, lock hash-table manipulation, checksum recalculations, and error-handling logic—that further consumes CPU. CPU saturation in turn slows lock acquisition and flush pacing, lengthening critical sections and making it even harder for waiting transactions to progress, while the persisting corruption continually re-injects failures. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another to create a self-amplifying degradation that can cripple an OLTP system until corruption is repaired, contention relieved, or compute resources expanded.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between table structures / indexes and workload access patterns forces inefficient access paths.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages and index structures are internally inconsistent or corrupted, making logical structures unreliable.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage subsystem is saturated, causing high read/write latency and queueing regardless of database configuration.

When all three root causes are present, the database simultaneously executes poorly tuned access paths, encounters unpredictable data-corruption‐induced plan fallbacks, and faces physical I/O saturation. Typical symptoms include: pervasive full-table or full-index scans that already strain disks; sudden, erratic result-set discrepancies or duplicate/missing rows caused by corrupt indexes; optimizer unexpectedly abandoning indexes and reverting to table scans, further inflating I/O; skyrocketing wait times for data-file, temp, and log I/O; alternating spikes of CPU (from repeated re-execution after corruption errors) and long stretches of I/O wait; integrity-check or consistency-check operations running longer than normal and themselves throttling on storage bandwidth; and a flood of engine alerts ranging from checksum failures to "slow I/O" warnings, making problem isolation difficult.

Causally, a sub-optimal physical design magnifies the demand for disk access, pushing the storage layer toward its throughput limits. Corrupted index or data pages then force the optimizer or runtime to discard otherwise efficient index paths, escalating to even heavier full-scan patterns and random probing that intensify disk pressure. The already saturated storage in turn prolongs recovery, consistency-check, and rebuild operations, leaving corrupted structures in place longer and increasing the likelihood of further corruption during stressed I/O conditions. This positive feedback loop between poor design, physical corruption, and I/O bottlenecks degrades performance, erodes data reliability, and complicates remedial actions, as each anomaly both masks and amplifies the others.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from application-level SQL that requests or manipulates far more data than required and from engine parameters that are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, so neither layer can compensate for the other’s inefficiencies.
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Inefficient or ill-scoped statements/transactions that inflate data access, hold resources too long, or create excessive round-trips beyond business need.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Misconfigured memory, logging, checkpoint, parallelism, or session limits that create artificial bottlenecks or under-utilize available hardware resources.

Combined phenomena: • Slow-query logs and statement statistics show extreme, erratic latencies; the same queries sometimes complete quickly and other times stall for minutes. • Wait-class distributions become skewed—e.g., concurrent scans spill to disk due to undersized work memory while CPU cores remain partially idle because parallelism caps are too low. • Prolonged transactions from chatty or scan-heavy logic trigger frequent checkpoints or log-flush storms configured too aggressively, causing I/O bursts followed by idle periods. • Lock waits, deadlocks, and connection pool exhaustion increase as sessions linger in resource waits created by both excessive work and tight limits. • Monitoring displays paradoxes such as high logical I/O but low physical I/O, or memory pressure alongside low buffer-cache hit ratios.

Causal chain: Verbose or poorly filtered SQL expands row sets, consumes more buffer cache, work memory, and redo space, pushing the engine toward its configured ceilings. Because critical parameters (buffer pool size, work_mem, max_parallelism, checkpoint_timeout, etc.) are mis-aligned, the inflated demand cannot be absorbed gracefully: memory spills to temp files, checkpoints fire prematurely, and log files wrap too quickly, each inducing additional waits. Conversely, if parameters are over-provisioned, each heavy query can monopolize large swaths of RAM or worker threads, starving other sessions and amplifying contention created by the flawed workload logic. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other—inefficient SQL raises resource pressure, while poor configuration converts that pressure into severe contention or wasted capacity—making performance regressions broader, harder to predict, and more difficult to diagnose.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Input metadata about data distribution is stale or inaccurate, misleading the optimizer and yielding systematically mis-estimated cardinalities and inefficient execution plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: The replication subsystem cannot receive, persist, or apply primary-side log records fast enough, producing sustained apply and log position lag between primary and replicas.

When both root causes are active, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: poorly costed queries inflate I/O, CPU, memory, and transaction duration on the primary, while the same bloated workloads generate larger, burstier redo streams that downstream replicas cannot keep up with. Monitoring may simultaneously show massive row-count estimation errors, sudden plan changes, lock escalation, and runaway temporary space on the primary, alongside widening replication lag, unresolved replication slots or relay logs, and rising primary log-device utilization. Read-only replica queries may return highly stale data, and planned failovers can take far longer due to both statistics-induced replay slowdowns and the backlog of unapplied log records. Administrators may misinterpret the symptoms because performance degradation appears on both primary and replicas with different surface metrics.

Causally, stale or incomplete statistics provoke the optimizer to choose plans that scan or sort far more data than necessary, elongating transactions and inflating the volume of generated undo/redo. The surge of log traffic stresses the replication channel; any pre-existing bandwidth, CPU, or threading limits on the replica amplify lag. In turn, the growing replication backlog prevents timely log truncation on the primary, further increasing storage pressure and I/O contention, which exacerbates plan performance problems. The prolonged replay times on replicas delay statistics refresh jobs often scheduled there, allowing statistics staleness to persist and creating a feedback loop that continuously degrades both query performance and replication health.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (e.g., buffer-pool size, work-memory, checkpoint and log sizing, parallelism caps) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload characteristics.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database process allocates, grows, and retains memory regions beyond the safe physical or virtual limits of the host, triggering OS-level pressure and cache churn.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, causing allocation failures and blocking persistence operations.

When these three root causes manifest concurrently, the system can exhibit cascading and hard-to-interpret symptoms:  • Erratic wait-event patterns such as log-write or flush waits even while I/O devices are under-utilised, coupled with memory-pressure stalls and sudden OOM terminations.  • Rapid growth of both memory pools and on-disk segments (data, temp, or log) until space ceilings are hit, leading to client-visible "no space left" or "cannot extend" errors.  • Frequent checkpoints and page-flush storms generated by aggressive configuration knobs that flood both RAM and disk, amplifying storage exhaustion while still leaving hot data evicted from caches.  • Node eviction, failover, or restart loops as the engine alternates between memory over-commit, forced checkpoints, and failed log or temp-file extensions.  • Monitoring tools may show contradictory signals—CPU idle yet high latch contention, disks idle then suddenly saturated, memory free then abruptly paged out—making diagnosis non-trivial.

Causal interaction: Mis-set configuration parameters can over-inflate memory allocations (e.g., oversized buffer pools, per-session work memory, or parallel worker buffers), directly triggering the Memory Allocation Anomaly. Excessive in-memory structures force aggressive checkpointing or spill temporary data, increasing redo and temp-file generation that accelerates Storage Space Capacity exhaustion. Conversely, dwindling disk space limits the engine’s ability to recycle logs or grow temp segments, causing it to retain more data in memory and to extend checkpoints more frequently, which feeds back into memory pressure. The escalating memory pressure prompts the engine to flush dirty pages prematurely, generating additional I/O and consuming remaining space faster. As each layer reacts to the stress induced by the others, the database enters a vicious cycle where mis-configuration drives memory bloat, memory bloat drives disk growth, disk exhaustion induces further mis-behaviour of configuration-dependent subsystems, ultimately degrading both throughput and availability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Page-level serialization inside the buffer manager where sessions compete for latches, pins, or hot pages, stalling access even though memory is available.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space reaches its hard limit, preventing further data-file, log, or temp-area growth and returning allocation-failed errors.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume nearly all host CPU cycles, pushing run-queue length and context-switch rates to saturation.

When all three root causes arise together, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: intense latch waits and buffer-busy events are interleaved with repeated allocation-failed errors while overall response time is further stretched by CPU starvation. Hot pages spin on latches yet cannot be evicted or flushed because datafiles or redo/archive destinations have no free space, causing dirty-page flush threads to loop futilely and burn CPU. Concurrent sessions observe a mixture of page-latch, space-allocation, and scheduler-related wait events, prolonged commit latency (logs cannot extend), surging spin CPU without throughput gain, and sudden statement failures once space or CPU is fully exhausted.

Causally, space exhaustion blocks checkpoints and background writers from completing, keeping dirty pages resident. These pages amplify latch contention because they cannot be flushed and released, lengthening hold times on buffer latches. The extended latch hold times drive up CPU utilization as sessions spin or context-switch while waiting, pushing the host toward CPU saturation. In turn, a saturated CPU slows the very maintenance tasks (file growth, log archival, buffer flush) needed to resolve space shortages and clear dirty pages, completing a feedback loop that escalates all three anomalies and can lead to widespread throughput collapse or instance hang.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks a sub-optimal execution plan—even with reasonable statistics—due to cost-model, plan-cache, or version/parameter issues.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Replication receivers or appliers cannot ingest or replay WAL/redo at the rate produced by the primary, producing widening log-position gaps and lag.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical data or index pages are corrupted or internally inconsistent, so access methods and integrity checks no longer trust the on-disk structures.

When all three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits a tangled failure signature: 1) erratic query latencies and plan flips on the primary and replicas, 2) explosive growth in I/O and CPU as bad plans trigger large scans or nested-loop explosions that read corrupted pages, 3) replication lag that oscillates or stalls because corrupted blocks or redo records cannot be applied, leading to repeated retries or worker crashes, 4) divergence between primary and replicas—some replicas may silently miss or duplicate rows due to underlying index inconsistencies while also being hours behind, and 5) administrative alerts about checksum errors, plan cache thrashing, and disk-space exhaustion from retained WAL segments.

Causally, corrupted data or index structures can distort optimizer statistics or cause runtime page-level errors that prompt the optimizer to abandon efficient access paths, increasing the likelihood of sub-optimal plan selection. These heavier plans generate larger volumes of undo/redo and prolonged locks, inflating the replication stream. Simultaneously, when corrupted pages propagate through WAL, replicas may repeatedly fail to apply them, stalling replay and amplifying synchronization lag; this backlog prevents log recycling on the primary, further stressing storage and exacerbating I/O contention that feeds back into poor plan choices. Thus, each anomaly reinforces the others: corruption undermines plan quality; bad plans inflate replication load; replication stalls surface more corruption and resource pressure, collectively degrading both primary and replica stability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism limits, etc.) are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, so the bottleneck originates from the parameters themselves rather than from any intrinsic resource shortage.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or log storage layer runs out of free bytes in data, temp, or archive locations, causing space-allocation failures and blocking growth or write activity.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, exhausting compute cycles and lengthening run-queue wait time for all work.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: frequent checkpoints or aggressive background writers (from poor configuration) generate surges of I/O and log activity that rapidly consume the remaining disk space, while simultaneously driving CPU to 100 % as the engine spends extra cycles on checkpoint processing, log archiving retries, space-error handling, and repeated scan or sort re-tries in shrinking temp areas. Applications may see a mixture of space-exhaustion errors, sudden latency spikes, timeouts, and alternating periods of near-idle disks (due to write throttling) and CPU run-queue waits. Monitoring views show mismatched indicators—high CPU and checkpoint/write wait events despite low actual I/O throughput, plus accelerating free-space depletion and recurrent autovacuum/autopurge backlogs.

Causally, mis-set configuration parameters (too small buffer pools, short checkpoint intervals, oversized parallelism) inflate write-amplification and log generation, pushing storage toward its capacity ceiling. As free space dwindles, the engine triggers more frequent checkpoints and log switches, which further raise CPU demand and intensify space pressure. Space errors force repeated allocation retries and rollback/redo processing, again consuming CPU. The resulting feedback loop—parameter-driven churn → space exhaustion → error handling → CPU saturation—escalates quickly, degrading both throughput and stability across transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback information outpaces background cleanup, inflating on-disk structures and visibility-check cost.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical read/write bandwidth or IOPS of the underlying storage is saturated, driving up latency and I/O wait while CPU remains under-utilised.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Available free space on data, log, temp, or archive volumes approaches or reaches hard limits, leading to allocation failures and write stalls.

When these three root causes manifest together, the database exhibits compounding symptoms: version stores, heaps, and indexes grow rapidly and consume the shrinking free space, while every page read or dirty-page flush contends with an already saturated I/O path, producing long device queues, soaring latency, and persistent "disk full" or "cannot extend" errors. Autovacuum/garbage-collection workers remain permanently backlogged, yet their own activity intensifies the I/O storm. Transaction response times swing from sluggish to outright timeouts; checkpoints, log flushes, and background writer operations stall, causing spikes in replication lag, lock retention, and risk of crash-recovery amplification. Monitoring shows simultaneous escalation of obsolete-row ratios, I/O wait events, and free-space depletion, making it difficult to attribute any single metric to a unique root cause.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn inflates the version store. The extra dirty pages and enlarged tables amplify read and write volumes, pushing the storage subsystem beyond its throughput envelope. Elevated I/O latency slows vacuum/cleaner progress, letting even more obsolete versions pile up and further enlarging the on-disk footprint. The bloated data structures, together with sustained high write rates, accelerate space consumption until capacity thresholds are crossed; at that point, failed extensions and frozen log recycling prevent new transactions, holding snapshots open and creating even more version retention. Thus each anomaly feeds the others: MVCC bloat drives I/O pressure and space usage, I/O saturation throttles cleanup, and space exhaustion blocks recovery actions—forming a self-reinforcing loop that can cripple an OLTP system.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design obliges the engine to scan, join, or retain far more data and for longer periods than business logic really requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The optimizer’s metadata about row counts, data distribution, and correlations is stale or incomplete, leading to systematic cardinality misestimates and poor plan choices.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate memory consumed by buffer caches, plan caches, per-query work areas, parallel workers, and background heaps grows beyond the host’s safe limit, provoking paging, swapping, or OOM events.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits extreme and erratic response times, sudden plan regressions, and node-level memory pressure. Queries already oversized by sub-optimal SQL logic are further mis-planned into hash joins, large sorts, or wide index scans because the optimizer under- or over-estimates cardinalities. These memory-hungry operators inflate work-area allocations, evict useful buffer pages, and bloat the plan cache with many ad-hoc variants generated by chatty application patterns. Concurrent long-running transactions keep locks and row versions alive, preventing page reuse and amplifying cache churn, while the OS shows sustained swap, NUMA rebalancing, or even process kills. End-users observe cascading timeouts, increased retry storms, and sporadic service unavailability that are difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL constructs expand the data footprint and prolong transaction lifetimes; stale or poor statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing memory-intensive physical operations on those inflated datasets; the resulting excessive work-memory grants, spilling, and cache growth breach physical limits, triggering memory pressure and reclaim cycles. Memory stress in turn slows automatic statistics refresh and intensifies plan cache bloat, locking the system into a feedback loop where each anomaly reinforces the others and degrades overall workload stability.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects or reuses a highly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonably accurate.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating the live data set.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space for data files, logs, temp areas, or archives is exhausted or about to hit hard limits.

Composite Definition
This composite anomaly describes a condition in which the database simultaneously suffers from (1) poor execution-plan choices, (2) runaway accumulation of MVCC garbage, and (3) dwindling physical or logical storage space. The workload therefore experiences the combined pressure of inefficient query execution, table and index bloat, and imminent space exhaustion.

Combined Observable Phenomena
• Queries that suddenly switch from index access to full or bitmap scans, run far longer than usual, and generate large temporary-space spills.
• Rapid growth of base tables, indexes, undo/rollback segments, and transaction logs; version-store or vacuum/cleaner processes remain perpetually backlogged.
• Free space graphs show step-function drops; auto-extend/auto-grow requests fail or pause; warning messages cite both "no space left" and "vacuum not keeping up" conditions.
• Statistics drift because bloated pages distort row counts, causing even more unstable plan flips and further execution-time variance.
• End-user symptoms include sporadic timeouts, "cannot allocate space" errors, and unpredictable throughput collapse during peak update or reporting windows.

Causal Chain and Reinforcement Mechanisms
1. Sub-optimal plans (e.g., full table scans or poorly parallelized nested loops) read and modify far more pages than necessary, inflating undo/redo and version chains.
2. The enlarged version store slows visibility checks, prolonging transaction lifetimes; long-running or stalled queries hold old snapshots, preventing cleanup workers from reclaiming dead rows.
3. As MVCC garbage accumulates, table and index bloat consume additional disk space, forcing the storage subsystem toward its capacity limits.
4. Approaching space limits throttle or fail further writes, which in turn can invalidate cached plans, trigger plan recompilations, or disable adaptive features—raising the likelihood of yet more sub-optimal plan choices.
5. The feedback loop—bad plans → more version churn → storage bloat → space pressure → plan instability—amplifies latency and risk of outright service interruption, making the composite failure harder to diagnose than any single anomaly in isolation.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit-path bottleneck where log generation, flush, switch, or archival throughput cannot keep pace with redo production.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion of physical or logical free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas, resulting in allocation failures rather than pure latency issues.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Saturation of host CPUs by database processes, leaving insufficient compute headroom for normal engine and operating-system tasks.

Combined phenomena: • Commit latency, LOG_FLUSH/LOG_SYNC waits, and checkpoint storms rise sharply while host CPU utilization remains pegged. • The log writer and archiver compete for scarce CPU, causing redo files to pile up and quickly consume remaining log and archive space. • Free-space alarms, auto-extend failures, and "device full" errors appear almost simultaneously with escalating run-queue depth and context-switch rates. • As space disappears, new log segments cannot be created or archived, forcing the database to stall user transactions; meanwhile foreground sessions spin or retry, amplifying CPU pressure. • Diagnostic logs show interleaved messages about log switch hangs, space allocation failures, and CPU-scheduler waits, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal chain: High CPU demand—often from inefficient or highly concurrent transactional workloads—starves the log writer and archiver, slowing flush and copy operations. The slowdown prolongs the occupancy time of each log segment; un-archived segments accumulate and rapidly consume the finite log and archive destinations, triggering a storage-capacity crisis. Once space is exhausted, the archiver can no longer off-load segments, which in turn blocks further log switches and forces the log writer to stall commits—feeding back into longer foreground waits that keep database sessions active and consuming even more CPU. Thus, CPU saturation, log-subsystem contention, and space exhaustion reinforce one another, driving the database into a cascading performance and availability degradation characteristic of this composite anomaly.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, partition, and data-type choices do not match workload access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written SQL into inherently expensive access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even with acceptable statistics, often because of cost-model quirks, parameter-sensitivity, or unstable plan-cache behaviour.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Instance-level parameters governing memory, parallelism, logging, and background processes are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, so bottlenecks arise even when the underlying resources are not truly saturated.

Combined phenomena: When all three root causes coexist, queries routinely fall into full scans, non-covering index probes, or bloated nested-loop joins, yet plan shapes can fluctuate unpredictably between executions as the optimizer wrestles with poor physical paths and misleading cost signals. Mis-sized buffer pools or work-memory settings magnify the impact—large scans evicted from cache thrash I/O, while underestimated work memory forces excessive spills. Checkpoint storms or undersized log files can stall already long-running statements, and plan instability after each cache flush or parameter change complicates troubleshooting. Performance counters show simultaneous I/O saturation bursts, CPU spikes from repeated re-optimizations, and idle gaps where throttling parameters (e.g., max parallel workers) prevent effective hardware usage.

Causal chain: A mismatching schema forces the optimizer to consider heavier plans; the optimizer’s cost model, already challenged, may settle on especially poor strategies or oscillate between them. Misconfigured memory, parallelism, or logging parameters then amplify the cost of whatever plan is chosen—small caches penalize the large scans induced by bad indexing, while excessive parallelism makes nested loops fight for resources, reinforcing the bad plan’s inefficiency. Conversely, aggressive or fluctuating configuration changes invalidate or reweight cost estimates, triggering further plan churn. The feedback loop among design flaws, plan mis-selection, and ill-suited runtime settings drives compounding latency, throughput collapse, and diagnostic ambiguity.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : The application issues queries or transactions whose written logic obliges the engine to scan, join, or hold far more data and time than the functional requirement dictates.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and undo records pile up faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check costs.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive host CPU utilisation to sustained saturation, exhausting compute cycles needed for timely request processing.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system experiences a compounded failure mode: chatty or over-broad application statements generate excessive row touches and protracted transactions; the resulting surge of updates and long-lived snapshots accelerates MVCC version bloat; the enlarged heaps and indexes make every future scan, probe, and visibility check more expensive, which in turn magnifies CPU consumption. Observable symptoms include: 1) rapidly rising table and index sizes despite stable business data volume, 2) a growing backlog of vacuum/clean-up tasks with workers permanently active yet unable to keep up, 3) host CPU utilisation pinned near 100 % with high run-queue lengths and scheduler waits, 4) widespread statement-level latency spikes and application timeouts even for read-only operations, and 5) repetitive slow-query log entries for the same logically simple but physically heavy statements.

Causally, inefficient SQL constructs (wide scans, missing predicates, oversized batches, long transactions) create high write-amplification and leave snapshots open, which delays version pruning. The swelling version store bloats on-disk and in-memory structures, causing each subsequent query—many of which are already sub-optimal—to traverse more pages and perform more visibility checks. This elevates CPU demand; once cores saturate, background cleaners are deprived of cycles, letting version debris accumulate further. The feedback loop between poor workload logic, MVCC housekeeping debt, and CPU exhaustion drives an escalating degradation that is difficult to disentangle unless all three contributing root causes are addressed together.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and bloating tables and indexes.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Memory, checkpoint, background-worker, and parallelism parameters are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, so internal subsystems receive too little or too much resource budget at the wrong cadence.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions repeatedly serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, producing buffer-busy waits, spin-loops, and latency spikes.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a feedback loop of bloat and contention: 1) tables and indexes swell with dead versions, causing sequential scans, index probes, and visibility checks to touch far more pages; 2) because the buffer pool is undersized or flushing too aggressively due to mis-set parameters, these extra page touches churn rapidly through the cache, driving up buffer-busy waits, page evictions, and latch acquisition times; 3) cleanup workers remain permanently behind, yet their activity competes with foreground queries for the same hot pages, further lengthening latch wait chains. Observable symptoms include simultaneously growing version-store metrics, high buffer-latch and buffer-pin waits, sustained CPU spin without full core utilization, erratic checkpoint spikes, and warning logs about both transaction-ID wraparound and I/O stall despite apparent hardware headroom.

Causal chain: Misconfigured memory, checkpoint, and autovacuum/autopurge parameters starve background cleaners and shrink effective cache capacity, letting dead tuples accumulate. The expanding heap forces every transaction to read and dirty more pages, which—in the tight cache—triggers frequent evictions and dirty-page flushes. Each flush or page replacement requires latches and I/O slots that many sessions now contend for, magnifying buffer-level serialization. The heightened latch contention slows both cleaners and user transactions, so version bloat grows even faster, further increasing page churn and latch pressure. Thus, configuration mis-tuning sparks a self-reinforcing cycle between MVCC debris build-up and buffer-cache contention, steadily degrading OLTP throughput and latency.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements or transaction patterns that obligate the engine to scan or modify more data, rows, or duration than the true business need demands.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks on the same resources, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated data, log, or temporary space is exhausted or nearly exhausted, preventing further allocations and blocking space-consuming operations.

When these three root causes coexist, the system experiences a compound failure mode: overly heavy or long-lived SQL requests inflate undo, redo, and temporary usage just as they hold locks for extended periods; meanwhile, shrinking free space slows or halts growth of data files, temp segments, and transaction logs. Observable effects include: 1) surging statement and transaction latency with frequent application timeouts, 2) expanding lock wait graphs where blockers cannot finish because they are stalled on space-allocation or log flush operations, 3) deadlocks followed by rollbacks that re-execute the same inefficient SQL, 4) rapid consumption of tablespace, log, or temp space culminating in allocation-failure errors that freeze active transactions mid-commit, and 5) escalating connection-pool saturation as sessions queue behind both locks and space shortages, making it difficult to isolate a single culprit.

Causally, chatty or scan-heavy SQL inflates row-level change sets and temp work files, which in turn intensify lock footprints and prolong transaction lifetimes. The prolonged holds amplify contention, increasing the number and duration of waiting transactions. Each blocked or retried transaction further multiplies DML volume and redo generation, accelerating consumption of data and log space. As space nears exhaustion, auto-extend or log-archive operations stall, preventing commit processing and keeping locks active even longer, which deepens the contention spiral. The feedback loop between space exhaustion, prolonged lock retention, and inefficient SQL processing can rapidly degrade OLTP throughput and force widespread rollbacks or outages.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks, creating blocking chains or deadlocks that halt forward progress until a waiter is granted the lock or a victim is aborted.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, undo records, and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them, inflating data pages and raising visibility-check overhead.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s write-ahead log fast enough, producing widening log-position gaps and preventing log-segment recycling.

Combined phenomena: The database may show long‐running transactions stuck in lock wait queues, a rapidly growing version store and table size, continuous vacuum/clean-up activity that never catches up, and ever-increasing replication apply lag. Lock bloat lengthens transaction lifetimes, so snapshots remain open, preventing version pruning; the extra row versions and larger tables in turn expand I/O and CPU time per statement, lengthening lock hold times and enlarging blocking chains. Meanwhile, the surging volume of undo and redo generated by repeatedly touching bloated pages produces larger log files that must be shipped to replicas, but the replicas are already behind, so additional log segments accumulate on the primary. As log recycling is held back by both open snapshots and replica retention needs, disk space usage spikes on the primary, and replicas deliver increasingly stale reads, reducing failover readiness.

Causal chain: Heavy lock contention freezes or prolongs transactions, pushing the MVCC horizon backward; this prevents cleaners from deleting dead tuples, causing table and index bloat that slows every subsequent statement and amplifies further lock contention. The extra update and cleanup churn inflates WAL generation, which, together with the long-lived transactions that keep old log segments active, overloads the replication pipeline. Replication lag then feeds back by holding even more log segments on the primary, consuming I/O bandwidth and storage that background cleaners and user transactions must now contend with, thereby reinforcing the original lock and version-maintenance problems and driving the system into a mutually aggravating spiral.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults, leading to disproportionate waits or bursts of background activity even when physical resources are not fully utilized.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database process allocates and retains more memory than the host can safely provide, triggering OS pressure, paging, or OOM events and causing volatile cache behavior.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures become physically or logically corrupted, breaking key order, page links, or checksums and making persisted data unreliable.

When these three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a tangled set of symptoms:  • Sudden memory pressure from oversized work areas or buffer pools coincides with erratic checkpoint storms and aggressive log flushing driven by mis-set parameters, amplifying latency spikes.  • Paging, swap, or forced restarts caused by memory exhaustion interrupt I/O patterns, after which corruption errors, checksum failures, or divergent index/heap row counts surface during crash recovery or routine queries.  • Administrators observe oscillations between CPU-bound spin waits (due to mis-tuned parallelism or background workers), I/O idle periods with heavy log-write waits, and integrity-check failures that force query plan fallbacks to full scans, making performance troubleshooting highly ambiguous.

Causal chain: inappropriate configuration settings (e.g., over-sized shared buffers, unlimited per-session work memory, aggressive checkpoint intervals) drive the engine to claim excessive memory. This sustained pressure provokes OS paging and ungraceful process terminations; the resulting write amplification, incomplete flushes, or aborted background operations heighten the probability of torn pages and index inconsistencies. Conversely, latent corruption can inflate memory usage—repeated retries, error logging, and forced cache invalidations—prompting administrators to further tweak parameters, unintentionally enlarging memory footprints. The feedback loop between bad parameters, runaway memory allocation, and emerging physical corruption degrades both performance and data reliability, placing the database into a progressively unstable state that affects transactional and analytical workloads alike.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously experiencing excessive lock contention and/or deadlocks in the lock manager, uncontrolled growth or exhaustion of engine-level memory regions, and physical corruption or logical inconsistency of on-disk data and index pages. All three root causes coexist during the same workload execution, creating a multifaceted failure mode that spans concurrency control, memory management, and storage integrity.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Long blocker-waiter chains, frequent deadlock victim rollbacks, and sharp drops in transaction throughput. 2) Escalating resident-set size, swapping or OOM events, plummeting cache-hit ratios, and CPU stalls caused by memory pressure. 3) Intermittent corruption errors, checksum failures, and mismatched row counts between index and heap scans. Because the faults reinforce one another, operators may also see: transactions stuck in lock wait while holding large private work buffers that cannot be freed; corruption-induced plan fall-backs to full scans that inflate both lock footprints and memory consumption; node restarts triggered by combined OOM kills and corruption-related assertion failures; and a surge of application-side timeouts and retry storms that obscure the true root causes.

Causal interaction: Damaged data or index pages can force the optimizer to abandon narrow index paths in favor of broader scans, which lock more rows or pages for longer periods, heightening lock contention. These heavier scans also allocate larger buffer and work areas, accelerating memory exhaustion. In turn, severe memory pressure prolongs execution time, delays lock release, and may trigger automatic lock-escalation, all of which deepen blocking chains. Prolonged lock waits keep dirty or inconsistent pages pinned in shared buffers, hampering checkpoint flush and increasing the likelihood that corrupted pages survive or propagate. Repeated crash recoveries due to OOM or corruption amplify concurrency storms when clients reconnect, recreating the contention–memory–corruption cycle and progressively degrading the overall database health.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing even well-written SQL into inefficient access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution metadata no longer represent reality, leading the optimizer to choose sub-optimal execution plans because of systematic cardinality errors.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log buffer, files, or archiving pipeline become the primary bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling write activity.

When all three root causes strike at once, the database shows a wide mix of symptoms: queries that should be index-seek or range-scan operations devolve into full-table scans; the optimizer’s row-count guesses are wildly off, so it sometimes picks nested-loop plans that explode into millions of logical reads, or hash/merge joins that spill to disk. These bloated read workloads generate excessive undo/redo and trigger large batch updates or page splits because the underlying index design is non-covering or poorly aligned with predicates. The extra redo volume quickly saturates the log buffer and forces frequent log flushes, leading to LOG_BUFFER_WAIT, LOG_FILE_SYNC, or similar waits; foreground sessions experience both query CPU spikes and commit stalls. Checkpoint storms, long-running auto-stats jobs, and emergency index rebuilds further amplify log traffic, while stale statistics prevent the optimizer from recognizing the true cost of these maintenance tasks. As a result, performance degradations appear both in read and write paths, and the root causes are easily misattributed to generic I/O or concurrency issues.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design makes almost every CRUD statement touch more rows or columns than necessary. This inflates I/O and redo generation. Because statistics are stale or inaccurate, the optimizer cannot compensate—it often picks plans that further widen the access path or use memory-hungry operators, compounding data modification volume. The surge in redo overwhelms the transaction log subsystem, which responds with longer flush times and throttled commit throughput. Those commit delays in turn slow DML completion, extending lock lifetimes and causing even more contention and blocking, which invites emergency maintenance (manual stats updates, index rebuilds) that again produces heavy redo. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others, creating a feedback loop that degrades overall database stability far beyond the impact of any single root cause.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses an execution plan that is markedly sub-optimal even though statistics are acceptable.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical devices that host database files are saturated, driving read/write latency and queue depth far above normal levels.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Critical data, log, temp, or backup volumes run out of free space, hitting hard limits that block further allocations.

When all three root causes occur together, the database shows erratic and degrading performance: execution plans that favour full scans or large hash operations collide with a storage layer that is already bandwidth-starved, causing exponential growth in I/O wait time. Simultaneously, space exhaustion events interrupt or abort the very same long-running statements, temp‐space sorts, or log flushes, leading to a mix of plan re-compilations, partial rollbacks, and repeated retries. Administrators observe a chaotic symptom set—frequent plan changes, skyrocketing I/O waits, sudden "out of space" errors, stalled checkpoints, and prolonged lock retention—making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single subsystem.

Causally, a poor plan often triggers excessive table or index scans that flood the I/O subsystem, pushing it past its throughput ceiling and lengthening statement duration. The longer run times and heavier spill-to-temp exacerbate space consumption, accelerating volume exhaustion. In turn, space shortages cause failed allocations that invalidate or flush plans, prompting the optimizer to recompile and potentially choose even worse plans, while also forcing the engine to retry I/O on already congested devices. This feedback loop amplifies latency, magnifies log-growth and temp usage, and can culminate in service outages where both performance and capacity limits are simultaneously breached.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table and index pages have become physically or logically corrupt, so the storage structures no longer match the logical contents they are supposed to represent.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot deliver the sustained read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database engine, causing prolonged I/O waits and stalled page and log traffic.

When both anomalies are present, the database exhibits a mixture of corruption-style and saturation-style symptoms: index and consistency checks intermittently fail while ordinary queries suffer unpredictable slowdowns; identical statements alternate between missing rows and hanging on I/O waits; recovery, backup, or CHECKDB-like operations may run for excessive durations and still report page, key-order, or checksum errors; log flush latency spikes co-occur with corruption detections, triggering repeated automatic page repairs, forced page flushes, or emergency readahead that further prolong I/O queues; monitoring shows rising wait times for both corruption-related retry logic and device-level bottlenecks, making it difficult to attribute the primary performance degradation.

The causal interplay stems from the fact that storage congestion increases the likelihood that partially written pages, torn writes, or incomplete index rebuilds persist long enough to escape detection, while corrupt blocks force the engine to perform extra physical reads, retries, and redundancy checks that inflate I/O volume and queue depth. Each corrupted page or index inconsistency often causes re-reads, repair attempts, or fallback full scans, all of which demand additional throughput from an already saturated storage subsystem. Conversely, sustained high queue depths and latency windows during peaks extend the vulnerability period for write interruptions (power loss, controller resets), thereby increasing the chance of structural corruption. Together, the two root causes form a feedback loop that amplifies both data-integrity risks and performance degradation, rapidly eroding overall database availability and reliability.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer statement or transaction design that forces the engine to process more data, rows, or time than business logic truly requires.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, leading to bloat and visibility-check overhead.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources such as file handles, shared-memory segments, or thread quotas that are outside the database engine’s direct control.

When all three anomalies occur together, the system exhibits an amplified symptom set: statement latency and slow-query log entries multiply, while table and index bloat lengthen sequential scans and skew planner estimates. Background autovacuum or purge workers run continuously yet fall further behind, and at the same time they intermittently fail to spawn or allocate I/O contexts because per-process file-handle or thread limits have been hit. Users see long-tail response times, timeouts, and sudden "cannot allocate shared memory / cannot create worker" errors. Disk footprint grows rapidly, checkpoint and backup times lengthen, and idle sessions that remain open across think-time exacerbate both version buildup and handle consumption, blurring the boundary between SQL inefficiency, storage bloat, and OS-level shortages.

Causally, chatty or scan-heavy SQL patterns generate excessive updates, deletes, and wide scans, inflating the version store. The bloated heap forces larger buffer and I/O footprints, pushing the engine to open more file descriptors and spawn more maintenance workers. As OS limits are reached, those workers throttle or fail, so version reclamation slows even further, letting bloat accelerate. The growing data size in turn lengthens already sub-optimal SQL operations, prolonging transactions and keeping snapshots open, which preserves even more dead rows. Thus, poor workload logic fuels version accumulation; version accumulation drives higher resource consumption; and OS resource ceilings choke the very background tasks needed to recover, locking the system into a downward performance spiral.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to touch far more data, rows, or time than the true business request requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects or reuses an execution plan whose cost model decision is sub-optimal despite having reasonably accurate statistics.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures on disk have become corrupted or internally inconsistent, making their logical contents unreliable.

When all three conditions coexist, the workload experiences extreme and erratic latency spikes, wide resource excursions, and unpredictable result-set correctness. Over-broad or poorly parameterized SQL keeps transactions open and touches large data ranges; the optimizer, already mis-choosing plans, may oscillate between full scans and inefficient nested loops; corrupted pages or mis-linked index structures further inflate I/O, cause repeated retries, checksum failures, or silent row omissions/duplications. Symptoms manifest as the same queries repeatedly entering slow-query logs with varying plans and row counts, sudden floods of checksum or logical-consistency errors, lock escalation or deadlocks due to long-running transactions stuck on corrupt pages, and application-side timeouts followed by inconsistent business results.

Causally, excessive and ill-scoped SQL amplifies the surface area that the optimizer must reason about and the storage engine must read, raising the probability of touching corrupted pages. Once such pages are accessed, error handling or silent corruption skews runtime statistics, which in turn feeds back into the plan cache and encourages the optimizer to pick even poorer plans on subsequent executions. Conversely, a bad plan that chooses an unnecessary full scan or hot spot index walk is more likely to hit corrupted structures, provoking retries, forced plan invalidations, or emergency fallbacks to slower scans. The interaction forms a vicious cycle: workload inefficiency increases I/O and execution time, the optimizer’s misjudgments magnify that cost, and underlying corruption injects further unpredictability, leading to cascading performance collapse and potential data-consistency exposure across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excess accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback data outpaces background cleanup, inflating on-disk structures and widening visibility checks.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Total in-process memory (buffers, work areas, caches, worker heaps) grows beyond physical limits, inducing OS pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Data, log, and temp areas reach or approach full utilisation, leading to allocation failures and stalled database activity.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the system shows a blended pathology: bloated tables and indexes consume ever-increasing disk space while their swollen pages are simultaneously cached, driving buffer-pool expansion and forcing the engine and operating system into memory pressure and swap thrash. Background vacuum/clean-up workers remain active yet ineffective, and their I/O competes with foreground queries already slowed by cache churn and frequent page faults. Free-space alarms, logfile or temp-space exhaustion, and sudden out-of-memory terminations can occur almost in lock-step. Query plans become erratic due to stale statistics and reduced cache hit ratios, and emergency autovacuum or space-reclamation tasks may be throttled or aborted because neither RAM nor disk space is available to complete them. Administrators observe runaway resident-set size, rapidly shrinking free disk, elevated I/O latency, checkpoint stalls, and a growing backlog of un-recycled transaction logs.

Causal interaction: Heavy update/delete activity produces large version stores that enlarge both the heap and associated indexes, rapidly consuming disk space. The inflated objects must also be read and written more frequently, prompting the buffer manager to allocate additional pages and evict working-set data, which amplifies memory consumption and cache churn. As RAM fills, the OS begins paging, slowing cleanup workers so that obsolete versions linger even longer, further inflating storage demand—a positive feedback loop. Simultaneously, swollen tablespaces and unreclaimed WAL or archive logs push the system toward physical space exhaustion; once disks near capacity, background processes throttle or stall, which again delays cleanup and forces even more memory buffering of dirty pages waiting for checkpoint. Thus, memory pressure, version bloat, and dwindling storage reinforce each other, escalating to widespread performance collapse or service outage if not arrested.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine-level settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, worker counts, etc.) are mis-tuned for the hardware, workload, or version, creating artificial pressure on internal resources.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, logs, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, triggering allocation failures and blocking growth-related operations.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas are reached, preventing the database from creating or accessing required OS objects.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the system exhibits compound symptoms: rapid log-file growth from aggressive checkpointing collides with insufficient disk space, producing log-write stalls, checkpoint storms, and frozen commit processing. Concurrently, the engine’s attempts to auto-extend files, spawn extra background or parallel workers, or allocate additional shared memory are denied by the OS, surfacing as "cannot allocate file descriptor / shared memory / thread" errors in both database and system logs. Sessions may hang in log-related waits while CPU usage oscillates between idle gaps (due to write throttling) and spin loops (from failed worker creation). Maintenance tasks meant to reclaim space or clean orphaned resources cannot launch, causing temp-space bloat and runaway diagnostic logs that further consume the dwindling disk.
