Overall, the workload experiences cascading slowdowns, sporadic transaction failures, and eventual instance-wide freeze or crash recovery cycles.

Causally, mis-set configuration parameters often increase churn: undersized redo logs force frequent checkpoints; small work-memory settings inflate temp spill volume; overly high connection or parallelism caps multiply file and semaphore consumption. These behaviors accelerate space consumption and inflate the count of kernel objects, pushing the system toward its storage and OS-limit ceilings sooner than normal. Once disk fills, the database cannot archive or recycle logs, prolonging checkpoints and inflating the number of open file handles; simultaneous OS denials of new handles or shared memory prevent the engine from adapting (e.g., creating new log segments or spawning cleanup workers). Each anomaly thus amplifies the others: configuration mis-tuning drives resource churn, space exhaustion blocks I/O progress, and OS limit saturation starves the engine of critical handles and memory, jointly intensifying contention, stalling recovery mechanisms, and precipitating full service outages.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, enlarging the version store and degrading visibility checks.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, file, flush, switch, archive) becomes the primary bottleneck, inflating commit latency and preventing timely log recycling.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing ever-growing replay lag and retention of old log segments on the primary.

When all three conditions co-exist, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: commits stall under prolonged log-flush and sync waits while log directories and version stores balloon simultaneously. Table and index sizes grow due to unreclaimed dead tuples, increasing scan times and skewing optimizer statistics. Replication lag widens, replicas fall minutes or hours behind, and primary-side log segments pile up because they cannot be recycled until both MVCC cleanup and replica replay advance the retention horizon. Background vacuum/cleanup, log archiver, and replication sender processes run constantly yet remain backlogged, leading to checkpoint storms, disk-space exhaustion warnings, and potential forced shutdowns or replica cascades.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn amplifies MVCC bloat, which in turn accelerates redo generation and stresses the transaction-log subsystem. As log write and flush latency increase, commit throughput drops, lengthening transaction lifetimes and further delaying version cleanup. Simultaneously, the replication slowdown prevents log truncation, locking old log segments in place; the enlarged log volume exacerbates I/O pressure on the log device and archiver, feeding back into higher commit latency. The expanding version store and retained logs both inflate disk usage, while each subsystem’s backlog deprives the others of progress, creating a reinforcing loop that degrades overall OLTP performance and threatens system availability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from stale or incomplete optimizer statistics and from runaway accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions, so both the optimizer’s picture of data distribution and the physical storage layout are drifting away from reality at the same time.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Estimates vs. actuals diverge even more sharply because dead tuples and page bloat make real row counts higher while statistics still reflect a much smaller live set. 2) Queries that formerly used selective index paths switch to serial or bitmap heap scans, yet those scans run markedly slower than expected owing to fragmented, low-density pages full of dead rows. 3) Autovacuum/cleanup workers show sustained backlog, while automatic statistics refreshes either do not trigger (percentage-based thresholds never met after size inflation) or run but take longer and block on bloated objects. 4) Execution plans oscillate after each manual ANALYZE or forced vacuum, producing unstable performance and making regression diagnosis difficult. 5) Storage usage, version-store metrics, and execution-plan row-count warnings all rise together, and I/O wait times increase on both data and temp spaces.

Causal chain and interaction: Heavy update/delete churn creates large volumes of dead tuples, inflating table and index size; this physical bloat invalidates prior statistics. Because the statistics module triggers on percentage of modified *live* rows, the enlarged object causes required thresholds to rise, delaying automatic statistics refresh and worsening staleness. In turn, poor cardinality estimates drive the optimizer toward full-table access paths that read every dead tuple, generating yet more visibility checks and I/O, further taxing VACUUM/cleanup workers already behind schedule. Long-running transactions that hold old snapshots block both vacuum reclaim and statistics for frozen XIDs, perpetuating the feedback loop. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other, accelerating performance degradation and storage growth until manual intervention (force vacuum + analyze) or resource exhaustion occurs.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Critical metadata such as row-count, histogram, and correlation statistics are stale, missing, or too coarse, causing systematic cardinality misestimation.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer’s costing logic or plan-cache reuse chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even when statistical inputs would in principle allow a better one.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log path—generation, buffering, flushing, switching, or archiving—cannot keep up with the volume of redo, becoming the primary bottleneck for commits and checkpoints.

When all three anomalies coexist, symptoms multiply and overlap:  
• Queries may oscillate between very different plans, often landing on an inefficient plan that amplifies row counts and random I/O because statistics are stale and the cost model mis-ranks alternatives.  
• Poor plans drive excessive row versioning, large sort runs, and wide index or table scans, sharply increasing redo generation; meanwhile the saturated log subsystem lengthens commit latency and holds locks longer, feeding back into even larger active-row sets sampled by future statistics or plan captures.  
• Execution plans show grossly inaccurate estimates, high actual vs. estimated rows, and unexpected operators (full scans, nested loops) together with surging LOG WRITE/LOG FLUSH waits, frequent log-file switches, and checkpoint storms.  
• Application perspective: sporadic but severe slowdowns on both read and write statements, timeouts during peak write bursts, and dramatic variance between executions of the same SQL text.

Causal chain and interaction: Stale or incomplete statistics mislead the optimizer, increasing the probability that the cost model will pick an already risky plan; the resulting plan then produces outsized data modifications, UNDO/REDO, and temp spill volume. This surge in redo overwhelms an undersized or poorly configured transaction-log subsystem, elongating commit and flush times. Extended commit latency lengthens transaction lifetimes, preventing timely auto-statistics refresh, and keeps heavily modified objects locked or pinned, which in turn skews future sampling and encourages further plan mis-selection. The feedback loop thus reinforces both the optimizer’s blindness and the log bottleneck, degrading throughput and predictability across the entire OLTP workload.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonably accurate statistics, causing excessive I/O, CPU, or memory consumption per statement.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long wait chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions accumulate faster than background cleanup can purge them, inflating table and index size and adding visibility-check overhead.

When all three root causes strike at once, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: expensive plans run far longer than expected, keeping row, page, or metadata locks open; these prolonged locks block other transactions, generating extensive wait chains and frequent deadlock rollbacks; while the blocking persists, update and delete activity continues to create new MVCC versions that cannot be reclaimed because readers are still attached to old snapshots and writers are stalled behind locks. Operators observe high CPU from poor plans, rising lock-wait time and deadlock reports, steadily growing table size, bloated indexes, widening gaps between planner estimates and actual row counts, and dramatic drops in overall transaction throughput coupled with surging application-level timeouts.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan often performs wide table scans or nested-loop explosions that touch many more rows than necessary, enlarging the lock footprint and lock duration. The resulting blocking keeps transactions open, preventing vacuum/cleanup workers from advancing the version horizon; this accelerates MVCC bloat. In turn, the swollen heap and indexes skew the optimizer’s cost calculations, making it even more likely to choose poor plans for subsequent compilations. The larger on-disk structures also lengthen lock hold times for index or page-level locks, intensifying contention. Meanwhile, the backlog of obsolete versions elevates I/O and CPU pressure, slowing both foreground statements and background cleaners, further aggravating plan quality and lock congestion in a self-reinforcing loop.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table structures, indexes, partitioning, or data types are mismatched to workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even when SQL is well written.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Catalog statistics are stale, incomplete, or misleading, causing the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and pick sub-optimal plans.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates more memory to caches and work areas than the host can safely supply, triggering OS pressure, paging, and cache churn.

When all three root causes coexist, the system shows a blend of symptoms: queries that should be index-seek driven are compiled into full scans because the needed indexes are missing or non-covering, while inaccurate statistics further mislead the optimizer into believing those scans are cheap. The resulting plans read far more pages than necessary, bloating buffer pools and spilling large hash and sort operations. Memory consumption rises rapidly, eroding cache hit ratios and provoking paging, temporary spill files, or out-of-memory terminations. Execution times become highly volatile: some requests stall on I/O, others throttle on memory grants, and background processes compete with the OS for RAM, causing node-level instability. Because each anomaly obscures the others, traditional tuning signals—such as adding an index or refreshing statistics—yield only partial relief and regress again under load.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design creates inherently heavy I/O plans; stale or incomplete statistics hide their true cost and steer the optimizer toward even heavier plans; these bloated plans inflate memory grants and enlarge the working-set size of buffer and work areas. The swollen memory footprint pushes the host into sustained pressure, which in turn degrades cache efficiency and amplifies the I/O impact of the original design flaw. Meanwhile, memory pressure may delay or cancel automatic statistics collection, keeping statistics stale and completing a feedback loop that reinforces all three anomalies. The combined effect is a self-perpetuating degradation cycle that progressively worsens both latency and stability across OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale or incomplete statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimation, leading the optimizer to choose sub-optimal access paths and join orders.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot pages, undersized cache, or slow I/O make sessions frequently block or spin on page pins, latches, or buffer I/O slots.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical structural inconsistency in data pages or index pages breaks the trustworthiness of persisted storage structures.

When all three anomalies coexist, the system exhibits a mixture of plan instability, erratic execution latency, and intermittent correctness failures. Queries may pick inefficient plans because of bad statistics, then spend excessive time waiting on buffer-busy or page-latch events once those plans hammer a small set of corrupted or hot pages. Corrupted index structures can amplify misestimation by returning duplicate or missing rows, causing row-count feedback to diverge even further from reality. Meanwhile, latch contention is magnified by repeated retries, table scans, or forced full-index rebuilds triggered by corruption detection; CPU usage spikes, I/O throughput plateaus, and error logs intermittently show checksum or key-order violations alongside bursts of statistics-related recompiles.

Causally, stale statistics direct traffic toward the wrong objects or access patterns, concentrating activity on a subset of pages and thereby creating hotspots that intensify latch contention. Prolonged contention increases buffer churn and I/O latency, stretching checkpoint and recovery windows and making corruption-prone pages stay dirty longer, raising the risk of incomplete writes or torn pages that deepen structural damage. Conversely, hidden corruption can distort sampling when statistics are collected, producing even worse estimates and feeding a feedback loop of poor plan choices. Together, these interactions degrade both performance and data correctness far more severely than any single anomaly would, complicating diagnosis because symptoms from one layer disguise or trigger failures in the others.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Pages or their associated latches become hot, forcing concurrent sessions to serialize on buffer-cache access and stall on lightweight synchronization primitives.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Persisted data or index pages are physically or logically corrupt, making on-disk structures unreliable and provoking verification or consistency failures.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes monopolize host CPU cycles, driving the machine toward saturation and elongating every code path that needs scheduler time.

When all three conditions arise together, the system exhibits a toxic blend of symptoms: 1) extreme buffer-busy and page-latch waits as sessions spin to acquire contended buffers, 2) intermittent or repeated checksum, page-link, or index-key errors as the same hot pages are found to be corrupt, 3) host CPU utilization pegged near 100 %, with spin-loops and retry logic crowding the run queue, and 4) workload-wide latency spikes or complete hang because threads waiting on latches are starved by other threads burning CPU on corruption retries or background verification tasks. Error logs may oscillate between latch time-out messages and corruption alerts; execution plans may flip from index to full scans, further inflating both latch pressure and CPU consumption.

Causal chain: corruption in a frequently accessed page forces the engine to re-read, re-verify, or fail-and-retry the page, extending the time that its buffer and latch are held. The prolonged hold amplifies latch contention, causing additional sessions to spin or sleep while the corrupt page is examined. Those spin loops translate directly into elevated CPU demand, which in turn slows the OS scheduler and lengthens latch wait times even more. The spiraling CPU saturation also delays background writer and check-pointer threads, impeding dirty-page eviction and increasing buffer-pool turnover, which raises the probability of repeatedly touching the same corrupt pages. Thus each anomaly reinforces the others, progressively degrading throughput and making root-cause isolation difficult until the corruption is repaired, latch pressure relieved, and CPU usage normalized.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution metadata are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and poor plan choices.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log files, archiver/replicator) is saturated or mis-configured, driving up commit latency and stalling write activity.

When these two root causes strike together, the database exhibits a mixture of optimizer-related and log-related symptoms that reinforce each other:  • Execution plans show grossly inaccurate estimates, leading to plan shapes that inflate redo generation (e.g., unnecessary row-by-row updates, wide nested loops, or missing batch merge operations).  • Concurrently, sessions accumulate high LOG* and COMMIT wait events, throughput collapses, and checkpoint or archival backlogs appear.  • Autovacuum/auto-stats or plan recompiles fire more often but finish later because they themselves suffer from log-flush delays.  • Spikes in buffer dirtiness, memory pressure from bloated hash/ sort operations, and lock contention extend transaction lifetimes, further multiplying log volume and commit queuing.  • Administrators may find it difficult to attribute slowdown to either the optimizer or the log subsystem alone because symptoms of one manifest as effects in the other.

Causal interaction: Stale or incomplete statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing row-oriented, non-batch, or overly parallel plans that touch many more rows than necessary, dramatically increasing redo generation and frequency of commits, thereby amplifying pressure on an already constrained log subsystem. The resulting log-write stalls prolong transaction duration and lock retention, preventing automatic statistics jobs from keeping pace with data changes and allowing statistics staleness to deepen. The feedback loop between inaccurate statistics (producing write-heavy, long-running plans) and log bottlenecks (delaying stats refreshes and transactional completion) spirals into severe throughput degradation and unpredictable query latency.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating on-disk structures and visibility-check overhead.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database process allocates more RAM and swap than the host can safely supply, driving paging, OOM events, and cache-turnover stalls.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Listener, socket, or network-path resources become saturated, leading to slow or failed connection establishment and stalled result transmission.

When all three anomalies manifest together the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: bloated tables enlarge I/O and memory footprints, pushing the buffer cache and worker arenas beyond physical limits; the ensuing memory pressure causes aggressive eviction, swap-outs, and stalled backends whose result buffers cannot be flushed because client networks are congested. Clients experience timeouts both while connecting and while awaiting results; the server side shows growing numbers of idle-in-transaction sessions holding old snapshots, high background-writer and vacuum duty cycles, runaway resident-set growth, frequent OOM kills or NUMA rebalancing spikes, and a swelling backlog of half-open sockets. Monitoring may report simultaneously dropping cache-hit ratios, escalating disk reads, and elevated round-trip times, making it hard to attribute performance collapse to any single layer.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn creates MVCC bloat that inflates the buffer cache requirement; this in turn accelerates memory exhaustion, which triggers kernel paging and prolongs every I/O. Memory stress delays background cleanup workers, letting version stores grow still faster—a positive feedback loop. Concurrently, memory-starved backends take longer to produce and transmit result sets; these longer-lived sessions monopolize network sockets and max out connection pools, which increases connection retries and amplifies network congestion. The congested network then slows snapshot-holding clients, further preventing cleanup of old versions. Thus, MVCC debris drives memory overcommit, memory pressure hampers cleanup, and impaired connectivity locks sessions in place, collectively deepening resource depletion and pushing the OLTP system toward cascading latency and availability failures.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from stale or incomplete optimizer statistics, severe transaction-level lock contention, and host-level CPU saturation. Each root cause is independently harmful, but when they occur together they create a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades throughput and response time in a highly concurrent OLTP workload.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Execution plans show large cardinality misestimates and select sub-optimal join orders or access paths, often choosing full scans or low-selectivity index probes. 2) Those plans increase the number of rows touched and the duration of data-modifying statements, inflating the lock footprint and prolonging lock hold times. 3) Concurrent sessions pile up in long blocker-waiter chains; deadlock reports, application timeouts, and rising lock-wait seconds are observed alongside surging CPU utilisation near 100 %. 4) The CPU run queue grows as sessions spin on latch/lock manager operations, while background statistics-update tasks and deadlock detectors compete for the same saturated cores. Symptoms become hard to attribute to a single layer because query plans, lock waits, and CPU pressure all appear as co-primary bottlenecks.

Causal chain: Stale statistics → cardinality misestimation → inefficient, work-expensive plans → longer statement execution and larger lock scopes → lock contention and deadlocks → increased context switching and spin-waiting in the lock manager → CPU saturation. The saturated CPUs in turn slow automatic statistics collection and prolong rollback or deadlock-victim cleanup, keeping statistics stale and locks held even longer, thereby amplifying both the contention and the compute bottleneck in a self-reinforcing cycle.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan cache, or background heaps that pushes the host into memory pressure, paging, or OOM situations.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Sustained saturation of host CPU by database processes, producing long run queues, context-switch storms, and system-wide latency spikes.

When all three root causes collide, the workload exhibits reinforcing symptoms: queries lacking proper indexing devolve into full scans and large hash/sort phases that allocate massive work buffers, rapidly inflating memory use. Memory pressure causes frequent buffer evictions, swap activity, and plan-cache churn, which forces additional physical reads and re-parses. The repeated large scans and reprocessing cycles drive CPU utilization to sustained saturation; concurrently, kernel and engine wait events show paging, scheduler contention, and memory latch waits. End-user latency and throughput fluctuate unpredictably as some statements time out under CPU exhaustion while others stall on memory faults or buffer re-loads, making performance problems appear both widespread and erratic.

Causally, a poor schema/index design initiates oversized I/O and compute work per statement. These bloated operations consume large per-query work areas and enlarge the buffer and plan caches, triggering the memory allocation anomaly. Once the host starts paging or throttling memory requests, every buffer miss forces extra CPU cycles for re-reads, decryption, decompression, and re-planning, driving the CPU resource anomaly. Elevated CPU pressure, in turn, slows background flushers and memory reclamation threads, delaying buffer recycling and exacerbating memory bloat. The vicious cycle—inefficient data access → excessive memory use → CPU saturation → slower reclamation → further memory and CPU stress—amplifies each constituent anomaly and pushes the database into a state where small workload surges or maintenance tasks can precipitate acute outages.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table, partition, and index structures do not match workload access patterns, forcing the optimizer into wide scans, non-covering lookups, and excessive index maintenance work.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries pile up faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating on-disk structures and visibility-check overhead.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Table and index files grow rapidly because bloat from dead MVCC versions is layered on top of redundant or poorly chosen indexes, driving up I/O volume for every scan. 2) Queries that should be selective are executed as full-table or full-index scans; the scans now traverse many more pages than the live data actually needs, so latency and buffer churn escalate. 3) Autovacuum or similar cleanup workers run almost constantly yet fail to catch up, their work slowed by the oversized and mis-aligned index set they must walk. 4) Statistics drift as the live-row density drops, further skewing the optimizer toward the already expensive plans. 5) Write throughput degrades because every UPDATE/DELETE must touch multiple unnecessary indexes and append more row versions, while also contending with long-running cleanup tasks.

Causal interaction: Sub-optimal schema and indexing choices increase the number and size of index entries that must be maintained for every data change, directly lengthening MVCC undo/redo chains and the work that vacuum processes must perform. As cleaners fall behind, version bloat expands the physical tables, magnifying the cost of the original design flaw by making sequential scans even heavier and rendering existing indexes less selective. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other: bad design slows version cleanup; delayed cleanup enlarges data structures and statistics errors, making the design mismatch more harmful. The feedback loop can quickly push an OLTP system into a state where both read and write performance deteriorate sharply and maintenance windows cannot recover in time.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical data model and indexing strategy do not match the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient full-table scans, excessive row lookups, and write hot-spots.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level memory, checkpoint, log, parallelism, or background-worker settings are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, causing avoidable waits and resource churn.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Data files, logs, or temporary areas reach or approach hard space limits, leading to allocation failures and cascading stalls.

Composite definition: The database is simultaneously hampered by a poor schema/index design, misaligned engine parameters, and shrinking free space. Each of the three root causes is independently sufficient to degrade performance, but their coexistence produces a more severe, multi-layer failure mode that blends logical inefficiency, runtime misallocation, and physical space exhaustion.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Queries that should be index-seek driven spill to large hash or sort operations because covering indexes are missing, filling up TEMP segments and triggering “no space left” errors. • Full-table scans driven by design flaws flood the buffer cache; at the same time an undersized buffer pool or overly aggressive work-memory setting forces frequent evictions, checkpoint storms, and log switches. • Checkpoints and log flushes stall because the log or archive destination is nearly full, yet CPU and I/O remain under-utilised due to throttling waits (e.g., LOG_FILE_SYNC, CHECKPOINT_QUEUE) caused by conservative parameter limits. • Administrators observe erratic latency spikes, mixed wait events (buffer-busy, temp-space, log-file-sync), and a rapid drop in free space that monitoring alarms cannot attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain: Inefficient access paths from the schema/index design generate excess I/O, temporary spill files, and enlarged redo logs. Misconfigured memory, work-area, and checkpoint parameters amplify this footprint by pushing data to disk more often and limiting in-memory reuse. The inflated I/O and log volume consume storage faster, accelerating the approach to space boundaries. As free space declines, checkpoints slow and temp allocations fail, which in turn make optimizer feedback and maintenance (e.g., index creation to fix the original design issue) harder or impossible. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another: design inefficiency → higher resource consumption; bad parameters → higher churn and lower tolerance; space exhaustion → new errors and blocked remediation, producing a vicious performance and stability spiral.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The log‐write, flush, switch, or archive path becomes the primary bottleneck, stalling commit processing and redo generation.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer saturates its read/write or IOPS capacity, elevating latency for any file on the affected volumes.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores are saturated by database processes, leaving little head-room for additional work and elongating run-queue waits.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database can exhibit a multi-layer performance collapse: commits and checkpoints queue behind slow log flushes; data and log I/O waits pile up because the storage subsystem itself is bandwidth-starved; meanwhile CPU remains pinned, so background writer, log writer, archiver, and user sessions all contend for compute cycles, lengthening every wait even further. Observable symptoms include: rapidly escalating commit latency, frequent log‐file switch warnings coupled with slow archive completion, device queue depths pegged, service times well above specification, scheduler and run-queue waits dominating wait-class views, and a system-wide slowdown where both short OLTP transactions and maintenance tasks time out or deadlock around resource starvation.

Causally, each anomaly amplifies the others. A slow storage plane prolongs every log write, which increases the lifetime of foreground sessions holding latches and therefore raises CPU pressure; the elevated CPU load in turn slows log-writer and I/O submission threads, lowering the effective IOPS they can push to an already saturated device. As checkpoints and archivers miss their windows, log directories bloat, producing larger, burstier write operations that further flood the constrained storage path. The vicious cycle leads to a feedback loop where storage stalls raise CPU usage (busy-waiting, context switches), high CPU usage throttles I/O throughput (delayed submissions), and both together deepen the log subsystem bottleneck, potentially driving the database into prolonged stalls or crash-recovery scenarios.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a physical-schema/index design that forces inefficient access paths, sustained saturation of host CPU resources, and exhaustion of kernel-enforced process or handle limits. The three layers—data model, compute, and operating system—are therefore all active bottlenecks, and any single-layer fix alone will be insufficient.

Combined phenomena: Queries show full-table scans, non-covering index lookups, or needless partition scans that inflate CPU time per statement. Host metrics reveal near-100 % core utilization, long run queues, and frequent context switches. In parallel, the engine or system logs record failures to create threads, open files, allocate shared memory, or start parallel workers; new sessions intermittently fail while existing ones slow dramatically. Application latency spikes, timeouts multiply, and performance becomes erratic—sometimes appearing as pure CPU saturation, other times as sudden "cannot allocate resource" errors—making diagnosis confusing.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and indexing force the optimizer toward scan-heavy or row-by-row execution, inflating CPU demand. The resulting surge in CPU usage lengthens query runtimes, causing connection backlogs and encouraging the engine to spawn more worker threads or parallel processes. This escalated process and descriptor count pushes the workload toward operating-system limits on file handles, threads, shared memory segments, and async-I/O contexts. Once those limits are hit, kernel denials prevent new workers from starting, which further queues work on already saturated CPUs, amplifying latency and resource thrashing. Conversely, when OS limits are low, even a moderate CPU spike caused by sub-optimal schema can tip the system into both CPU starvation and kernel-resource exhaustion, creating a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades throughput far faster than any of the three anomalies would individually.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously suffers from stale or incomplete optimizer statistics and an overgrown MVCC version store whose cleanup has fallen behind. As a result, the cost-based optimizer makes decisions on metadata that are both outdated and distorted by heap and index bloat, producing systematically mis-estimated and sub-optimal execution plans.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Extreme and erratic divergences between estimated and actual row counts, with estimates often orders of magnitude off due to statistics that no longer reflect the swollen base tables. 2) Query plans flip unpredictably between index scans and full-table or bitmap scans as the optimizer struggles to evaluate heavily bloated relation sizes. 3) Execution times elongate because plans chosen to access small perceived row sets instead confront large on-disk footprints and must wade through many dead tuples, incurring excessive random I/O, CPU spent on visibility checks, and memory consumed by mis-sized hash or sort operations. 4) Autovacuum or background purge workers appear saturated yet ineffective; meanwhile, automatic statistics refresh jobs are throttled or miss their windows, causing a persistent feedback loop of poor plans and further bloat.

Causal chain and interaction: MVCC version accumulation inflates table and index pages, rapidly invalidating previously accurate statistics and increasing the skew between logical row counts and physical storage size. The optimizer, lacking fresh or sufficiently detailed statistics, underestimates result sizes and selects access paths that intensify I/O and CPU pressure. These heavier plans prolong query execution and hold snapshots open longer, which in turn delays version reclamation and forces the version store to grow even faster. The enlarged version store makes maintenance operations costlier, causing further delays in both vacuum/purge cycles and statistics refresh, thereby reinforcing the downward spiral of bloat, misestimation, and degraded performance.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer choices.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Excessive serialization on hot buffer-cache pages and their latches or pins, causing sessions to stall or spin while competing for page access and flush slots.

When these two root causes coexist, queries are not only forced into full-table scans, non-covering index probes, or hot-page insert patterns by poor schema/index design, but they must also fight for the same overcrowded buffer pages, latches, and I/O slots. Observable symptoms therefore include: 1) widespread full-object or non-selective index scans that inflate buffer churn, 2) surging buffer-busy/latch wait events concentrated on a few root or data pages, 3) CPU spikes from spin-locks coupled with high I/O service times, 4) erratic query latency where some executions stall far longer than optimizer estimates, and 5) write throughput collapses during bulk loads or hot-spot inserts despite otherwise adequate hardware resources.

Causally, the sub-optimal physical design creates access patterns (e.g., range scans on unpartitioned, unindexed columns, monotonic inserts into a single data or index page, or repeated lookups requiring back-to-table fetches) that funnel many concurrent sessions toward the same limited set of buffer pages. This concentrates reads, updates, and dirty-page flushes on those pages, inflating latch acquisition and buffer pin times. In turn, the resulting latch contention prolongs page residency, reduces effective cache capacity, and magnifies the penalty of the original design flaws—encouraging yet more full scans and page churn. The feedback loop between design-induced hot spots and low-level buffer contention can degrade both transactional and analytical workloads, making the underlying issues harder to diagnose because symptoms appear both at the execution-plan level and deep inside the storage engine’s synchronization layer.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, or auxiliary memory regions that pushes the database process and host beyond safe physical-memory limits, triggering paging, OOM events, or node eviction.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Replicas, subscribers, or downstream consumers are unable to receive, persist, or apply primary transaction-log records at the rate they are generated, causing widening log-position gaps, replay lag, and retention of old log segments.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data pages or index structures become internally inconsistent—checksum failures, broken page links, key ordering errors—leading to wrong or missing results and corruption-related engine errors.

When these three root causes are concurrent, the system exhibits a compounded failure profile: memory pressure on the primary and replicas grows as bloated buffer/plan caches coexist with ever-expanding retained WAL / redo segments held for lagging replicas; intensive retry loops and corruption checks amplify CPU usage and stall foreground queries. Replication delay masks or propagates latent page and index corruptions, so stale replicas may serve inconsistent reads or, upon catch-up, replay corrupt blocks that trigger crash-recovery cycles, further bloating memory with repeated recovery allocations. Operators observe erratic throughput, sharp drops in cache hit ratios, frequent OOM killer or instance restarts, rapidly filling disks due to unrecycled logs, replica apply processes stuck on corrupt pages, and divergence between primary and replica query results that is hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, runaway memory allocation on the primary inflates per-process RSS and can throttle background tasks that recycle log segments, causing prolonged WAL retention exactly when replicas are already behind. The swelling log backlog forces replicas to allocate large relay buffers and extend on-disk log stores, exacerbating their own memory and I/O pressure and slowing apply latency further. As replicas eventually replay large bursts of changes, latent data-block or index corruption—possibly originating from earlier memory-pressured writes or storage faults—surfaces during redo or validation, halting apply threads and freezing replication. The primary, unable to recycle logs because of stalled replicas, accumulates even more un-flushed cache and log pages, increasing the probability of additional memory exhaustion and corruption events. This feedback loop tightens the coupling between allocation pressure, replication lag, and structural corruption, driving the cluster toward cascading failures and data-availability risks.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between tables, indexes, partitions, data types, or constraints and the workload, forcing queries into full scans, non-covering lookups, or unbalanced partition access.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Unbounded or badly sized buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and session heaps that push the host into sustained memory pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Exhaustion of free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas, leading to allocation failures, auto-extend errors, and stalled write or sort operations.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the engine exhibits a cascade of symptoms: full-table scans triggered by poor indexing inflate the amount of pages pulled into the buffer cache and enlarge per-query hash/sort work areas, accelerating memory growth; once memory is saturated, these operations spill to temporary segments, which rapidly erode remaining disk space and provoke temp-file or tablespace full errors; concurrent paging, swap thrashing, and temp-space saturation magnify I/O latency, so even simple OLTP statements and maintenance tasks stall, while log files and backups cannot grow or rotate, risking transaction blockage and recovery gaps.

Causally, inefficient schema design is the first amplifier—forcing wide data reads that demand large memory and temp resources. The enlarged memory footprint hastens the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly; under pressure, the engine spills intermediate results to disk, directly feeding the Storage Space Capacity Anomaly. Conversely, dwindling disk space prevents further temp spills or index creation, forcing more in-memory work that exacerbates memory exhaustion. This positive feedback loop between design-induced I/O, runaway memory use, and shrinking storage surfaces as a compounded, hard-to-diagnose performance and availability degradation that is far more severe than any of the three issues in isolation.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Excessive serialization while acquiring buffer-cache pages, page pins, or latches, causing CPU spin and inflated buffer-busy waits.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Exhaustion of free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas, leading to allocation failures, stalled checkpoints, or log switches.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Saturation or instability in the client/server network or connection pool, producing connection timeouts, refused sessions, and socket-level backlog.

Combined anomalous phenomena: When all three root causes strike together, sessions that finally obtain a connection experience erratic response times dominated by buffer-busy and page-latch waits, only to hit "no space left" or "cannot extend" errors mid-statement. Concurrently, stalled checkpoints and blocked log switches—caused by full filesystems or tablespaces—hold dirty buffers in memory longer, enlarging latch hold times and raising CPU spin. The prolonged execution makes back-end processes occupy network sockets for extended periods, filling listener backlogs and depleting connection slots; new clients see escalating connection latency, retransmissions, and authentication failures. Monitoring views show a mélange of symptoms: soaring latch and buffer busy wait counts, near-zero storage free space with frequent auto-extend attempts, growing queues of idle-in-transaction sessions, and spikes in aborted or half-open TCP connections.

Causal interaction: Space exhaustion slows or blocks checkpoint, log archive, and background flush activity, preventing dirty pages from being evicted; this forces active sessions to compete longer for the same hot buffers, amplifying latch contention. The resulting execution slow-downs lengthen transaction lifetimes and increase the number of simultaneously active back-end processes, pushing the server toward its connection and socket limits. As connections pile up and clients retry after timeouts, network and listener resources become congested, feeding back additional latency that further stretches transaction duration and buffer residency. The intertwined feedback loops between storage stalls, in-engine contention, and network overload create a cascading degradation that can rapidly incapacitate both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution metadata are outdated or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation during cost-based planning.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup, bloating tables and indexes and increasing visibility-check overhead.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Total memory reserved by buffer caches, work areas, and background structures grows beyond the host’s safe limits, driving OS-level pressure, paging, and potential OOM events.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the engine exhibits compound symptoms: execution plans are chosen on the basis of stale statistics that underestimate the now-bloated relation sizes, producing pathologically sub-optimal strategies such as nested-loop joins that iterate over swollen heaps or sequential scans that spill to disk because inflated memory footprints have triggered global memory pressure. Concurrently, vacuum/cleanup workers compete for scarce memory and I/O while struggling to reclaim runaway version stores, and their backlog further enlarges table and index sizes. Operators report wildly divergent estimated versus actual row counts, steadily declining cache hit ratios, sudden bursts of swap activity, and erratic query latencies punctuated by out-of-memory terminations or instance restarts.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn creates surplus row versions; if automatic statistics refresh is suppressed by that same churn or by long-running snapshots, the optimizer’s view of table cardinalities lags behind reality. The resulting mischosen plans often scan far more pages than expected, escalating buffer-pool turnover and prompting the engine to allocate additional work memory for spills and re-reads, which in turn aggravates global memory pressure. Heightened memory stress slows background cleaners and may throttle their work via cost-based back-off, allowing even more dead tuples to pile up. The enlarged storage footprint feeds back into further cardinality drift and memory consumption, forming a vicious cycle that degrades transactional throughput and endangers system stability.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Inefficient or overly broad application-issued statements and transaction patterns that force the engine to process more data or hold resources longer than business logic requires.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters that misalign memory, logging, checkpoint, parallelism, or worker settings with actual hardware and workload needs.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced limits such as file handles, shared memory segments, or thread quotas, restricting the database process regardless of internal configurations.

When these three root causes occur simultaneously, the workload generates excessive scans, large result sets, and long-running transactions while the engine is hamstrung by sub-optimal buffer sizes, work memory, checkpoint cadence, and worker pools. The inflated demand collides with artificial ceilings imposed by the operating system, producing a compound symptom set: long-tail and highly variable statement latency, frequent slow-query log entries, sudden spikes of log-write or buffer-flush waits that do not match actual device utilization, intermittent "cannot allocate shared memory / open file" errors, failed connection or parallel-worker startups, and partial outages where active sessions stall yet CPU and I/O metrics appear under-utilized. Diagnostic views may show bloated memory evictions, repeated checkpoint storms, and escalating kernel error messages about resource exhaustion, making it difficult to pin the problem on any single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL inflates resource consumption, driving up memory pressure, dirty-page generation, and concurrent session counts. Misconfigured parameters prevent the engine from absorbing this pressure—small buffer pools force excessive I/O and checkpoints, while oversized per-session memory or parallelism settings multiply the footprint of every bad query. The heightened demand accelerates consumption of kernel objects (file descriptors, shared memory, threads); once OS limits are reached, new allocations fail, which in turn causes retries, rollbacks, and further stretches transaction lifetimes. Each layer amplifies stress on the others: poor SQL magnifies the impact of bad configuration, while both together push the process into the hard wall imposed by operating-system limits, resulting in a feedback loop of escalating latency, resource thrashing, and intermittent errors that degrade overall database availability and performance.

Name: CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host-level compute cores are saturated by database processes, driving load averages and run-queue waits to the point where even lightweight tasks compete for CPU time.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database engine and its worker processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings such as file-handle, thread, shared-memory, or cgroup quotas, preventing new resources from being allocated even though the engine itself is willing.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The network or listener layer cannot accept or service the rate of incoming connections or data transfer, causing socket backlog growth, refused sessions, retransmits, and client-side timeouts.

When these three root causes appear simultaneously, symptoms overlap and amplify: CPU saturation stretches every code path, including process creation, authentication, encryption, and packet handling, so connection handshakes linger and pile up in the listener backlog. The backlog itself grows until kernel socket or file-descriptor limits are reached, at which point new sockets are refused. Meanwhile, the engine cannot spin up additional back-end threads or parallel workers because both CPU cycles and per-process thread quotas are exhausted, producing a mixture of "cannot create process/thread", "too many connections", and client timeout errors. Existing sessions exhibit inflated statement latency from CPU queuing, periodic stalls while waiting on kernel objects, and prolonged client-read/client-write waits as network buffers drain slowly under high CPU contention. Monitoring views may concurrently report elevated run-queue depth, rising OS error counters for resource exhaustion, and spiking network retransmissions, making it hard to attribute the primary bottleneck.

Causally, heavy CPU demand—often from inefficient queries or runaway parallelism—drives up context switches and kernel calls, accelerating consumption of file descriptors, threads, and async I/O contexts. As OS limits are hit, the engine’s ability to accept or spawn connection handlers degrades, forcing clients to back off and retry, which in turn inflates connection churn and socket creation rates, feeding further into descriptor exhaustion. Simultaneously, degraded CPU availability slows TLS handshakes and packet processing, elevating network latency and retransmissions; the longer sockets stay open, the more descriptors are occupied, deepening the OS-level shortage. The intertwined feedback loops between compute starvation, kernel resource depletion, and network saturation produce a cascading failure mode where relieving only one layer is insufficient—the anomalies reinforce each other to magnify overall performance collapse and partial service outages.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions contend for mutually incompatible locks, forming long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or downstream replicas fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply the primary’s log stream at the production rate, widening replay lag.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space in data, log, archive, or temp areas approaches exhaustion, threatening further allocations and log recycling.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set: transactions on the primary block each other and remain open longer, inflating commit latency and enlarging transaction-log records. The swollen log must be shipped and applied downstream, but replicas already lag, so unsent or unapplied segments accumulate. Because log truncation or recycling is now gated by both open transactions and replica confirmation, primary-side log volumes balloon, quickly consuming the remaining storage budget. Operators observe sharp rises in lock-wait time, deadlock reports, client timeouts, replication delay metrics, runaway disk usage in log or archive areas, and eventual "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors that can halt new transactions and stall recovery replay on replicas.

Causally, severe lock contention lengthens transaction lifetimes, delaying commit acknowledgments that replication relies on, thereby increasing replica lag. The growing lag prevents the primary from reclaiming old log segments, so every additional blocked or retried transaction produces more unreleased log data. The expanding log footprint accelerates storage exhaustion; once space becomes scarce, auto-extension failures or forced checkpoints slow down data-file and log writes, which further degrades throughput and raises lock-hold times—feeding back into even worse contention and replication backlog. This positive feedback loop can cascade into a full outage affecting both primary OLTP processing and downstream read scalability or disaster-recovery objectives.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model, indexing, or partitioning choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans, lookups, or data rewrites.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Aggregate buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and background heaps outgrow available physical memory, provoking paging, allocation churn, and OOM events.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Underlying disks or storage fabric are unable to sustain the read/write volume demanded, driving up queue depths and latency.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload experiences a cascade of symptoms: poorly indexed queries generate excessive logical reads that overflow the buffer cache, evicting hot pages and inflating physical I/O. The inflated I/O stream collides with already saturated storage, so read and write latencies spike, amplifying wait events such as buffer busy, read-IO, log flush, and temp I/O stalls. Concurrently, memory pressure causes frequent buffer recycling, hash/sort spills to disk, plan-cache flushing, and even OS-level swapping, further multiplying physical I/O and prolonging CPU stalls. End users observe erratic but persistently high response times, batch jobs overrun maintenance windows, and nodes may terminate due to out-of-memory or I/O timeout conditions, making it difficult to attribute slowness to any single layer.

Causally, a deficient schema/index design is the first trigger: full scans, non-covering probes, and unpruned partitions enlarge the working-set size and inflate per-query work memory. This heightened demand pushes the engine to allocate more buffers and work areas, breaching memory limits and inducing cache churn or swapping—hallmarks of the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly. As hot buffers are prematurely evicted and large hash/sort regions spill to disk, the volume of physical reads and temp writes surges, directly pressuring the storage subsystem. Because the Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly is already present, the storage layer cannot absorb the compounded load, so latency balloons, which in turn prolongs query lifetimes. Longer-running sessions hold onto memory and latches even longer, feeding back into memory exhaustion and perpetuating the vicious cycle of cache misses and I/O saturation. The intertwined anomalies therefore reinforce each other, leading to severe and escalating deterioration of overall database performance and stability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from hot-page/latch contention inside the buffer manager, a stalled replication pipeline that cannot keep up with primary log generation, and approaching or reached exhaustion of physical or logical storage space. Each problem alone can degrade performance, but their coexistence creates a tightly-coupled failure scenario that endangers both throughput and data safety.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Users notice sharp and erratic response-time spikes as sessions spin on buffer latches while dirty pages linger in memory. Checkpoints and background flushers run more aggressively yet free space continues to shrink because archived or shipped log segments accumulate—replicas lag behind, preventing log recycling. Monitoring dashboards show simultaneously high buffer-busy and page-latch wait events, widening replication lag metrics, rapidly declining free-space alarms, and possibly "cannot extend" or "out-of-space" errors. CPU usage is elevated without proportional throughput; I/O queues deepen from forced flushes; and replica read consistency deteriorates as standby snapshots fall minutes or hours behind.

Causal Interaction: 1) Buffer and latch contention slows transaction completion, lengthening the time dirty pages and unflushed log records stay active. 2) The replication subsystem, already unable to consume WAL/redo fast enough, leaves log files retained on the primary, inflating disk usage. 3) Growing log retention and churn consume the remaining free space; once space becomes scarce, data-file or log auto-extension fails, causing emergency checkpoints that intensify buffer flushing and further magnify latch contention. Conversely, space pressure can throttle background writers and archivers, making dirty-page eviction slower and keeping hot pages pinned longer, which heightens buffer contention. The feedback loop between clogged replication, latch hot spots, and space exhaustion accelerates degradation, potentially culminating in system-wide stalls or forced shutdown.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resource, causing blocking chains or deadlocks managed by the lock manager.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings for memory, checkpointing, logging, and parallelism are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, creating artificial bottlenecks unrelated to true resource exhaustion.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, breaking key order, page links, or heap-index mappings and making the storage layer unreliable.

When these three root causes strike at once, the system can exhibit an intertwined symptom set: lock wait times and deadlock-victim rollbacks surge, yet host CPU, I/O, or memory metrics appear only partially utilized because mis-set parameters throttle useful work while allowing idle hardware cycles. Queries that do complete may return inconsistent row counts, fail with page-verification errors, or fall back to table scans, further enlarging the lock footprint and lengthening blocking chains. Checkpoint or flush storms triggered by mis-tuned settings increase I/O pressure exactly when corrupted pages require rereads or retries, amplifying latency spikes. Application threads pile up in both connection-pool wait queues and retry loops as they encounter alternating lock-timeout, deadlock, or corruption exceptions, making the overall performance degradation hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, poor configuration can be the catalyst that magnifies both locking and corruption effects: undersized buffer pools or overly aggressive checkpoints force frequent disk access, raising the probability that transactions touch damaged pages. When a corrupted index forces the optimizer to abandon an efficient access path, the resulting full scans acquire many more row, page, or table locks, intensifying contention. Long I/O stalls on bad blocks keep locks held longer, widening wait chains; deadlock detection may fire more often, causing rollbacks that re-enter execution and re-encounter the same corrupted structures. Simultaneously, mis-aligned log or memory parameters slow recovery from these aborts, allowing blockage to propagate through the workload. Thus, each anomaly reinforces the others: corruption inflates lock scope and duration, mis-configuration prevents timely progress or recovery, and the compounded lock contention spreads the performance collapse across the whole OLTP system.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, or correlation statistics are stale, missing, or insufficient, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal execution-plan choices.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or degraded network, listener, authentication, or socket resources limit connection establishment and data transfer between clients and the database.

When these two root causes act concurrently, the database can choose overly expensive or chatty execution plans (e.g., large hash joins, full scans, massive result sets) precisely while the network layer is least able to carry the inflated traffic. Observable effects include: • Sharp spikes in query latency and server CPU as misestimated plans over-produce rows. • Prolonged client-side waits during result fetching, intermittent timeouts, and cascading application retries that inflate connection counts. • Server processes stuck in client-read/client-write or network send waits, while execution-plan statistics show grossly inaccurate cardinality estimates. • Frequent plan recompilations after bulk loads that coincide with rising socket backlog, retransmissions, and authentication stalls, making it difficult to pinpoint whether slowness is inside the engine or on the wire.

Causal chain and interaction: Stale or inadequate statistics drive plans that emit far more data than intended or that require excessive remote look-ups, multiplying the volume and duration of network traffic. The bloated data streams saturate already constrained network and listener resources, increasing round-trip latency and connection hold times. In turn, network slow-downs extend query runtimes, delaying automatic statistics refresh jobs, prolonging lock holds on tables undergoing statistics collection, and permitting statistics to drift even further from reality. This feedback loop amplifies both anomalies, leading to widespread throughput collapse, session pile-ups, and unstable performance across transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical or logical corruption of on-disk data and index pages such that page checksums, key order, or heap-to-index mappings are no longer trustworthy.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores become saturated by database processes, leaving insufficient compute capacity for the rest of the workload.

When both faults occur simultaneously, the system exhibits a compound failure mode: corruption-induced full table scans, repeated page rereads, checksum retries, or error-handling loops multiply CPU demand, while the already maxed-out CPUs slow internal recovery routines, verification passes, and client queries. Observable symptoms include near-100 % CPU utilization alongside a spike in physical-corruption messages in the error log, sudden plan switches from index seeks to exhaustive scans, dramatic divergence between index and heap row counts, time-outs in integrity-check utilities, and pervasive latency across unrelated sessions as the scheduler queue length explodes.

Causally, damaged pages or broken index pointers force the optimizer or storage layer to fall back to costlier access paths, reread pages, or invoke on-the-fly repair logic—each action consuming additional CPU cycles. The elevated CPU load lengthens I/O and latch holding times, increasing the window for further corruption to surface and complicating post-failure recovery. In turn, CPU starvation delays background validation jobs and checkpoint processing, allowing more corrupted pages to remain undetected and propagating inconsistent data to replicas or backups. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other, escalating from isolated page issues or momentary CPU spikes into a widespread performance and data-integrity crisis.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Multiple sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages or latches, stalling while trying to pin or modify pages held by others.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or subscriber nodes cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo fast enough, producing widening log-position gaps and retained primary logs.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying volumes hit their physical IOPS/throughput ceiling, driving up read/write latency and I/O wait time.

When all three root causes are active, the database exhibits a compounded failure pattern: 1) CPU spin and prolonged page-latch waits on the primary, 2) storage queues and device latency spiking on both primary and replicas, 3) rapidly expanding write-ahead logs, relay logs, or retained segments, 4) replication lag that grows despite normal network health, 5) checkpoint and background-writer activity that cannot drain dirty pages, and 6) cascading response-time and throughput degradation that is hard to attribute to a single tier because buffer, storage, and replication metrics all show distress.

Causal chain: Hot pages and latch contention generate bursts of physical I/O (dirty-page flushes and replacement reads); this extra traffic pushes the storage subsystem past its throughput limit, further lengthening flush times and keeping pages pinned longer, which in turn intensifies latch contention. The same saturated storage slows WAL writes and replay on replicas, so replay lags behind, preventing log recycling on the primary. The growing retained log set increases storage usage and write volume, feeding back into the storage bottleneck and extending latch hold times. Thus each anomaly reinforces the others, producing a feedback loop that degrades buffer concurrency, disk service levels, and replication freshness simultaneously.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer reuses or chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though the underlying statistics are adequate.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks.

When both root causes strike together, inefficient plans (e.g., full-table scans, unordered nested loops, or missing parallelism) hold larger lock footprints for longer durations, while the resulting lock waits postpone plan-dependent work in other sessions. Observable symptoms include: sudden plan flips followed by explosive lock-wait time, dramatic drops in throughput, erratic query runtimes where some executions finish quickly while others stall behind blockers, frequent deadlock reports after a plan change, and lock-escalation events triggered by the inflated I/O and row count of the poor plan. Performance tools show both high CPU/I/O from the bad plan and a lock table filled with long-lived blockers and victims.

Causal interaction: a sub-optimal plan inflates the amount of data touched and lengthens transaction duration, expanding the window during which locks are held. The enlarged lock scope (row → page → table) amplifies contention, which in turn prolongs queues in the lock manager. Extended wait times keep transactions open longer, preventing plan-cache turnover and fostering further reuse of the bad plan across parameter values, reinforcing poor plan selection. The feedback loop between plan inefficiency and lock contention thus deepens and perpetuates both problems, degrading overall OLTP system stability.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer reuses or chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite correct statistics, leading to inefficient access paths, inappropriate join methods, or unstable plan flips.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages or index structures causes missing/duplicate rows, checksum failures, or unexpected engine errors, making the storage layer untrustworthy.

When both root causes are present, the database may exhibit extreme and erratic behaviour: the optimizer may alternate between inefficient full-table scans and corrupt-index-driven lookups, producing wildly varying runtimes, sporadic spikes in I/O and CPU, and unpredictable result sets that sometimes show missing or duplicated rows. Execution plans that appear reasonable in the cache can still fail at runtime with corruption or latch time-outs, while integrity-check errors surface intermittently. Sudden plan recompilations triggered by corruption-induced statistics divergence or failed index seeks can cause flurries of ad-hoc plans, exhausting cache memory and further destabilizing performance. Troubleshooting becomes difficult because poor performance, wrong results, and physical corruption errors mingle, obscuring which symptom stems from which layer.

Causally, damaged index or data pages distort cardinality feedback and may force the optimizer to rethink or invalidate previously good plans, increasing the likelihood of sub-optimal plan selection. Conversely, an already poor plan that overuses a corrupt index amplifies read amplification and exposes the corruption more frequently, accelerating error propagation and potential crash recovery events. The feedback loop between unreliable storage structures and volatile plan choices can therefore reinforce each anomaly, degrading throughput and reliability across both OLTP and analytic workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Excessive or poorly-written application statements and transaction demarcations that drive the engine to touch more rows, return larger result sets, or keep transactions open longer than the true business need.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced objects such as file handles, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, preventing the database process from acquiring the operating-system resources it requests.

When these two root causes strike simultaneously, users observe an extreme long-tail of statement latencies, frequent timeouts, and sporadic "cannot allocate resource" or "too many open files" errors. Queries that already scan or lock large data ranges because of sub-optimal SQL now stall mid-execution when the engine cannot obtain additional file descriptors, worker threads, or shared memory. Connection storms triggered by application-level retries further deplete process or thread quotas, leading to partial outages where existing sessions hang in uninterruptible I/O or lock-wait states while new sessions are refused. Monitoring shows CPU and I/O utilisation well below capacity, yet wait-time histograms are dominated by OS-level resource acquisition waits and user-level lock/latch contention amplified by the prolonged transactions.

Causally, poorly tuned SQL inflates the demand for kernel resources—longer scans keep file handles, buffers, locks, and threads alive, while batched or Cartesian operations require more temporary files and memory mappings. This pushes the database process toward the fixed OS limits faster than anticipated. Once limits are hit, the kernel denies new allocations, which in turn causes the database to pause or retry internal operations, lengthening execution time and holding application locks even longer. The extended lock holds and session backlogs feed a positive feedback loop, aggravating both the workload-logic inefficiency and the OS resource scarcity, eventually cascading into widespread performance degradation and intermittent service outages.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free physical or logical space for data, logs, or temporary areas reaches exhaustion limits.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes drive the host CPU close to saturation, leaving too few cycles for the rest of the workload.

When all three root causes are present, the database exhibits a cascade of intertwined symptoms: a plan regression suddenly switches selective index access to full scans or hash joins that spill to disk, inflating both CPU consumption and temporary-space usage. Temp segments and growing undo or redo logs fill remaining storage, triggering allocation failures, auto-extend stalls, log-archive back-pressure, and "out of space" errors. At the same time, the CPU remains pegged, lengthening every I/O request, catalog access, and background maintenance task, so space-reclamation jobs, log shipping, and plan-cache management all slow down. The result is erratic but severe query latency, widespread enqueue and scheduler waits, repeated plan recompilations due to cache eviction, and sudden session aborts when space or CPU limits are finally breached.

Causally, a poor plan initiates excessive buffer touches, parallel threads, and large intermediate result sets, directly driving CPU load and temp-space consumption. Elevated CPU utilization delays checkpoint, archive, and cleanup processes, preventing timely space recycling. As storage fills, the optimizer may abandon previously viable plans that require work areas or create new plans that favor CPU-heavy in-memory operations, further worsening CPU saturation. Space exhaustion can also invalidate or flush plans, forcing more compilations and again increasing CPU pressure. This feedback loop between bad plans, CPU saturation, and space shortages rapidly degrades overall database stability and makes single-factor remediation ineffective until all three dimensions are addressed together.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer repeatedly chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to excessive I/O, CPU, or memory use per statement.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions acquire incompatible locks on the same resources, causing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall throughput.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages or index structures makes the physical representation of rows or keys unreliable.

Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal plan choices, heavy lock contention, and underlying data/index corruption.
