Each of the three root causes is active at the same time, so queries may execute with inefficient plans, fight over locks, and occasionally hit corrupt pages or broken index structures—all within the same workload execution window.

Combined anomalous phenomena: (1) Query texts randomly alternate between fast and extremely slow runtimes as the optimizer selects poor plans, sometimes forced into full table scans when damaged indexes are skipped. (2) Large scans and mis-estimated cardinalities inflate lock footprints, leading to long blocking queues, frequent deadlocks, and application timeouts. (3) Corrupted pages or malformed index links surface as sudden I/O errors or silent row omissions; when detected, the engine may escalate to table locks for recovery or consistency checks, further amplifying contention. Monitoring will show erratic query plans, surging lock-wait and deadlock statistics, escalating I/O retries, and integrity checker or error-log reports—all interleaved without a single dominant symptom.

Causal chain and interaction: Index or data corruption can distort statistics and force the optimizer to abandon otherwise selective access paths, pushing it toward full scans or unhelpful join orders—triggering the Query Plan Selection Anomaly. These inflated scans touch far more rows and pages, acquiring many more row or page locks, which lengthens critical sections and intensifies Transaction Lock Contention. In turn, prolonged blocking keeps versions or pages pinned, hampering background scrub or repair processes and increasing the window during which corruption affects additional queries. The resulting deadlocks cause transaction rollbacks that force the optimizer to re-evaluate statements, potentially caching yet more unstable plans. Together, the three issues form a reinforcing loop that degrades performance, jeopardizes data integrity, and complicates root-cause isolation in high-concurrency OLTP environments.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages or their protecting latches, causing stalls and CPU spin without overall memory exhaustion.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply primary log records at source speed, leading to widening replay lag and retention of old log segments.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database process hits kernel-enforced limits for handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or similar objects, preventing it from allocating new kernel resources even though engine-level quotas appear free.

When all three root causes manifest together, the system shows a blended symptom set: 1) intense page-latch and buffer-busy waits, high CPU spin, and throughput collapse on the primary; 2) replication lag that grows erratically, with relay or retained WAL files piling up, replicas reporting apply throttling, and fail-over readiness deteriorating; 3) intermittent OS-level allocation errors—failure to open additional file descriptors, spawn parallel or apply workers, or allocate shared memory—which surface both in database logs and kernel dmesg output. Because OS limits block the creation of extra background writers, flushers, or replication apply threads, latch pressure is not relieved and replication catch-up workers cannot scale, making the combined performance degradation appear as a single, opaque bottleneck rather than three distinct issues.

Causal chain: heavy latch contention on a small set of hot pages inflates active session count and prolongs critical sections, rapidly consuming kernel objects such as threads, asynchronous-I/O contexts, and file handles. Hitting those OS limits prevents the primary from launching additional buffer-flush or checkpoint helpers, so dirty pages linger longer, keeping latches held and further aggravating buffer contention. Simultaneously, the same kernel caps restrict WAL sender/receiver and apply workers, throttling the replication pipeline. Replica lag rises, which in turn forces the primary to retain more log segments, growing disk usage and increasing buffer-pool turnover—all of which feed back into latch contention. Thus the three anomalies reinforce one another in a vicious loop that degrades throughput, inflates latency, and jeopardizes recovery objectives across both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, causing page-level stalls regardless of total memory size.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes collectively saturate host CPU, driving high run-queue pressure and system-wide latency.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a multifaceted bottleneck pattern: CPU utilization hovers at or near 100 %, yet throughput stays flat because many runnable threads spin or block on buffer-busy and latch waits. Wait-event views report an alternating mix of latch, buffer-busy, and scheduler/run-queue waits; OS metrics show high context-switch and spin time with pockets of idle I/O capacity. Checkpoint storms or aggressive background writers triggered by mis-set parameters extend the dirty-page queue, prolonging latch hold times and further bloating CPU usage. End-user queries suffer from unpredictable latency spikes and throughput collapse that do not improve even when more CPU cores are provisioned or when isolated configuration knobs are tweaked.

Causally, ill-chosen configuration parameters (e.g., undersized buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint interval, excessive worker or parallelism limits) create hot pages and rapid buffer churn, which magnify latch contention inside the buffer manager. The same mis-configuration often spawns too many runnable workers; as they fight for the same latches, they spin, driving up CPU consumption and inflating the run queue. Elevated CPU pressure in turn lengthens the time to service background flushes and checkpoints, keeping dirty pages in memory longer and re-intensifying latch contention—a feedback loop that obscures the original mis-configuration and makes the combined anomaly more severe than any single root cause alone.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Bottleneck in generation, flushing, archival or retention of write-ahead log records, stalling commit processing and write throughput.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages have become corrupted or internally inconsistent, making persisted structures logically or physically unreliable.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server transport, listener or connection-handling resources are saturated or unstable, delaying or aborting session establishment and data transfer.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database may exhibit a multi-layered failure signature: commits hang or time-out, yet even successful transactions later surface missing or duplicated rows due to latent corruption; error logs show alternating bursts of log-flush and log-sync waits, page-checksum failures and connection-refused messages; clients experience a mix of slow authentication, dropped sessions, and data-integrity exceptions. Recovery utilities and background check-pointers run continuously but fall behind because log archival stalls, while network retransmissions and half-open sockets amplify commit latency. Administrative attempts to rebuild indexes or run integrity checks are throttled by both log I/O saturation and unreliable network channels, making the true extent of corruption hard to assess.

Causal chain: network congestion and listener saturation increase round-trip latency for commit handshakes and archiver file transfers, lengthening the time each transaction occupies the log buffer. The swollen log backlog forces aggressive checkpointing and log switches; if the underlying data pages are already corrupt, these checkpoints repeatedly hit verification errors, provoking partial rollbacks and even more redo generation, further overloading the log subsystem. Conversely, corruption in indexes or data blocks can trigger excessive redo (e.g., repetitive page-clean operations or index rebuild attempts) that drives the log system into saturation. The resulting log-flush stalls prolong transaction hold-times, thereby keeping sockets open longer and inflating the population of active connections, which worsens the existing network bottleneck. This self-reinforcing loop degrades both durability and consistency guarantees, making OLTP workloads unable to meet latency or correctness SLAs while obscuring the primary point of failure.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings such as buffer-pool size, work-memory, checkpoint cadence, log-buffer length, and parallelism are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, creating artificial pressure that is not rooted in the underlying resources themselves.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, physical log files, flushing, switching, and archiving—cannot keep up with redo generation, causing commit stalls, checkpoint storms, or backlog in replication/archiving pipelines.

When both conditions arise concurrently, the database exhibits compounding symptoms: sharp spikes in commit latency, bursts of log-flush and log-write waits while I/O devices appear under-utilised, repeated emergency checkpoints that evict hot pages from an undersized buffer pool, rapid growth of log and archive directories, and oscillations between CPU spin and I/O idle time. Sessions may pile up on "log sync" or "flush" waits, while background cleaners and recovery workers lag, leading to autovacuum/compaction debt, bloated tables, and unpredictable throughput. Monitoring may show paradoxical metrics—high wait times alongside low physical device utilisation—making diagnosis harder.

Causally, mis-set configuration parameters often amplify inherent weaknesses in the log subsystem: a too-small log buffer or overly aggressive synchronous commit policy forces every transaction to flush, driving the already constrained log files and archiver into saturation. Conversely, when the log subsystem stalls, mis-configured checkpoint intervals shrink recovery windows, triggering emergency checkpoints that flood the log further and thrash the buffer pool. Oversized per-session work memory and excessive parallel workers increase concurrent redo generation, while inadequate connection or background-worker limits delay log archival, causing retention pressure. The feedback loop between mis-tuned parameters and a bottlenecked log path escalates latency, jeopardises durability guarantees, and can ultimately halt write processing.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are valid, leading to excessive resource demand per statement.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or downstream replicas fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply WAL/redo as fast as the primary generates it.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate host CPU, starving other activities and lengthening scheduling latency.

When these three root causes coincide, the sub-optimal plans inflate CPU consumption on the primary and, once shipped, on every replica that must re-execute the same inefficient SQL during logical or physical apply. The resulting CPU saturation slows local query execution, background housekeeping, and the replica apply threads simultaneously. In parallel, the replication channel begins to lag; monitoring views show rapidly widening LSN/SCN gaps, growing retained logs, and increasing replica staleness. On both primary and replicas, users observe longer query latencies, stalled failover readiness, and escalating disk usage as log recycling is blocked by outstanding replication positions.

Causally, poor plan selection is the ignition point: inflated row loops, missing pruning, or mis-estimated joins drive CPU and generate larger transaction logs. The surge in CPU demand pushes the host to saturation, lengthening process run-queue times and slowing the single-threaded or lightly parallelized apply workers on replicas. As apply throughput falls behind the primary’s heightened log generation rate, replication lag compounds, which in turn prevents log truncation and keeps more redo on disk, increasing I/O pressure. The feedback loop—sub-optimal plans → CPU exhaustion → slower apply → larger backlogs—propagates across all nodes, making each individual anomaly harder to diagnose in isolation and severely degrading overall database performance and resilience.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written so inefficiently that they drive the engine to process far more data or hold locks far longer than the true business requirement dictates.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, or partition design does not match access patterns, forcing even well-written statements into full scans, non-covering lookups, or write-amplified index maintenance.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated free space for data files, indexes, logs, or temporary areas reaches hard limits, causing allocation failures and write stalls rather than pure I/O bandwidth saturation.

Combined phenomena: When all three root causes coexist, long-running or chatty SQL generated by the application meets a schema lacking the right supporting structures, leading to massive full-table or full-index scans, spill-to-disk hash/ sort operations, and bloated intermediate results. These operations create excessive temporary segments, huge redo/transaction logs, and frequent index leaf splits, accelerating space consumption. As free space dwindles, the engine triggers emergency auto-extend, space scavenging, or outright allocation failures, which in turn prolong statement latency, trigger lock timeouts, block writers, and surface "out-of-space" errors to the application. Performance degradation and space exhaustion therefore appear together, with slow queries, intermittent write stalls, aborted DML, sudden log-archive backlog, and cascading replica lag all occurring in the same time window.

Causal chain: Inefficient workload logic inflates the volume of data read and written; the missing or ill-suited indexes magnify this volume by preventing selective access and by adding maintenance overhead on every DML. Both factors exponentially increase the size of temporary work areas, undo/redo logs, and secondary index pages. The burst of space demand rapidly consumes tablespace and log capacity, pushing the system into autogrowth events or hard space limits. Once space becomes scarce, allocation pauses and log recycling delays further slow or block the very workload that is already running long, creating a reinforcing feedback loop that degrades throughput, heightens contention, and can ultimately cause service-level outages.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and increasing visibility-check work.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine settings for memory, background workers, checkpointing, and parallelism are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, so internal subsystems operate with inappropriate resource budgets or cadences.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Data files, log areas, or temporary/backup destinations run out of free space, producing allocation failures, stalled writes, and growth-limit errors.

When all three root causes strike at once, the database exhibits a compounding failure pattern: dead tuples and rollback segments bloat tables and indexes, while mis-configured memory and worker limits prevent vacuum/garbage-collection processes from keeping up, causing version stores and relation files to balloon until the underlying tablespace, log, or temp volumes exhaust their physical capacity. Operators see a convergence of symptoms: rapidly escalating disk-usage alarms, sudden log-archive or data-file growth spikes, longer and less predictable query latencies due to enlarged heap scans and bloated indexes, frequent autovacuum or cleanup workers stuck or thrashing, checkpoints triggering under duress yet unable to flush because target filesystems are full, sessions receiving "no space left on device" or "cannot extend" errors, and wait events oscillating between space-allocation stalls and version-visibility scans.

Causally, excessive MVCC churn is the initial generator of extra pages and undo records. Mis-tuned configuration parameters (e.g., undersized cleanup worker budgets, conservative vacuum cost limits, small log segments, overly aggressive checkpoint intervals, or insufficient temp/maintenance memory) throttle the very mechanisms that should reclaim that space, so the bloat progresses unchecked. The swollen relation and log files rapidly consume the finite storage allotment, pushing the system into a capacity crisis. Once space becomes scarce, checkpoint and vacuum operations slow further because they cannot allocate new segments, which in turn leaves even more dead versions on disk, forming a positive feedback loop that magnifies latency spikes and increases the probability of outright service outage. Together, the three anomalies reinforce one another, turning what would be benign bloat, mild mis-tuning, or manageable space usage in isolation into a self-amplifying OLTP outage scenario.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are accurate.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, leaving too few cycles for the rest of the workload.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server transport or connection-handling infrastructure becomes a throughput bottleneck, causing delays in establishing or servicing sessions.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal plan selection, host-level CPU saturation, and constrained network/connection capacity. Together these three root causes create a multilayer performance crisis in which inefficient plans generate excessive CPU demand while the network layer cannot move data or establish sessions fast enough, amplifying latency and error rates across the entire workload.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Drastic and frequent plan flips that favor full scans or over-parallelized execution, driving CPU usage to sustained 90-100 %. 2) Run-queue depth, context switches, and CPU-bound wait events coincide with surges in client-side connect or read timeouts, "too many connections" errors, and growing server backlog queues. 3) Statement latency and throughput become highly variable; some sessions wait on CPU, others stall on client-read/client-write waits, and retry storms escalate both CPU and network pressure. 4) Monitoring shows a mismatch between cached plan costs and actual resource consumption, steep spikes in network retransmissions, and a sudden plateau in completed transactions per second despite rising workload demand.

Causal interaction: Sub-optimal plans inflate row processing, parallelism, and result-set size, directly raising CPU cycles consumed per statement and volume of bytes sent over the wire. The surge in CPU contention slows process scheduling, lengthening every network handshake, authentication, and data send, which in turn keeps back-end sessions open longer and exhausts listener sockets. Connection stalls and retries feed an even higher request rate into the server, causing the optimizer to compile more ad-hoc statements and cache additional poor plans, closing the feedback loop. The intertwined effects of inefficient planning, CPU starvation, and network congestion therefore reinforce one another, driving the system into a self-amplifying saturation state that is harder to diagnose because symptoms span optimizer, operating-system, and network layers simultaneously.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log pipeline (buffer, writer, flush, switch, archive, and replication retention) is saturated or stalled, inflating commit latency and halting forward progress of write activity.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages have become physically or logically corrupt, breaking key order, links, or checksums so that the storage structures can no longer be trusted.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively consume and contend for CPU cycles to the point of host-level saturation, slowing every CPU-bound activity.

When these three root causes strike at the same time, the system exhibits a multilayer failure signature: commits and checkpoints hang behind growing log backlogs while overall response times balloon; wait-event views show simultaneous LOG_FLUSH, ARCHIVE, and CPU_RUN_QUEUE contention; integrity-check jobs or auto-repair tasks report checksum, page-verification, or index-key errors yet take unusually long to complete; query plans degrade from indexed lookups to full scans, amplifying CPU consumption and redo generation; error logs interleave corruption reports with "log file switch/checkpoint not complete" warnings; replication or backup processes stall because both corrupt pages and unarchived logs block their progress.

Causally, corruption in data or index pages can force the optimizer or recovery components to perform full-table scans, index rebuilds, or page rereads, multiplying CPU demand and drastically increasing redo production. The surge of log records stresses an already constrained log subsystem; slower log flushes lengthen commit hold times, causing active sessions to accumulate and consume even more CPU while waiting. In parallel, CPU saturation slows the log writer, archive, and integrity-check threads, further delaying log persistence and corruption repair. The feedback loop—corruption-driven redo volume → log subsystem bottleneck → session pile-up → CPU exhaustion → slower corruption handling and log flushing—escalates until the database experiences severe throughput collapse or enters protective shutdown.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks and must wait or deadlock, throttling throughput.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive or apply primary log records fast enough, widening replay lag.

When all three anomalies strike together, the database simultaneously runs inefficient execution plans, suffers heavy blocking inside the primary, and falls behind on shipping or applying its redo stream. Symptoms compound: badly chosen plans generate large scans or high-fan-out nested loops that touch far more rows than necessary, inflating lock footprints and lock hold times. This magnifies wait-for chains and deadlock frequency, driving up transaction latency, connection-pool exhaustion, and application timeouts. The same bloated work inflates the primary’s redo volume; because replicas are already CPU- or I/O-bound, their apply processes cannot keep up, causing rapidly growing replication lag, swollen log retention on the primary, and endangered failover objectives. Administrators may observe simultaneous plan flip events in the cache, spikes in lock-wait statistics, deadlock reports, and replica replay delays, making it difficult to attribute slowdowns to any single layer.

Causal interaction: a poor plan increases row touches and I/O, which prolongs transaction duration and enlarges the lock scope and hold time, directly intensifying lock contention. Extended blocking inflates commit latency, which in turn bursts redo generation when the blocks finally clear; the resulting log spikes overwhelm replication channels already strained by the same inefficient plans running on secondaries. Conversely, replication lag can delay conflict resolution and apply-side locks, feeding back into longer lock retention on replicas and, in multi-primary or read/write split architectures, propagating contention hot spots back to the primary. Thus each root cause amplifies the others, creating a feedback loop that degrades both local transaction throughput and cross-node consistency guarantees.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers (1) an on-host transaction-log write/flush bottleneck, (2) an off-host replication receive/replay backlog, and (3) saturation of the network and connection-handling layer that transports client traffic and ships the log stream. Together these three intertwined faults cripple the end-to-end commit, ship, and replay pipeline that protects transactional durability and availability. 

Amplified Observable Phenomena: • Application commits stall with soaring log-flush and log-sync waits, while archive or redo directories grow rapidly because completed segments cannot be recycled. • Replication monitoring shows diverging LSN/SCN gaps, increasing send/receive/replay lag, and bloated relay logs. • Listener queues fill, new sessions experience authentication or TCP timeouts, and established sessions pile up in client-read/client-write waits; network interfaces report retransmits and elevated RTT. • Checkpoint storms, frequent log switches, and "cannot allocate log" or "replication retention" alerts appear concurrently, and failover readiness drops as replicas fall hours behind. The combination makes it difficult to determine whether the primary, the network, or the replicas are at fault, while all three layers exhibit degraded performance.

Causal Interaction: A slow or full transaction-log device lengthens commit latency and forces aggressive log switching; each switch amplifies the volume of log data that must traverse the network to replicas. Constrained network bandwidth, high packet loss, or listener saturation then throttles log shipping, enlarging replication lag and forcing the primary to retain additional log segments. This retention prevents log recycling, further filling the already stressed log disk and intensifying the log write/flush bottleneck. Meanwhile, frustrated applications open more connections or retry failed attempts, swelling connection pools and exhausting socket and backend slots, which in turn worsens network congestion and listener delays. The reinforcing loop between log I/O saturation, replication backlog, and network/connection exhaustion leads to cascading slowdowns, potential log-device exhaustion, and risk of primary unavailability under OLTP workloads.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply transaction-log records at the rate the primary emits them, causing widening log-position gaps and retained WAL segments.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, exhausting compute cycles and inflating run-queue and scheduler waits across all workload components.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, socket, or connection-slot resources between clients/replicas and the server are unable to sustain the offered throughput, yielding timeouts, retransmissions, and refused sessions.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, symptoms compound: replication lag grows rapidly while both primary and replica CPUs remain pegged, yet neither side can clear backlogs because network throughput and connection-handling capacity are throttled. Clients observe slow or failed connections, rising statement latency, and stale read-only replica data. Primary disk usage surges as unrecycled WAL accumulates; OS metrics reveal high context-switch rates, swollen socket queues, retransmissions, and long run queues. Monitoring views show replication replay delay, CPU-bound wait events, and client-read/client-write waits intertwined, making it difficult to attribute latency to a single layer.

Causally, network congestion or listener exhaustion first restricts log streaming and client traffic, causing the primary to retain WAL. The replica, receiving data in bursts, spikes its apply workers and saturates CPU, further delaying catch-up. Concurrently, CPU saturation on the primary slows both query processing and the network stack, amplifying packet loss and connection backlog, which in turn worsens replication lag. Each layer therefore reinforces the other: network bottlenecks throttle replication, replication lag inflates CPU bursts during catch-up, and CPU exhaustion degrades network I/O handling. The feedback loop drives escalating lag, widespread latency, and degraded failover readiness until at least one resource pressure is relieved.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model and indexing choices do not match workload access patterns, forcing inefficient plans and excess I/O.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or related log/temporary areas run out of free space, leading to allocation failures and halted operations.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, threads, or similar objects are exhausted, preventing the database from creating or accessing required resources.

When all three root causes are present, symptoms intertwine: poorly indexed queries trigger large full-table scans and spill to temp segments, rapidly consuming tablespace and temp space; background growth of data files or logs fails because host file-descriptor quotas or filesystem space are simultaneously exhausted; error logs show a mix of "no space left on device" and "too many open files" while query latency escalates and write operations stall. Autovacuum, index rebuilds, and backup jobs may start but abort mid-way due to both space exhaustion and lost OS resources, leaving partially created objects that further waste space and ties up additional file handles. End-user experience degrades from slow responses to outright session failures as new connections cannot allocate shared memory or temp work areas.

Causally, the inefficient physical design inflates I/O volume and temporary allocations, accelerating consumption of both disk space and kernel objects (e.g., temp files, workfile descriptors). Rapid space growth forces frequent file extensions, each of which requires additional file handles and shared memory mappings, pushing the system toward OS limits. Conversely, once OS handle or memory limits are hit, auto-extension and cleanup tasks fail, preventing space reclamation and exacerbating space shortages. The mutual reinforcement of design-driven bloat, space exhaustion, and OS limit saturation produces a feedback loop that intensifies resource starvation and makes the composite anomaly harder to diagnose than any single constituent issue.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data model and indexing choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even when statements are well written.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Catalog statistics are stale, incomplete, or inaccurate, causing the optimizer to mis-estimate cardinalities and pick sub-optimal plans.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU cores, leaving insufficient compute capacity for the rest of the workload.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a mis-aligned physical schema, misleading optimizer statistics, and sustained CPU saturation. Together these root causes make queries both logically and physically inefficient while the engine lacks compute headroom to mask the deficiencies.

Combined phenomena:  • Execution plans show full scans or nested-loop cascades on large tables where selective index probes should occur, with estimated row counts far from the actual figures.  • Plan shapes flip unpredictably after data changes or recompiles, yet all alternatives consume abnormally high CPU, driving overall host utilization to near 100 %.  • Wait-event views alternate between CPU-bound waits and I/O stemming from unnecessary scans; end-user latency spikes sharply during peak periods, and tuning changes that address only one layer (e.g., adding an index or updating stats) yield partial or short-lived relief.  • Automatic statistics jobs or index-rebuild tasks themselves compete for CPU, lengthening maintenance windows and creating further contention.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design expands the amount of data each statement must touch. Stale or inadequate statistics then mislead the optimizer into believing these wide scans or non-covering lookups are cheaper than they are, cementing inefficient plans. The inflated work per statement aggregates into heavy CPU demand; as CPU saturates, collection of fresh statistics and index-creation tasks are delayed or throttled, allowing statistics to drift even further from reality. The reinforcing cycle—bad design → bad estimates → bad plans → CPU saturation → deferred maintenance → even worse estimates—amplifies performance degradation across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction demarcations are written so that they scan or modify more data and hold transactions open longer than business logic truly requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, keys, or tables, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort work.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine parameters governing memory, logging, checkpoints, parallelism, or connection limits are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, degrading internal subsystems without the physical resources being saturated.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database exhibits extreme and erratic latency spikes, frequent deadlock terminations, surges of lock-wait and log-write wait events, sudden freezes during checkpoint storms, and application timeouts that persist even when CPU, I/O, or memory usage appear modest. Slow, chatty, or over-broad SQL keeps transactions open long enough for lock queues to grow; mis-sized memory pools and overly aggressive checkpoint or parallelism settings magnify the time locks are held and lengthen recovery after deadlock rollbacks. Administrators may observe fluctuating throughput, bloated lock tables, escalating connection-pool backlogs, and oscillations between underutilized and saturated hardware states that defy single-factor explanations.

Causally, inefficient workload logic inflates read and update footprints, extending transaction duration and expanding the scope of acquired locks. These enlarged lock footprints collide under high concurrency, giving rise to intense blocking and deadlocks. Simultaneously, sub-optimal configuration—such as too small a buffer pool, low lock-table memory, or tight checkpoint intervals—slows I/O, increases page latch times, and prolongs lock retention during physical writes or rollback processing. The misconfiguration therefore amplifies the delays introduced by poor SQL logic, while the swelling lock contention further stresses memory and logging subsystems already constrained by bad parameter choices, creating a feedback loop that degrades OLTP performance severely and obscures individual root-cause signals.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, causing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort work.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine's cumulative memory footprint for caches, work areas, and background heaps exceeds safe physical limits, provoking host-level pressure, paging, or OOM terminations.

When both root causes manifest together, the system shows a blended symptom set: lock wait time, deadlock reports, and application time-outs rise while, in parallel, process resident-set size climbs, OS swap activity surges, cache hit ratios fluctuate, and sporadic OOM or eviction events appear. Queries blocked on locks hold private work buffers longer, inflating overall memory use; conversely, memory pressure can throttle or pre-empt processes, stretching statement execution time and prolonging lock ownership, so blocking trees lengthen rapidly. Connection pools fill as sessions queue behind both lock and memory bottlenecks, throughput collapses, and recovery routines such as lock-timeout victim selection or kernel OOM killer may trigger cascading rollbacks and node restarts.

Causally, heavy lock contention forces many concurrent sessions to remain active and retain their per-session allocations, expanding memory consumption. Growing memory pressure induces CPU stalls, swapping, or task cancellation, slowing query completion and extending the lifetime of held locks. This positive feedback loop amplifies each anomaly: lock waits create more resident memory, while memory starvation prolongs lock holds, together degrading transactional latency and risking systemic instability.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions acquire mutually incompatible locks on the same resources, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort work. 
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine’s memory consumers collectively exceed safe physical limits, triggering paging, allocation throttling, or OOM terminations. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Stand-by or downstream replicas fall behind because they cannot receive, persist, or apply log records at the rate produced by the primary. 

When all three conditions co-exist, the system exhibits severe and interleaved symptoms: lock wait queues lengthen while primary and replica memory footprints grow uncontrollably; backend processes stall on both lock acquisition and memory allocation, driving CPU idle time interspersed with kernel paging spikes. Replication lag balloons as apply workers blocked on locks or starved for memory defer redo, causing log files to accumulate and consume additional memory for in-flight buffers. Application sessions experience timeouts, intermittent deadlock errors, and sudden disconnects when OOM killers or crash-recovery events fire; monitoring shows rising lock-wait and memory-pressure counters alongside widening replica delay, making it hard to discern the dominant bottleneck.

Causally, heavy lock contention elongates transaction lifetimes, inflating in-memory lock tables, undo/redo buffers, and per-session work areas, which accelerates memory exhaustion. Memory pressure in turn slows buffer-cache lookups and forces paging, lengthening critical sections and increasing the window during which locks are held, thereby aggravating contention. Both factors throttle the primary’s commit rate, yet the generated WAL still outpaces replicas whose apply threads now compete for scarce memory and encounter the same lock conflicts when replaying changes, deepening replication lag. The expanding replica delay prevents log truncation, causing additional memory and storage usage for retained log segments, which feeds back into the overall memory-allocation crisis and further stresses lock management, creating a vicious amplification loop that can culminate in cluster instability or forced failover.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer selects or reuses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are accurate, inflating execution cost and runtime footprint.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions contend for incompatible locks, generating long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall throughput.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process hits kernel-enforced limits on objects such as file handles, processes/threads, or shared-memory segments, preventing further resource allocation.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload may exhibit extreme and erratic slowdowns: a sudden plan switch to a full-table scan or wide nested loop holds many row or page locks for far longer than usual, magnifying lock-wait times, deadlock frequency, and application time-outs. Sessions that pile up behind the blockers spawn additional server processes or threads until the operating-system quota for PIDs, file descriptors, or semaphore sets is reached, after which new connections, background workers, or parallel query helpers fail to start. Operators may observe a mixture of symptoms—escalating lock-wait graphs, deadlock-victim errors, optimizer plan regressions in execution-plan caches, and kernel log messages about "too many open files" or "cannot allocate memory"—making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal chain: a poor plan (1) dramatically lengthens critical sections, enlarging the time windows in which locks are held; (2) the prolonged locks throttle other transactions, causing them to queue and accumulate; (3) each waiting or retrying session consumes additional database back-end processes, file descriptors, and shared-memory objects; (4) once kernel limits are saturated, even diagnostic queries or deadlock-detector threads may fail to start, further delaying lock resolution and forcing the engine into partial outage. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another—sub-optimal planning triggers lock storms, which in turn drive the system to exhaust OS resources, amplifying the performance collapse and complicating recovery.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer repeatedly chooses or reuses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonable, causing excessive logical I/O, wrong join methods, or unnecessary parallelism.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot pages, page-latch conflicts, or limited I/O slots force sessions to serialize on buffer-manager structures, inflating page-latch and buffer-busy waits and elongating critical sections.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes drive the host’s CPU usage to sustained saturation, creating long run-queues, high context-switch rates, and global latency inflation.

Combined manifestation: When a bad plan that over-scans or over-probes data is executed concurrently by many sessions, it floods the buffer pool with unnecessary page touches, hammering a small set of index root or table pages. The resulting latch storms increase wait time while every process also burns CPU cycles in spin loops and plan work operations. Operators observe a toxic mix of symptoms: (1) abrupt plan flips followed by dramatic rises in both page-latch and CPU-scheduler waits; (2) CPU usage pegged near 100 %, yet throughput stagnates because sessions stall on buffer latches; (3) alternating spikes of logical I/O, latch contention, and scheduler delay in performance dashboards; (4) identical SQL text showing different plans and wildly different resource footprints within minutes; and (5) amplified latency variability that is hard to attribute to any single layer because optimizer, buffer manager, and CPU all appear as top consumers.

Causal chain and reinforcement: A sub-optimal plan multiplies the number of page accesses, focusing pressure on a small working set. The intensified page churn heats up specific buffers and latches, extending their hold times. As more sessions queue on those latches, some spin-wait on CPU, driving processor utilization toward saturation. High CPU load in turn lengthens latch spin loops and slows the optimizer’s background tasks, delaying statistics refreshes and plan invalidations, which prolongs the life of the bad plan. Meanwhile, latch contention stalls dirty-page flushes, shrinking effective buffer capacity and further penalizing the plan’s I/O pattern. The feedback loop—bad plan → latch contention → CPU saturation → slower recovery mechanisms—creates a self-reinforcing state where all three anomalies aggravate one another and degrade the entire workload until the root causes are resolved.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, store, or replay transaction-log records as fast as the primary generates them, causing sustained replication lag.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated disk or logical free space for datafiles, logs, archives, temp areas, or backups is exhausted, leading to allocation failures and stalled database operations.

Composite definition: Both anomalies manifest concurrently—the replication pipeline is backlogged while one or more nodes (primary or replicas) are simultaneously running out of space needed to write or retain log and data blocks.

Combined phenomena: 1) Rapidly widening replication-position gaps alongside shrinking free space on primary and/or replica volumes. 2) Retained WAL/redo or relay-log files piling up because they cannot be recycled until replicas catch up, hastening space exhaustion on the primary. 3) On replicas, full disks prevent new relay logs from being written, which in turn halts apply threads and pushes lag even higher. 4) Error messages such as "no space left on device," "cannot allocate WAL segment," or "replication receiver stalled" appear together, and failover readiness metrics degrade sharply. 5) User transactions may start failing when the primary can no longer allocate new log segments or when temporary-space shortages collide with long-running queries.

Causal chain: Replication lag forces the primary to retain extra log segments; these retained files consume space that would normally be reclaimed, accelerating space depletion. Once storage reaches critical thresholds, archive, backup, or checkpoint processes fail, further preventing log recycling and deepening the lag. Conversely, initial space pressure on a replica (e.g., from unchecked data growth or oversized temp usage) can block the writing of incoming relay logs, which stalls replay and propagates back to the primary, increasing file retention there. The two root causes thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop that escalates from mild lag or moderate disk usage into a compound failure affecting durability, availability, and recovery objectives.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database instance is simultaneously mis-configured at the parameter level, constrained by an overstressed transaction-log subsystem, and suffering from host CPU saturation. The three root causes coexist and interact, so the platform is neither tuned for the hardware nor able to absorb the log-write volume it produces, while CPU time is exhausted trying to keep up with both normal workload processing and log-related background activity.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Commit latency and log-flush waits rise sharply even when underlying storage metrics show spare IOPS; 2) Checkpoint storms, frequent log-file switches, and growing archive backlogs coincide with OS run-queue spikes and near-100 % CPU utilization; 3) Wait-event views show an interleaving of log-write, CPU scheduler, and configuration-driven background worker waits; 4) After a parameter change or version upgrade, throughput falls off cliff-like, with application threads alternately spinning on CPU and blocking on log-sync, while monitoring tools report buffer pools or per-session work memory either overcommitted or too small; 5) Secondary symptoms such as replication lag, autovacuum/cleanup backlog, and plan-cache thrashing become harder to attribute to a single layer because every mitigation attempt (e.g., raising parallelism or lowering checkpoint frequency) quickly pushes the system into a different but equally constrained state.

Causal chain and interaction: Poorly chosen configuration parameters (e.g., undersized log buffer, aggressive synchronous-commit, or checkpoint-completion target set too low) increase the frequency and immediacy of log flushes. This drives the transaction-log subsystem toward its throughput limit; once the log path slows, foreground sessions hold latches longer and CPU spin-time rises, inflating overall CPU utilization. The elevated CPU demand further delays log-writer and archiver threads, deepening log congestion. Meanwhile, CPU saturation prevents background processes from performing adaptive tuning or deferred I/O, so configuration mis-matches (such as small buffer pools or excessive parallel workers) cannot self-correct and instead generate even more redo. The feedback loop—mis-configuration → log pressure → CPU thrashing → slower log processing—amplifies each individual anomaly, producing a compounded failure mode that is more severe and harder to diagnose than any of the three issues in isolation.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks on the same data or metadata objects, causing queues, blocking chains, or deadlocks that throttle throughput and force rollbacks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, logging, checkpoints, parallelism, or connection limits are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, so internal subsystems stall or thrash despite no real shortage of physical resources.

When both root causes strike together, the system exhibits lock wait times and deadlock rates that rise erratically in tandem with configuration-induced stalls. Symptoms include long-lasting blocker–waiter trees that suddenly cascade after checkpoints, deadlock storms following aggressive lock-escalation, CPU cores oscillating between idle and spin while sessions are stuck on lock waits, transaction-throughput saw-toothing as mis-sized log buffers force frequent flushes that hold critical locks, and application timeouts escalating even though raw hardware utilization appears modest.

The causal chain is mutually reinforcing: sub-optimal parameters (e.g., too small buffer pool, undersized log or overly frequent checkpoints, inflated work-mem driving spill and lock-escalation) lengthen statement execution and keep transactions open longer, enlarging their lock footprint and probability of collision. Simultaneously, heavy blocking stretches transaction lifetimes, inflating in-memory structures and redo volume, which magnifies the impact of any memory, logging, or background-worker misconfiguration. Each feedback loop intensifies the other, pushing the database into a state where locks and mis-tuned internals alternately throttle progress and obscure each other's contribution, complicating diagnosis and recovery.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries outpaces background vacuum/clean-up activity, inflating the version store and visibility-check overhead.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, worker limits, etc.) are misaligned with hardware and workload, causing secondary inefficiencies that are not due to the raw resources themselves.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log becomes the primary bottleneck because flushing, switching, or archiving cannot keep up with redo generation, leading to commit stalls and log-space pressure.

Combined phenomena: When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits simultaneous bloat of table and index pages, soaring version-store or undo-segment size, growing transaction-log directories, and chronic background-worker backlogs. Commit latency and "log flush" wait events spike, yet CPU, I/O, or memory meters may show headroom, confusing first-level diagnostics. Vacuum/cleanup workers contend with aggressive checkpoints and log switches triggered by mis-tuned parameters; the resulting I/O storms further delay version pruning. Query planners misestimate both row counts and I/O cost because live-row density is low and statistics are stale, leading to erratic plan choices and unpredictable response times. Alerts about approaching transaction-ID wrap-around, exhausted log space, or stalled archivers may appear nearly simultaneously.

Causal chain: Heavy update/delete churn inflates the version store. Because checkpoint cadence, buffer-pool size, log-buffer length, and cleanup cost limits are poorly configured, background workers cannot reclaim space before new versions arrive. The growing undo/version space in turn amplifies redo generation, driving the transaction log faster toward capacity. Log saturation forces more frequent checkpoints and full-page writes, which consume I/O bandwidth that cleanup processes also need, creating a feedback loop. Each subsystem starves the others: mis-tuned parameters throttle vacuum bandwidth, vacuum delays raise redo volume, and log pressure forces yet more aggressive checkpoints. The intertwined effects compound latency spikes, storage growth, and risk of service interruption far beyond what any single anomaly would cause in isolation.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive growth of database memory regions (buffer/plan caches, work areas, parallel-worker buffers, etc.) drives the host beyond its safe physical or virtual memory envelope.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively saturate available CPU cores, exhausting compute bandwidth irrespective of the individual query or plan inefficiencies behind the demand.

When both anomalies surface together, the system shows a mix of memory-pressure and compute-pressure symptoms: resident-set sizes and swap traffic rise while run-queue depth and context-switch rates spike; page-fault handling, memory-reclaim daemons, and database background threads all compete for CPU, inflating overall latency. Query response times, log-flush and checkpoint operations, and cluster heartbeat intervals all elongate, and node evictions or OOM kills may coincide with scheduler wait events and spin-loop back-offs. Performance counters oscillate unpredictably as memory thrashing generates additional CPU load, making it difficult to attribute slowdowns to a single layer.

Causal chain: memory bloat forces the OS to spend more CPU cycles on page management; the resulting page-fault storms amplify CPU saturation. In turn, CPU starvation slows down individual queries and background tasks, prolonging their memory retention windows and causing further cache/work-area inflation. Parallel workers spawned to speed up lagging queries multiply both the memory footprint and the CPU demand, closing a feedback loop that rapidly depletes remaining resources. The intertwined pressure on memory and compute therefore reinforces itself, accelerating degradation until workload throttling, component failure, or manual intervention occurs.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more data, rows, or time than business logic truly requires.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupt, making access paths and stored data unreliable.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, hitting hard allocation limits.

When all three anomalies manifest together, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: queries that already scan or modify excessive data stumble into corrupted pages, returning inconsistent row counts, checksum errors, or forced full-table scans. The extra I/O, temp sorting, and bloated undo/redo generated by the inefficient workload rapidly consume remaining space, leading to allocation failures for data pages, temp segments, or archive logs. Space exhaustion, in turn, halts index rebuilds, corruption repairs, and normal checkpoint or log-recycle operations, so corruption symptoms and slow-query entries grow unmitigated. Users observe a mix of long-tail latencies, intermittent "row not found" or duplication errors, unexpected full-scan plans, and sudden "no space left" or "cannot extend" failures, often within the same session.

Causal chain: Poorly written SQL drives large scans and massive DML, inflating data and log footprints and steadily eroding available space. Shrinking free space increases the likelihood of partial writes, failed auto-extends, and out-of-space conditions during critical write-ahead logging or page splits, which can introduce new corruption or leave indexes half-updated. Existing corruption forces the optimizer to abandon damaged indexes and fall back to even broader scans, multiplying the workload’s space and I/O consumption. Repair attempts, re-writes, or repeated application retries further bloat logs and temp usage. Thus, each anomaly intensifies the others: logical inefficiency accelerates space depletion; space pressure elevates corruption risk and blocks remediation; corruption feeds back by degrading access paths, amplifying the workload footprint and pushing the system toward a cascading failure state.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently selects a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, causing excessive CPU, I/O, or memory consumption per statement execution.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Stand-by or downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply transaction-log records at the pace the primary generates them, leading to widening replay lag and log-retention growth.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, or temporary areas falls to, or reaches, hard limits, triggering allocation failures and stalled database components.

When these three root causes strike at the same time, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: query executions swing unpredictably between fast and extremely slow; the primary’s transaction-log directory, archive area, or replica relay logs grow rapidly but cannot be recycled; replication delay spikes and failover readiness drops; data-file and temp-space auto-extend attempts fail, surfacing "no-space" errors to users; monitoring shows both runaway disk consumption and increasing replica lag, while execution-plan history shows frequent plan flips or a single bloated plan reused across skewed parameter sets.

Causal chain and interaction: The sub-optimal plan inflates row reads, sort volumes, and log generation per transaction. This surge in redo volume overwhelms the replication channel, lengthening log-retention windows because old segments cannot be discarded until replicas catch up. The retained segments, together with the oversized temp objects and data bloat created by the bad plan, consume disk rapidly, pushing the system into a storage-capacity anomaly. As free space shrinks, auto-extension or logging failures slow query execution further and can force the optimizer to re-optimize under degraded statistics, making poor plan choices even more likely. Meanwhile, replicas fall further behind because they must replay the same inefficient work but may also run into their own space shortages, halting apply threads and preventing log recycling on the primary. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another: bad plans create excess data and log volume, replication lag blocks space reclamation, and space exhaustion degrades execution and replication performance, forming a self-amplifying feedback loop that rapidly threatens overall database availability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level runtime parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload, leading to behavior that is sub-optimal even though the underlying resources themselves are not yet saturated.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, producing buffer-busy and page-latch waits that inflate latency while CPUs appear either under-utilised or spinning.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: The database or log storage layer runs out of allocatable space, provoking allocation failures, forced checkpoints, and write stalls.

Combined anomalous phenomena: When all three root causes coexist, the instance exhibits pronounced and intertwined symptoms. Mis-sized buffer-pool, checkpoint, and log-size parameters cause aggressive page eviction and frequent checkpoints that amplify latch waits on hot pages. The extra dirty-page flushes and log switches rapidly consume the already limited free space, leading to intermittent "out-of-space" or "cannot extend" errors. As space nears exhaustion, background writers and checkpoint processes throttle foreground work, holding critical latches longer and causing latch wait and CPU spin spikes. Performance monitoring shows a perplexing mix of buffer-busy waits, log-write stalls, and space-allocation errors, while hardware I/O and CPU utilisation fluctuate between idle gaps and short saturation bursts.

Causal chain and interaction: Sub-optimal configuration (e.g., undersized buffer pool, small log files, overly aggressive checkpoint interval) increases the churn of dirty pages and log segments. This churn heightens buffer-cache turnover and concentrates access on a reduced set of hot pages, elevating latch contention. Simultaneously, the frequent checkpoints and log switches allocate space at an accelerated pace, depleting the already constrained storage. As free space shrinks, write operations block on space availability, prolonging the duration that pages remain pinned and latches are held, which in turn worsens contention. The stalled writes force additional checkpoints and emergency autovacuum or purge activity, each governed by the same poor parameter settings, creating a feedback loop that propagates latency, raises the risk of transaction timeouts, and can ultimately push the database into read-only or shutdown states.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Cardinality-estimation inputs are stale or incomplete, so the optimizer chooses plans on wrong row-count and data-distribution assumptions.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate buffer-cache, work-area, and background allocations grow beyond physical limits, provoking paging, OOM events, or cache thrashing.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Listener, socket, or transport capacity is saturated, delaying connection establishment and slowing result transmission between server and clients.

When these three root causes co-exist, symptoms overlap and intensify: queries compile into sub-optimal, memory-hungry hash joins or sorts that immediately inflate per-query work areas; the swollen memory footprint pushes the host into swap, dropping cache hit ratios and lengthening CPU scheduling gaps. Degraded execution speed means sessions stay open longer, holding memory and result buffers while simultaneously occupying network sockets that trickle data to slow or intermittently stalled clients. Connection pools fill, new sessions face authentication delays or refusals, and retry storms multiply backend processes, further inflating memory demand. Execution-plan reports show severe estimate-to-actual row count divergence, high physical I/O from spilled workfiles, increasing "client read/write" or "socket wait" times, rising OS swap and retransmission counters, and abrupt process terminations or node failovers.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into selecting execution strategies that require large in-memory structures. These oversized allocations accelerate memory exhaustion; under memory pressure, the engine evicts buffers and spills to disk, increasing latency. Longer runtimes and blocking expand the active connection footprint, while network congestion slows result delivery, holding server memory and worker threads hostage. Prolonged network handshakes and half-open sockets raise the number of simultaneously connected backends, which, in turn, allocate additional memory for session state and plan caches, amplifying the memory-allocation anomaly. The resulting swap thrashing slows automatic statistics collection and exacerbates statistic staleness, completing a feedback loop that perpetuates poor plans, memory overload, and connection saturation.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: This anomaly denotes a situation in which Transaction Lock Contention, Storage Space Capacity exhaustion, and CPU Resource saturation all strike the database simultaneously, so the lock-manager, storage allocator, and CPU scheduler are each a primary, co-existing bottleneck.

Combined observable phenomena: Lengthening blocker–waiter chains, frequent deadlock victim errors, and surging lock-wait time appear in parallel with "no space left" or "cannot extend" messages for data, log, or temp areas. Checkpoints, log flushes, and space-reclamation tasks stall, causing commit freezes and widespread statement latency spikes. Host CPU utilization sits near 100 %, run-queue depths rise, and both user sessions and internal housekeeping processes (deadlock detectors, log writers, auto-extenders, cleaners) consume large amounts of CPU. Application layers experience cascading timeouts and aggressive retry storms, inflating connection pools and further amplifying contention. Monitoring views show interleaved lock, I/O-allocation, and CPU scheduler waits that are difficult to disentangle.

Causal interaction: Heavy lock contention prolongs transaction lifetimes, inflating undo/redo volume and retaining row versions that impede space reuse, thus accelerating consumption of data, log, and temp space. As free space dwindles, allocation failures force the engine to pause writers and invoke purge or auto-extension paths that hold additional locks, deepening blocking chains. Each stalled or repeatedly aborted transaction, along with intensified background housekeeping, drives CPU demand upward; the ensuing CPU saturation slows lock acquisition, deadlock detection, and space-management threads, further extending lock hold times and delaying space reclamation. The three resource crises therefore reinforce one another in a positive feedback loop that rapidly degrades throughput and can culminate in complete service unavailability unless all contributing factors are relieved together.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level runtime settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, log size, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload demands.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log records becomes the principal bottleneck on the write path.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures become physically or logically corrupt, rendering access paths and checksums unreliable.

When these three root causes manifest together, the system may exhibit a confusing blend of symptoms: 1) commit latency and log-flush waits surge while overall I/O and CPU metrics appear under-utilised; 2) sudden checkpoint storms, repeated log-file switches, or archiver backlogs coincide with query plans unexpectedly falling back to full table scans or returning inconsistent row counts; 3) integrity-check utilities report page or index corruption just as background workers throttle or stall due to mis-sized memory pools and aggressive checkpoint parameters; 4) application workloads experience intermittent dead-time where writes hang, followed by bursts of redo, page-verification errors, and emergency auto-recovery cycles.

Causal interaction: Mis-configured memory and checkpoint parameters can inflate redo generation rates and shrink log-buffer headroom, quickly pushing the transaction-log subsystem into saturation. Prolonged log pressure delays checkpoint completion and increases dirty-page residency, making any latent page or index corruption more likely to surface during forced flushes or crash-recovery cycles. Conversely, the presence of corrupted pages triggers extra recovery and validation work, amplifying log-write volume and stressing both the mis-configured buffers and the already constrained log path. The three factors therefore reinforce one another: bad parameters create excess log traffic, log saturation prolongs exposure to corrupt data pages, and corruption events in turn force additional I/O and recovery processing, all of which feed back into the mis-tuned configuration and exacerbate throughput collapse and data-quality risks.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The database engine allocates and retains more memory than the host can safely provide, driving paging, swap activity, and cache thrashing.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical disks or storage fabric are unable to sustain the read/write throughput or IOPS demanded by data, temp, or log files, forcing long device queues and high latency.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Network paths, listeners, or connection slots are saturated or unstable, delaying session establishment and data transfer between clients and the database.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the system exhibits a multi-layer performance collapse: memory pressure forces dirty pages and large work areas to spill to disk exactly when the underlying storage is already throughput-bound, amplifying device queues and read/write latency. Stalled I/O keeps backend processes in active states, each holding scarce memory, sockets, and worker threads, which in turn inflates overall memory footprint and accelerates paging. Prolonged statement execution and commit latency lengthen transaction lifetimes, causing application connection pools to exhaust, inflating the volume of concurrent connection attempts, listener backlogs, and network retransmissions. Clients observe erratic response times, frequent timeouts, and sporadic "too many connections" errors, while the server shows simultaneous spikes in page-fault rates, disk wait events, and socket queue depths that are difficult to disentangle.

Causally, excessive in-engine memory allocation pushes the operating system to evict buffer pages, initiating large amounts of swap and checkpoint traffic that overwhelms storage bandwidth. Storage saturation elongates every I/O, trapping sessions in wait states and preventing memory from being released, thus worsening the memory shortfall. The elongated waits propagate up the stack as slow or hanging queries; clients keep connections open longer and retry failed attempts, which saturates network and listener resources. Network congestion and connection storms then feed back into the database by further delaying commit acknowledgements and result-set drains, keeping server processes resident in memory and perpetuating high buffer and work-area allocations. The intertwined feedback loops among memory pressure, I/O bottlenecks, and network contention magnify each anomaly, driving the database into cascading degradation or forced restarts.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction design force the engine to touch far more data, rows, or time than the business requirement demands.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer metadata no longer reflects real data distribution, causing systematic cardinality and cost misestimation that leads to poor plan choices.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally large share of CPU, saturating host compute capacity and slowing all work.

When these three root causes appear together, symptoms overlap and intensify: the same SQLs dominate slow-query and CPU-time lists, their execution plans show severe row-estimate errors, and each run consumes many more CPU cycles than expected. Global host metrics hover near 100 % utilization with long run queues, while engine views report both scheduler waits and wide discrepancies between estimated and actual row counts. Automatic statistics jobs and background maintenance fall behind because of CPU starvation, causing fresh data changes to remain un-analyzed. End-user sessions experience extreme and erratic latency, timeouts, and transaction rollbacks, and any plan change—good or bad—can swing performance unpredictably.

Causally, inefficient workload logic initiates excessive data access. Stale or incomplete statistics then misinform the optimizer, amplifying the inefficiency by selecting full scans, Cartesian joins, or over-parallelized plans. The compounded CPU demand drives the server into sustained saturation, which in turn delays automatic statistics refresh tasks and forces the optimizer to rely even longer on bad metadata, closing a feedback loop that continually degrades plan quality. High CPU pressure also slows individual query execution, keeping transactions open longer and further increasing contention and resource demand. The interaction of bad logic, bad statistics, and exhausted CPU thus produces a self-reinforcing spiral that can cripple both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements or transaction boundaries are written in ways that force the engine to scan or move more data than the business case requires.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes saturate host CPU, leaving too few cycles for timely request processing.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The network or connection-handling path between clients and the server becomes a bottleneck, delaying connection establishment or data transfer.

When all three root causes are active, the system exhibits cascading symptoms: inefficient SQL generates excessive logical I/O and large result sets that inflate both CPU demand and outbound payload. The over-consumption of CPU lengthens execution time for every statement, causing run queues, context switches, and scheduler waits to spike. Meanwhile, the same bloated result sets congest network interfaces and exhaust server-side connection resources, producing elevated connection-setup latency, socket backlog growth, and client-side timeouts. Latencies propagate up the stack, leading to stalled application threads, retry storms that further inflate workload volume, and an overall perception of intermittent or widespread outage.

Causally, poor workload logic initiates the spiral by amplifying per-request resource consumption. The swollen CPU usage not only slows query processing but also extends the lifetime of each network transfer, keeping sockets open longer and pushing the listener and kernel queues toward exhaustion. In parallel, delayed network handshakes hold server threads in authentication or client-read waits, preventing them from returning to the pool and increasing CPU pressure on remaining schedulers. The resulting feedback loop—inefficient SQL → CPU saturation → slower execution → prolonged and enlarged network traffic → connection contention—magnifies both resource anomalies and can drive the database into thrashing or partial denial-of-service despite each individual layer appearing only moderately loaded in isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design obliges the database engine to touch more data, rows, or time than the true business requirement demands.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer metadata is stale, incomplete, or inaccurate, provoking systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal plan selection.

When both root causes coexist, the database exhibits severe and erratic performance degradation: statements already scanning or joining excessive data are paired with execution plans that underestimate or overestimate row counts, leading the optimizer to choose nested-loop scans where hash joins are needed (or vice-versa), to allocate wrong memory grants, and to spill to disk.
