Slow-query logs show the same statements with wildly different runtimes, blocking chains lengthen as mis-estimated queries hold locks longer, and resource monitors report oscillating CPU spikes, temp-space surges, and bursty I/O. Autonomic tuning and statistics refresh operations may thrash, causing frequent recompilations without relief, while application tiers experience cascading timeouts, retries, and throughput collapse.

Causally, inefficient SQL shapes created by the application magnify the impact of bad statistics: wide scans, non-sargable predicates, and bulky IN lists increase the sensitivity of plan quality to accurate cardinality estimates. Conversely, stale or missing statistics deprive the optimizer of the information it needs to mitigate poor SQL patterns, so it selects plans that further inflate data access, memory use, and lock duration. The feedback loop—sub-optimal SQL inflating row counts, statistics misestimation hiding the real cost, and the resulting plans compounding both—drives the database into progressively worse performance and stability states.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and bloating on-disk structures.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The generation, flushing, switching, or archiving of write-ahead log records becomes the bottleneck on the commit path, inflating commit latency and log storage.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated, so read/write latency, queue depths, and IOPS limits are exceeded across data, temp, and log volumes.

When these three root causes occur together, the database exhibits a compound symptom pattern: 1) rapidly expanding tables, indexes, version store, and transaction-log directories; 2) soaring commit and checkpoint latency dominated by log-flush and device-I/O waits; 3) long-running queries and autovacuum/clean-up workers that never catch up; 4) device-level queues pegged, with wait profiles simultaneously showing MVCC visibility checks, log-related waits, and generic data-file I/O stalls; 5) escalating risk of transaction-ID or log-segment wraparound, emergency checkpoints, and sudden write stalls that block both OLTP traffic and background maintenance.

Causally, high update/delete churn inflates the version store, which in turn increases redo generation because every version change must be logged; this heavier log stream stresses the transaction-log subsystem. Frequent log flushes and larger log archives multiply write pressure on the same storage back-end that is already servicing bloated data-file writes and long sequential scans caused by MVCC bloat. As the storage layer saturates, log flush latency rises, stretching transaction completion times and prolonging snapshot retention; the longer snapshots further delay version reclamation, feeding back into MVCC bloat. The intertwined feedback loops—more versions ⇒ more log writes ⇒ more physical I/O ⇒ slower cleanup ⇒ even more versions—can rapidly degrade throughput and threaten database availability.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata and become blocked or deadlocked in the lock-manager layer.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server transport, authentication, or socket resources are saturated or unstable, causing slow or failed connection establishment and prolonged data transfer.

When both anomalies manifest simultaneously, the database exhibits long chains of waiting transactions, increasing deadlock victim rollbacks, and sharply deteriorating throughput while, at the same time, clients experience connection timeouts, refused sessions, or stalled result delivery. Lock-wait time, deadlock reports, and connection retry counts rise in tandem; backend threads accumulate in both "lock wait" and "client read/write" states, and connection pools overflow even though the server still shows CPU and I/O headroom. Application logs reveal a mixture of deadlock errors and network/socket exceptions, making it difficult to attribute latency to a single layer. The dual stress can lead to sudden surges of aborted transactions followed by retry storms that further inflate both the lock queue and the listener backlog.

Causally, impaired network paths slow down client request submission and response consumption, lengthening transaction lifetimes and holding locks for longer than normal; these extended lock tenures increase the probability of blocking chains and deadlocks. Conversely, severe lock contention keeps server backends idle while waiting, prolonging their ownership of network sockets and authentication slots, thus reducing the pool of available connections and inflating the server’s socket queues. As blocked transactions time out, clients reconnect and retry, injecting additional connection load that exacerbates the already constrained network resources. The feedback loop between prolonged lock holding and degraded connectivity amplifies both problems, driving the database into a state where progress stalls despite seemingly adequate compute resources.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical layout of tables, partitions, and indexes does not align with the workload’s access patterns, forcing statements into wide or non-covering scans and inflating the amount of data touched per operation.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, causing wait chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Old row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, expanding the physical data set and raising visibility-check overhead.

When all three conditions coexist, the database shows a blend of severe symptoms: queries that should be selective instead trigger large table or index scans, which hold locks on many more rows or pages than necessary. The enlarged lock footprints increase the likelihood and length of blocking chains and deadlocks; blocked transactions that sit idle prolong the lifetime of their snapshots, preventing garbage collection of obsolete versions. Meanwhile, the unchecked version buildup fattens tables and indexes, making subsequent scans even longer and further extending lock durations. Administrators observe skyrocketing lock-wait and deadlock rates, rapidly growing table and index sizes, deteriorating cache efficiency, longer checkpoint and vacuum/cleanup cycles, increasing I/O and CPU usage for both query execution and background maintenance, and application timeouts even on moderately complex requests.

Causally, poor schema and index design initiates wide scans and non-covering lookups, which touch and therefore lock far more data than necessary. The inflated lock scope intensifies contention; transactions wait longer and remain open, prolonging MVCC snapshots. These long-lived snapshots keep obsolete versions alive, causing version bloat. The growing heap and index size then slow future scans, further extending lock hold times and amplifying contention. Simultaneously, the overworked cleanup workers struggle to reclaim space because blocking transactions retain old versions, leading to a feedback loop where version bloat, lock contention, and inefficient access paths reinforce each other and collectively degrade OLTP performance.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, index, partition, and datatype choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans or excess maintenance work.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, producing growing replication lag and log-retention pressure.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are internally corrupt or inconsistent, making some data unreadable, duplicated, or missing even when access paths are correct.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a mixed symptom set:  • Primary queries show unpredictable latency—some slowed by full scans or non-covering index probes, others failing with corruption errors.  • Index or data corruption causes intermittent "tuple not found" or checksum failures on both primary and replicas; replicas may repeatedly disconnect or stop applying when they hit corrupt log records or pages.  • Replication lag balloons because the primary’s inefficient plans generate excessive I/O and write-amplified redo, while corrupt pages force retries, conflict resolution, or skip/repair operations on the apply side.  • Log files and replica relay logs accumulate, consuming disk space and delaying log recycling.  • Monitoring shows diverging row counts between primary and replicas, stale read traffic on replicas, and escalating lock contention from repeated repair, VACUUM, or rebuild attempts.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and indexing inflate row fetches and index maintenance, producing larger transactions and higher redo volume. The replication pipeline, already bandwidth- or CPU-constrained, falls behind, extending retention windows for old log segments that reference damaged pages. Any latent data/index corruption therefore persists longer and is transmitted to replicas, where it can break apply workers, forcing rollbacks or halts that further increase lag. Conversely, corruption-induced apply failures cause retries and re-streaming, multiplying network traffic generated by the sub-optimally indexed workload. The sustained backlog also prevents timely vacuuming or index rebuilding on both primary and replicas, allowing corruption and design flaws to compound and degrade overall system reliability and performance.

Name: CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
CPU Resource Anomaly : Saturation of host CPU cycles by database-related processes, driving run-queue growth and system-wide latency. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Exhaustion or slowdown of network, listener, or connection-handling resources, inflating connect times and socket waits. 

This composite anomaly represents the simultaneous exhaustion of compute and network/connection resources on the database server. While the CPU is near saturation, the server is also unable to accept, authenticate, or transmit client traffic at the required rate, so both statement execution and session establishment are impaired concurrently.

Combined manifestations include: • sustained CPU utilization >90 % with long OS run queues while listener or connection-pool queues back up; • spikes in both CPU-bound wait events (e.g., CPU_BUSY, RUNQ) and network events (client read/write, socket wait, accept) in engine views; • widespread query latency where time is split between CPU and network waits, making single-point diagnosis difficult; • increased application timeouts, retransmissions, and connection errors coinciding with elevated context switches and TCP retransmits; • feedback loops in which client retry storms multiply session attempts, further inflating CPU load on authentication and session setup threads, and keeping sockets open longer, which in turn increases kernel interrupt and protocol-stack CPU consumption.

Causal chain: high CPU usage slows every server-side operation, including network I/O, accept() and SSL handshake processing, thereby lengthening connection lifecycles and filling socket queues. The congested network layer then stalls query result delivery, causing server worker threads to remain runnable longer and perform additional copy/checksum work, which pushes CPU utilization higher. Client retries triggered by network delays inflate request rates, adding parsing, authentication, and encryption work that further stresses CPU. This positive feedback loop between CPU saturation and network congestion amplifies latency and error rates, potentially leading to cascading application failures.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path becomes the primary bottleneck, throttling commit throughput due to slow log generation, flushing, switching, or archiving.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database engine or its background workers hit kernel-enforced ceilings for handles, shared-memory, threads, AIO contexts, or cgroup quotas, blocking further allocation of critical OS objects.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from log-path saturation and exhaustion of kernel-level resources, so every commit must fight both slow I/O on the log device and the kernel’s refusal to grant the file handles, shared memory, or threads required to advance the log pipeline.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Commit latency, log-write waits, and log-sync waits rise sharply and unpredictably. 2) Log switches or archive operations intermittently fail with OS-level "too many open files", "cannot create thread", or shared-memory errors, causing long stretches where no new log segment can be created. 3) Background writers, checkpoint workers, or replication archivers disappear or refuse to start, leaving redo files to accumulate and filling the log mount. 4) The engine may enter a partial outage: existing sessions hang in commit, new sessions are rejected due to lack of processes or memory, and alert logs alternate between log-related stalls and OS resource-limit errors, making the root cause appear fragmented.

Causal chain: Heavy transactional throughput drives intense redo generation, which increases the frequency of log buffer flushes, segment switches, and archiver invocations—all of which open files, allocate AIO contexts, and spawn or awaken threads. This burst of kernel requests pushes the host toward its per-process or cgroup limits. Once those limits are hit, the engine cannot create the next log file or start the archiver that would free space, so the log device remains busy and fills up, deepening the original log bottleneck. Conversely, the stalled log subsystem lengthens commit paths and multiplies waiting sessions, inflating the number of active processes and open descriptors, thereby accelerating OS resource depletion. The two root causes thus form a feedback loop that amplifies stalls, propagates errors across components, and can culminate in a full transactional freeze.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) do not align with workload access patterns, forcing any query to traverse inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer, despite having usable statistics, chooses or reuses an execution plan whose cost model decisions are markedly sub-optimal for the current parameter set and runtime context.

When both root causes are present simultaneously, the database exhibits a blend of structural and planning symptoms: frequent full-table or full-index scans alternate unpredictably with unstable index probes; the same statement may oscillate between several inefficient plans, each still burdened by non-covering or missing indexes. CPU and I/O surge during both reads and writes, latch/lock contention rises due to longer scan durations, and plan cache bloat appears as the optimizer repeatedly compiles variants attempting to compensate for design flaws. Performance tuning becomes confusing because adding hints or forcing plans yields only temporary relief—subsequent executions regress whenever data distributions, parameter values, or cache states change. End-user latency is highly variable, with some executions timing out while others complete acceptably after index-rebuilds or manual plan fixes.

Causally, an ill-suited physical schema narrows the set of viable access paths, pushing the optimizer toward plans that are already at a disadvantage. The optimizer’s cost model, facing inadequate or overly broad indexes and non-selective partitions, may misrank the remaining alternatives, leading to erratic plan choices. Each poor choice amplifies the cost penalties inherent in the flawed schema, while the unstable plans obscure the underlying design defect by making performance appear non-deterministic. Conversely, plan churn can mask which structural changes would help, delaying corrective indexing or schema redesign. Together, the two anomalies form a feedback loop in which weak structures invite bad plans, and bad plans magnify the impact of weak structures, resulting in chronic, hard-to-diagnose performance degradation across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model and indexing choices do not match workload access patterns, forcing the optimizer into full scans, non-covering lookups, and excessive maintenance overhead that inflate I/O and log volume.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber systems cannot ingest or apply the primary’s change stream fast enough, producing growing log-position gaps, replay lag, and retention of un-archived log segments on the primary.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Allocated data, temp, or log areas approach exhaustion, leading to allocation failures, halted extensions, and stalled recycling of log/temporary space.

When all three root causes co-exist, the database experiences cascading symptoms: 1) poorly indexed queries generate large scans, temp spills, and bloated undo/redo, elongating transactions; 2) the surge in log volume overwhelms replication apply threads, widening replication lag and forcing the primary to retain ever-growing log segments; 3) retained logs, enlarged indexes, and temporary spill files rapidly consume remaining disk space, triggering auto-extend failures, halted DML, aborted queries, and replica disconnections. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in query latency, checkpoint age, replica delay, and space usage, making it difficult to attribute blame to any single subsystem.

Causally, inefficient schema and index design is the first amplifier: every read and write becomes heavier, generating more undo/redo and larger index updates. The inflated log stream must be shipped and replayed downstream; limited apply throughput on replicas turns this into chronic replication backlog. Because the primary cannot recycle log segments that replicas have not replayed, space consumption on both primary and replica storage rises sharply. As free space shrinks, auto-extension or archive operations fail, which in turn stalls new writes and further delays replication, establishing a feedback loop that degrades performance and can culminate in an outage. The intertwined nature of design inefficiencies, replication lag, and space exhaustion complicates diagnosis, as each anomaly masks and intensifies the others.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : A static mismatch between table structures, index and partition layout, data types, and integrity rules and the actual access patterns, forcing the optimizer to rely on inherently inefficient access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, missing, or inaccurate statistics on row counts, distributions, and correlation, driving systematic cardinality errors and mis-costed execution plans.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Approaching or hitting hard limits on data, log, or temporary storage, causing allocation failures, auto-extension stops, and spill-area exhaustion.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode: queries that already lack proper supporting indexes are further mis-optimized by incorrect statistics, often devolving into full-table scans, large hash joins, and massive sort or spool operations. The resulting bloated I/O, oversized workfiles, expanded indexes, and prolonged transaction logs rapidly consume remaining free space. As space dwindles, temp-segment allocations, index rebuilds, bulk loads, and even automatic statistics refresh jobs begin to fail, triggering error messages, session aborts, and emergency space-management operations. Performance becomes erratic—some statements hang on space waits while others oscillate between radically different plans after forced recompilations, making troubleshooting difficult.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design inflates the amount of data each statement must touch; stale statistics prevent the optimizer from recognizing any residual selectivity, locking queries into scan-heavy plans that magnify I/O and temporary space consumption. The surge in transient and persistent storage use accelerates space exhaustion. Once free space is scarce, the database may cancel or skip statistics gathering, shrink sample sizes, or abort index-creation and maintenance tasks—thereby keeping both the design mismatch and the statistics in a degraded state. In turn, allocation failures in data, temp, or log areas can interrupt DML and maintenance operations, leading to fragmented or partially applied schema changes that further deteriorate access paths. The feedback loop between bad design, wrong statistics, and shrinking space compounds latency, raises error rates, and can ultimately bring the workload to a standstill.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpoints, etc.) that distort resource usage patterns and introduce artificial bottlenecks independent of true hardware limits.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores are genuinely saturated or oversubscribed by database processes, causing elevated run-queue delays and system-wide latency.

When both root causes coexist the system presents a confusing mixture of symptoms: CPU utilisation hovers at or near 100 %, yet individual sessions may simultaneously report waits that suggest they are "spinning" or throttled by configuration limits (e.g., small work-memory forcing excessive batch-loop processing, aggressive parallel-worker allocation leading to context-switch storms, or checkpoint storms producing bursts of log-flush CPU). Wait-event histograms show an interleaving of CPU-bound activity (CPU time, scheduler waits) and configuration-induced waits (buffer-pin, log-write, flush-queue), and performance counters may oscillate as background processes kick in late due to CPU starvation. Response-time spikes appear across both read and write paths; even after workload subsides, recovery and autovacuum/cleanup tasks lag because mis-sized maintenance workers cannot acquire CPU.

Causally, sub-optimal configuration settings inflate the amount of CPU work per transaction (e.g., too-small caches trigger extra page decompression and checksum verification, over-parallel plans multiply worker threads, tight checkpoint intervals force frequent flush bookkeeping). This artificial demand pushes the host CPU past sustainable limits, producing a true CPU Resource Anomaly. In turn, sustained CPU saturation amplifies the negative impact of the bad settings: background writers miss their cadence, causing larger and more expensive checkpoints, while worker shortages lead the optimizer to fall back to inefficient serial plans that again raise per-query CPU cost. The feedback loop between poor configuration and CPU exhaustion deepens latency, obscures which layer is primary, and can ultimately stall throughput or trigger failover mechanisms.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously impaired by (1) a bottleneck in the write-ahead logging subsystem that restricts log generation, flushing, switching, archiving, or retention capacity, and (2) physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk data blocks and index structures. The system must therefore cope with both stalled commit processing and unreliable persistent structures at the same time.

Combined observable phenomena: Users experience rising commit and DML latency, "log write / log sync" wait spikes, and frequent log-file switch or archive backlog messages while, in parallel, queries randomly miss or duplicate rows, integrity-check utilities flag page-checksum or index-ordering errors, and the engine emits corruption or recovery warnings. Recovery or redo‐apply operations may loop or slow dramatically, checkpoints can thrash, and replication or backup jobs may halt because damaged pages cannot be read while required log segments remain unarchived, causing log directories to grow uncontrollably. The overlap of symptoms makes it difficult to attribute stalls solely to I/O or corruption, as each condition amplifies the other.

Causal interaction: Corrupted pages or broken index links often trigger extra page reads, forced validation scans, repetitious page splits, or emergency repairs, all of which generate surges of redo records that saturate an already constrained log subsystem. The resulting log backlog delays checkpoints and archive operations, extending the time that corrupted pages stay in service and increasing the risk of additional inconsistencies. Conversely, when the log device reaches capacity or flush latency grows, incomplete commits and prolonged recovery windows raise the likelihood of torn-page or lost-write scenarios, seeding further data and index corruption. Replication or backup retries against corrupt pages can pin log segments for longer retention, intensifying log file exhaustion. Thus the two root causes form a feedback loop that progressively degrades write throughput, data correctness, recovery time, and overall system availability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns forces inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer choices.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Bottleneck in generation, flushing, archiving, or retention of write-ahead log records that inflates commit latency and can stall write traffic even when general I/O bandwidth is adequate.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk pages or index structures causes missing/duplicate rows, checksum failures, and unpredictable plan changes.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern:  • Queries already slowed by missing or non-covering indexes degrade further because every extra random lookup or full scan produces a surge of row modifications to non-optimal indexes, inflating redo volume and saturating the transaction-log writer. • Commit latency spikes and frequent log-flush waits coexist with erratic query runtimes, unexpected full scans, and mismatched row counts. • Integrity-check utilities or background scrubbers may detect page or index corruption, and their repair activity generates additional redo, compounding log congestion. • Repeated plan fallbacks (due to corrupt indexes) increase data-page reads and undo lookups, stressing I/O channels shared with the log, while stalled commits hold locks longer, magnifying concurrency waits and user-visible timeouts.

Causal chain: Poor schema and indexing force heavier I/O and larger redo generation per transaction; the swollen write-ahead log stream overwhelms inadequately sized or placed log files, causing log-flush bottlenecks. Prolonged log flush times lengthen recovery windows and extend lock hold times, heightening the probability of crashes or forced shutdowns. Any abrupt stop or incomplete recovery, in turn, raises the risk of data-block or index corruption. Conversely, pre-existing subtle corruptions invalidate indexes, driving the optimizer toward full scans and further amplifying redo volume, which stresses the log subsystem even more. The feedback loop between design inefficiencies, log saturation, and structural corruption accelerates performance collapse and data-integrity degradation, making isolation of the individual root causes difficult and requiring coordinated remediation across schema redesign, log-subsystem tuning, and physical repair.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is concurrently affected by (1) SQL Workload Logic Anomaly—application-level statement or transaction patterns that generate excessive or inefficient data manipulation, (2) Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly—commit-path bottlenecks related to log buffering, flushing, or archival, and (3) Storage Space Capacity Anomaly—approaching or reached hard limits on physical or logical free space for data, log, archive, or temporary areas.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Statement latency and slow-query frequency rise sharply while commit latency, log-flush waits, and log-sync waits increase in lockstep. • Log files switch more often, archives pile up, and free space in both active log volumes and archive destinations plummets, triggering space-related alerts. • When log segments cannot be recycled because archives lag or space is exhausted, new writes stall, causing application timeouts and long-running transactions to linger even longer, holding locks and further inflating contention. • Auto-extension failures, "out of space" errors, and checkpoint storms occur simultaneously with runaway redo generation and prolonged user transactions, making the symptoms appear as a single, escalating performance and availability incident.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Inefficient SQL patterns (wide scans, over-sized batches, long open transactions) inflate redo volume per transaction. The surging redo stresses the transaction-log subsystem, driving more frequent flushes, switches, and archive operations. Because the storage layer is already at—or near—capacity, log and archive files cannot grow or be archived fast enough, which in turn blocks further log allocation. Blocked log allocation stalls commits, elongates transaction lifetimes, and amplifies the workload logic anomaly’s original resource footprint. The prolonged transactions occupy additional temp and undo/rollback space, accelerating overall space exhaustion. Thus, each root cause reinforces the others: inefficient SQL generates excessive redo; excessive redo overwhelms the log subsystem; the overwhelmed log subsystem consumes and fragments remaining space, and tight storage capacity feeds back to block log processing, creating a self-amplifying degradation loop that jeopardizes OLTP throughput and system availability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : The engine is started with sub-optimal runtime parameters (memory pools, parallelism, checkpoint cadence, etc.), so the database behaves inefficiently even though the underlying hardware may still have headroom. 
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive the host CPU to sustained saturation, producing long run-queues, high context-switching, and broad latency inflation across statements. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database reaches kernel-enforced ceilings such as file-handle, thread, or shared-memory limits, causing allocation failures or the inability to spawn new workers.

When all three anomalies coincide the system shows a confused and rapidly degrading performance pattern: CPU utilization hovers at or near 100 %, yet some cores sit idle because mis-tuned parallelism, work-memory, or background-worker settings keep useful tasks from being dispatched while kernel limits silently block new threads. Wait-event histograms simultaneously report CPU-bound waits, configuration-specific waits (e.g., excessive checkpoint or log-write stalls), and sporadic "cannot allocate resource" errors from the OS. Throughput becomes erratic: bursts of work briefly clear, then stall again when the engine hits a kernel object limit or triggers a heavy checkpoint, causing run-queue spikes. Monitoring tools may mislead—showing CPU exhaustion that persists even after cancelling the top SQL—because background flushers and orphaned worker threads are spinning but unable to acquire the kernel resources they need.

Causal chain: a mis-set configuration (e.g., overly aggressive parallelism and tiny checkpoint segments) first inflates CPU demand and spawns many workers; the surge pushes total runnable threads toward the host’s logical-CPU count, creating a CPU Resource Anomaly. As more workers are launched, they collectively exhaust kernel limits on threads, file descriptors, or AIO contexts, triggering an Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly. The OS denials then force the engine to retry or spin, which consumes yet more CPU, while configuration parameters such as short checkpoint intervals amplify I/O and flush activity, further increasing thread creation and handle usage. Each anomaly therefore feeds the next: bad parameters create excess work, excess work saturates CPU, CPU saturation and worker proliferation hit OS ceilings, and the resulting allocation failures loop back to make the configuration’s side effects (checkpoint storms, parallelism thrashing) even harder to resolve, deepening the overall performance collapse.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Stale, missing, or insufficient statistics misrepresent real data distribution and lead the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and costs.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Even with acceptable statistics, the optimizer chooses or reuses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan because of cost-model bias, plan-cache effects, or version/configuration shifts.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Network paths, listeners, authentication, or socket resources are saturated or unstable, delaying connection establishment and throttling data transfer between clients and the DBMS.

When all three root causes are present, database sessions experience extreme and erratic latency. Misestimated cardinalities steer the optimizer toward plans that are already poor; subsequent plan-selection pathologies (e.g., bad plan reuse, loss of parallelism) can further inflate execution time and I/O. The prolonged queries hold server back-end processes and large result sets open, which, combined with limited network throughput or frequent retransmissions, keeps sockets busy, inflates client-read waits, and exhausts connection pools. Symptoms include: dramatic swings between very fast and very slow runtimes for the same statements, execution plans whose estimates diverge wildly from actual rows, sudden shifts to full scans or nested-loop explosions, spikes in network wait events and TCP retransmits, growth of half-open or idle-in-transaction connections, application-side timeouts, and bursts of session reconnect attempts that hit listener backlog limits.

Causally, outdated or low-quality statistics are the first domino, skewing cost calculations. The optimizer may then lock in a flawed plan or reuse one unsuitable for current data, multiplying resource consumption. The heavier CPU, memory, and I/O load lengthens query and fetch phases, causing result sets to dribble over congested or lossy networks. Extended response times keep connections open longer, pushing the network layer toward saturation; conversely, network stalls can trigger query cancellations and forced recompilations, increasing plan churn and making statistic-driven misestimates more frequent. The positive feedback between bad plans and network contention amplifies both bottlenecks, degrading overall throughput and stability across OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and visibility-check costs. 
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Write-ahead log generation, flushing, or archival becomes the bottleneck, stalling commits and growing the log store. 
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, creating system-wide compute starvation regardless of which layer drives the load. 

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a cascade of symptoms: commit latency and "log write/log flush" waits soar while user transactions also spend more time on MVCC visibility scans and vacuum/garbage-collection contention. Table and index sizes balloon, leading to longer buffer misses and heavier background I/O. Simultaneously, CPU utilization remains pegged; cleanup workers, log-flush daemons, and application sessions compete for cycles, causing elevated run-queue times and mixed wait profiles (CPU, log I/O, MVCC lookup) that are difficult to disentangle. Checkpoints may fire more frequently yet complete more slowly, archiver lag grows, and planner misestimates rise as row-density statistics drift, further inflating CPU and log pressure.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn produces large volumes of undo/redo, first stretching MVCC storage and then flooding the transaction log. The bloated heap forces longer visibility checks, which consume extra CPU; at the same time, intensified log flushing and background vacuum both demand CPU and I/O bandwidth. As CPU saturation lengthens every worker’s service time, cleanup and archiver processes fall further behind, letting dead versions and unarchived logs accumulate. The feedback loop—more dead versions → more log generation → more CPU demand → slower cleanup/flushing—amplifies each anomaly and can tip the database into a write-path stall or emergency shutdown due to version-store or log-space exhaustion.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine parameters governing memory, workers, checkpointing, and parallelism are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, introducing artificial bottlenecks and untimely background activity.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages and index structures contain physical or logical corruption that breaks key order, page links, or checksum verification, making access paths unreliable.

Combined phenomena: When all three root causes are active, the system shows explosive table and index growth, chronic autovacuum or purge backlogs, and erratic query plans that oscillate between bloated index scans and full table scans because of missing or duplicated rows. Checkpoints and log flushes may surge immediately after parameter changes, yet the storage subsystem remains under-utilised. Background cleaners report "skipped corrupted page" or stall on invalid page links, leaving ever more dead tuples behind. Integrity-check utilities and engine logs intermittently emit checksum, page-level, or index-order errors, while wait-event charts are dominated by version visibility checks, corruption-related retries, and idle CPU gaps that do not match the apparent workload pressure. Application sessions may experience sudden serialization failures, duplicate-key errors on inserts, or silent data loss when queries miss rows that are present in the heap but absent from a damaged index.

Causal chain: Mis-tuned parameters (e.g., undersized cleanup workers, disabled page checksums, aggressive checkpoint throttling, or oversized work_mem that bloats per-session memory) throttle version reclamation and extend transaction ID horizons, allowing MVCC debris to pile up. The enlarged heap and index footprint forces more page IO and longer maintenance windows, increasing the chance of power events, firmware bugs, or out-of-memory conditions that precipitate physical corruption. Once corruption appears, cleanup workers may skip or loop on damaged pages, further slowing or halting version reclamation. The lingering MVCC bloat in turn amplifies the stress on misconfigured memory and checkpoint parameters, causing additional checkpoint storms and weakened durability settings that make future corruption more likely. The three anomalies therefore reinforce each other in a feedback loop that degrades performance, jeopardises data integrity, and complicates root-cause diagnosis.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses or reuses an execution plan that is substantially sub-optimal even though statistics are reasonably accurate.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating table size and visibility-check cost.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply transaction-log records as fast as the primary generates them, causing replay lag and log-retention growth.

When these three root causes strike together, the system shows a blend of symptoms: 1) query plans alternate between index probes and full scans or stick to a poor plan, yet execution times lengthen regardless because heaps and indexes are bloated with dead rows; 2) long-running or repeatedly re-planned queries emit far more I/O and WAL, which rapidly widens replica write/flush/replay lag; 3) replication lag, in turn, keeps old snapshots open on standbys, preventing garbage collection on the primary, so the version store and table bloat swell further; 4) statistics collected on the enlarged tables exaggerate row counts, confusing the optimizer and prompting additional mis-plans; 5) the primary’s pg_wal / redo or archive area grows because segments cannot be recycled until replicas catch up, exacerbating storage pressure already heightened by MVCC bloat.

Causal chain: heavy OLTP churn creates many dead versions; delayed vacuum leads to bloated relations and skewed cost estimates, encouraging the optimizer to switch to full table scans or poorly chosen join orders, which inflate execution time and emit more WAL. The surge in WAL overwhelms replicas whose apply threads are already slowed by replaying large, poorly batched updates, so replication lag increases. That lag holds replication snapshots open, preventing further vacuum progress on the primary and locking in the version bloat that triggered the plan regression. This feedback loop steadily degrades query performance, bloats storage, and erodes recovery point objectives, making the composite anomaly significantly more damaging than any individual root cause alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is concurrently affected by (1) sub-optimal or erroneous application SQL and transaction design, (2) saturation or mis-configuration of the write-ahead logging path, and (3) latent corruption or structural inconsistency inside persistent data and index pages. Together they create a multi-layer fault that spans the workload, the log write pipeline, and the on-disk structures themselves.

Combined Observable Phenomena: End-user operations and background jobs show extreme and highly variable latency; some sessions wait on log flush or sync events while others hang on full-table or full-index scans that return incorrect or duplicated rows. Slow-query and deadlock logs grow rapidly, intermixed with engine messages about log switch storms, archive backlog, page-checksum failures, and forced plan fallbacks from indexed probes to sequential scans. Commit times spike, replication lags, checkpoints lengthen, and recovery/consistency verification utilities intermittently detect corruption, prompting automatic page repairs or instance restarts. The overlapping symptoms obscure clear attribution because each layer (application, log, storage) both masks and amplifies the others.

Causal Interaction: Inefficient SQL patterns (wide scans, large batch INSERT/UPDATE, long-lived transactions) generate excessive redo, driving the transaction-log subsystem to its throughput limits. Log buffer pressure and prolonged flush cycles extend transaction lifetimes, increasing lock hold times and exposure windows for any latent data-block flaws. Simultaneously, existing page or index corruptions force the optimizer to abandon efficient access paths, inflating I/O and redo volume further and triggering still more log activity. Log bottlenecks delay checkpoints and recovery, which in turn defer detection and repair of structural corruptions, allowing them to propagate. The feedback loop between heavy, poorly scoped workload operations, stressed log infrastructure, and damaged on-disk structures culminates in cascading slowdowns, elevated risk of transaction timeouts or rollbacks, and potential data loss on crash recovery.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written in a way that forces the engine to scan or modify far more data and to keep transactions open longer than business logic requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress until a lock is granted or a victim is rolled back.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot supply the read/write bandwidth or IOPS demanded by the workload, causing rising device-level latency and queue depths.

When all three anomalies strike together, the database shows a multilayered slowdown: slow-query logs fill with the same heavyweight statements, while lock-monitoring views reveal growing blocker–waiter trees and frequent deadlock reports. Commit latency and 99th-percentile response times soar; sessions pile up in both lock-wait and I/O-wait states; CPU utilization stays modest even as overall throughput collapses. Checkpoints, log flushes, and temp-space spills linger on disk, replica or backup lag widens, and connection pools exhaust, triggering application timeouts and retries that further inflate concurrency.

The causal chain begins with inefficient SQL that touches large row sets and performs wide updates, multiplying the volume of physical I/O. The saturated storage subsystem answers with elevated latency, lengthening statement execution and therefore the lifetime of every lock those statements hold. Extended lock hold times make it far more likely that other transactions will collide on the same rows or ranges, deepening lock queues and spawning deadlocks. Each rollback or retry triggered by lock contention restarts the expensive I/O-heavy statements, injecting still more traffic into an already bandwidth-limited storage fabric. This positive feedback loop binds workload inefficiency, I/O saturation, and lock contention into a single compound failure mode that can freeze an OLTP system.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table structures, indexes, partitions, or data types do not match workload access patterns, forcing queries into non-selective or non-covering scans that inflate work per statement.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively drive the host’s CPU cores into sustained saturation, so scheduling delays, run-queue waits, and system load grow independent of any single query plan choice.

When both root causes are present, the workload experiences a cascade of symptoms: execution plans show full-table or wide index scans that iterate over large row sets, while the CPU remains pegged near 100 %. The mismatch in physical design multiplies the number of rows each statement must touch; the resulting surge of predicate evaluations, hash computations, and buffer-management operations overwhelms the processor cache and elevates context-switch and run-queue waits. End-user latency rises sharply and unpredictably, auto-throttling or queuing appears in the application layer, and maintenance tasks such as index rebuilds or statistics jobs fall behind, further masking or amplifying the issue.

Causally, poor schema and index design inflates logical I/O and amplifies CPU demand per query. The aggregate of these inefficient plans pushes total CPU consumption to the saturation point, triggering a CPU Resource Anomaly. In turn, CPU bottlenecks slow optimizer feedback loops, prolong lock holding, and extend transaction lifetimes, which increases contention and intensifies the cost of every additional row fetch imposed by the design flaw. The two factors therefore reinforce each other: deficient physical design generates excessive CPU load, while CPU saturation magnifies the latency penalty of the design flaw and complicates diagnosis by making all queries appear slow, masking the original indexing deficiency.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating the version store and visibility-check work per statement.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical devices or virtual volumes cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency budget demanded by the database workload.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Host CPU cores are driven to sustained saturation by database processes, leaving little headroom for other tasks.

When all three root causes manifest simultaneously, the system shows a blended pathology: data and indexes grow rapidly while auto-vacuum or purge workers run constantly yet make no headway; buffer-pool miss rates climb, leading to more physical reads that wait in long device queues; foreground sessions exhibit both high I/O wait and elevated CPU run-queue latency; query plans that must scan bloated heaps spend extra CPU cycles on version visibility checks, only to stall again on slow block delivery; background writer, checkpointer, and log-flush threads extend commit latency, and overall transaction response times and batch windows stretch unpredictably. Monitoring views reveal swollen rollback segments, disk queues pegged, and CPU usage near 100 %, making it difficult to isolate any single dominant wait class.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn expands the version store, inflating table and index footprints. The larger on-disk working set overwhelms the storage subsystem, elevating I/O latency. Slow I/O in turn delays cleanup workers, allowing even more dead versions to accumulate and further bloat storage. As each user query now touches more pages and performs extra visibility checks, CPU demand rises. With CPUs already saturated, context-switch overhead grows, further slowing background tasks such as vacuuming and checkpoint flushing, which then generate burstier I/O patterns that intensify storage contention. The feedback loop among unchecked version buildup, degraded I/O throughput, and exhausted CPU cycles drives the database into a self-reinforcing degradation spiral that is difficult to recover from without addressing all three underlying resource constraints together.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Sustained physical read- and write-volume overruns the bandwidth or latency capability of the underlying storage devices.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Critical database volumes run out of free space, preventing further allocation to data, log, temp, or backup files.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or AIO contexts are reached by database processes.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences a compound failure mode: rising I/O queue depths and latency slow every read and write, just as space-allocation operations and background writers begin to fail, while the engine is intermittently denied new file handles, shared-memory segments, or AIO slots needed to continue processing. Observable symptoms co-exist and amplify one another—high I/O wait time alongside space-exhaustion or auto-extend errors, cascading log-archive stalls, sudden "too many open files" or "cannot allocate shared memory" errors, checkpoints that cannot complete, and sessions hanging in both I/O and kernel wait states. Batch windows stretch, OLTP requests time out, and portions of the engine may appear up yet accept no new work.

Causally, storage-bandwidth saturation elongates every write, delaying checkpointing, archiving, and space-reclaim tasks, which accelerates space consumption. As free space dwindles, emergency auto-extension, log-switch, and purge operations raise the number of concurrent file opens and asynchronous I/O requests, pushing the process toward kernel limits. Once OS resource ceilings are hit, the engine is unable to create new files or I/O contexts, further throttling throughput and blocking the very maintenance needed to relieve space pressure. In parallel, failure to create or extend files feeds back into higher I/O retry traffic and excessive log buildup, worsening both throughput saturation and space exhaustion. The intertwined feedback loops of bandwidth starvation, capacity depletion, and kernel denials drive the database into a progressively deeper stall or partial outage until at least one of the constraints is lifted.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Persistent exhaustion or near-exhaustion of physical or logical free space assigned to data files, logs, temp areas, backups, or diagnostics, causing allocation failures and space-related errors.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Sustained saturation of host CPU by database processes, driving run-queue growth and broad response-time inflation across the workload.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced quotas such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or cgroup limits, preventing the database from acquiring required OS resources.

When all three conditions occur together, the database exhibits compound symptoms: rapid space depletion accompanies soaring CPU utilisation and a surge of kernel-level allocation failures. Checkpoints, log switches, and temp operations repeatedly fail or stall, while foreground sessions and background workers spin or retry, inflating CPU load and run-queue depth. Simultaneously, the mounting number of retries, orphaned handles, and emergency maintenance threads consume additional file descriptors and process slots, triggering "too many open files", "cannot create thread", or shared-memory errors. Application traffic sees erratic latency, timeouts, and abrupt disconnections as the engine alternates between CPU starvation, space allocation failures, and OS denials, making the root cause appear multi-faceted and intermittent.

Causally, shrinking free space forces the engine to perform frequent auto-extension checks, logging, and aggressive space-management work (e.g., checkpoints, archive generations, purges), each of which elevates CPU demand and opens additional files, pushing both CPU utilisation and OS resource consumption upward. The resulting CPU saturation slows background cleaners and log archivers, delaying space reclamation and accelerating space pressure. In parallel, the expanded number of active sessions or retry loops inflates file-handle and thread usage until kernel limits are hit; once those limits are breached, the engine cannot create new files, extend tablespaces, or spawn workers, further preventing space recovery and amplifying CPU spin and wait events. The feedback loop among space exhaustion, CPU overload, and OS limit exhaustion drives the system into cascading stalls or outages far more severe than any single anomaly would cause alone.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite acceptable statistics, leading to inefficient access paths, excessive work, or poor parallelism.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes or sessions hit kernel-enforced limits for files, memory, threads, or other OS objects, preventing new allocations and throttling normal engine activity.

When these two root causes strike simultaneously, the database may show volatile and erratic performance: some statements swing from fast to extremely slow as bad plans drive up I/O, memory, or worker-thread demand, which in turn collides with exhausted OS quotas. Operators observe frequent plan flips, sudden full-table scans that flood buffer cache, spikes in context switches, parallel-worker start-up failures, "cannot allocate memory/handle" errors, and sessions hanging in compilation or execution. Existing connections limp along with degraded throughput while new logins, background tasks, or parallel workers are refused by the kernel, making it difficult to diagnose whether the bottleneck is inside the optimizer or below the database layer.

Causal interaction: a sub-optimal plan typically inflates resource consumption—opening many files, scanning large data regions, spawning extra threads, or allocating larger memory areas. This surge accelerates exhaustion of kernel-level limits (file descriptors, shared memory, process IDs, AIO contexts). Conversely, once those limits are reached, the optimizer may be forced to recompile without access to parallel workers or temp-space files, pushing it toward even worse plans and provoking further plan churn. The feedback loop between poor plan choices and OS denials amplifies latency variance, expands partial outages, and obscures root-cause isolation because each anomaly masks and triggers the other.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are accurate, leading to excessive CPU, I/O, or memory consumption per statement.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or downstream replicas cannot receive or apply log records at the rate the primary generates them, causing widening replication lag and retained WAL segments.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server or server-to-replica network paths and connection-handling resources are saturated or unreliable, throttling data transfer and session establishment.

When these three root causes strike together, the system shows a compound symptom set: 1) unpredictable query latency spikes and CPU/I/O bursts on the primary due to poor plans; 2) rapidly growing replication send, write, and replay lag because the heavier plans inflate the volume of WAL generated per time unit; 3) simultaneous network queuing, retransmissions, and connection timeouts that slow both client traffic and the streaming of WAL to replicas. Monitoring dashboards may reveal alternating bottlenecks—some intervals dominated by query-execution waits, others by replication backlog, and still others by listener-queue saturation—making the true culprit difficult to isolate. Fail-over readiness degrades as replicas fall behind while end-user sessions experience both execution slowdowns and intermittent connection errors.

Causal interaction: The sub-optimal plans increase row touches, temp-space spills, and index maintenance, amplifying WAL generation and stressing the replication pipeline. The swollen outbound log stream must traverse the same constrained network paths and connection pools that are already suffering congestion, further slowing delivery to replicas and feeding back pressure to the primary, which must retain more log segments and may stall commits when synchronous replication is configured. In turn, network saturation lengthens client round-trip times; connection retries inflate session counts, consuming listener and socket resources and reducing the budget of backends available to execute queries. The resulting execution slowdowns give the optimizer volatile runtime feedback, encouraging still more erratic plan selection. Thus, each anomaly reinforces the others, driving a vicious cycle of heavier workload, growing lag, and deteriorating connectivity that degrades both transactional and analytical performance.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data or metadata resources, creating blocking chains or deadlocks inside the lock-manager layer.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log file, archiver, or sync pipeline) becomes the primary bottleneck, stretching commit latency and stalling write activity.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space for data, log, or archive destinations falls to (or below) critical thresholds, causing allocation failures and preventing log or data growth.

When all three root causes surface simultaneously, the database can enter a cascade of reinforcing symptoms: commits slow down because log flushes wait on saturated log devices or on archiver/replication lag created by space shortages; transactions keep their locks for much longer, inflating lock-wait time, expanding blocking chains, and multiplying deadlock incidents. Blocked sessions accumulate in connection pools, while error logs alternate among lock timeouts, "log write stall", and "no space left" messages. Checkpoint storms, repeated log-switch attempts, and emergency autogrowth retries further increase I/O contention, amplifying both log and lock delays. Overall throughput collapses and application timeouts spike, yet the overlapping symptoms obscure which layer is the primary trigger.

Causally, dwindling storage space throttles the archiver or prevents log segment recycling, forcing the transaction log subsystem to pause commits until space frees up. These elongated commit phases keep transactional locks active far beyond their normal duration, igniting severe lock contention. In turn, the growing queue of blocked and retried transactions inflates redo generation and temp usage, accelerating space exhaustion and putting even more pressure on the log subsystem. The feedback loop between space starvation, log stall, and prolonged lock holding drives the system into a self-reinforcing degradation spiral that can culminate in widespread transaction aborts or a full outage.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Runtime parameters governing memory, I/O cadence, background workers, and parallelism are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload characteristics, or version defaults.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database memory regions (buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, parallel worker buffers, etc.) grow beyond the physical limits of the host, causing sustained operating-system memory pressure.

When both root causes exist concurrently, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: sudden or sustained spikes in paging, swap or OOM killer events occur alongside wait-event distributions that do not align with actual resource usage (e.g., log flush waits while disks are idle, CPU spin while cores are under-utilized). Checkpoints, log flushes, or background cleanup may thrash because incorrectly sized parameters force frequent flushes, while at the same time memory pressure evicts hot buffer pages, driving down cache hit ratios and inflating I/O. Parallel queries can stall or be force-cancelled when the per-worker memory set by configuration oversubscribes RAM already depleted by runaway allocations, leading to unpredictable latency, connection aborts, or instance restarts that are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, mis-tuned parameters often initiate excessive or fragmented memory reservations—large buffer pools, overly generous per-query work memory, or inflated parallel-worker caps—that push the engine into physical memory overcommit, triggering the memory-allocation anomaly. In turn, the resulting OS memory pressure feeds back into the database: evicted pages slow operations, which prompts even more intensive background activity (checkpoints, re-reads, cache repopulation) that was already scheduled too aggressively by the faulty configuration. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other, creating a loop where configuration-induced over-allocation exhausts memory and memory exhaustion amplifies the performance pathologies caused by the bad configuration, degrading both OLTP and OLAP workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) stale or missing optimizer statistics that drive systematic cardinality misestimates, (2) replication channels that cannot receive or apply the primary’s change stream in real time, and (3) on-disk data or index corruption that compromises physical page and key integrity. Together these three independent root causes create a multi-layer failure in which the optimizer, the replication pipeline, and the storage layer are all impaired at once.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Queries on the primary may flip unpredictably between long-running full-table scans and erroneous index probes, showing extreme plan regressions and wildly inaccurate row-count estimates. These inefficient plans inflate I/O, CPU, and transaction-log generation, which in turn floods the replication queue; standbys display rapidly widening replay lag, swollen relay / retained log segments, and intermittent apply errors or pauses. Corrupted pages or index structures can surface first on replicas during redo-apply, manifesting as replication-side checksum failures, apply-phase panics, or forced replica restarts, while the primary reports page-verification warnings and begins discarding corrupted indexes, triggering further plan shifts and emergency full scans. Application symptoms range from time-outs and stale read results on replicas to inconsistent row counts or silent data errors on the primary.

Causal Interaction: Stale or incomplete statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing plans that generate excessive I/O and large batched modifications, expanding the volume and burstiness of redo traffic. The inflated and irregular log stream overstresses an already bandwidth- or CPU-constrained replica set, deepening replication lag and increasing the window during which un-recycled log segments must be retained. Simultaneously, latent data or index corruption causes additional I/O retries and error handling on the primary and may corrupt log records that must be shipped. When these damaged blocks reach the replica, apply failures force repeated retries or pauses, compounding lag. The stalled or broken replication prevents off-host integrity checks and hampers failover options, while the corruption itself can block automatic statistics refreshes, perpetuating the optimizer’s misinformation. Thus each anomaly feeds the others: bad statistics create heavy workloads, heavy workloads overload replication, and corruption both triggers and is masked by the other two issues, driving the system into a spiraling degradation of performance, consistency, and availability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer input metadata (row counts, histograms, correlations) is stale or incomplete, provoking systematic cardinality misestimation.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime settings for memory, parallelism, checkpointing, and other behaviors are mis-tuned for the actual hardware, workload, or version, causing non-resource constrained stalls and regressions.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Aggregate memory consumed by caches, work areas, and background components exceeds safe physical limits, triggering OS pressure, paging, or OOM events.

When these three root causes coexist, the system exhibits erratic and mutually reinforcing symptoms: query plans fluctuate between under- and over-allocation of memory; inaccurately costed plans may request excessive hash/sort buffers that the mis-configured memory ceilings still allow, leading to sudden resident-set growth, swap storms, and plan evictions. Checkpoint storms or aggressive background workers spawned by poor configuration contend with bloated caches for RAM, while misestimated row counts cause the optimizer to either underutilize or over-utilize parallel workers, amplifying CPU spin waits and buffer thrashing. Operators chosen on bad statistics (e.g., multi-way hash joins, large sorts) aggravate memory pressure; once paging begins, previously minor log-write or I/O waits balloon, and feedback loops of plan recompilation and memory churn create workload instability. Symptoms therefore span: wildly diverging execution times, chronic memory pressure alarms, CPU under- or over-utilization unrelated to actual data volume, frequent plan cache flushes, and post-upgrade regressions that defy single-cause attribution.

Causally, stale or missing statistics misguide the optimizer into selecting memory-intensive or improperly parallelized plans. Mis-set configuration parameters (e.g., inflated work_mem, oversized buffer pool, aggressive parallelism, or lax memory overcommit) permit those plans to reserve more memory than the host can sustain. The resulting memory over-allocation pushes the database process into OS paging or OOM territory, triggering automatic memory eviction, plan recompilations, and emergency checkpoints, all of which further distort statistics and raise background-worker activity. Each anomaly therefore feeds the others: bad statistics provoke wasteful memory usage, misconfiguration fails to constrain it, and memory exhaustion in turn disrupts statistics collection and background maintenance, creating a vicious cycle that severely degrades both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions block or deadlock on mutually incompatible locks, forcing sessions to wait or be aborted by the lock manager.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume an abnormally high share of CPU, driving the host to sustained compute saturation.

Composite definition: This anomaly denotes a workload state in which severe lock blocking/deadlocks and host-level CPU saturation arise at the same time, each rooted in its own layer yet jointly degrading throughput and latency.

Combined observable phenomena: Lock-wait queues, deadlock reports, and victim rollbacks appear together with OS run-queue inflation, near-100 % CPU utilization, and pervasive scheduler wait events. Queries and transactions stall both on locks and on CPU scheduling, causing erratic response times, sharp drops in TPS, rapid growth of connection-pool backlogs, and surges of application-side timeouts or retried statements. Deadlock victims and retry loops can inflate statement counts, while blocked sessions hold locks longer, inflating both wait chains and CPU consumption once they resume, making the overall performance picture noisy and harder to diagnose.

Causal chain and interaction: Heavy lock contention lengthens transaction lifetimes; the sessions that finally obtain locks often perform their work in CPU-starved conditions, extending lock hold times and propagating blocking to more sessions. Simultaneously, deadlock victim retries, spin-loops, and repeated lock acquisition attempts add extra CPU load, feeding the saturation. The saturated CPU, in turn, slows lock-manager bookkeeping, prolongs detection of deadlocks, and delays the execution and commit phases that would release locks, thereby intensifying contention. This positive feedback loop between prolonged locking and depleted CPU cycles amplifies both anomalies, accelerating performance collapse unless one of the root causes is relieved.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine-level settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload demands, so the problem originates from the parameter choices themselves rather than from true resource scarcity.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions repeatedly serialize on buffer-cache pages, latches, or page-pin structures, causing buffer-busy waits, CPU spin, and I/O stalls even when aggregate resources appear sufficient.

When both root causes are present, the system simultaneously suffers from mis-sized or overly aggressive configuration parameters and from intensified contention inside the buffer manager. Observable symptoms blend and amplify:  
• Extreme and oscillating buffer-busy/latch wait counts alongside spikes of log-write, checkpoint, or background-writer waits that do not correlate with actual hardware usage.  
• CPU cores alternate between idle periods (due to throttling by mis-tuned parameters) and 100 % spin-loops (due to latch storms).  
• Sudden latency cliff after configuration changes or upgrades, followed by cascading stalls in buffer I/O, prolonged checkpoint completion, and lock escalations at higher tiers.  
• Monitoring tools may falsely suggest memory pressure, yet page-in/out rates stay high because the undersized buffer pool forces constant eviction, further aggravating hot-page contention.  

Causal chain: misconfigured parameters—such as a too-small buffer pool, overly frequent checkpoints, or an excessive max_parallelism value—create rapid page churn and frequent dirty-page flushing. This churn elevates demand on shared hotspot pages and on the buffer manager’s latch structures. The heightened contention lengthens critical sections, causing spin-loops that waste CPU cycles and delay I/O completion. The resulting throughput collapse, in turn, leads administrators to raise connection or parallel-worker limits, which further magnifies both latch pressure and configuration misfit. Thus, the two anomalies reinforce each other: poor configuration provokes buffer-level thrashing, and the ensuing latch contention obscures the original tuning fault, jointly degrading performance far more than either issue alone.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, causing table bloat and visibility-check overhead.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database memory regions (buffers, work areas, caches, temporary segments) grow past safe host limits, triggering OS-level pressure, paging, or OOM events.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high and sustained share of CPU, saturating cores and lengthening run-queue waits.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: bloated heaps and indexes inflate the buffer-cache footprint, which in turn competes with per-query work areas and background workers for RAM. Memory pressure forces the operating system to page, and every faulted-in page or reclaimed version must still be visibility-checked, driving up CPU cycles per row. The escalating CPU demand keeps all cores near saturation, prolongs cleaner and checkpointer cycles, and further delays version reclamation. Observable symptoms therefore include explosive growth of on-disk table size, runaway resident-set size, swap activity, soaring CPU utilisation, high scheduler/run-queue waits, persistent autovacuum or purge workers unable to keep up, mis-estimated plans due to bloated statistics, cache-hit ratio collapse, and widespread query latency spikes that blur the boundary between I/O, memory, and CPU bottlenecks.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn produces excessive dead versions; the enlarged version store inflates buffer-pool usage and forces more aggressive caching, pushing overall memory consumption past safe thresholds. Paging and memory throttling slow cleaner threads, letting even more dead tuples accumulate. Each subsequent access must traverse larger page chains and perform more visibility checks, amplifying CPU usage. Near-saturated CPUs delay both user queries and background maintenance, so version cleanup and memory reclamation fall further behind, creating a feedback loop where MVCC bloat drives memory exhaustion, memory pressure amplifies CPU demand, and CPU saturation prevents recovery—ultimately degrading throughput and threatening system stability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, missing, or incomplete optimizer statistics cause systematic misestimation of predicate selectivity and cardinalities, leading the planner to choose sub-optimal access paths and join orders.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excess accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries causes table and index bloat, heavier visibility checks, and persistent background-cleanup pressure in a high-churn OLTP system.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or congested network and connection-handling capacity limits the rate at which clients can establish sessions or transfer result sets, creating connection backlogs and socket-level waits.
