When all three defects co-exist, the database exhibits a blend of execution-plan instability, growing on-disk and in-memory footprints, and erratic end-to-end latency. Misestimated plans may trigger full-table scans or inefficient nested loops that read vast swaths of bloated heaps; the extra I/O magnifies MVCC-induced scan times because more dead tuples must be skipped. Long-running queries inflate the number of concurrent backends holding snapshots, slowing version cleanup even further. As heap and index sizes swell, the optimizer’s already stale statistics become progressively less representative, compounding estimation errors. Concurrently, enlarged result sets generated by sub-optimal plans congest outbound network buffers, while prolonged query runtimes keep connections open, exhausting listener slots and causing connection attempts to time out. Clients observe sporadic spikes in response times, query cancellations, and authentication failures, while DBAs see divergent estimated vs. actual rows, rising autovacuum lag, blazing version-store growth, swelling relation sizes, and OS socket queues overflowing.

Causally, MVCC bloat inflates table size and skews data distribution, which degrades the accuracy of existing statistics; the optimizer therefore chooses plans that scan or join far more data than anticipated, lengthening query execution. The longer queries run, the longer snapshots stay alive, delaying version reclamation and accelerating version-store growth—a positive feedback loop. The heavier I/O and CPU demand further slows background cleanup workers, letting bloat expand. Meanwhile, the oversized result sets and extended query durations hold server processes and network sockets, pushing connection pools and listener queues to their limits. Connection contention triggers client retries, amplifying network load and session churn, which in turn increases transaction open/close activity and further burdens MVCC bookkeeping. The intertwined effects of poor statistics, MVCC bloat, and network saturation thus reinforce each other, driving the system into a deteriorating performance spiral.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings such as log-buffer size, checkpoint cadence, synchronous-commit flags, parallel apply threads, and memory limits are mis-tuned with respect to hardware capacity and workload intensity.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The primary’s write-ahead log buffer, files, or archive pipeline cannot generate, flush, or recycle log records quickly enough, turning the log path into the dominant bottleneck on commits.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, flush, or apply the shipped log stream at the rate the primary produces it, leading to growing positional lag and retained log segments.

When all three root causes coexist, symptoms overlap and amplify: commit latency and log-flush wait events surge even though storage and CPU utilization appear modest; massive log backlogs accumulate because slow replication prevents log recycling; checkpoints and log-switch storms fire more often yet fail to relieve space pressure; replica replay lag widens, causing stale reads, delayed failover readiness, and possible cascading stalls on synchronous replicas; primary-side disk consumption grows unpredictably, while monitoring shows erratic spikes in background-worker CPU, network retransmissions, and I/O bursts that do not correlate cleanly with foreground workload volume.

Causally, mis-configured parameters (small log buffers, undersized log files, aggressive synchronous-commit or archiving settings, insufficient apply-worker threads) throttle the transaction-log subsystem, inflating commit and flush latency. The slowed log path, in turn, reduces the throughput margin available for replication shipping. As replicas fall behind, the primary must retain additional log segments, further expanding the already stressed log file set and forcing more frequent checkpoints and file switches—each of which revisits the poorly tuned parameters that caused the initial slowdown. The feedback loop between configuration mis-tuning, log-path saturation, and replication lag therefore compounds pressure on memory, disk, and network, degrading OLTP performance and increasing the risk of outage.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same objects, producing long waiter chains or deadlocks that stall statement execution.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and undo records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating storage, scan cost, and snapshot–visibility work.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Generation, flush, or archival of write-ahead log records becomes a bottleneck, stretching commit latency and stalling writers.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits a compound slowdown: transactions block each other at the lock manager, pile up in connection pools, and hold snapshots that prevent vacuum/garbage-collection from advancing. The unreclaimed version bloat enlarges tables and indexes, lengthening lock hold times for range or page locks and further stressing the lock manager. Meanwhile every stalled or rolled-back transaction generates additional redo; the growing version store and frequent deadlock retries inflate log volume, overwhelming the already saturated log buffer, checkpoint, and archiver paths. Observable symptoms include soaring lock-wait and deadlock counts, rapidly expanding table and index sizes, constantly active yet ineffective cleanup workers, exploding write-ahead log directories, prolonged commit and rollback times, and eventually global throughput collapse accompanied by application-level timeouts and storage-space alerts.

Causally, intense lock contention causes sessions to stay open longer, freezing their MVCC snapshots and stopping version pruning; this fuels version-store growth. The bloated heap increases I/O per statement, extending transaction durations and the lifespan of locks, which in turn deepens contention. Both phenomena raise redo generation (due to repeated updates, rollbacks, and cleanup activity) just as prolonged commit waits tie up locks even longer, forming a feedback loop that strains the transaction-log subsystem. A saturated log path then delays commit acknowledgement and rollback processing, prolonging lock holds and snapshot lifetimes, amplifying version bloat, and perpetuating the cycle—ultimately producing a severe, intertwined availability and performance crisis.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and undo/rollback records because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update-delete churn.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Total memory consumed by caches, working areas, and background structures grows beyond the safe host envelope, provoking OS-level pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read-write demand from data, temp, and log files saturates the bandwidth/IOPS capacity of the underlying storage, producing long device queues and high latency.

When all three conditions co-exist, the system exhibits a compounded failure pattern: tables and indexes swell with dead versions, inflating buffer-pool residency and exhausting memory; as the engine pages dirty and clean buffers more frequently under memory stress, the already overtaxed storage layer experiences further surges of random and sequential I/O. Checkpoint and vacuum/cleaner processes run constantly but fall behind, causing rollback segments and version stores to balloon on disk. Operators observe runaway RSS growth followed by paging or OOM kills, steep drops in cache hit ratios, soaring read/write latencies, prolonged lock-holder lifetimes, misestimated plans due to bloated statistics, and a vicious oscillation between CPU stalls on memory reclamation and waits on disk I/O.

Causally, heavy update/delete workloads first trigger MVCC bloat, enlarging both on-disk heaps and in-memory buffers. The extra pages inflate the buffer cache and plan cache demand, tipping the system into memory over-commitment; the resulting eviction and swap activity converts what could have been memory hits into physical I/O. This amplification pushes the storage subsystem toward saturation, where higher latency further slows cleanup workers, allowing even more version accumulation. In turn, the expanding on-disk structures require larger memory allocations and longer I/O operations, forming a feedback loop in which MVCC maintenance, memory exhaustion, and storage bandwidth starvation continuously reinforce each other, rapidly degrading throughput and stability of the transactional workload.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database concurrently suffers from a sub-optimal execution-plan selection by the optimizer, mis-tuned engine configuration parameters, and restrictive operating-system resource limits. Although each factor alone can cause performance degradation, their simultaneous presence creates a multifaceted failure in which query plans are poor, engine subsystems are ill-provisioned, and the host kernel blocks further resource allocation.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Workloads exhibit erratic performance with the same SQL sometimes using efficient index probes and other times reverting to table scans or serial plans. CPU and I/O utilization metrics look inconsistent with wait-event reports—sessions show long log-write or memory allocation waits while disks and CPUs are under-utilized. Sudden bursts of checkpoints or background-writer activity coincide with spikes of "cannot allocate shared memory," "too many open files," or "failed to create thread" errors coming from the OS. Parallel queries intermittently fall back to single-threaded execution because worker pools cannot grow, causing unpredictable query runtimes. Plan cache churn grows as failed worker creation or memory shortages force frequent recompilations, and overall throughput collapses in waves rather than gradually.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Mis-set database parameters (e.g., undersized buffer pool, aggressive work-memory limits, or overly frequent checkpoints) inflate true execution costs, but the optimizer—already prone to selecting borderline plans—may overestimate or underestimate those costs and choose plans that rely on resources the engine cannot effectively supply. When such a plan attempts to allocate additional memory, workers, or I/O contexts, it collides with tight operating-system limits on file handles, shared memory, or threads, resulting in run-time errors or implicit plan downgrades. These failures invalidate or evict plans, prompting fresh compilations that again suffer from the same flawed cost model and parameter landscape, creating a feedback loop. Meanwhile, engine background tasks triggered by the mis-configuration (e.g., checkpoint storms) consume the very kernel resources that user queries lack, amplifying contention and making the overall performance regression sharper and harder to diagnose.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more rows, hold transactions open longer, or perform extra round-trips beyond business needs.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long wait chains or deadlocks managed by the lock manager.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database process hits kernel-enforced ceilings such as file-descriptor, thread, or shared-memory limits, preventing new workers or I/O operations.

When these three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: individual statements run slowly and appear repeatedly in slow-query logs; lock-wait and deadlock statistics surge, producing victim rollbacks and application retries; and, simultaneously, the engine logs failures to open files, spawn threads, or allocate shared memory, causing partial connection or worker starvation. Blocking sessions linger because the lock manager cannot grant locks, while new sessions or parallel workers cannot be created due to exhausted OS resources, amplifying queue length at both the database and application tiers. Observable effects include steep drops in throughput, rising response-time variance, connection-pool exhaustion, and oscillations between lock timeouts, transaction aborts, and "resource cannot be acquired" engine errors.

Causal chain: chatty or scan-heavy SQL inflates transaction scope and lock footprint, lengthening the time each lock is held and turning otherwise brief conflicts into chronic blocking or deadlock scenarios. Prolonged waits keep server processes alive and idle for longer, inflating the number of simultaneously active threads, file handles, and asynchronous I/O contexts. This sustained pressure drives the database process toward OS-level resource ceilings. Once those limits are reached, the engine can no longer spawn new worker threads to service blocked or retrying sessions, which in turn magnifies lock contention because fewer transactions can progress to release their locks. The positive feedback loop between over-heavy SQL, extended lock holding, and kernel resource exhaustion pushes the database into a severe, self-reinforcing degradation state that is difficult to resolve without addressing all three layers.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, swelling the version store and bloating heap and index pages.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions stall while fighting for buffer-cache pages, lightweight latches, and dirty-page flush slots, causing CPU spin and prolonged page waits.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical data or index pages become internally inconsistent—checksums fail, key order breaks, or page links go missing—so logical access paths can no longer be trusted.

When these three root causes strike together, the system shows a tangled mixture of symptoms: rapidly growing tables and indexes raise the buffer-pool residency pressure; the same hot, bloated, or corrupted pages are repeatedly pinned, evicted, and reread, amplifying latch and I/O waits; index or heap corruption forces query planners to fall back to full scans that must wade through mountains of obsolete versions; integrity-verification or auto-recovery tasks repeatedly touch damaged pages, further heating contention hotspots; cleanup workers run constantly yet make little visible progress, while sessions see latency spikes, duplicate or missing rows, and intermittent corruption warnings.

Causal interaction: excessive version churn expands the number of dirty and frequently accessed pages, lengthening the time each page stays in the buffer pool and widening the window for latch contention. Prolonged latch holds and buffer pressure delay vacuum or purge workers, letting even more obsolete versions accumulate. The sustained write amplification increases checkpoint volume and I/O stress, heightening the risk of torn-page events or incomplete flushes that introduce on-disk corruption. Once corruption appears, every access to the damaged pages triggers additional retries, verification reads, or full-page writes, keeping the pages perpetually hot and further intensifying latch contention and cleanup backlog. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another in a feedback loop that degrades throughput, threatens data correctness, and complicates diagnosis.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The system simultaneously suffers (1) heavy lock-manager conflicts that block or deadlock concurrent transactions, (2) runaway accumulation of obsolete MVCC versions that background cleaners cannot reclaim in time, and (3) sustained saturation of host CPU resources by database processes. The three root causes coexist and interact, jointly degrading throughput, increasing latency, and threatening availability on a write-intensive OLTP workload.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 
• Long blocker-waiter chains and periodic deadlock victim errors coincide with rapidly growing table and index footprints, swollen undo/version stores, and vacuum/cleaner workers stuck in backlog. 
• Global CPU utilisation hovers near 100 %, run-queue length rises, and CPU-related wait events dominate performance views; at the same time, lock wait time, query latency, and application timeouts climb steeply. 
• Select queries encounter larger visibility-check costs due to bloated page contents, while update/delete statements both wait on locks and spend extra CPU sifting through long version chains. 
• Background cleanup workers, starved of CPU and blocked by long-running transactions, fall further behind, allowing version bloat and storage usage to snowball. 

Causal interaction: Lock contention prolongs transaction lifetimes and increases the number of in-flight snapshots, preventing garbage collection of obsolete versions and accelerating MVCC bloat. The enlarged version store forces foreground queries to scan more row versions, inflating CPU consumption, while overworked cleanup processes intensify CPU demand yet make little progress because they are pre-empted by user back-ends and impeded by still-held locks. Rising CPU saturation slows both application and maintenance tasks, lengthening lock hold times and further delaying version reclamation. This feedback loop amplifies each individual anomaly, driving the database into a state where blocking, storage growth, and CPU exhaustion reinforce one another, culminating in severe throughput collapse and potential service outages.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead. 
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk heap or index pages become physically or logically corrupted so that key ordering, page links, or row mappings are no longer reliable. 
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume nearly all available CPU, starving the rest of the workload and elongating every wait path.

When all three anomalies coexist, the engine faces simultaneous version-store bloat, structural corruption, and compute saturation. Observable symptoms merge and intensify: table and index sizes balloon while integrity-check utilities flag page or key-order errors; long-running queries switch from index to full scans yet still miss or duplicate rows; VACUUM/autovacuum or purge workers run constantly but make little progress, monopolising CPU and I/O; error logs show a mix of "transaction-id wraparound imminent", "page checksum mismatch", and scheduler/run-queue wait events; overall latency spikes unpredictably as corruption forces redundant visibility checks and error-handling retries on an already CPU-starved host.

Causally, page or index corruption can block or abort version cleanup by causing workers to loop, restart, or skip damaged ranges, allowing obsolete versions to accumulate unchecked. The growing version store inflates heap and index footprints, increasing the number of pages that must be scanned and validated, which further raises CPU demand. Sustained CPU saturation slows both foreground queries and background repair tasks, extending snapshot lifetimes and exacerbating version bloat. In turn, the larger and increasingly corrupted data structures heighten per-tuple visibility checks and checksum validations, feeding back into higher CPU consumption. The intertwined feedback loop accelerates storage inflation, widens corruption impact, and pushes the transactional system toward critical failure thresholds such as transaction-ID wraparound or irreversible data loss.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite anomaly definition: The database concurrently experiences on-disk data/index corruption, sustained saturation of the underlying storage devices, and near-maximum consumption of host CPU resources. The coexistence of these three root causes causes intertwined integrity faults, I/O bottlenecks, and compute starvation that jointly threaten both correctness and performance across transactional and analytical workloads.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Operators that rely on indexes intermittently miss or duplicate rows while their response times swing unpredictably; repeated checksum failures, page-repair attempts, and forced re-reads inflate read amplification and drive I/O queues to their limits, causing device latencies to spike into seconds. Simultaneously, database worker threads spin on retries and error handling, pushing CPU utilization to 100 %, swelling run queues, and surfacing scheduler and I/O wait events side-by-side. Batch jobs overrun maintenance windows, OLTP transactions time out or deadlock on corrupted pages, recovery processes loop, and monitoring shows a mixture of physical corruption alerts, persistent PAGEIOLATCH/IO_COMPLETION waits, and high CPU_TIME rankings for error-handling routines.

Causal interaction: Corrupted data or index pages force the engine to issue repeated physical reads, trigger consistency checks, and invoke page-repair or rebuild tasks, all of which amplify demand on an already saturated storage subsystem. The heightened I/O contention elongates each access, causing worker threads to block and then surge when I/O completes, which in turn spikes CPU consumption through excessive context switching, spin-locks, and retry logic. Conversely, CPU saturation slows background tasks such as checksum validation, buffer flushing, and recovery, prolonging the window during which corrupted pages remain in circulation. The prolonged I/O queues also increase the chance of further write interruptions or incomplete flushes, potentially deepening the underlying corruption. The feedback loop among corruption handling, storage overload, and CPU exhaustion drives the database into a degraded and unstable state where both performance and data integrity are simultaneously compromised.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, forcing them to queue or deadlock in the lock-manager layer.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, causing allocation failures and engine stalls unrelated to I/O bandwidth.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process hits kernel-enforced limits such as file descriptors, shared memory, or thread quotas, preventing creation or expansion of required OS objects.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences compound symptoms: lock-wait and deadlock statistics surge while space-allocation and OS-resource errors appear in engine and system logs; DML or DDL commands freeze holding locks, blocking whole lock chains; new sessions, parallel workers, or log-writer threads fail to start because the OS will not grant additional file handles or memory; data-file or log-segment auto-extend requests hang or abort due to full devices, leaving transactions open and their locks retained; application time-outs, retry storms, and partial node outages become frequent and hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, each anomaly amplifies the others. Space exhaustion or OS handle limits can interrupt a transaction while it is still holding locks, stretching lock durations and propagating blocking to unrelated sessions. Prolonged lock waits inflate the inflight transaction count, consuming more process slots, memory, and kernel objects, which accelerates hitting OS resource ceilings. At the same time, high concurrent activity and stalled commits drive log and temp growth, hastening space depletion. The feedback loop among extended lock holding, failed space extensions, and denied kernel allocations degrades throughput far faster than any single anomaly would, potentially cascading into a full outage that spans storage, OS, and concurrency control layers.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload intensity, or version defaults.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging pipeline—log buffer, files, flush/switch/archive processes—cannot keep pace with redo generation, stalling commits and checkpoints.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or I/O contexts throttle database processes independently of the engine’s internal resource governance.

When these three issues strike concurrently, symptoms overlap and amplify: commit latency and log-flush waits spike even though storage and CPU appear under-utilized; checkpoints and log-file switches occur in erratic bursts, sometimes failing with "unable to open file" or shared-memory allocation errors; background writers, archivers, and replication senders fall behind, causing bloated log directories and prolonged recovery point objectives; new sessions or parallel workers intermittently fail to start, and the engine may enter a partial hang where active transactions linger in commit wait while resource-starved background tasks cannot progress. Performance counters show low device saturation but high wait times on log and kernel primitives, confusing first-level diagnostics.

Causally, mis-sized configuration parameters (e.g., too small log buffer, aggressive checkpoint_timeout, excessive max_connections) inflate the churn on the transaction log. The surge in file creation, flush, and archive activity collides with operating-system limits on file descriptors, asynchronous I/O contexts, and shared memory, causing kernel denials that further slow or block log operations. Each blocked flush extends transaction hold times, boosting in-memory log pressure and triggering even more checkpoints, which in turn amplifies I/O and resource requests to the OS. This feedback loop escalates until both the logging subsystem and the kernel resource pools are saturated, yielding a compounded performance and availability degradation characteristic of this composite anomaly.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer consistently or intermittently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to excessive CPU, I/O, and memory consumption per statement.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database exhausts or is about to exhaust physical or logical free space in data files, log destinations, or temporary areas, triggering allocation failures and stalls rather than pure latency slow-downs.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes or sessions reach kernel-level ceilings for file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other OS-governed objects, causing hard errors when attempting to allocate additional kernel resources.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, symptoms become intertwined and harder to triage:  • Queries may flip unpredictably between different bad plans as plan-cache invalidations occur after space-related DDL, or as failed worker spawns force the optimizer to re-cost without parallelism.  • Sub-optimal plans generate ballooning intermediate results that overflow into TEMP, growing files faster than auto-extension can provide and amplifying space exhaustion.  • Log growth from long-running, poorly planned transactions collides with already constrained file-handle limits, producing alternating "no space" and "cannot open file" errors.  • Existing sessions may hang on waits for space or kernel objects, while new sessions fail to start because OS quotas are reached, producing a mix of engine-level and kernel-level error messages.  • Overall throughput collapses as the database oscillates between plan re-compilations, space allocation retries, and kernel denials.

Causal chain: a bad plan inflates I/O and temp-space usage, accelerating the consumption of data, log, and TEMP files. Growing files and frequent auto-extend operations open many new file handles, pushing the process toward OS handle and inode limits. Once these kernel limits are hit, further file growth or parallel-worker creation fails, forcing the optimizer to fall back to even less efficient serial plans, which in turn run longer and generate more redo, worsening space pressure. Simultaneously, space exhaustion triggers background cleanup and checkpoint activity that opens additional files and semaphores, further stressing OS quotas. The mutual reinforcement among poor plan selection, space depletion, and kernel-level resource starvation drives the database into a compounded failure state that is more severe than any individual anomaly acting alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a static mismatch between the physical data model and workload access patterns (Schema and Index Design Anomaly), the optimizer is selecting sub-optimal execution plans despite reasonable statistics (Query Plan Selection Anomaly), and the lock manager is experiencing intense blocking or deadlocks among concurrent transactions (Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly). Together, these three root causes form a reinforcing performance pathology that degrades OLTP throughput and increases response-time variance.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Queries that should be index-seek driven instead perform full scans, hold locks on large page or table ranges, and run much longer than expected. • The same statement text may alternate between inefficient scan-heavy plans and marginally better plans, creating unpredictable spikes in CPU, I/O, and lock-wait time. • Transaction throughput drops sharply; connection pools back up while lock-wait queues and deadlock reports grow. • Lock escalation from row to page/table level becomes frequent because long-running, scan-oriented plans read large portions of hot tables lacking proper indexing or partitioning. • Performance improves dramatically only when missing or better-aligned indexes are added AND plan stability mechanisms are introduced, confirming the multi-layer nature of the issue.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Poor schema and index design expands the data footprint each statement must touch; the optimizer, already prone to misestimation or plan-reuse mistakes, often chooses or reuses plans that amplify the footprint even further (e.g., full table scans instead of selective seeks). These bloated plans acquire and hold many more locks for longer durations. The inflated lock scope raises the probability of conflicting requests from other concurrent transactions, triggering blocking chains, lock escalation, and deadlocks. Conversely, the elevated lock contention lengthens query runtimes, causing feedback loops in which the optimizer’s adaptive mechanisms capture skewed runtime statistics and cement the bad plans. The combined effect is a vicious cycle where design shortcomings and plan mis-selection magnify lock contention, and the resulting waits further degrade optimizer choices and throughput.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) and workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Excessive competition for buffer pages, latches, and page-level locks causes waits, CPU spin, and stalled I/O beneath the lock manager.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas approaches exhaustion, producing allocation failures, forced checkpoints, or background cleanup stalls.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the system exhibits a layered pathology: poorly designed tables and non-optimal indexes push queries toward full scans and large, non-covering lookups that flood the buffer cache with extra pages. The resulting hot pages and elevated dirty-page generation amplify latch and buffer-busy waits, while the inflated I/O footprint rapidly consumes remaining disk and temp space. Near-full datafiles and log destinations trigger auto-extend attempts, emergency checkpoints, or log switches that further increase latch contention and stall sessions. Administrators observe a mix of symptoms—massive logical I/O, soaring page-latch waits, checkpoint and log-archive pauses, sudden "out of space" errors, and erratic latency spikes—making it difficult to attribute performance degradation to a single tier.

Causally, an inadequate schema and index design forces the engine to touch far more pages than necessary. This surge in page demand churns a limited buffer pool, driving up latch contention and increasing the volume of dirty pages that must be flushed. Persistent flush activity collides with shrinking free space; once space nears exhaustion, background writers and checkpoint processes throttle foreground workloads while contending for the same latches already stressed by hot pages. Conversely, space pressure can disable optimal index creation or trigger auto-growth stalls, feeding back into the design inefficiency. The intertwined effects create a feedback loop where design inefficiency inflates page traffic, page traffic magnifies latch contention, and both accelerate space consumption, ultimately degrading throughput and threatening availability.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency limits of the underlying volumes are reached, throttling every engine component that issues I/O.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space on data, log, temp, or backup volumes is exhausted or approaches hard limits, leading to allocation failures and stalled write activity.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host compute cores are saturated by database processes, driving run-queue contention and global latency increases.

When all three conditions appear simultaneously, the database experiences a multi-dimensional resource collapse. End-users see sharp and widespread response-time spikes, batch jobs overrun their windows, checkpoints, log flushes, and sort/hash work accumulate in ever-lengthening wait queues, and critical statements fail with both "out of space" and "too busy"-style errors. I/O statistics show disks pegged at maximum service time while queue depths lengthen; meanwhile CPU load averages hover at or above core count, yet the additional work done per second diminishes because threads are blocked on both I/O latency and space-allocation retries. Monitoring surfaces a cacophony of device-level I/O waits, space-allocation errors, and scheduler waits, making it difficult to isolate any single bottleneck.

Causal interaction: Space exhaustion forces aggressive auto-extension, log switching, and frequent allocation checks; these operations themselves generate extra synchronous writes and metadata updates, inflating I/O demand on volumes that are already throughput-bound. The longer latency holds back foreground tasks, the more connected sessions remain active, amplifying CPU consumption through context switches and spin waits. Conversely, CPU saturation slows the purge, compression, and cleanup jobs that would reclaim space, accelerating capacity depletion. As operations struggle to complete, they re-issue reads, writes, and retries, further driving both I/O bandwidth and CPU cycles while the shrinking free space leaves less room for write coalescing or spill-to-temp optimizations. The feedback loop among limited throughput, vanishing space, and maxed-out CPU intensifies until the system reaches a stall or fails with multiple simultaneous resource errors.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The database’s local write-ahead logging path is saturated or stalled, so commit processing, log buffering, flushing, or archiving becomes the performance bottleneck.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas or change-data consumers fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply log records at the pace the primary generates them, creating widening log-position gaps and retention of old log segments.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: One or more storage areas—data files, log volumes, archive destinations, temp, or backup locations—approach or reach full utilization, resulting in allocation failures and preventing normal growth or recycling.

Combined phenomena: With all three conditions active, the database exhibits escalating commit latency, prolonged log-flush and log-sync waits, and frequent pauses or timeouts for foreground transactions. Replication lag grows rapidly; replicas report increasing receive and replay delay, and failover readiness degrades. Log and archive directories expand uncontrollably until the underlying volume exhausts free space, after which both primary commits and replica apply threads may halt with "out of space" or "cannot allocate log segment" errors. Checkpoints and archive/relay-log purges trigger more often but complete slowly, leading to checkpoint storms, lock contention, and excessive CPU usage in background processes. Monitoring dashboards show simultaneous spikes in log-related waits, replication delay, and disk-space alerts, making it difficult to attribute the primary symptom to a single layer.

Causal chain and reinforcement: Saturated transaction-log I/O slows commit throughput, which lengthens the queue of unsent log records to replicas. The growing replication backlog forces the primary to retain older log segments, blocking log recycling. This retention, combined with high redo generation, rapidly consumes remaining disk capacity on both primary and replica log or archive volumes, triggering the storage space anomaly. Once space becomes scarce, log switches or archive writes may hang, further increasing commit latency and deepening replication lag. Conversely, if storage fills first, log archiving and replica relay writing stall, which feeds back into the log subsystem by preventing segment reuse and inflating the in-memory log buffer. The intertwined feedback loops among log I/O saturation, replication backlog, and space exhaustion create a self-amplifying failure that can culminate in a total halt of transactional processing and replication.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements or transaction patterns that request or manipulate more data, rows, or time than business logic actually requires, leading to excessive scans, joins, and long-running transactions.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages or index structures that breaks key ordering, page links, or heap-to-index mappings, making persisted structures unreliable.

When these two root causes coexist, the database simultaneously executes wasteful or poorly scoped SQL while relying on corrupted storage structures. The workload’s already inflated scans, Cartesian joins, or repeated single-row probes collide with missing or duplicated rows, checksum failures, and sudden plan shifts to full table scans. Symptoms include extreme and widely scattered statement latencies, frequent plan changes, dramatic variance between repeated executions, explosions in lock contention as long-running transactions touch damaged pages, surge in application timeouts and retries, and integrity-check or page-verification errors interleaved with slow-query log entries. Result sets may appear inconsistent across executions, and retries undertaken by the application can further stress corrupted pages, provoking additional engine error logs or crash recovery cycles.

Causally, heavy and inefficient SQL patterns magnify the surface area and frequency of page and index access, increasing the probability of reading or writing corrupt structures. Conversely, corruption can invalidate indexes, forcing the optimizer to discard efficient plans, which in turn drives the engine toward broader scans and larger data movement—effects that mimic or exacerbate the original workload-logic inefficiencies. The combination forms a feedback loop: bloated queries amplify I/O against damaged objects, while structural corruption forces ever less efficient execution paths, collectively accelerating performance collapse, lock amplification, and potential availability incidents.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses a highly inefficient execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to excessive I/O, CPU, or memory demand per statement.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions fight for hot buffer-cache pages and the latches that protect them, producing long page-latch waits and spin CPU with limited throughput gain.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client/server communication paths or connection slots are saturated, causing connection delays, socket-level back-pressure, and session wait events on client reads or writes.

When all three root causes strike together, the workload experiences a multilayer slowdown: (1) bad plans drive up logical and physical I/O, inflating demand on the buffer pool; (2) the resulting surge in page pins and dirty-page churn amplifies latch contention and buffer busy waits; (3) the elongated execution and commit times hold server processes and network sockets open longer, swelling session counts and outbound data queues. Symptoms may include erratic plan flips accompanied by sudden spikes in page-latch and buffer-busy waits, CPU saturation from spin loops, growing numbers of connections in authentication or established-idle states, and cascading client time-outs. Performance views may show high variance in execution plans, hot-page contention centred on index roots or sequencing tables, and network retransmissions or listener backlog exhaustion, making it hard to attribute latency to a single tier.

Causally, a poor plan that scans large data ranges floods the buffer pool, evicting useful pages and forcing frequent page replacement. This heightens latch pressure as many sessions attempt to pin or dirty the same root and leaf pages. The prolonged critical-section holds extend statement duration, so each session monopolizes its backend thread and TCP socket for longer, pushing the connection pool and listener toward saturation. Conversely, network slowdowns or connection-establishment delays can elongate transaction lifetimes, aggravating buffer residency pressure and increasing the window during which latch contention manifests. The intertwined feedback loop means that relieving only one layer often yields limited benefit; comprehensive remediation must address plan stability, buffer/latch hot spots, and network or connection scaling parameters in concert.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count and data-distribution metadata no longer reflect reality, forcing the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and to pick sub-optimal, often I/O- or CPU-heavy, execution plans.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical read/write demand exceeds the bandwidth, IOPS, or latency capacity of the underlying storage stack, causing prolonged I/O waits and throttling the database engine.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Aggregate database processing saturates available CPU cycles, driving run-queue growth and widespread latency once cores are fully utilized.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the workload exhibits mixed and mutually amplifying symptoms: execution plans with severe row-count misestimates choose overly large scans or sub-optimal join methods that inflate both buffer gets and physical I/O. The inflated I/O queue collides with an already congested storage layer, producing escalating read/write latencies, stalled checkpoints, and log-flush back-pressure. As the engine waits for I/O, ready tasks accumulate; when I/O finally completes, cascades of workers awaken and contend aggressively for already scarce CPU, spiking context switches, run-queue length, and further elongating response times. Performance dashboards oscillate between I/O wait and CPU saturation states, masking the true multi-layer nature of the bottleneck and complicating diagnosis.

Causally, stale or incomplete statistics steer the optimizer toward plans that generate needless data volume—large full-table or partition scans, Cartesian joins, or excessive parallelism—which dramatically raise both logical and physical I/O. The bloated I/O demand quickly exhausts storage throughput ceilings, lengthening I/O wait times and causing query threads to sleep. Once I/O eventually returns, accumulated workers resume simultaneously, driving sudden CPU spikes that oversubscribe cores and trigger scheduler delays. The ensuing CPU contention slows the database’s background tasks (autostats refresh, checkpoint writing) and prolongs I/O operation submission, feeding back into the storage bottleneck. This feedback loop means each anomaly worsens the others: bad statistics create wasteful work, storage saturation stretches that work out, and CPU starvation prevents the optimizer and maintenance processes from correcting statistics or rebalancing load, thereby locking the system into a spiraling degradation state.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer keeps selecting or re-using an execution plan whose estimated cost is low but whose actual runtime is high, despite reasonably accurate statistics.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages and their protecting latches, causing excessive buffer-busy and page-latch waits rather than outright memory shortage.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings such as file-descriptor, shared-memory, semaphore, or thread limits, restricting the engine’s ability to allocate or grow critical resources.

When these three root causes manifest together, symptoms appear in multiple layers: 1) unstable plans suddenly flip from index to full table scans or from parallel to serial execution; 2) the sub-optimal plan amplifies touch rates on a few index or table pages, so latch and buffer-busy waits surge and CPU spins without throughput gain; 3) as the engine tries to spawn extra workers, open more files, or enlarge shared memory to compensate, it is blocked by OS limits, resulting in errors for new sessions, failures to start parallel workers, and bursts of "cannot allocate resource" messages in system logs. Overall latency oscillates unpredictably, with apparent optimizer issues, internal latch storms, and sporadic OS-level allocation failures all visible yet hard to disentangle.

Causally, a poor plan (e.g., full scan or nested-loop with high outer cardinality) dramatically increases buffer-cache pressure and concentrates access on a narrow set of pages. This fuels latch contention, prolonging critical-section hold times and driving up request queues. The prolonged waits expand task runtimes, which in turn prolongs plan age and keeps the hot pages in constant circulation, reinforcing contention. As the engine reacts—attempting more parallelism, larger I/O queues, or additional background flushers—it consumes extra file handles, threads, and shared-memory segments, quickly exhausting kernel quotas. Once OS ceilings are hit, the database cannot spawn the very workers or I/O contexts that could alleviate contention, so both plan inefficiency and buffer hot-spotting persist, creating a vicious loop that degrades overall throughput and stability.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The log-writer path (log buffer, log files, archive/replication pipeline) becomes the bottleneck, inflating commit and log-flush latency.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer saturates its IOPS/MB-per-s capacity, driving up read-write latencies and queue depths for all database files.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, asynchronous-I/O contexts, shared memory, or process threads are reached, preventing the database from issuing or completing additional I/O or spawning helper tasks.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database experiences compound symptoms: commit operations stall behind saturated log devices whose writes themselves wait in deep OS-level I/O queues; data and log read/write latencies climb simultaneously, obscuring whether slowness originates in the engine or the device; background tasks such as checkpoint, archiver, and replication sender processes intermittently fail to open new log segments or allocate AIO contexts, producing error bursts in both database and system logs; queue build-up in the log subsystem triggers frequent checkpoints and aggressive log switches, which further inflate I/O pressure on an already bandwidth-starved storage array; overall throughput collapses while CPU remains under-utilised and sessions time out.

Causally, log-heavy OLTP traffic generates sustained redo that must be flushed. The undersized or co-located log files hit the physical throughput ceiling of the shared storage, lengthening sync times. As waits accumulate, the database spawns more helper processes and AIO requests, quickly consuming kernel file-handle and AIO limits. Once those limits are breached, new I/O submissions are throttled or fail, forcing the engine to fall back to synchronous, single-threaded or buffered I/O, which further degrades throughput and amplifies storage congestion. The persistent storage backlog, in turn, keeps log segments open longer, blocks checkpoints, and inflates recovery-related disk activity, creating a feedback loop that deepens the performance crisis and can escalate into a full write stall or service outage.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpointing, etc.) are mis-aligned with hardware and workload characteristics.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Total memory consumed by caches, work areas, and background structures grows beyond safe host capacity.

When all three conditions are present simultaneously, the system exhibits a blend of erratic plan changes, parameter-driven resource imbalance, and escalating memory pressure. Symptoms may include: plans oscillating between parallel full scans and single-threaded index access as the cost model reacts to shifting memory availability; sudden bursts of hash or sort memory that push the instance into paging, followed by emergency re-planning; CPU cores alternately over- and under-utilized because mis-set parallelism caps clash with the optimizer’s plan choices; checkpoint or log-flush storms triggered when inflated buffer pools contend with swap activity; and highly variable response times where the same statement alternates between milliseconds and minutes.

Causal chain: mis-tuned configuration parameters (e.g., oversized work memory, aggressive parallel-worker limits, or an over-grown buffer pool) permit individual queries to claim far more memory than the host can supply. The optimizer, unaware of real-time OS pressure, may favor memory-intensive hash joins or large parallel plans—amplifying consumption initiated by the configuration mistake. As memory saturates, the operating system begins paging, which slows I/O, disrupts feedback loops, and triggers re-optimizations that may select even less efficient plans. The resulting vicious cycle—bad parameters enabling greedy plans, greedy plans exhausting memory, and memory pressure provoking further unstable plan selection—magnifies latency, throughput variability, and the risk of OOM termination.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, leading to inefficient access paths, poor parallelism choices, or pathological join orders.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating table and index size and lengthening visibility checks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions compete for hot buffer pages and their latches, causing wait events, spinning, and throughput collapse.

When all three faults coexist, the workload exhibits cascading performance degradation: execution plans flip between selective index probes and full scans over bloated base tables; scans and joins touch far more pages because of MVCC bloat, which in turn overpopulates the buffer cache and keeps hot root and visibility-map pages under heavy latch pressure. Operators that the optimizer mistakenly favored (e.g., nested loops on underestimated row counts) encounter massive I/O and latch waits, producing sharp latency spikes, CPU spin, and stall chains that are hard to attribute to any single layer. Autovacuum or cleanup workers may run continuously yet fail to catch up, while query plans churn in the cache as statistics drift due to the bloated heap, further destabilizing performance.

The causal loop is self-reinforcing: sub-optimal plans increase I/O volume and prolong statement execution, which delays transaction completion and lengthens the lifespan of old snapshots, thereby slowing MVCC cleanup and enlarging the version store. The growing heap and index bloat enlarge the working-set footprint, forcing more pages through a limited buffer pool and creating hot-page hotspots where many sessions contend for latches. Elevated latch waits extend query runtimes, giving the optimizer more chances to mis-select plans based on stale or skewed runtime feedback, and stretching transactions even further. This spiraling interaction among poor plan choice, MVCC bloat, and buffer contention can push an OLTP system into a persistent low-throughput, high-latency state until all three issues are addressed in concert.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical runtime parameters (memory, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, parallelism, connection limits, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload profile, or version defaults.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, logs, archives, temp areas, or backups is exhausted or approaching hard limits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network bandwidth, latency, socket/connection slots, or listener resources are insufficient to handle the connection rate and data flow between clients and the database.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: 1) Sudden or cascading "out of space" errors, aborted checkpoints, and stalled DML as log or data files cannot extend; 2) Spike in application timeouts, refused or half-open connections, and client-read/write waits even though in-engine CPU and I/O counters appear low; 3) Dramatic skew in wait-event distribution—sessions pile up on log-write, client-read, buffer-pin, and space-allocation waits concurrently; 4) Long-running transactions and idle-in-transaction sessions accumulate, consuming per-session memory far beyond what the mis-configured work-mem and connection limits can sustain; 5) Background workers (vacuum, cleanup, archiver) fall behind because checkpoints thrash and network copies of archives or backups cannot complete, further accelerating space depletion and widening performance variance.

Causal interaction: Mis-sized parameters (e.g., too small log files, overly aggressive checkpoint targets, oversized per-session work memory, or an inflated max-connections setting) generate excess redo, temp data, and long-lived backends, driving faster space consumption. As free space dwindles, checkpoints and archive processes run more frequently and for longer, inflating I/O bursts and producing additional log segments that must be shipped or copied. Simultaneously, a saturated or flaky network slows archive shipping, backup streaming, and client traffic, preventing timely space reclamation and causing connection retries that further overload listener and backend slots already mis-tuned. Each layer feeds the next: bad parameters accelerate space growth, space exhaustion prolongs I/O stalls that keep transactions and sockets open, and network bottlenecks block the very maintenance operations meant to relieve space and memory pressure—creating a reinforcing loop that can culminate in complete service outage or forced instance shutdown.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, or data types are not aligned with workload access patterns, forcing the optimizer into unnecessarily wide scans and non-covering lookups regardless of statistics or parameter settings.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical disks or storage subsystem are unable to sustain the read/write throughput, IOPS, or latency demanded by the database, producing long device queues and I/O waits even when the database engine is correctly configured.

When both root causes strike together, the workload generates an excessive volume of physical I/O because of missing or sub-optimal indexes, large table scans, and extra row fetches, while the underlying storage cannot absorb this load. Symptoms include: execution plans that fall back to full scans or repeated bookmark lookups, buffer cache churn, and spill-to-temp operations; concurrent surges in data-file, temp-space, and log-flush waits; device queue depths pinned high with service times that grow non-linearly; CPU utilization oscillating between idle (waiting on I/O) and spikes during short bursts of work; dramatic, workload-wide latency variability where individual statements appear to "hang" and batch or ETL windows overrun.

Causally, inadequate schema and index design magnifies the volume of physical reads and writes, quickly pushing the storage subsystem past its sustainable bandwidth. Once disks are saturated, I/O latency lengthens, which in turn makes the inefficient access paths even more expensive, causing the optimizer to favor still broader scans or additional spilling, thereby further compounding the load. The intertwined feedback loop means that neither redesigning storage tiers nor merely adding indexes alone will fully resolve performance issues; both the data model and the storage capacity must be addressed together to restore stable and predictable performance.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Runtime parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload characteristics, or version defaults, causing sub-optimal use of memory, log, checkpoint, worker, or parallelism resources.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or downstream nodes cannot receive, persist, or apply primary log records fast enough, leading to widening log-position gaps, retention of old log segments, and increasing fail-over risk.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage layer is saturated on throughput, IOPS, or latency budget, elevating read/write service times for data, temp, and log files.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a multi-layer performance collapse: replication lag grows explosively while primary-side log segments pile up because mis-sized checkpoint and log parameters generate larger bursts of I/O that the saturated storage cannot absorb, and replicas cannot catch up. Primary sessions see erratic response times dominated by log-write, buffer-flush, and replication-slot waits; replicas show both apply-worker CPU stalls and severe I/O waits. Monitoring dashboards may misleadingly report normal CPU headroom yet display runaway disk-space consumption on the primary, high network utilization without corresponding replay progress on standbys, oscillating checkpoint duration, and sudden spikes of background cleanup debt.

Causal chain: mis-tuned configuration (e.g., oversized shared buffers, undersized WAL segments, aggressive checkpoint timeout, or insufficient parallel replay workers) amplifies the volume and burstiness of redo generation. This inflates the write pressure on an already throughput-bound storage subsystem, elongating local commit latency. The same storage bottleneck throttles replica apply speed, while the configuration’s limited replication worker parallelism and fragmented checkpoints further slow downstream consumption. The resulting backlog prevents WAL recycling, which pushes even more I/O to the stressed disks and forces emergency checkpoints, creating a feedback loop that aggravates both storage saturation and replication delay, ultimately threatening availability and performance for both OLTP and analytical queries.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical data model and indexing strategy are misaligned with workload access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written statements into inherently inefficient access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale or inaccurate, misleading the optimizer into systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan selection.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.

Combined anomalous phenomena: When a poor physical design lacks selective or covering indexes and statistics no longer represent actual data, the optimizer may choose wide table or index scans, nested-loop joins on vastly underestimated row sets, or plans that touch far more rows than expected. These long-running, I/O-heavy statements acquire large lock footprints, hold them for extended periods, and may escalate from row to page or table level. As concurrency rises, wait queues, deadlock reports, victim rollbacks, application timeouts, and sudden throughput collapses all appear, often immediately after data-skewing events or bulk loads. Performance tuning signals become noisy: execution plans show both gross misestimates and missing indexes, while lock-monitoring views simultaneously display growing blocker/waitee chains.

Causal chain: Faulty schema design starts the problem by depriving critical queries of efficient access paths, inflating the number of rows and pages they must touch. Stale statistics compound the issue by hiding the true cost of these scans, so the optimizer avoids any remaining selective indexes or chooses join orders that maximize locking scope. The resulting queries run longer and lock more rows, creating hotspots that multiple sessions hit concurrently, triggering blocking and deadlocks. Prolonged blocking, in turn, delays commit points and automatic statistics maintenance, which makes statistics even staler and further obscures the need for new indexes—forming a vicious feedback loop that degrades both read and write performance across the OLTP workload.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The optimizer relies on stale, incomplete, or missing statistics, systematically misestimating cardinalities and choosing inefficient execution plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or downstream replicas fall behind the primary because they cannot receive, write, or apply WAL/redo at the pace it is generated.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The database engine or its background workers hit kernel-enforced ceilings such as file-descriptor, shared-memory, semaphore, or thread limits, causing allocation failures and process throttling.

When all three anomalies co-exist, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: queries on the primary choose bloated plans that spill to disk, saturate I/O, and generate unusually large redo streams; replicas show rapidly widening log-position gaps, growing retained WAL segments, and stale read data. Meanwhile, the mounting number of open log files, temporary spill files, parallel-worker threads, and lingering replication processes exhaust kernel limits on file handles, shared memory, or process counts. Operators observe a mixture of plan-estimate skew warnings, replication lag alarms, and intermittent "too many open files", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "failed to fork worker" errors. Automatic statistics jobs and replication apply workers may crash or refuse to start, making it difficult to distinguish whether performance problems stem from the optimizer, replication, or the host OS.

Causally, stale or missing statistics cause the optimizer to favor plan shapes that read or sort far more data than necessary, driving up CPU, memory, and especially write-ahead logging volume. The inflated WAL stream overwhelms network, I/O, and CPU capacity on replicas, triggering replication synchronization delays. As lag accumulates, the primary is forced to retain ever-growing sets of log segments and file descriptors. The surge in simultaneously open WAL, temp files, and worker processes pushes the database up against operating-system limits; once those limits are reached, new background workers (including auto-analyze and replication apply processes) fail to start, preventing statistics refreshes and further slowing replay on replicas. This feedback loop amplifies all three root causes, leading to severe performance degradation, disk exhaustion risk, impaired failover readiness, and partial service outages.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine runtime settings (memory, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, creating artificial pressure or idle gaps that do not reflect real resource limits.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions block or spin while fighting for access to hot buffer-cache pages, page pins, or latches, causing serialization inside the buffer manager rather than at the row-lock layer.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical devices or virtual storage layers hit their bandwidth / IOPS ceiling, stretching read- and write-latencies and driving up I/O wait times.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits a confused mix of symptoms:  • Bursts of buffer-busy, page-latch, log-write, and file-I/O waits appear side-by-side.  • Checkpoint or background-writer storms trigger prolonged dirty-page flushing that holds buffer latches, freezes modifying sessions, and inflates read/write latency at the device.  • CPU alternates between under-utilization (blocked on I/O) and futile spin-loops (contending for latches), while overall throughput collapses and response-time variance widens.  • Wait-event histograms show both high in-engine spin / latch time and deep storage queue depths, yet OS-level memory and CPU headroom remain.

Causal chain: Misaligned configuration parameters—such as too small a buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint intervals, or an undersized async I/O batch size—force pages to be evicted and flushed more often than necessary. The heightened flush frequency drives up physical I/O, quickly exhausting the storage subsystem’s throughput budget and inflating device latency. Slower I/O prolongs dirty-page residency and latch hold times, intensifying buffer and latch contention. In turn, the elevated contention magnifies the sensitivity to the original configuration errors, prompting more retries, spin-loops, and timeout-driven flushes. The feedback loop between bad configuration, I/O saturation, and internal latch contention compounds stalls across all sessions, degrading both transactional and analytical workloads simultaneously.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries pile up faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, bloating the heap and indexes.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Stand-by or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot ingest or replay the primary’s WAL stream at the rate it is produced.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database-related processes saturate host CPU, starving both foreground queries and essential background workers of compute cycles.

When all three root causes strike together, the system shows a compound symptom set: sustained near-100 % CPU, long run queues, and pervasive latency spikes; rapidly growing table and index sizes with falling live-row density; sequential scans and UPDATE/DELETEs slowing as visibility checks touch ever-larger version chains; replication views displaying widening receive, flush, and replay lags together with a swelling stock of retained WAL segments; VACUUM or equivalent cleanup workers reported as backlogged while still consuming high CPU; replica read traffic returning increasingly stale data; and disk usage rising on both primary (due to unrecycled WAL) and replicas (due to redo backlog).

Causal chain: excessive update/delete churn or long-running snapshots start the version buildup. The bloated pages force foreground scans and background VACUUM to do more work per row, driving CPU demand upward. CPU saturation slows both cleanup workers and the single-threaded or poorly parallelized replication apply processes, letting more dead versions and unreplayed WAL accumulate. In turn, replication lag prevents the primary from advancing its "oldest xmin" horizon, blocking further removal of dead tuples and accelerating heap bloat. The feedback loop—MVCC bloat → higher CPU → slower replication → frozen xmin → even more MVCC bloat—can quickly spiral, degrading throughput, enlarging storage footprints, and eroding failover safety.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonably accurate statistics, often because of flawed cost estimation, unstable plan reuse, or version/option changes.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings for memory, parallelism, logging, and background tasks are mis-tuned, so runtime behavior no longer matches hardware capacity or workload needs.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, leading to unreliable access paths and incorrect row visibility.

When all three problems coexist, the database exhibits a volatile and hard-to-triage performance and correctness pattern: identical queries oscillate among radically different plans; some executions fall back to full table scans because damaged indexes fail validation, while others keep inefficient index-based nested loops due to sticky bad plans in the cache. Mis-sized memory or parallelism parameters aggravate the situation—small work or buffer pools force excessive I/O for the accidental full scans, whereas over-allocated settings trigger OOM kills or throttling waits without the CPUs or disks actually being saturated. Concurrently, corruption-induced checksum errors, page-verification failures, or silent row omissions surface intermittently, sometimes only after a checkpoint or log flush storm initiated by the same misconfiguration. The mixed symptom set—plan churn, unexplained wait spikes, sporadic error logs, and mismatched result counts—creates a noisy diagnostic picture in which any single anomaly can masquerade as the primary culprit.

Causally, mis-tuned configuration parameters distort both the optimizer’s cost model (e.g., reduced effective cache size, altered parallelism thresholds) and the runtime resource envelopes, increasing the likelihood that it picks or reuses fragile plans. Those fragile plans amplify the impact of latent page or index corruption by exercising edge code paths (e.g., random I/O probes, backward scans) that hit bad pages earlier and more often. In parallel, overly aggressive checkpoint or log settings—another facet of the configuration anomaly—can precipitate or expose corruption by forcing rapid page recycling or recovering from frequent crashes. Once corruption invalidates indexes or forces the engine to disable them, the optimizer’s already misguided plan repertoire grows even worse, and the subsequent performance degradation feeds back into more emergency configuration tweaks, perpetuating the vicious cycle. Together, the three anomalies reinforce one another, leading to compounded performance regression, unpredictable query results, and elevated risk of data-loss events.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Exhaustion of physical or logical storage space allocated to data files, logs, temp areas, or backups, resulting in allocation-failed or no-space errors.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced limits such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or process/thread quotas, preventing the database from obtaining necessary OS resources.

When both conditions arise simultaneously, the database may encounter a compound failure mode: writes, log switches, temporary-object growth, or backup operations stop because storage is full, while at the same time new sessions, background workers, or file opens fail due to OS-level limits. Observable symptoms include a rapid succession of "no space left on device" and "too many open files" errors, stalled checkpoints that cannot flush dirty pages, archiver or logger processes that crash or hang, backup jobs that start but abort immediately, and connection storms where existing sessions hang in I/O wait while new logins are refused. Monitoring dashboards may show normal CPU usage yet a steep rise in transaction latency and an abrupt drop in throughput, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, the two root causes can reinforce each other: log or temp spills caused by space pressure force the engine to open additional files, exhausting file-handle limits; conversely, reaching the file-handle or shared-memory ceiling can block housekeeping tasks (log rotation, purge, auto-extend) that would otherwise release or allocate new space, accelerating disk exhaustion. Attempts to auto-extend datafiles fail first on OS limits (unable to create or open the next file) and then on physical space scarcity, leading to cascading transaction aborts. The interaction traps the system in a feedback loop where neither space nor OS resources can be reclaimed, pushing the database into partial or complete outage until both constraints are relieved.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive growth of engine buffer caches, work areas, and ancillary heaps drives the database process beyond the safe physical-memory or swap envelope of the host.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for objects such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, independent of database-level quotas.

When both conditions surface concurrently, the system exhibits a blended failure pattern: resident-set size balloons until the kernel begins paging, while at the same time new threads, shared-memory extents, or file handles cannot be granted. Administrators observe escalating swap usage, cache-hit degradation, and memory-pressure-induced CPU stalls alongside erratic "cannot allocate memory / resource temporarily unavailable" errors, inability to spawn parallel workers, and partial service where existing sessions limp on but new logins, sorts, or I/O requests fail. Restart storms may occur because an out-of-memory killer terminates the process just as unreleased kernel objects accumulate, causing the next startup to inherit or exceed tight resource caps.

Causally, aggressive memory allocation magnifies the likelihood of breaching kernel limits: each session or parallel worker spawned to service the enlarged workload reserves its own stack, file handles, and asynchronous I/O contexts, accelerating exhaustion of per-process quotas.
