In turn, once the kernel refuses additional handles or threads, the database engine cannot offload or flush memory through background tasks, so buffers remain pinned and continue to grow, intensifying host memory pressure. This feedback loop turns two individually manageable issues into a compound outage where memory bloat feeds kernel-resource starvation and vice versa, rapidly degrading overall database stability.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: Simultaneous occurrence of transaction-level lock conflicts, low-level buffer or latch serialization, and saturation of network/connection resources. The database engine is therefore impeded at three tiers—lock manager, buffer manager, and client connectivity—causing stacked waits that severely limit progress of OLTP requests.

Observable Manifestation: Users see sharp and erratic increases in response time, timeouts during statement execution as well as during connection establishment, frequent deadlock or lock-wait victim errors, surging page-latch/buffer-busy waits, CPU spin without throughput gains, and a growing backlog of client sessions blocked in socket read/write or authentication phases. Internal monitoring shows long blocker-waiter chains, elevated lock-wait and deadlock detector activity, hot data pages with prolonged latch hold times, saturated buffer flush or I/O slots, and operating-system socket queues filling up. Overall, transaction throughput collapses while resource utilization oscillates between CPU spin (latch contention), I/O stalls (buffer churn), and idle waits on network operations.

Causal Interaction: Network congestion or connection-pool exhaustion makes each client round-trip slower, holding transactions open longer and extending the lifetime of their locks and page pins. These extended lifetimes intensify lock contention; blocked transactions in turn keep buffer pages and their latches occupied, amplifying buffer-level serialization. Meanwhile, latch contention and slow page access prolong critical sections inside the engine, further delaying lock releases and enlarging blocking chains. The resulting backlog of inactive yet connected sessions overwhelms listener sockets and authentication workers, feeding back into the network/connectivity bottleneck. Together, the three layers reinforce each other in a positive feedback loop that degrades concurrency, inflates wait times across all tiers, and risks systemic throughput collapse.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) a physical data-model and indexing layout that forces excessive or non-selective data access and heavy index maintenance, (2) a transaction-log subsystem that cannot absorb or flush the resulting surge of redo records, and (3) storage that is approaching or has reached its free-space limits. Together, these three root causes create a feedback loop in which inefficient data access multiplies write volume, overwhelms log handling, and rapidly exhausts available space, crippling both query execution and commit processing.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Queries that should be index-efficient devolve into full scans, row-by-row lookups, or repeated non-covering index probes, causing inflated I/O and redo generation. • Concurrent DML shows rising commit and checkpoint latency, with spikes in LOG_WRITE / LOG_FLUSH waits, frequent log switches, and archiver backlogs. • Free space in data, temp, and especially log or archive destinations plummets; auto-extend and allocation failures, "out of space" errors, and emergency space reclamation events appear. • Application sessions observe a mixture of slow query response, stalled commits, temporary-space errors, and, in extreme cases, database‐wide hang as log segments cannot be created or recycled. The overlapping symptom set can obscure diagnosis because performance waits (from design flaws) and hard space errors (from storage pressure) manifest simultaneously with log-related stalls.

Causal interaction: Suboptimal schema and missing/oversized indexes inflate the amount and size of data modified per transaction and multiply index maintenance work. This drives up redo generation and forces the transaction-log subsystem to flush larger volumes more frequently. As the log subsystem approaches its throughput ceiling, commits queue and log switches accelerate, generating even more archived segments. The elevated churn, combined with space-wasting indexes and fragmented tables, rapidly consumes disk capacity. Shrinking free space further slows both data and log I/O, while full archive or data destinations prevent log recycling, amplifying commit stalls. The inability to rebuild or drop problematic indexes due to space scarcity locks the system in a self-reinforcing degradation loop that severely impacts OLTP workload throughput and availability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Statistics on tables or partitions are stale, missing, or insufficiently granular, causing systematic cardinality misestimates.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer’s decision logic or plan‐reuse strategy chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even when statistical inputs could be acceptable.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpoint cadence, etc.) are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, distorting resource availability and costing assumptions.

Composite anomaly definition: The database concurrently suffers from inaccurate or out-of-date statistics, flawed plan selection logic, and mis-configured engine parameters, meaning the optimizer is making cost decisions on bad input data, with a cost model that is already choosing poorly, while running on a platform whose runtime knobs further mislead cost estimates and distort actual execution behavior.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Aggressive plan flip-flopping—each new execution may alternate between index seeks, full scans, and poorly parallelized plans as both statistical errors and parameter changes invalidate previous cost assumptions. 2) Massive gaps between estimated and actual rows accompanied by execution memory spills or early aborts because work-memory and parallelism settings are wrong for the chosen plan. 3) Wait-event profiles that oscillate between CPU spin, log-write stalls, and page I/O even though system-level metrics show spare capacity, making bottlenecks hard to diagnose. 4) After bulk loads or partition swaps, performance can degrade catastrophically and persist until statistics are refreshed, plan cache is cleared, and parameters are re-tuned—yet no single remedy fully restores performance.

Causal chain interaction: Stale or missing statistics skew cardinality estimates, which the optimizer combines with misaligned cost-model parameters (e.g., incorrect CPU vs. I/O weightings or parallelism caps) to choose an already fragile plan. Misconfigured memory and parallelism settings then amplify any estimation error: underestimated row counts cause hash tables to spill, while overestimates trigger unnecessary parallel workers that contend for an undersized buffer pool. The resulting resource pressure delays automatic statistics updates and forces more frequent plan invalidations, perpetuating the cycle. Thus, each root cause reinforces the others, producing a multi-layered performance regression that is far worse than the sum of its parts.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously impacted by on-disk data/index corruption, sustained saturation of the underlying storage throughput budget, and exhaustion of operating-system-level resource limits. Together these three root causes create a complex failure domain in which physical structures are unreliable, I/O paths are throttled, and the kernel refuses to grant additional critical resources to the database engine.

Combined anomalous phenomena: In addition to checksum failures, index–heap mismatches, and corruption errors, administrators observe erratic yet persistently high read/write latency with queue depths stuck near maximum while overall CPU remains modest. Integrity-verification utilities report escalating page or key-order errors, yet corrective operations such as CHECKDB, index rebuilds, or page re-writes stall or fail due to storage stalls and kernel denials to open new files, map buffers, or spawn worker threads. Session spikes or maintenance jobs may intermittently hang on I/O or emit “too many open files,” “cannot allocate shared memory,” or “AIO context limit reached” messages. Performance baselines collapse: queries unpredictably fall back to full table scans because damaged indexes are marked unusable, but the scans themselves are slowed by storage saturation; meanwhile background recovery or redo replays lag because log-write bandwidth is throttled and additional recovery workers cannot be forked.

Causal chain and interaction: Latent or newly introduced physical corruption forces the engine to reread pages, trigger verification logic, or rebuild indexes, multiplying I/O demand exactly when the storage subsystem is already bandwidth-constrained, worsening queue buildup and latency. The prolonged I/O wait extends the lifetime of sessions and background tasks, increasing consumption of file descriptors, AIO contexts, shared-memory segments, and worker threads until the operating system’s hard limits are reached. Once those limits are hit, the engine can no longer allocate the resources required for corruption-repair tasks or for normal workload processing, leading to cascading errors, partial outages, and an escalating backlog of dirty pages whose delayed flushing perpetuates both corruption exposure and storage congestion. The mutually reinforcing cycle of corrupted structures (requiring more I/O), saturated storage (slowing every operation), and kernel resource exhaustion (blocking new work and recovery actions) drives the system into severe instability that is difficult to diagnose if each symptom is viewed in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating table and index size and lengthening visibility checks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions fight for access to hot buffer-cache pages and their associated latches, causing spin-waiting, prolonged page pins, and I/O slot starvation.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database back-end or auxiliary processes exhaust kernel-enforced quotas on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or AIO contexts, leading to failed allocations and worker start-ups.

Combined phenomena: A system suffering all three anomalies simultaneously shows explosive growth of the version store and on-disk relation size, steadily rising buffer-busy/latch wait times, and sporadic but escalating OS-level "too many open files", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "failed to create thread" errors. Autovacuum, purge, or undo-cleanup workers run continuously yet make little progress, while their attempts to fork new workers or open additional segments are rejected by the kernel. Checkpoints slow down, dirty pages linger, and hot root or freelist pages become choke points, pushing CPU usage into spin loops. Application sessions pile up behind both MVCC visibility checks and latch waits; some fail to connect at all once OS limits are hit, producing partial outages and time-outs that are hard to attribute to a single subsystem.

Causal chain: Heavy OLTP update/delete churn inflates the MVCC version store, enlarging heaps and indexes so that more pages must reside in the buffer cache. The expanded working set and incessant background cleanup amplify buffer churn and concentrate access on hot meta-pages, triggering latch contention. As latch waits lengthen, session counts rise and the engine spawns additional cleanup, checkpoint, and I/O helper processes; the surge in file handles, shared memory, and threads pushes the host kernel over its configured limits. Once the kernel starts denying resources, cleanup workers terminate or fail to start, allowing even more version bloat, while existing sessions hold latches longer, further intensifying contention. Thus each anomaly feeds the next in a reinforcing loop that degrades throughput, inflates latency, and risks complete service saturation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) backlog in removing obsolete MVCC versions, (2) uncontrolled growth of in-process and shared memory allocations, and (3) replication receivers or apply workers that cannot keep pace with the primary’s WAL stream. The three issues coexist and interact, producing a compound failure mode that crosses the storage, memory, and replication subsystems.

Combined observable phenomena: Dead-tuple density, version-store or rollback-segment length, and table/index sizes all rise quickly while autovacuum or purge workers remain constantly busy yet ineffective. At the same time the database processes’ resident memory and swap usage climb, leading to OS-level memory pressure, cache-eviction churn, and occasional OOM kills. On both primary and replicas the WAL/redo backlog grows; replication lag and relay-log retention widen, preventing log recycling and inflating disk usage. Administrators may see query slowdowns from bloated scans, erratic execution plans due to stale statistics, elevated CPU usage from memory thrashing, and degraded failover readiness because replicas are minutes or hours behind.

Causal chain and reinforcement: Heavy OLTP update/delete churn creates excessive dead versions, inflating table size and producing larger WAL records. The enlarged working set must reside in buffer caches and plan/work areas, pushing total memory consumption beyond safe limits; memory pressure throttles autovacuum, purge, and replication apply workers, further delaying version cleanup and redo replay. Simultaneously, replication lag keeps old snapshots open on replicas (or via synchronous feedback slots), which in turn blocks HOT pruning and vacuum on the primary, locking more dead versions in place. The stranded WAL segments required for lagging replicas consume additional memory and disk, and their accumulation further stresses the memory allocator and I/O subsystem. This positive feedback loop makes each individual anomaly harder to remediate, accelerating systemic degradation until throughput collapses or the cluster experiences forced restarts.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : The application issues inefficient SQL or transaction patterns that force the engine to process and move more data than business logic actually requires.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot deliver the sustained read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency demanded by the engine.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other OS objects are exhausted by the database process.

When these three root causes coexist, the database shows a compound symptom set: statements already slow from poor SQL logic wait even longer on saturated storage queues; overall latency and variance spike, with slow-query logs filling rapidly and application timeouts multiplying. Simultaneously, the engine begins to emit file-open, async-I/O, or thread-creation errors as OS quotas are hit, causing new sessions, parallel workers, or log writer helpers to fail intermittently. Wait-event profiles oscillate between buffer-I/O, log-write stalls, and OS-level resource-acquisition waits, making diagnosis non-trivial. Long-running transactions hold locks and pins while they repeatedly retry failed I/O or background task creation, further inflating contention and cascading delays across otherwise independent workloads.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL logic amplifies data volume and row touches, inflating buffer misses and forcing heavier physical I/O. The excess I/O drives the storage subsystem past its throughput ceiling, lengthening every read/write and inflating device queue depth. Prolonged I/O completion times keep database worker threads busy for longer, increasing the concurrent demand for kernel objects—more open file descriptors, async-I/O contexts, and waiting threads—until OS-imposed limits are breached. Once those limits are hit, new I/O requests or worker threads fail or block, which in turn triggers additional retries and longer transactions inside the database engine, further increasing data volume and I/O pressure. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others, creating a feedback loop that degrades throughput, elevates tail latency, and risks partial or total service outage.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : contention for hot buffer-cache pages, latches, pins, and dirty-page slots stalls CPU threads and throttles page access.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : physical or logical corruption inside data or index pages makes on-disk structures unreliable and can force scan fall-backs or error aborts.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : shortages or instability in sockets, listener threads, or network bandwidth delay or terminate client/server communication.

When all three conditions coexist, the system presents a layered, self-reinforcing failure pattern. Clients observe sporadic connection timeouts, authentication delays, and mid-stream result stalls. Sessions that do connect frequently hang on buffer-busy or page-latch waits; when pages are finally read, checksum mismatches or broken index links trigger retries, error propagation, or crash-recovery cycles. These extra retries enlarge connection pools and keep server backends alive longer, further depleting socket and worker resources. Corruption-induced plan shifts from targeted index probes to full scans explode buffer-pool churn, pinning and dirtying more pages and sharply increasing latch spin as many sessions converge on the few remaining uncorrupted root or allocation pages. Meanwhile, network congestion prolongs result transmission, extending buffer-pin lifetimes and exacerbating contention hot spots.

Causally, page and index corruption can force workload patterns (full scans, repeated fetch attempts) that inflate buffer-cache pressure; the resulting latch contention lengthens query execution times, which in turn holds network connections open and propagates retry storms that exhaust listener backlogs and socket tables. Simultaneously, network slowdowns raise session counts and idle-in-transaction periods, compounding buffer residency and latch hold times. The vicious cycle among corrupted storage structures, in-memory contention, and connection saturation rapidly degrades throughput and makes isolation of any single fault difficult, driving the database into a multi-layered degradation spiral.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing metadata (row counts, histograms, correlations) is stale or incomplete, driving systematic cardinality errors and sub-optimal execution-plan choices.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for incompatible locks, causing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort workload threads.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating table size and adding visibility-check overhead.

When all three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a mixture of planning errors, long-running and frequently killed queries, swelling table and index footprints, and sharply rising response-time variance. Cardinality misestimates lead the optimizer to prefer plans that scan or update far more rows than necessary; these over-wide scans touch many pages, hold locks for longer intervals, and create large numbers of new or updated row versions. The inflated I/O and extended lock hold times intensify blocking, lengthen deadlock cycles, and cause more frequent victim rollbacks, which in turn spawn even more dead tuples and rollback records. Cleanup workers, already lagging behind, fall further behind due to persistent lock waits on hot pages, so version bloat and statistics staleness both worsen. Monitoring views show simultaneously exploding lock-wait seconds, growing version-store or autovacuum backlogs, and widening gaps between estimated and actual row counts in execution plans.

Causally, stale or missing statistics first misguide the optimizer into choosing lock-heavy or scan-heavy plans, expanding the lock footprint and prolonging transaction duration. The resulting lock contention not only slows foreground work but also blocks background statistics refreshes and version-cleanup tasks, allowing both statistics staleness and version bloat to reinforce themselves. Accumulated dead tuples distort future statistics, further degrading plan quality, while the swollen heap forces longer scans that keep locks active, fueling a feedback loop that degrades throughput and risks transaction-ID or version-store exhaustion.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, join, or retain far more data and hold locks longer than business logic requires.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes collectively drive the host’s CPU to sustained saturation, throttling execution and inflating latency across the workload.

When both root causes are present, inefficient SQL patterns rapidly consume CPU cycles, and the resulting CPU saturation further slows those same statements, lengthening their execution time and keeping transactions open even longer. Observable symptoms escalate in a feedback loop: 1) run-queue and load-average spikes, 2) widespread statement slowdowns and timeout/retry storms, 3) prolonged lock holding and blocking chains, 4) engine wait profiles dominated by CPU scheduler waits intertwined with full-scan or function-wrapped predicate executions, and 5) an expanding set of queries appearing in slow-query and high-CPU lists that grows as concurrency rises.

Causally, non-selective predicates, Cartesian joins, and oversized result sets inflate per-statement CPU demand; this pushes aggregate CPU utilization to the saturation point. In turn, cores starved for compute stretch each statement’s wall-time, which amplifies active session counts and keeps the problematic SQL in flight longer, further increasing CPU load—a vicious cycle. The overlapping anomalies mask each other: DBAs may blame hardware limits while the root inefficiency in SQL logic persists, and tuning individual execution plans may miss the systemic CPU ceiling already reached. The interaction can cascade into broader instability, making the database appear under-provisioned even if capacity would be sufficient with well-written workload logic.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive or apply WAL/redo fast enough to keep up with the primary, widening the log-position gap.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, causing allocation failures and stalls.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or similar objects are reached, preventing the database from creating or accessing required resources.

When all three conditions arise together, the database estate experiences a spiraling failure mode: replication lag grows, retained WAL or relay logs accumulate, and the resulting surge in on-disk log volume drives the underlying storage toward full. At the same time, exhausted OS limits prevent archiver, cleanup, or apply processes from opening additional files, allocating shared memory, or spawning workers, so neither the primary nor the replicas can reclaim space or accelerate catch-up. Symptoms include rapidly inflating disk usage on primaries and standbys, replica replay lag jumping while apply workers crash or refuse to start, repeated "no space" or "too many open files" errors in both database and system logs, stalled checkpoints, disabled autovacuum or compaction tasks, and an increasing number of read-only queries served stale data from far-behind replicas.

Causal chain and reinforcement: (1) Initial OS resource exhaustion (e.g., file-descriptor limits) throttles replication apply processes and archive writers; (2) slowed apply causes WAL retention on the primary, inflating log volume; (3) the sudden consumption of disk space triggers storage-capacity breaches that further block WAL archiving and temp-space operations; (4) with storage full, retry storms and additional worker spawns push the system even harder against the same OS limits, causing more process failures; (5) the feedback loop leaves both primary and replicas unable to advance, risking total outage or data-loss exposure if the primary crashes before replicas catch up.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, forming long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupt, making navigation paths unreliable and forcing the engine to surface corruption errors or fall back to expensive full scans.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server communication or listener capacity is saturated or unstable, lengthening connect, read, or write operations and exhausting backend connection slots.

When all three faults coexist, the database exhibits a blended failure pattern: transactions obtain locks and then linger because corrupted pages or forced full-table rescans slow I/O, while simultaneous network slowdowns stretch round-trip times and postpone lock release. Blocker–waiter chains grow rapidly, deadlock detector activity spikes, and corruption-induced retries or failed statements multiply the number of sessions competing for locks and connections. Clients observe erratic response times, intermittent corruption or deadlock errors, authentication or connection-timeout failures, and dramatic drops in throughput as both in-engine and network wait events dominate performance dashboards.

Causally, page or index corruption degrades access paths, inflating I/O latency and statement duration; these long-running statements hold locks longer, heightening the likelihood of contention and deadlocks. Prolonged lock waits keep transactions open, increasing the population of active connections just as network bottlenecks restrict new session establishment and slow result streaming. Network stalls further delay commits and rollbacks, extending lock lifetimes and compounding contention. The ensuing retries and connection churn feed back into the network layer, while repeated scans of corrupt structures exacerbate I/O and CPU load, creating a self-reinforcing loop that destabilizes both concurrency control and connectivity handling, potentially cascading into widespread application timeouts and availability loss.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback data because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update-/delete-churn, inflating storage footprints and visibility-check cost.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Unbounded growth of buffer, work, and auxiliary memory areas that pushes the host into heavy paging, OOM kills, or node eviction.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures become internally inconsistent, causing logical/physical corruption and unreliable access paths.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode: version bloat swells table and index sizes, driving up buffer-cache demand and temporary-work memory; the overstressed memory subsystem begins paging, which slows background vacuum/cleaner threads, further accelerating version accumulation. Simultaneously, memory pressure and incessant dirty-page churn shorten write-back intervals and increase I/O bursts, heightening the risk of torn pages or incomplete writes that manifest as page-checksum errors, mismatched heap-to-index entries, and sudden "could not read block" or "index corrupted" errors. Symptomatically, administrators observe: rapidly growing disk usage, declining live-row density, long-running snapshot queries, vacuum workers perpetually lagging, escalating RSS and swap use, intermittent OOM terminations of worker or autovacuum processes, sporadic integrity-check failures, index scans returning inconsistent row counts, and emergency restarts that only partially resolve corruption reports.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn initiates sustained version buildup. The bloated heap and indexes enlarge the buffer pool footprint and lengthen cleaner cycles, forcing the engine to allocate ever-more memory for caching and for the large intermediate sort/hash operations now needed to handle expanded data ranges. Once physical memory is exhausted, the operating system pages or kills processes, interrupting vacuum or checkpoint activity mid-operation. These aborted maintenance actions, together with write storms from swap-in/swap-out and aggressive check-pointing, create windows where critical pages are only partially written, amplifying susceptibility to block corruption. Corruption, in turn, invalidates indexes and requires full-table scans, which touch even more bloated pages, feeding back into memory pressure and leaving cleaners powerless to advance the version horizon. The intertwined feedback loops among version bloat, memory exhaustion, and structural corruption rapidly degrade both performance and data reliability in transactional workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition:
This anomaly represents the simultaneous occurrence of (1) application-level SQL that processes more data and holds transactions open longer than necessary, (2) heavy lock-manager conflicts among concurrent transactions, and (3) intense competition for buffer-cache pages and their protecting latches. The three layers—statement semantics, lock management, and buffer management—interact to form a single cascading performance failure.

Combined Observable Phenomena:
• Very long or highly variable statement and transaction latencies; the same queries dominate slow-query and wait-event logs.
• Large, persistent blocker–waiter chains, frequent deadlock detections, and a surge in lock-wait and deadlock-victim rollback statistics.
• Concurrent spikes in buffer-busy and page-latch wait events, elevated CPU spin time, and stalled I/O submission as dirty pages accumulate.
• Connection pools exhaust, application threads back up, timeouts and retries rise, and overall throughput collapses even though hardware utilization appears erratic (some CPUs spinning, others idle).

Causal Chain and Interaction:
Inefficient SQL logic expands the number of rows scanned, updated, or locked and keeps transactions active across longer code paths. The enlarged lock footprint and extended hold time greatly raise the probability of conflicting lock requests, triggering blocking and deadlocks in the lock manager. While sessions wait, they still pin buffer pages and retain latches, making those pages hot spots. Simultaneously, the same overly broad scans repeatedly touch a small working set (e.g., index root or hot counter pages), driving up latch and buffer-busy contention. Latch stalls lengthen statement execution, which in turn prolongs transaction duration and exacerbates lock contention—a feedback loop that further amplifies blocking chains. The intertwined waits at the statement, lock, and buffer levels obscure root-cause isolation and push the database into a throughput-limiting congestion spiral.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to read or manipulate more data, rows, or time than the business need truly requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses or reuses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to inefficient access paths or join strategies.

When both flaws appear at once, the workload issues written at the application layer are executed through a plan that is already inefficient, creating a multiplicative performance penalty. Observable effects include: extreme and unpredictable statement latency spikes; the same SQL text showing wildly different runtimes across executions; transactions holding locks far beyond user think-time; CPU spikes, buffer-cache churn, and temp-space explosions as full-table or Cartesian scans iterate over bloated predicate sets; rapid oscillation between time-outs and apparent normalcy as bind-sensitive plans flip while the underlying query text remains logically bloated; and an unusual mix of application-side retries and optimizer-related plan cache growth.

Causally, ill-written SQL increases row counts, widens projections, or keeps transactions open, thereby enlarging the search space the optimizer must cost. This raises the probability that the cost model misjudges join orders, access paths, or degree of parallelism, producing a poor plan. Conversely, once a bad plan is chosen, its inefficiencies magnify the excess work mandated by the workload logic—e.g., a full scan on a table already over-read by non-sargable predicates—further stretching lock durations and resource usage. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other: workload logic bloats the operational footprint, while plan selection defects prevent the engine from mitigating that bloat, together degrading both OLTP and analytical performance.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously burdened by (1) inefficient or over-broad SQL workload logic, (2) an overwhelmed MVCC cleanup subsystem that cannot reclaim obsolete versions fast enough, and (3) saturated physical storage whose read/write bandwidth and IOPS are already at or beyond capacity.

SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction patterns fetch, scan, or modify far more data than business needs, keeping transactions open longer and inflating row-touch counts.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, undo records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background vacuum/cleanup workers can remove them, expanding table and index size and lengthening visibility checks.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying volumes hit their throughput or latency ceiling, driving up I/O wait time for data, log, and temp files even though the database engine keeps submitting requests.

Combined observable phenomena: 
• Very long statement and transaction latency with high variance.
• Steadily growing table, index, and version-store size; bloat ratios far above normal.
• Storage metrics showing queue depths pegged, read/write latencies multiples of baseline, and sustained log flush delays.
• Autovacuum/vacuum, purge, or garbage-collection workers running constantly yet falling further behind.
• Wait-profile dominated by buffer-I/O, data-file read, log-file write, and transaction visibility checks; CPU utilization remains moderate while sessions pile up on I/O and row-version scan waits.
• Application timeouts, retry storms, and potential dead-tuple or transaction-ID wraparound alarms.

Causal chain and reinforcement: Inefficient SQL patterns initiate large scans, wide updates, and long-lived transactions, immediately generating heavy I/O demand and a flood of new row versions. The surplus versions bloat heap and index pages, forcing subsequent queries—including the same flawed SQL—to read more pages and perform more visibility checks, further increasing I/O. As storage throughput becomes saturated, both foreground queries and background cleanup workers slow down; the throttled cleaners fall even further behind, allowing version bloat to accelerate. The enlarged on-disk structures amplify each read and write, which in turn deepens the storage backlog. This positive feedback loop ties the three root causes together, rapidly degrading OLTP responsiveness and threatening operational stability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Systematic cardinality misestimation caused by stale, incomplete, or missing optimizer statistics.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk data and index pages, causing unreliable access paths and incorrect result sets.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Exhaustion of allocated space for data files, logs, or temporary areas, leading to allocation failures and stalled background maintenance.

Composite definition — The database simultaneously suffers from inaccurate optimizer statistics, latent corruption inside data/index pages, and critical depletion of free storage. Together, these root causes distort cost estimation, break logical consistency, and impede the engine’s ability to allocate space for corrective actions, forming a compound failure mode that degrades both query correctness and availability.

Combined observable phenomena — Queries show extreme and erratic plan choices with grossly wrong cardinality estimates; some executions unexpectedly return missing or duplicate rows or switch to full table scans when indexes are flagged as suspect. Integrity-check utilities and engine logs intermittently report checksum or key-order errors but are unable to repair because REBUILD or DBCC commands abort on "out of space" conditions. Simultaneously, statistics-auto-update and index-rebuild tasks are skipped or cancelled due to space exhaustion, causing estimates to diverge further. End-user sessions experience a mix of slow response times, wrong results, and allocation-failed errors, while background processes flood the log with both corruption and no-space diagnostics, making the symptoms appear unrelated and hard to triage.

Causal interaction — Corrupted pages or orphaned index entries can inflate apparent table size and fragment free space, accelerating storage consumption and triggering capacity exhaustion. Once space is scarce, automatic statistics collection, online index rebuilds, and corruption-repair utilities cannot acquire work space, so neither data integrity nor statistics accuracy can be restored. In turn, stale or inaccurate statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing index paths that touch corrupted structures more frequently or into preferring full scans that exacerbate I/O and space pressure via large spool or temp segments. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another: corruption increases space use, space shortage blocks repair and stats refresh, and bad statistics drive workloads toward the very structures that are damaged, spiraling the system into deeper performance and reliability degradation.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime settings are mis-tuned with respect to hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults, creating artificial memory, I/O, or parallelism bottlenecks.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages are physically or logically corrupt, breaking key ordering, page links, or checksum validation and making persisted structures unreliable.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other process resources are reached, preventing the database from allocating required OS objects.

When these three root causes are present together, symptoms overlap and intensify: checksum or index-integrity errors may appear intermittently as the engine retries I/O using sub-optimal paths forced by bad configuration; sudden spikes in log-write or buffer-flush waits coexist with unexplained failures to spawn background workers or open files; query plans oscillate between full scans and index access, yet both can return inconsistent row counts; checkpoints or crash-recovery phases stall because corrupted pages trigger re-reads while the process simultaneously waits for additional file descriptors or shared-memory segments that the kernel refuses to grant. The administrator may observe idle CPU despite high wait events, bursts of corruption messages after parameter changes, and partial outages where existing sessions hang in I/O or lock waits while new connections are rejected by the OS.

Causally, mis-configured memory pools, log sizing, or parallel-worker limits can inflate the number of files, threads, and shared-memory objects the engine attempts to allocate, hastening the exhaustion of OS resource limits. Once those limits are hit, failed writes or incomplete background jobs increase the window during which torn pages or unfinished index modifications are exposed, aggravating latent on-disk corruption. Conversely, corruption that forces repeated retries, page reads, or index rebuild attempts drives additional kernel object consumption and accentuates the impact of tight OS quotas, while the same corruption can be masked or surfaced depending on buffer-pool and checkpoint parameters. The feedback loop between bad configuration, resource-limit exhaustion, and structural corruption accelerates workload degradation and complicates diagnosis because each layer surfaces errors that appear unrelated yet stem from their interaction.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Critical engine parameters (memory, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, durability, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, so bottlenecks arise from the settings themselves rather than from true resource exhaustion.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions serialize on buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots, producing elevated buffer-busy and page-latch waits, CPU spinning, and stalled throughput.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk data or index structures become physically or logically corrupt, causing checksum failures, mismatched row counts, or engine-reported corruption errors.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, the system exhibits a confusing blend of symptoms: bursts of log-write or checkpoint waits coexist with idle hardware, latch waits skyrocket on a small set of pages, and queries intermittently return wrong or missing rows. Integrity-check utilities report corruption while ordinary workload execution shows latency spikes and throughput collapse. Checkpoint or background-writer storms triggered by mis-tuned parameters keep dirty pages in memory longer, amplifying latch contention, while corruption on hot pages forces repeated latch retries, buffer invalidations, or emergency page reads, further inflating wait events. Operators may observe oscillating CPU usage—periods of spin-loop contention followed by long I/O stalls during corruption-induced page rereads—and error logs filled with both configuration warnings and corruption messages.

Causal chain: Misconfigured parameters (e.g., undersized buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint cadence, disabled or weakened page-verification settings) increase page churn and expand the window during which pages remain dirty, raising the probability that any latent storage fault or power loss will leave unfinished writes and introduce data corruption. The resulting corrupt pages tend to be hot root or index pages that are already under heavy access, so each access attempt collides on the same latches, multiplying contention. In turn, the elevated latch waits and stalled I/Os mislead adaptive tuning components, which may further adjust memory or background-worker settings in harmful directions, reinforcing the misconfiguration. The three anomalies therefore feed into one another: bad parameters create stress that promotes corruption, corruption localizes workload on a few damaged pages that intensify latch contention, and the intensified contention drives further reactive parameter changes or workload shifts that deepen the misconfiguration loop.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (e.g., buffer-pool size, work-memory limits, checkpoint cadence, parallelism caps) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload so that they themselves become the bottleneck.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Total memory consumed by caches, work areas, background workers, and sessions grows beyond safe physical capacity, leading to OS pressure, paging, and OOM events.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, write, or replay WAL at the pace the primary emits it, causing widening log-position gaps and blocked log recycling.

When all three root causes occur concurrently the system exhibits a mixed symptom set: sustained OS memory pressure, sporadic or continuous OOM kills, and cache-churn driven latency spikes on the primary; at the same time replicas show accelerating receive/write/replay lag, stale read-only queries, and ever-growing retained WAL segments that inflate both memory-mapped log buffers and on-disk archives. Checkpoint storms or aggressive autovacuum triggered by mis-set parameters may overlap with memory-hungry hash/sort bursts, further depleting memory and pushing the primary and replicas into swap. Administrators may notice wait-event patterns that keep alternating between memory-allocation waits and replication-send/receive waits, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single layer.

Causally, unsafe configuration parameters (oversized work-mem, undersized checkpoint segments, overly aggressive parallelism) inflate per-query and background memory footprints, directly instigating the Memory Allocation Anomaly. The ensuing OS memory pressure throttles I/O and CPU scheduling on both primary and replicas, slowing WAL generation as well as WAL apply. Slower apply causes Replication Synchronization Anomaly, which in turn forces the primary to retain additional log segments in memory-mapped buffers and on disk, further increasing its memory demand and amplifying the original memory pressure. This feedback loop leads to escalating lag, rising swap usage, and increased likelihood of crash or fail-over, producing a composite failure state that is more severe than each anomaly in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excess accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries overwhelms background cleanup, inflating the version store and visibility-check costs.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot pages and limited buffer-manager synchronization resources force sessions to serialize on latches or spin on buffer pins.

When both root causes strike together, the system exhibits a mixture of version-store bloat symptoms and severe buffer-level waits. Dirty, bloated data pages churn through a constrained buffer pool, so every logical read or cleanup pass contends for already-hot pages and their latches. Wait-event dashboards show a blend of long MVCC visibility checks, buffer-busy waits, and latch spin time; checkpoint and auto-vacuum workers stay active yet fall behind, while foreground transactions report rising latency, especially on UPDATE/DELETE-heavy tables whose root index pages are constantly reloaded or latched. Disk usage and I/O grow rapidly, yet CPU idle time shrinks because sessions alternate between spinning on latches and scanning oversized heaps.

Causally, unchecked MVCC bloat multiplies the number of pages that must reside in or cycle through the buffer cache, inflating pressure on limited buffer frames and the latches that guard them. Each cleanup, scan, or index probe must touch more pages, increasing the frequency with which many sessions converge on the same hot root or visibility map page, intensifying latch contention. In turn, heavy latch waits delay autovacuum or cleaning workers, allowing even more obsolete versions to accumulate and perpetuating the vicious cycle. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other: version bloat amplifies buffer contention, and buffer contention slows the very tasks needed to remove the bloat, driving the database into progressive performance degradation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design that forces the engine to touch more rows, pages, or time than the business need requires.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot pages or undersized cache cause sessions to serialize on buffer-pool latches and page pins rather than progress in parallel.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The log buffer, log files, or archiver cannot keep pace with redo generation, so commits stall waiting for log I/O or space.

Composite definition: The database is concurrently stressed by chatty or over-broad SQL, by latch congestion inside the buffer pool, and by an overloaded transaction-log path. All three root causes manifest at the same time, producing a multi-layer bottleneck chain that spans application logic, in-memory page access, and durable write-ahead logging.

Combined anomalous phenomena:  • End-user calls experience highly variable latency, with both statement execution time and commit time spiking.  • Engine wait views show a mixed profile of buffer-busy waits, page-latch spins, and log-flush or log-sync waits.  • CPU utilisation oscillates between spin-loops on hot latches and idle periods while sessions sleep on log-related events.  • Slow-query logs are flooded with the same wide-scan or chatty statements, and those statements frequently appear at the top of latch-contention reports.  • Checkpoints and archive processes run more often as the log grows rapidly, amplifying I/O pressure and extending latch hold times on dirty pages.  • Overall throughput collapses earlier than expected as concurrency rises because each layer feeds back into the others.

Causal interaction: Verbose or non-set-oriented SQL produces excess logical reads and redo; the surplus page touches concentrate access on a limited set of index roots and data hotspots, escalating latch contention. While sessions wait or spin on those latches, they continue to generate redo for partial work, further increasing the log generation rate. The congested log subsystem then delays commit acknowledgement, lengthening transaction duration and keeping buffers and latches pinned for longer, which intensifies buffer-cache pressure and widens the latch hotspot window. This feedback loop—over-broad SQL → latch contention → prolonged commit → extended latch hold—propagates across many sessions, causing a systemic throughput cliff and severe tail latency even though no single resource is fully exhausted in isolation.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, or parallel-worker heaps pushes total engine memory beyond the safe capacity of the host.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages and index structures on disk become internally inconsistent, leading to checksum failures, broken key ordering, or incorrect heap–index mappings.

When both root causes manifest simultaneously, the system may exhibit a mélange of symptoms: relentless OS-level paging or OOM kills interleaved with corruption warnings in engine logs; queries oscillating between slow full scans (triggered by corrupted indexes) and abrupt termination due to memory exhaustion; recovery or checkpoint phases that repeatedly crash or hang because corrupted pages are re-read into an already overcommitted buffer pool; and diagnostic utilities that report both cache pressure and structural corruption, making it difficult to isolate one primary culprit.

Causal interaction: (1) Runaway memory allocation reduces the headroom required for clean check-pointing and orderly flushes; an ensuing OOM or forced restart can interrupt write-ahead logging, heightening the likelihood of on-disk corruption. (2) Once corruption exists, query plans fall back to table scans, index rebuilds, or error-handling code paths that allocate large sort/hash buffers, further inflating memory usage. (3) The feedback loop of memory pressure → crash/restart → incomplete recovery → deeper corruption → heavier memory demand accelerates degradation, ultimately risking data loss and prolonged downtime.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and deleted index entries pile up faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them, causing version-store growth and heavier visibility checks.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers fall behind the primary, accumulating un-replayed log records and widening receive, flush, and replay lags.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes exhaust kernel-enforced quotas such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or process slots, preventing new workers or I/O contexts from being created.

When all three conditions co-exist, the system exhibits an intertwined symptom set: the heap and index bloat lengthen scans and expand the volume of write-ahead logging; the swollen WAL stream cannot be shipped or applied fast enough, so replica lag and retained log segments grow sharply; the primary keeps thousands of unrecycled log files open while vacuum and replication workers proliferate, collectively hitting per-process file-handle, shared-memory, or thread limits. Operators may see persistent autovacuum backlogs, replication slot disk usage exploding, replica replay delay climbing into hours, and sudden failures to spawn additional vacuum, apply, or client workers despite plenty of CPU and RAM.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn first inflates MVCC garbage, forcing aggressive cleanup activity that emits large volumes of WAL. The surge in log traffic overwhelms replication channels, extending log-retention windows because segments cannot be recycled until replicas catch up. The ever-growing set of retained segments and extra background workers raises the count of open files, shared-memory requests, and threads until kernel limits are hit. Once OS limits are breached, new vacuum workers and replication sender/receiver processes fail to start, further delaying garbage removal and replica catch-up. This feedback loop amplifies each anomaly, accelerating storage consumption, degrading query performance, and eroding high-availability guarantees.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply primary-generated log records at the pace they are produced, causing growing log-position gaps and replay lag.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages are physically or logically corrupted so that stored structures no longer match the expected logical contents, yielding wrong or incomplete query results and engine corruption errors.

When both root causes are present, the database estate exhibits a compound failure surface: replicas fall behind while simultaneously applying corrupt or inconsistent pages, leading to divergent data sets. Symptoms include replay lag that never clears, replica crashes or endless retries on specific LSNs, replication pipelines stalling on checksum or key-order errors, primary log segments retained indefinitely, unexpected duplicate or missing rows on replicas, inconsistent read results between primary and replicas, and integrity-check utilities flagging escalating corruption footprints on both sides. Failover readiness is severely degraded because the most current replica is both out-of-date and structurally unreliable, and monitoring tools may misattribute performance degradation to network or I/O saturation while underlying corruption silently spreads.

Causally, sustained replication lag lengthens the window during which damaged pages created on the primary (or introduced by storage faults on a replica) propagate. Conversely, corrupted pages encountered during apply can throttle or halt the single-threaded replay worker, amplifying lag and causing the primary to retain more WAL, which increases I/O pressure and the chance of further corruption on an already stressed storage subsystem. The feedback loop—corruption causing replay stalls, and stalls increasing exposure of corrupted state—accelerates divergence and magnifies both anomalies, ultimately threatening data consistency, availability, and recoverability across the cluster.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or missing optimizer statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimation and mis-costing of execution plans.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write capacity of the underlying storage is saturated, driving high I/O latency, deep device queues, and dominant I/O wait time in the database.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, async-I/O contexts, threads, or processes are reached, preventing the engine from allocating essential OS resources.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload is exposed to a compounded failure mode: misestimated plans choose I/O-heavy access paths and excessive spool/temporary operations; the resulting surge in physical reads, writes, and temp-file activity collides with an already bandwidth-constrained storage layer, inflating latency and queue depths. Prolonged I/O waits keep sessions and background workers alive longer, driving descriptor, thread, and AIO-context usage up to or beyond kernel limits. Once those limits are hit, new workers, parallel threads, and statistics-gathering jobs fail to spawn, producing errors about file or resource exhaustion and further preventing corrective statistics refresh.

Causal chain and mutual reinforcement: (1) Inaccurate statistics steer queries toward volume-scanning or temp-spilling plans, multiplying I/O demand. (2) Storage saturation lengthens every I/O, amplifying the cost of those suboptimal plans and delaying automatic statistics maintenance, leaving statistics even staler. (3) High latency and prolonged session lifetimes consume more OS handles, async-I/O slots, and threads; once OS limits are reached, additional I/O contexts cannot be opened, throttling the database below its configured parallelism and exacerbating throughput bottlenecks. (4) The failure of auto-stats jobs due to missing workers or file handles locks the system into a vicious cycle of ever-worsening plan quality, I/O pressure, and resource exhaustion, leading to widespread slowdowns, partial outages, or complete service interruption.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to read, join, or hold more data than the business requirement actually needs.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Instance-level settings for memory, parallelism, logging, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores are saturated by database processes, throttling all other work even if other resources are still available.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms from each layer amplify one another: long-running or chatty queries generated by the workload logic push large volumes of work into the executor; mis-sized work-memory, buffer, and parallelism parameters force the engine either to spill, over-parallelize, or repeatedly flush checkpoints, creating bursts of CPU demand that drive core utilization to sustained saturation. Observable phenomena therefore include: a slow-query log crowded with the same expensive statements, CPU wait events dominating wait-class views, run-queue lengths spiking during checkpoints or sort/hash phases, sudden latency cliffs whenever statement concurrency rises, and apparent hardware under-utilization of I/O or network despite high end-to-end response times.

Causally, inefficient workload logic is the initial generator of excessive CPU instructions and memory pressure. Mis-tuned configuration parameters remove the safety valves that could have absorbed or mitigated that pressure—e.g., too little work memory forces repetitive in-memory operations, while excessive parallelism multiplies the CPU footprint of each bad plan. The compounding effect drives the system into true CPU saturation, which in turn lengthens query runtimes, keeping transactions open longer and further increasing concurrency and memory churn. The feedback loop masks the individual contribution of each root cause, making the overall anomaly harder to diagnose and capable of crippling both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously burdened by application-side SQL that processes and commits far more data than the business logic truly needs (SQL Workload Logic Anomaly) and by a replication pipeline that cannot receive, flush, or replay the resulting log stream fast enough to stay current with the primary (Replication Synchronization Anomaly).

Combined observable phenomena: 1) End-user statements and transactions show long-tail latency, large row scans, and timeouts on the primary. 2) At the same time, replication-state views report rapidly growing LSN/SCN gaps, high replay lag, expanding relay or retained log segments, and stale data on read replicas. 3) Disk usage on the primary inflates because old log segments cannot be recycled, while replica hosts exhibit elevated CPU/IO saturation as they struggle to apply backlogged redo. 4) Failover readiness drops, and any read-scaling tier begins returning increasingly outdated or inconsistent data, making the slow-query symptoms harder to attribute to either the workload, the replicas, or both.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient SQL inflates the volume and size of transactions—scanning more rows, updating more tuples, and holding locks longer—thereby producing a heavier, burstier write-ahead log. This surge stresses the replication channel; network, apply threads, or storage on replicas fall behind, deepening lag. The accumulated lag, in turn, prevents log truncation on the primary, extending the lifetime of large transactions and amplifying contention that already exists due to the sub-optimal workload logic. Long-running or bulk transactions also serialize apply workers on the replica, further slowing catch-up. The two root causes thus reinforce each other: bad SQL logic creates excess redo; replication bottlenecks prevent its timely drainage, which in turn feeds back into longer transaction lifetimes, higher resource pressure, and even slower statement execution on the primary.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, parallelism, etc.) are mis-calibrated with respect to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions thrash on hot buffer pages and their associated latches, causing serialization and CPU spinning rather than true memory exhaustion.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log path—log buffer, flush, switch, archive, replication retention—cannot keep pace with redo generation, stalling commits and checkpoints.

Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from mis-tuned configuration parameters, severe buffer-cache/latch contention, and a saturated transaction-log subsystem. Together they create a feedback loop where write throughput is throttled at multiple layers while internal synchronization points become hot spots.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Commit latency and overall response time spike, with wait-event views showing a mixture of log-flush waits, buffer-busy/page-latch waits, and background-writer or checkpoint waits. 2) CPU usage oscillates between idle gaps (when sessions sleep on I/O or log flush) and spin-loops (while contending for latches). 3) Checkpoints fire more frequently, ejecting dirty pages and intensifying latch contention on the buffer freelist, yet still fail to relieve log pressure because log files are undersized or archiver lagging. 4) Performance regressions appear immediately after a configuration change or version upgrade, but traditional resource monitors show disks and CPUs only partially utilized, making the root cause hard to isolate.

Causal chain: Undersized log segments or slow archiving lengthen commit flush times; administrators react by tightening checkpoint intervals or enlarging work-memory, inadvertently pushing more dirty pages into the buffer pool. The higher dirty-page churn amplifies contention on buffer hash chains and page latches, causing threads to spin and burn CPU without progress. The resulting stall lengthens transaction durations, which in turn sustains a higher volume of concurrent sessions and redo generation, keeping the log subsystem overwhelmed. Because the mis-set parameters (checkpoint cadence, buffer-pool size, parallelism, log buffer length) govern both the buffer manager and the log writer, their poor calibration creates circular amplification: slow log flushes trigger aggressive checkpoints; aggressive checkpoints raise latch contention; latch contention delays the very transactions that must flush the log, thereby deepening the bottleneck. Without correcting all three layers, tuning any single layer in isolation provides only transient relief.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer reuses or chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonably accurate.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, page latches, or related lightweight locks, stalling on buffer-manager structures rather than row-level locks.

When both root causes are active, the database experiences a feedback loop in which a poor plan amplifies latch pressure and the resulting contention magnifies the performance penalty of the bad plan. Observable symptoms include: 
• Sudden plan switches from index seeks to full scans that explode logical and physical I/O, immediately followed by spikes in BUF_BUSY/PAGE_LATCH wait events. 
• High CPU spin time with little throughput while multiple sessions run the same cached but sub-optimal plan. 
• Hot-spot pages such as index roots, sequence blocks, or a narrow range of heap pages becoming latch bottlenecks because the inefficient plan drives excessive, repetitive accesses. 
• Wide variance in query latency; some executions hang on latch waits while others recompile and obtain yet another unstable plan, making performance diagnosis confusing.

Causal chain: A flawed plan can dramatically increase the number of page touches (e.g., table scans or nested loops with large outer row counts). This floods the buffer pool, concentrates access on a small set of pages, and lengthens dirty-page residency, all of which raise latch acquisition times. The heightened contention slows query completion, keeping the bad plan active longer and increasing concurrency on the same hot pages, further reinforcing the contention. In turn, the elongated execution times and fluctuating runtime statistics may trigger opportunistic recompilations that choose different but still sub-optimal plans, perpetuating the cycle and degrading overall system stability.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonably accurate and the query text is unchanged.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk heap pages or index structures become physically or logically corrupted, breaking key order, page links, or heap–index correspondence.

Combined phenomena: 1) Sudden plan flips from index probes to full scans on tables whose physical size has exploded from version bloat or whose indexes have become unreliable, 2) huge gaps between estimated and actual row counts because corruption and bloat distort statistics, 3) escalating I/O, CPU, and memory consumption during long-running OLTP statements, 4) vacuum/cleanup workers stuck or failing on corrupted pages while plan cache thrashes with ever-changing bad plans, 5) user-visible symptoms ranging from intermittent wrong-result sets (duplicate or missing rows) to query-timeouts and engine warnings about both wraparound danger and page checksum errors.

Causal chain: MVCC version bloat enlarges tables and skews visibility statistics, which misleads the optimizer into choosing cost-based plans that look cheaper but are disastrous in practice. Corrupted index or heap pages further undermine the optimizer’s cardinality feedback, triggering even worse plan choices or forcing full scans that magnify the impact of the bloated storage layer. In turn, the poor plans often perform wide scans and high-churn updates that generate yet more row versions and touch damaged pages, hampering cleanup workers whose failure allows both bloat and corruption to deepen. The three faults therefore reinforce one another, driving a feedback loop of growing storage, deteriorating plan quality, rising resource usage, and increasing risk of data-access errors in a live OLTP workload.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the heap and version store.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply transaction-log records at the rate the primary generates them, leading to widening replication lag and retention of extra log segments.

When both root causes are active, the system shows a compound pattern: dead‐row ratios, table and index sizes, and version-store length rise sharply while, at the same time, replica-side receive/flush/replay positions drift further behind the primary. Autovacuum or equivalent cleaners remain busy yet ineffective because replication-held snapshots prevent pruning; primary log-segment archives grow because neither cleanup nor replica acknowledgment frees them. Application sessions may see slower reads due to bloated pages, delayed failover readiness, and inconsistent read staleness on replicas. Monitoring views report simultaneously high "dead tuples" and escalating "replication lag", with disk pressure mounting on both primary (unrecycled WAL) and replicas (backlog of unapplied redo).

Causally, replication lag lengthens the global xmin or equivalent transaction-age horizon, freezing the visibility of old row versions and blocking their removal. The stalled cleanup enlarges the heap and forces the primary to emit more full-page images and update records, which in turn amplifies WAL volume and further overloads the already lagging replicas. The positive feedback loop—replica lag preventing cleanup, and unchecked version churn inflating WAL traffic—creates a self-reinforcing degradation that can exhaust storage, throttle throughput, and endanger recovery objectives.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot buffer-pool pages, pins, or latches become a serialization bottleneck, forcing sessions to stall or spin while trying to access the same in-memory page frames.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages are physically or logically corrupt, breaking key order, page links, or heap-to-index mappings and causing inconsistent query results and checksum errors.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage layer cannot sustain the read/write throughput or latency demanded by the workload, producing long device queues and elevated I/O wait times.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences an intertwined set of symptoms: 1) elevated buffer-busy, latch, and page-pin waits coexist with 2) intermittent corruption errors, failed index probes, or sudden fall-back to full scans, while 3) read and write latencies from the storage layer remain persistently high. The corruption forces repeated page rereads, verification retries, or index rebuild attempts, each of which lengthens latch hold times and inflates buffer churn. Meanwhile, storage saturation stretches dirty-page flush cycles, so hot pages stay pinned and dirty for longer, further amplifying latch contention. The blend of corrupt structures and slow I/O also leads to erratic query plans, duplicate or missing rows, prolonged recovery checkpoints, and CPU spin loops that do not translate into useful work, making the overall performance degradation severe and hard to attribute to a single subsystem.

Causally, storage throughput exhaustion slows every physical read and write, increasing the window during which pages remain latched or pinned in the buffer cache. The longer latch hold times exacerbate buffer contention, especially on the corrupt or hot pages that require extra verification or recovery work. Conversely, corruption inside data blocks and index pages causes additional I/O—forced rereads, page restores, or index repairs—which pushes more requests onto an already saturated storage system, deepening the throughput deficit. The prolonged flush and recovery cycles keep dirty or suspect pages resident and locked, causing further latch pile-ups. Thus, each anomaly feeds the others: corruption drives more I/O, slow I/O extends latch lifetimes, and latch contention hinders timely resolution of corruption and flush queues, creating a reinforcing loop that degrades both correctness and performance.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: The submitted statements, transaction boundaries, or batching strategy are written in a way that forces the engine to touch more rows, transfer more bytes, or hold locks longer than the functional requirement dictates.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: The transport layer between client and database cannot sustain the offered connection or data-transfer rate because of socket, listener, authentication, or physical network limitations.

When these two root causes manifest simultaneously, the database exhibits a super-position of engine-side latency and network-side latency. Over-wide scans, bulky result sets, and long-lived transactions generated by the logical workload flaw inflate the volume and duration of data that must traverse the network. At the same time, constrained connection slots, high round-trip time, handshake overhead, or packet loss delay the delivery of each oversized request and response. Operators may observe: a surge of identical slow-query log entries intertwined with client-read/client-write wait events; application timeouts during both connection establishment and statement execution; exponential growth of half-open sockets and idle backends stuck in network waits; elevated retransmission rates exactly when statement latency histograms show long tails; and connection pool exhaustion even though the server’s CPU and I/O metrics remain moderate.

Causally, the verbose SQL workload amplifies pressure on every stage of the network pipeline by demanding more result bytes per transaction and by holding sessions open longer, which in turn ties up limited connection slots and increases the backlog on the listener. Conversely, network congestion or authentication delays stretch each already-inefficient transaction, causing application retries that re-issue the same sub-optimal statements and further multiply load on the engine. The feedback loop between chatty or bloated SQL patterns and network resource scarcity deepens lock hold times, inflates memory used for result buffering, and starves new sessions, ultimately degrading overall throughput and making it difficult to isolate whether the primary bottleneck is intra-engine processing or inter-host transport.
