Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, absent, or inaccurate statistics mislead the cost-based optimizer, generating execution plans whose cardinality and cost estimates deviate sharply from reality. 
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions request incompatible locks on the same resources, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Data, log, or temporary storage nears or hits capacity limits, causing allocation failures and engine stalls. 

When these three root causes coexist, the database experiences a compound failure pattern: poorly estimated queries choose scan-heavy or overly granular access paths that touch far more rows or pages than necessary, inflating the lock footprint and duration of each statement. The enlarged lock scope multiplies blocking and deadlock frequency, while space exhaustion in data, log, or temp areas slows or aborts operations that need to extend objects, create workfiles, or flush transaction logs. Wait queues, deadlock victim rollbacks, repeated plan recompiles, and out-of-space errors appear interleaved in monitoring dashboards, obscuring which fault started the degradation.

Causal interaction: 1) Bad statistics produce inefficient plans that run longer and hold locks longer, intensifying lock contention. 2) Blocked transactions keep undo and redo entries active and prevent log truncation, accelerating consumption of the very space that is already scarce. 3) Approaching space limits force auto-grow or allocation waits, further lengthening statement runtime and lock hold time; any rollback triggered by a deadlock or timeout must write additional log records, consuming yet more space. 4) Space-related aborts invalidate or flush plans, and on recompile the optimizer still relies on stale statistics, perpetuating the cycle. The feedback loop between misestimation, prolonged locking, and space exhaustion can quickly cascade into widespread timeouts, aborted transactions, and ultimately a full service outage if not broken by corrective action on all three fronts.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them, enlarging the version store and bloating tables and indexes.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Total in-engine memory demanded by caches, work areas, and background components pushes the host into sustained pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages and latches, creating wait spikes and CPU spin without corresponding throughput gains.

Combined anomalous phenomena: While the version store and heap bloat grow, ever-increasing dirty pages and old row versions must be kept in memory. This expands the buffer pool footprint and forces the engine to reserve more private and shared work memory, driving the overall RSS upward. Under pressure, the operating system begins paging; page faults slow down cleanup workers, which in turn fall further behind, allowing even more dead tuples to accumulate. Hot pages such as index roots, free-space-map pages, and version-chain heads become latch hotspots because both foreground queries (doing long MVCC visibility scans) and background cleaners (doing deletes and vacuum-style work) continuously touch them. Users observe a mix of high buffer-busy/latch waits, rising memory usage, erratic cache-hit ratios, longer table scans, frequent checkpoints, and occasional OOM terminations or instance restarts that are hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causal chain and reinforcement: Heavy update/delete churn produces large numbers of dead tuples, inflating both the heap and the version store. The extra pages must be cached and flushed, directly increasing memory consumption; when memory caps are exceeded, the OS pages out, lengthening I/O latency. Slower I/O prolongs latch hold times on dirty or hot pages, amplifying buffer contention. At the same time, memory pressure throttles or starves background cleaners, so version buildup accelerates, creating a feedback loop: more dead tuples ⇒ larger memory footprint ⇒ higher paging and slower cleaners ⇒ still more dead tuples. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another in a vicious cycle that degrades OLTP throughput and latency far more severely than any of them would in isolation.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot or churned buffer-cache pages and their associated latches become a serialization point, forcing sessions to spin or wait while trying to pin, read, or modify pages.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo at the rate the primary generates it, leading to growing log gaps and retention of old log segments.

When both root causes are active, the primary experiences elevated page-latch waits and CPU spin loops that inflate commit latency and throughput variance, while at the same time replication lag widens because the standby must re-read or re-apply the same hot pages under contention. Observable symptoms include: 1) extreme and uneven latency spikes on the primary for statements that touch hot index root or sequence pages, 2) sustained "buffer busy" or "page latch" wait events co-occurring with escalating replication receive/replay delay, 3) rapidly growing on-disk log retention because replay cannot advance, and 4) replicas showing intermittent apply stalls coupled with their own buffer-pin or latch waits as large batches of redo hit the same contended pages.

Causal chain: hot-page contention on the primary lengthens transaction commit and increases WAL generation bursts (dirty pages flushed multiple times, frequent full-page images), producing larger or more clustered redo packets that replicas must ship, write, and apply. The replicas in turn encounter the same page-level hot spots during redo, which slows their apply speed, further enlarging the replication gap. The growing gap prevents log recycling on the primary, keeping more dirty and historical pages resident and intensifying buffer churn; meanwhile, backpressure from replication retention can raise checkpoint frequency, putting additional write and latch pressure on the already contended buffer cache. Thus, each anomaly amplifies the other, creating a feedback loop that degrades both local performance and replication health.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records outpaces background cleanup, causing version-store growth and visibility-check overhead.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data files, logs, or temp areas is exhausted, producing allocation failures and write stalls.

When these two root causes strike simultaneously, the database shows an explosive rise in disk usage, steep declines in live-row density, and a shrinking pool of free blocks. Autovacuum or purge workers run constantly yet make no headway; at the same time their I/O requests contend with data-file auto-extension and log archiving that are repeatedly failing due to lack of space. Transactions may begin to receive no-space-left or cannot-extend errors, large scans slow dramatically because they wade through bloated heaps, and the planner misestimates both row counts and cost. Checkpoint, archive, or temp-space operations start to stall, and engine alerts escalate from version-store wraparound warnings to imminent tablespace exhaustion.

Causal interaction: heavy update/delete churn creates surging MVCC garbage, inflating tables and indexes until they consume the remaining free extents; the resulting space pressure prevents cleanup workers from allocating new pages they need for rewriting pages or writing index-cleanup batches, so version reclamation slows further. Meanwhile out-of-space conditions can pause WAL recycling and force longer retention of old segments, which in turn widens the snapshot horizon and keeps old row versions alive. This feedback loop makes each anomaly reinforce the other, quickly degrading performance and threatening database availability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or page-pin structures, causing CPU spin and stalled logical I/O rather than exhausting memory capacity.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log generation, flushing, or archiving path becomes the bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling write traffic.

When both root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a mixed symptom set: 1) surging buffer-busy, page-latch, log-flush, and log-sync waits appearing together in wait-event views; 2) commits that intermittently freeze while foreground processes simultaneously spin on latches; 3) sharp throughput drops with CPU usage oscillating between idle (waiting for log flush) and 100 % spin (contending for latches); 4) checkpoint and archive storms that evict hot pages, forcing even more latch acquisitions; and 5) dramatic latency spikes concentrated on hot index roots or monotonically growing tables whose insert activity pours redo into an already saturated log.

Causal chain: intense latch contention on hot pages heightens the volume and burstiness of redo records (each latched modification adds log entries), which in turn overloads the log subsystem; delayed log flushes prolong transaction commit times, keeping row-level and page-level latches held longer than usual and feeding back into buffer-cache contention. Frequent checkpoints triggered by log-file pressure churn the buffer pool, creating new hot pages and further latch clashes. Conversely, slow log archiving can extend checkpoints, keeping dirty pages pinned and limiting buffer recycling, thereby concentrating access on a shrinking set of resident pages. The two bottlenecks therefore reinforce each other in a positive feedback loop that magnifies latency, reduces concurrency, and risks complete write-path stalls.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer-input metadata (row counts, histograms, correlations) is stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan choices.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Engine memory regions (buffer pool, work areas, plan cache, background heaps) expand beyond the safe envelope of the host, provoking OS pressure, paging, or OOM events.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive or apply log records at the rate produced by the primary, creating widening log-position gaps and retention of unrecycled log segments.

When these three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: the optimizer repeatedly selects memory-hungry or parallel plans due to inaccurate statistics, inflating per-query work buffers and hash tables; this enlarges overall memory consumption, drives the database process into paging and stalls, and further slows local log generation and background I/O. The impaired primary now produces transaction logs in bursts with uneven latency, while replicas—already lagging—fall further behind because their replay threads contend for scarce memory and suffer the same mis-estimated plans. Observable symptoms therefore include: 1) dramatic divergence between estimated and actual rows in both primary and replica plans, 2) resident-set size and swap usage climbing in lock-step with plan cache and work-area footprints, 3) steep replication delay and unrecycled WAL/redo segments exhausting primary storage, 4) intermittent query timeouts, replica read staleness, and destabilising failover readiness.

Causally, stale statistics can trigger memory pressure by choosing plans that favor large in-memory sorts, hashes, or excessive parallelism. The resulting memory allocation anomaly not only degrades local execution but also starves the replication sender and receiver processes, slowing log shipping and apply throughput. Growing replication lag, in turn, prevents log file recycling, expanding the I/O footprint and exacerbating memory pressure through larger buffer-pool churn. Meanwhile, delayed replicas keep their own statistics ever more outdated, reinforcing the optimizer statistics anomaly on the replay side. Thus the three root causes reinforce each other in a feedback loop that degrades query performance, memory stability, and replication health simultaneously.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are acceptable.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures are internally inconsistent with the logical contents of the database, leading to unreliable access paths and data retrieval.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : A hard limit is reached on data files, temp areas, logs, or backup destinations, preventing further space allocation.

Composite definition: This anomaly represents the database instance in which (1) the optimizer is selecting poor plans, (2) underlying data and index pages are corrupted or inconsistent, and (3) the storage layer is at or beyond its space capacity—all at the same time while the workload is executing.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Identical SQL statements oscillate between radically different plans; many fall back to full table scans because damaged indexes are marked unusable or return incorrect results. • Full scans, bad join orders, and loss of parallelism inflate I/O volume, temp-space usage, and redo generation, rapidly consuming the last free blocks in data, temp, and log areas. • Queries that do find and use corrupt indexes may return wrong or duplicate rows, causing application retries that drive even more log growth and temp spills. • Space-exhaustion errors ("cannot allocate extent", "log full", "temp space exhausted") interleave with corruption messages (checksum failures, key-order violations) and plan-cache invalidations, making the root cause set hard to distinguish. • Recovery or repair utilities abort mid-run because the required work space or logs cannot be extended, leaving additional orphaned segments and further plan instability.

Causal chain and interaction: Corrupted indexes mislead the optimizer, producing drastic mis-estimates that trigger sub-optimal plans and heavy resource usage. The inflated I/O, sort, and redo volume quickly depletes the already scarce storage, converting latent space pressure into hard allocation failures. In turn, space exhaustion prevents index rebuilds, online repair, or even clean checkpointing, allowing corruption to persist and spread. The sudden invalidation of unusable indexes forces the optimizer to re-optimize and often choose even less efficient plans, which further accelerates space growth, creating a vicious feedback loop that degrades both performance and data reliability.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Definition: A composite condition where the optimizer selects sub-optimal execution plans while, at the same time, the underlying storage subsystem cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded by the workload. Both root causes are active concurrently, so poor plans inflate the amount of physical I/O exactly when the storage layer is least able to absorb it.

Combined anomalous phenomena: • Rapid plan flips from index access to full or partial table scans that drive a surge in random and sequential I/O. • Execution plans that suddenly escalate parallelism, hash operations, or temp-space usage, causing long stretches of I/O wait even though CPU remains under-utilised. • Device queue depths pinned, read/write latency climbing, and database wait events dominated by both I/O-bound events and plan-related spills (e.g., workfile or spool I/O). • Query response times and batch windows inflate non-linearly; minor plan mis-estimates yield major slow-downs because each extra page read is throttled by saturated storage. • Performance variability is extreme across executions: identical SQL may run fast when the plan is good or during low I/O contention, yet crawl when an inferior plan coincides with peak device saturation, making diagnosis appear intermittent.

Causal interaction: A sub-optimal plan often multiplies logical I/O (e.g., scanning whole partitions, materialising large join inputs, spilling to temp), thereby exerting additional pressure on storage throughput. Conversely, chronic storage saturation elongates I/O service times, which can distort runtime feedback, invalidate adaptive plan features, and provoke the optimizer to abandon previously efficient access paths (e.g., choosing broad scans over point lookups because the perceived random I/O cost becomes prohibitive). The two anomalies thus form a feedback loop: bad plans create excess I/O, the slow I/O worsens plan execution cost, and subsequent recompilations may entrench even worse plans, driving the database into a sustained low-throughput, high-latency state that affects both OLTP and OLAP workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously affected by (1) application-layer SQL that processes more data or holds transactions longer than business logic requires, (2) stale or insufficient optimizer statistics that cause systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan choices, and (3) a write-ahead log subsystem whose generation, flushing, or archival capacity is saturated. All three root causes coexist and interact during the same workload execution.

Combined observable phenomena: Queries show extreme and erratic latency, with execution plans exhibiting large mismatches between estimated and actual row counts, wide scans, or inappropriate join orders. Transactions remain open far longer than normal, consume excessive locks, and generate unusually large volumes of redo. Commit, checkpoint, and log-flush waits spike, archive or replica-shipping queues back up, and application sessions face timeouts or cascading retries. Performance degradations may appear suddenly after data loads or schema changes, yet persist because inefficient SQL continues to execute against misinformed plans while the log subsystem throttles all write traffic, making the individual symptoms difficult to isolate.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient SQL logic expands data touched per statement; when paired with inaccurate statistics, the optimizer selects plans that further magnify row processing, I/O, and sort or hash spill volumes. The bloated work units inflate redo generation and prolong transaction duration, driving a surge of log records that must be flushed and archived. The overwhelmed log subsystem lengthens commit latency, which in turn holds locks and latches for longer periods, inflating concurrency conflicts and extending transaction lifespans. These longer transactions keep snapshot versions and index pages "in flight," preventing automatic statistics refresh from triggering and thereby keeping statistics stale. The feedback loop—poor SQL logic → bad cardinality → excess redo → log bottleneck → longer transactions → delayed stats upkeep—amplifies systemic slowdown until all three layers are addressed together.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between table structures / index layout and workload access patterns forces inefficient scans and excessive maintenance work, independent of statistics freshness or plan-selection logic.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records outpaces background cleanup, bloating tables/indexes and raising visibility-check overhead in high-churn environments.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas fall behind because they cannot receive or apply primary-generated log records at the production rate, causing widening log lags and retention of old WAL segments.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits compounded symptoms:  • Queries on the primary perform long full-table or non-covering index scans against increasingly bloated storage, showing step-function latency spikes and misestimated plans.  • Update/delete-heavy workloads generate surging version stores; vacuum or purge workers remain perpetually active yet fail to reclaim space, leading to runaway disk growth on both primary and replicas.  • Excessive WAL produced by large, fragmented heaps and nonselective indexes saturates network and I/O channels, so replicas accumulate growing replay lag, expose stale data to read traffic, and hold back log recycling on the primary.  • Failover readiness deteriorates; maintenance windows lengthen as index rebuilds, vacuums, and catch-up replays compete for resources. Distinguishing which layer is at fault becomes difficult because every observed slowdown (scans, vacuums, replication) appears mutually reinforcing.

Causally, ineffective schema and index design first increases I/O per query and amplifies row churn (e.g., heap-only tuple updates prevented by missing HOT-friendly indexes). The heavier churn inflates MVCC version chains; without supportive indexes, cleanup workers scan whole tables, fall behind, and leave more dead tuples. This bloat inflates each checkpoint’s WAL volume and lengthens full-table scans, further stressing CPU and storage. The swollen and write-intensive WAL stream then overwhelms replication channels; replicas that also suffer from the same poor indexing and version bloat replay changes even more slowly, extending apply lag. The prolonged retention of old snapshots on lagging replicas in turn delays VACUUM’s ability to reclaim dead versions on the primary, accelerating disk growth and perpetuating the vicious performance spiral.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Inaccurate or stale optimizer metadata causes systematic misestimation of cardinalities and costs.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, making their contents unreliable.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The storage subsystem is unable to deliver the needed read/write bandwidth or latency, leading to persistent I/O waits.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, execution plans are chosen on the basis of wrong cardinality assumptions, may access corrupt indexes or pages, and then wait excessively on saturated storage devices. Observable effects include: wildly fluctuating plan shapes, repeated plan recompilations, queries that return missing or duplicate rows, checksum or page-corruption errors in engine logs, sudden fall-back to full table scans that amplify I/O volume, disk queues pinned at maximum depth, prolonged lock or latch holding due to slow I/O, and batch windows or SLA response times degrading unpredictably. Because misestimated plans may mask corruption (e.g., skipping damaged index ranges) while corruption forces the optimizer to choose scan-heavy plans that overload the already saturated storage, symptoms intertwine and are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain and reinforcement: corrupted indexes or pages can invalidate previously collected statistics, causing the optimizer to rely on stale or misleading data; the resulting sub-optimal plans drive higher I/O, which pushes the storage layer past its throughput limits. Sustained storage saturation lengthens write-ahead-logging and checkpoint cycles, increasing the vulnerability window in which additional corruption can occur during power loss or crash recovery. Prolonged I/O queues also delay automatic statistics jobs, keeping statistics stale even longer. The feedback loop of bad statistics → poor access paths → excessive I/O → deeper corruption risk and staler statistics progressively deteriorates overall database health and makes recovery and diagnosis significantly harder.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer reuses or picks a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network, listener, authentication, or socket resources between clients and the database are saturated, delayed, or exhausted.

When all three anomalies strike together, the system exhibits a multi-layer performance collapse: 1) poor plans inflate statement runtimes and touch far more rows or pages than necessary, 2) the prolonged execution holds locks for longer periods, creating extensive blocker–waiter trees and frequent deadlocks, and 3) stalled or retried client connections accumulate, exhausting connection slots and further delaying both new sessions and network I/O for running ones. Operators may observe rapidly oscillating or contradictory symptoms—e.g., alternating spikes of CPU, lock-wait time, and client-read waits; sudden bursts of deadlock victim errors followed by connection-timeout errors; and highly variable execution plans in the cache that correlate with rising network retransmissions.

Causal chain: a sub-optimal plan increases execution time and result-set size, which keeps locks and sockets open longer. The extended lock hold causes other sessions to queue, swelling the active session count and driving up connection demand exactly when the listener or socket queues are already saturated. Simultaneously, network slowdowns delay result delivery, further prolonging transaction lifetimes and amplifying lock contention; the backlog of waiting sessions provokes more hard-parses, heightening the risk of the optimizer selecting yet another bad plan under different parameter bindings. Each layer therefore reinforces the next, producing a feedback loop that degrades throughput far more severely than any single anomaly would.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The cost model receives stale or incomplete statistics, resulting in systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan shapes.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Cumulative memory reserved for caches, work areas, and background structures exceeds the safe limits of the host, provoking paging, cache shrinkage, or OOM termination.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, producing buffer-busy and latch waits that throttle throughput.

When all three root causes surface concurrently, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: queries choose memory-intensive operators (hash joins, large sorts) based on misestimated cardinalities; these operators overrun available work memory, forcing the engine to evict clean pages, shrink caches, and escalate to temporary spill or OS swap. The resulting buffer churn and reduced cache residency turn frequently accessed index root pages into hotspots, driving latch spin and wait amplification. Observable symptoms include wildly inaccurate plan estimates, sudden plan regressions after data changes, escalating resident-set size, swap-daemon or cgroup throttling, plummeting buffer-cache hit ratios, surges in PAGE_LATCH_* or BUFFER_BUSY waits, CPU spin without progress, and query runtimes that grow super-linearly with concurrency.

Causal interaction: stale statistics mislead the optimizer to request much more (or much less) memory than is actually needed; over-allocated work areas aggregate across many sessions, tipping the instance into global memory pressure. As the engine trims the buffer pool to free memory for work areas, hotter pages cycle in and out more frequently, extending the hold time of latches protecting those pages. Longer latch waits elongate query execution, keeping their memory allocations alive and further intensifying pressure. Conversely, memory shortages can inhibit automatic statistics refresh jobs, perpetuating statistics staleness, while latch contention slows data-modification operations, leaving partitions in states that diverge further from recorded statistics. The three anomalies thus form a feedback loop that magnifies latency, degrades throughput, and risks stability far more severely than any single anomaly would in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously affected by unchecked growth of obsolete MVCC row versions/rollback records and by depletion of available disk or tablespace capacity; the version store inflates faster than it can be cleaned while free space shrinks toward a hard boundary.

Combined observable phenomena: free-space monitoring shows a steep, unexplained drop that coincides with sharply rising counts of dead tuples and rollback segments; data-file auto-extension or tablespace growth requests begin to fail, while VACUUM/PURGE workers run constantly yet report little progress. Sequential scans, index range scans, and visibility checks take longer because of page bloat, and the query planner misestimates row counts. Users may first see "no space left" or "cannot allocate version record" errors, stalled DML statements waiting for space, log-archive back-pressure, and emergency wraparound warnings all at once, making the root cause appear as a generalized outage rather than two specific issues.

Causal interaction: heavy update/delete churn produces a flood of obsolete versions that inflate heap and index pages; this ballooning rapidly consumes remaining disk space and pushes the system into a storage-capacity crisis. Conversely, once free space is scarce, background cleanup cannot allocate the working space it needs to rewrite pages or extend rollback areas, so it falls further behind, allowing even more obsolete versions to accumulate. As space approaches exhaustion, checkpoints and log archiving stall, which in turn prolongs active snapshots and prevents version pruning—creating a positive feedback loop that amplifies both anomalies and accelerates system degradation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and heap size.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Stand-by or downstream replicas cannot receive or apply transaction-log records at the rate the primary generates them, producing sustained replication lag.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures become internally inconsistent, causing logical/physical corruption and unreliable access paths.

When all three root causes coexist, the system shows a blended symptom set: the primary’s tables and indexes grow rapidly while replication monitoring reports widening write/flush/replay gaps; VACUUM/cleanup workers stay permanently backlogged and may repeatedly abort or skip ranges because they encounter corrupted pages; replica apply workers stall on the same corrupt blocks, causing cascading log retention on the primary. Query plans on both primary and replicas degrade—some scans slow down due to bloated heaps, others fall back to full scans after detecting unusable indexes, and read-only replicas deliver increasingly stale or incorrect results. Disk consumption spikes on every node (heap bloat on the primary, retained WAL on the primary, expanded relay logs on replicas), and administrative utilities report both version-age horizon warnings and page-checksum or key-order errors.

Causal interaction: heavy update/delete churn creates large WAL streams and rapid version accumulation. Replication lag prevents the primary from advancing its replication-xmin horizon, so VACUUM cannot prune old versions, further enlarging the version store. The swollen version store in turn magnifies WAL volume, worsening replication lag in a feedback loop. Concurrently, any latent on-disk block or index corruption causes VACUUM or replica apply processes to error out or slow down, freezing progress at exactly the pages that need cleanup or replay; this halting behavior amplifies both the version-maintenance backlog and the replication gap. Conversely, the prolonged presence of corrupted pages inside an ever-growing heap complicates detection and repair because corruption signatures are buried under layers of obsolete versions. The three anomalies therefore reinforce each other, accelerating storage growth, degrading query correctness, and eroding failover readiness far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures, indexes, partitions, and data types do not match workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging pipeline—generation, buffering, flushing, archiving—cannot keep pace with redo volume, causing commit stalls and log-related waits.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume sustained, near-saturation CPU, leaving insufficient cycles for other work and inflating run-queue latency.

When all three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits a blended symptom set: queries that already scan whole tables or fetch many rows because of missing or non-covering indexes amplify redo generation, which in turn overwhelms the log buffer and I/O band­width. As commits wait for log flushes, user sessions pile up, yet they remain CPU-hungry while looping on retries or scanning data, driving host utilization to saturation. Observers see mixed wait profiles—log-flush and CPU scheduler waits spike together—alongside escalating query latencies, checkpoint storms, and sharp drops in TPS. Monitoring dashboards may misleadingly attribute the slowdown to any one layer, while in reality lock contention, log stalls, and CPU thrashing are interleaved.

Causally, inefficient schema and index design multiplies the amount of data each DML or SELECT touches, inflating both CPU cycles and redo bytes per transaction. The surplus redo intensifies pressure on the transaction-log subsystem; once log-flush latency lengthens, foreground sessions hold locks longer and re-execute scans, compounding CPU load. Elevated CPU utilization then slows background log writer and archive processes, further delaying flushes and creating a feedback loop. The synergy of these root causes therefore magnifies performance degradation far beyond what each would inflict in isolation, pushing an OLTP system into a cascading slowdown that is difficult to diagnose without recognizing their mutual reinforcement.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model does not align with workload access patterns, forcing queries into inefficient full-scan or non-covering-index paths and creating write hot-spots.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, causing CPU spin and wait spikes even when total memory is sufficient.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot ingest or apply primary-side log traffic fast enough, leading to widening log-position gaps and retention of un-recycled log segments.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: 1) queries and DML repeatedly hammer a small set of ill-designed tables or index root pages, inflating buffer-busy and page-latch waits; 2) the resulting stall and retry behaviour increases transaction duration and the volume of generated redo, so the primary’s log grows faster while flush cycles are lengthened by buffer contention; 3) replicas fall further behind because they must replay the same inefficient access patterns and also compete for their own buffer latches, showing escalating replay lag and ballooning relay-log or retained WAL storage. End-user latency oscillates with both local latch storms and downstream back-pressure, and administrative alarms may simultaneously report buffer-cache hotspots, high WAL retention, and replication lag, making the root cause hard to pinpoint.

Causally, the sub-optimal schema design creates concentrated page accesses that become latch hot-spots; this latch contention slows foreground DML and prolongs checkpoints, generating bursts of dirty pages and large transaction logs. The enlarged and sustained log volume overloads the replication pipeline, whose own apply threads are further hampered by the same poor index layout, re-creating latch contention on the replica side and reducing catch-up throughput. As replicas lag, the primary is forced to retain additional log segments, keeping more pages dirty and resident, which intensifies buffer churn and latch pressure—forming a reinforcing loop that degrades both primary performance and replica freshness.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The engine allocates and holds more memory than the host can safely supply, driving paging, swap use, or OOM terminations.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database-related processes saturate CPU cores, creating run-queue backlogs and global latency inflation.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced limits on handles, shared memory, threads, or other objects are exhausted, preventing the engine from creating new workers or allocating critical kernel resources.

When all three root causes manifest together, the platform exhibits a multilayer resource meltdown: memory pressure triggers heavy paging that competes for CPU time, while CPU saturation prolongs critical sections that keep kernel objects open longer, causing file-handle, thread, and shared-memory limits to be hit sooner. Symptoms include simultaneous spikes in swap I/O, load average, and kernel allocation failures; sessions hang while trying to attach to shared memory, spawn parallel workers, or allocate work buffers; wait-event views show interleaved memory pressure waits, scheduler waits, and OS-resource acquisition waits; and even lightweight operations stall because the engine cannot obtain either CPU slices or the kernel objects needed to proceed.

Causally, runaway memory allocation enlarges each process’s resident set, provoking the kernel to reclaim pages and schedule I/O, which in turn escalates CPU demand for memory management and I/O handling. The inflated CPU usage lengthens the lifetime of threads in critical sections, delaying their release of file descriptors, semaphores, and other kernel objects, thereby pushing the system faster toward the configured OS limits. Once those limits are reached, new workers or buffers cannot be created; the engine reacts by retrying or spawning additional management threads, amplifying both memory footprint and CPU consumption. This positive feedback loop between memory over-commitment, CPU saturation, and kernel-level resource exhaustion accelerates degradation, leading to cascading failures, partial outages, or full instance termination.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes sustain near-saturation CPU consumption, starving other work and inflating latency.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or thread counts, causing allocation failures.

When all three root causes are active, the system shows a compound failure signature: vacuum or purge workers spin at 100 % CPU yet make little progress, overall host load and context-switch rates soar, and the engine begins to log errors about failing to spawn new workers, open files, or extend shared memory. Query latencies rise non-linearly; some sessions stall on visibility checks of bloated tables while others are rejected outright by the kernel. Monitoring views show both a growing version store and a backlog of blocked or aborted background jobs. Administrators may observe that even emergency maintenance commands refuse to start because required handles or processes cannot be created.

Causal chain: heavy UPDATE/DELETE churn inflates the version store, awakening more cleanup workers; these workers consume additional CPU cycles and create more kernel objects (threads, file handles, async-I/O contexts). The extra CPU demand pushes the host to saturation, lengthening task-switch queues and slowing all workers—including those needed for cleanup—so the MVCC bloat worsens. Meanwhile, the multiplication of worker threads and open files drives the process toward OS resource ceilings; once those limits are reached, new vacuum workers and client sessions fail to start, eliminating the very mechanisms that could relieve version pressure. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another: MVCC bloat triggers CPU saturation, CPU saturation accelerates kernel object creation, OS denials block remediation, and the feedback loop rapidly degrades overall database availability.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, or correlation metadata no longer reflect the real data distribution, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan choice.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating table size and adding visibility-check overhead.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced caps on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other OS objects are reached, preventing the database from allocating needed resources.

When these three root causes strike together, the system exhibits a blend of misleading planner estimates, suddenly slow queries, rising disk and memory footprint, and intermittent OS-level allocation failures. Execution plans may flip from index probes to full scans just as the underlying tables become bloated with dead tuples; the resulting surge in I/O, buffer usage, and parallel worker demand quickly consumes file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or thread slots. Administrators may see autovacuum or cleanup workers stuck or crashing due to fork/handle limits, statistics collectors unable to write new stats, and a vicious circle of plan instability, longer execution times, and mounting OS error messages. Symptoms appear scattershot—poor plans, bloated storage, and sporadic "cannot open file", "cannot create thread", or "cannot attach to shared memory" errors—making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal chain: heavy update/delete activity grows the version store, enlarging tables and indexes. The inflated objects exacerbate the optimizer’s existing stale statistics, further skewing estimates and leading it to select plans that touch far more data than expected, which increases CPU and I/O pressure. To cope, the engine spawns more workers and opens more files, but the concurrent demand collides with tight OS limits. Cleanup and statistics refresh processes are among the first to fail under these limits, so dead-tuple bloat and statistic staleness worsen, reinforcing each other. The positive feedback loop ultimately degrades throughput, triggers OS allocation errors, and pushes the database toward partial or total outage.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot ingest and apply primary WAL at the rate it is produced, widening log-position gaps and preventing log recycling.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, driving load-average and run-queue pressure and slowing every code path that requires compute time.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database hits kernel-enforced ceilings on handles, processes/threads, shared memory, or similar objects, blocking new work even though engine-level slots still exist.

When all three root causes strike together the system exhibits a compound failure signature: replica lag explodes while both primary and replica show near-100 % CPU, yet error logs also record ‘cannot allocate shared memory / open file / create thread’ messages. DML and queries on the primary slow because WAL flushes are throttled by back-pressure from stalled replicas, autovacuum or parallel workers fail to start due to kernel limits, and monitoring shows both high scheduler wait events and replication wait events. Replica apply workers repeatedly fall behind or crash-restart when they cannot obtain file handles or shared-memory segments, further inflating CPU as they respawn, while primary-side WAL segments accumulate, threatening disk exhaustion and jeopardizing failover readiness.

Causal interaction: CPU saturation lengthens every system call, causing replication sender and receiver processes to miss network deadlines and aggravate apply lag. Growing apply lag forces more WAL traffic and larger relay logs, which in turn require additional CPU to process, forming a positive feedback loop. Simultaneously, the elevated process and thread count spawned by retrying replication and maintenance tasks drives the system past kernel resource ceilings; each allocation failure triggers more retries and logging, consuming yet more CPU. Hitting OS limits also prevents the database from spawning extra apply or parallel workers that might have alleviated lag or distributed CPU load, thereby entrenching both replication backlog and CPU starvation. The three anomalies thus reinforce one another, producing a blended symptom set that is broader, more severe, and harder to attribute to a single layer.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite accurate statistics, often because of faulty cost modeling or unstable plan reuse.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall throughput.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings for memory, parallelism, checkpointing, etc., are mis-tuned, so resource management behavior is misaligned with the workload and hardware.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload experiences extreme and erratic slowdowns: poorly chosen plans (e.g., full table scans or expansive nested-loop joins) touch far more rows and pages than necessary, inflating the lock footprint and duration per statement. The enlarged critical sections collide under high concurrency, producing deep blocker-waiter chains, frequent deadlocks, and surging lock-wait and retry rates. Meanwhile, mis-configured memory limits, work-memory, or parallelism caps throttle query operators and prolong execution and lock holding times, while aggressive or insufficient checkpoint and log settings amplify I/O spikes that further delay lock acquisition and query progress. Symptoms include sudden plan flips followed by immediate lock pile-ups, CPU and I/O under- or over-utilization that does not correlate with wait events, oscillating throughput, rising application timeouts, and deadlock graphs that implicate statements whose plans recently changed after a configuration tweak.

Causal chain: A mis-tuned configuration (e.g., low work-mem, disabled plan baselines, too high parallelism) nudges the optimizer toward cheaper-on-paper but wider scans or nested-loops, creating a Query Plan Selection Anomaly. The bloated plan expands the number and duration of locks held, which under heavy OLTP concurrency triggers Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly. In turn, lock waits elongate transaction lifetimes, keeping more locks active and feeding back into the optimizer’s cost feedback or adaptive plan mechanisms, potentially causing further plan instability. Simultaneously, the same mis-set parameters (e.g., small buffer pool, aggressive checkpoint) starve running statements of resources, lengthening lock retention and magnifying contention. Thus the three anomalies reinforce each other, creating a compounded performance collapse that is far worse than any single issue alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model, indexing, partitioning and data-type choices do not fit workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths independent of statistics freshness.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or related log/temporary areas are close to or at space exhaustion, leading to allocation failures and blocked growth operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport and connection-handling layer cannot sustain the offered session or data-transfer rate, producing refused or stalled connections and socket-level waits.

When all three issues strike concurrently, the database shows a blend of symptoms: queries already slowed by full scans or non-covering index lookups take longer to return, holding server processes and network sockets open while large result sets dribble across congested links. Those prolonged sessions accumulate, inflating active connection counts until listener or OS socket queues overflow and new clients are rejected or time out. Meanwhile, the excessive I/O generated by the poor schema design (unnecessary table scans, row lookups, temp-space sorts) accelerates tablespace growth, temp-file inflation, and redo/undo generation, quickly consuming the remaining free space. Space shortages then cause auto-extend or log-archive stalls that freeze write operations mid-transaction; frozen backends remain connected, further saturating the limited connection pool and network backlog. Administrators may observe a mixed pattern of slow queries, intermittent "out of space" errors, rising waits on client read/write events, and periodic connection storms that mask which layer is primary.

Causally, inefficient schema design drives higher disk and temp usage as well as larger result sets, pushing the storage subsystem toward capacity limits. The same inefficiency prolongs statement execution times, increasing the duration each backend holds a network socket, which magnifies the impact of pre-existing network constraints. As space becomes scarce, allocation failures pause or abort writes; these partial or hung transactions keep locks and connections open, creating more network pressure and client retries. Retried connections and replayed workloads then amplify both space consumption (duplicate writes, additional temp objects) and connection demand, creating a reinforcing loop that rapidly degrades overall availability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime settings (e.g., buffer-pool size, per-session work memory, checkpoint cadence, connection limits) are mis-aligned with hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database components collectively consume more physical memory or swap than the host can safely supply, leading to paging, OOM events, or node eviction.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, authentication, or socket resources cannot sustain the offered connection or data-transfer rate, producing connection errors, backlog growth, or elevated client-read/write waits.

When all three root causes appear together, symptoms overlap and amplify: connection storms and retry loops inflate backend counts that already exceed mis-tuned connection limits; every new session reserves oversized work memory, rapidly exhausting RAM and triggering operating-system paging or OOM kills. Memory pressure stalls backends, lengthening query turnaround and enlarging in-flight result sets, which in turn hold sockets open and deepen network backlog. Wait-event charts show simultaneous client-read/client-write stalls, log-write or checkpoint spikes divorced from actual I/O utilization, and CPU time lost to memory-pressure spin waits. The database may repeatedly restart, dropping TCP sessions and forcing clients into further reconnect attempts, while half-open sockets accumulate because listener backlog and keepalive timers are set too low.

Causal chain: misconfigured parameters (high work_mem, high parallel-worker counts, lenient connection caps) initiate excessive per-session memory reservation. The resulting memory exhaustion slows or terminates backends, which increases latency and provokes client retries, swelling the active connection pool and socket queues. Network bottlenecks then prolong each session’s lifetime, causing even more memory to remain pinned. Conversely, dropped or timed-out connections create bursts of new logins that re-invoke the misconfiguration and allocation cycle. Thus, each root cause reinforces the others—parameter mis-tuning drives memory over-consumption, memory pressure magnifies network latency, and network congestion feeds back into connection growth—producing a cascading degradation that is more severe and harder to diagnose than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonably accurate, leading to inefficient access paths, incorrect join orders, or inappropriate parallelism settings.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates or leaks so much memory to caches, work areas, and background structures that the host experiences sustained RAM pressure, paging, or OOM events, degrading every component that depends on predictable memory availability.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging machinery—log buffers, redo files, flush and archive operations—cannot keep pace with the workload’s commit rate, causing log-related waits and potential stalls on the write path.

When these three root causes occur concurrently, the system exhibits a blended failure pattern: a poor query plan may trigger excessive logical and physical I/O, large hash or sort buffers, and elevated redo generation; the inflated memory footprint from those work areas—combined with uncontrolled plan and buffer cache growth—pushes the host into memory pressure and paging, which in turn slows log buffer flushes and data-file I/O. The log subsystem, already undersized or on a saturated device, now faces a spike in redo volume and longer flush times, driving commit latency higher and forcing additional waits inside sessions already executing inefficient plans. Symptoms therefore include: rapid oscillation between different bad plans, surge in memory reservations per session, abrupt drops in page-cache hit ratios, escalating log write/sync waits, frequent checkpoint or log-switch storms, and eventual process throttling or termination by the OS as swap fills—making it difficult to isolate a single culprit.

Causally, an ill-chosen plan (e.g., nested loops on skewed data) multiplies row processing and generates large temporary structures, inflating per-query work memory. This accelerates memory exhaustion, which induces OS-level paging; the resulting I/O contention further degrades plan performance and extends transaction lifetimes, amplifying redo generation. The overtaxed log subsystem must now flush bigger, bursty redo streams while competing with paging and data reads, lengthening commit durations. Prolonged commits keep locks held longer, increasing concurrency and memory usage, which feeds back into higher cache bloat and additional sub-optimal plan selections as the optimizer misinterprets transient statistics. Thus, each anomaly intensifies the others, creating a self-reinforcing loop that can cripple an OLTP system.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, partitions, and indexes are not aligned with access patterns, forcing the optimizer into inefficient full scans, non-covering look-ups, and excessive maintenance work.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Generation, flushing, or archiving of write-ahead logs cannot keep up with the commit rate, causing commit stalls and log-related wait events.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport paths, listeners, or connection slots are saturated or unreliable, delaying session establishment and result transmission.

When all three root causes strike together, the database exhibits a mixed pattern of symptoms: 1) queries perform unnecessary full scans that inflate I/O and redo volume, 2) the oversized redo stream accumulates in the log buffer and waits for slow log flushes, lengthening commit latency, and 3) clients waiting on congested network channels or exhausted back-end slots experience timeouts and retry storms. End-to-end response times fluctuate wildly; small write transactions intermittently block behind log-sync waits, while read requests pile up inside the engine because client sockets cannot drain result sets quickly enough. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in logical and physical I/O, LOG_WRITE or LOG_FLUSH waits, and CLIENT_READ/CLIENT_WRITE waits, making it hard to attribute delays to a single layer.

Causally, the poor schema and index design amplifies redo production and buffer-cache churn, putting sustained pressure on the transaction log subsystem. The log subsystem, already tuned too tightly for peak throughput, elongates commit cycles; longer commits hold latches and row locks for extra time, which in turn stretches the duration that back-end processes occupy network sockets. As network resources saturate, new sessions and retries further raise concurrency, driving even more ad-hoc queries through sub-optimal access paths and accelerating redo generation. This positive feedback loop—inefficient data access → excess redo → log-flush bottleneck → prolonged transactions → connection pile-ups → higher concurrency → more inefficient work—creates a cascading performance collapse that is far more severe than any individual anomaly would cause.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resource, creating blocking chains or deadlocks that stall forward progress.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate memory consumed by caches, work areas, and session heaps surpasses the safe capacity of the host, provoking paging or out-of-memory pressure.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing is throttled because log buffers, log files, or archiving pipelines cannot absorb the volume of redo being generated.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set: lock-wait time and deadlock frequency rise while commit latency simultaneously elongates; worker threads pile up in both lock-manager wait queues and OS run queues starved for memory; RSS and swap usage climb until the operating system steals cache pages, further degrading buffer-cache hit ratios; log-flush and log-write waits spike, exaggerating the apparent duration of locks held during COMMIT; connection pools saturate, application timeouts increase, and recovery/instance restarts may occur when memory exhaustion or stalled log archival triggers fault-management logic.

Causally, each anomaly amplifies the others. Memory pressure slows SQL execution (extra paging, reduced cache efficiency), lengthening transaction lifetimes and thereby prolonging lock holds that intensify contention. The enlarged lock backlog inflates per-session memory footprints (lock structures, row versions, private work areas), deepening the memory shortfall. Prolonged transactions also generate more redo per unit of business work and keep old log segments active, causing log files to fill faster; in turn, delayed log flushes extend commit duration so locks remain held even longer, feeding the contention loop. Finally, frequent flushes and checkpoint storms consume additional CPU and memory buffer space, tightening the memory bottleneck and creating a self-reinforcing triad that can bring an OLTP system to a near standstill if not addressed holistically.

Name: CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database-related processes saturate host CPU capacity, driving run-queue growth and system-wide latency.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes exhaust kernel-enforced quotas such as file descriptors, threads, or shared-memory segments, blocking further allocations.

Composite definition:
The system simultaneously suffers from severe CPU saturation and the exhaustion of one or more operating-system resource limits, creating a multi-layer bottleneck where compute cycles are scarce and new kernel objects cannot be obtained. 

Combined anomalous phenomena:
• Sustained 90-100 % CPU utilization, long run queues, and increased context switches coincide with frequent engine or kernel errors about "unable to create thread", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "too many open files".
• Session creation, parallel-worker spawning, or I/O submission intermittently fails; surviving sessions run slowly because every task competes both for CPU time-slices and for scarce kernel objects.
• Wait-event views show a mix of CPU run-queue waits and kernel-resource waits; application logs show unexplained timeouts alongside low-level allocation failures.
• Latency spikes and throughput collapse spread across otherwise unrelated queries, making performance degradation appear chaotic and difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain and interaction:
High CPU demand causes threads to execute longer and context-switch more frequently, accelerating consumption of per-process file descriptors, async-I/O contexts, and thread IDs. As these kernel limits are approached or reached, the database attempts to spawn additional workers or open more files to cope with the workload, but the kernel denies the requests, forcing retries and idle waits that further extend CPU hold times. The longer each thread sits runnable but unscheduled, the more the run queue grows, intensifying CPU saturation. Conversely, when kernel limits block thread or I/O creation, existing threads must shoulder more work, increasing CPU load even further. This feedback loop amplifies both anomalies, rapidly degrading overall throughput and potentially leading to partial or complete service outage.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Inefficient or overly broad application-level SQL and transaction design that forces the engine to scan, lock, or return more data than the business case requires.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Contention or saturation in the write-ahead logging pipeline—buffer, file groups, flushing, archiving, or replication retention— that inflates commit latency and stalls write activity.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or unstable network and connection-handling capacity that slows or interrupts client/server data transfer and session establishment.

When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the database exhibits a mixed pattern of symptoms: long-running queries and transactions generate excess redo volume, driving up log-flush and commit waits; at the same time, clients experience intermittent connection timeouts, slow result streaming, and elevated retry storms. Engine wait statistics show both LOG FILE SYNC / LOG BUFFER SPACE and CLIENT READ/WRITE or SOCKET WAIT events rising together. Slow-query logs capture repetitive, heavy statements whose commit phases are further delayed by log I/O back-pressure, while monitoring tools report swollen log directories, archiver backlogs, growing transactional back-logs, and a spike in half-open connections. Application servers may exhaust connection pools as sessions remain tied up during prolonged commit and network send phases, amplifying perceived end-user latency and error rates.

Causally, inefficient SQL inflates row-change volume and result-set size, which in turn increases redo generation and network payloads. The bloated redo stream overwhelms undersized or mis-configured log buffers and log devices, lengthening fsync cycles and extending transaction commit time. These longer commits keep server processes engaged, holding locks and consuming connection slots. Simultaneously, the enlarged result sets traverse congested or resource-starved network paths, further delaying session completion. Prolonged sessions prevent connection reuse and escalate pool exhaustion, which triggers more connection attempts and authentication overhead, feeding into the already stressed log and network subsystems. The feedback loop between chatty, over-fetching workload logic, log subsystem saturation, and degraded network throughput drives a compound degradation that is more severe and harder to diagnose than any individual anomaly alone.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database cluster is simultaneously suffering from (1) replication pipelines that cannot keep up with primary-side log generation, (2) physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk data and index pages, and (3) host-level CPU saturation that deprives all engine components of compute cycles. The three conditions interact so that neither the primary nor its replicas can progress, recover, or serve workload in a timely and reliable manner.

Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys or downstream consumers lag behind because they cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo at the rate it is produced.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Disk pages or index structures are corrupted or inconsistent, making storage contents untrustworthy and triggering verification or access failures.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume the available CPU to the point of saturation, inflating run-queue time and global response latency.

Combined Phenomena:  • Replication views show rapidly widening receive, write, and replay lag while replica error logs emit page-checksum or index-consistency errors.  • Apply workers on replicas spin on repeated redo-apply retries or corruption-handling routines, driving CPU usage to 100 % on affected cores.  • On the primary, accumulating unrecycled WAL segments inflate disk usage because replicas cannot confirm receipt.  • Queries served from replicas return stale or inconsistent results, and corruption-induced full-table scans or forced rechecks further intensify CPU demand on both primary and replica nodes.  • Cluster-wide latency spikes, failover eligibility drops, and maintenance utilities such as CHECKDB or VACUUM/ANALYZE stall or abort due to lack of idle CPU and inaccessible pages.

Causal Chain: Corrupted data pages arriving through the replication stream—or already present on the replica—cause apply workers to encounter errors, forcing retries, validation passes, and potentially single-threaded corruption-repair logic. These loops monopolize CPU, leaving fewer cycles for normal redo apply and query execution, which in turn widens replication lag even further. The growing lag prevents WAL recycling, bloating storage on the primary and lengthening crash-recovery times. Elevated CPU utilization also slows any background index-rebuild or corruption-repair jobs, prolonging the period during which bad pages remain in the active dataset. Conversely, CPU starvation on the primary can lengthen transaction commit times and enlarge transactions, generating burstier WAL that replicas—already throttled by corruption handling—cannot absorb, completing a feedback loop that magnifies both replication backlog and corruption exposure across the cluster.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The metadata that feeds the optimizer—row counts, histograms, correlation and partition statistics—is stale, incomplete or inaccurate, causing systematic cardinality misestimation.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer’s decision logic or plan-reuse mechanism chooses a sub-optimal execution plan even though the statistical inputs are generally available and sound.

When both root causes occur simultaneously, the database can exhibit an amplified mix of symptoms: extreme gaps between estimated and actual row counts, rapid oscillation among widely different plans, sudden regressions after data loads or cache flushes, and high variance in response times for the same SQL text. Plan changes may appear random—sometimes driven by bad statistics, other times by a flawed cost model—making regression patterns hard to reproduce. You may see alternating use of full scans and deeply nested loops, intermittent spills to disk, erratic parallelism activation, and excessive plan recompilations as the optimizer tries to compensate for conflicting cues.

Causally, stale or poorly sampled statistics skew the cost estimates fed into the optimizer, while the plan-selection anomaly magnifies the impact of those skewed numbers by failing to choose a resilient plan or by reusing a parameter-sensitive one. Conversely, even where statistics are marginally acceptable, an overly aggressive or outdated cost model can pick a brittle plan whose performance collapses after the next data change, prompting further statistics churn. The two issues thus reinforce each other: bad statistics mislead the cost model, and a vulnerable plan-selection strategy makes the system more sensitive to every minor statistics deviation, leading to a feedback loop of plan thrashing and performance instability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : The submitted SQL, transaction, or batch logic forces the engine to touch far more rows, pages, or result bytes than the business task actually needs.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical devices or storage-virtualization layer cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth or IOPS demanded by the workload, so I/O queues and latencies explode.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The free space on data, temp, or log volumes nears exhaustion, producing allocation failures, auto-extend stalls, or log-archive back-pressure.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits an escalating mix of symptoms:  • SQL statements appear repeatedly in slow-query logs with highly variable and growing latency.  • Device-level and database wait statistics show both deep I/O queues and space-allocation waits.  • Temp, undo, and log segments bloat during the long-running queries, consuming the last remaining free blocks; auto-extend attempts pause behind already saturated storage paths, and eventually raise out-of-space errors.  • Checkpoints, log flushes, and writes from other sessions are starved, so even read-only statements see elevated latencies.  • Administrators observe contradictory signals—moderate CPU, but soaring I/O wait, shrinking space, and a flood of timeout and "cannot allocate extent" errors.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL logic creates large scans, wide result sets, and oversized transactions that bombard the storage subsystem with reads, spills, and writes. The surge in physical I/O quickly saturates the available throughput; as queues deepen, each I/O takes longer, stretching the lifetime of every open transaction. Prolonged transactions hold temp and log space for longer periods while simultaneously growing those areas, accelerating space depletion. As free space approaches zero, space-allocation failures force additional retries and background clean-ups, which in turn generate more I/O on the already throttled devices. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another in a vicious cycle—heavy logic drives high I/O, high I/O inflates latency, inflated latency magnifies space consumption—culminating in widespread performance collapse and potential service outages.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or pin structures because the buffer manager cannot grant concurrent access fast enough.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log becomes the bottleneck for commit processing, log flushing, or archiving, stalling foreground writes.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages have become physically or logically corrupt, breaking key ordering, page links, or checksums.

When these three root causes strike together, the system shows an entangled symptom set: extreme and erratic commit latency, bursts of CPU spin on page latches, log-flush and buffer-busy wait events appearing side by side, and query results intermittently missing or duplicating rows as corrupted index pages are visited under high latch pressure. Frequent checkpoint storms and forced log switches lengthen the time buffers are held dirty, magnifying latch hold times. Integrity check utilities may hang or block behind the same latch and log waits, and recovery or failover attempts can stall because the damaged pages sit in dirty buffers that cannot be flushed while the log device is saturated.

Causal chain: heavy write traffic first overdrives the log subsystem, stretching commit and checkpoint intervals. Extended checkpoints keep more dirty pages in memory, inflating buffer-pool turnover and intensifying latch contention on the hottest pages. Prolonged contention means pages stay pinned longer, so any latent corruption on popular data or index blocks surfaces more often and under higher concurrency, triggering retry loops, error logging, or full table scans that further inflate redo volume. The extra redo amplifies log saturation, while corrupted pages that cannot be flushed cleanly force additional I/O retries and keep buffers in a permanently dirty state, feeding back into both latch contention and log backlog. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another, driving a vicious cycle of rising latency, shrinking throughput, and escalating data-integrity risk.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects or re-uses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, inflating the cost of individual statements.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer is unable to supply the required read/write bandwidth or latency, so database requests accumulate in the I/O subsystem.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, the system exhibits a compound failure pattern: poorly chosen plans perform large table scans, Cartesian joins, or serial executions that issue many more logical and physical I/Os than a good plan would. The excessive I/O meets an already saturated storage layer, so each physical read or write is delayed. Statements therefore hold row, key-range, or table locks for far longer, lengthening blocking chains. Waiting sessions pile up behind both locks and I/O, driving transaction response times to spike, connection pools to exhaust, and deadlock detectors to fire. Performance metrics show a mixture of high lock-wait time, high I/O wait time, low CPU utilization, erratic plan changes in the cache, and sudden throughput collapses that are difficult to attribute to a single subsystem.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan is the initiating amplifier: it multiplies the amount of data touched and the duration locks are held. The longer lock hold times increase the probability and depth of lock contention. In turn, blocked transactions remain active and continue to issue or retry I/O requests, further stressing the storage layer and aggravating the I/O throughput anomaly. The storage bottleneck feeds back by slowing every I/O-bound statement, which stretches lock lifetimes even more and gives the optimizer more chances to pick or reuse bad plans under changing cache and parameter conditions. The intertwined feedback loops between inefficient plans, prolonged lock contention, and saturated storage create a self-reinforcing degradation that can bring an OLTP system to a standstill unless all three root causes are addressed together.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between table/partition layout, index set, data types, and the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written queries into inefficient scans or lookups.
