Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level memory, I/O, parallelism, or background-worker settings that are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, causing bottlenecks or wasted resources even when the underlying components are healthy.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside heap pages or index structures that makes persisted data and index entries unreliable or unusable.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms overlap and intensify: queries that already suffer from missing or non-covering indexes choose full scans that are further slowed by mis-sized buffer pools or aggressive checkpoint storms, while corrupted pages or mis-linked index leaves cause unpredictable row omissions, duplicates, or engine errors. Operators may observe alternating patterns of plan regressions, sudden I/O bursts, fluctuating CPU spin on lightweight locks, rising retry or deadlock rates during maintenance tasks, and intermittent corruption warnings. Autovacuum, consistency-check, or index-rebuild operations may stall because configuration limits starve them of memory or I/O quota, yet their failure leaves structural damage uncorrected, feeding back into even costlier scan plans. Overall performance and correctness become erratic, and separating design flaws from runtime mis-tuning or corruption side effects becomes extremely difficult.

Causally, a poor schema and index design inflates table and index footprints, increasing buffer-pool and checkpoint pressure; if memory and I/O parameters are already mis-tuned, the engine is forced into more frequent flushes and page evictions, amplifying latency spikes. Vigorous churn from inefficient queries and oversized structures lengthens maintenance windows, raising the likelihood of interrupted writes or partial rebuilds that introduce on-disk corruption. Conversely, latent data-block or index damage can mask the benefits of any later design improvements and lead DBAs to over-allocate memory or alter checkpoint settings in futile attempts to recover performance, deepening the configuration mismatch. The intertwined feedback loop between static design flaws, dynamic mis-configuration, and lurking physical corruption drives the database into a degraded and unstable state that affects both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution metadata are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation by the optimizer.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log file group, buffer, or archival pipeline cannot keep pace with redo generation, so commits stall on log-flush or log-switch waits.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously the database exhibits a compounded performance collapse: poorly estimated plans choose wide scans, large hash builds, or inappropriate join orders that touch far more rows than necessary. The over-sized data touch amplifies lock footprint and hold time, lengthening blocker-waiter chains and raising the probability of deadlocks. At the same time the excessive I/O created by those plans inflates redo volume; commit latency rises as the saturated log subsystem struggles to flush bigger log buffers, further prolonging the duration that locks are held. Symptoms therefore include: explosive growth in both estimated-vs-actual row-count gaps and lock-wait time, surging deadlock reports, escalating log-flush wait statistics, and a backlog of unarchived or unreplicated log segments. Application users perceive slow or hanging transactions followed by timeout or deadlock-victim errors, while internal monitoring shows overlapping cardinality-error warnings, lock-manager waits, and log-write bottlenecks.

Causally, the three anomalies reinforce one another in a feedback loop: 1) Stale statistics mislead the optimizer into selecting plans that scan or update large data regions, inflating redo generation and obtaining many or coarse-grained locks. 2) The bloated lock footprint heightens contention; blocked sessions hold locks and transactional state open longer, generating still more redo during rollbacks or retries. 3) The overloaded log subsystem slows every commit or rollback, extending lock hold times and preventing blocked statements from completing, which in turn prevents automatic statistics refreshes that could have corrected the original misestimates. The intertwined effects continuously degrade throughput until manual intervention breaks the cycle by refreshing statistics, relieving lock hot spots, or expanding and tuning the log subsystem.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Cross-node log receive and apply path falls behind the primary’s log-generation rate.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk data or index pages become physically or logically corrupt or inconsistent.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage devices cannot sustain the read/write bandwidth or latency demanded by the database engine.

When all three root causes strike together, the system exhibits a compound failure surface: replication lag widens rapidly while both primary and replica I/O wait times spike; integrity-check utilities or background scrubbing jobs report page or index corruption; relay or retained WAL segments accumulate on the primary, consuming space and further increasing write latency; replicas may repeatedly disconnect or crash on encountering corrupt pages, causing replay gaps that leave them far behind and unusable for read traffic or failover; normal query traffic experiences elongated response times, and emergency repair actions (reindex, checksum verification, physical copy) run slowly or stall because storage bandwidth is already exhausted.

Causal interaction: saturated storage reduces the throughput of both the primary’s log writer and the replicas’ redo apply threads, directly inflating replication lag. The same I/O pressure increases the chance that incomplete or torn writes occur, leading to new block or index corruption. Conversely, encountering corrupted pages during replay forces replicas to perform additional random reads, error handling, or crash-recovery cycles, which in turn drive up I/O demand and deepen the storage bottleneck. Because replicas cannot advance past the corrupt regions, the primary must retain ever-growing WAL, further stressing disk capacity and write throughput; this retention prevents log recycling, perpetuating high I/O queues and making both replication and corruption recovery progressively harder. The feedback loop among I/O saturation, corruption, and replay lag amplifies each anomaly and can push the cluster into a state where neither failover nor on-line repair is feasible without first relieving the storage constraint.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or poorly controlled growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, and other engine heaps pushes total resident and swap usage beyond the safe limits of the host. 
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log (WAL) records becomes the principal bottleneck on the write path, inflating commit latency and stalling writers. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas are reached before database-level limits, preventing the engine from allocating additional OS objects that it needs to progress. 

When these three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: rapidly growing process RSS, paging spikes, and NUMA or cgroup memory throttling coincide with surging log-flush waits and commit stalls. Archiver or replication lag amplifies, while the engine emits errors for exhausted file handles, shared-memory, or thread creation failures. Checkpoint storms and forced log switches appear alongside sudden process terminations or node reboots triggered by out-of-memory killers. Administrators may observe that despite sufficient raw I/O bandwidth, write performance collapses unpredictably, and new sessions, background workers, or parallel executions intermittently fail to start even though workload pressure persists. 

Causally, aggressive memory allocation fills buffer and work caches until the OS starts paging and tightening kernel limits; this heightens CPU queuing and elongates the path to persist log buffers, directly aggravating the Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly. In turn, elevated commit latency encourages session buildup and longer retention of in-memory state, forcing the engine to request more memory, file descriptors, log segments, and IPC objects, which pushes it harder against OS limits. Once kernel caps are hit, log writers and archivers cannot open new files or allocate additional shared memory, freezing log progression and blocking all transactional work. The feedback loop between memory pressure, stalled log flushing, and OS resource exhaustion accelerates degradation, driving the database into cascading stalls, partial outages, or full instance failure.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL and transaction design forces the engine to touch far more data or hold locks far longer than the business requirement demands.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Metadata about data distribution is stale, missing, or misleading, causing systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal plan choices.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Instance-level settings for memory, parallelism, checkpoints, logging, and background workers are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload.

When all three root causes appear together, symptoms compound: the same business operation may exhibit runaway latency, wildly fluctuating execution plans, and resource waits that do not match real hardware utilization. Statements already written with broad scans or chatty row-by-row access patterns are paired with estimates that radically under- or over-count rows, steering the optimizer toward plans that spill to disk, fan out nested-loop joins, or serialize otherwise parallelizable work. Mis-sized work memory and buffer pools then exaggerate I/O bursts, trigger checkpoint storms, and prolong lock holding, while disabled or throttled statistics maintenance hides the true row-count drift. The resulting picture in monitoring views is a confusing mix of slow queries, frequent plan recompiles, memory pressure, idle hardware, and application timeouts.

Causally, the inefficient SQL logic inflates the volume of data the optimizer must reason about, making it hypersensitive to statistics quality. Stale or coarse statistics mislead the cost model, often selecting plans whose fragility is exposed by the oversized SQL patterns. Meanwhile, mis-configured memory, parallelism, or checkpoint cadence both throttles automatic statistics refresh and limits the engine’s ability to amortize the extra work, feeding back into even staler statistics and longer execution times. Each layer therefore reinforces the next: poor SQL magnifies the impact of bad statistics; bad statistics force plan paths that are intolerant of resource mis-tuning; and mis-tuned parameters slow the corrective mechanisms that could otherwise mitigate SQL or statistics flaws, driving a self-sustaining performance spiral.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is simultaneously suffering from replication-path backlog (standbys cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL fast enough) and front-end network / connection saturation (clients and internal feeders contend for limited transport and connection resources). The two root causes coexist and interact, producing a compound failure surface that spans both cross-node log shipping and client connectivity.

Combined Phenomena: Administrators observe widening replication-lag and log-position gaps while, at the same time, clients hit connection-establishment timeouts, "too many connections" errors, and elevated round-trip times. Retained WAL segments or relay logs accumulate on the primary, disk usage climbs, and replica read-only queries become increasingly stale. Listener backlog queues fill, half-open or idle sockets linger, and authentication or TLS handshakes stall. Because replication streaming uses the same network and socket infrastructure, packet loss or latency spikes show up as both replay delay on replicas and long client-read / client-write waits on the primary. Failover readiness drops, yet manual switchover attempts may also fail because new replication or monitoring sessions cannot attach.

Causal Chain: Network congestion, firewall inspection, or exhausted server socket slots first throttle throughput for both application sessions and replication streams. Diminished bandwidth causes the replica to fall behind; the primary therefore retains additional WAL segments, increasing disk-I/O pressure and prolonging every subsequent network transfer. The growing backlog lengthens replication sockets’ lifetime, holding server processes and TCP ports open and further depleting connection capacity. Conversely, replication delay pushes read traffic back to the primary when replicas become too stale, inflating client connection demand and amplifying the original network bottleneck. The two anomalies thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop that degrades throughput, inflates latency, and jeopardizes durability and high-availability objectives.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, flush, or apply WAL/redo at the rate produced by the primary, creating growing log-position gaps.

Composite definition: The system simultaneously suffers from mis-calibrated runtime parameters and an over-stressed replication pipeline. Configuration flaws on the primary or replicas both distort local resource usage and prevent replicas from keeping up, producing a blend of internal wait imbalances and cross-node lag.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Rapidly growing replication lag, retained WAL segments, and mounting disk consumption on the primary even though storage and network throughput appear under-utilised; 2) Bursty checkpoint or page-flush activity triggered by an inappropriate checkpoint interval, which in turn floods replication with spikes of redo; 3) Walsender and apply-worker queues backed up while CPU cores remain partly idle because work-memory or parallelism caps throttle apply threads; 4) Stale read-only queries on replicas, increased failover RPO/RTO, and sudden performance regressions following parameter changes, version upgrades, or instance resizing events.

Causal chain: Mis-tuned parameters (e.g., too small max_wal_senders, aggressive checkpoint_timeout, undersized work_mem, or poorly chosen apply-worker parallelism) raise the volume and burstiness of WAL generation and/or limit the number of threads that can ship and replay it, directly intensifying replication synchronization pressure. As replicas fall behind, the primary is forced to retain extra log files, inflating disk usage and lengthening checkpoints, which further exposes the impact of the faulty configuration (longer fsync queues, cache flush storms). Conversely, apply lag on replicas masks the true effect of the parameter mis-tuning, delaying feedback signals such as CPU or I/O saturation and making root-cause isolation harder. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other: bad parameters magnify replication backlog, and the backlog amplifies the adverse side-effects of the misconfiguration, degrading both primary and replica performance and resilience.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The cost model relies on stale, incomplete, or skew-blind statistics, producing systematic cardinality misestimates that misguide plan selection.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating table and index size and adding visibility-check overhead.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Frequently accessed pages and in-flight I/O slots are protected by latches that become hot under pressure, forcing sessions to stall or spin while waiting for buffer-cache access.

When these three conditions coexist, the database can display a compound symptom set: queries suddenly flip from index to full-table scans over massively bloated heaps and indexes; the scans drag huge numbers of dead tuples into the buffer pool, displacing useful pages and amplifying buffer churn; latch and buffer-busy waits soar, CPUs spin on hot root pages, and overall throughput collapses. Execution-plan estimates diverge drastically from reality, autovacuum or purge workers remain saturated yet fall further behind, checkpoint and background-writer activity spike, and storage consumption and I/O latency rise concurrently. Administrators may observe alternating bursts of high I/O, CPU spin, and memory pressure, with query plans oscillating unpredictably as statistics age and data volume grows.

Causal chain: heavy OLTP update/delete traffic generates MVCC bloat, swelling the physical size of tables and indexes. Because statistics are not refreshed at the same pace, the optimizer still believes row counts are low and selects plans (e.g., nested-loop joins or index probes) that, once executed, touch many more pages than expected. The unexpected I/O inflates buffer-pool turnover; hot index and freelist pages needed for version look-ups suffer latch congestion. Meanwhile, the enlarged object footprints and constant churn consume buffer slots, lengthening dirty-page queues and prolonging latch hold times, which in turn slow vacuum/cleanup workers, allowing even more dead versions to accumulate. This feedback loop ties stale statistics, MVCC bloat, and buffer/latch contention into a self-reinforcing composite anomaly that can cripple transactional workloads unless all three root causes are addressed together.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses or re-uses an execution plan that is materially sub-optimal even though statistics are reasonable.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on buffer-pool pages or their latches, causing CPU spin waits and latency spikes.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or log areas run out of free space, leading to allocation failures and stalled writes.

Composite definition: The workload encounters all three conditions concurrently—poor execution plans drive excessive I/O and buffer hot spots, those hot spots intensify low-level latch contention, and the amplified I/O churn quickly consumes the remaining physical or logical storage space, eventually hitting space exhaustion boundaries.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Identical statements flip between index scans and table scans, producing unexpected full-table or hash-join plans that touch far more pages than normal. 2) Buffer-busy, page-latch, and IO wait events rise together; CPUs show high spin time while throughput flattens. 3) Free-space monitors drop precipitously; auto-extend or archive operations fail, and DML or log writes stall. 4) Performance volatility escalates—each plan flip can suddenly flood the buffer cache, evicting useful pages and forcing more physical reads against an already space-starved storage layer.

Causal chain: A sub-optimal plan (e.g., full scan instead of index access) multiplies page touches and dirty-page generation. The surge of concurrent accesses to a small set of root or data pages creates intense latch contention, elongating critical sections and prolonging transaction lifetimes. Longer transactions and extra I/O amplify log growth and data-file expansion, rapidly consuming remaining disk space. As space approaches exhaustion, autogrowth pauses and checkpoints slow, further extending latch holds and causing the optimizer to invalidate or recompile plans more frequently, which can select even worse plans. The feedback loop between poor plan choice, buffer/latch pressure, and shrinking free space magnifies latency and eventually leads to workload-blocking space errors.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from heavy lock-manager blocking/deadlocks and from excessive accumulation of obsolete MVCC versions, so each transaction is at risk of both waiting on incompatible locks and wading through bloated heaps and indexes whose cleanup is lagging behind.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Administrators will see long lock wait queues, deadlock victim rollbacks, and rising application time-outs together with rapidly growing table and index sizes, a persistently busy or backlogged vacuum/cleanup process, and planner misestimates caused by low live-row density. Throughput and latency variability become extreme: sessions that finally acquire their locks still run slowly because scans must traverse many dead versions, while lengthy scans keep locks held for longer, enlarging blocking chains. I/O and CPU usage rise concurrently—disk reads driven by bloat, and CPU cycles consumed by lock management and version visibility checks—yet business transactions per second keep falling.

Causal Interaction: Lock contention prolongs the lifetime of update and delete transactions, keeping their snapshots and row versions alive and preventing background cleaners from advancing the version horizon; this accelerates version-store growth. The resulting table and index bloat lengthens read and write execution times, so transactions hold locks for longer and are more likely to collide, escalating row locks to page or table level and deepening contention. Cleanup workers may also be throttled by locks that protect hot pages, causing them to yield and fall further behind. Thus each anomaly amplifies the other in a positive feedback loop that degrades both concurrency control and storage health until manual intervention or a workload drop breaks the cycle.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine allocates more process memory than the host can safely provide, leading to paging, swap storms, or OOM terminations.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Threads stall on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O-slot primitives because many sessions compete for the same cache frames or page states.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing is throttled by slow log buffering, flushing, or archiving, making the log device or pipeline the primary write-path bottleneck.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: commit latency and page-access latency rise together, CPU usage oscillates between spin-loops on latches and kernel time servicing memory pressure, and throughput collapses unpredictably. Wait-event views show a mix of MEMORY_PRESSURE, PAGE_LATCH_*, LOG_FLUSH, and IO_SCHEDULER waits. Buffer-pool hit ratios fluctuate as pages are evicted by memory pressure while the same hot pages are immediately re-read, amplifying latch waits. Concurrently, log flushes slow down because the kernel is paging and the log device queues are saturated, causing transactions to queue behind both latch acquisition and commit synchronization. Administrators may mis-attribute the slowdown to any single subsystem because symptoms overlap and mask each other.

Causal interaction: oversized work areas and plan/cache bloat inflate the resident-set size, forcing the OS to reclaim pages and lengthening dirty-page flush cycles. Prolonged flush cycles keep buffer frames pinned, intensifying latch contention on the hot pages that remain. At the same time, the memory-starved kernel delays log-buffer flushes, so transactions that finally obtain buffer latches still block on LOG_SYNC before completing. The stalled commits, in turn, hold locks and retain buffer pins longer, feeding back into latch pressure and extending the lifetime of in-memory structures, which further swells memory consumption. The three subsystems therefore reinforce one another in a vicious circle that degrades both read-modify-write and pure write workloads and can culminate in cluster node eviction or forced instance restart.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement and transaction design forces the engine to scan or modify far more data, rows, and pages than business logic requires.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot buffer pages and their protecting latches become serialization points, causing sessions to spin or block while trying to pin or modify pages.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage subsystem cannot supply read or write bandwidth fast enough, so database I/O queues grow and service times climb.

When these three root causes strike together, the workload issues excessive page accesses, the hottest of which pile up in the buffer cache and contend on latches while the same pages are also waiting for slow physical reads or flushes. Observable symptoms are an explosive mixture of long-tail SQL latency, severe buffer-busy and page-latch waits, sustained I/O wait events, and CPU spin with little progress. Slow-query logs fill with the same heavyweight statements; wait-event histograms show alternating spikes of latch waits and I/O waits; checkpoint or dirty-page flush operations linger, causing transaction commit latency and drawing more latch contention on the log buffer. Application threads may time out, retry, and further magnify the concurrent pressure.

Causally, the chatty or scan-heavy SQL multiplies the number of buffer touches; the surge in touched pages raises the probability that many sessions target the same index root, data hotspot, or insert location, intensifying latch contention. Because storage bandwidth is already saturated, pages stay in flight or dirty longer, prolonging the time latches must be held and increasing the likelihood of spin or block. Conversely, the latch pile-ups delay page release, throttling page recycling and forcing still more physical reads, which deepens the storage backlog. The result is a feedback loop in which inefficient SQL amplifies buffer-level hot spots, latch serialization keeps pages locked in memory, and constrained storage throughput prevents timely I/O completion, collectively driving runaway latency and throughput collapse.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Critical metadata such as row-count estimates, histograms, and correlation statistics are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer’s plan-choice logic selects a poor execution plan even though, in principle, an efficient plan is available.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, temp, or log areas is exhausted or approaching hard limits, leading to allocation failures and stalled processing.

When all three root causes co-exist, the database may display compound symptoms: execution plans swing unpredictably between full scans and deeply nested loops, produce vastly inaccurate estimated vs. actual rows, and generate outsized workfiles, spill areas, undo, or redo that rapidly deplete the already scarce storage. Auto-growth events occur frequently but fail or hang, hash or sort operations abort with "no space" errors, and emergency log switches block user sessions. Operators observe oscillating plan behavior after each statistics refresh attempt, yet refresh jobs themselves may fail because temp or sample segments cannot be allocated.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics mislead the cost model, increasing the likelihood that the optimizer selects an inefficient plan; even when statistics are refreshed, the selection logic may still cache or reuse the earlier bad plan. The resulting plan often performs unnecessary full-table scans, large hash aggregates, or excessive spill-to-disk operations, which consume temp and log space far beyond what the allocator predicted. As space dwindles, auto-stats collection, plan compilation tests, and maintenance jobs are unable to create work segments, leaving statistics stale and forcing the optimizer to continue using or reusing flawed plans. Each component therefore reinforces the others, producing a feedback loop that accelerates performance degradation and culminates in space-related service outages.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log generation, buffering, flushing, switching, or archiving path on the primary becomes the main bottleneck, inflating commit latency and preventing timely log-space reuse.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or change-data consumers cannot receive, store, or apply the primary’s log stream at the required rate, producing widening log-position gaps and retaining old log segments on the primary.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-level caps on file descriptors, processes, shared memory, or other OS resources are reached, hindering the database and its background workers from allocating essential kernel objects.

When these three root causes manifest together, the database shows a compound failure pattern: transaction commits slow or stall while replication lag expands in lock-step; alert logs fill with log-flush, log-sync, and replication-apply wait events alongside OS errors such as “too many open files” or “cannot allocate shared memory.” Log files, archive destinations, and relay logs balloon because log recycling is blocked both by replication retention and by the engine’s inability to create or close files under exhausted OS limits. Checkpoints and log switches become more frequent yet less effective, replicas fall progressively further behind, and failover readiness degrades. Administrators observe simultaneous pressure on primary I/O, soaring disk consumption, throttled network throughput to replicas, and sporadic failures to start new background or apply processes.

Causal chain: slow log flush/switch operations leave less headroom in the active log area, forcing the primary to retain segments longer. The growing backlog magnifies replication workload; replicas already constrained by I/O or apply throughput fall even further behind, extending the retention window. Both effects cause the primary and archiver to open ever-more log, archive, and relay files while keeping existing ones pinned. As file handles, asynchronous-I/O contexts, and process slots accumulate, they collide with OS-level limits, triggering allocation failures that in turn further impede log writes and replication apply threads. The three anomalies reinforce each other in a feedback loop: log pressure → replication lag → handle/process accumulation → OS denials → even slower log/replication progress, eventually leading to transaction freezes, replica disconnects, and potential outage.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to process far more data or rows than the true business need. 
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database-related processes saturate host CPU cycles, creating system-wide compute contention. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, threads, shared memory, or similar objects are reached, preventing the database from acquiring additional OS resources. 

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a layered failure pattern: statement latencies grow long and variable; CPU utilization hovers at or above core capacity with high run-queue lengths; meanwhile, new sessions, parallel workers, or I/O requests intermittently fail with "too many open files," "cannot create thread," or shared-memory errors. Slow-query logs and performance views show repeated, bloated SQL with extreme CPU time, while the error log and system journal simultaneously record kernel resource-limit denials. End-user symptoms range from sporadic timeouts and retries to partial outages where existing sessions crawl while new connections are rejected.

Causally, inefficient SQL constructs (wide scans, Cartesian joins, long-lived transactions) drive excessive CPU demand. The resulting saturation lengthens task runtimes and escalates context switches, increasing the number of concurrent threads, open file descriptors, and asynchronous I/O contexts the database tries to allocate. As CPU pressure rises, the engine spawns more background or parallel workers in an attempt to keep up, rapidly depleting kernel-level quotas. Once an OS limit is hit, the database cannot create additional execution or I/O resources, which forces even well-written queries to queue behind stuck tasks, further extending transaction lifetimes and compounding CPU consumption. The feedback loop—inefficient SQL → CPU exhaustion → kernel limit exhaustion → wider systemic slowdown—amplifies each individual anomaly and can culminate in cascading service degradation or outage.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Sustained physical-device bandwidth and latency limits are reached, so every read or write request queues and waits.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space on data, log, temp, or backup volumes is exhausted or about to exhaust, preventing further allocations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: The network path, listener, or connection-handling layer cannot accept, transmit, or maintain the required number of client sessions or bytes in flight.

When all three exist simultaneously, the database shows a volatile mix of symptoms: I/O wait events soar while read/write latencies fluctuate; auto-extension, log switch, temp usage, or backup operations intermittently fail with out-of-space errors; connection establishment and result-set delivery stall or time out, and clients see both "no space" and "cannot connect" errors. Backend processes may accumulate in client-read/client-write and buffer-I/O waits at once, queue depths on storage devices remain full, and network socket queues overflow, making it difficult to attribute the primary bottleneck. Batch windows elongate, checkpoints linger, archiving falls behind, and retry storms from the application add further load across all three constrained resources.

Causally, the three root causes amplify one another: slow storage throughput lengthens the time each write holds file handles and network sockets, pushing up concurrent session counts and exhausting listener backlogs. At the same time, reduced throughput delays log archival and backup jobs, accelerating space consumption until capacity thresholds are hit, which in turn forces additional synchronous space checks and allocation overhead that further degrades I/O performance. Network congestion or connection thrashing slows remote copy or replication traffic, preventing space-reclaim operations and keeping disks fuller for longer, while client retries multiply transactional I/O and network chatter. The feedback loop among limited bandwidth, shrinking space, and choking connectivity drives the database into a compounded degradation state that is more severe than any single anomaly alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic actually requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are reasonably accurate.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine allocates or holds more memory than the host can safely provide, leading to OS-level pressure or paging.

When these three root causes coexist, the workload issues compound. Verbose or poorly-scoped SQL drives voluminous data access; the optimizer then occasionally locks in plans that further magnify I/O and CPU demand (e.g., full scans, hash joins, or blown-out nested loops); the resulting surges in buffers, work areas, and plan cache cause memory footprints to balloon beyond physical limits. Observable symptoms include: extreme and highly variable statement latency, repeated slow-query log entries, frequent plan flips between bad alternatives, sudden spikes in buffer-cache churn and work-memory usage, sustained OS paging or swap-ins, query cancellations or out-of-memory terminations, and cluster node eviction or database instance restarts. Session traces may reveal wide scans combined with excessive hash or sort space, while memory monitors show resident-set size climbing in step with each batch or ad-hoc burst.

Causally, the inefficiencies introduced at the SQL layer inflate row counts and intermediate result sizes; this expands the search space the optimizer must cost, increasing the likelihood it will misjudge the best plan or reuse an ill-suited cached plan. Once a poor plan is chosen—such as a full table scan or an unbounded hash aggregate—it requests large work buffers and floods the buffer cache with pages that have little re-use value. The inflated memory demand erodes headroom for all sessions, causing global memory pressure. Under pressure the engine may evict hot pages prematurely or swap, which slows subsequent parts of the same long-running statements, creating feedback that further prolongs transaction duration and keeps memory allocated even longer. Thus, inefficient SQL, sub-optimal plan selection, and runaway memory consumption reinforce one another, amplifying latency variability and risking stability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of statistics or optimizer choice.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data or metadata objects, producing wait chains or deadlocks that stall or abort workload execution.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes collectively saturate host CPU, driving run-queue growth, context switching, and broad latency inflation independent of any single SQL statement.

When all three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern: queries perform full scans or non-covering index lookups that touch many rows, inflating the lock footprint and holding row/page/table locks far longer than expected. The enlarged critical sections create dense blocker–waiter trees and frequent deadlocks, while the excessive I/O and predicate evaluation work drives CPU utilization toward saturation. Under high CPU load, the lock manager itself slows, lengthening detection and wake-up cycles, so blocking and deadlock resolution take longer. Applications see sharp spikes in response times, timeouts, and retry storms; monitoring shows near-max CPU usage, long lock-wait queues, repeated deadlock victim messages, and plan shapes dominated by scans that could be selective with proper indexing.

Causally, poor schema and index design is the initiating factor: missing or non-covering indexes force broad data access, which increases the number and duration of locks acquired. The prolonged locks raise the probability of collisions and deadlocks, producing Transaction Lock Contention. As sessions wait, blocked tasks may still consume CPU through spin-loops or wake-ups, while unblocked sessions keep issuing inefficient scans, jointly driving a CPU Resource Anomaly. Elevated CPU usage slows lock acquisition, latch operations, and deadlock detection, further extending transaction lifetimes and deepening contention. The feedback loop—inefficient access ➔ longer locks ➔ higher contention ➔ CPU saturation ➔ slower lock processing—amplifies each symptom until overall OLTP throughput collapses.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer bases its cost estimates on stale, incomplete, or missing statistics, systematically misestimating cardinalities and choosing inefficient execution plans.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data items, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger roll-backs.

When both root causes strike at once, the database experiences a compound failure mode in which poor plan choices amplify locking pressure and the resulting blocks further hinder statistics maintenance. Observable symptoms include: 1) huge gaps between estimated and actual row counts, 2) plans that scan or sort far more rows than expected, 3) sudden lock-wait time spikes, deadlock reports, and lock-escalation events, 4) throughput collapse accompanied by CPU and I/O under-utilization while sessions wait on locks, 5) repeated plan recompiles that fail to stabilize, and 6) deferred or aborted automatic statistics updates because the objects they target are locked for long periods.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into selecting plans that touch many unnecessary rows or use sub-optimal join orders, expanding lock footprints from key to page or table scope and lengthening transaction duration. The enlarged concurrency window increases the likelihood of lock collisions, intensifying blocking chains and deadlocks. In turn, the prolonged locks prevent the statistics engine from acquiring the short-term metadata locks it needs to refresh statistics, allowing statistics staleness to persist or worsen. This feedback loop progressively degrades plan quality and concurrency, leading to severe and self-reinforcing performance deterioration.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than the true business requirement demands.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Instance-level runtime parameters are mis-tuned so that memory, background workers, checkpoint cadence, or parallelism no longer match hardware capacity or workload profile.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, page pins, or lightweight latches, creating a bottleneck inside the buffer manager rather than running out of memory itself.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a compound symptom pattern: 1) statement latency outliers and repeated slow-query entries; 2) bursty or sustained waits on page latches and buffer-busy events even when global CPU, I/O, or memory utilization looks moderate; 3) rapid oscillations between CPU spinning and idle periods; 4) checkpoint or background-writer storms triggered earlier than expected; 5) application timeouts escalating into long-running transactions that hold hot pages even longer, magnifying contention footprints; and 6) diagnostic views showing both inefficient SQL plans and suspicious configuration ratios (e.g., undersized buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint_target) that fail to alleviate the hot-page churn.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL logic inflates the volume and frequency of page touches, turning a few index root pages or sequence blocks into extreme hot spots. A mis-sized buffer pool or ill-timed checkpoint/worker scheduling (configuration anomaly) prevents those pages from staying resident or being flushed smoothly, increasing the turnover of the cache and the number of threads simultaneously demanding the same pages. As concurrency rises, the probability of latch collisions on the overused pages skyrockets, producing Buffer Cache and Latch Contention. In turn, the contention inflates the latency of each already inefficient statement, extending transaction lifetimes and redo generation windows, which further stresses the mis-tuned memory and checkpoint parameters. The three issues therefore reinforce one another in a feedback loop that degrades throughput far more severely than any single anomaly in isolation.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of database memory regions (buffer/plan caches, work areas, etc.) that pushes the host into severe memory pressure, paging, or OOM conditions.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Hot-page or latch serialization inside the buffer manager that forces sessions to spin or wait when pinning, accessing, or flushing shared pages.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo at the rate the primary generates it, leading to widening log‐position and replay lag.

When all three root causes are active, the database shows an intertwined failure pattern: memory pressure inflates buffer-replacement churn while hot pages and latch waits spike, driving CPU spin and elongated service times on the primary. The same saturation reduces headroom for the replication sender process, and the stalled page flushes needed to recycle dirty buffers restrain checkpoint progress, so retained log segments and relay logs balloon. On replicas, backlog growth forces larger memory footprints for relay/applier buffers, possibly inducing their own memory exhaustion and further slowing apply. Observability surfaces reveal simultaneous high memory utilization, escalating page-latch or buffer-busy waits, replication apply/flush lag, and log recycling frozen by both memory and latch bottlenecks; symptoms blur together, making single-cause diagnosis difficult.

Causally, uncontrolled memory allocation amplifies buffer pool turnover; as pages are evicted prematurely, they become hot and are immediately re-read, intensifying latch contention. The extra CPU and I/O consumed by this churn slows checkpoint and log flush threads, throttling the replication sender’s ability to stream redo. Replication lag then prevents log truncation, extending the primary’s active log set and enlarging memory-resident replication queues, which feed back into overall memory pressure. On replicas, delayed apply keeps buffer pages dirty longer, prolonging their latch holding time and echoing contention downstream. This positive feedback loop between memory exhaustion, latch serialization, and replication backlog escalates latency, risks OOM or node eviction, and undermines HA objectives.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures (tables, partitions, indexes, datatypes, constraints) do not match the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths and inflating DML and query cost.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : The replication pipeline cannot receive, persist, or apply primary-side log records fast enough, causing widening apply lag and retention of log segments on the source.

When these two root causes strike at the same time, the database exhibits a mixed set of local performance issues and distributed data-movement symptoms: primary queries suffer from full scans, non-covering index lookups, and write slow-downs due to oversized or missing indexes, while replicas simultaneously fall further behind because the bloated change stream (extra page writes, larger redo records, unnecessary index maintenance) overwhelms network, I/O, and apply threads. Monitoring may show high CPU and I/O on both primary and replicas, growing replication lag, expanding WAL/binlog retention, hot-spot pages locked on the replicas during re-indexing, and unpredictable read staleness that cannot be eliminated merely by tuning replication parameters.

Causally, the poor physical design inflates every data modification—each insert, update, or delete touches more pages and indexes, enlarging transaction-log volume and increasing per-statement latency. The heavier log stream must traverse the replication channel, stressing network and replica resources; as replicas fall behind, retained log segments accumulate on the primary, further consuming I/O bandwidth and storage and lengthening checkpoint and vacuum cycles. Conversely, sustained replication lag prevents timely feedback about design fixes (e.g., new indexes) and can hold metadata locks, delaying online schema evolution and perpetuating the sub-optimal design. Together, the two anomalies reinforce each other, degrading both local workload performance and the availability of up-to-date replicas, thereby compromising overall system throughput, latency, and resilience.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database concurrently suffers from runaway MVCC version-store bloat, mis-tuned engine parameters that distort internal housekeeping cadence, and hard ceilings imposed by operating-system resource limits. The result is a compound failure mode where version cleanup cannot catch up, engine subsystems are configured in ways that mask or worsen the backlog, and the kernel refuses additional resources just when the database tries to recover.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Administrators observe steep growth of obsolete row versions and rollback records while autovacuum/cleanup workers stay permanently busy yet ineffective. Checkpoint, log-flush, or background-worker waits spike despite storage and CPU still showing spare capacity; at the same time, new parallel workers, back-end processes, or I/O contexts intermittently fail to start with kernel-level "too many open files", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "resource temporarily unavailable" errors. Page and index sizes expand quickly, sequential scans slow down, and the planner misestimates row counts, all while wait-event samples oscillate between engine-level maintenance waits and kernel-level allocation failures. After manual restarts or configuration tweaks, short periods of relief are followed by even faster deterioration because workers launched to catch up immediately collide with OS quotas.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Heavy update/delete churn produces large numbers of dead versions (MVCC anomaly). Misaligned configuration parameters—such as an undersized buffer pool, too-low autovacuum cost limits, or overly aggressive parallel-worker settings—delay cleanup and inflate the number of background workers the engine tries to spawn (configuration anomaly). These extra workers demand more file descriptors, shared memory segments, and threads; when host-level limits are set conservatively or have been exhausted by lingering handles from earlier crashes, the kernel denies the requests (OS-limit anomaly). Each denial prevents cleanup or checkpoint activity from scaling, causing further version buildup, larger tables, longer checkpoints, and yet more worker spawn attempts, forming a positive feedback loop that rapidly degrades transactional throughput and risks complete stall.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions hold or request incompatible locks on the same resources, causing wait chains or deadlocks that stall or abort statements.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, enlarging data structures and slowing visibility checks.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or other OS objects, preventing further allocations.

When all three root causes strike together, the database experiences compound symptoms: long lock-wait times and deadlock retries surface alongside rapidly growing version stores, bloated tables, and constantly busy autovacuum/cleaner tasks. Simultaneously, background workers, parallel query helpers, or even ordinary sessions intermittently fail to start because the process exhausts file-handle, semaphore, or shared-memory limits. Administrators see lock-manager wait graphs, surging deadlock victim counts, soaring disk usage from version bloat, cleanup workers stuck or throttled, and operating-system logs complaining about resource exhaustion. From the client side this manifests as unpredictable latency spikes, timeouts, aborted transactions that must be retried, and sporadic "cannot allocate OS resource" errors.

Causal chain: heavy OLTP update/delete activity creates many row versions; long-running or blocked transactions (due to lock contention) keep old snapshots alive, preventing version cleanup and inflating the version store. The swelling version store enlarges on-disk structures and lengthens checkpoint and vacuum cycles, which in turn extend lock durations and increase contention. To cope, the database spawns more cleanup or parallel worker processes—quickly approaching or exceeding OS limits on file descriptors, shared memory, or process counts. Once those limits are hit, new workers cannot start, further stalling vacuum and deadlock-detector activity, so both version bloat and lock queues worsen. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others, driving a feedback loop that degrades throughput and may culminate in partial or full service outage.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating the version store and bloating on-disk structures.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log (WAL) records becomes the bottleneck, stretching commit latency and stalling write throughput.

Composite definition: Both version-store bloat and log-subsystem saturation are active at the same time, so every modifying transaction must cope with heavier MVCC bookkeeping while also waiting longer for its corresponding log records to be flushed and archived.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Commit times rise unpredictably because transactions spend extra CPU cycles scanning swollen version chains and then block on congested log-flush waits. 2) Table and index files grow rapidly alongside the WAL directory, causing storage exhaustion warnings for both data and log areas. 3) Autovacuum or purge workers run continuously yet fall further behind, while checkpoint and log-archive processes report backlog; checkpoint storms triggered by the log side amplify IO pressure on already bloated heaps. 4) Planners misestimate row counts due to table bloat, producing scan plans that magnify the I/O amplified by frequent checkpoints, making it difficult to attribute latency spikes to one layer alone.

Causal chain and reinforcement: High update/delete churn first inflates the version store; the extra redo produced by deleting and relinking MVCC versions accelerates WAL generation. The swollen WAL in turn forces more frequent checkpoints and log-file switches, throttling background cleaners that need IO bandwidth to prune dead tuples, so MVCC bloat accumulates even faster. If archive or replication lag prevents log recycling, disk space pressure can suspend new transactions; long-running snapshots retained by slow replicas also keep old versions alive, preventing cleanup. Thus each anomaly feeds the other, creating a positive feedback loop that degrades throughput, inflates storage, and risks full-stop outages.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution statistics are stale, missing, or insufficient, causing systematic cardinality misestimates that mis-guide the optimizer’s cost calculations and plan selection.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates or leaks memory beyond the safe capacity of the host, producing sustained OS memory pressure, paging, or OOM events that disrupt normal processing.

When both root causes are present, the workload can exhibit a cascade of symptoms: queries choose overly memory-hungry plans (e.g., large hash joins, multi-GB sorts) because of bad cardinality estimates, while the engine is already under memory stress. This leads to rapid inflation of work areas, frequent hash/sort spills, thrashing between buffer cache eviction and OS swapping, frequent plan recompilations with wildly fluctuating shapes, prolonged execution times, degraded cache hit ratios, and intermittent session or instance terminations. Monitoring tools may show both extreme estimate-vs-actual row count gaps and concurrently escalating resident-set sizes, swap activity, and memory-pressure wait events, making isolation of the primary trigger difficult.

Causally, stale or poor statistics steer the optimizer toward plans that demand excessive memory. Those allocations accelerate exhaustion of available memory, intensifying the Memory Allocation Anomaly. In turn, heavy memory pressure can throttle or abort automatic statistics collection and cause background processes to skip or down-sample statistics updates, perpetuating or worsening the statistics inaccuracy. The feedback loop between misestimation-driven memory-greedy plans and memory scarcity amplifies both issues, resulting in systemic performance collapse and heightened risk of crashes or cluster failovers.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously suffers from runaway accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions and from saturation or instability of the network / connection-handling layer, so that internal storage-management pressure and external communication bottlenecks coexist and interact to degrade OLTP throughput and availability.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Administrators observe ballooning table and index sizes, escalating autovacuum or purge backlogs, and steadily worsening sequential-scan times while, at the same moments, clients experience slow or failed connection attempts, intermittent time-outs, and prolonged fetch latencies. Backend processes pile up in client-read or client-write waits, yet overall transaction throughput drops because statements also spend more time traversing bloated heaps and indexes. Listener queues fill, socket counts spike with half-open or idle connections holding old snapshots, and version-store wrap-around alarms coexist with operating-system warnings about exhausted file descriptors or TCP retransmissions. The mixed symptoms can obscure root-cause isolation because server-side I/O amplification mimics network slowness, while network stalls extend transaction lifetimes and hide version-bloat effects until space or XID horizons are suddenly reached.

Causal interaction: Network congestion or connection-pool exhaustion delays transaction commit/close messages, leaving sessions in long-running states that keep their old snapshots alive. These snapshots hold back the global xmin or equivalent reclaim horizon, preventing vacuum/purge workers from removing dead tuples and deleted index entries. As obsolete versions accumulate, on-disk and in-cache data structures grow, increasing the work each query must perform and lengthening result-set transmission times. Larger result sets and slower scans in turn prolong client/network usage per transaction, further stressing listener backlogs, socket buffers, and bandwidth, creating a positive feedback loop that amplifies both anomalies and accelerates resource exhaustion. Ultimately, the intertwined issues can culminate in transaction-ID wraparound risks, critical disk-space pressure, widespread connection failures, and severe OLTP service degradation.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite usable statistics, often because of flawed cost comparisons, plan reuse pathologies, or version/configuration changes.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database hits kernel-enforced ceilings on objects such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, threads, or async-I/O contexts, causing failures outside the engine’s own resource governance.

When both root causes are present, workloads exhibit erratic and hard-to-explain behaviour: the same statement may alternate between fast and extremely slow executions; some runs error out with OS-level "cannot create thread/file/shm" messages, while others limp through with degraded performance. Parallel queries may start but stall after only a subset of workers appear, leading to skewed execution, temp-spill explosions, or repeated plan abort/retry cycles. System-wide, operators observe sudden surges in CPU and I/O from full scans or massive hash builds selected by the optimizer, coinciding with spikes in kernel resource-exhaustion logs. Session creation, background autovacuum or checkpoint processes, and I/O completion threads intermittently fail, producing partial outages that disappear once load subsides.

Causal chain: a poor plan often allocates far more resources than a well-tuned one—opening many table/index files, spawning numerous workers, or spilling to large temporary files. This accelerates consumption of kernel-limited objects, pushing the system over OS quotas. Once limits are reached, the database cannot create additional workers, files, or I/O contexts, causing in-flight queries to abort or replan. The optimizer, unaware of the external constraint, may repeatedly choose the same high-resource plan, triggering a feedback loop of retries, plan cache pollution, and further resource churn. Conversely, OS denials can invalidate or refuse parallel plans, forcing the optimizer to fall back to less efficient serial scans, which lengthen execution time and keep resources busy even longer. The mutual reinforcement of bad plan choices and kernel resource exhaustion amplifies latency variance, throughput collapse, and operational instability across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, forming long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress until victims are rolled back.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and undo records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating the version store and degrading visibility checks.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Buffer caches, work areas, and other in-memory structures grow beyond the host’s safe capacity, provoking paging, OOM kills, or instance restarts.

When these three root causes strike at once, the database exhibits a toxic mix of symptoms:  
• Sessions pile up in lock-wait or deadlock retry loops while overall transaction throughput and application responsiveness collapse.  
• Heap and index footprints balloon because cleanup workers are prevented from advancing the snapshot horizon, inflating on-disk size, slowing sequential scans, and further stressing shared buffers.  
• The surging version store and proliferating lock objects consume large amounts of shared memory; combined with unbounded per-query work areas and buffer-cache churn, this tips the host into heavy paging or OOM events.  
• Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in lock-wait time, deadlock detections, bloat and vacuum/autovacuum lag, rapidly growing memory RSS, and degraded cache hit ratios; emergency restarts may occur, wiping in-flight work and masking the underlying dual/triple interaction.

Causal interaction: Hot rows or long-running transactions first create lock contention. Blocked or orphaned transactions hold snapshots open, freezing the MVCC cleanup horizon and causing rapid version accumulation. The expanding version store must be cached or paged, driving up shared-memory and OS memory consumption. Rising memory pressure slows background cleaners, which further delays version reclamation, while paging elongates lock-hold durations as transactions struggle to read bloated pages. This positive feedback loop tightens lock contention, accelerates bloat, and amplifies memory exhaustion, ultimately threatening database availability through deadlocks, timeouts, and process termination.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal physical schema/index design, heavy transaction lock contention, and excessive or poorly managed memory allocation. Together they create a feedback loop in which inefficient access paths inflate lock footprints and execution time, while bloated memory structures contend for limited RAM, all under a concurrency-intensive workload.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Queries that should be index-efficient instead scan large portions of tables or non-covering indexes, holding row/page/table locks far longer than expected. 2) Lock-wait graphs and deadlock reports show long chains and frequent victim rollbacks, accompanied by application timeouts and retry storms. 3) Overall memory consumption of buffer pools, work areas, and plan cache rises sharply as full scans flood the buffer cache and ad-hoc plans accumulate; the OS may exhibit paging, swap activity, or OOM kills that further lengthen lock-hold times. 4) Throughput decays and latency becomes highly variable; short transactions occasionally stall for seconds or minutes, and node restarts or failovers can occur under sustained memory pressure.

Causal chain and interaction: Missing or misaligned indexes force even selective OLTP statements into full-table or wide index scans. These scans not only read more pages, bloating the buffer cache and plan cache, but also acquire more and coarser locks, enlarging the lock footprint. The longer I/O and CPU time of each statement increases the interval during which locks are held, escalating the probability of concurrent conflicts and deadlocks. Simultaneously, the excess pages and work memory consumed by the scans drive the system toward memory pressure; when physical RAM is exhausted and the OS starts paging, query execution slows further, extending lock durations and deepening blocking chains. Conversely, lock buildup stalls transactions that would normally release buffers, causing more sessions to accumulate private work areas and pinned pages, aggravating memory exhaustion. Thus, poor schema/index design multiplies lock contention, lock contention amplifies memory residency, and memory pressure feeds back to slow execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle that degrades OLTP performance and stability.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data or metadata objects, leading to long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall foreground work until a waiter times out or a victim is aborted.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical devices or storage fabric cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database, causing prolonged page-in, log-write, and temp-space waits despite adequate CPU and memory.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client/server links, listeners, authentication paths, or socket resources are saturated or unstable, inflating connection-setup time, stalling result streaming, and exhausting backend connection slots.

When all three root causes are active, symptoms intertwine: transactions hold locks longer because disk reads, writes, or fsyncs are sluggish, lengthening the lifespan of critical sections. The extended lock tenure propagates deeper blocker-waiter trees, raising lock-wait timeouts, deadlock frequency, and application retries. At the same time, slow or dropped network interactions delay transaction commit/rollback acknowledgements and result-set drains, further prolonging lock ownership and holding server backends occupied. Connection pools fill with sessions stuck in lock or I/O waits, while new clients experience connection refusals or handshake stalls. Overall throughput collapses, CPU appears under-utilised relative to response-time explosions, and monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in lock-manager waits, storage read/write latency, and network retransmissions or connection-queue depth.

Causally, inadequate storage bandwidth forces foreground operations to wait for pages and log flushes, stretching transaction duration and keeping locks active. These prolonged locks exacerbate contention, causing more sessions to block and pile up. Blocked or aborted transactions trigger bursts of application-side retries that open fresh connections, amplifying pressure on listener sockets and backend process pools already strained by network slowdowns. Conversely, network latency and dropped packets slow client request arrival and response draining, inflating server-side idle-in-transaction time and further delaying lock release. The mutual reinforcement between slow I/O, prolonged locking, and congested connectivity thus creates a feedback loop that severely degrades OLTP workload performance and stability.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a highly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, inflating resource consumption per statement.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive or apply WAL / redo records at the rate the primary produces them, causing widening replication lag.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, throttling database reads and writes.

When all three surface together, the database exhibits extreme and hard-to-diagnose slowdown: suddenly changed plans trigger large table scans, hash spills, or explosion of nested-loop iterations that issue far more physical I/O and generate excessive redo. The bloated I/O stream collides with an already-constrained storage subsystem, driving up queue depths and latency on both data and log devices. As commit latency grows, the primary’s WAL archive accumulates, replicas fall minutes to hours behind, their replay workers stall on the same saturated disks, and read-only workloads on replicas see stale or inconsistent data. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in logical I/O from plan churn, physical I/O wait from device saturation, and steep climbs in replication send, write, and replay lag, making it unclear which layer is primary.

Causally, a bad plan magnifies data-page and log traffic, pushing the storage layer past its throughput ceiling. Prolonged storage saturation lengthens commit times and slows WAL shipping, directly aggravating replication lag. In turn, the replica’s delayed apply holds WAL segments open on the primary, preventing log recycling and forcing yet more physical writes to already bottlenecked volumes. The feedback loop—poor plan → excess I/O → storage saturation → replication backlog → retained WAL → further I/O pressure—creates a self-reinforcing degradation that compromises both OLTP responsiveness and analytical query SLAs.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction scopes are written in a way that forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic really needs.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, causing prolonged blocking or deadlocks within the lock manager.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, breaking the correspondence between stored data and its indexes.

When all three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits a multi-layer failure pattern: ill-formed queries and over-long transactions magnify the number and duration of lock acquisitions; corrupted pages or broken index chains make ordinary lookups fall back to broader scans or trigger repeated lock retries, further extending lock hold times. The engine’s monitoring surfaces show a mixture of symptoms—spiking statement latency, swollen slow-query lists, escalating lock-wait and deadlock counts, diverging row counts between index and heap scans, checksum or page-corruption errors, and waves of application timeouts followed by retries that compound the congestion.

Causally, bad workload logic initiates oversized scans and keeps transactions open, inflating the lock footprint and creating hotspots. These longer-running locks increase the probability and depth of blocking chains. Simultaneously, underlying page or index corruption forces the optimizer and storage engine to abandon efficient access paths or to attempt page repairs, adding extra I/O and lock revalidation steps that stall holders and waiters alike. The resulting feedback loop—inefficient queries → extended locks → heightened contention → corruption-induced rescans/rollbacks → even longer transactions—can rapidly degrade throughput, exhaust connection pools, and jeopardize data consistency as forced rollbacks meet structural corruption.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale, missing, or incomplete, causing systematic optimizer cardinality misestimation.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures are corrupted or inconsistent with logical data, making on-disk storage unreliable and leading to incorrect or missing rows.

When these two root causes coexist, the database exhibits a blend of cardinality-driven plan instability and corruption-driven data access failures: estimates diverge wildly from actual rows while index probes intermittently miss, duplicate, or corrupt result sets; the optimizer oscillates between inefficient full scans and reliance on damaged indexes; execution plans that appear optimal at compile time catastrophically underperform at run time; repeated recompilations, sudden "inaccurate page" or checksum errors, and alternating error codes for corruption and statistics invalidation are observed. Application symptoms range from severe latency spikes and deadlocks (due to unexpected scan types) to incorrect query results and aborted transactions.

Causally, corrupted data blocks distort row counts returned by sampling or validation routines, further polluting already stale statistics. In turn, bad statistics drive the optimizer to choose access paths (e.g., non-clustered index seeks) that intensify exposure to the very pages that are corrupt, multiplying read errors and forcing emergency fallbacks. Corruption can also prevent automatic statistics maintenance from scanning affected objects, letting staleness persist. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other: corruption hides behind misestimation, and misestimation keeps the workload focused on corrupt structures, accelerating overall degradation of performance, reliability, and data accuracy.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Page-level serialization inside the buffer manager forces sessions to wait or spin on buffer pins, latches, and I/O slots, throttling access to hot data pages.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively saturate host CPU cycles, inflating run-queue length, context switches, and statement latency across the workload.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, threads, shared memory, or other OS objects are reached, preventing the database from allocating additional kernel resources.

When these three issues strike together, the system exhibits an interleaved symptom set: extreme CPU utilisation with sizable spin-loop time on buffer latches, elevated buffer-busy and scheduler wait events, sudden spikes in failed thread or file-descriptor creations, and uneven but rising transaction latencies. Hot pages trapped in the buffer cache cause worker threads to spin, inflating CPU usage; simultaneous OS resource exhaustion stops new workers or I/O contexts from being created, so existing threads queue longer, amplifying latch contention. Performance views show both CPU-bound statements and waits for latches and kernel resources; error logs report "too many open files", "cannot create thread", or shared-memory allocation failures, while throughput plummets despite all CPUs appearing fully utilised.

Causally, heavy latch spinning drives persistent CPU saturation. The high CPU load lengthens the time threads hold latches, further deepening buffer contention.
