Meanwhile, the large number of active threads created by the database to cope with queuing pushes the process toward OS limits on threads, file handles, or AIO contexts; once reached, new worker or I/O requests fail, forcing more work onto existing threads. This feedback loop—hot-page contention → CPU burn → thread proliferation → OS limit breaches → reduced parallelism → longer latch holds—causes a cascading degradation that is markedly worse than any single anomaly alone, culminating in widespread stalls, errors, and potential partial outage.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, producing long blocker-waiter chains or deadlocks and throttling throughput.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, undo records, and deleted index entries pile up faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check overhead.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages, index structures, or page links become physically or logically inconsistent, making access paths unreliable and raising corruption errors.

When all three conditions co-exist, the database experiences an intertwined failure mode: corruption in data or index pages forces the optimizer to abandon efficient index probes in favor of wide scans over bloated heaps swollen by unreclaimed MVCC debris. These scans hold locks far longer than normal, intensifying lock queues, deadlock frequency, and application time-outs. Simultaneously, pervasive blocking stalls vacuum/cleanup workers exactly when the version store is already expanding, while the corrupted pages they must touch repeatedly abort or skip their passes, letting dead versions accumulate still further. The runaway bloat amplifies I/O and buffer-cache pressure, prolonging lock hold times and increasing the chance that recovery or page-verification reads will surface additional integrity faults. Corruption in index or heap pages can also cause spurious lock retention by orphaned transactions, exacerbating contention.

Causally, each root cause reinforces the others: (1) integrity faults trigger plan shifts and retries that lengthen transactions and widen their lock footprint; (2) the resulting lock contention delays snapshot-advancing commits and blocks autovacuum or purge tasks, accelerating version buildup; (3) excessive version chains enlarge tables and indexes, driving more page splits and writes that raise the probability of further physical corruption on stressed storage; and (4) repeated corruption-induced rollbacks inject yet more undo records, feeding the MVCC store. The feedback loop degrades concurrency, inflates storage, and threatens data correctness, making recovery increasingly difficult without coordinated intervention.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing metadata (row counts, histograms, correlation statistics) is stale, missing, or incomplete, causing systematic misestimation of cardinalities and sub-optimal plan choices.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions request incompatible locks on the same resource, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger rollbacks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, background workers, checkpoint cadence, or parallelism are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, so internal subsystems either starve or over-allocate resources.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload is exposed to a compound failure mode: the optimizer repeatedly selects inefficient, lock-prone plans; those plans inflate the number and duration of row or page locks, while mis-sized memory, log, and parallelism parameters lengthen critical sections and slow the resolution of blocking. Observable effects include extreme divergence between estimated and actual row counts, sudden drops in TPS accompanied by surging lock-wait and deadlock events, erratic CPU and memory utilization (some cores idle while others spin), checkpoint or log-flush bursts that coincide with lock spikes, frequent automatic plan recompiles that still fail to relieve blocking, and application timeouts that persist even though hardware is under-utilised.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics lead the optimizer to choose plans that scan or update far more rows than necessary, expanding the lock footprint. Because configuration parameters are sub-optimal—e.g., work memory too small, max parallelism too high for the buffer pool, or checkpoint intervals too short—each bloated plan holds locks longer, competes for limited memory, and may force excessive log flushes. The prolonged execution time of these poor plans increases the window in which other transactions request conflicting locks, magnifying blocking chains and raising the probability of deadlocks. In turn, the resulting wait storms and victim rollbacks trigger additional auto-stats invalidations and plan recompiles, perpetuating the feedback loop and pushing overall transactional throughput into collapse.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Engine and background components consume more physical memory and swap than the host can safely provide, causing OS-level memory pressure and database OOM or eviction events.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, leading to excessive buffer-busy waits, CPU spin, and stalled page access.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server transport, listener, socket, or connection-pool resources saturate, producing slow or failed connects and prolonged client I/O waits.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database shows a convoluted mix of symptoms: resident-set size and swap continually rise while CPU usage swings between spin waits on buffer latches and idle time caused by blocked or disconnected clients. Wait-event dashboards light up with alternating memory-pressure stalls, buffer latch waits, and client read/write or connection establishment waits. Checkpoint and dirty-page flush latency grows because hot pages linger in memory under contention, further bloating memory with dirty buffers. Meanwhile, clients experience erratic query latencies, intermittent "too many connections" or timeout errors, and retransmissions on the network as over-subscribed back-ends struggle to send or receive data that must first be fetched from an overcommitted, latch-contended buffer pool.

Causal chain: memory over-allocation inflates each backend’s footprint and shrinks effective buffer cache, forcing heavier churn and making individual pages hotter; this magnifies latch contention and CPU spin. The prolonged execution times that result keep sessions and their sockets open longer, which raises connection counts and floods listener backlogs, pushing the system toward the network/connectivity limit. Conversely, slow or reset network links leave server backends blocked in client I/O, holding buffer pins and memory allocations alive, which further tightens memory pressure and extends latch hold times. The reinforcing loop among memory exhaustion, buffer-level serialization, and stalled network endpoints amplifies resource starvation across all tiers, threatening systemic throughput collapse and potential node eviction or crash.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks or re-uses an execution plan whose estimated cost is far lower than its real runtime cost, even though statistics are adequate.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating table and index size and adding visibility-check overhead.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Redo/commit log generation, flushing, or archival becomes the primary bottleneck, driving up commit latency and stalling write activity.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal plan selection, runaway MVCC version buildup, and saturation of the transaction-log path. All three root causes are active at the same time, creating a compound performance and stability issue that spans the optimizer, storage engine, and durability layer.

Combined phenomena: 1) Queries that once completed quickly now switch between table scans and poorly parameterized index paths, inflating row touch counts. 2) The excess row touches manifest as a surge of UPDATE/DELETE and vacuum traffic, causing the version store and on-disk heap to grow rapidly. 3) Checkpoints, log-flush waits, and archive-lag alerts appear alongside rising commit latency; long-running queries held open by bad plans keep old snapshots alive, preventing cleanup and forcing the log manager to retain older segments. 4) Planner misestimates grow worse because bloat skews statistics, leading to even heavier scans, more undo/redo generation, and longer transaction lifetimes, making it increasingly difficult to isolate any single symptom from the others.

Causal chain: Sub-optimal plans amplify row accesses and modification volume, which explodes MVCC version creation. The inflated version store increases physical I/O and statistics drift, feeding back into even poorer plan choices. The heightened DML throughput and prolonged transactions generate large bursts of redo; simultaneously, the MVCC cleanup lag forces the log subsystem to retain old segments for snapshot visibility, pushing log buffers, disk groups, and archivers past capacity. Log-flush delays lengthen commit times, extending transaction lifespans, which further pins row versions and perpetuates the cycle. The intertwined feedback loops among the optimizer, MVCC cleaner, and log manager thus escalate latency, resource consumption, and risk of outage far beyond what any of the individual anomalies would cause in isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written in a way that touches more rows, larger result sets, or longer transactions than business logic truly requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, partition, and index layout does not align with actual access patterns, forcing the optimizer into wide scans, row lookups, or write-amplifying structures.

When both root causes coexist, the database engine is simultaneously burdened by over-demanding requests and by structures incapable of serving those requests efficiently. Observable symptoms intensify: the same statements dominate slow-query and wait-event logs with extreme and erratic latency; execution plans show full-table scans or non-covering index probes combined with non-SARGable predicates; buffer pool churn, I/O saturation, and lock wait chains lengthen because transactions hold resources for far longer than expected; retry storms, deadlocks, or replica lag may emerge as write paths are slowed by oversized or redundant indexes that the chatty workload must maintain.

Causally, poorly written predicates, joins, and batch patterns magnify every weakness in the physical design—missing or non-covering indexes turn each excessive predicate or Cartesian join into a full scan, while oversized index sets make every superfluous update or long-running transaction more expensive to log and replicate. Conversely, an inadequate schema masks the true cost of the logic flaw, causing developers to add even larger batches, broader IN lists, or ad-hoc hints that further bloat resource consumption. Together, the two anomalies create a feedback loop in which inefficient code and misaligned structures reinforce each other, exhausting CPU, memory, and I/O bandwidth and degrading both transactional and analytical workload performance.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and workload access patterns forces inefficient access paths and excessive I/O. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or downstream replicas cannot receive, write, or apply primary log records fast enough, producing widening replication lag and retained logs. 
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate host CPU, driving high run-queue lengths and system-wide latency once compute capacity is exhausted.

When all three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a blend of severe symptoms: primary queries show full-table scans and multiple non-covering index lookups that spike CPU consumption; CPUs on both primary and replicas run near 100 %, inflating context switches and scheduler waits; replication lag explodes as replicas choke on compute-heavy, poorly indexed redo application; primary retains ever-growing write-ahead logs, leading to disk-space pressure and prolonged failover times; application requests observe erratic latency due to CPU starvation, while read replicas deliver increasingly stale or inconsistent data. Performance troubleshooting becomes difficult because each layer (query design, system load, and replication health) appears to be the bottleneck at different moments.

Causally, sub-optimal schema and missing/inefficient indexes inflate the CPU cost of every read and write. The excess CPU load on the primary slows transaction processing and inflates generated redo volume through larger scan and update operations. The same flawed schema exists on replicas, so their single-threaded or limited-parallelism apply processes struggle even more, consuming CPU cycles to re-execute costly statements and intensifying replication lag. Growing lag prevents log recycling on the primary, increasing disk pressure and forcing additional checkpoints that further tax CPU. The sustained high CPU utilization on both primary and replicas feeds back into longer query times and slower replication apply, forming a reinforcing loop that degrades throughput and jeopardizes recovery objectives.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path on the primary instance is saturated or frequently stalled when generating, flushing, or switching log segments, causing commit latency and log growth. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or subscribers cannot receive or apply those same log records fast enough, leading to rising replay lag and retention of un-archived log segments.

When both anomalies co-exist, the database experiences compounding symptoms: commits stall not only because the local log device is busy but also because retention of old segments—held for lagging replicas—forces the primary to pause for log switches or archiving. Wait-event dashboards show simultaneous spikes in LOG_FLUSH/LOG_SYNC waits and replication-send or apply waits; disk usage in the log and archive areas grows rapidly; buffer cache pressure surfaces as dirty pages accumulate, yet checkpoints cannot advance while required log positions remain active. Application sessions observe volatile response times, periodic freeze-ups during log switch attempts, and sudden throughput collapses when the primary throttles writers to keep replicas in sync.

Causally, slow or undersized log files make each commit more expensive, inflating the volume of in-flight redo that must be shipped to replicas. The resulting backlog slows replica apply rates, which in turn prevents the primary from recycling old log segments, lengthening log switch and archive operations and further amplifying log-path contention. This feedback loop widens replica lag, holds critical resources (log buffer space, archive slots, checkpoint advancement), and forces the primary to serialize write traffic, thereby intensifying the overall performance degradation.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between table structures, indexes, partitions, and the workload’s access predicates that forces the optimizer onto wide scans, non-covering index probes, or hot-page insert patterns.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Intensive competition among sessions for buffer-pool pages, page pins, and latches that serialises access, causes CPU spin or waits, and throttles throughput even when higher-level locks are free.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources—file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, thread slots, AIO contexts, cgroup quotas—preventing the database from allocating memory, buffers, or worker processes.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload exhibits extreme and erratic latency, bursty throughput, and frequent transient errors. Full-table scans and non-selective index access flood the limited buffer cache, evicting useful pages and triggering constant physical I/O. The undersized or starved buffer pool amplifies buffer-busy waits and page-latch contention as hot root pages, sequence blocks, or last pages of append-only tables are thrashed by concurrent sessions. Simultaneously, the operating system intermittently refuses additional shared-memory allocations, file opens, or thread spawns, leading to sudden query failures, stalled background writers, or disabled parallel plans. Monitoring views show a mix of high logical I/O, spikes in BUFFER_BUSY/LATCH_* waits, and kernel-level "Too many open files", "ENOMEM", or "semget failed" messages, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single layer.

Causally, the poor schema and index design enlarges the I/O footprint and concentrates activity on a small set of pages. This load magnifies buffer-pool pressure; because OS-level limits cap the cache size or the number of shared-memory segments, the engine cannot keep enough pages resident, leading to relentless eviction and reload cycles. Each reload requires latches and I/O slots, increasing contention inside the buffer manager. As contention lengthens critical-section hold times, latch spin and sleep escalate CPU consumption, while OS resource denials further reduce available worker threads or AIO descriptors, stretching I/O completion times and checkpoint flushes. The three issues thus form a reinforcing loop: sub-optimal data access inflates buffer demand, restricted OS resources prevent the cache or process pool from scaling, and the overstressed buffer manager becomes a hotspot, collectively degrading both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, so the bottleneck stems from the parameter choices themselves rather than true resource exhaustion.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions stall on buffer-pool page pins, latches, and other lightweight synchronization points because hot or churning pages force serialised access and CPU spin-waiting.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process collides with kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, aio contexts, processes/threads, or cgroup quotas, blocking further allocations even though database-level resources appear free.

When these three root causes strike together, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: 1) extreme and erratic wait-event mixes in which buffer-busy/latch waits, log-write waits, and kernel resource-allocation errors appear in the same time slices; 2) bursts of checkpoint-driven I/O that stall on both latch contention and OS aio/file-handle shortages, causing sharp latency spikes and temporary query freezes; 3) CPU saturation by spin loops despite low measured user throughput; 4) sudden connection or worker-spawn failures accompanied by kernel messages about ENFILE, EMFILE, or shared-memory limits, leading to partial outages while existing sessions themselves are trapped behind hot-page latches; 5) highly variable performance after configuration changes, instance restarts, or workload surges, making the individual anomalies hard to distinguish because each masks or amplifies the others.

Causally, mis-sized engine parameters (e.g., an undersized buffer pool, overly aggressive checkpoint target, or excessive parallel-worker cap) increase buffer turnover, concentrate access on a small set of pages, and flood the I/O and logging paths, which in turn magnifies latch contention inside the buffer manager. As latch pressure rises, sessions hold internal resources longer and attempt to open more files, spawn more background workers, or allocate larger shared-memory segments to cope with the backlog, quickly bumping into restrictive OS limits. Conversely, once the kernel refuses new handles, shared memory, or threads, the database cannot expand buffer pools or I/O contexts, forcing even tighter reuse of the existing cache and further intensifying page churn and latch waits. The feedback loop between bad configuration, internal contention, and external resource caps can thus cascade into severe throughput collapse and erratic, hard-to-diagnose performance degradation.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, and other engine heaps drives the database process beyond the physical-memory envelope, provoking paging, swapping, or OOM events.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log records becomes the principal bottleneck on the write path, inflating commit latency and stalling forward progress when log space or bandwidth is exhausted.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate host CPUs, keeping run queues full and starving other components of compute cycles, thereby inflating response times across the workload.

When these three conditions co-exist, the platform experiences a multilayer resource crisis. Memory pressure forces the engine and operating system to page frequently, which inflates CPU time spent in kernel mode and raises contention on memory latches. Simultaneously, the log subsystem cannot flush or archive fast enough, so commit and checkpoint waits accumulate. Because every commit now lingers on log I/O, client sessions remain active longer, holding onto memory allocations and consuming additional CPU while spinning on log-related waits. The prolonged session lifetimes and retry storms further expand plan and buffer caches, aggravating the memory shortfall, and the elevated CPU utilization slows both log-writer threads and page-reclaimer daemons, creating a feedback loop that deepens stalls. Symptoms therefore blend: escalating commit latency, soaring CPU load averages, runaway RSS growth, swap storms, and ultimately node eviction or crash recovery triggered by failed commits or OOM kills.

Causally, high redo generation drives the log subsystem to its limits; stalled commits elongate transaction lifetimes, which in turn prevent memory buffers from being released and keep worker threads runnable, pushing CPU toward saturation. The CPU bottleneck then slows log flushing and memory reclamation, while memory scarcity induces additional CPU overhead through paging and spin-lock contention. Each anomaly reinforces the others, turning what might have been isolated pressure points into a systemic failure that degrades throughput for write-intensive OLTP workloads and risks abrupt service interruption.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer is fed with stale, incomplete, or misleading statistics, leading to systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal execution plan choices.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log generation, flushing, or archiving path becomes the critical bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling write workloads.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical pages or index structures on disk are corrupted or internally inconsistent, causing incorrect or failed row retrieval and forcing fallback access methods.

When all three conditions coexist, the database may exhibit an erratic mix of severe symptoms:  • Queries oscillate between long-running full scans (chosen because of bad statistics or disabled indexes) and repeatedly aborted index scans (failing integrity checks).  • Commit operations intermittently freeze behind log-flush waits, causing application time-outs and holding locks that magnify contention.  • Emergency index rebuilds triggered by detected corruption generate bursts of redo that saturate the already constrained log subsystem, further delaying recovery operations and increasing checkpoint frequency.  • Repeated recompilations show wildly divergent cost estimates, and execution plans flip-flop after every statistics refresh or corruption-induced index disablement.  • Integrity-check utilities and alert logs report page verification errors alongside "log file switch/archive required" warnings, making it difficult to distinguish performance from correctness issues.

Causal interaction: (1) Stale or skewed statistics drive the optimizer to prefer damaged indexes or overly aggressive join orders, which in turn surface latent corruption through run-time errors. (2) Detection of corruption prompts index rebuilds or table rewrites that emit large volumes of redo, rapidly filling and switching log files. (3) The already throttled transaction-log subsystem becomes saturated, extending checkpoint and commit times; these elongated transactions prevent timely automatic statistics refresh and keep locks active, producing more contention and blocking DML. (4) Elevated redo pressure increases the risk of incomplete flushes during failures, potentially widening the corruption footprint and perpetuating the statistics/plan instability cycle. Collectively, the intertwined failures in metadata accuracy, physical data integrity, and log throughput degrade both performance and reliability, making diagnosis and recovery substantially harder.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer relies on stale, incomplete, or otherwise inaccurate statistics, leading to systematic cardinality misestimation.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : Despite reasonably accurate statistics, the optimizer may still choose a sub-optimal execution plan because of cost-model flaws, plan-cache reuse, or version/configuration changes.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall throughput.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a blend of inaccurate row-count estimates, erratic or degraded plan choices, and severe lock waits. Misestimated cardinalities or a poor plan (e.g., an unexpected full table scan or a broad nested-loop join) can dramatically enlarge the number or duration of row touches, thereby inflating the lock footprint and extending lock hold times. The swollen execution latencies feed back into the lock manager, lengthening wait queues, triggering deadlocks under high concurrency, and generating bursts of lock-wait/timeout errors alongside frequent plan recompilations or plan flips. Performance becomes highly unpredictable: some executions complete quickly, others stall behind long blockers, and overall throughput and SLA compliance collapse, making it difficult to distinguish whether the primary culprit is the optimizer or the lock subsystem.

Causally, stale or missing statistics first mislead the optimizer, and any surviving misestimation gaps that the cost model fails to correct push the optimizer toward inefficient plans. These bloated plans touch more rows or use inappropriate join orders, which in a busy OLTP environment increases lock acquisition and hold times. The resulting lock contention slows down data-modifying statements, prolongs transactions, and further skews the data distribution, making statistics even staler and encouraging additional plan recompilations. This positive feedback loop amplifies both the optimizer defects and the locking bottlenecks, creating a compounded performance crisis that cannot be resolved by addressing only one of the underlying root causes.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleaners can purge them.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The database allocates buffer, work-area, and cache memory beyond the host’s physical or virtual limits, provoking paging or OOM events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or address space are hit, blocking further allocations or process creation.

When these three conditions coexist, the system exhibits an intertwined failure pattern. Version bloat inflates table and index sizes, expanding the buffer cache and working-set footprint, while long-running transactions and cleanup lag pin even more pages in memory. The swelling resident set collides with fixed OS memory, handle, and shared-memory quotas; the host begins paging, and kernel logs show ENOMEM, EMFILE, or EAGAIN errors as new connections, background workers, or I/O contexts fail to start. Autovacuum or purge workers, already overwhelmed by the volume of stale versions, are themselves throttled or denied resources, causing version-store growth to accelerate. Query plans degrade as the optimizer misjudges bloat, sequential scans lengthen, cache hit ratios oscillate due to aggressive page eviction, and users experience sporadic timeouts, failed statements, or partial node outages.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn produces excessive MVCC debris that must be kept in memory and the buffer pool until cleaned. This amplifies overall memory consumption, driving the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly. Rising memory pressure leads the engine to request more shared buffers, work memory, or background processes, which in turn collide with operating-system limits on virtual memory, shared segments, or open files—triggering the Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly. Once the OS begins refusing allocations or swapping aggressively, cleanup workers slow further, allowing even more version accumulation and cache bloat in a positive feedback loop that can culminate in out-of-memory kills, inability to spawn essential workers, and a cascading service degradation or outage.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to process far more data or hold resources much longer than business logic requires.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk pages or index structures makes stored data and access paths unreliable.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or similar objects prevent the database from obtaining required OS resources.

When all three root causes occur concurrently, the system experiences a multi-layer failure mode in which excessive or inefficient SQL drives high I/O, memory, and worker-thread demand; corrupted pages or indexes introduce unpredictable access-path fallbacks, retries, or error storms; and exhausted kernel resources prevent new file opens, buffer allocations, or background-worker spawns needed for recovery or normal execution. Observable symptoms converge and amplify: the same slow or timing-out statements repeatedly hit corrupted pages, triggering checksum or logical-consistency errors; automatic plan fallbacks to full table scans magnify the already bloated workload, pushing file-handle and shared-memory usage to hard OS limits; connection spikes caused by application retries encounter "too many open files," "cannot map shared memory," or "failed to start worker" errors, while index versus heap row counts diverge and integrity-check utilities cannot allocate the resources required to repair. Admins may see alternating patterns of statement-level timeouts, corruption warnings in engine logs, and kernel messages denying resource allocations, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal chain: Inefficient SQL amplifies resource consumption, bringing the process close to OS quotas. Near the saturation point, any additional overhead—such as the engine switching from index seeks to full scans because of corrupted structures—rapidly exhausts remaining kernel objects and memory. Simultaneously, resource denials can interrupt checkpointing, index rebuilds, or page flushes, causing partial writes or failed recovery steps that deepen on-disk corruption. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others: logic-level overwork accelerates resource exhaustion; resource exhaustion hinders I/O and recovery, increasing corruption risk; corruption forces heavier access patterns, which in turn magnify both workload inefficiency and OS-level pressure, culminating in cascading performance degradation and potential service outage.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request mutually incompatible locks on the same resource and therefore wait, block, or deadlock.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database exhausts free space in data, log, temp, or archive areas so that further page, extent, or segment allocations fail.

When both root causes strike at once, sessions already queued on locks find their waits prolonged by space-allocation stalls, while space-related errors trigger rollbacks that propagate new lock requests and deadlocks. Observable effects include rapidly rising lock-wait time, deadlock and victim reports interleaved with "no space left" or "cannot allocate extent" errors, frozen or hung DML/DDL statements, exploding connection-pool wait lists, log file growth that plateaus at the capacity ceiling, checkpoint or log-switch delays, and application retries that add more concurrent lock contenders.

Causally, long-running or blocked transactions hold locks and referenced undo/redolog segments open, preventing log recycling and freeing of extents; this accelerates space exhaustion in log and data areas. Conversely, once the storage boundary is hit, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations pause on space-allocation paths, lengthening their lock tenure and enlarging blocking chains. Rollback operations triggered by allocation failures can further inflate undo and redo volumes, immediately reclaiming no space and deepening the capacity crisis. The mutual reinforcement between lock persistence and space starvation can drive the system into a feedback loop of mounting contention, cascading rollbacks, and service-level degradation unless both dimensions are relieved simultaneously.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages have become physically or logically corrupt, making access paths unreliable and occasionally incorrect.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume persistently high CPU, saturating host compute resources and throttling all concurrent work.

When these three root causes strike together, the system exhibits an extreme mix of symptoms: statements already bloated by poor SQL design run even longer because index corruption pushes them from targeted probes to full table scans; the extra scanning work magnifies CPU saturation, driving run-queue spikes, context-switch storms, and widespread latency. Applications see inconsistent or missing rows on some requests and duplicated rows on others, while timeouts, retries, and lock waits mushroom as overloaded CPUs delay execution and corrupt structures force expensive consistency checks. Engine logs may alternate between slow-query entries, corruption alerts, and CPU-throttling or scheduler wait events, making diagnosis ambiguous.

Causally, inefficient workload logic inflates I/O and CPU demand; if the targeted indexes or data pages are corrupt, the optimizer abandons or retries access paths, escalating demand further through full scans and revalidation work. The resulting CPU saturation lengthens checkpoint, recovery, and background verification cycles, which can in turn defer detection of additional corruption and prolong transaction lifetimes, increasing the window for ill-formed SQL to lock larger data sets. The feedback loop between excessive logical workload, structural corruption, and compute exhaustion amplifies each individual issue, degrading performance, correctness, and stability far more than any single anomaly would in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries that outpaces background cleanup, inflating the version store and increasing visibility-check and I/O overhead.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency in on-disk data or index pages, leading to broken page links, bad checksums, or mismatched heap-to-index mappings.

When both root causes strike together, administrators may observe an explosive growth of disk space and severe query divergence: sequential scans lengthen because of massive dead tuples, while index scans intermittently miss or duplicate rows due to corrupt leaf pages. Autovacuum or purge workers can run continuously yet fail, repeatedly crashing or skipping damaged pages, so the dead-row ratio and version store continue to climb unchecked. CHECKDB-style utilities report both bloated heaps and structural defects; execution plans oscillate between slow full scans (triggered by planner distrust in corrupt indexes) and mis-guided index probes that still return incorrect results. Error logs may alternate between "cannot find snapshot/clog" warnings and "page checksum mismatch" or "index inconsistent" errors, making isolation of a single culprit difficult.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn first inflates the MVCC version store; the enlarged heap and index structures expand the surface area for I/O and memory faults, increasing the probability of physical corruption. Conversely, once block or index corruption appears, cleanup workers may abort or skip corrupted pages, allowing even more obsolete versions to linger and accelerating version-store exhaustion and table bloat. Repeated crash-recovery cycles caused by corruption can interrupt vacuuming windows, further delaying reclamation. The feedback loop between failed cleanup and structural corruption amplifies performance collapse, risks transaction-ID wraparound or undo-segment exhaustion, and ultimately threatens data correctness and availability.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions on the primary database compete for mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, creating long blocker-waiter chains or deadlocks that inflate wait time and suppress throughput.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, enlarging log-position gaps and delaying replica replay.

When both root causes manifest together, the database experiences compounded symptoms: on the primary, sessions stall behind lock queues while commit latency rises; simultaneously, the replication pipeline shows rapidly growing receive/replay lag, bloated log retention, and stale read replicas. Application traffic may shift to the primary as replicas become outdated, further intensifying lock pressure. Deadlock-victim rollbacks, connection-pool exhaustion, and sudden surges of catch-up I/O on replicas appear concurrently, making it difficult to attribute slowdowns to either subsystem alone.

Causally, heavy lock contention slows transaction completion, prolonging the lifespan of open transactions and delaying log generation, flush, and truncation. These lingering transactions prevent log recycling and force the primary to retain ever-larger log segments, which must still be shipped to replicas. On the replica side, apply workers encountering the same conflicting lock patterns (e.g., hot-spot updates or DDL) are blocked, reducing apply throughput and amplifying replication lag. The growing lag, in turn, prompts read workloads to be redirected to the already lock-saturated primary or triggers administrative actions (e.g., pausing apply, promoting a lagging standby) that further disturb lock ordering, creating a feedback loop that worsens both locking and synchronization delays. The intertwined effects degrade overall OLTP performance and erode high-availability guarantees.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database host simultaneously suffers from storage-subsystem saturation (throughput, IOPS, or latency limits reached on underlying volumes) and exhaustion of kernel-enforced process or memory-mapping resources (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, threads, AIO contexts, etc.), creating a compounded bottleneck that is external to the database engine’s own configuration knobs.

Combined Observable Phenomena: End-to-end response times and batch windows extend unpredictably as physical read/write latency spikes coincide with intermittent engine errors such as "cannot allocate shared memory", "unable to open file", or "failed to spawn worker". Wait-class statistics show heavy data-file, log-file, and durability flush waits alongside sudden surges of metadata, latch, or connection-management waits caused by stalled background workers. CPU utilisation may appear moderate but with rising run-queue lengths when threads block on both I/O completion and kernel resource acquisition. System logs reveal kernel I/O queue overruns, IOPS throttling, plus EMFILE/ENFILE or ENOMEM errors. The overlap can lead to partial or rolling outages: long-running sessions persist yet new connections, parallel workers, or checkpoint helpers fail to start, while I/O queues deepen and checkpoint completion timeouts threaten crash recovery windows.

Causal Interaction: Sustained storage saturation elongates I/O completion times, causing a buildup of database processes and background tasks waiting on disk; this increases concurrent open files, AIO requests, semaphore consumption, and thread count, pushing the system toward its kernel resource limits. Conversely, once file-handle, AIO, or memory-mapping limits are reached, the database engine may be forced to retry or serialize I/O operations, further inflating I/O queues and intensifying storage latency. The feedback loop between physical device overload and kernel resource exhaustion thus amplifies contention at both layers, degrading throughput, starving new work, and complicating diagnosis because symptoms from each layer mask or mimic the other.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-issued statements or transaction boundaries are written so that they process more data or hold resources longer than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine runtime parameters are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload mix, or version defaults, causing non-ideal resource behavior.

When these three root causes coexist, the database experiences a multilayered performance regression. Poorly written SQL generates excessive logical work; the optimizer then multiplies the cost by selecting inefficient plans (e.g., full scans, bad join orders, missing parallelism); finally, mis-set memory, parallelism, or I/O parameters prevent the engine from masking these inefficiencies, exposing the system to compounded stalls. Operators observe a flood of slow-query log entries whose execution plans oscillate between variants, long-running transactions that monopolize locks and latches, dramatic swings in CPU and I/O utilization unrelated to real hardware saturation, and checkpoint or logging spikes that appear disconnected from actual data-change volume. End-users perceive unpredictable latency, timeouts, and sporadic throughput collapses, while monitoring shows both plan instability and resource wait patterns that do not align with host-level metrics.

Causally, problematic SQL shapes the workload toward large scans, wide result sets, and chatty access patterns. The optimizer, already challenged by this input, may misjudge costs or recycle an ill-suited cached plan, amplifying the data touched per execution. Misconfigured parameters—such as undersized buffer pools, inadequate work memory, or aggressive parallelism—then throttle the engine’s ability to execute even a good plan, let alone a bad one, leading to spill-to-disk, excessive context switching, or checkpoint storms. Conversely, sub-optimal plans inflate memory and I/O demand, making otherwise safe configuration settings suddenly inadequate. The feedback loop between inefficient SQL, fragile plan selection, and mis-aligned configuration accelerates resource contention, heightens variability, and obscures the root cause, thereby worsening the overall database state.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine and background components consume memory or swap beyond the safe limits of the host, provoking OS-level pressure, paging, cache churn, or OOM terminations.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply log records as fast as the primary generates them, causing growing log-position gaps, replay lag, and log-retention bloat.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport links, listeners, socket buffers, or authentication paths between clients/replicas and the server saturate or stall, yielding connection timeouts, retransmissions, and backlog overflows.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: 1) primary and replica nodes show escalating resident-set sizes, swap activity, and cache thrash; 2) replication delay widens rapidly, with retained WAL or relay logs ballooning in both memory and disk, exhausting further resources; 3) clients and replicas experience sporadic disconnects, SYN backlog drops, increased round-trip times, and authentication stalls. Monitoring dashboards may reveal intertwined spikes in memory usage, network retransmits, and apply lag, making it difficult to attribute the dominant bottleneck. Failover readiness deteriorates as replicas fall behind while simultaneously suffering from memory pressure and network instability.

Causally, heavy memory over-allocation on the primary competes with the kernel for page cache and socket buffers, curtailing throughput of the WAL sender and elevating TCP retransmission rates. Network congestion and handshake retries slow log streaming further, forcing the primary to retain more unshipped segments—which occupy additional shared memory and disk—amplifying the original memory pressure. On the replica side, delayed reception plus its own memory contention hampers redo apply, causing relay logs to accumulate in RAM and on disk, which in turn exacerbates memory exhaustion. The feedback loop between memory shortages, impaired network I/O, and escalating replication backlog can culminate in cascading stalls, OOM kills, or split-brain failovers across the cluster.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, missing, or insufficient statistics distort the optimizer’s cardinality estimates and costing inputs, driving systematically poor plan choices.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall throughput.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for handles, memory segments, semaphores, threads, or similar OS objects, preventing new allocations and halting growth of work.

Combined phenomena: When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits severe and erratic slowdowns. Misestimated row counts lead the optimizer to pick plans that scan or update far more data than necessary, inflating lock footprints, extending lock hold times, and triggering cascades of blocking and deadlocks. Sessions that become stuck waiting on locks or deadlock retries remain logged in, consuming connections, file descriptors, shared-memory slots, or semaphore entries until global OS quotas are exhausted. Once kernel limits are reached, new client logins, background workers, or parallel query processes fail to start, causing partial outages and amplifying application time-outs. Monitoring may show exploding lock-wait queues, skyrocketing wait-on-OS resource allocation failures, drastic drops in throughput, and sudden bursts of deadlock victim errors, all while execution plans display grossly inaccurate cardinality estimates.

Causal chain: (1) Stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing high-cost, bulk-locking execution plans (e.g., full table scans without useful indexes), thereby lengthening transaction duration and widening the scope of acquired locks; (2) the prolonged and enlarged lock holding intensifies lock contention, inducing blocker-waiter trees and frequent deadlocks; (3) each blocked or orphaned backend continues to hold kernel objects—file handles, semaphores, threads—pushing the database toward OS resource limits; (4) once those limits are hit, new sessions and maintenance workers (including auto-statistics refresh jobs) cannot start, preventing correction of the stale statistics and forcing more sessions into lock waits. This feedback loop compounds latency, throughput collapse, and availability degradation in OLTP workloads.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, log files, archiver, or replication-retention pipeline—cannot persist or advance redo fast enough, stalling commits and checkpoints.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Client/server communication or connection-handling facilities—network links, listeners, socket queues, authentication threads—are saturated or unstable, delaying session establishment and data transfer.

When both anomalies manifest concurrently, users experience a mixture of severe commit latency, intermittent session timeouts, and sudden pauses in workload progress. Commit, log-flush, and log-sync waits rise sharply while, at the same time, new or idle sessions encounter long TLS handshakes, SYN backlog drops, or "too many connections" errors. Queued transactions hold locks and pins, causing cascading contention that further lengthens response times. Archive and replication lag grows because log files cannot be shipped over an already congested network, leading to log-file directory bloat and eventual log-space exhaustion; once log switches stall, write workloads freeze and a surge of client retries floods the overstressed listener.

Causally, packet loss, high round-trip times, or exhausted connection workers slow archive/replica transport, which in turn prevents timely log segment clearance; retained segments fill the log device, throttling new log writes and elongating commit paths. Conversely, prolonged commit latency forces application threads to remain in open transactions longer, inflating connection counts and data queued for client delivery, thereby intensifying network socket pressure and retransmissions. The positive feedback loop between an overwhelmed log subsystem and degraded connectivity accelerates resource exhaustion on both fronts, making the composite failure mode harder to diagnose and more disruptive than either anomaly in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions, undo records, and dead index entries that outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and scan costs.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters (memory, checkpointing, parallelism, background workers, etc.) that create artificial resource bottlenecks or disable timely maintenance despite hardware capacity.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Saturation or mismanagement of connection, socket, or network transport resources that delays or interrupts client–server communication and query execution.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a blended failure signature:  • Version store and table bloat grow rapidly, while autovacuum/vacuum or purge workers remain perpetually behind because configuration limits throttle their throughput.  • Checkpoint storms or overly aggressive WAL flushing amplify I/O pressure, yet actual CPU and disk utilization appear imbalanced due to sub-optimal parameter settings.  • Clients experience intermittent connection timeouts, authentication delays, and prolonged result-set transfers; simultaneously, backend processes pile up in client-read/write and tuple-visibility check waits.  • System views report soaring dead-tuple ratios, rising transaction-ID age, swelling redo/backlog sizes, and a high count of idle-in-transaction sessions holding snapshots open.  • Latency and throughput vary erratically: moments of network congestion or socket exhaustion compound with sudden maintenance bursts, making performance regressions hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causal chain: Misconfigured memory, checkpoint, and worker parameters slow or starve the vacuum/purge subsystem, allowing MVCC debris to accumulate. The bloated data footprint increases I/O volume and stretches transaction-commit and query-execution times, keeping sessions open longer. Prolonged session lifetimes enlarge the active connection pool, consuming more server processes/threads and sockets. This raises pressure on the listener backlog and network stack, producing connection stalls and retransmissions that further elongate transactions. The resulting feedback loop—sluggish cleanup ➝ heap/index bloat ➝ longer queries ➝ extended and additional connections ➝ network and listener saturation—magnifies both the storage-level visibility overhead and the parameter-induced resource mismatch, ultimately degrading OLTP responsiveness and risking transaction-wraparound or outage.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, datatypes, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns forces otherwise well-written SQL to use inherently inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer selects a markedly sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonably accurate statistics, often due to cost-model quirks, plan-cache reuse, or version/configuration changes.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client ↔ server transport, authentication, or socket resources become saturated or unstable, causing connection stalls, retransmissions, or session back-pressure outside the core execution engine.

When all three root causes coexist, symptoms compound: queries lacking proper indexes or partitioning are prone to be costed poorly and may receive volatile or outright bad plans (full scans, non-covering index probes, or bloated parallel plans). These heavier plans generate excessive I/O and large intermediate/result sets that take longer to ship across the network. The protracted data transfer holds server worker threads in client-write waits, inflates transaction response times, and keeps connections open longer. Meanwhile, plan thrashing and retries—triggered by timeouts or aborted sessions—inflate the number of concurrent parses and connections, quickly exhausting listener backlogs, socket buffers, or backend process slots. Operators observe a mixture of symptoms: alternating execution plans, sudden latency spikes, CPU and I/O surges, growing queues of half-open or idle-in-transaction sessions, client timeouts, and rising network retransmission or authentication wait counters.

Causally, the poor physical design starves the optimizer of efficient options, increasing the probability that any small costing bias or plan-cache quirk yields a disastrous plan. Those bloated plans, in turn, magnify network load and session lifetimes, making the system more sensitive to existing bandwidth limits or connection-slot ceilings. Network slowdowns feed back into the database: lingering result transfers delay cursor closure, prolong locks, and trigger client-side retries that invalidate or pollute the plan cache, further destabilizing plan selection. The intertwined feedback loops between inefficient physical access, unstable plan choice, and constrained connectivity drive a runaway degradation that is far more severe than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, and other in-engine memory regions exhausts physical RAM or swap on the host, causing paging, OOM terminations, or node eviction.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data pages or index structures become logically or physically corrupt, leading to missing/duplicated rows, checksum failures, and forced scan or recovery behavior.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or unstable network, listener, or socket resources prevent timely establishment or servicing of client connections, producing timeouts, retries, and connection-slot exhaustion.

When these three root causes manifest concurrently, the database displays a compounded failure pattern: memory pressure triggers frequent process restarts that interrupt active sessions, while latent or ongoing page/index corruptions cause queries to fall back to full table scans that inflate buffer allocations and prolong response times. The resulting sluggishness drives clients to exceed retry thresholds, flooding the listener with new connection attempts just as server memory is constrained, exhausting socket queues and backend slots. Administrators observe oscillating RSS growth, OOM kills, repeated crash-recovery cycles reporting page-checksum or index-link errors, surges in network retransmissions, and a rapid rise in refused or half-open connections. Diagnostic utilities show diverging row counts between scans, while monitoring stacks report simultaneous spikes in memory faults and network wait events, making it difficult to attribute slowdowns to any single layer.

Causally, corrupted data structures can inflate memory demand by forcing table scans and generating large work areas, pushing the engine toward the memory-allocation cliff. Memory exhaustion, in turn, precipitates abrupt backend terminations or instance restarts that may interrupt in-flight writes, amplifying the risk of additional on-disk corruption. Each restart or stall disrupts active sessions, prompting application drivers to issue aggressive reconnect loops that saturate listener backlogs and network stacks. The clogged connection layer further delays transactional retries, lengthening query lifetimes and keeping oversized result sets and work buffers resident in memory. This feedback loop—corruption-induced memory bloat, memory-pressure crashes aggravating corruption, and connection storms intensifying memory and I/O churn—drives the database into an unstable state where availability, correctness, and performance are simultaneously degraded.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The engine allocates or leaks more RAM and swap than the host can safely provide, inflating buffer pools, plan caches, work areas, and background heaps until the operating system or the instance experiences memory pressure, paging, or OOM terminations.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots, producing excessive buffer-busy waits, CPU spin, and throughput stalls despite adequate raw CPU availability.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Persistent table or index pages become physically or logically corrupt—checksum failures, broken page links, or out-of-order keys—making on-disk structures unreliable and forcing retries, error handling, or full-scan fall-backs.

When all three anomalies surface together, the database alternates between memory exhaustion, low-level latch storms, and corruption-triggered retries. Symptoms include: 
• Rapid, uneven growth of the buffer cache and per-query work areas followed by OS paging or OOM kills.
• Spikes in buffer-busy/latch wait events as many sessions hammer a shrinking set of hot, repeatedly dirtied or corrupted pages that cannot be evicted promptly because memory is saturated and dirty-page flush queues are backlogged.
• Intermittent checksum or page-verification errors appearing alongside latch timeouts; queries that fall back from index access to full scans further inflate memory use and prolong latch holding times.
• Erratic performance: bursts of CPU spin mixed with periods of deep stalls while the engine retries failed I/Os, re-parses plans discarded under memory pressure, or restarts after crash recovery triggered by corruption or OOM.

Causal chain: Excessive memory allocation fills physical RAM, delaying or stalling background flushers. Dirty pages linger longer, increasing latch hold times and aggravating Buffer Cache and Latch Contention. Prolonged retention of dirty or repeatedly written pages raises the probability of torn writes during any forced restart or OOM kill, seeding Data Block and Index Integrity Anomalies. Conversely, encountering corrupted pages forces extra I/O retries, consistency checks, or full table scans, which allocate additional work memory and flood the buffer pool, amplifying memory pressure. The resulting feedback loop—memory overcommit → latch contention → corruption exposure → heavier memory and latch demand—degrades throughput, destabilizes the instance, and raises the risk of repeated crash-recovery cycles.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to read, write, or keep alive far more data and rows than the true business task requires.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in datafiles, logs, temp areas, or backups shrinks to, or reaches, an exhaustion point, preventing further allocations.

When both conditions exist simultaneously, the database experiences an accelerating feedback loop: overly large scans, joins, sorts, and long-running or chatty transactions quickly inflate data files, undo/redo logs, temporary segments, and diagnostic output, while the shrinking free space prevents the engine from extending these structures. Observable symptoms include: rapid and non-linear space depletion immediately following the execution of heavy or poorly written SQL; sudden "out of space" or "cannot allocate extent" errors in the middle of statements; hash or sort operations that spill to temp and then fail; log, archive, or backup destinations filling and halting commit processing; application timeouts, lock wait explosions, and repeated retries clogging connection pools; and slow-query logs swollen with the same problematic statements that precipitate space exhaustion events.

Causally, inefficient workload logic drives up data churn—scanning whole tables, materializing large intermediate results, and extending transactions across long user think-times. Each of these behaviors multiplies the volume of undo, redo, temp, and result-set data written to disk, rapidly consuming free bytes. As capacity thresholds are crossed, the storage exhaustion blocks further allocations for temp work areas, index growth, or log switching, which forces statement aborts and triggers rollbacks that themselves need yet more space. The inability to allocate space prolongs transaction lifetimes, exacerbating lock contention and amplifying the latency already caused by the initial bad SQL patterns. The two root causes thus reinforce each other: poor workload logic accelerates space consumption, and space shortages magnify the performance and stability impact of the inefficient workload, potentially cascading into system-wide stalls or outages.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer selects a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to inefficient access paths, wrong join methods, or inappropriate parallelism.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates or retains more memory than the host can safely supply, causing OS-level pressure, paging, or out-of-memory events.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage subsystem cannot sustain the read/write demand, so device queues, latencies, and I/O waits grow until the database becomes I/O-bound.

When all three root causes strike simultaneously, symptoms overlap and reinforce each other: poorly chosen plans trigger large table scans, hash builds, and wide parallel fan-out that demand excessive work memory and flood buffer caches. The inflated memory footprint collides with existing cache, sort, and hash allocations, pushing the host into swap and forcing the database to evict hot pages while still waiting on I/O. As caches churn and spill operations erupt, physical reads and writes spike, driving the already-stressed storage subsystem beyond its throughput ceiling. The resulting latency amplifies statement runtimes, leaving memory-hungry queries active longer, pinning even more memory, and generating further I/O. Observed metrics show oscillating or steadily worsening plan changes, memory pressure alarms, swap- or OOM-killer events, soaring I/O wait time with moderate CPU utilization, erratic query latencies, and sudden node or instance restarts that obscure a single clear culprit.

Causally, a sub-optimal plan is the spark: choosing full scans or large hash joins magnifies per-query memory needs and multiplies physical I/O. The bloated memory allocations exceed host limits, triggering eviction and spilling that redirect what should be in-memory operations to disk, thereby aggravating storage load. Conversely, storage saturation delays page and temp-space requests, prolonging query execution so that memory remains allocated longer and more concurrent sessions accumulate, escalating memory pressure. This vicious cycle between bad plans, runaway memory usage, and saturated storage quickly degrades overall throughput, masks the origin of the slowdown, and may culminate in service interruption if not disentangled promptly.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Critical metadata about data distribution is stale, incomplete, or missing, causing the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal execution plans.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Heavy concurrent access to a small set of hot pages or an undersized buffer pool forces sessions to serialize on buffer latches and page pins, inflating wait times and CPU spin.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas are reached, preventing the database from allocating additional low-level resources.

Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from incorrect optimizer statistics, severe buffer-cache/latch contention, and exhaustion of critical OS-level resources. Poor plan choices amplify page hot spots, while latch storms and multiplied background activity consume kernel objects until hard limits are hit, jointly throttling throughput and raising latency.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Execution plans with grossly inaccurate row-count estimates repeatedly choose nested loops or index range scans that hammer the same root, inner-table, or index pages. 2) Buffer-busy and page-latch wait events surge; CPU utilization shows high spin without corresponding work completion. 3) As sessions accumulate in latch waits, new connections, parallel workers, or I/O requests start failing with "too many open files," "cannot allocate shared memory," or "unable to create thread" errors logged by both the engine and the OS. 4) Automatic statistics refresh jobs abort due to unavailable OS handles, keeping statistics stale and locking the system in a degradation loop. Diagnosis becomes difficult because symptoms oscillate between optimizer misestimates, latch waits, and sporadic OS allocation errors.

Causal chain: Stale or low-quality statistics lead the optimizer to route a large fraction of queries through plans that over-concentrate activity on a narrow set of pages (e.g., small hash tables, root index pages, or hot partitions). The resulting hot-page pattern drives intense latch contention in the buffer manager. Prolonged latch waits inflate session counts, background I/O, and retry loops, which in turn consume additional file handles, semaphores, and thread slots. Once OS resource limits are breached, new workers and auto-statistics jobs fail, preventing corrective statistics collection and reinforcing misestimation. Simultaneously, limited OS resources slow checkpoint and flush operations, keeping hot pages resident and further intensifying latch storms—forming a self-reinforcing feedback loop that degrades both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses substantially sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are reasonably accurate.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing is throttled because generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log records is the primary bottleneck.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages are physically or logically corrupted, invalidating key order, page links, or checksums.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits erratic plan flips, long-running queries that suddenly devolve into full table scans, surging redo generation from excessive row touches or emergency index rebuilds, and sharply rising log-flush and commit latencies. End-user symptoms include intermittent time-outs, dead-session pile-ups, and inconsistent query results (missing or duplicated rows). Engine alerts may simultaneously report page-checksum failures, log-write or log-sync wait events, repeated log-file switches, and frequent plan-cache invalidations. Because corruption forces the optimizer to avoid or mistrust indexes, even read-heavy statements inflate redo traffic through unnecessary row versioning or sort-based spill writes, further stressing the already saturated log subsystem. The overlapping noise of plan churn, integrity errors, and log stalls makes it difficult to attribute slowdowns to any single layer.

Causally, latent page or index corruption degrades the optimizer’s visibility of accurate access paths, leading it to select expansive scans or Cartesian joins (Query Plan Selection Anomaly). These inflated operations dramatically increase row modifications to worktables, temp segments, or repair attempts, thereby driving up redo volume. The heightened write-ahead log rate overruns an undersized or slow log subsystem (Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly), escalating commit delays and extending lock-hold times. Prolonged transactions hinder timely page clean-up and checkpointing, allowing additional corrupted pages to propagate and causing more plan invalidations, which in turn perpetuate poor plan selection. The feedback loop among misguided plans, log saturation, and structural corruption amplifies performance instability and data-quality risks, pushing the database toward acute availability incidents if not promptly remediated.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, or data types are ill-suited to the workload, forcing the optimizer into systematically inefficient access paths independent of statistics freshness or plan choice.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level memory, I/O, parallelism, and background-worker settings are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload mix, so internal subsystems operate outside their optimal envelopes even when the physical resources are not inherently scarce.
CPU Resource Anomaly : The host’s CPU cores are saturated by database processes, producing run-queue buildup, scheduler waits, and global latency spikes across queries.

When these three root causes coincide, the workload experiences cascading and mutually reinforcing symptoms: queries that lack proper indexing fan out into large scans and excessive row lookups, inflating CPU demand; at the same time mis-sized buffer pools, work-memory, and parallelism parameters amplify the CPU pressure by provoking redundant I/O, spill-to-disk operations, and over-parallel execution. The result is chronic CPU saturation, long run-queue delays, and erratic throughput. Execution plans show full table scans and noncovering-index probes, while wait-event histograms alternate between CPU-run, memory-allocation, and I/O-related waits despite overall storage and memory not being fully utilized. Checkpoints or background autovacuum/autopurge tasks may trigger storm-like episodes that momentarily seize all CPU, further degrading foreground query latency and causing timeouts.

Causally, the missing or sub-optimal indexes inflate logical I/O and predicate evaluation work, directly driving up CPU usage. The misconfigured parameters then prevent the engine from absorbing or smoothing this load: undersized buffer pools force repeated physical reads, over-aggressive parallelism multiplies CPU threads per query, and poorly timed checkpoints inject extra compute overhead. The resulting CPU saturation feeds back into longer query runtimes, which in turn sustain higher memory and worker consumption, exhausting the mis-set limits and increasing context switches. Thus, static design flaws, dynamic misconfiguration, and hard CPU exhaustion lock the system into a self-reinforcing performance spiral that is difficult to attribute to any single layer without holistic analysis.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, or data types are not aligned with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient physical access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Catalog statistics are stale or insufficient, causing systematic misestimation of row counts and selectivity during plan generation.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced quotas on files, memory segments, processes, or other OS objects cap the database’s ability to allocate required resources.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: queries choose and execute sub-optimal plans (e.g., full scans, non-covering index probes) that already over-consume I/O and CPU; estimation errors hide or exacerbate the bad physical design, leading the optimizer to deploy even more I/O-intensive or parallel plans; meanwhile, the surge in physical work and connection retries pushes the instance against OS-level ceilings, triggering sporadic "cannot open file", "cannot create thread", or "shared memory exhausted" errors. Auto-stats jobs, index rebuilds, and plan compilation may intermittently fail due to insufficient OS resources, while query latency becomes wildly unstable—sometimes stalling not only on data access but also on the inability to spawn workers or allocate I/O contexts.

Causally, the poor schema/index design increases the cost of every logical request, inflating resource consumption (handles, memory, parallel workers). This heavier footprint accelerates exhaustion of kernel limits. Once limits are hit, essential background tasks such as statistics collection or index maintenance abort, keeping statistics perpetually stale and preventing corrective indexing actions—thereby reinforcing both the statistics and design anomalies. In turn, the optimizer, deprived of accurate statistics and constrained by disabled parallelism, produces even more resource-hungry plans, which further stress the already saturated OS resources. This feedback loop magnifies latency, raises failure rates, and can culminate in partial or full service degradation despite no single anomaly appearing catastrophic in isolation.
