Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries pile up faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Stand-by or downstream replicas cannot receive or apply the primary’s WAL/redo stream at the rate it is generated.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space for data files, transaction logs, temp areas, or archives is exhausted or about to hit a hard boundary.

When all three conditions co-exist, the system shows a compound failure pattern: version stores, heap and index files, and retained WAL segments grow rapidly; replicas fall ever further behind, reporting escalating receive, flush, and replay lags; primary-side log directories, tablespaces, and temp areas approach 100 % usage; autovacuum or purge workers run continuously yet remain ineffective; long-running queries on replicas see increasingly stale data; and once space is fully consumed, new transactions, temp operations, or log writes error out, potentially bringing both primary and replicas to a halt. Monitoring may report contradictory signals—high bloat on primary tables, massive log backlogs, and space exhaustion alarms—making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal chain: heavy update/delete churn inflates MVCC bloat, which in turn drives up WAL volume. The surging WAL stream overwhelms replicas, forcing the primary to retain additional log segments until they have been replayed. Those unrecycled segments, along with the enlarged tables, consume disk rapidly, pushing the system toward space exhaustion. As free space shrinks, checkpoints, autovacuum, and replica apply processes compete for I/O and fail more often, slowing cleanup and replay still further. The positive feedback loop—bloat ➝ more WAL ➝ replication lag ➝ retained logs ➝ space pressure ➝ slower cleanup/apply ➝ more bloat—amplifies each constituent anomaly and jeopardizes both data freshness and service availability.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions are forced to serialize on hot or pinned buffer-cache pages and their associated latches, causing CPU spin, buffer-busy waits, and latency spikes.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical data or index pages become inconsistent, producing checksum errors, broken links, and mismatched row counts that undermine the reliability of access paths.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Data, log, temp, or archive areas run out of free bytes or cannot extend, leading to allocation failures, stalled checkpoints, and halted DML or DDL operations.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a multilayered failure pattern: extreme buffer-busy and page-latch waits mount while queries intermittently return wrong or duplicate rows, and sessions suddenly abort with "no space left/on­device" or "corruption detected" errors. Dirty pages linger in the buffer pool because checkpoints cannot allocate extra extents or recycle full log segments, increasing latch hold times and CPU spin. Simultaneously, corruption on hot pages causes repeated read-retry or logical consistency checks, amplifying contention as many sessions revisit the same damaged buffers. Administrators may see a chaotic mix of space-exhaustion alerts, corruption traces, and soaring latch wait graphs, making the individual symptoms hard to disentangle.

Causally, space exhaustion can stall or abort write-ahead logging and checkpoints, leaving pages partially flushed and heightening the risk of on-disk corruption. Corrupted or half-written pages then become hot spots as the engine repeatedly retries I/O and consistency verification, escalating latch contention within the buffer manager. The prolonged residency of dirty or suspect pages further reduces usable cache space, intensifying buffer churn and spin waits. In turn, the elevated contention slows down page flushing and file-growth operations, causing log and data files to reach capacity even faster. This vicious circle intertwines the three anomalies, degrading both performance and data integrity across transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even when plans are correctly chosen.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned instance parameters (memory, parallelism, logging, checkpointing, worker pools, etc.) that make the engine behave sub-optimally compared with the hardware and workload characteristics.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient or unstable network/connection capacity between clients and the DBMS, leading to slow or failed session establishment and data transfer.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload experiences compounding symptoms across execution, engine, and transport layers:  • Queries already slowed by full table scans or non-covering index probes take longer to acquire scarce buffer-pool pages or work memory, then stall again while transmitting large intermediate result sets over congested network links.  • Wait-event profiles show an interleaving of I/O reads, buffer-pin or work-mem spills, log-write or checkpoint waits, and client read/write or socket waits, none of which individually reach hardware saturation, making diagnosis difficult.  • Connection pools observe sporadic timeouts and elevated latency; back-end processes accumulate in idle-in-transaction or client send waits, yet CPU and disk metrics appear under-utilised.  • After configuration changes meant to relieve memory or parallelism pressure, checkpoint storms or background-worker starvation may coincide with network retransmissions, causing sudden throughput collapses and erratic response-time outliers.

Causally, poor schema/index design inflates I/O volume and row counts per query, bloating memory demand and increasing result-set sizes that must traverse the network. Mis-sized memory pools, work-mem, or parallelism settings then exacerbate this by triggering spills, excessive checkpoints, or worker thrashing, extending execution windows and keeping connections open longer. The prolonged sessions and enlarged result streams intensify network utilisation, pushing listener queues, socket buffers, and client pools toward exhaustion; in turn, elevated connection delays amplify application retry storms that further load the database. Meanwhile, network slowdowns lengthen query elapsed time, which feeds back into higher concurrency, larger working-set pressure, and more aggressive background activity driven by sub-optimal parameters. The positive feedback among design inefficiencies, misconfiguration, and connectivity constraints compounds latency and throughput degradation beyond what any single anomaly would cause.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the database engine to read, process, or return more data than the business logic truly requires.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying disk or storage-virtualization layer cannot supply read/write throughput or latency within the budget required by the database, causing device-level saturation and elevated I/O waits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Transport, listener, authentication, or socket resources between clients and the database server are exhausted or slow, impeding connection establishment and data transfer.

When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the system exhibits a multi-layer slowdown: statements already inflated by poor SQL logic drive excessive physical reads and writes that hit a saturated storage layer, multiplying I/O wait times, while the resulting long-running transactions occupy connections and emit large result sets that congest network links and exhaust listener or socket queues. Observed symptoms include a surge of slow queries in engine logs, soaring disk queue depths and read/write latencies, rising client connection timeouts, increased "too many connections" errors, and CPU idling while sessions wait alternately on I/O and client network sends. End-users perceive erratic response times, sporadic authentication failures, and stalled pages as both data access and result delivery degrade.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies physical I/O demand, pushing the storage subsystem past its throughput capacity; the ensuing storage latency elongates every statement’s execution window, holding locks and server processes longer. These extended transaction lifetimes keep network sockets open and flush larger or delayed result sets, which intensify network utilization. Network slowdowns and connection retries, in turn, inflate session counts and keep queries active even longer, further hammering the already saturated storage. The feedback loop between chatty, data-heavy SQL, overtaxed storage, and constrained network/connection resources cascades into systemic performance collapse, making each individual root cause harder to isolate and remediate.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer reuses or chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite accurate statistics, producing inefficient access paths or join orders.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk pages or index structures causes data retrieval errors, missing/duplicate rows, or forced scan fall-backs.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, threads, or other OS objects prevent the database from allocating required resources, leading to partial or total service denial.

When these three root causes coexist, the database may exhibit erratic and hard-to-diagnose behavior: identical queries intermittently toggle between good and disastrous plans; some executions fail outright with OS-level ‘too many open files’ or ‘cannot map shared memory’ errors; others succeed but return wrong, missing, or duplicate rows due to corrupted indexes. Plan instability compounds the visibility of corruption—bad plans may unexpectedly bypass damaged indexes via full scans, masking inconsistencies, while resource-limit failures interrupt index rebuilds or statistics collection, prolonging exposure. Administrators may observe a swirl of symptoms: sudden performance cliff-drops, exploding I/O from scan fallbacks, sporadic session or worker creation failures, checksum or page-verification errors in engine logs, and wide variance between estimated and actual row counts as the optimizer is misled by silently corrupted structures.

Causally, the resource-limit anomaly can impede routine maintenance (checksum verification, vacuum, or index rebuild jobs) and suppress parallelism, allowing latent block/index corruption to persist and spread. Corrupted indexes in turn mislead the optimizer, increasing the likelihood of terrible plan choices or forcing plan recompilations after repeated runtime errors. These mischosen plans may drastically inflate memory, file-handle, or thread consumption, accelerating exhaustion of already tight OS limits and triggering further allocation failures. The feedback loop between plan mis-selection, structural corruption, and OS resource starvation amplifies performance volatility, data correctness risks, and availability outages far beyond what any single anomaly would cause in isolation.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The costing inputs that drive plan selection (row counts, histograms, correlation, etc.) are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate buffer cache, work-area, and auxiliary memory growth pushes the host into sustained pressure, paging, or OOM scenarios.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical disks or storage fabric are saturated in IOPS, bandwidth, or latency, so read/write requests queue and slow down regardless of database intent.

When all three conditions coexist, the workload experiences erratic and worsening performance: queries are compiled into sub-optimal plans that favor either hash joins, large sorts, or table scans based on bad statistics, which in turn allocate excessive work memory and drive up buffer-cache churn. The inflated memory footprint exhausts physical RAM, causing the kernel to start paging exactly while the storage subsystem is already operating at or beyond its throughput limits. Swapping competes with normal data, temp, and log I/O, so I/O queues back up even further. Execution plans then encounter both severe memory pressure (work-area spills, frequent eviction of hot pages) and disk stalls (elevated read/write latency), leading to unstable runtimes, timeouts, and possible instance crashes.

Causally, stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing data-hungry execution strategies (e.g., full scans, multi-gigabyte sorts) that inflate memory requests. These oversized allocations accelerate consumption of buffer cache and per-query work memory, tipping the system into OS-level paging. The resulting swap traffic lands on already saturated storage, deepening I/O queues and latency. Conversely, high I/O latency slows down statistics collection jobs, prolonging staleness and reinforcing bad plans, while memory pressure can evict cached statistics objects, further degrading estimation accuracy. The feedback loop among poor statistics, runaway memory usage, and storage saturation drives a spiral of degrading performance across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction patterns request, scan, or lock more data than the business case requires, inflating logical work and execution time.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model lacks the indexes, partitions, or data types needed to support the workload’s access paths, forcing otherwise valid statements into inefficient full scans or lookups.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage devices or shared-storage tier cannot deliver the read/write throughput or latency demanded by the database engine, causing long I/O waits even for correctly issued requests.

When all three root causes coexist, the database experiences a cascade of amplified symptoms: statements already bloated by poor SQL logic and missing indexes trigger large full-table or index scans that generate surges of physical I/O; these surges immediately hit the ceiling of an I/O subsystem that is itself throughput-constrained. Observable effects include extreme and widely variable statement and transaction latencies, slow-query logs filled with repeated business operations, execution plans showing scan-heavy access with high physical read counts, buffer pool churn, sustained queue depths and read/write latencies at the device level, elevated lock wait times as long-running transactions hold resources, and application timeouts or retries that further multiply the workload.

Causal chain: ill-formed SQL and chatty transaction logic expand the amount of data the engine must touch. Because the schema lacks selective or covering indexes, the optimizer has no alternative but to choose scan-oriented plans, converting excess logical work into massive physical I/O. The inflated I/O demand overwhelms an already bandwidth-limited storage layer, stretching device queues and service times. As storage stalls lengthen, open transactions remain active longer, keeping locks and latches held and feeding back into even more contention and retry traffic. Thus, weaknesses at the workload layer and schema layer magnify the stress on storage, while storage saturation in turn exposes and aggravates every inefficiency in the upper layers, resulting in a self-reinforcing performance collapse that is difficult to attribute to any single tier without holistic diagnosis.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, write, or apply WAL/redo fast enough to keep pace with the primary, leading to growing replication lag and retention of log segments.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages become physically or logically corrupt, breaking key order, page links, or checksums and causing inconsistent query results or engine errors.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : The database or log storage reaches or nears its physical or logical size limit, preventing further allocations or log recycling and causing allocation failures.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits compounding symptoms: replication lag widens while retained primary log segments balloon; the enlarged log volume, unrecycled due to replica delay and corruption-triggered recovery retries, rapidly consumes remaining disk space until data files, archive areas, or temporary spaces hit hard limits. Corrupted pages or indexes surfaced on the replica may propagate back as apply failures, causing replication worker crashes, skipped transactions, or repeated retries that further increase lag. On the primary, space exhaustion and unrecycled logs generate "no space left" errors, stall checkpoints, and block new transactions, while read replicas deliver stale or inconsistent query results because of both replay delay and local corruption.

Causally, storage capacity pressure and replication backlogs reinforce each other: corruption encountered during replay forces replicas to halt or loop on failing records, which prevents log-position advancement; the primary therefore retains more WAL segments, accelerating space consumption. As free space dwindles, both primary and replica I/O subsystems may switch to synchronous archiving or halt allocations, further slowing write throughput and exacerbating replication lag. Simultaneously, corruption inside data or index pages can trigger larger redo generation (e.g., forced page writes or index rebuild attempts), inflating log volume when the replica is already behind. The intertwined feedback among replication delay, corruption-induced replay failures, and shrinking storage headroom drives the database toward a cascading failure that impairs availability, data integrity, and recovery options.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Optimizer inputs (row counts, histograms, correlation data) are stale or incomplete, leading the planner to choose systematically mis-costed execution plans.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate because background cleanup is throttled or blocked, inflating on-disk objects and visibility-check overhead.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log path (generation, flush, switch, archive, retention) becomes a bottleneck, stretching commit latency and stalling writers.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a multi-layer performance collapse:  
• Queries adopt inefficient plans—e.g., index probes where true cardinalities demand scans, or vice-versa—because statistics reflect the pre-bloat data shape rather than the current, heavily versioned heap.  
• Table and index bloat from unreclaimed versions drastically lengthens I/O paths; the mischosen plans amplify I/O and CPU consumption, further stressing the buffer pool and cache hierarchy.  
• Concurrently, surging redo from update/delete churn and from the faulty plans’ extra work overwhelms the log buffer and log device, inflating commit latency, causing frequent log-flush waits, and delaying checkpoints and archival.  
• Long-running transactions that keep version snapshots open also prevent log segment recycling, so log directories and version stores grow together, consuming space and triggering emergency autovacuum or checkpoint storms.  
• Background statistics jobs, vacuum/cleanup workers, and log archivers all contend for I/O and CPU, falling further behind and creating a feedback loop where stale statistics, bloat, and log pressure reinforce each other.  

Causally, excessive MVCC bloat inflates table sizes and redo generation, which in turn magnifies transaction-log throughput requirements. Log subsystem saturation slows commits and prolongs active snapshots, blocking vacuum from pruning dead tuples and perpetuating version accumulation. The expanding heap and skewed dead/live row ratios render existing statistics obsolete; suppressed or delayed statistics refreshes (due to long transactions or choking maintenance workers) lock the optimizer into poor plans that intensify CPU and I/O demand, generating even more undo/redo. This vicious cycle can escalate to severe space exhaustion, widespread query slowdowns, and potential outage if log or transaction-ID horizons are reached.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite reasonably accurate statistics, leading to inefficient access paths, wrong join methods, or unstable plan switches.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, enlarging the physical tables and indexes and inflating visibility-check overhead.

When both conditions coexist, the database exhibits hybrid symptoms: queries intermittently flip to full-table scans or poorly parameterized nested-loop joins that must wade through bloated heaps and indexes packed with dead tuples. Execution times surge non-linearly, buffer-cache churn intensifies, and I/O rises as enlarged objects no longer fit in memory. Autovacuum or cleanup workers run constantly yet fail to catch up, while the optimizer’s mischosen plans multiply the number of pages touched, further extending snapshot-scanning time. Administrators observe wildly varying runtimes for the same statement, rising latency for hot OLTP paths, escalating memory and I/O utilization, and misleading planner cost estimates due to distorted table statistics.

Causally, excessive dead tuples from the MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly distort table and index statistics, widening the gap between estimated and actual cardinalities just enough to tip the optimizer into Query Plan Selection Anomalies. Once a poor plan (e.g., sequential scans or Cartesian joins) is selected and possibly cached, it exacerbates the bloat problem by reading and rewriting more pages, producing yet more version churn and delaying cleanup progress. The two anomalies therefore form a feedback loop: version bloat misguides the optimizer, and the optimizer’s sub-optimal plans accelerate bloat growth and resource consumption, degrading overall transactional performance until both issues are addressed together.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to scan or modify far more data, rows, or time than business logic actually requires.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and undo/rollback segments outpaces background cleanup, inflating on-disk structures and visibility-check cost.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from poorly written workload logic that drives unnecessary row accesses and prolonged transactions, while MVCC version garbage is not reclaimed fast enough. Together, these conditions form a feedback loop where bloated version stores degrade performance and further magnify the inefficiencies of the SQL workload.

Combined observable phenomena:  • Sharp and erratic tail latencies, frequent application timeouts, and growing slow-query logs.  • Rapid growth of table and index size despite stable business data volume; rising dead-to-live row ratios and increasing checkpoint or vacuum runtimes.  • Long-running transactions that pin old snapshots, causing vacuum freezes, and in turn exacerbate bloat.  • Escalating I/O and memory consumption as wide scans touch many stale pages, leading to cache churn, higher CPU spent on visibility checks, and potential autovacuum saturation.  • Optimizer misestimates due to inflated statistics, yielding even less efficient plans and reinforcing the original workload inefficiencies.

Causal interaction: Inefficient SQL patterns (e.g., bulk updates without selective predicates, chatty ORM loops, transactions left open across think time) generate high churn of updates/deletes and create extensive undo/version chains. Those same long transactions also hold old snapshots, preventing garbage collection. As background cleaners fall behind, table and index bloat increases, making each subsequent oversized query or scan more expensive, which prolongs execution and transaction lifetimes. The compounded effect is a vicious cycle: bad workload logic produces more MVCC debris, the unreclaimed debris slows queries and elongates transactions, and the prolonged transactions inhibit cleanup, driving the system into progressively degraded throughput and escalating resource consumption.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, scan, or hold far more data and resources than the true business logic requires.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Internal buffer-manager hot pages and their associated latches become points of intense contention, stalling sessions on page access, pin, or flush operations.

When both conditions exist simultaneously, end-user statements display extreme and highly variable latency, slow-query logs fill with repetitive statements, CPU usage oscillates between long spin-loops and idle waits, and wait-event views show surges in buffer busy waits, page/latch waits, and I/O stalls. Hot root or leaf pages of frequently scanned tables and indexes become choke points, while oversized scans and long-lived transactions keep those pages in memory and pinned, amplifying contention. Application retries and lock time-outs rise, throughput collapses under concurrency, and even background tasks such as checkpoints or purge/clean-up jobs begin to lag.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL patterns (full-table scans, wide projections, chatty ORM loops, or monotonic inserts) read and dirty large numbers of pages, driving rapid buffer turnover and concentrating access on a small subset of pages. This inflates latch acquisition frequency and duration on those pages. The resulting latch waits extend statement and transaction lifetimes, which in turn leave pages pinned longer, exacerbate page hot-spotting, and further reduce effective cache capacity. The two anomalies thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop where poor workload logic produces the very contention that magnifies its own performance cost, degrading both transactional and analytical operations across the system.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Execution-plan cost inputs no longer match the true data distribution, causing systematic cardinality and cost misestimates that bias plan selection.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-wide settings for memory, parallelism, logging, and background workers are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, so runtime behavior is limited or destabilised even when physical resources are sufficient.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport path or server-side connection handling cannot sustain the offered request or result-set volume, leading to connection stalls, retransmits, and socket exhaustion.

When all three root causes are present, the database shows a multi-layer performance collapse: queries choose wildly sub-optimal plans (e.g., serial nested-loop joins on billions of rows or overly parallel hash joins that spill), backends over-allocate or under-allocate memory because of incorrect parameter values, and the resulting oversized or long-running result sets flood an already constrained network layer. Symptoms may include: extreme divergence between estimated and actual row counts, sudden spikes in buffer flushes, work-memory spill storms, CPU threads idling while sessions wait on client read/write or connection slots, erratic throughput with bursts of "too many connections" or authentication timeouts, and seemingly random latency outliers immediately after data loads or configuration changes. Monitoring may show low to moderate server CPU and I/O utilisation while application response times soar and network retransmission counters, socket backlog depth, and background-worker queues all climb together.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics drive execution plans that generate unexpected I/O and data transfer volumes; mis-sized memory, parallelism, and checkpoint parameters amplify these inefficiencies, causing larger intermediate results, aggressive workfile spills, or excessive concurrent backends. The inflated data flows and prolonged query runtimes then saturate connection slots and network bandwidth, increasing round-trip times and retransmissions. In turn, network slowdowns lengthen query execution even further, delaying feedback-based statistics refresh and prolonging locks and memory occupation, which deepens the impact of the configuration mis-tuning. The intertwined feedback loops between optimizer misestimation, resource-governing parameter errors, and constrained connectivity culminate in a self-reinforcing degradation that is difficult to diagnose when each layer is inspected in isolation.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request conflicting locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, producing long blocker-waiter chains or deadlocks that suspend or abort work until locks are released.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot supply the needed read/write bandwidth or IOPS, driving up I/O latency and queue depths for data, log, and temp files.

Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously suffers from severe lock-manager contention while the underlying storage subsystem is saturated, so that blocking waits and deadlock retries are compounded by prolonged physical I/O delays, creating a feedback loop that cripples transactional throughput.

Combined observable phenomena: Lock-wait and deadlock graphs lengthen and recur more frequently; sessions stay in lock-wait states far longer than usual because the holders of critical locks are themselves stalled on slow disk reads or log flushes. Overall response times and commit latency spike, CPU usage remains modest, and connection pools back up as both lock and I/O wait classes dominate performance monitors. Deadlock victims may rise, yet retries often re-encounter the same blocked resources because the underlying I/O bottleneck prevents rapid forward progress. Batch windows stretch, and application timeouts increase even for read-only workloads due to lock queues behind long-running write transactions.

Causal chain interaction: Storage saturation lengthens the execution and commit duration of transactions, extending the lifetime of their locks and increasing the probability that other sessions will conflict with them. Those blocked sessions accumulate, enlarge lock queues, and may form deadlock cycles that force rollbacks and retries, which in turn generate additional I/O and further stress the already constrained storage subsystem. Conversely, the surge of retried or piled-up transactions multiplies random I/O requests, exacerbating device queue depths and widening latency, creating a vicious circle where lock contention and I/O bottlenecks reinforce each other and jointly deteriorate overall OLTP system performance.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Composite anomaly definition: The system concurrently suffers from (1) the optimizer choosing sub-optimal execution plans, (2) intense lock-manager contention that blocks or deadlocks transactions, and (3) runaway memory consumption that pushes the database process or host into sustained memory pressure. All three root causes are present at the same time and jointly degrade workload performance.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Application sessions experience long and highly variable response times as poorly chosen plans amplify row visits and prolong critical sections, which in turn lengthen lock-hold durations and enlarge blocker–waiter chains. Concurrently, inflated work areas, plan-cache bloat, and growing buffer caches drive the process RSS beyond physical memory, triggering operating-system paging or OOM killer events. Monitoring shows oscillating or flip-flopping execution plans, escalating lock-wait counters, frequent deadlock victim messages, rapid growth of memory allocations and swap, drop-offs in cache hit ratios due to churn, CPU stalls caused by memory thrashing, and eventual connection timeouts or node restarts that further disturb plan stability and lock recovery.

Causal chain and interaction: A bad plan (e.g., full table scan instead of index seek) inflates I/O and keeps row-level or page locks active far longer, increasing the probability and duration of blocking and deadlocks. The same inefficient plan may require oversized hash/sort buffers or spawn excessive parallel workers, accelerating memory consumption. Elevated memory pressure leads the engine or operating system to evict clean pages, flush caches, or invoke swapping, extending I/O times and further slowing statement completion—thereby lengthening lock hold times and widening contention. Repeated plan invalidations caused by memory pressure or crash recovery prompt the optimizer to regenerate and possibly pick different sub-optimal plans, creating performance whiplash. The feedback loop among bad plans, lock buildup, and memory exhaustion can cascade into severe throughput collapse and service instability, making isolated tuning of any single layer ineffective until all three contributing root causes are addressed together.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, often because of cost-model issues, plan reuse pathologies, or version/configuration changes.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates or leaks memory beyond safe host limits, producing OS pressure, swapping, and cache churn due to unbounded work areas, plan-cache bloat, or excessive parallelism.

Composite anomaly definition: Both a poor plan choice and runaway memory consumption coexist, so the workload executes under an execution plan that is already inefficient while the engine is simultaneously stressed by memory over-allocation.

Combined observable phenomena: SQLs that abruptly switch from efficient indexed access to broad scans or high-fan-out nested loops also show exploding memory footprints for hash joins, sorts, or parallel worker buffers. Operators that the optimizer mistakenly deems cheap reserve large work areas, causing rapid growth of process resident-set size, frequent eviction of buffer pages, degraded cache hit ratios, increased I/O, CPU stalls due to paging, and even out-of-memory kills. Performance instability becomes pronounced: the same statement may be lightning-fast at one moment and then timeout or crash the instance minutes later. Monitoring dashboards reveal correlated spikes in hard-parse counts, plan cache entries, work-memory grants, and OS swap activity.

Causal interaction: A sub-optimal plan often drives heavier operator memory grants (e.g., full hash aggregates instead of indexed lookups) which accelerates memory pressure; conversely, memory pressure can trigger plan cache evictions, forcing re-optimization that re-selects or pins the bad plan, perpetuating the cycle. Excessive parallelism chosen by the flawed plan multiplies per-worker buffers, exhausting memory faster and amplifying pressure. As the OS begins swapping, the already inefficient plan lengthens execution time, keeping its large allocations alive longer, further aggravating memory exhaustion. The intertwined feedback loop of poor plan selection and escalating memory allocation degrades overall throughput and can culminate in instance instability or crash.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to touch far more data, rows, or time than business logic truly requires.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records pile up faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check costs.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures become physically or logically corrupted, undermining confidence in access paths and data correctness.

When all three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: long-tail statement latencies and frequent application timeouts intertwine with ever-growing table and index sizes, elevated I/O for version scans, and erratic query plans that suddenly devolve into full-table scans as the optimizer distrusts or disables damaged indexes. Cleanup workers struggle, cycling endlessly over bloated version stores that include corrupted or unreachable pages, while integrity checkers report escalating page-checksum and key-order errors. Lock-free but version-heavy scans inflate undo/redo volume, lengthen checkpoint times, and amplify storage pressure, leading to increased risk of further corruption during crash recovery. From the user’s perspective, intermittent data mismatches, missing rows, and duplicate results accompany severe performance variability, making diagnosis elusive.

Causally, poorly written workload logic initiates excessive updates, deletes, and long-running transactions, accelerating MVCC version accumulation. The swollen version store expands on-disk structures, heightening I/O churn and prolonging maintenance windows. This persistent stress magnifies the chance of write-amplification, torn pages, or half-completed page splits, which in turn precipitate data block and index integrity faults. Once corruption forms, index probes may fail, forcing broader scans that read even more outdated versions, further slowing queries and delaying vacuum/clean-up progress. The corrupted structures also impede effective version pruning, trapping old versions and creating a feedback loop that compounds bloat, corruption exposure, and application-level inefficiencies. The interplay of excessive logical workload, runaway MVCC debris, and physical structure corruption thus degrades both performance and data reliability in transactional workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statement or transaction design forces the engine to process, scan, or return more data and to hold locks longer than functionally required.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or subscribers cannot receive or apply primary WAL/redo at production rate, leading to growing replication lag and log-retention pressure on the primary.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport and connection-handling path between clients and the database is saturated or unstable, throttling session establishment and data transfer.

When all three anomalies occur together the system experiences an acute mix of long-running, data-heavy transactions, widening replica apply delay, and deteriorating client connectivity. Clients observe erratic response times, frequent timeouts both during query execution and connection setup, stale reads from lagging replicas, mounting numbers of aborted or retried transactions, and explosive growth of primary-side WAL or binlog storage. Monitoring shows bloated slow-query logs, replication delay graphs climbing in parallel with network retransmission rates, ballooning counts of idle-in-transaction or client-read waits, and listener backlogs filling while replicas fall further behind.

Causally, chatty or data-intensive workload logic inflates result sets and transaction sizes, increasing primary log volume. The surge of log traffic must traverse the same constrained network links that already struggle to serve front-end clients; packet loss or bandwidth saturation slows both client I/O and replica streaming. As replicas slip, the primary is forced to retain additional log segments, further stressing local storage and lengthening checkpoints. In turn, the extended transaction durations caused by sub-optimal SQL keep locks and snapshots open longer, amplifying replica apply contention and prolonging network socket occupancy. The intertwined effects create a feedback loop where poor workload design generates excess data, congested networks delay its delivery, and replication lag feeds back into longer client wait times and heavier retry storms, collectively degrading overall database performance and availability.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or unconstrained growth of database engine memory regions (buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, etc.) that pushes the host into sustained memory pressure, paging, or OOM scenarios.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside on-disk data and index pages, causing checksums, key order, or page link verification to fail and making persisted structures unreliable.

When both root causes are present, the system may show a compound symptom set: 1) escalating memory consumption and swap activity, 2) intermittent or repeated detection of checksum or index-order errors, 3) erratic query plans that oscillate between index scans and full scans, 4) crash-recovery or instance-eviction cycles that arise from OOM killers or corruption panics, 5) heavy buffer churn as the engine attempts to reread or repair damaged pages, amplifying cache-miss rates and memory allocations, and 6) longer maintenance windows because integrity-check, repair, or restore tasks run concurrently with memory-hungry workloads, further stressing RAM.

Causal interaction: runaway memory allocations shrink the effective buffer cache and push clean pages out, increasing I/O and the likelihood that already-corrupted pages are reread and dereferenced. Every emergency checkpoint or abrupt shutdown triggered by OOM heightens the risk that partially flushed dirty buffers leave pages in an inconsistent state, deepening corruption. Conversely, encountering corrupted pages forces the engine to allocate extra diagnostic and recovery work areas, inflate error queues, and potentially pin suspect pages, all of which consume additional memory and aggravate the original memory pressure. The feedback loop between memory exhaustion and structural corruption accelerates system instability, turning what would be isolated faults into widespread service degradation and potential data loss.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Composite Anomaly Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from accelerated accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions and saturation of the underlying storage-subsystem’s read/write throughput. The version store keeps expanding while the physical devices that must hold, read, and clean those extra pages are already at or beyond their performance envelope.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Administrators will notice rapidly growing table and index sizes, soaring obsolete-to-live row ratios, and autovacuum/cleaner workers that run constantly yet make little progress. At the same time, I/O wait events dominate wait-class statistics; average and p-99 latencies for data-file, log, and temp-space operations rise sharply; queue depths remain full; and overall transaction response times elongate even though CPU utilization is modest. Sequential scans and index probes both touch many more pages because of bloat, compounding physical I/O. Planner misestimates lead to poor plans, while checkpoints, WAL flushes, and batch jobs overrun their windows due to throttled bandwidth. Alerts may escalate for near-term transaction-ID wraparound, version-store exhaustion, or log flush timeouts.

Causal Interaction: Excessive update/delete churn produces large numbers of dead tuples that background cleanup workers must remove. Each cleanup cycle issues additional reads and writes, inflating I/O demand. When the storage layer is already throughput-constrained, these maintenance I/Os contend with foreground queries and deferred writes, slowing both application workload and cleanup itself. The slowdown lets even more obsolete versions pile up, further bloating on-disk structures and increasing every future I/O operation’s cost. This positive feedback loop—version bloat increasing I/O volume, and I/O saturation throttling bloat removal—drives the system into a self-reinforcing degradation spiral that jeopardizes performance, space availability, and transactional safety.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive or runaway allocation of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine heaps pushes total database memory demand beyond the safe limits of the host.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path—generation, flushing, switching, or archiving of redo—becomes the primary bottleneck, inflating commit latency and stalling write activity.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical volumes that service data, temp, and log files are saturated in IOPS, bandwidth, or latency, making device service time the limiting factor for I/O.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database exhibits a blended failure signature: memory pressure drives aggressive dirty-page eviction and larger, more frequent log flushes just as the log subsystem itself struggles to switch or archive segments on an already saturated storage layer. Observable effects include surging commit and checkpoint latency, oscillating buffer-cache hit ratios, prolonged foreground and background waits on log file sync, buffer IO, and direct path read/write events, escalating paging or swapping on the host, and periods of near-stall where sessions block behind log space or I/O completion while CPU remains under-utilized. Monitoring may show the database process’s resident set swelling, log and data volumes with deep device queues, archive destinations ballooning, and ultimately instance eviction or crash due to out-of-memory or inability to advance the redo pointer.

Causally, excessive memory allocation shortens the usable in-memory write-back window, forcing the engine to flush dirty buffers and large log batches more aggressively. Those extra writes hit a transaction-log subsystem that is already size- or configuration-limited; the backlog there prolongs commit and checkpoint completion, causing yet more buffers to accumulate and further elevating memory pressure. Meanwhile, both the forced buffer flushes and the heavy redo traffic converge on an over-subscribed storage layer whose throughput ceiling amplifies every flush and sync delay. The three anomalies therefore form a positive feedback loop: memory over-consumption accelerates log pressure; log stalls extend buffer lifetimes and increase memory usage; both inflate I/O volume, which hammers the storage subsystem and propagates latency back up the stack, degrading overall database stability and performance.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously affected by runaway accumulation of obsolete MVCC versions, on-disk data-block or index corruption, and imminent exhaustion of allocated storage space. This convergence means the version store cannot be cleaned up, the physical structures that should be reclaimed are partly corrupted or inconsistent, and the shrinking free space prevents corrective maintenance and normal DML from completing.

Expected manifestations: Administrators may observe rocketing counts of dead tuples, rollback records, and logically deleted index entries while VACUUM/clean-up workers remain busy yet ineffective. In parallel, queries that rely on indexes begin to miss or double-count rows, checksum or page-verification errors appear in logs, and integrity-check utilities flag key-ordering or linkage violations. At the same time, tablespaces, WAL/redo logs, or temp areas report critically low free bytes, leading to auto-extend failures, rejected allocations for new versions or undo segments, stalled checkpoint or log-archiving processes, and sudden transaction aborts. Planner misestimates, long-running sequential scans, repeated statement retries, and emergency shutdowns triggered by corruption or out-of-space situations may all appear together, making symptom attribution difficult.

Causal interaction: Excess MVCC bloat inflates table and index sizes, directly accelerating consumption of limited disk space; as free space disappears, background cleaners lose the ability to allocate new pages for version rewriting, further slowing or halting garbage collection and causing an even faster rise in obsolete versions. Simultaneously, latent or newly introduced page or index corruptions can prevent space-reclaim operations such as vacuum, defragmentation, or index rebuilds from completing, leaving corrupted pages locked and their space unrecoverable. Space pressure constrains crash-safe writes and check-pointing, increasing the risk of torn-page or incomplete-redo corruption, which in turn exacerbates integrity anomalies. The feedback loop among bloated version stores, structural corruption, and dwindling capacity drives the system toward a state where both user workloads and recovery/repair utilities fail, threatening data availability and consistency.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks on shared rows, pages, or metadata, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Stand-by or replica nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, persist, or apply primary-generated log records at the produced rate, inflating replication lag and retaining excess log segments on the primary.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Transport or connection-handling bottlenecks—bandwidth saturation, packet loss, socket exhaustion, or authentication backlogs—impede data flow between clients or replicas and the database server.

When these three issues arise together, the database exhibits compound symptoms: application sessions pile up in both connection pools and lock wait queues; ordinary statements appear to "freeze" as they wait for locks held by transactions whose clients are themselves stalled on sluggish networks; deadlock detector activity and victim rollbacks surge; replica replay lag grows rapidly because lock-intensive transactions commit slowly and because network congestion throttles log shipping; primary WAL or binlog disks fill due to unrecycled segments retained for lagging replicas; monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in lock-wait time, replication apply delay, network retransmissions, and refused or idle sockets, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single layer.

Causally, degraded network paths first throttle both client traffic and replication streaming. Prolonged round-trip times cause application transactions to hold locks longer, increasing the probability of blocking and deadlocks on the primary; these stalled commits in turn reduce commit throughput while still accumulating unflushed WAL. Because the same network impairment also limits the rate at which replicas receive or acknowledge log data, the primary cannot recycle its growing log, further stressing disk subsystems. On the replica side, apply workers encountering lock conflicts left by large or long-running transactions replay even more slowly, amplifying lag. The feedback loop—network-induced latency inflating lock duration, lock contention elongating transactions and generating larger bursts of WAL, and replication backlog preventing log cleanup—drives a systemic degradation that impacts both write and read traffic and complicates root-cause isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : The application issues inefficient or over-broad SQL or transaction patterns that force the engine to scan, sort, or lock far more data than business logic actually requires.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply the primary’s log stream at the rate it is generated.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated in throughput, IOPS, or latency, throttling reads, writes, and durability flushes across data, temp, and log files.

When all three anomalies arise together, the database exhibits extreme and persistent slowness across both primary and replica tiers: primary sessions show long-tail statement latencies, high read and write waits, and prolonged transaction lifetimes; slow-query and statement-statistics views list the same heavyweight SQL repeatedly. On replicas, log-position gaps widen rapidly, apply lag grows from seconds to minutes or hours, relay logs bloat, and read-only workloads return increasingly stale data. Administrators observe escalating disk-queue depths, soaring device-level latency, checkpoints that take longer to complete, and log segments accumulating because replication cannot advance. Failover readiness deteriorates, and application retries may amplify concurrency and locking conflicts, masking whether the bottleneck is in SQL design, storage, or replication.

Causally, inefficient SQL and long-running transactions generated by the SQL Workload Logic Anomaly create large volumes of table and index I/O as well as oversized redo bursts. These heavy I/O demands collide with pre-existing or induced Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly, causing data-file reads, temp spills, and log flushes to queue behind saturated devices. The inflated redo stream must traverse the replication channel; however, the same storage bottlenecks now slow both transmission and apply on replicas, triggering the Replication Synchronization Anomaly. As replicas lag, the primary is prevented from recycling log segments, further increasing write pressure on the already stressed storage layer. The feedback loop among verbose workload, throttled storage, and backlog in replication amplifies each symptom, making the overall system progressively less responsive and complicating root-cause isolation.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys, read replicas, or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo records as fast as the primary produces them, causing widening log-position gaps and replay lag.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical devices that host data, temp, and log files are saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, driving up read/write wait times and elongating database operations.

When both root causes strike together, the system exhibits extreme and intertwined symptoms: commit latency on the primary increases as log flushes queue behind a congested storage layer, while replicas fall increasingly behind because their own disks cannot ingest or replay the incoming log stream. WAL segments pile up on the primary and relay logs balloon on replicas, accelerating disk-space consumption and triggering emergency retention policies. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in storage wait events (data-file, log-file, durability flush) and replication metrics (send/receive/replay lag). Failover readiness rapidly degrades, read-only workload freshness collapses, and maintenance windows overrun as both I/O stalls and replication gaps reinforce each other.

Causally, inadequate storage throughput throttles the very I/O operations—log writes on the primary and log reads/writes on replicas—needed for timely replication. As disks struggle, primary commit flushes slow, lengthening the log queue to replicas; the larger backlog forces replicas to perform bursty catch-up replays that in turn spike their own I/O demand on already saturated volumes, further delaying apply. The growing backlog prevents log recycling, inflating disk usage and deepening the storage bottleneck on the primary, while replica lag perpetuates retention of old segments. This feedback loop magnifies both anomalies, making the overall database increasingly unstable and at risk of outage.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Inaccurate, missing, or stale optimizer statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimation and mis-costing, leading the optimizer to select sub-optimal execution plans. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced caps on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other OS resources are exhausted, preventing the database from allocating processes, memory, or I/O contexts that it logically requires. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Listener, socket, or network-path capacity is insufficient or unstable, producing connection refusals, timeouts, and slow or stalled client/server data transfer.

When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the database exhibits multilayer symptoms: 1) query plans flip unpredictably or lock into inefficient full scans or serial plans due to wrong row-count estimates; 2) those inefficient plans inflate memory, file-descriptor, worker, and I/O demands, accelerating exhaustion of the already tight OS resource limits and triggering "cannot fork", "too many open files", or "cannot allocate shared memory" errors; 3) as backend and listener resources saturate, new client connections back up, causing rising TCP SYN backlog, authentication stalls, mid-stream socket disconnects, and application-side timeouts. Performance telemetry shows extreme variance—some sessions hang on client read/write waits, others are terminated by internal errors, while surviving sessions run with degraded plans and long runtimes. Diagnosis is complicated because plan misestimates, kernel denials, and network failures surface in overlapping time windows, obscuring singular blame.

Causal chain: Stale or incomplete statistics steer the optimizer toward plan shapes that open many files, allocate large temp segments, or request numerous parallel workers. These bloated resource requests collide with low or already near-exhausted OS limits, causing allocation failures that leave partially initialized backends, leaked file descriptors, and half-open sockets. The accumulation of such orphaned kernel objects further shrinks available OS quotas, amplifying the resource-limit anomaly. Meanwhile, aborted sessions and retrying application pools inflate connection churn, deepening the network and listener overload. Conversely, network-level slowdowns prolong transaction lifetimes, delaying statistic-gathering jobs and prolonging locks on objects, which keeps statistics stale and perpetuates misestimation. The feedback loop among poor statistics, OS-level exhaustion, and network saturation thus cascades, driving widespread performance collapse across both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating on-disk and in-memory footprints and lengthening visibility checks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions repeatedly serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, and I/O slots, stalling while trying to pin, read, or flush shared pages.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, starving other work and enlarging run-queue and scheduler waits.

When these three conditions coexist, the system exhibits a feedback loop of stress signals: rapidly growing table and index sizes inflate the working-set beyond the buffer pool, causing constant page evictions and refills. Hot root pages and version chains become latch hot-spots, producing surges of buffer-busy and latch waits. Spin-loop retries and repeated visibility checks consume CPU, pushing host utilization to the ceiling. Checkpoint and background-writer processes fight for CPU and I/O, while cleanup workers fall further behind, seen as ever-rising dead-tuple ratios, lengthening autovacuum runtimes, and warnings about transaction-ID or UNDO wraparound. Application queries experience both CPU-bound queuing delays and IO-induced latency spikes, making performance unpredictable and hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, heavy update/delete churn triggers MVCC bloat; the swollen relation footprint overwhelms an already tight buffer pool, amplifying buffer churn and latch contention. Each failed latch acquisition can induce spin-waiting, directly inflating CPU demand. As CPUs saturate, background cleaners and checkpointers lose scheduling opportunities, slowing version reclamation and dirty-page flushing. The slower cleanup further escalates bloat, which in turn increases buffer pressure and contention, closing a vicious cycle that degrades throughput and threatens outages from transaction-horizon or space-exhaustion limits.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical table, index, and partition design does not match workload access patterns, forcing inefficient full scans, non-covering index probes, and excessive row/memory churn.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log buffer, file groups, or archiver cannot absorb or flush redo fast enough, so commits wait on log-write, log-flush, and log-sync events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced caps on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, I/O contexts, or process/thread counts are reached, preventing the database from allocating required OS resources.

When these three root causes coexist, the workload experiences an explosive mix of symptoms: poorly indexed DML and wide range scans generate abnormally large redo streams that quickly fill the log buffer and force frantic log-file switches. Commit latency, "log file sync/write" and "log buffer space" waits surge, while background archiver or replication workers fall behind, swelling archive directories. As sessions queue behind stalled commits, the database tries to open more files, allocate additional shared memory, start extra log writer or archiver threads, and spawn parallel workers—actions that collide with tight OS limits. Soon the error logs show alternating database wait events and kernel denials (EMFILE, ENOMEM, ENOSPC, semaphore limits), new sessions or workers fail to start, and parts of the system enter a semi-hung state where reads limp along but writes time out or abort.

Causally, the inefficient schema/index design inflates the volume and frequency of data modifications and undo/redo generation. This elevated redo rate saturates an already undersized or mis-placed transaction-log subsystem, prolonging commit paths and increasing the lifetime and number of active log files. The resulting backlog drives the engine to open more descriptors, maintain more control files, grow log buffers, and spawn additional background tasks, all of which consume kernel objects. If OS limits are conservative or have been depleted by earlier failures, these requests begin to fail, which in turn prevents log switches, flushes, or worker creation, aggravating log congestion and magnifying the performance collapse. Thus, each root cause amplifies the others, producing a severe, intertwined bottleneck that is far more debilitating than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced per-process or system-wide resources such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or address space that the database engine depends on but does not directly control.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Saturation or misconfiguration of the network, listener, socket, or connection-management layer that prevents clients or replicas from reliably establishing, maintaining, or using database connections.

When these two root causes manifest together, the database may enter a cascading failure mode: bursts of incoming sessions or large result transfers inflate the number of sockets, file handles, and threads until kernel limits are hit; concurrently, network congestion or listener backlog saturation drives up connection latency and retry storms. Observable symptoms include frequent client timeouts, "too many open files" or "cannot create thread" errors in server logs, spikes of half-open and TIME_WAIT sockets, abrupt termination of background or parallel workers, authentication stalls, and a mix of network wait events and OS-level resource allocation failures. The overlap of network-layer socket buildup with tight kernel limits makes it hard to distinguish whether outages stem from the network or the host itself.

Causally, elevated connection rates or slow data transfer inflate the number and lifespan of sockets and backend processes. Each additional socket consumes a file descriptor and kernel memory; each authenticated session spawns a process or thread. If OS limits on descriptors, processes, or shared memory are low, normal retry behavior from network slowdowns will quickly exhaust those limits, preventing new workers from spawning and amplifying connection queuing. Conversely, once the OS refuses new descriptors or threads, the listener cannot accept or process connections, causing clients to back off and retry, which further floods the network and listener backlog. This positive feedback loop intertwines the two anomalies, escalating from partial degradation to complete service outage and making remediation require simultaneous relief of both kernel resource caps and network/connectivity bottlenecks.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database concurrently suffers from (1) stale or inaccurate optimizer statistics that drive systematic cardinality misestimation, (2) runaway memory consumption that pushes the instance and host beyond safe memory limits, and (3) saturation of the transaction-log generation / flush path. Together, these three orthogonal yet interacting root causes form a compound failure state that degrades both query processing and commit throughput under OLTP workloads.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Execution plans show severe row-estimate errors, often selecting hash or sort strategies that demand excessive work memory. The inflated work areas, plus bloated buffer and plan caches, exhaust physical RAM, leading to paging, memory pressure waits, or OOM terminations. At the same time, commit latency, LOG FLUSH/WRITE waits, and log-buffer stall events spike because log flushing competes with paging I/O, frequent checkpoints, and large redo bursts produced by mis-planned bulk or spill operations. Users see alternating patterns of slow queries, aborted transactions, and periods where the entire instance freezes or is force-restarted by the cluster manager.

Causal Interaction: Stale statistics first mislead the optimizer into choosing memory-intensive plans (e.g., multi-GB hash joins, over-parallelized sorts). These plans inflate per-session work areas and swell the buffer cache with mispredicted read-ahead, pushing the engine into memory overcommit. The resulting OS paging and cache churn slow down datafile and log-file I/O alike, lengthening log flush times. Prolonged commits keep log buffers full, forcing back-pressure on application threads and increasing transaction duration; the longer transactions retain log segments, causing more frequent log switches and checkpoints, which in turn intensify both memory usage (dirty-page queues) and disk traffic. Memory pressure also impedes the archiver and replication workers, keeping log files active longer and exacerbating log-space shortages. Thus, cardinality misestimation fuels memory exhaustion, which magnifies log contention, and the stalled log subsystem further propagates memory retention—creating a feedback loop that drives the database into severe throughput collapse.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale, missing, or inaccurate, causing systematic cardinality misestimates that mislead the optimizer during plan generation.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime parameters (memory, parallelism, checkpoint, etc.) are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, so performance limits are hit even when physical resources are not fully utilized.

When both conditions exist simultaneously, the workload exhibits plan choices that are not only sub-optimal but also collide with ill-sized memory pools, worker limits, and I/O cadences. Symptoms include: execution plans that swing between inefficient serial scans and over-parallelized joins; sudden spool, sort, or hash spills despite apparently ample server memory; erratic CPU and I/O utilization where some resources idle while sessions wait on memory, workfile, or replan events; frequent recompilations after data changes followed by checkpoint or flush storms triggered by mis-set checkpoint parameters; and highly variable response times where identical statements alternately run fast and then stall on waits that do not match observed hardware saturation.

Causally, incorrect statistics drive the optimizer to favor plans whose resource demands—join order, parallel degree, memory grants, spill behavior—are based on wrong cardinality assumptions. Misaligned configuration parameters then fail to supply, or grossly oversupply, the required resources, turning what might have been a modest inefficiency into severe contention or wasted capacity. Conversely, undersized work memory or buffer pools force more frequent I/O, which can invalidate sampling assumptions and accelerate data churn, making statistics stale even faster. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other: bad statistics choose bad plans; bad configuration magnifies their cost, leading to oscillating performance, noisy wait patterns, and an opaque diagnostic picture that masks the true dual origin of the problem.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys or downstream consumers cannot read, persist, or apply WAL/redo fast enough, causing ever-growing log-position gaps and replica lag.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical devices or storage fabric are saturated, driving up read/write latencies and queue depths and slowing all database I/O.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Allocated disk or logical volume free space is exhausted for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas, producing allocation failures and blocking further growth.

When these three issues occur together, the database experiences compounding symptoms: replication delay widens rapidly while primary and replica disks show both high latency and dwindling free space. Primary log segments accumulate because they cannot be recycled until replicas catch up, but the replicas themselves are replaying slowly due to saturated I/O paths. The retained logs, growing relay logs, and stalled archiving consume the remaining disk capacity on both tiers, causing space-exhaustion errors, forced pauses of replication or checkpoint activity, prolonged commit acknowledgment times, escalating application latency, and eventually write failures that can freeze the entire workload. Monitoring dashboards show soaring replication lag, elevated storage wait events, device queues at maximum depth, and critical free-space alarms firing almost simultaneously.

Causally, an underlying Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly throttles both the primary’s log flushes and the replicas’ redo apply rates. This slowdown makes replicas fall behind, which prevents the primary from removing old log segments. The retained logs rapidly consume disk, triggering a Storage Space Capacity Anomaly on both primary and standby volumes. As space tightens, background checkpoints and archiving intensify I/O pressure, further degrading throughput and creating a positive feedback loop that worsens replication lag and accelerates space depletion. The intertwined nature of insufficient I/O bandwidth and shrinking free space amplifies the replication backlog, culminating in systemic stalls, potential replication stoppage, and risk of primary outage due to full disks.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions contend for mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, leading to wait chains or deadlocks that stall forward progress.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging pipeline (log buffer, log file, archiver, replication retention) cannot keep pace with redo generation, inflating commit latency and pausing writers.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupt, so look-ups, scans, or modifications encounter checksum, linkage, or key-order violations.

When these three root causes strike at once, the database experiences a multilayered slowdown and instability: lock wait times and deadlock victim errors rise while commits stall on log flushes, stretching the duration that locks are held and enlarging blocking trees. Corrupted pages or indexes trigger automatic verification retries, forced page rereads, or error-driven transaction rollbacks, further prolonging lock holds and generating bursts of redo that exacerbate log-flush congestion. Applications observe erratic response times, timeouts, and repeated failures; monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in lock waits, log-related waits, deadlock detections, and corruption or checksum error reports. Performance tuning in one layer appears ineffective because pressure simply resurfaces in another, masking the true intertwined nature of the outage.

Causally, page or index corruption can provoke long-running consistency checks, table scans, or error-handling rollbacks that hold locks far longer than usual, amplifying lock contention. These extended transactions in turn generate excessive undo/redo as they are retried or rolled back, driving up log volume and stressing the log subsystem. Conversely, a saturated log device delays commit processing, lengthening the period that locks remain acquired and increasing the likelihood of deadlock cycles. Prolonged recovery or repeated crash restarts initiated by corruption can also intensify log traffic and re-acquire locks, while log backlog may postpone the writing of page images needed to repair corruption. The feedback loop among corrupted structures, lock retention, and log flush bottlenecks deepens the outage and complicates diagnosis, as symptoms from each layer propagate and obscure the original triggers.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (table layout, partitioning, indexes, data types, constraints) and workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Optimizer chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite adequate statistics, due to cost-model or plan-reuse issues, causing erratic or poor performance.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data or index pages breaks key ordering, page links, or heap-to-index mappings, making storage structures unreliable.

When all three anomalies arise together, the database exhibits extreme and confusing symptoms: queries oscillate between full scans and corrupt index probes, some result sets contain missing or duplicated rows, while others hang in long-running nested-loop storms or trigger sudden recompilations. Rebuilding or adding indexes may temporarily help a few statements yet make others worse, and integrity-check utilities intermittently report low-level page or key errors. Plan caches fill with divergent plans for the same statement, latch contention and I/O spikes appear without clear correlation to workload changes, and corrective actions aimed at any single layer fail to stabilize performance.

Causal chain: a poor schema/index design first pushes the optimizer toward heavy scanning or non-covering lookups; this increases I/O and page churn, heightening the likelihood of latent storage or index corruption surfacing under load.
