Corrupted pages then feed inconsistent cardinality and access-path signals to the optimizer, provoking highly variable or outright wrong plan choices and further amplifying performance variance. Conversely, unstable plan selection stresses already mis-designed structures with bursty access patterns, accelerating fragmentation and exposing more integrity flaws. The intertwined feedback loop among design flaws, bad plans, and physical corruption degrades both performance and correctness, making the composite anomaly far more severe than any individual root cause alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process or retain far more data, rows, or time in flight than the true business requirement demands.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing metadata is stale, incomplete, or inaccurate, driving the optimizer to mis-estimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal execution plans.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, temp, or log areas falls to or past hard limits, producing space-allocation failures and knock-on stalls.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits an extreme and nonlinear degradation pattern: poorly written or chatty SQL generates large scans, bloated intermediate results, and long-running transactions; the misaligned statistics cause the optimizer to underestimate these result sizes, selecting plan shapes (nested loops, memory-hungry hash joins, spill-prone sorts) that further amplify I/O and temp usage; the excessive data movement and prolonged transactions rapidly consume datafiles, temp segments, and redo/undo logs, driving the system into critical low-space territory. Operators observe a cascade of symptoms—exploding temporary-space consumption, sudden "out of space" or auto-extend failures mid-query, runaway statement latency with estimates far below actual rows, lock retention due to aborted space allocations, repeated plan recompiles as statistics auto-updates struggle against space limits, and erratic application-level timeouts and retries.

Causally, inefficient workload logic is the initiator, inflating data volume and transaction lifetimes. Stale or missing statistics mask the true cost of this bloat, preventing the optimizer from choosing mitigative plans and sometimes reintroducing plan instability that widens space usage variance. The inflated runtime footprints accelerate space exhaustion, while space shortages trigger temp-file extension failures, redo log stalls, and emergency autovacuum or checkpoint storms that further slow or roll back the already heavy queries—feeding back into longer transaction windows and more space held. Thus each anomaly reinforces the others, creating a feedback loop that magnifies performance degradation and increases the likelihood of hard failures.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is concurrently suffering from sub-optimal application SQL logic, internal buffer-cache/latch hot-spotting, and saturation of the client-server network or connection layer. All three root causes are present at the same time, so the engine must execute needlessly heavy statements, arbitrate intense in-memory page access, and move large result sets across congested or resource-starved network paths.

Combined Observable Phenomena: 1) Statement-statistics and slow-query logs show wide scans, huge row counts, and long-running transactions. 2) Wait-event views report spikes in buffer-busy, page-latch, and lightweight latch waits, with CPU spin yet little throughput gain; hotspot index root pages and sequence pages are frequently pinned. 3) Simultaneously, clients experience intermittent connection establishment failures, higher round-trip times, and long "client read/client write" waits; server-side listener backlogs, socket queues, or backend process pools approach their limits. The combination amplifies long-tail latencies: extended execution times hold latches longer, which in turn prolongs network hold-ups, causing more sessions to pile up and further overstress the buffer cache.

Causal Chain and Reinforcement: Inefficient SQL logic multiplies the amount of data touched and returned, driving up buffer-pool pressure and repeatedly targeting the same root or leaf pages; this creates latch contention. The prolonged latch waits lengthen transaction and session lifetimes so that connections stay open while still occupying network sockets. Large and delayed result sets then congest the network layer, slowing packet delivery and further extending the time pages remain pinned or dirty. Network slowdowns feed back into the workload by holding workers in active yet stalled states, increasing concurrent demand on the same hot pages and deepening latch contention. The three layers therefore form a vicious loop—poor SQL inflates memory contention, memory contention elongates connection duration, and network bottlenecks prevent timely completion—driving overall throughput down and tail latency up across both OLTP and analytical queries.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between table/ index / partition design and workload access patterns forces inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer or statistics quality.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Accumulation of obsolete row versions and dead tuples outpaces background cleanup, inflating storage and adding visibility-check overhead.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Saturated or unstable network, listener, or connection-pool resources delay session establishment and data transfer between clients and the database.

When all three root causes strike together, the database must scan bloated heaps and non-covering indexes while also navigating layers of stale MVCC versions; each statement therefore touches far more pages, returns larger intermediate result sets, and holds server back-ends open longer. The elongated execution widens the window in which network sockets remain active, increasing the likelihood of socket-buffer exhaustion, retransmissions, and connection timeouts. Clients experience erratic response times: some calls stall during table or index scans, others hang during result transmission or authentication, and retries triggered by perceived timeouts multiply the incoming connection load. On the server side, statistics show ballooning on-disk relation sizes, vacuum/cleanup workers perpetually busy yet ineffective, rising full-scan counts, swelling per-backend memory, and a growing backlog of connections waiting on client I/O or slot availability.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design forces wide scans that prolong transaction duration; these longer transactions widen the oldest-xmin horizon, throttling MVCC cleanup and accelerating table and index bloat. The expanding data footprint further degrades scan speed, intensifying the performance hit from the design flaw. The heavier I/O and longer query runtimes keep network sockets busy, while the increased volume of data transferred (due to larger tables and lack of selective indexing) stresses bandwidth and server process limits. Network slowdowns, in turn, extend transaction lifetimes even more, delaying VACUUM or purge processes and allowing dead versions to accumulate. The three anomalies thus create a feedback loop in which design inefficiency, version bloat, and network congestion amplify each other, driving the system into a state of chronic latency, high resource consumption, and escalating risk of transaction-ID or connection exhaustion.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries because background cleanup cannot keep pace with update/delete churn, inflating the version store and scan/visibility overhead.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas falls to critical levels, causing allocation failures and write stalls.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or similar objects are reached, preventing the database from creating or accessing required OS resources.

When all three anomalies co-exist, the database exhibits compounding symptoms: rapid growth of data files, rollback segments, and indexes consumes remaining disk space, while the engine’s attempts to extend files, write WAL/redo, build temp objects, or create new version segments start to fail with no-space errors. Simultaneously, the profusion of version and temp files inflates the number of open file handles and shared-memory allocations, driving the system into kernel-level limit breaches that manifest as sporadic session failures, inability to fork background or parallel workers, and repeated "too many open files" or "cannot allocate shared memory" messages in both database and system logs. Autovacuum/cleanup workers run constantly yet make little progress because they cannot allocate additional disk or OS resources, leading to escalating transaction-ID wraparound warnings, runaway checkpoint and archive backlogs, deteriorating query latency, and eventual cluster-wide freeze.

Causally, heavy update/delete activity generates large volumes of dead tuples; if cleanup workers are throttled or blocked by long-running snapshots, the version store swells. The bloated heap and indexes rapidly deplete free storage, pushing the system into space-pressure territory. Near-full filesystems force frequent, fragmented auto-extensions and generate many small segment files, multiplying the number of file descriptors the engine must keep open. This surge, combined with intensified cleanup and retry logic, drives consumption of kernel objects (FDs, semaphores, threads) until OS limits are hit. Once either space or OS resources are exhausted, cleanup workers fail to start or complete, further accelerating MVCC bloat and space consumption in a vicious feedback loop that culminates in service outages, data-modification failures, and degraded read performance.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical data model, indexes, partitions, and data types are mis-aligned with workload access patterns, obliging the optimizer to choose scan-heavy or non-covering access paths that inflate read and write volume.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Core engine settings for memory pools, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, and background workers are wrongly sized for the hardware and workload, creating artificial pressure on caches, log flushes, and background I/O activity.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying disks or storage fabric cannot deliver the throughput or latency demanded, so I/O queues lengthen and device wait times dominate response time.

When these three root causes strike together, the database experiences runaway I/O amplification: poorly designed tables and missing or redundant indexes force excessive random and full-table scans; the undersized buffer pool, aggressive checkpoint intervals, or mis-set work-memory parameters keep hot pages from staying in cache and trigger frequent dirty-page flushes; meanwhile the saturated storage layer cannot absorb the elevated read/write traffic, driving up I/O wait events, log write stalls, and checkpoint storms. End-user symptoms include highly variable query latencies, sharp throughput drops at moderate concurrency, CPU cores idling while sessions wait on data-file and log-file I/O, and dramatic slow-downs during data-modification bursts or reporting jobs. Performance tools show a confusing mix of plan inefficiencies, buffer-cache churn, and device-level saturation, making the true scope of the problem hard to pinpoint.

Causally, inefficient schema and index choices raise the baseline I/O demand. Misconfigured memory and background-writer parameters prevent the engine from masking that demand through caching or paced flushing, instead releasing large spikes of I/O during sorts, hash builds, or checkpoints. These bursts hit a storage subsystem that is already at or near its throughput ceiling, causing queue buildup and exponential growth in latency. Rising I/O times feed back into the engine as longer lock holds, stalled worker threads, and further cache eviction, which in turn forces even more physical I/O due to the poor access paths. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another, producing a severe, self-amplifying degradation that is far worse than any of the individual issues in isolation.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model, indexing, partitioning, or datatype choices are misaligned with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient execution paths independent of statistics or optimizer faults.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Allocated data, index, log, or temp space approaches or reaches exhaustion, causing allocation failures, halted growth, and stalled background maintenance.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from sub-optimal schema/index design and imminent or actual exhaustion of critical storage areas. Poor data layout magnifies space consumption while also generating inefficient I/O patterns that accelerate space depletion, so application activity is constrained both by slow queries and by hard space limits.

Combined observable phenomena:  • Growing tables and non-covering or redundant indexes balloon disk usage, shrinking free space far faster than capacity planning assumes.  • Queries already performing full table or full index scans spill to on-disk sorts or hash areas, rapidly filling TEMP segments and triggering "out of space" errors.  • DML operations against poorly clustered or over-indexed tables hit "cannot allocate extent" or "autoextend failed" messages mid-transaction, causing rollbacks, lock retention, and user-visible timeouts.  • Emergency index rebuilds or partition maintenance meant to mitigate poor designs cannot complete because of insufficient work space, leaving bloated structures in place and worsening performance.  • Monitoring shows interleaved patterns of escalating latency and sudden statement failures related to space, making the root cause appear intermittent and multifaceted.

Causal interaction: Inefficient schema and indexing choices inflate row length, duplicate data in overlapping indexes, and prevent effective partition pruning; this amplifies data and index growth, quickly consuming tablespace, log, and temp capacity. As free space dwindles, the database's ability to allocate new extents, write redo/undo, or create temporary segments degrades, leading to frequent space errors that interrupt queries already slowed by poor access paths. Conversely, space pressure blocks corrective actions such as adding proper covering indexes, reorganizing tables, or implementing partitioning, locking the system into a feedback loop where design inefficiencies accelerate space exhaustion and space shortages prevent design remediation. The intertwined root causes thus reinforce each other, producing severe throughput collapse, elevated latency, and operational instability across both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Critical metadata about data distribution is stale or incomplete, causing the optimizer to systematically misestimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal execution plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive, write, or apply the primary’s change stream at production speed, enlarging log-position and apply lags.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical volumes hosting data, log, or temp spaces are saturated for bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, driving up I/O wait times across the engine.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a multilayered performance collapse: the optimizer generates plans that unexpectedly scan or sort far more (or fewer) rows than anticipated, inflating I/O demand on already saturated storage. The excess physical reads and writes amplify device queue depths and latency, which in turn slows both local transaction processing and the replica’s redo apply. As the replica struggles to fetch and replay bloated redo streams, replication lag widens, primary log segments accumulate, and long-running queries or batch jobs on the primary experience escalating wait events for I/O, buffer access, and log-space reclamation. Monitoring tools simultaneously report severe cardinality-estimation errors, soaring physical-I/O waits, and rapidly growing replication delay, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, stale or poor-quality statistics mislead the optimizer into favoring plans with large table scans, excessive hashing, or inappropriate join orders, dramatically increasing physical I/O. The inflated I/O volume saturates the storage subsystem, elevating latency for both data access and log flushes. Higher log-flush latency reduces the rate at which the primary can recycle or ship WAL/redo, forcing replicas to ingest bigger batches less frequently and fall further behind. The growing replication backlog, in turn, prolongs retention of old log segments on the primary, compounding storage pressure and perpetuating the I/O bottleneck. Together, the three anomalies create a feedback loop where bad plans generate surplus I/O, storage saturation throttles both query execution and log shipping, and replication lag increases disk usage and operational risk, severely degrading overall system performance and availability.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Saturation or stalling of the write-ahead logging pipeline (log buffer, log files, flush/sync, archival or replication) that delays commit processing and other write activity.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical or logical corruption of on-disk data pages or index structures that causes inconsistencies between stored bytes and the logical contents expected by the database engine.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-managed resources (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, AIO contexts, cgroup quotas, etc.) that prevents the database from performing normal I/O and process management.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database exhibits a compounded failure pattern: commit latency and log-flush waits rise sharply while the engine intermittently fails to open or extend log and data files due to depleted file handles or address space. Archive or redo-shipping workers throttle or abort, causing log directories to balloon and checkpoints to storm. Concurrently, corrupted pages or indexes surface as checksum errors, duplicate or missing rows, and emergency plan fall-backs to full scans; recovery attempts may repeatedly fail or loop because required log segments cannot be written, read, or archived. Administrators observe a mixture of engine corruption panics, "unable to allocate shared memory / file handle" errors from the kernel, and prolonged application write stalls, making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, tight OS resource limits can starve the log subsystem of file descriptors, AIO slots, or thread quotas, slowing or blocking log writes and archives; prolonged stalls increase the window during which partially flushed or torn pages may be exposed, heightening the risk of data and index corruption if a crash or timeout forces an abort. Conversely, existing page or index corruption triggers extra recovery, verification, and redo activity, inflating log generation and magnifying pressure on the already constrained log pipeline and OS resources. The mutual reinforcement between log congestion, kernel-level resource starvation, and structural corruption can drive the database into cascading failures, escalating from performance degradation to systemic outage and data-loss risk.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, incomplete, or missing statistical metadata causes systematic cardinality misestimates that misguide the optimizer into choosing inefficient execution plans.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Physical or logical corruption inside data pages or index structures breaks key ordering, page links, and row visibility, making persisted structures unreliable and forcing error handling or access-path fall-backs.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high share of CPU cycles, driving the host into sustained saturation and lengthening all run-queue–related waits.

When these three root causes co-exist, their symptoms overlap and amplify: misestimated cardinalities push the optimizer toward full scans or overly parallel plans that inflate CPU demand; corrupted indexes provoke repeated scan restarts, error logging, or forced heap scans, further compounding CPU consumption; meanwhile the saturated CPU stretches latch acquisition, recovery, and page-verification work, prolonging lock holds and blocking other sessions. End users observe sharp and erratic latency spikes, intermittent wrong-result or "row missing/duplicate" complaints, sudden plan thrash with exploding compile counts, engine errors reporting checksum or logical inconsistencies, and operating-system metrics showing cores pinned at or near 100 % utilization.

Causally, corruption in data or index pages can invalidate row counts that automated statistics collection relies on, accelerating the drift between optimizer assumptions and reality. The resulting bad plans create excessive CPU pressure, which in turn delays or cancels maintenance tasks such as statistics refreshes and online index rebuilds, letting both corruption effects and statistics staleness persist. High CPU also stresses IO and memory paths, increasing the likelihood of additional write-omissions or torn-page events that deepen structural corruption. Thus, each anomaly reinforces the others in a vicious cycle: corruption distorts statistics, bad statistics drive CPU-heavy plans, CPU saturation hampers repair and refresh operations, and the overall database health deteriorates rapidly.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, partition, or datatype choices mismatch workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even when queries are well written.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Catalogued statistics no longer reflect true data distribution, causing systematic cardinality misestimates and poor plan selection.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupt, producing inconsistent or missing rows and forcing plan fall-backs.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a convoluted mix of symptoms: queries swing unpredictably between full scans caused by bad schema design and emergency scans forced by index corruption; estimated versus actual row counts diverge wildly, yet re-gathering statistics yields unstable or non-deterministic plans because corrupt or poorly designed indexes supply misleading sampling data; repeated recompilations, sudden plan switches, lock escalation, and erratic latency spikes occur. Maintenance operations such as index rebuilds or statistics collection may abort with integrity errors, while write operations suffer from both oversized, non-covering, and possibly corrupted indexes, inflating I/O, blocking, and recovery times. Troubleshooting becomes difficult because each anomaly masks or mimics the symptoms of the others—for example, missing rows might stem from either bad join plans, poor schema alignment, or physical corruption.

Causal interaction: a flawed schema and index design increases index size, depth, and page churn, which in turn raises the likelihood of physical page or linkage corruption. Corrupted or bloated indexes distort sampling and histogram creation, making statistics rapidly inaccurate; conversely, stale or coarse statistics obscure the need for design fixes and can direct the optimizer to rely on damaged indexes, amplifying data-corruption symptoms. Together, the three anomalies form a feedback loop: design flaws create stress and complexity, corruption degrades the very structures relied on to compensate for design gaps, and statistics mislead the optimizer into repeatedly choosing the worst possible paths, driving up load, I/O, and failure probability across both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free physical or logical space for data, logs, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, halting allocation and growth operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Network links, listener, socket, or session-handling resources saturate or stall, preventing timely establishment and servicing of client connections.

When both conditions manifest concurrently, the database experiences compounded symptoms: connection attempts pile up while existing sessions hang on client-read/client-write waits; DML or bulk-load operations abruptly fail with out-of-space errors that cascade into log-archive backpressure, yet the related error and retry storms further overload the listener and network queues. Monitoring may show plummeting free space metrics alongside soaring connection backlog, retransmissions, and authentication latencies. Application tiers observe unpredictable timeouts—sometimes during login, other times mid-transaction—making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, space exhaustion can indirectly amplify network stress: failed commits and log pushes trigger client retries and connection churn, inflating socket counts and listener workload. Conversely, network stalls slow log shipping, backup writes, and archiving, delaying space reclamation and causing filesystems or tablespaces to fill more quickly. The vicious cycle of space pressure generating retry traffic, and connectivity limits preventing cleanup or maintenance from freeing space, accelerates service degradation and risks a complete outage if neither resource constraint is relieved promptly.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements or transaction design force the engine to process and retain far more data, rows, or time in flight than business logic really requires.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Engine and session memory structures grow beyond the safe capacity of the host, provoking paging, OOM events, cache churn, or instance restarts.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, breaking key order, page links, or heap-to-index consistency.

When these three root causes coincide, their symptoms interleave and intensify: oversized scans and long-running transactions inflate buffer-pool residency and per-query work areas, driving sustained memory pressure; this in turn accelerates paging, CPU stalls, and unplanned restarts. Each crash or forced restart increases the likelihood that unsettled dirty pages are left partially written, surfacing new checksum or index-consistency errors. Meanwhile, existing corruption forces the optimizer to abandon selective indexes, converting many requests into full scans that further bloat memory demand and prolong lock holding, thereby amplifying the long-tail latency already introduced by sub-optimal workload logic. Administrators may observe a feedback loop of repeated slow-query log entries, escalating RSS growth, OOM killer or cluster eviction events, intermittent duplicate or missing rows, and sudden plan regressions that are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL design begins the spiral by overstressing memory. The resulting pressure heightens the chance of engine stalls, spill-to-disk, or crash recovery gaps that can corrupt pages or indexes. Once corruption appears, the engine compensates with full scans and page rereads, inflating memory consumption and extending transaction lifetimes, which in turn perpetuates memory exhaustion. The intertwined effects of logical inefficiencies, memory starvation, and structural corruption thus reinforce each other, degrading performance, stability, and data correctness across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Replicas or downstream consumers are unable to receive or apply primary transaction-log records at the rate they are generated, producing widening replication lag.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data files, logs, or temporary areas is exhausted or approaching hard limits, leading to allocation failures and blocked recycling.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database or related processes saturate host CPU cores, creating run-queue buildup and pervasive latency.

When all three conditions arise together, the database experiences a compound failure mode in which replication lag grows rapidly, on-disk log segments and relay files accumulate until file systems or tablespaces fill, and the CPU remains pegged as both primary and replica processes fight for compute time to generate, transmit, and replay an ever-growing backlog. Observable symptoms include:  
• Exponential increase of replication "write/flush/replay" delay accompanied by near-full disk or object-store usage on both primary and replica nodes.  
• Frequent "cannot allocate space", "write failed", or "archive destination full" errors interleaved with scheduler and CPU spin waits.  
• Periodic stalls where foreground user transactions block on log-space or checkpoint waits, followed by bursty catch-up periods that again spike CPU to 100%.  
• Monitoring shows rebounding replication lag after every attempted recovery cycle, with replica apply threads starved for CPU while also contending with I/O stalls caused by full disks.

Causal interaction: CPU saturation on either primary or replica slows log generation, network processing, and redo apply threads, which in turn inflates replication lag. The unresolved lag forces the primary to retain past WAL segments, rapidly consuming storage and pushing both primary and archive destinations toward capacity limits. As free space dwindles, checkpoints, auto-extension, and archive writes pause foreground activity, but these pauses cause queues to build, after which surges of deferred work reignite CPU pressure. On the replica side, limited CPU prolongs apply times, so retained relay logs bloat local storage, risking replay halts when disks fill. Conversely, once space exhaustion triggers excessive garbage collection, error logging, or retry loops, additional CPU is consumed, further aggravating saturation. The feedback loop among slow replication, shrinking space, and CPU overload can cascade into systemic outage or forced failovers if not interrupted.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently selects sub-optimal execution plans even though statistics are accurate, leading to inefficient operator choices, excessive work, or inappropriate degrees of parallelism.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, log file set, flush/sync, or archival pipeline—cannot keep pace with redo generation, inflating commit latency and stalling write activity.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes monopolize CPU cycles, driving host utilization toward saturation and lengthening run-queue and scheduling waits.

Combined phenomena: When all three anomalies manifest together on an OLTP system, poorly chosen plans generate unnecessary row accesses, joins, and sorts that dramatically inflate CPU consumption as well as redo volume. The spike in CPU usage lengthens execution times, which in turn extends transaction hold time and keeps log flushes outstanding longer. Concurrently, the overworked transaction-log subsystem becomes the primary choke point; commit latency, log file sync, and log buffer space waits soar. Users observe erratic query latency, batch timeouts, and periods of near system freeze where both CPU run queues and log-related wait events climb in lockstep. Because each anomaly masks and amplifies the others, standard plan-stability or I/O tuning efforts appear ineffective until the intertwined root causes are disentangled.

Causal chain analysis: A bad plan (e.g., full scans or Cartesian joins) dramatically increases CPU cycles and generates excess redo for each DML operation. The resulting CPU saturation slows down log flush threads that compete for the same cores, so log writes take longer, lengthening commit paths and forcing additional back-pressure on application sessions. Meanwhile, the overwhelmed log subsystem forces foreground transactions to wait, extending their execution window and keeping the sub-optimal, CPU-hungry plans active even longer, further intensifying CPU pressure. This feedback loop aggravates both resource domains, producing a cascading slowdown that can culminate in write stalls, severe throughput collapse, and unstable performance across the entire OLTP workload.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction patterns that force the engine to touch far more data or hold locks longer than business logic requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, and partition design that fails to support the workload’s access paths, forcing even well-written queries into inefficient scans or lookups.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Replication pipeline in which replicas cannot receive or apply log records as quickly as the primary produces them.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms compound across layers: 1) the primary experiences long-tail query latency, oversized result sets, and extended transaction lifetimes; 2) execution plans show full-table scans, row-by-row lookups, and high index-maintenance overhead; 3) the extra I/O and redo generated by these queries enlarge transaction logs and widen replication lag, with replicas reporting increasing receive, flush, and replay delay; 4) standbys that share the same sub-optimal schema struggle to re-execute the heavy statements, further deepening backlog, while primary log segments cannot be recycled, inflating disk usage and threatening failover freshness.

Causal chain: chatty or bulk-scanning application queries (logic anomaly) encounter missing or non-covering indexes (design anomaly), driving up CPU, I/O, and redo generation on the primary. The larger, longer transactions emitted under this inefficient schema bloat the write-ahead log. Replicas inherit the same schema deficiencies, so their apply threads reproduce the expensive scans and index maintenance, slowing replay throughput below the primary’s production rate (replication anomaly). The resulting lag feeds back to the primary by preventing log truncation and increasing checkpoint and flushing pressure, which in turn amplifies query latency and heightens the probability of further application-level retries—creating a reinforcing loop that degrades both primary performance and replication health.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic truly demands.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, partition, or datatype choices do not fit the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written statements into inefficient access paths.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, due to cost-model or plan-reuse issues.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms at every observation layer intensify and blur together: statements originally written with broad predicates or poor batching trigger full-table or non-covering index scans because the necessary supporting indexes or partitions are missing, while the optimizer simultaneously misjudges the remaining access options, producing erratic plan flips between inefficient scans and explosive nested loops. As a result, the same queries may alternate between long tail latencies and catastrophic stalls, saturating I/O and memory, prolonging lock holds, and cascading into application timeouts, deadlocks, and retry storms. Execution-statistics and performance dashboards show extreme variance: high logical I/O, frequent plan cache churn, bloated temp usage, and atypical CPU spikes during both read- and write-heavy windows.

Causally, sub-optimal SQL logic (e.g., non-sargable predicates, Cartesian joins, oversized batches) magnifies the penalty of a weak physical design by driving large row counts through tables that lack selective or covering indexes. In turn, the impoverished index/partition layout restricts the optimizer’s viable plan space, increasing its reliance on brittle cost estimates; even small cardinality errors or bind-value changes cause dramatic plan swings. Meanwhile, mischosen plans reinforce the workload’s inefficiencies, amplifying I/O and contention, which lengthen transaction lifetimes imposed by the original poor logic. The feedback loop among ill-formed SQL, mismatched schema structures, and unstable plan selection escalates resource consumption and variability, degrading both transactional and analytical operations across the system.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously affected by (1) inefficient or over-broad SQL issued by the application, (2) the optimizer selecting sub-optimal execution plans for those statements, and (3) the operating-system denying additional kernel-level resources required by the database processes. The co-existence of these three layers of faults forms a single composite anomaly that magnifies latency, resource contention, and outright failures far beyond what any individual anomaly would cause in isolation.

Combined anomalous phenomena: End-user requests frequently time out or are retried; slow-query logs and statement-statistics views show the same statements with wildly fluctuating execution times and alternating plans (e.g., index seeks vs. full scans). Transactions stay open longer, holding locks and blocking others, while parallel workers or new sessions sporadically fail to start with kernel error messages about exhausted file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or thread quotas. Monitoring shows escalating CPU and I/O demand from bad plans, but throughput plateaus as the engine hits OS-imposed limits, leading to queue build-up, lock waits, and partial service outages. Plan changes intended to alleviate workload pressure appear ineffective or revert unpredictably because the plan cache is being continuously invalidated by resource-related errors.

Causal chain and interaction: Poorly written SQL forces the optimizer to consider large search spaces and high-cost alternatives; when the optimizer misjudges this workload, the resulting plans amplify row and page touch counts, inflating CPU, memory, and parallel-worker demand. The inflated demand accelerates consumption of kernel objects (file handles, threads, AIO contexts, shared memory), pushing the system over OS resource ceilings. Once those ceilings are reached, the operating system rejects new allocations, causing the database engine to drop or retry workers, invalidate plans, and reparse statements, which in turn increases parse and planning overhead. The feedback loop intensifies: every OS denial forces more plan churn and longer transactional hold times, which exacerbate lock contention and widen the performance tail. Thus the three root causes reinforce each other, producing a complex, self-perpetuating performance and stability degradation that is harder to diagnose than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, index, datatype, or partition design mismatches workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans and excessive index maintenance work.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup processes can purge them, inflating storage and visibility-check cost.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Memory, background-worker, checkpoint, and parallelism settings are mis-tuned for the hardware and workload, so internal subsystems receive too few or too many resources at the wrong moments.

When these three root causes coexist, the database experiences a feedback loop of bloat, latency spikes, and erratic resource utilisation. Poorly chosen or missing indexes drive large table and index scans that touch every page, but those pages are swollen with dead tuples because vacuum/garbage-collection cannot keep up. Each scan therefore reads more data than expected, further extending execution times and holding snapshots open longer, which in turn slows or blocks version reclamation. Misconfigured memory and worker-pool parameters exacerbate the situation: undersized buffer pools cause constant cache churn of the bloated objects, while too-small or too-aggressive maintenance-worker, checkpoint, or autovacuum settings alternately starve or overload I/O, producing bursts of write amplification and log-write waits even when the underlying disks are not fully utilised. Statistics become stale quickly, so the optimizer keeps choosing full scans over non-covering or missing indexes, reinforcing the cycle.

Causally, the deficient schema design raises the baseline I/O and write-amplification costs, generating more dead tuples per transaction (e.g., non-covering indexes force extra lookups and updates). The surging update/delete churn feeds the MVCC version store; if configuration parameters throttle cleanup workers or limit maintenance memory, reclamation lags behind growth. The swelling heap and indexes then consume buffer cache and elongate checkpoints, which, when ill-tuned, intensify I/O storms that pre-empt regular queries. Longer-running queries hold old snapshots, delaying version reuse and causing still more bloat. Thus, each anomaly magnifies the others, pushing the system into a degrading spiral of increasing storage, CPU, and latency costs under transactional workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more data, rows, or time than functionally required.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on the same buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, causing stalls and CPU spin without exhausting total memory.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages, index structures, or page links are physically or logically corrupt, making stored data structures unreliable.

When all three conditions coexist, the system is confronted with a mixed logical, concurrency, and physical failure mode. Long-running, data-heavy statements generated by sub-optimal workload logic pound a small set of hot tables and indexes. This concentrates traffic on a limited set of pages whose internal structures are already partially corrupt. Sessions therefore experience extreme and erratic latencies: extended runtime and timeouts from oversized scans, surges of buffer-busy and page-latch waits, sudden switch-overs to full table scans when index corruption is detected, duplicate or missing rows in result sets, increased deadlocks as transactions hold latches longer, intermittent checksum or page-verification errors, and a flood of retries or connection aborts at the application tier.

Causally, inefficient SQL drives excessive reads and writes against a narrow range of index and data pages, turning them into hotspots. The resulting latch pressure amplifies dwell time on those pages, magnifying the impact of any latent block or index corruption: corrupt pages are touched more often, triggering repeated checksum failures, forced page invalidations, or costly consistency checks. Conversely, corruption can invalidate index access paths, forcing the optimizer to fall back to full scans that exacerbate the already heavy workload, further swelling the buffer churn and latch queues. The feedback loop between bad SQL patterns, contention for shared buffers, and structural corruption degrades throughput, increases error rates, and can ultimately lead to service outages or emergency recovery operations.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction scopes are written so inefficiently that they process more data, rows, or time than business requirements mandate.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, or partition structures are mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing even well-written queries onto sub-optimal access paths.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Old row versions and rollback information accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating storage and visibility-check cost.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits compounded symptoms: end-user requests and background jobs show extreme and highly variable latencies; execution plans tilt toward full table or index scans that traverse bloated heaps and sparsely populated pages; slow-query logs are dominated by repetitive, wide-scan statements whose response times deteriorate steadily over the lifetime of the instance; buffer cache hit ratios fall despite rising memory pressure because enlarged tables consume more pages; DML operations stall during index maintenance and VACUUM/garbage-collection contention, and long-running transactions keep old snapshots alive, preventing space reclamation. Administrators may observe runaway table and index sizes, relentless autovacuum or purge activity that never catches up, escalating I/O utilisation, and application-level timeouts that are hard to attribute to a single layer.

Causally, inefficient SQL logic initiates excessive reads and writes, amplifying row churn and version creation. Because the underlying schema lacks selective or covering indexes, these statements must scan large portions of tables, touching many more rows than necessary and generating a high volume of MVCC undo or version records. The resulting bloat further degrades access paths, as query plans now operate on swollen data structures, worsening scan cost and skewing statistics. Simultaneously, the schema’s deficient indexing slows cleanup workers, which must traverse non-pruned partitions and wide indexes to locate obsolete versions. As long-running, chatty transactions from the flawed workload hold snapshots open, background cleaners cannot advance the version horizon, so space consumption and visibility-check overhead spiral upward. Each anomaly thus feeds the next: bad SQL intensifies data churn, poor physical design magnifies I/O and lock footprint, and overwhelmed MVCC maintenance inflates storage and latency, creating a self-reinforcing performance collapse in OLTP environments.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-formed queries into broad scans or non-covering lookups.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Excessive or conflicting lock requests among concurrent transactions that lead to long blocking chains or deadlocks, degrading throughput and provoking rollbacks.

When these two root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blend of I/O-heavy access paths and severe lock queuing. Queries that should have been quick, selective index probes instead scan whole tables or large index ranges, acquiring and holding many row, page, or even table locks for extended periods. This inflates lock footprints, lengthens critical-section times, and causes cascades of blockers and waiters. Observable symptoms include simultaneous spikes in logical/physical I/O, CPU usage, lock wait time, deadlock frequency, connection-pool exhaustion, and dramatic variance in response times; execution plans show scans while lock-diagnostic views reveal growing wait chains often ending in deadlock victim rollbacks.

Causally, poor schema and index design enlarges the scope and duration of locking: missing or non-covering indexes force full scans that touch many rows, causing transactions to acquire more locks and hold them longer. The broadened lock scope increases the probability of conflict with other concurrent transactions, intensifying lock contention. In turn, prolonged blocking and repeated deadlocks further delay statement completion, keeping scans active even longer and amplifying the performance penalty of the design flaw. The feedback loop between inefficient access paths and escalating lock waits can drive the database into a state of chronic congestion where both throughput and user experience deteriorate sharply.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from on-disk data/index corruption and from host-level resource exhaustion, so that logical storage structures are damaged while the engine is also prevented from obtaining the kernel objects (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, threads, etc.) it needs to detect, isolate, or repair the corruption.

Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures have become internally inconsistent, breaking key order, page links, checksums, or heap–index mappings and causing wrong, lost, or duplicated rows.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or related objects are hit, denying the database process further allocations and impairing normal operation.

Combined observable phenomena:  • Queries intermittently fail or return wrong result counts due to corrupted indexes, while other sessions receive "unable to open file", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "failed to start worker" errors.  • Integrity-checking or backup utilities may abort early because they cannot acquire additional descriptors, leaving corruption only partially reported.  • Recovery or checkpoint operations may stall: the engine detects damaged pages yet also cannot allocate the I/O contexts or background workers required for recovery, causing prolonged startup times, replication lag, or sudden crash-looping.  • Monitoring shows rising I/O errors, checksum failures, and a plateau of kernel resource counters (open files, semaphores) at their limits.  • Performance degrades unpredictably as the optimizer switches from corrupted indexes to full scans, which in turn spawn additional temporary files whose creation fails due to file-handle exhaustion.

Causal interaction: Resource limits can precipitate or exacerbate physical corruption—for example, a shortage of file descriptors or asynchronous I/O slots can interrupt checkpoint flushing, leaving pages only partially written and vulnerable to torn-page corruption. Conversely, once corruption exists, the database engine may attempt aggressive background validation, index rebuilds, or repeated retries, each consuming extra threads, memory arenas, or kernel objects and thereby accelerating exhaustion of the already tight OS limits. This feedback loop masks the true origin of errors, producing overlapping symptoms that complicate diagnosis and prolong outage duration.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database is simultaneously affected by (1) stale or incomplete optimizer statistics that drive systematic cardinality misestimation, (2) heavy lock-manager blocking/deadlock situations among concurrent transactions, and (3) exhaustion or slowdown of network/connection-handling resources between clients and the server.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Inaccurate or missing statistics misguide the cost-based optimizer, producing sub-optimal access paths and join orders.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Incompatible lock requests from concurrent transactions create long blocking chains or deadlocks, throttling throughput.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Limited or unstable network, listener, socket, or authentication capacity delays session establishment and enlarges result-set transfer times.

Combined phenomena: Affected systems exhibit erratic query plans with unexpectedly large scans that lock many rows or pages, quickly generating extensive blocker–waiter trees. As blocked sessions pile up, client threads remain connected but idle, inflating session counts until the listener or socket backlog is saturated. Users observe a mixture of symptoms—slow or timed-out connections, sudden surges in lock wait time, deadlock error bursts, intermittent plan regressions after data loads, and highly variable response times—making root-cause isolation difficult.

Causal interaction: Misestimated cardinalities can cause the optimizer to choose plans that touch far more data than necessary (e.g., full table scans instead of index seeks), increasing the number, scope, and lifetime of locks held by each statement. The enlarged lock footprint heightens the probability and duration of lock contention and deadlocks. Prolonged blocking slows statement completion, so application sessions stay active longer, which in turn drives up the number of concurrent connections competing for limited listener threads, socket buffers, and network bandwidth. Conversely, network or authentication slowdowns extend transaction round-trip times, delaying commit/rollback and keeping locks in place even longer, thereby intensifying contention. The feedback loop between poor plans, prolonged locks, and network saturation can quickly degrade overall OLTP throughput and stability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine parameters cause internal components such as memory pools, checkpoint frequency, logging, parallelism, or worker counts to operate out of alignment with hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU cycles, driving run-queue depth and scheduler waits regardless of the SQL-layer reason for the demand.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The network path, listener, authentication, or session-slot layer cannot keep pace with attempted client traffic, leading to backlog, retransmissions, or connection exhaustion.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the system exhibits intertwined symptoms: 1) end-users observe sporadic slow logins, connection time-outs, and sudden query latency spikes; 2) server-side metrics show near-continuous CPU saturation even while some cores idle waiting on client I/O or log flushes; 3) wait-event profiles oscillate between client read/write, socket backlog, spin waits, and log/checkpoint stalls; 4) operating-system socket tables fill and clear in bursts, coinciding with periods of runaway context switches and load-average peaks; 5) post-upgrade or recent parameter changes precipitate flurries of checkpoints and background-writer activity that steal CPU from already strained listener and worker threads, amplifying queueing on both the network and execution layers.

Causal interaction: An ill-chosen configuration (e.g., overly aggressive parallelism, undersized work-memory, tight checkpoint intervals, low connection limits) inflates CPU demand and background activity, pushing the host toward compute saturation. As CPU headroom disappears, listener and authentication threads slow down, prolonging connection setup and increasing socket backlog, which in turn causes clients to retry, compounding network traffic. The surge of half-open sessions and retransmissions further taxes kernel networking stacks and database process scheduling, while misaligned memory and logging parameters trigger additional flushes and context switches that keep CPUs busy but unproductive. The reinforcing loop—misconfiguration driving CPU pressure, which hampers network handling, which then provokes more retries and engine overhead—creates a systemic bottleneck that disrupts both transactional and analytical workloads until configuration is corrected, capacity is added, or traffic is throttled.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: The cost-based optimizer relies on stale, absent, or corrupt statistics, so row-count and distribution estimates deviate sharply from reality and drive sub-optimal plan choices.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The database engine allocates more buffer cache, work memory, and auxiliary heaps than the host can safely supply, triggering swap, allocation failures, or forced evictions.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical pages or index structures on disk are corrupted, breaking key order, page links, or checksums and rendering persisted data unreliable.

When these three root causes occur together, the workload may exhibit a volatile mix of symptoms:  • Queries suddenly switch to memory-hungry hash or sort plans based on bad cardinality guesses, inflating per-query work buffers just as global memory is already under pressure.  • The inflated memory footprint accelerates paging, process thrashing, or cluster node evictions, while corruption forces repeated retries, table scans, or on-the-fly index rebuilds that further consume cache and temp space.  • Execution plans may appear to "flap"—oscillating between different shapes as statistics are auto-recalculated, corrupted pages invalidate plans, or memory pressure triggers re-optimization.  • Integrity check failures and checksum errors surface intermittently because aggressive buffer flushing and page writes, driven by memory scarcity, expose damaged blocks more frequently.  • Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in logical/physical I/O, memory faults, and severe estimate-to-actual row count gaps, making it difficult to attribute performance regressions to any single layer.

Causal chain: Corrupted data or index pages can poison or prevent correct statistics collection, seeding the optimizer with misleading cardinalities. These misestimates favour large in-memory joins, sorts, or parallel plans that allocate excessive work areas. The resulting memory inflation pushes the engine and operating system into heavy paging, which in turn increases I/O and the likelihood of encountering additional corrupted pages, leading to more consistency checks, plan invalidations, and emergency rewrites. Meanwhile, ongoing memory pressure can starve background tasks that would normally refresh statistics or run integrity scrubbing, allowing both statistics staleness and physical corruption to deepen. The feedback loop among bad statistics, runaway memory allocation, and latent page/index corruption amplifies instability, culminating in severe, hard-to-diagnose performance degradation, query failures, and potential service outages.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite reasonably accurate statistics, leading to excessive I/O, row visits, or parallelism misuse.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating tables/indexes and adding visibility-check overhead.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database back-end and maintenance processes drive host CPU utilization to saturation, creating run-queue waits and pervasive latency spikes.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a blended failure pattern: queries flip to or remain on inefficient plans that scan or join far more rows than necessary; the scanned pages are bloated with dead tuples, so every logical row access requires extra visibility checks and additional buffer churn; the surplus work manifests as sustained CPU saturation, causing system-wide slowdowns. Autovacuum or garbage-collection workers run constantly yet make little progress because they compete for the same exhausted CPU, while critical user queries also stall on CPU run-queue waits. Statistics drift as table bloat grows, amplifying plan instability and fostering new mis-plans. Symptoms include erratic plan changes, explosive growth of table and index size, skyrocketing CPU wait events, and workload latency that degrades non-linearly with concurrency.

Causally, poor plan choices initiate oversized scans and high row lookups, inflating CPU consumption and prolonging transaction lifetimes; the longer execution times delay cleanup horizon advancement, letting MVCC garbage pile up. The ensuing table bloat further skews cardinality estimates, nudging the optimizer toward even worse plans—especially when plan reuse locks in bad strategies—creating a vicious feedback loop. Meanwhile, the compounded read-amplification from dead rows and the CPU-intensive mis-plans jointly saturate the processor, throttling both foreground queries and background vacuuming. The throttled cleanup then falls further behind, intensifying version accumulation and perpetuating the cycle until the system experiences severe throughput collapse or reaches transaction-ID wraparound danger.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and actual workload access patterns forces intrinsically inefficient access paths independent of statistics or optimizer choices.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Optimizer chooses or reuses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, due to cost-model or plan-cache issues, leading to unexpected full scans, bad join orders, or loss of parallelism.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared memory, threads, or other OS objects, causing failures to allocate required resources despite sufficient logical capacity inside the DB engine.

When all three root causes coexist, workloads encounter a multilayered performance and stability collapse: poorly designed or missing indexes inflate the amount of data each statement must touch; simultaneous optimizer mis-decisions steer execution toward full scans, Cartesian joins, or serial plans that intensify I/O, memory, and worker-process demands; and as these bloated executions proliferate, the database tries to open many more files, allocate larger shared buffers, or spawn extra workers, quickly exhausting OS-level limits. Symptoms include extreme and erratic query latency, bursts of plan flips with divergent runtimes, sudden errors such as “too many open files,” inability to create parallel workers, partial outages where new sessions fail while existing ones slow to a crawl, and log files showing both optimizer plan hashes oscillating and kernel resource-exhaustion messages.

Causally, the deficient schema/index design first widens the resource footprint of every logical operation. This magnifies the cost sensitivity of the optimizer, increasing the chance it will pick unstable or poor plans that appear cheapest under its imperfect model. The resulting heavier plans (e.g., table scans, large hash joins) drive up file-handle usage, shared-memory allocation, and thread counts, rapidly approaching or breaching OS quotas. Once kernel limits are hit, the engine cannot create additional I/O contexts, open segment files, or spawn background/parallel workers, which in turn forces further plan re-optimization and emergency fallbacks to even less efficient serial execution paths. The feedback loop between bad design, volatile plan selection, and hard OS ceilings culminates in compounded performance degradation, plan thrashing, and intermittent availability loss that is difficult to attribute to any single layer without holistic diagnosis.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or tables, producing blocking chains or deadlocks managed by the lock-manager subsystem.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions stall while contending for buffer-cache pages, latches, or I/O slots inside the buffer manager, leading to long page-latch waits and CPU spin.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, write, or replay primary log records fast enough, causing growing log-position lag and retention of un-recycled WAL segments.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits a blended symptom set: soaring lock-wait and deadlock counts, surges in buffer-busy and page-latch events, elevated CPU usage with little useful work, rising transaction latencies, and sharp drops in throughput. Simultaneously, replication monitoring shows widening replay delay, swelling retained log files, and replicas that serve increasingly stale reads or fall out of sync, jeopardizing recovery point objectives. From the application side, users encounter time-outs, slowed commit acknowledgments, and unpredictable replica freshness, making troubleshooting difficult because waits oscillate between lock, latch, I/O, and replication states.

Causally, hot rows or pages first induce lock contention; transactions blocked on locks keep buffer pages pinned and their latches held longer, amplifying latch contention for other sessions that need the same pages. Prolonged latch waits lengthen transaction execution times, extending lock hold durations and enlarging commit batches, which in turn inflate the volume and burstiness of generated log records. The heavier and more uneven log stream overwhelms replication apply threads already slowed by their own lock and latch conflicts while replaying changes, deepening replication lag. As replicas fall behind, the primary is forced to retain additional log segments, limiting checkpoint progress; this inflates dirty-page residency, increases buffer-flush pressure, and extends latch hold times during I/O. The positive feedback loop between lock waits, latch contention, and replication backlog drives the system into a compounded degradation state where each anomaly reinforces the others and accelerates overall performance collapse.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent sessions request mutually incompatible locks on the same objects, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall transaction progress.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Database components collectively consume more physical memory than the host can safely supply, leading to paging, OOM events, and cache-churn side effects.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate available CPU cores so that runnable tasks pile up and every operation experiences scheduler delay.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers heavy lock waits, runaway memory growth, and CPU saturation. Each symptom originates in its own layer but co-exists in the same runtime window, producing an OLTP environment where sessions are both blocked on locks and starved for memory and CPU, making the overall system appear hung or intermittently unresponsive.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Lock-wait and deadlock diagnostics show long blocker–waiter chains, yet even unblocked requests execute slowly because CPU run queues are full and memory paging stalls I/O. 2) Process RSS and OS swap metrics rise while lock tables stop shrinking because victim rollbacks themselves need memory and CPU to complete. 3) Application timeouts, connection-pool exhaustion, and surge in retry storms coincide with host load averages pegged near core count and kernel swapping spikes, creating erratic throughput and latency outliers.

Causal chain and mutual reinforcement: Excessive memory allocation inflates the working set, provoking the OS to swap; paging overhead steals CPU cycles and pushes the run queue higher. CPU starvation lengthens every critical section, so transactions hold locks longer, deepening contention and increasing the probability of deadlocks. Conversely, lock blockage forces sessions to stay active, retaining their work buffers and execution state, which amplifies memory pressure. When victims are rolled back, they often re-execute, adding even more CPU demand and memory churn. The three anomalies therefore form a feedback loop—memory pressure and CPU saturation slow lock release, extended locking enlarges session memory footprints, and the retransmission of aborted work keeps CPU utilization maxed—driving the database into a progressively worsening spiral until intervention or load shedding occurs.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and rollback records outpaces background cleanup, inflating version stores, bloating storage, and slowing visibility checks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Mis-tuned engine settings for memory, checkpointing, logging, parallelism, or worker budgets cause resource-usage patterns that do not align with actual hardware capacity or workload demands.

Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from excessive MVCC version buildup while critical configuration parameters (e.g., autovacuum thresholds, maintenance work memory, checkpoint intervals, log and buffer sizes) are mis-aligned with the update-heavy workload. The twin conditions coexist, so version store growth is unchecked just as the subsystem meant to reclaim it is throttled or mistimed by sub-optimal settings.

Combined anomalous phenomena:  • Rapid expansion of table and index sizes, soaring obsolete-to-live row ratios, and long sequential scans.  • Cleanup workers that appear active yet never reduce bloat because cost limits, memory quotas, or parallel-worker caps are too low.  • Repeated emergency checkpoints or log-file saturation despite under-utilised I/O bandwidth, coinciding with escalating visibility-check CPU time.  • Planner misestimates and query latency spikes intermixed with seemingly unexplained background I/O storms right after every forced checkpoint.  • Monitoring shows both version-store wraparound warnings and configuration-related wait events (e.g., excessive log flush waits while disks are idle).

Causal interaction: Poorly chosen configuration parameters throttle or mis-schedule the very maintenance tasks needed to prune old versions, letting bloat compound. The swelling version store, in turn, inflates redo volume and dirty-page pressure, triggering more frequent checkpoints and log flushes—events whose impact is magnified by the same mis-tuned parameters governing log size, checkpoint cadence, and buffer pools. As each anomaly feeds the other, the database enters a feedback loop: growing MVCC debris raises I/O and memory demand, while configuration limits prevent timely cleanup, accelerating performance degradation and bringing the system closer to transaction-ID exhaustion or out-of-space failures.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, partitions, indexes, datatypes, constraints) and workload access patterns forces inefficient access paths even when SQL is well-written.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Replication pipeline cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo at the pace the primary generates it, causing widening log-position gaps and lag across nodes.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying storage subsystem is saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, so physical reads and writes queue up, inflating I/O wait times for data, temp, and log files.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a compounded performance collapse: primary queries perform full scans and excessive random look-ups due to poor schema and index design, inflating read and write volumes exactly when the storage layer is already throughput-bound. The bloated I/O stream amplifies storage queue depths, elevates data-file and log-file latencies, and slows checkpoint and flush operations. Simultaneously, the replication channel falls further behind because the primary’s overloaded log writer produces a high volume of change records while the replica’s apply threads stall on the same storage bottlenecks. Monitoring shows runaway query latency, surging buffer cache misses, prolonged commit times, rapidly growing replication lag, retention of old WAL segments on the primary, and near-continuous storage wait events on both primary and replicas, making it difficult to attribute delays to any single layer.

Causally, inefficient access paths caused by poor schema and indexing multiply the physical I/O demand. This burst of disk activity collides with limited storage throughput, extending read/write latencies and commit times. Longer commit paths inflate the volume and lifespan of log data waiting to be shipped, so replication lag widens. As replicas struggle with the same sub-optimal schema and the shared storage bottleneck, their apply rate drops, which in turn prevents the primary from recycling log segments, further increasing disk usage and pressure on the constrained storage subsystem. The vicious cycle of excessive I/O, storage saturation, and replication backlog can ultimately threaten both performance and availability of the entire database environment.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer, despite having usable statistics, chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan because of cost-model or plan-cache issues.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU, creating system-wide compute contention that slows all workload components.

When these three root causes arise together, the database experiences extreme and erratic latency. Verbose or chatty SQL generated by the application multiplies the number of logical operations the optimizer must plan; a mischosen plan then inflates the physical work per statement—often turning what should be index seeks into full scans, spawning excessive parallel workers, or causing runaway nested-loop joins. The bloated execution demand drives CPU utilization to sustained saturation, pushing run-queue lengths and context switches high. Symptoms include: recurrent appearance of the same statements in slow-query and CPU-top lists, rapid oscillation between wildly different plans for identical SQL text, steep degradation after plan-cache invalidations or parameter shifts, widespread increases in service latency, and resource-wait events shifting from I/O to CPU-scheduler contention. Because CPU is the shared bottleneck, even well-written queries begin to stall, masking the original logical and planning flaws.

Causally, inefficient SQL logic supplies an overlarge search space to the optimizer; if the optimizer then selects or reuses a poor plan, per-statement CPU demand skyrockets. The inflated demand aggregates across many sessions, quickly exhausting CPU headroom. Once CPU is saturated, run-queue delays elongate execution times, which in turn keep transactions open longer, amplifying the footprint of the already chatty workload and further biasing the optimizer toward low-concurrency but high-CPU plans. This positive feedback loop intertwines the three anomalies, making remediation impossible unless all contributing layers—application SQL, plan stability, and CPU capacity—are addressed in concert.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to touch more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer selects or reuses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot supply the read/write bandwidth or IOPS demanded, causing sustained device-level saturation.

When all three root causes are active, the database exhibits extreme and erratic latency: the same statements repeatedly surface in slow-query and wait-events logs with swings between moderate and catastrophic response times; buffer cache hit ratios collapse, page read and write latencies spike, and long-running transactions accumulate large lock-hold times. Execution plans may oscillate between inefficient full scans and cached sub-optimal plans, amplifying I/O volume precisely when the storage subsystem is already saturated.
