Application sessions experience timeouts, deadlock retries, and connection pool exhaustion, while system metrics show moderate CPU, soaring I/O wait, deep device queues, and excessive redo/transaction log flush delays.

Causally, overly broad or chatty SQL (Workload Logic Anomaly) inflates the logical work the optimizer must translate into physical access paths. If the optimizer then selects a poor plan (Query Plan Selection Anomaly)—such as hash or nested-loop joins that read vast table portions or disable partition pruning—the physical I/O demand balloons. This surge in random and sequential reads/writes drives the underlying disks or flash tiers past their throughput limits (Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly). In turn, the elevated I/O latency feeds back to the optimizer’s feedback mechanisms and to application latency thresholds, increasing the likelihood of plan invalidations, parameter-sensitive plan flips, and additional retries that further increase the workload volume. The intertwined effects create a self-reinforcing spiral where bad logic produces bad plans, bad plans overload storage, and storage saturation magnifies every inefficiency, severely degrading overall database performance and stability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model structures, indexing, partitioning, or column definitions do not align with workload access paths, forcing inefficient scans and extra look-ups.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level runtime settings for memory, logging, parallelism, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware and workload, introducing artificial bottlenecks or bursts of maintenance activity.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply primary transaction-log traffic at source speed, causing growing apply lag and retention of log segments.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: primary queries show high latency and erratic plan shapes (full scans, excessive random I/O); checkpoint, log-write, and work-memory waits spike even though raw CPU and I/O remain under-utilised; at the same time replica lag widens rapidly, retention of log segments inflates primary disk usage, and read-only workloads on replicas see increasingly stale data. Performance troubleshooting becomes harder because any point-in-time metric may show multiple saturated subsystems (buffer cache churn, background writer thrashing, replication apply backlog), yet none individually explains the full degradation.

Causal interaction: poorly designed schemas generate larger row sets and bloated indexes, inflating the volume of dirty pages and redo that the primary must handle. Mis-configured memory and checkpoint parameters then accelerate flush storms, fragment the buffer cache, or throttle worker memory, amplifying query cost and redo generation even further. The swollen and bursty log stream must be shipped to replicas, but their apply threads—already contending with the same inefficient schema structure—fall behind, creating replication lag. As log segments cannot be recycled until all replicas acknowledge them, disk pressure on the primary rises, triggering additional checkpoints and background cleanup that again interact with the mis-tuned parameters. The three root causes therefore reinforce each other in a feedback loop that degrades primary throughput, replica freshness, and overall system stability far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, store, or apply WAL/redo data as fast as the primary generates it, causing widening replication lag and retained logs.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, threads, sockets, or other OS-level objects, blocking new work or I/O even though engine-level quotas appear sufficient.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, or socket resources between clients/peers and the server become saturated or unreliable, yielding connection errors, retransmissions, and stalled I/O.

When all three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits compounding symptoms: replicas fall ever further behind while the primary’s WAL directory and replica relay logs mushroom, yet attempts to diagnose or remediate are hampered by flurries of “too many open files,” “cannot allocate shared memory,” or “could not create socket” errors. Clients and replication processes both suffer connection timeouts, half-open TCP states accumulate, authentication stalls increase, and parallel-apply or WAL-sender workers fail to spawn. Failover readiness erodes as replicas report severe replay lag, and primary storage may fill because old log segments cannot be recycled. Monitoring shows spiking network RTT and retransmissions, OS kernel logs of resource denials, and replication views with ballooning write/flush/replay delay—all intertwined and temporally correlated, making single-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, network congestion or unstable links slow the flow of WAL to replicas, inflating in-flight buffers and socket counts; this accelerates consumption of file descriptors, shared memory message queues, and async-I/O contexts until OS limits are breached. Once limits bite, new sockets, threads, or shared-memory allocations for WAL sender/receiver or client sessions fail, which further throttles or stalls replication, deepening lag and forcing the primary to retain even more log files—amplifying handle usage and storage pressure. Simultaneously, replication workers that crash or hang leave orphaned semaphores and sockets, further exhausting OS quotas and exacerbating connection-layer backlog. The mutual reinforcement between network-level bottlenecks, OS resource starvation, and replication slowdown can drive the cluster into a cascading degradation or complete service outage unless both infrastructure capacity and kernel limits are addressed together.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from a static physical-design mismatch (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints that do not fit the workload) and a saturated transaction-log subsystem (log buffer, log files, archiving, or replication pipeline unable to keep up with redo generation). Both root causes are active at the same time, so even correctly written applications experience inefficient access paths while every data change competes for limited log-write bandwidth.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Queries that should be index-seek driven devolve into full scans or non-covering index lookups, inflating I/O and CPU. 2) DML and commit operations show pronounced LOG FLUSH, LOG WRITE, and LOG SYNC waits, with frequent log-file switches, growing archive backlogs, and checkpoint storms. 3) Because poorly chosen or missing indexes force extra row lookups and maintain redundant or bloated index structures, redo volume spikes; this aggravates log-file growth, causes longer checkpoint and replication lag, and lengthens transaction response times. 4) End users observe erratic latency patterns: reads slow due to scan overhead, writes stall during log flush pressure, and mixed workloads exhibit lock contention and time-outs as transactions stay open longer. Performance improves only after both design and log bottlenecks are addressed.

Causal interaction: The design anomaly inflates the amount and frequency of data modifications (extra index entries, wider rows, unnecessary full-row updates), directly increasing redo generation per transaction. The swollen redo stream overwhelms an already constrained transaction-log subsystem, extending commit times and prolonging lock hold durations. Prolonged transactions, in turn, intensify contention on the poorly designed tables and indexes, causing even more row versioning, index splits, and undo/redo traffic. This feedback loop magnifies I/O pressure on both data and log devices, masks the root causes behind multiple overlapping wait events, and can ultimately bring an OLTP system to throughput collapse until both the schema/index layout and the log subsystem capacity are corrected together.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is concurrently affected by mis-tuned engine runtime parameters and impending or actual exhaustion of physical or logical storage space, causing both resource-governance inefficiencies and hard space limits to surface at the same time.

Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Critical settings for memory, checkpoints, background workers, parallelism, logging, or connection limits are misaligned with hardware capacity, workload patterns, or version defaults, degrading performance even when raw resources are available.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: The data, log, temporary, or backup areas approach or reach full utilization, producing allocation failures, auto-extend errors, and write stalls unrelated to bandwidth limitations.

Combined Phenomena: When these two root causes overlap, the system exhibits a mixture of misleading and self-reinforcing symptoms—e.g., frequent checkpoint storms caused by undersized log files co-occurring with actual log-destination fullness; intense log write waits, buffer flush surges, or autovacuum/autopurge backlogs while I/O devices appear under-utilised; sudden query or DDL failures due to "out of space" errors intermixed with erratic latency from over-aggressive background processes; and oscillating CPU usage as incorrectly configured work-memory or parallelism triggers repeated spill-to-disk operations that then fail or stall because temporary space is depleted. Monitoring dashboards may show paradoxical metrics such as low CPU or I/O throughput alongside severe wait events and aborted transactions.

Causal Chain Analysis: Misconfigured parameters can accelerate space consumption (e.g., excessive log generation from too-frequent checkpoints, bloated temp segments from oversized work memory, or unbounded session counts each creating temp files). At the same time, shrinking free space constrains the database’s ability to honor configuration settings that rely on disk growth (log file extensions, temp-space allocation, auto-grow datafiles), forcing the engine into emergency or aggressive housekeeping modes that further increase I/O and CPU pressure. The feedback loop between poor configuration and dwindling storage manifests as amplified contention, unexpected throttling, and ultimately service outages, making root-cause isolation difficult without recognizing that both parameter mis-tuning and space depletion are jointly responsible.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer input metadata is stale, incomplete, or otherwise inaccurate, causing systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal plan selection.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high and sustained share of CPU, saturating the host’s compute capacity.

Composite definition: This anomaly represents the concurrent presence of stale or missing optimizer statistics that generate inefficient execution plans while, at the same time, the database host is already CPU-saturated. The workload therefore runs under both poor plan quality and a hard compute bottleneck.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Execution plans show large row-count estimate errors alongside wide or deeply nested loop joins, excessive hash-table builds, or serial plans that spill to disk; 2) Average and p-99 query latencies increase sharply, with CPU-related wait events (e.g., RUN_QUEUE, SCHEDULER_YIELD) dominating the wait profile; 3) Host metrics reveal load averages well above core count and high context-switch rates; 4) Automatic statistics refresh, recompile, or adaptive plan mechanisms may struggle to complete on time because the CPU is already saturated; 5) Performance spikes appear immediately after large data loads or partition swaps, and the entire workload—not just the affected queries—slows down due to contention for cores.

Causal chain and interaction: Stale statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing CPU-intensive plans—such as full table scans, overly parallel plans, or repeated function evaluations—that inflate CPU demand. The inflated demand pushes the system into CPU saturation, which in turn prolongs query runtimes and keeps sessions active longer, further delaying automatic statistics maintenance tasks that could have corrected the estimates. The feedback loop amplifies both problems: bad statistics create high CPU pressure; high CPU pressure prevents timely statistics refresh and plan re-optimization, leading to progressive degradation of overall database performance.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer input metadata (row counts, histograms, correlations) is stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimates and mis-costed execution plans.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Available space for data, indexes, logs, temp, or backup areas falls to critical levels or is exhausted, producing allocation failures and blocking I/O activity.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database or co-located processes drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, starving other work of compute cycles and inflating run-queue waits.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a compound failure mode: poorly costed plans spawn inefficient, CPU-intensive scans, joins, and sorts that try to spill to temporary or redo space that is already near full, while global CPU saturation lengthens every I/O, log flush, and space-management operation. Observed symptoms include: wildly inaccurate row-count estimates in plans that nevertheless keep reusing bad cache entries; sudden spikes of CPU and context-switch waits; temp-segment or log-file space errors mid-query; aborted DML due to "no space left" conditions; slow or failed statistics jobs; and an escalating pattern of lock contention, statement timeouts, and instance-wide latency as both compute and storage headroom disappear.

Causal interaction: Stale or absent statistics provoke the optimizer to choose plan shapes that scan or sort much more data than expected, inflating CPU consumption and generating excess temp and redo usage. The resulting CPU saturation slows background tasks responsible for automatic statistics refresh, file auto-extension, log archival, and space reclamation, allowing space to deplete even faster. In parallel, shrinking free space limits the ability of queries to create temp segments or extend data/log files, causing repeated retries and latch contention that further burn CPU. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others: bad statistics drive CPU and space demand upward; CPU exhaustion throttles corrective maintenance and inflates I/O wait times; space pressure blocks the very operations (statistics refresh, sorts, index builds) needed to restore plan quality—creating a vicious feedback loop that can culminate in widespread query failures or a complete database outage.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, correlation, or partition statistics are stale or incomplete, so the optimizer systematically misestimates cardinalities and chooses sub-optimal execution plans.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log buffer, files, or archiver become a throughput or latency bottleneck, inflating commit time and stalling write-intensive operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-to-server transport, listener, socket, or authentication resources are saturated or unstable, causing connection failures, retransmissions, and session stalls.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a blended symptom set: queries compile into inefficient, row-hungry plans that generate excessive data modifications, undo, and temporary spill, inflating redo volume exactly when the log subsystem is least able to absorb it. Commit latency and log-flush waits rise, provoking application time-outs and an explosion of concurrent sessions as connection pools retry. The overloaded network layer meanwhile amplifies perceived database slowness—handshakes, result-set transfers, and commit acknowledgements linger in TCP queues—so client connections pile up, OS socket tables fill, and listener backlog overflows. Monitoring shows severe cardinality error warnings, surging log I/O waits, and escalating client-side timeouts all in the same window, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to a single tier.

Causal chain: stale or missing statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing plans that scan or update far more rows than expected, producing a spike in redo generation. The bloated redo stream overruns undersized or contended log groups, stretching commit durations. Prolonged commits hold transactions open, extending lock lifetimes and keeping network connections busy while clients wait, which in turn consumes socket descriptors and increases traffic bursts when retries fire. Concurrently, network congestion or listener saturation slows log-flush acknowledgements for synchronous commits, further throttling the log writer. The feedback loop—poor statistics → heavier logging → slower commits → longer-lived connections → network saturation → even slower commit acks—drives compound degradation, making the overall database state markedly worse than any single anomaly would cause alone.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write demand overwhelms the throughput, IOPS, or latency capacity of the underlying storage devices, making storage the immediate bottleneck.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database server CPUs run at or near saturation, limiting the cycles available for query execution and background tasks regardless of SQL-level causes.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client-server transport, listener, or connection-handling resources are unable to keep pace with incoming requests, causing connection stalls, retransmits, or refusals.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a multilayer performance collapse: (1) soaring statement and batch latencies as sessions queue first for connection slots or socket bandwidth, then for CPU scheduling, and finally for completion of slow physical I/O; (2) rampant wait-event inflation spanning client read/write, run-queue, and I/O-related classes, making it difficult to attribute delay to any single layer; (3) exaggerated feedback loops where blocked sessions hold open connections and consume memory while retry storms and connection pool exhaustion multiply front-end network traffic; (4) system-wide throughput instability in which intermittent I/O pauses cause CPU utilisation to oscillate between thrashing saturation and idle, further disturbing TCP windowing and increasing packet loss.

Causally, storage saturation elongates I/O service times, keeping server worker threads busy longer and driving up CPU time spent in spin-locks, context switches, and poll loops. Elevated CPU utilisation in turn slows listener and authentication processing, raising connection setup latency and pushing more clients into retry cycles that inflate network load. The expanding backlog of waiting or half-open sessions elevates transaction concurrency, amplifying buffer cache churn and prompting additional physical reads that further tax the constrained storage subsystem. Each layer’s bottleneck therefore reinforces the next: slow disks raise CPU pressure, busy CPUs throttle network acceptance, and network contention feeds back by spawning more concurrent retrying sessions—all combining to degrade both transactional and analytical workloads across the board.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer statement or transaction design forces the engine to process or return more data than business logic requires.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive or apply primary WAL/redo at production rate, creating widening replay lag.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced limits on handles, threads, shared memory, or similar objects choke database and auxiliary processes.

When these three root causes strike together, the system shows an extreme mix of symptoms: end-user statements experience long-tail latency and timeouts; primary-side WAL files and replica relay logs accumulate rapidly; replica read staleness and failover RPO/RTO violations grow; and both primary and replica emit errors about failing to open files, fork workers, allocate shmem, or schedule async I/O. Monitoring may reveal surging transaction durations, massive unresolved replication backlogs, sudden pauses in apply threads, and spurious partial outages where established sessions limp on while new sessions, background writers, or logical decoding workers fail to start.

Causally, inefficient SQL inflates row scans, I/O, and transaction sizes, driving up WAL generation. The heavier WAL stream must traverse the replication channel; apply workers already slowed by CPU or I/O contention now meet even steeper backlogs. As lag balloons, the server retains more WAL segments and spawns extra sender, receiver, and apply processes to catch up, sharply increasing demands for file handles, shmem, semaphores, threads, and AIO contexts. If OS limits are low or already close to saturation, these extra processes hit hard caps, causing replication workers to crash or stall, further delaying apply and magnifying backlog. The vicious circle tightens: larger backlog leads to more retained WAL, which consumes more descriptors and disk, while application logic continues to generate oversized transactions. Ultimately the interplay of excessive workload, replication stress, and kernel resource exhaustion destabilizes both primary and replicas, complicating diagnosis because each layer manifests errors that mask the others.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-layer statements and transaction scopes are written so inefficiently that the database engine must scan or modify far more rows and keep transactions open far longer than the business task requires.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, undo segments, and dead index entries accumulate faster than background cleaners can reclaim them, inflating on-disk and in-memory storage and adding visibility-check overhead.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : The transport, listener, authentication, or socket layer cannot provide enough bandwidth, round-trip performance, or connection slots to satisfy the client request rate, leading to connection stalls, retries, or drops.

When these three root causes strike together, the workload exhibits an extreme long-tail of statement latencies, high counts of slow or timed-out transactions, ballooning table and index sizes, surging connection attempts, and back-end processes stuck in client-read/client-write or vacuum/clean-up states. Bulk or chatty queries created by sub-optimal SQL logic send oversized result sets over a saturated network, prolonging transaction lifetimes. The prolonged transactions, in turn, hold old MVCC snapshots that prevent version cleanup, so each retry or leaked connection leaves more dead tuples behind. As tables bloat, the optimizer underestimates row counts, causing even heavier scans and further swelling result sets, which exacerbates network congestion and connection pool exhaustion. Meanwhile, overworked vacuum or purge workers compete for I/O with the now larger user queries, deepening latency spikes and amplifying retry storms.

Causal chain: Inefficient application SQL multiplies the amount of data touched and the duration of each transaction, creating large intermediate and final result sets. These long-lived, update-heavy transactions generate and retain many obsolete versions, pushing MVCC maintenance into perpetual backlog. The enlarged on-disk structures slow subsequent scans, inflating response times and producing even bigger network transfers. The heightened latency causes clients to hold or reopen more connections, which overloads listeners and exhausts socket and process pools, introducing additional waits and failures. Each layer’s slowdown feeds the others: network stalls prolong transactions, stalled transactions impede version cleanup, version bloat slows queries, and inefficient SQL sustains the pressure, leading to a self-reinforcing degradation spiral across application, storage, and connectivity tiers.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Simultaneous requests for incompatible locks create long blocker-waiter chains or deadlocks in the lock-manager layer, stalling transactional progress.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Mis-tuned engine settings (memory, parallelism, checkpoint, commit, etc.) mis‐align system behavior with hardware and workload characteristics, introducing artificial bottlenecks.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log’s buffering, flushing, or archiving path becomes saturated, lengthening commit latency and stalling write traffic.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database experiences a feedback loop of delay and congestion: mis-sized log buffers, aggressive synchronous-commit or checkpoint settings, or undersized log files throttle log throughput; each commit pause keeps locks held longer, amplifying lock queues and deadlock frequency. Growing blocking chains in turn prolong the lifespan of open transactions, preventing log truncation and pushing log files to switch or archive more often, which further taxes the already constrained log subsystem. Operators observe a mosaic of symptoms—skyrocketing lock-wait and log-flush wait events, surging deadlock alerts, dramatic drops in transaction throughput, sudden checkpoint storms, expanding log directories, and application timeouts—even though CPU and storage may appear only moderately utilized.

Causally, unfortunate parameter choices (e.g., minimal log buffer, tight max log file size, over-aggressive checkpoint intervals, or enforced synchronous durability) first slow down log flushes. The resulting commit latency extends the duration for which transactions retain locks, seeding blocker chains. As locks pile up, some transactions remain active for so long that checkpoints cannot advance and reused log space is withheld, intensifying log file pressure and triggering more frequent flushes and switches. Each subsystem therefore exacerbates the others: configuration mis-tuning throttles the log path; log stalls lengthen lock hold times; expanded lock contention further blocks log-space–releasing commits, ultimately spiraling into system-wide throughput collapse and repeated deadlock victimizations.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : The physical data model, indexes, partitions, constraints, and data types are mismatched to workload access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer decisions.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage media or controller cannot deliver the read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database, so physical I/O becomes the dominant wait state.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network links, listener processes, or connection-handling resources become saturated or unstable, delaying connection establishment and result transfer between clients and the database server.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, performance symptoms appear at every layer. Queries already forced into full-table scans or non-covering index lookups generate excess physical I/O that clashes with an undersized or congested storage subsystem, driving up disk queue depths and read/write latencies. The prolonged execution times keep server back-end sessions busy longer, inflating the active connection count just as network sockets, listener backlogs, or authentication threads are themselves bottlenecked. Clients observe timeouts both when establishing sessions and while waiting for large result sets; meanwhile the database shows a mixture of storage waits (data-file, log flush, temp I/O) and client/network waits (socket send/receive, TCP retransmits). CPU may appear under-utilised because time is consumed in I/O and network waits, masking the underlying schema inefficiencies.

Causally, poor schema and index design increases the volume and randomness of I/O. On an already throughput-limited storage layer this magnifies latency, which in turn prolongs transactions and amplifies concurrent session counts. The bloated execution windows and larger result sets place sustained pressure on network pipelines and connection pools, making network saturation and socket exhaustion more likely. Conversely, intermittent network slow-downs extend the life of each database session, reducing buffer cache turnover and forcing more dirty pages to accumulate and flush under constrained storage bandwidth, worsening I/O stalls. This feedback loop leads to cascading slowdowns: design flaws create excessive I/O, storage limits throttle throughput, and network/resource contention further extends query lifetimes—jointly degrading both transactional and analytical workload performance.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently chooses a sub-optimal execution plan despite having reasonably accurate statistics, leading to excessive CPU, I/O, or memory consumption per statement.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes cannot receive or apply WAL / redo as fast as the primary produces it, causing growing log-position gaps and replay lag.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced limits on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or similar resources prevent the database from opening new objects or spawning background workers.

When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the system exhibits a blend of symptoms that blur subsystem boundaries:  
• Queries that used to be fast suddenly slow down or fluctuate because the optimizer has switched to scan-heavy or single-threaded plans; parallel workers may be missing due to OS thread limits.  
• The inefficient plans inflate transaction duration and generate excessive redo, which in turn causes replication send and apply queues to balloon; monitoring shows rapidly widening WAL/LSN gaps and replicas falling minutes or hours behind.  
• At the same time, OS resource ceilings are hit—log-sender or apply processes fail to open additional files, allocate shm segments, or start extra apply threads—leading to error messages in both database logs and kernel logs, further throttling replication and occasionally aborting query executions.  
• The primary’s pg_wal or redo area grows uncontrollably because old segments cannot be recycled while replicas lag, risking full disks and cascading slowdowns.  
Overall, users observe erratic response times, timeouts, stale read traffic on replicas, and declining fail-over readiness, yet the individual symptoms overlap enough to obscure the multi-layered root cause.

Causal interaction: A poor plan elevates I/O and CPU load, inflating the volume and rate of transaction log generation. This heavier WAL stream must traverse the replication channel, but replicas already struggle because OS-level limits cap the number of receiver/apply workers and restrict kernel objects (file handles, AIO contexts). The constrained replication workers fall further behind, which prevents log recycling on the primary, amplifying storage pressure and increasing contention for file descriptors—tightening the OS resource squeeze. Simultaneously, the exhausted kernel quotas prevent the optimizer from spawning parallel execution or maintaining plan cache structures, encouraging more plan switches and further entrenching sub-optimal plans. The feedback loop between wasteful plans, replication backlog, and kernel-level throttling drives the database into a degraded, unstable state.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from (1) a physical schema-and-index layout that forces excessive random and non-selective access, (2) saturation of the underlying storage layer’s throughput/IOPS capacity, and (3) exhaustion of kernel-enforced process, file-handle, and asynchronous-I/O limits. Acting together, these three root causes create a self-reinforcing performance and stability collapse that is not attributable to any single layer alone.

Combined observable phenomena: Queries that should be index seeks devolve into full scans, driving abnormally high physical read and write volumes. Storage latencies, device queue depths, and database I/O wait events spike, yet database CPU utilisation remains uneven because workers stall on I/O. As latency stretches, sessions, parallel workers, and background tasks linger, inflating the count of open files, AIO contexts, and threads until operating-system limits are hit. At that point the database emits "cannot open file", "cannot allocate shared memory", or "failed to start worker" errors, new connections hang or fail, checkpoints prolong, and log flush times grow, increasing recovery-point exposure. Performance troubleshooting becomes difficult because symptoms oscillate between classic I/O bottlenecks and sudden OS-level allocation failures.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient schema and missing or non-covering indexes multiply the number of blocks each query must touch. The resultant surge in physical I/O drives the storage subsystem to its throughput ceiling, raising service times and leaving requests queued. Prolonged I/O wait elongates transaction lifetimes and inflates the number of concurrently active sessions, each holding file descriptors, AIO handles, shared-memory latches, and threads. As these kernel objects accumulate, they collide with conservative per-process or cgroup limits. Once limits are reached, further I/O submission or session creation fails, causing retries, partial task aborts, and even more backlog against the already saturated storage. Conversely, kernel rejections of I/O contexts or file handles force the database to fall back to less efficient synchronous or serial paths, which put additional pressure on both the storage layer and the poorly indexed schema. The feedback loop of excessive logical I/O → storage saturation → longer runtimes → kernel resource exhaustion compounds latency, jeopardises throughput, and can precipitate cascading outages.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level settings (memory, checkpoint, logging, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload demands, creating artificial bottlenecks or bursts of background activity.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk table or index pages are physically or logically corrupt, causing incorrect or failed access to stored rows and keys.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas exhausts, leading to allocation failures and stalled write-ahead logging.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a tangled failure pattern: mis-sized memory pools and aggressive checkpoint or autovacuum settings drive elevated log generation and page flush activity; simultaneous hidden corruption produces sporadic checksum errors, failed index lookups, and forced full-table scans that inflate I/O and space consumption; meanwhile, limited free space prevents growth of datafiles, logs, or rebuild work areas. Operators may observe oscillating CPU spin on internal retry loops, surges of log-write and page-flush waits even while devices report inconsistent utilization, sudden query failures with “no space” or “corrupt page” errors, repeated crash-recovery cycles, and integrity-check tools reporting new corrupt objects after each restart.

Causally, aggressive or ill-fitting configuration parameters (e.g., undersized checkpoint segments, oversized work-memory, excessive parallel workers) accelerate data churn and checkpoint frequency, amplifying write pressure. This heightened I/O stream consumes remaining disk capacity faster, raising the likelihood of out-of-space events that interrupt normal write-ahead logging. Abrupt log pauses or failed extensions in turn increase the window for partially written pages, intensifying the risk of physical corruption, while corruption itself can force emergency rewrites or index rebuilds that require additional space the system no longer has. The feedback loop between mis-tuned parameters, space exhaustion, and corruption escalates from intermittent slowdowns to systemic outages, making isolation of any single root cause difficult and leaving the database in an unstable and potentially unrecoverable state.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Costing inputs (row counts, histograms, correlations) are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plans.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level memory, I/O, parallelism, and checkpoint/redo settings are mis-tuned for the actual hardware and workload, distorting runtime behavior regardless of physical capacity.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or downstream replicas cannot receive or apply WAL/redo as fast as the primary generates it, leading to growing replication lag and log-retention pressure.

Composite definition: The database concurrently suffers from inaccurate optimizer statistics, ill-calibrated configuration parameters, and impaired replication throughput. Together they create a multi-layer performance and availability degradation in which poor plan quality, resource misallocation, and backlog in the replication pipeline reinforce one another.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Queries on the primary intermittently swing between very fast and severely slow executions, with explain plans showing grossly off row-count estimates, high memory spills, or runaway parallelism. 2) Mis-sized buffers, work-mem, or checkpoint intervals inflate redo generation and increase flush storms, amplifying log-write waits even while CPU or storage remain under-utilised. 3) Replication monitor views show widening receive/replay lag, growing retained log segments, and replicas serving progressively staler data; failovers become risky as retained logs approach disk limits. 4) After bulk loads or schema changes, statistics staleness triggers massive sequential scans whose bloated I/O, memory, and redo output collide with poorly tuned background writer and WAL parameters, further starving replication workers and extending apply latency. Symptoms cross domains, obscuring root causes: log bloat may be misattributed to storage when it is jointly driven by bad plans and sub-optimal checkpoint sizing.

Causal interaction: Stale or missing statistics generate inefficient plans (e.g., full-table scans, oversized hash aggregates) that explode I/O and redo volume. Because configuration parameters (buffer pool, work_mem, checkpoint_timeout, wal_buffers, parallelism limits) are mis-set, the engine cannot absorb the extra load, leading to more frequent checkpoints, longer log flush times, and head-of-line blocking. The surge in WAL traffic overwhelms replication channels already operating near capacity; as replicas fall behind, the primary must retain additional log segments, increasing disk pressure and further lengthening checkpoints. Elevated write and memory contention from mis-configured resources slows statistics auto-collection, perpetuating staleness and creating a reinforcing loop where each anomaly exacerbates the others, culminating in severe performance volatility, storage exhaustion risk, and degraded high-availability posture.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process or return far more data than business logic actually requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer cost inputs are stale, incomplete, or misleading, causing systematic misestimation of cardinalities and sub-optimal plan choices.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage layer is saturated, so physical read/write latency, IOPS, or bandwidth become the dominant bottleneck.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits extreme and highly variable response times, runaway I/O wait percentages despite available CPU, repeated slow-query log entries for the same statements, frequent plan recompilations with wildly shifting row-estimate errors, prolonged lock holding, and application timeouts or cascading retries. Execution plans often show full or large index scans chosen on the basis of bad statistics, while the sheer volume of unnecessary data access generated by poorly written SQL floods the already saturated storage subsystem, driving queue depths and device wait times even higher. Batch windows stretch, checkpoint and log-flush operations compete with data reads, and both OLTP and analytical sessions experience head-of-line blocking on I/O.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies the impact of stale statistics: wide scans and non-selective predicates make the optimizer’s reliance on accurate cardinalities critical; when those statistics are outdated, it is more likely to choose plans that exacerbate data access. The resulting surge in physical I/O pushes the storage layer to or beyond its throughput limits, inflating latency. Elevated I/O latency in turn prolongs statement and transaction duration, delaying or suppressing automatic statistics refresh and leaving poor plans in place longer. The feedback loop between bad SQL, bad estimates, and saturated storage compounds resource contention, driving the database into a persistent degraded-performance state.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine allocates and retains more memory and swap than the host can safely supply, inflating buffer pools, work areas, plan caches, and other heaps until the operating system is under sustained memory pressure.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Multiple sessions concurrently fight for access to hot buffer-cache pages, latches, and I/O slots, stalling on lightweight synchronization points rather than on row-level locks and causing CPU spin or wait inflation.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read- and write-request volume overwhelms the bandwidth, IOPS, or latency envelope of the underlying storage devices, keeping queue depths saturated and stretching out every I/O-bound database activity.

When these three root causes strike at once, the system displays a blend of memory exhaustion symptoms (OS paging, resident-set bloat, OOM kills), extreme buffer-busy/latch waits, and escalating I/O wait times. Cache-hit ratios plunge as hot pages churn out of a shrunken or fragmented buffer pool; each miss forces synchronous disk access that is already throttled by saturated storage, elongating latch hold times and propagating wait chains across sessions. CPU usage oscillates between futile spin-loops on latches and idle time blocked on I/O, while overall throughput collapses and latency becomes erratic. Clustered or virtualized environments may add node evictions or failovers as memory and I/O pressure propagate at the host or storage fabric level.

Causal interaction: Excessive memory allocation reduces free RAM, triggering the kernel to reclaim pages and expel dirty buffers, which immediately amplifies physical I/O demand. The surge in disk traffic collides with an already over-subscribed storage layer, driving up service times and inflating the duration for which buffer pages stay pinned or dirty. Prolonged disk flushes delay latch release, so more sessions queue for the same hot pages, intensifying latch contention. In turn, threads that spin or wait longer keep their per-session work areas allocated, further straining memory and encouraging the engine to evict clean pages more aggressively—feeding yet more I/O. The feedback loop among memory starvation, I/O saturation, and buffer-level serialization rapidly degrades both read and write paths, making the composite anomaly far more severe than any individual issue encountered in isolation.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to read, process, or retain more data and locks than business logic really requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, or partitioning choices do not align with access patterns, obliging the optimizer to scan or maintain excessive data even for selective tasks.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The generation, flushing, or archival of write-ahead log (WAL/redo) records becomes a bottleneck, prolonging commit latency and stalling write activity.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits extreme and erratic response times: large or poorly filtered statements trigger wide scans and massively inflate redo generation; missing or non-covering indexes force full data movement into the log, while row-by-row access patterns multiply log records. The bloated transactional footprint keeps locks and latches active for longer, raising contention and deadlock rates. Commit, checkpoint, and replication latencies surge as the undersized or saturated log subsystem struggles to flush the amplified redo stream. Administrators observe simultaneous slow-query spikes, runaway log growth, frequent log-switch alerts, and application timeouts whose duration varies with background archive or replication backlog.

Causally, sub-optimal SQL logic is the first amplifier, turning simple business operations into bulk scans or chatty cursors that touch many rows. Because the physical schema lacks appropriate indexing or partitioning, each operation translates into more I/O and produces larger update, undo, and redo volumes. This excess redo saturates a marginal log subsystem; log buffers fill, checkpoints advance aggressively, and commits stall while waiting for disk or archival space. The prolonged transactions caused by the workload logic keep locks active, further delaying other sessions already slowed by log waits, creating a feedback loop that degrades throughput and jeopardizes both read and write performance across the OLTP system.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical runtime settings (memory, checkpointing, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload profile, or software version, so the engine’s internal behavior itself becomes the bottleneck.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Stand-by or subscriber nodes cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo traffic as fast as the primary produces it, causing widening log-position gaps and retention of log segments.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network paths, listener sockets, or connection-handling resources are saturated or unstable, impeding data flow or session establishment between hosts and clients (including replicas).

When these three conditions overlap, the database exhibits a multi-layer degradation pattern: replication lag surges while primary-side WAL files pile up and cannot be recycled; replicas report both I/O or apply backlogs and frequent disconnect/reconnect churn; monitoring shows bursts of write-intensive waits on the primary even though storage and CPU are under-utilised, alongside steep increases in network retransmissions, half-open sockets, and authentication queueing. End-user sessions experience sporadic timeouts, stale reads from lagging replicas, and sudden latency spikes after each forced checkpoint or replica catch-up. Operations such as failover, switchover, or scaling out read traffic become risky because replicas are simultaneously behind and unstable.

Causally, an unfitting configuration (e.g., aggressive checkpoint_interval, undersized wal_sender timeout, or excessive max_connections) drives high redo generation and spawns more background and connection processes than the host or network can handle. The inflated WAL rate stresses the replication pipeline; meanwhile, network congestion or socket exhaustion slows delivery to replicas, amplifying apply lag. The primary, seeing replication slots behind, is forced to retain additional log segments, inflating disk pressure and triggering even more frequent checkpoints—feedback that intensifies the original configuration problem. Replicas, burdened by delayed apply and intermittent network drops, further throttle back acknowledgement, convincing the primary to hold more WAL and fueling a vicious cycle that degrades both local performance and cross-node consistency.

Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : Persistent on-disk table or index pages contain logical or physical corruption, breaking key order, page links, or heap–index correspondence.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database’s processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, address space, or cgroup quotas, independent of database-level limits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Server-side listener, socket, or transport resources are insufficient, or network path quality is poor, causing connection establishment failures, stalled sessions, or retransmissions.

When all three root causes manifest concurrently, failure signals overlap and amplify: corrupted indexes force full table scans that open far more data files and consume extra buffer, handle, and I/O contexts, hastening exhaustion of per-process file-descriptor or asynchronous-I/O limits. Stalled or repeatedly failing queries remain active longer, holding backend processes and sockets; meanwhile new clients encounter connection-handshake timeouts, too-many-connections errors, or kernel-level "cannot create socket / thread" denials. Integrity check errors, page-checksum failures, or sudden plan fallbacks coincide with spikes in operating-system alerts about EMFILE, ENOMEM, or semaphore limits, plus rising counts of half-open TCP connections, retransmissions, and authentication drops. These interleaved symptoms complicate diagnosis because each layer reports distinct yet causally related errors.

Causal chain: latent or newly introduced page/index corruption triggers heavier I/O and longer-running statements, inflating the number and lifetime of file handles, buffer pins, background workers, and client sockets. The inflated footprint collides with tight OS limits, producing resource allocation failures that block new sessions and recovery tasks, leaving corruption unrepaired and forcing additional client retries. Simultaneously, resource exhaustion in the kernel (e.g., depleted sockets, shared memory, or threads) degrades listener throughput and amplifies network wait times, causing application-side reconnection storms that further flood the already limited socket and process pools. The feedback loop between structural corruption–induced workload inflation, OS limit saturation, and deteriorating connectivity accelerates service degradation, risking partial or full outage and complicating both detection and remediation.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite reasonably accurate statistics, leading to inefficient operator choices, wrong join orders, or inappropriate degrees of parallelism.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, parallelism, logging, or background workers are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, creating systemic pressure or artificial throttling independent of actual resource capacity.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes drive the host CPUs to sustained saturation, producing high run-queue depths, context switching, and widespread latency spikes.

When these three root causes manifest together, symptoms intertwine and intensify: the system oscillates between radically different plans, some of which spawn excessive parallel workers or CPU-heavy operators just as configuration mis-settings (e.g., over-aggressive max parallelism, undersized buffer pool, or tiny work-memory limits) force the engine to rely on CPU-intensive re-execution or spill-heavy strategies. Checkpoints or background cleaners triggered by poor parameter choices contend for the same overcrowded CPU cores, so wait-event views simultaneously show CPU-bound runqueue waits and configuration-driven stalls such as log flush or buffer eviction pauses. Performance becomes erratic—queries that sometimes fly collapse into severe slowdowns after plan cache invalidations, while overall throughput plateaus even though I/O and memory appear under-utilised.

Causally, misconfigured parameters first distort the optimizer’s cost landscape (e.g., inaccurate CPU vs. I/O weighting, inflated parallelism limits, or constrained memory per operation). These distortions bias plan selection towards CPU-intensive paths. The resulting heavy compute demand pushes the host into saturation, triggering the CPU Resource Anomaly. In turn, the congested CPU environment slows background tasks governed by the same mis-tuned parameters, causing more frequent plan recompiles, cache flushing, and checkpoint storms that invalidate or evict plans—further increasing the likelihood of sub-optimal plan selection. This feedback loop amplifies latency variability, reduces throughput, and makes isolating any single layer’s contribution difficult, as optimizer misjudgments, parameter miscalibration, and genuine CPU exhaustion continuously reinforce one another.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Static mismatch between the physical data model (table layout, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer or statistics quality.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Excessive or conflicting lock acquisition by concurrent transactions, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort OLTP statements.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources (file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, etc.) that prevents the database from opening additional objects or spawning workers even though in-engine capacity remains.

When all three root causes coexist, the system shows a blended symptom set:  
• Queries that should be selective devolve into full scans, inflating the number and duration of row/page locks they hold.  
• Lock-wait time, deadlock frequency, and transaction retries climb sharply; application sessions pile up in connection pools or remain idle in transaction.  
• As blocking lengthens, background processes and new sessions attempt to open more files, allocate shared buffers, or spawn additional lock-manager and I/O workers, quickly reaching OS limits.  
• The engine begins emitting "cannot open file/too many open files", "cannot create thread", or "out of shared memory" errors, compounding the perceived outage.  
• Performance troubleshooting is complicated because lock-wait views, execution-plan analysis, and operating-system logs all surface critical alerts simultaneously, making it hard to isolate any single culprit.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and indexing enlarge the footprint and duration of each statement, increasing the volume and granularity of locks requested. The swollen lock set exacerbates contention among concurrent transactions, producing longer blocker chains and more deadlocks. Prolonged blocking encourages session buildup and retries, which inflate the number of active connections, held locks, open file handles, and background helper threads. This surge in kernel object usage pushes the database toward operating-system resource limits; once those limits are reached, the engine cannot create additional locks, files, or worker threads, further stalling lock acquisition and query execution. In turn, transactions hold locks even longer while waiting for scarce OS resources, reinforcing the lock contention and creating a feedback loop that degrades overall throughput and can precipitate a partial or full service outage.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same data or metadata resources, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress until a waiter times out or the engine aborts a victim. 
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine parameters (memory, checkpoint cadence, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, causing subsystem behavior that is sub-optimal even though the underlying resources are not yet exhausted. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer becomes a hard bottleneck as sustained reads or writes exceed the throughput, IOPS, or latency capacity of the devices that host data, temp, or log files.

When all three root causes manifest together, the database experiences a reinforcing storm of symptoms: lock wait queues grow while overall I/O wait events dominate session profiles; transactions linger in locked states because every page or row access incurs inflated disk latency; checkpoint or log-flush surges—driven by mis-sized buffers or too-aggressive durability settings—collide with an already saturated storage subsystem, further stretching lock hold times. Users observe erratic response times, frequent deadlock victim errors, sporadic application timeouts, and sharp drops in throughput even though CPU may appear lightly loaded. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in lock waits, log write waits, buffer-I/O stalls, and background writer or checkpoint activity, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to any single layer.

Causal chain: sub-optimal configuration (e.g., undersized buffer pool, overly frequent checkpoints, small log files, or excessive parallel workers) forces the engine to issue more physical I/O and to flush dirty pages or logs more often. The increased I/O demand pushes the storage system past its throughput limit, inflating read/write latencies. Longer I/O times lengthen transaction execution and commit phases, extending the duration that locks are held. Prolonged lock ownership heightens the probability of conflicting lock requests, spawning longer blocking chains and deadlocks. In turn, the growing population of waiting sessions can exhaust connection and memory quotas already constrained by poor configuration, provoking further swapping, emergency checkpoints, or log stalls that deepen the storage overload. The three anomalies thus amplify one another, creating a feedback loop that degrades both concurrency control and physical I/O, culminating in severe throughput collapse for transactional workloads.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer input metadata (row counts, histograms, correlation stats) is stale, missing, or inaccurate, causing systematic cardinality misestimation.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table and index pages are physically or logically corrupted, breaking key ordering, page links, or heap-to-index consistency.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other OS objects are exhausted, preventing the database from allocating critical resources.

When all three root causes coexist, symptoms intertwine: queries may flip from efficient index plans to full table scans because the optimizer underestimates or overestimates row counts while simultaneously distrusting corrupted indexes and encountering OS errors when attempting to open alternate access paths, spawn parallel workers, or read recovery segments. Estimated-vs-actual row gaps, repeated plan recompilations, and integrity check failures surface alongside sporadic "cannot open file" or "cannot create shared memory" engine errors. Administrators may observe erratic performance spikes, partially missing result sets, and intermittent session or background-worker failures; corruption repair or index rebuild attempts may abort midway due to OS resource denials, leaving objects in even less consistent states.

Causal chain: stale or absent statistics can drive the optimizer to favor access paths that intensively exercise particular indexes or create large temporary workfiles, increasing I/O and handle usage; this added pressure accelerates the exhaustion of OS-level limits. Once limits are hit, critical maintenance tasks—such as automatic page verification, index rebuilds, or statistics refreshes—fail to complete, allowing existing block and index corruptions to persist and spread. Conversely, latent page corruption can trigger repeated plan invalidations and emergency scans that inflate resource consumption, hastening resource-limit breaches and deferring statistics collection that relies on full object scans. The mutual reinforcement of bad statistics, structural corruption, and kernel resource starvation creates a feedback loop that steadily degrades both query correctness and engine availability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical table, index, or partition design mismatches the workload, forcing inefficient access paths even with correct statistics.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Optimizer chooses or reuses a sub-optimal plan despite acceptable statistics, often due to flawed cost model or plan-cache behavior.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume sustained, abnormal CPU, saturating host cores and degrading overall workload performance.

When all three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits severe and wide-spread latency spikes, throughput collapse during peak traffic, and erratic plan flips that coincide with CPU saturation. Typical observations include:  
• Queries oscillate between full table scans (from missing/inefficient indexes) and occasionally cached but poor plans, inflating logical I/O and CPU time.  
• Run-queue lengths and context-switch rates climb, while wait-event views show a mix of CPU queue waits and I/O reads from unselective scans.  
• Minor data-skew or parameter changes trigger drastic performance variability because every new plan choice must fight for already scarce CPU resources.  
• Maintenance DML or batch jobs magnify the problem by hammering oversized index structures, further crowding cores and displacing execution plans in the cache.  
• Tuning actions that address only one layer (e.g., forcing a plan or adding CPU) yield limited benefit because the intertwined flaws at all three layers remain.

Causal chain: Poor schema and index design forces the optimizer to consider expensive access paths. Even when statistics are adequate, the cost model may still misjudge alternatives, yielding sub-optimal plans. These heavyweight plans drive excessive CPU consumption; the resulting saturation feeds back into the optimizer’s runtime feedback and plan caching, promoting additional plan instability. High CPU pressure further degrades plan quality through reduced search effort or forced parallelism and delays background statistics refreshes, which in turn perpetuate reliance on bad schema structures. The intertwined feedback loop thus amplifies latency and resource contention far beyond what any single anomaly would cause in isolation.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot or rapidly recycled buffer pages, pins, or latches force sessions to serialize access to shared in-memory data structures, inflating buffer-busy, page-latch, and spin wait times.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing and log maintenance are throttled by insufficient log buffer, log file, or archiver bandwidth, driving up log-flush and log-write waits and stalling foreground writers.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying disks or storage fabric reach their IOPS / bandwidth limits, lengthening physical read-write service times for data, temp, and log files.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database experiences a multi-layered stall: foreground transactions queue first on log-flush or commit waits, then hold buffer-cache latches longer than normal, while background check-point, buffer-flush, and archiver processes fight for the same saturated I/O channels. Observable symptoms include: 1) extreme variability in commit latency coupled with growing log file and archive backlogs; 2) explosive growth in buffer-busy/latch contention statistics as sessions spin on hot pages already pinned by log-waiting transactions; 3) device queues pinned at maximum depth, with both data-file and log-file latencies far exceeding their baselines; and 4) runaway CPU usage with little throughput gain, accompanied by periodic freezes when global cache or log buffers must be flushed.

Causally, slow physical storage elongates every data-file and log-file I/O, directly triggering the Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly. Prolonged log writes propagate upstream, converting short commit paths into long log-flush waits; transactions already holding page latches remain in critical sections, thereby intensifying Buffer Cache and Latch Contention. The heightened contention forces additional retry loops and may inflate the buffer churn rate, which in turn issues more dirty-page flushes and advances checkpoints, further loading the already saturated storage subsystem and increasing redo generation. This positive feedback loop between I/O saturation, blocked log flushing, and latch hold-time amplification cascades into severe throughput collapse typical of write-heavy OLTP systems.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Excessive accumulation of obsolete row versions, undo/rollback records, and stale index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating data structures and extending visibility-check work.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path—generation, flush, switch, or archival—becomes the primary bottleneck, stretching commit latency and stalling further DML until log space or I/O bandwidth is freed.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Client/server transport, listener, or socket resources saturate or flap, delaying connection establishment and slowing or interrupting result streaming.

When all three root causes strike concurrently, the database exhibits a compound pathology: 1) commits and statement completions slow first at the server (log-flush and version-chain scanning waits) and then at the client (network send/receive stalls); 2) transaction throughput collapses while session counts, half-open sockets, version-store bytes, and unarchived log segments all climb in tandem; 3) planner estimates drift because of table bloat, causing long-running scans that emit large result sets which further congest the network, amplifying front-end timeouts and retry storms; 4) monitoring shows cleanup workers, log writer, and archiver pegged, yet disk devices may appear only moderately busy because pauses are dominated by dependency back-pressure rather than raw I/O saturation.

Causally, heavy update/delete activity produces a flood of redo records that must be flushed, growing the transaction log. Log flush slowdowns delay commit completion, stretching transaction lifetimes and preventing MVCC cleanup from advancing its snapshot horizon; this in turn accelerates version bloat, generating still more redo and further enlarging the log. Meanwhile, the increasing payload of bloated table scans and prolonged transactions expand result sets and keep backend processes open longer, consuming connection slots and network buffers. Network congestion or socket exhaustion feeds back by raising commit acknowledgment and client-ack wait times, which lengthens transactions even more, giving rollback segments additional time to swell. The intertwined feedback loops among version buildup, log saturation, and network pressure cause a reinforcing spiral that degrades overall OLTP performance and complicates diagnosis because symptoms from one layer mask or exacerbate those in the others.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Statistics on tables and indexes are stale, incomplete, or missing, causing systematic cardinality mis-estimation.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses an execution plan that is sub-optimal despite reasonably accurate statistics because of cost-model or plan-cache issues.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes oversubscribe CPU cores, driving sustained CPU saturation and run-queue contention.

When these three root causes coexist, the workload experiences volatile and often catastrophic performance swings: grossly inaccurate cardinality estimates feed the cost model, which in turn selects poor or erratic plans that consume excessive CPU. The resulting CPU saturation starves concurrent sessions, inflates run-queue and context-switch waits, and lengthens response times across the system. Rapid back-to-back hard parses may cache alternating bad plans, so successive executions of the same statement oscillate between different, CPU-hungry strategies (e.g., serial full scans versus massively parallel nested loops). Because CPUs are already pegged, even small misestimations translate into severe slowdowns, and the statistical discrepancies become harder to detect—the usual tell-tale gaps between estimated and actual rows are obscured by global resource queuing. End-users observe unpredictable latencies, timeouts, and throughput collapse, while DBAs see both plan-quality warnings and system-level CPU alarms firing simultaneously.

Causally, stale or poor-quality statistics misguide costing; the optimizer, already susceptible to plan-selection pitfalls (e.g., parameter-sensitive reuse, version changes, missing hints), is more likely to lock in an inefficient plan. That plan inflates CPU demand—via unnecessary scans, mismatched join methods, or excessive parallelism—driving the host into sustained CPU saturation. High CPU pressure, in turn, expands parse times and reduces the effectiveness of adaptive mechanisms, delaying automatic statistics refresh jobs and making it harder for the optimizer to re-evaluate plans, thus reinforcing the feedback loop. The intertwined effects of bad statistics, wrong plan choices, and compute exhaustion therefore amplify each other, producing a severe composite anomaly that degrades both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is simultaneously suffering from (1) severe buffer-cache page and latch contention, (2) a saturated or stalled transaction-log subsystem, and (3) imminent or actual exhaustion of physical or logical storage space. These three root causes coexist and interact, creating a self-reinforcing bottleneck that impairs both read and write paths, inflates CPU usage, and threatens service availability.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Users experience sharp spikes in response time for both read and commit operations. Wait-event statistics show surging buffer-busy, page-latch, log-flush, log-sync, checkpoint, and space-allocation waits. Checkpoints and log switches fire more frequently yet take longer to finish; archive or replica-shipping lag grows. Free-space alarms oscillate near 0 %, autoextend and archive writes fail, and "cannot allocate extent" or "out of space" errors appear. Dirty buffers pile up because they cannot be flushed promptly—first due to log flush delays, then because datafiles or log destinations have no room—causing hot pages to remain latched and provoke CPU spin as sessions queue. Overall throughput collapses while CPU, log-file I/O, and storage error counters soar.

Causal Interaction: Slow or blocked log flushing elongates commit latency and stretches checkpoint intervals, keeping many buffers dirty and pinned. These long-lived pins elevate latch contention on hot pages, amplifying the buffer-cache anomaly. Simultaneously, dwindling storage space prevents timely auto-extension of datafiles and the creation or archival of new log segments, further stalling log writes. Each stalled log write prolongs dirty-page residency, which in turn increases buffer turnover pressure and latch competition. The clogged log and space exhaustion thus feed buffer contention, while the intensified write bursts generated by retried transactions and checkpoint storms accelerate space consumption, pushing the system into a cascading failure loop.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress inside the lock-manager layer.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process exhausts kernel-enforced resources such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, or thread quotas, causing allocation failures outside the engine’s internal limit system.

When both root causes manifest together, sessions already stalled behind lock waits are joined by new sessions or engine workers that cannot even start because the operating system refuses additional kernel objects. Symptoms therefore include: rapidly growing lock-wait and deadlock counts, rising transaction latency, and surging client timeouts, plus sporadic errors about "too many open files," "cannot create thread," or "out of shared memory." The engine may appear to freeze: existing transactions are blocked by locks, while new connections, background tasks, or deadlock detector threads fail to spawn, making the blocking invisible or unresolvable. Monitoring shows simultaneous saturation of lock queues and OS resource counters, with connection pools backing up despite adequate database-level capacity.

Causally, heavy lock contention lengthens transaction lifetimes and inflates the number of concurrent sessions, lock objects, and file handles each one holds; this accelerates consumption of kernel resources until OS limits are breached. Once those limits are hit, the engine can no longer create new worker threads or lock structures, preventing deadlock detection or victim cleanup and allowing blocking chains to grow unchecked—thereby further intensifying lock contention. The feedback loop between prolonged locks and resource starvation degrades throughput sharply and can escalate to a partial or total outage if either condition is not relieved.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings such as memory pools, checkpoint cadence, log sizing, parallelism, or worker counts are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload profile, or version defaults, degrading internal subsystems even though underlying resources are not yet saturated.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby or downstream replicas cannot receive, write, or apply primary-generated redo fast enough, producing widening log-position gaps and sustained replication lag.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, temp, or log areas is exhausted, causing allocation failures, halted log recycling, and stalled foreground work.

When all three root causes coexist, the primary instance may emit excessive log volume because of sub-optimal parameter choices (e.g., tiny checkpoint intervals or oversized per-statement work memory), while replicas fall behind, forcing the primary to retain large amounts of unapplied WAL/redo. The retained logs, together with mis-sized data and temp areas, quickly consume the remaining disk space. Operators observe a compound symptom set: chronic replication lag, growing numbers of retained or relay log segments, persistent write-ahead-log or archive directories nearing 100 % capacity, checkpoint storms that spike I/O yet leave CPU and network partially idle, sudden client errors for "no space left on device," and degraded failover readiness. Diagnostic views show misaligned buffer or work-memory usage, replication apply workers blocked, and space alarms firing simultaneously, making individual blame hard to assign.
