Causally, aggressive or poorly chosen configuration parameters inflate redo generation and restrict log file size or checkpoint frequency, pressuring both replication throughput and disk usage. The resulting replication bottleneck prevents log truncation on the primary, accelerating space consumption. As free space diminishes, background checkpoints and archive writes slow further, feeding back into longer stall times and even larger log backlogs. Conversely, disk-full conditions on replicas throttle their apply rate, deepening lag and forcing the primary to retain yet more logs. The intertwined feedback loops between misconfiguration, replication drag, and space exhaustion amplify each issue, potentially culminating in a full-disk outage and loss of high-availability guarantees.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same objects, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, background activity, or concurrency are mis-tuned for the hardware or workload, so internal resources are throttled or over-committed in ways unrelated to true capacity limits.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Aggregate memory consumed by buffer caches, work areas, parallel workers, and other heaps grows beyond safe physical limits, provoking OS pressure, paging, or OOM terminations.

When these three root causes strike together, the system experiences extreme and often confusing stress signals: lock-wait and deadlock events surge while overall throughput collapses; wait statistics show both prolonged lock waits and memory-pressure induced CPU stalls; background check-pointers, vacuum/cleaner, or lock-monitor threads contend for CPU cycles already inflated by mis-sized work-memory and excessive parallelism; sudden paging amplifies the latency of lock acquisition, causing lock queues to snowball and triggering deadlock detectors more frequently. Application sessions pile up in connection pools, retries multiply redo generation, and after each inevitable OOM or forced restart, recovery replays the same bloated, lock-heavy workload, lengthening downtime windows.

Causally, poorly chosen configuration parameters (e.g., oversized per-session work memory, unchecked parallel workers, or minimal lock-manager hash buckets) allow individual transactions to reserve large private arenas while encouraging high concurrency. This accelerates total memory consumption until the host comes under OS memory pressure, where swapping and CPU thrashing lengthen critical sections inside transactions. The longer each transaction remains active, the longer it holds its locks, raising the probability of collisions and deadlocks. In turn, escalating lock contention causes sessions to accumulate in wait queues, increasing the number of simultaneously connected back-end processes and their memory footprints, which further exacerbates the memory shortfall. The feedback loop between mis-tuned parameters, runaway memory growth, and prolonged lock holding produces a self-reinforcing spiral that cripples OLTP responsiveness and stability.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) runaway accumulation of obsolete row versions that outpaces background cleanup, (2) a saturated write-ahead logging path that cannot flush or archive redo fast enough, and (3) exhaustion of critical operating-system limits such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, or I/O contexts. Together these three root causes form a reinforcing feedback loop that stalls write throughput, hampers maintenance workers, and degrades overall availability of an OLTP system.

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Rapid growth of table and index sizes, high dead-tuple ratios, and autovacuum/cleaner processes that appear permanently backlogged. • Escalating commit latency with prominent log-flush or log-sync wait events, frequent log-switch alerts, and expanding on-disk/archived log volumes. • Intermittent errors when opening additional WAL files, spawning vacuum or archiver workers, or allocating shared memory; kernel logs show "too many open files", "cannot allocate memory", or semaphore exhaustion. • Checkpoints and recovery operations lengthen, long-running transactions hold old snapshots that block log truncation and heap cleanup, and front-end sessions experience time-outs or hang during commits or scans. • Monitoring dashboards show both rising version-store and log-file consumption while system calls related to file I/O or memory mapping start failing under OS limits.

Causal Chain and Interaction: Heavy update/delete churn generates large volumes of WAL records, inflating both the version store and the transaction log. Bloated heaps slow scans and prolong transactions, which in turn keep old snapshots active; this prevents VACUUM/cleanup and log recycling, so log segments and obsolete versions accumulate even faster. As the log subsystem approaches capacity, it requires additional file handles, buffers, and background archiver threads; simultaneous MVCC cleanup workers also ask for these kernel resources. If OS-level limits on open files, shared memory, or processes are too low, the database cannot create or manage the extra WAL segments, vacuum workers, or archivers it needs. The resulting failures further delay log archiving and version cleanup, causing a vicious cycle: un-truncated logs retain old row versions, ballooning storage; excessive storage and I/O amplify log-flush times; rising latencies prolong transactions and hold even more snapshots open. Ultimately the intertwined pressures of version bloat, log saturation, and kernel resource exhaustion can bring write traffic and maintenance to a halt, risking data-loss windows and prolonged recovery times.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
Description:
Composite Anomaly Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) application-level statements and transaction patterns that process far more data or hold resources much longer than business logic requires (SQL Workload Logic Anomaly), (2) stale or incomplete optimizer statistics that drive systematic cardinality misestimates and poor plan choices (Optimizer Statistics Anomaly), and (3) heavy blocking and deadlock situations inside the lock manager as concurrent sessions compete for the enlarged lock footprint produced by the first two problems (Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly).

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Extreme and highly variable statement and transaction latencies, with the same SQLs dominating slow-query and deadlock logs. • Execution plans showing gross mismatches between estimated and actual row counts, frequent recompiles after data changes, and sudden plan regressions. • Long blocker–waiter chains, lock-wait time spikes, automatic lock escalation to page or table level, and periodic deadlock victim errors driving application retries. • Connection pools saturate, application threads time out, and overall throughput collapses even while CPU and I/O utilization appear moderate because many sessions are stalled on locks.

Interaction and Causal Chain: Inefficient SQL or over-wide transactions generated by the application touch far more rows than necessary, dramatically inflating the number and scope of locks acquired. Because optimizer statistics are stale or lack correlation information, the engine routinely misestimates cardinalities, often selecting scan-heavy or poorly ordered plans that further expand the data and lock footprint. These oversized, mis-planned operations run longer, block more resources, and trigger lock-escalation or deadlock scenarios. The resulting lock contention feeds back into application behavior—timeouts cause retries, which issue the same inefficient queries again—exacerbating concurrency pressure. Meanwhile, the inflated workloads delay automatic statistics refreshes, keeping the optimizer blind and locking the system into a vicious cycle of bad plans, long transactions, and escalating contention that degrades OLTP performance end-to-end.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine memory regions that pushes the database process beyond the safe physical-memory or swap envelope of the host. 
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages and index structures that breaks key ordering, page links, or checksums, making persisted structures unreliable. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Sustained read/write demand that exhausts the throughput, IOPS, or latency headroom of the underlying storage subsystem, causing long device queues and elevated I/O wait times.

Composite-anomaly phenomena: When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the system shows a multi-layer failure pattern. Memory pressure drives aggressive paging and frees dirty buffers that must be flushed through a storage layer that is already saturated, elongating checkpoint, redo, and temp-space I/O times. While these writes grind, on-disk corruptions surface or worsen, leading to checksum errors, torn pages, or broken indexes; subsequent retries intensify I/O load and force more memory churn as damaged pages are evicted and reread. The workload experiences sharp spikes in latency, erratic query results (missing or duplicated rows), sudden plan shifts to full scans, frequent lockups due to stalled buffer-pool latches, and possible instance crashes or node evictions triggered by out-of-memory or unrecoverable corruption events. Troubleshooting is complicated because symptoms oscillate between memory exhaustion, I/O saturation, and data-integrity faults, masking their intertwined origins.

Causal interaction: Excessive memory allocation increases dirty-page volume and checkpoint intensity; when the storage subsystem is already throughput-bound, these spikes prolong write-back duration, leaving pages unflushed and heightening vulnerability to power loss or crash scenarios that seed further data and index corruption. Emerging corruption, in turn, provokes repeated read retries, page repairs, or forced table/index rebuilds that generate additional random I/O, aggravating the existing storage bottleneck. Corruption-related cache invalidations and error handling flush large swaths of buffers, recycling memory and amplifying allocation churn, which can reignite memory pressure and OOM risks. The feedback loop among memory over-commitment, constrained I/O bandwidth, and structural corruption accelerates degradation, ultimately threatening availability and data safety across both transactional and analytical workloads.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions, rollback records, and logically-deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating on-disk structures and lengthening visibility checks.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively drive host CPU utilization to sustained saturation, creating run-queue backlogs and wide-spread latency inflation independent of any single query plan.

When these two root causes strike at the same time, the database exhibits a compounded failure mode: bloated tables and indexes force more CPU-intensive visibility checks and larger memory copies during scans, while already maxed-out CPUs slow the very autovacuum, purge, or garbage-collection workers that should reclaim space. Observable effects therefore include (1) dramatic growth of version stores and table files, (2) steadily rising CPU usage that remains pegged at or near 100 %, (3) escalating query latencies that worsen faster than either anomaly alone would suggest, (4) cleanup workers falling further behind despite higher scheduling priority, and (5) misleading planner estimates as statistics age, causing even more CPU-heavy plans and feedback loops of overload.

Causally, excessive version churn increases per-row visibility evaluation and page pruning efforts, directly inflating CPU demand; that heightened CPU demand pushes the host into saturation, lengthening every task’s runtime—including garbage-collection cycles—so obsolete versions persist even longer. In turn, the bloated heap and index pages amplify CPU consumption for both user statements and maintenance tasks, closing a vicious loop that accelerates performance degradation and risks transaction-ID or version-store exhaustion. The interplay therefore magnifies both space and compute pressure, making the composite anomaly more severe than the sum of its parts.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from runaway accumulation of obsolete MVCC versions, severe buffer-cache/latch contention, and impending exhaustion of allocated storage space. These three root causes coexist and interact, leading to compounded performance degradation, space shortages, and amplified concurrency stalls.

MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records outpace background cleanup, bloating data structures and lengthening visibility checks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot or rapidly churning pages cause sessions to compete for buffer pins and latches, inflating CPU spin time and wait events.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Data, log, or temp areas approach hard size limits, provoking allocation failures, log-switch stalls, and emergency space conservation behaviors by the engine.

Combined Phenomena: While version churn expands tables and indexes, the working-set footprint in the buffer pool swells, forcing more pages to be loaded, dirtied, and flushed. The oversized version store and growing data files accelerate buffer turnover, increasing buffer-busy and page-latch waits. As space fills, background checkpoints and auto-extension attempts intensify, causing longer write-back stalls that hold latches even longer and block foreground operations. Clients may observe escalating latency spikes, frequent "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors, sudden slowdown of both reads and writes, and erratic query plans due to inaccurate statistics on the bloated heap. Cleanup workers, throttled by latch waits and lack of free disk space for new segment allocation, fall further behind, causing a positive feedback loop of storage growth, contention, and stalled transactions.

Causal Interaction: Heavy update/delete workloads create large version chains that inflate on-disk structures, rapidly consuming storage and enlarging the hot set of pages. The swollen data footprint forces more frequent page replacements, increasing the probability that many sessions converge on the same root or index pages, which amplifies latch contention. Simultaneously, shrinking free space lengthens and serializes checkpoints and dirty-page evictions, because each flush now competes for scarce allocation units and log space. These prolonged I/O and latch holds slow down autovacuum/cleanup tasks, allowing even more dead versions to pile up, thereby accelerating space exhaustion. The three anomalies hence reinforce one another: MVCC bloat drives space consumption and hot-page pressure; latch contention throttles cleanup and I/O; and near-full disks further delay writes and cleanup, culminating in widespread throughput collapse and potential service outages.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-layer statement or transaction design forces the engine to scan, join, or retain more data than the business requirement really needs.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space for data, logs, or temporary areas is exhausted or approaching hard limits.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database-related processes saturate host CPU, leaving too few cycles for the rest of the workload.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, the database experiences a compound failure mode in which user-written queries chew through excessive rows, fan out large intermediate result sets, and keep transactions open longer. Those bloated operations quickly consume CPU time, while the inflated intermediate and persistent objects (work tables, spill files, growing tables, and never-committed LOBs) burn through remaining disk and log space. Observable symptoms therefore overlap and amplify: statement latency grows non-linearly, slow-query logs and OS run-queue metrics spike together, "out of space" or "cannot extend" errors interleave with CPU-bound wait events, checkpoints or log archival stall because the log destination is full, and emergency space-reclaim tasks fail to run because the server is already CPU-saturated.

Causally, inefficient workload logic is the primary generator of both CPU demand and ballooning data footprints. The ensuing CPU saturation slows DML, causing redo and undo segments to remain active longer and accumulate more bytes, which in turn drives faster space consumption in datafiles and logs. Once space becomes scarce, allocation failures trigger retries and error handling paths in the application, spawning even more short-lived sessions and compiler activity that fight for already limited CPU. The feedback loop—poor query logic → high CPU → slow I/O recycling → accelerated space exhaustion → error-driven resubmissions → even higher CPU—can push the system into runaway degradation or outright outages unless all three contributing layers are addressed together.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Run-away or poorly governed growth of buffer caches, work areas, and other engine heaps that pushes the database process beyond the amount of physical memory the host can safely provide.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Depletion of free bytes in data, log, archive, temp, or backup destinations until new allocations, extensions, or log switches fail.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced quotas such as file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or address space, preventing the database from obtaining new kernel objects.

When all three conditions surface together the system is bombarded by overlapping symptoms: resident-set size and swap usage climb while dirty pages cannot be flushed because datafiles, tempfiles, or log destinations are full; simultaneously the engine emits ENOSPC, EMFILE, ENOMEM, or "cannot allocate shared memory/thread" errors. Checkpoints, log writers, and background workers may hang waiting for space or kernel objects, causing user sessions to stall, new connections to be refused, and cluster watchdogs to evict the node. Operating-system logs show paging storms, out-of-memory kills, and resource-limit denials, while database views report both shrinking free space and plummeting cache hit ratios driven by allocation churn.

Causally, unchecked data growth or failed housekeeping fills disk, preventing log rotation and forcing the buffer cache to retain dirty pages longer, inflating memory consumption. The bloated memory footprint heightens kernel pressure; once physical RAM is exhausted the engine requests additional shared memory, threads, or temp files, quickly colliding with conservative ulimit or cgroup quotas. At the same time, space exhaustion blocks creation of on-disk temp segments, pushing more work areas to reside in RAM and further amplifying memory pressure. Each anomaly therefore reinforces the others—disk fullness prolongs memory residency, memory bloat increases the number of file handles and shared-memory requests, and tight OS limits convert what would be recoverable pressure into hard allocation failures—culminating in a compound failure state that is more severe and harder to remediate than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution statistics are stale, missing, or inaccurate, driving systematic cardinality misestimates and sub-optimal execution-plan choices.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions acquire incompatible locks on the same resources, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall or abort transactions.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Physical read/write demand exceeds the bandwidth or IOPS that the underlying storage can deliver, inflating I/O latency and queue depth.

When all three root causes arise together, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: bad statistics make the optimizer favor full scans, hash joins, or broad index ranges that inflate the physical I/O footprint. The resulting surge of page reads and log writes pushes the storage subsystem beyond its throughput limits, lengthening every I/O. Statements and transactions therefore hold row, page, and metadata locks far longer than usual, causing long blocker-waiter chains, frequent deadlocks, and application timeouts. Meanwhile, auto-update statistics jobs and user-initiated ANALYZE commands are themselves delayed by lock waits and slow I/O, so the statistics remain stale, plans stay poor, and the cycle perpetuates. Symptom telemetry shows extreme divergence between estimated and actual rows, soaring PAGEIOLATCH/WRITELOG or comparable wait classes, lock and deadlock graphs growing in width and depth, and CPU trending moderate because execution is throttled by I/O and lock waits rather than computation.

Causally, inaccurate statistics start the chain by producing plans that overrun the storage system; saturated I/O then stretches lock hold times, directly amplifying contention in a transactional workload. In turn, heavy blocking prevents timely statistics collection and keeps I/O-intensive maintenance or checkpoint activities queued, which sustains the storage bottleneck. Each anomaly thus reinforces the others, driving a feedback loop that degrades throughput and undermines both concurrency control and optimizer accuracy.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch far more rows, columns, or pages than business logic requires.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical or virtual storage layer is saturated, so read/write latency, IOPS, or bandwidth no longer meet engine demand.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume nearly all available CPU cycles, driving run-queue pressure and broad latency inflation.

When these three root causes coexist, the database experiences a compound failure mode in which overly chatty or bloated SQL drives a flood of physical reads, large writes, and long-running transactions. The excessive I/O demand collides with a storage subsystem already at or beyond its throughput limits, generating steep I/O wait times, deep device queues, and stalled checkpoints or redo flushes. Simultaneously, CPU cores become saturated by the sheer volume of data processing, predicate evaluation, and context switching spawned by the inefficient workload and by threads waiting and retrying after I/O stalls. The mixed wait profile alternates between high CPU usage and prolonged I/O waits, producing erratic yet persistently high statement latencies, lock hold times, application timeouts, and unpredictable throughput that can cascade into connection pool exhaustion and node failovers.

Causally, sub-optimal SQL logic is the ignition point: wide scans, Cartesian joins, and long transactions amplify both I/O and CPU demand. This surplus demand overwhelms the storage layer first; as I/O slows, worker threads stay active longer, consuming additional CPU for predicate re-evaluation, buffer management, and lock maintenance. The resulting CPU saturation prevents the engine from efficiently issuing asynchronous I/O or processing completed I/O interrupts, which in turn further depresses effective I/O throughput. The feedback loop between bad SQL, clogged storage, and starved CPU resources escalates resource contention across all tiers, making each individual anomaly more severe and masking the original source of the problem.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, data types, constraints) and actual access patterns forces inefficient scans and look-ups.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and rollback records outpace background cleanup, causing table and index bloat and longer visibility checks under concurrent OLTP traffic.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Aggregate memory consumed by buffers, work areas, plan cache, and background workers exceeds available physical RAM, triggering paging, OOM events, and cache churn.

When these three root causes manifest together, the database exhibits compounded symptoms: tables and indexes grow rapidly from both design-induced full scans and MVCC bloat, swelling the buffer cache and temporary work areas until the host faces sustained memory pressure, swap thrashing, and sporadic process terminations. Queries that already suffer from missing or non-covering indexes now read ever-larger bloated relations, producing longer execution times, misestimated plans, and runaway hash/sort buffers. Background vacuum or purge processes stay perpetually active yet ineffective, while their own memory use competes with foreground sessions, further depressing cache hit ratios and inflating I/O. Administrators may observe steeply rising disk usage, frequent checkpoint or eviction storms, and a feedback loop of degraded throughput, erratic latency spikes, and heightened crash risk.

Causally, poor schema and index design forces excessive sequential scans and wide updates/deletes that generate large numbers of new row versions. The surge in version creation stresses MVCC cleanup; as autovacuum or purge workers fall behind, heaps and indexes expand, multiplying the data each scan must touch. The swelling on-disk structures inflate buffer-pool demand and per-query memory needs; combined with uncontrolled work-area allocations, this pushes the engine beyond physical memory limits, invoking the operating system’s paging or OOM killer. Memory pressure slows both user queries and cleanup workers, allowing even more version accumulation and bloat. Thus, each anomaly accelerates the others, creating a vicious cycle that severely impairs OLTP performance and stability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Runtime settings governing memory, checkpoints, parallelism, etc. are mis-tuned relative to hardware, workload, or version defaults.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive or apply WAL/redo at the rate the primary produces it, leading to widening log-position gaps and replay lag.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages and index structures are physically or logically corrupted, causing checksums, ordering, or mappings to diverge from expected states.

When these three root causes manifest together, the system exhibits an intertwined symptom set: replication lag grows erratically while the primary shows unusual wait patterns (e.g., log-write stalls without storage saturation), standby apply threads hit corruption errors that pause or crash replay, primary log segments are retained far beyond normal because corruption prevents truncation and replication prevents recycling, checkpoint storms triggered by mis-configured parameters stress I/O, and replicas remain perpetually behind, delivering stale or inconsistent reads and jeopardizing failover readiness. Administrators may observe cascading alert storms—parameter-related wait events, replication lag metrics, and integrity-check failures—without an obvious single point of failure, and traditional tuning or repair actions taken in isolation fail to restore stability.

Causally, mis-tuned engine parameters can inflate checkpoint frequency or shrink log buffers, increasing the volume and burstiness of WAL traffic that replicas must ingest. This amplified throughput collides with latent data-page or index corruption on standbys—or surfaces hidden corruption on the primary—which forces replication apply processes to halt or retry, further widening lag. Simultaneously, corruption that blocks log recycling holds additional segments on the primary, exacerbating space pressure and triggering even more aggressive checkpointing dictated by the misguided configuration. The feedback loop between excessive WAL generation, replication backlog, and corruption-induced replay failures drives the system into a degraded state that neither single-dimension tuning nor isolated page repair can resolve.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks inside the lock-manager layer.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions stall while fighting over hot buffer-cache pages, latches, or page pins, so every logical page access may spin or sleep before proceeding.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical devices or storage virtualization tier are saturated, stretching read- and write-service times far beyond the engine’s expectations.

When these three root causes strike together, the database exhibits extreme and baffling slowdowns: lock-wait and deadlock diagnostics explode while buffer-latch and I/O wait events spike; CPU may oscillate between idling (tasks sleeping on I/O) and frantic spinning (latch retries); transaction throughput collapses, statement latencies become highly variable, and connection pools back up. Autovacuum, checkpoints, or log flushes linger in the I/O queue, holding buffer-cache pages dirty and pinned, which in turn prolongs lock hold times. Application layers experience timeouts and cascading retries, masking whether the dominant bottleneck is logical locking, latch hot spots, or raw device saturation.

Causally, saturated storage stretches page read and flush times, so backend processes keep buffer pages and their latches for longer, inflating latch-queue lengths. Extended latch ownership delays row-level operations, meaning locks on those rows or pages are held longer, propagating larger blocker-waiter trees and increasing the likelihood of deadlocks. Simultaneously, growing lock queues raise the number of active sessions that are all poised to proceed, so when a latch or page finally frees, a burst of threads hits the same hot page, further intensifying latch contention. The feedback loop between prolonged I/O, held latches, and extended lock durations amplifies each symptom, creating a compound performance cliff that is far steeper than any individual anomaly would cause on its own.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly chooses sub-optimal execution plans despite having reasonably accurate statistics, leading to erratic or inefficient statement performance.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, logging, parallelism, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload needs, causing systemic inefficiencies that are not rooted in actual resource exhaustion.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL / redo data as quickly as the primary produces it, resulting in widening replay lag and retention of log segments.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits compound symptoms: 1) the same query may oscillate between fast and slow executions or fall back to full scans, 2) CPU, memory, or I/O usage appears either under-utilized or intermittently saturated without a clear pattern, 3) checkpoint storms or oversized log bursts coincide with sudden optimizer plan flips, and 4) replica lag spikes unpredictably, with large log backlogs held open by long-running or poorly planned queries whose resource footprints are inflated by mis-configured memory and parallelism settings. Administrators may observe plan-cache churn, bloated work-memory allocations, growing un-recycled WAL segments, and replicas stuck replaying expensive plans that amplify apply latency.

Causally, misaligned configuration parameters (e.g., overly large work_mem, insufficient shared buffers, aggressive checkpoint intervals, or excessively high max_parallelism) skew the optimizer’s cost model, leading it to prefer plans that assume more memory, CPU, or I/O bandwidth than the system can actually deliver. These bloated plans run longer and generate disproportionate redo, inflating the primary’s transaction log volume. The surge of log output must traverse the replication channel, but downstream nodes already constrained by sub-optimal apply plans and limited resources fall behind, deepening replication lag. The growing backlog prevents log truncation on the primary, which in turn increases disk usage and can trigger further emergency checkpoints, compounding pressure on the mis-tuned buffer and I/O subsystems. Thus, the initial mis-configuration amplifies poor plan choices, both of which magnify redo generation and hinder replication, creating a feedback loop that degrades performance and availability across the entire deployment.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from lagging or stalled replication streams, underlying physical corruption of data or index pages, and exhaustion of kernel-enforced resources (file descriptors, shared-memory segments, thread slots, etc.). The coincidence of these three root causes yields a compound failure state in which recovery, failover, and normal workload processing are all jeopardized.

Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo as fast as the primary produces it.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are physically or logically corrupted, making storage contents unreliable.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: The DBMS process hits kernel limits on critical resources such as open files, shared memory, semaphores, or threads, impeding normal engine operation.

Combined observable phenomena: 
• Rapidly expanding WAL retention or relay logs on the primary due to replicas falling behind while also being unable to purge corrupted or locked segments.
• Sudden replication apply errors triggered by corrupted pages reaching replicas, causing frequent replay crashes, cascading replica restarts, and further widening of replication lag metrics.
• Engine and kernel logs interleaving page-checksum failures with "too many open files", "cannot create thread", or "out of shared memory" messages as background workers and recovery processes fail to allocate kernel objects needed for corruption handling or log shipping.
• Stale or inconsistent read results from replicas, intermittent query failures, and unexpected full-table scans on the primary as indexes are marked unusable while repair utilities cannot run due to OS resource exhaustion.
• Escalating storage consumption and degraded throughput on the primary because unrecycled WAL and blocked autovacuum or checkpoint workers contend for the same limited file handles and shared memory.

Causal interaction: Physical corruption in data or index pages often surfaces first on replicas during redo, triggering replication halts that inflate apply lag. The stalled replication, in turn, forces the primary to retain ever-growing log segments, greatly increasing the number of files and shared memory descriptors the engine must keep open. This surge collides with tight operating-system limits, causing worker-spawn failures and further reducing the engine’s capacity to ship, apply, or repair WAL. Meanwhile, OS resource exhaustion can prevent integrity-check utilities, index rebuilds, or page-repair mechanisms from allocating the resources they need, allowing corruption to persist and repeatedly poison the replication stream. The feedback loop between corruption-induced apply failures, replication backlog, and kernel resource starvation amplifies both availability risk and data-consistency exposure, leading to a severe, multi-faceted outage scenario.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements and transaction boundaries are written in a way that touches far more rows, columns, or time than the business logic really requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, partition, and index layout is mis-aligned with the workload’s access patterns, forcing even well-written queries into inefficient scans and lookups.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The database engine allocates or leaks more memory than the host can safely supply, creating sustained OS pressure, paging, or OOM terminations.

When these three root causes strike together, the database experiences a multi-layer performance collapse. Poorly scoped SQL drives large scans; the absence of adequate indexes prevents selective access; and the excessive data volume inflates sort, hash, buffer-cache, and work-area allocations until the memory subsystem is saturated. Observable symptoms include: extremely long and highly variable statement latency, waves of slow-query log entries paired with full-table or non-covering index scans, temporary-segment or spill activity escalating to disk, rapid growth and churn of buffer-pool pages, shrinking cache hit ratios, spike-and-stall CPU patterns caused by memory contention, lock and latch waits that snowball as transactions stay open longer, and eventually paging storms or OOM crashes that take down nodes or entire clusters. Because each layer masks or amplifies the others, plan-level diagnostics alone may not reveal the full problem, and fixes applied at a single layer often show only transient relief.

Causally, inefficient SQL logic initiates oversized data access. The deficient schema and index design removes any opportunity for the optimizer to prune this workload, so the engine must physically process the bloated result set. The resulting scans, joins, and sorts demand large work areas and flood the buffer cache. As memory consumption climbs, the allocator competes for scarce RAM, triggering eviction of useful pages, spilling of intermediate results to temporary space, and OS-level paging. Elevated latency keeps transactions open longer, further enlarging memory footprints for session state and undo/redo, which feeds back into even higher memory pressure—a positive feedback loop that magnifies both performance degradation and stability risks.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale or incomplete, leading the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and pick inefficient plans.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Critical engine parameters for memory, parallelism, logging, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware, workload mix, or version defaults, so the engine’s internal resource governance does not match real demand.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other OS objects are reached, blocking the database from allocating the resources it requests.

When these three root causes coexist, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: queries suddenly switch to plans that demand far more memory, I/O, or worker processes than the engine or kernel can grant; execution plans show huge gaps between estimated and actual rows, while concurrent sessions stall on memory-allocation, file-open, or worker-spawn errors. Wait events oscillate between CPU-bound parallel workers and OS-reported resource-exhaustion waits; checkpoint storms or log-write stalls appear even though storage and CPU remain under-utilised. Administrators may observe flurries of statement re-plans, background process restarts, and kernel messages about ENOMEM, EMFILE, or EAGAIN, all interleaved with optimizer-related recompiles and configuration warnings, making single-cause diagnosis difficult.

Causally, stale statistics drive the optimizer to over- or under-estimate work, which, under mis-set memory/parallelism parameters, inflates per-query resource requests (e.g., oversized hash tables, excessive parallel workers). These exaggerated requests push the database to the brink of configured limits; when the engine then asks the OS for large shared-memory extents, additional threads, or many file descriptors, it collides with tight kernel quotas. Each rejection by the OS triggers retries, plan invalidations, or emergency fallbacks that further skew workload timing and data distributions, which in turn exacerbate statistics staleness and prompt more aggressive (but still misguided) plan and parameter usage. The feedback loop among bad statistics, poor configuration, and OS denials amplifies contention, degrades throughput, and can precipitate partial or total service outages.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Redo generation, buffering, flushing, or archiving becomes the bottleneck on the write path.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Critical free-space exhaustion anywhere in the database storage hierarchy, causing allocation failures rather than pure latency problems.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced limits on file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or similar objects are reached, preventing the database from acquiring additional OS resources.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences a multi-layer blockage on every path needed to persist and manage redo. Commits begin to queue behind long log-flush waits; alert logs show rapid log-file switches that cannot complete; archiver and backup processes report "device full" or "cannot open file" errors; free space in both active log and archive destinations plummets; and parallel workers or new client sessions intermittently fail because the engine cannot obtain additional file descriptors, shm segments, or threads. The overlapping symptoms make it appear as a generic "database hang," but metrics reveal concurrent spikes in commit latency, space-usage alarms, and kernel denials.

Causal chain: Heavy transactional load pushes the log subsystem to create and switch log segments at a high rate. This accelerates space consumption; once archive or log destinations near capacity, switches stall, trapping active transactions in "log file switch (checkpoint incomplete)" waits. Meanwhile, the same churn inflates the number of open log files, archive handles, and background workers, quickly exhausting per-process or cgroup file-handle and thread limits. Hitting OS limits causes archiver and checkpoint processes to fail at opening new files, which in turn prevents log recycling and releases no space, pushing the storage tier to full even faster. Conversely, storage exhaustion forces the engine to keep more log files open and retry writes, further leaking kernel objects and accelerating the breach of OS quotas. The feedback loop between log bottlenecks, space exhaustion, and OS resource starvation amplifies latency, precipitates commit freezes, and can culminate in a full outage that persists until all three constraints—log throughput, free space, and OS limits—are relieved together.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: The workload issues overly broad, chatty, or long-running statements/transactions that fetch, scan, or lock more data than business logic requires.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: The database engine grows buffer pools, work areas, and other heaps beyond the safe capacity of the host, inducing paging, swapping, or OOM conditions.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Physical data, temp, or log volumes reach or exceed their sustained IOPS/throughput limits, driving up device-level latency and queue depths.

When all three root causes coexist, end-to-end latency escalates sharply: chatty or scan-heavy SQL floods the buffer cache and temp space, inflating per-query work memory and provoking aggressive cache growth. Memory pressure triggers paging, which redirects random and spill-to-disk access to already saturated storage; in turn, the overtaxed I/O subsystem elongates read, write, and checkpoint times, further stretching transaction duration and increasing the number of concurrent sessions and memory consumers. Observables include skyrocketing resident-set size, frequent page-in/page-out activity, plan-cache and work-memory bloat, sustained disk queues, elevated buffer-I/O and log flush waits, and application timeouts with retries that multiply the load.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies both memory and I/O demand by expanding result sets, causing large sorts/hashes, and keeping transactions open longer. The expansion forces the engine to allocate more buffers and work areas, pushing the host toward memory exhaustion. As the OS begins to swap, every logical read can devolve into a physical I/O, compounding the storage bottleneck. Simultaneously, the storage subsystem’s throttling feeds back into the database, slowing buffer flushes and extending transaction lifetimes, which keeps memory allocations active and magnifies plan-cache and session-state footprints. The reinforcing loop among bloated workload logic, unchecked memory growth, and saturated storage throughput degrades both throughput and stability, ultimately risking node eviction or service outage.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model and index structures do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans, non-covering look-ups, and excess data modification work.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Hot buffer pages and their protecting latches become shared bottlenecks, causing sessions to spin or wait while accessing or modifying cached pages.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage layer cannot sustain the read/write volume demanded, so I/O queues saturate and latency rises beyond acceptable thresholds.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits a compounded symptom set: massive full-table or non-covering index scans push large data volumes through an already undersized or hot buffer pool, flooding it with page replacements; concurrent sessions pile up on buffer-busy and page-latch waits as they compete for a handful of root and hotspot pages; meanwhile every read or dirty-page flush must traverse an over-taxed storage subsystem, so I/O latencies balloon, checkpoint and background flush cycles elongate, and CPU alternates between spinning on latches and idling on I/O waits. Response-time variance explodes, batch windows slip, and lock or log-flush queues grow even though the server still shows unused CPU or memory capacity.

Causally, poor schema and index design drives unnecessary page accesses and writes, magnifying the demand placed on the buffer cache. The inflated churn heats specific pages (root index blocks, allocation maps, monotonic insert pages), extending latch hold times. Longer holds amplify latch contention, which in turn delays page release and aggravates buffer pressure. Simultaneously, the surge in physical I/O overwhelms disk throughput, further prolonging page fetch and flush operations; this stretches latch occupancy and deepens contention. The feedback loop between design-induced I/O amplification, buffer-level serialization, and storage saturation triggers a self-reinforcing degradation that is markedly worse—and diagnostically more opaque—than any of the individual anomalies in isolation.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions hold or request mutually incompatible locks, forming long blocker–waiter chains or deadlocks that stop progress until a lock is released or a victim is rolled back.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead log buffer, disk, switch, or archive pipeline cannot keep pace with redo generation, so commit, flush, or log-switch operations stall foreground writers.

When both conditions arise together, the database exhibits sharp and erratic slow-downs: transactions wait first to obtain locks and, once granted, may still hang on COMMIT while the log flush queue grows. Deadlock detectors fire alongside log-write timeouts; application retries exacerbate the surge in active sessions, swelling lock tables, connection pools, and redo volume. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in lock-wait and log-related wait events, with throughput collapsing, response-time histograms bifurcating into fast and extremely slow tails, and sudden waves of rollback traffic after deadlock or timeout victims are chosen.

Causally, the two root causes reinforce each other. Prolonged lock holds caused by slow commits (due to log flushing delays) lengthen blocking chains and increase the probability of deadlocks. Conversely, when lock contention forces transactions to queue or abort and retry, overall redo generation rises (additional row-version undo, repeated DML, compensating transactions), which further saturates the already constrained log subsystem. The feedback loop—the log becoming slower, extending lock duration, which in turn inflates redo volume—can drive the system into a self-perpetuating spiral of latency, throughput collapse, and escalating recovery workload.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, index, partition, and datatype layout does not match workload access paths, forcing scans, large lock footprints, and inefficient I/O regardless of statistics or optimizer choices.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger roll-backs.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys or downstream replicas cannot receive or apply WAL/redo at the rate produced by the primary, creating growing log-position lag and delaying fail-over readiness.

When all three root causes coexist, the workload suffers a compound pathology: poor schema and index choices expand the number of rows touched per statement, inflating the lock scope and duration of every read or write. This bloated locking footprint magnifies blocker–waiter chains and deadlock frequency, stretching transaction execution times and leaving locks held longer. The prolonged transactions, in turn, enlarge commit records and postpone commit timestamps, so the primary emits heavier, burstier redo streams. Replicas, already stressed by having to replay inefficient plans on sub-optimal data structures, fall further behind, and their apply processes may themselves encounter the same lock conflicts, amplifying replication lag. Observable symptoms therefore include simultaneous full-table scans with high logical and physical I/O, long lock-wait and deadlock statistics on the primary, application time-outs, rapidly growing replication write/replay delay, swelling retained transaction logs on the primary, and replicas serving increasingly stale data.

Causally, the static design flaws set the stage by making every transaction touch more data and hold more locks. This raises the probability and depth of lock contention; stalled or rolled-back transactions then produce larger, less frequent commit batches and force retries that inflate traffic. The resulting spike in log generation must traverse the replication channel, but the replicas, hampered by the same sub-optimal schema and by replay-time locking conflicts, cannot keep pace. Thus each anomaly reinforces the others: bad design drives contention; contention bloats and bursts the log stream; replication lag feeds back by delaying conflict resolution and vacuum/recovery processes, which further extends lock lifetimes on the primary. The intertwined effects degrade OLTP responsiveness and erode high-availability guarantees far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction patterns that force the database to process more data, rows, or time than the business demand actually requires.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Exhaustion or near-exhaustion of physical or logical free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas, leading to allocation failures and stalled database operations.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Insufficient network bandwidth, socket resources, or listener/connection slots causing connection establishment failures or slow data transfer between clients and the database.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences a multi-layered failure mode. Inefficient SQL holds locks and produces oversized result sets that must be written to temp and log areas already running out of space, while the same bloated result sets traverse an over-subscribed network and backlog limited connection slots. Observable effects include: runaway query runtimes, escalating temp-space and log-space consumption culminating in ‘out of space’ or ‘cannot allocate extent’ errors, sudden connection drops or authentication stalls, clients timing out during both execution and fetch phases, and an explosion of slow-query, space-allocation, and network-socket warning messages in logs. Because each layer (SQL, storage, network) reports symptoms that can mask or mimic the others, diagnostic signals become noisy and intermittent, complicating root-cause isolation.

Causally, sub-optimal workload logic is the spark: wide scans, large result sets, and long-lived transactions generate excessive data movement and temporary spill. This accelerates space consumption in tablespaces, logs, and temp segments, pushing the system toward capacity limits. As storage nears saturation, auto-extension failures and log reuse stalls elongate commit paths, further prolonging transaction lifetimes and inflating the volume of data queued for network transmission. Concurrently, the oversized result sets and prolonged sessions monopolize network sockets and bandwidth, increasing latency and connection churn; retry storms amplify both network load and transactional pressure, causing additional temp objects and logs to accumulate. The positive feedback loop between chatty or bloated SQL, shrinking free space, and degrading connectivity can cascade into systemic slowdown or outage unless all three layers are addressed in concert.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
This composite anomaly represents the concurrent existence of three independent but mutually reinforcing root causes: application-layer SQL design flaws, stale or incomplete optimizer statistics, and saturation or instability in the client-to-server network/connection tier.

Combined observable phenomena:
• Statements written with non-sargable predicates, Cartesian joins, or oversized result sets already exhibit long runtimes; inaccurate statistics further mislead the optimizer into choosing sub-optimal access paths (e.g., full table scans, wrong join order), magnifying execution time and resource usage.
• Misestimated cardinalities inflate memory and spool requirements, causing back-pressure that lengthens transaction duration; these longer-running queries hold server processes open, increasing their exposure to network latency, retransmissions, and socket-queue limits.
• Clients experience a mix of symptoms—slow statement completion, sporadic timeouts during execution, and failed or delayed connection attempts. Slow data retrieval caused by poor plans produces larger, prolonged result transfers that collide with limited network throughput, raising client-read wait events and swelling slow-query and connection-error logs simultaneously.
• Operational metrics show divergent indicators: high logical/physical I/O and CPU from misplanned scans, extreme estimated/actual row-count gaps, growing counts of half-open sockets, listener backlog saturation, and application-level retries that further increase workload pressure.

Causal interaction and amplification chain:
1. Faulty SQL patterns drive inherently heavy scans or large result sets.
2. Because optimizer statistics are stale or insufficient, the cost model underestimates the work, selecting plans that exacerbate data access volume and execution time.
3. Extended runtimes keep database backends and network sockets busy longer, inflating concurrent connection counts.
4. Network congestion or connection-handling bottlenecks slow data delivery and session establishment; this, in turn, stretches transaction lifetimes, aggravating lock holds and delaying statistics refresh windows.
5. The protracted, oversized workload hinders automatic statistics maintenance (due to ongoing long-running transactions) and triggers client retry storms, feeding an escalating loop that degrades both query performance and connectivity reliability.

The three anomalies thus reinforce one another: poor SQL logic inflates workload, bad statistics select worse plans for that workload, and network constraints prevent timely completion, together driving severe end-to-end latency, resource exhaustion, and operational instability.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Critical runtime settings (memory, checkpoint, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload, resulting in systemic inefficiencies that are not rooted in true resource exhaustion.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes fail to receive, write, or apply WAL/redo fast enough, producing widening log-position gaps, retained segments, and stale replicas.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume or contend for nearly all available CPU cycles, driving run-queue pressure and global latency spikes.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, the system enters a feedback loop in which mis-configured parameters inflate CPU demand (e.g., overly aggressive parallel workers, undersized buffers forcing extra processing), the saturated CPUs starve both foreground queries and replication apply threads, and the throttled replicas in turn prevent WAL recycling, provoking more frequent checkpoints and log flush storms dictated by poorly chosen checkpoint and log-size settings. Operators observe conflicting signals: near-100 % CPU utilization alongside idle I/O devices, rapidly growing primary log storage, replication lag that oscillates or monotonically increases, sudden latency spikes at checkpoint boundaries, and runaway background-worker queues.

Causally, bad configuration is the initiating factor—small checkpoint_segments or low shared_buffers force the engine to flush and generate WAL at a rate disproportionate to actual transactional throughput. The inflated redo stream drives higher CPU usage on the primary and demands faster apply on replicas. Because parallelism, work_mem, or autovacuum settings were also mis-tuned, CPU use on both primary and replicas climbs, lengthening replication apply times. The accumulating lag keeps log segments pinned, which the primary tries to purge via even more checkpoint activity, further stressing CPU loops. Thus, configuration errors ignite a chain reaction that both causes and magnifies CPU saturation, while the impaired CPU capacity directly degrades replication throughput, resulting in a self-reinforcing composite failure mode that is difficult to attribute to a single layer.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data model and indexing choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing otherwise well-written queries into inherently inefficient access paths.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : The optimizer relies on stale, missing, or biased statistics, causing systematic cardinality errors that mislead plan generation.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage layer cannot sustain the read/write demands placed on it, leading to persistent I/O saturation and elevated latency.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compounded symptom set: queries that already use sub-optimal access paths (full scans, non-covering index probes, excessive lookups) are paired with plans produced from wildly inaccurate row-count estimates, often selecting even more I/O-intensive strategies such as hash joins, broad parallel scans, or redundant bitmap probes. The resulting flood of random and large-volume I/O pushes the storage subsystem beyond its throughput and IOPS limits, driving queue depths high, inflating wait events (buffer reads, write-log flushes, temp-spill I/O), and creating long tail latencies perceived by both OLTP and analytical sessions. Performance becomes highly unstable: small data changes or plan recompiles can swing execution times from seconds to minutes, batch windows overrun, while foreground transactions experience intermittent stalls despite moderate CPU utilization.

Causally, a poor physical design forms the groundwork for heavy data movement; stale or missing statistics then misinform the optimizer, selecting plans that magnify the design inefficiencies; the amplified physical I/O finally collides with a saturated storage layer, turning what would have been tolerable inefficiency into a critical bottleneck. The feedback loop intensifies: slow I/O lengthens maintenance windows, delaying statistics refreshes; delayed refreshes perpetuate bad plans; prolonged write activity aggravates storage saturation. Together, these factors reinforce each other, degrading overall throughput, increasing lock durations, and eroding service-level objectives far more severely than any single anomaly alone.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages, page pins, or latches, stalling foreground work and consuming CPU in spin or sleep loops.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing and write-ahead logging are throttled by slow or saturated log buffers, files, or archiver/replication pipelines, inflating log-related wait events and commit latency.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or AIO contexts are reached, preventing the database from allocating required OS objects.

When these three root causes strike together the database exhibits a tangled symptom set: 
• Sharp spikes in buffer-busy, page-latch, log-flush, and log-sync waits, with foreground sessions oscillating between CPU spin on latches and sleeps on log writes.
• Commit latency and overall transaction response times become highly erratic; small transactions pile up behind log flushes while also contending for hot index or sequence pages.
• System and engine alert logs show failures to open files, allocate shared memory, or start background workers (e.g., archivers, checkpoint or buffer-flush helpers), and may report "too many open files" or semaphore exhaustion.
• Throughput collapses as latch spin amplifies CPU usage, while log files fill faster than they can be archived, leading to log-switch storms and potential "out of space" or "cannot allocate log buffer" errors.
• Performance tools reveal overlapping plateaus of CPU saturation, I/O queue buildup on the log device, and kernel resource allocation errors, making it difficult to attribute the slowdown to any single layer.

Causal chain and interaction: Intense OLTP activity concentrates reads and writes on a few hot pages, extending latch hold times and inflating redo generation. The surge in commit requests drives the transaction-log subsystem to its throughput limits; prolonged log flushes keep transactions open longer, which in turn keeps latches and buffer pins held, deepening buffer-cache contention. As sessions and background processes retry I/O and spawn additional helper threads, they consume extra file handles, AIO contexts, and semaphores. If OS resource limits are already tight, these retries quickly exhaust kernel quotas, causing further failures to allocate log files, buffer I/O slots, or worker threads. The three anomalies therefore reinforce one another in a positive feedback loop—buffer contention prolongs transactions, inflated commit volume stresses the log, log stall increases latch hold duration, and both layers drive up kernel object usage until OS limits impose a hard stop—culminating in severe, workload-wide stalls or outages.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, causing long blocker-waiter chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical volumes that host data, temp, or log files are saturated for bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, forcing the engine to stall on reads, writes, and durability flushes.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process reaches kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, async-I/O contexts, threads, or shared-memory objects, preventing timely creation or completion of new I/O and background tasks.

When all three conditions arise together, transactions simultaneously wait on locks, on slow or stalled physical I/O, and on the operating system’s refusal to grant additional kernel resources. Observable symptoms merge and intensify: lock-wait and deadlock reports spike while overall I/O wait time soars; buffer cache miss penalties grow because reads linger in the OS and storage queues; log flushes back up, lengthening commit latency; background workers, parallel query threads, or asynchronous I/O slots fail to start, producing OS-level "too many open files" or "cannot allocate resources" errors. Application sessions accumulate in connection pools, some timing out due to lock waits, others during disk stalls, and new connections may be rejected outright as process or handle limits are hit. Monitoring dashboards show high lock-wait percent, elevated I/O latency and queue depths, moderate CPU utilization, and surges in kernel error counters.

Causally, storage saturation elongates every physical read and write, forcing transactions to hold row and metadata locks far longer; the resulting backlog increases the number of concurrent sessions and lock requests, amplifying contention and raising the likelihood of deadlocks. Prolonged waits and growing session counts exhaust kernel objects such as file handles, AIO contexts, and threads, triggering OS resource denials that further constrain the engine’s ability to dispatch I/O or spawn lock-manager workers. Each root cause thus feeds the others—slow I/O inflates lock duration, lock pile-ups increase session and handle usage, and OS limits throttle the very mechanisms (I/O threads, background flushers, deadlock detectors) needed to relieve pressure—culminating in a feedback loop that degrades OLTP performance and may escalate into partial or complete service outages.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks, causing blocking chains or deadlocks in the lock-manager layer.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Commit processing is throttled by slow redo generation, flushing, or archiving in the write-ahead log subsystem.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate host CPU capacity, leaving too few cycles for other work.

When all three root causes occur together the database experiences a compounded slowdown: commits are delayed by log-flush waits, so transactions hold locks longer, creating larger blocker–waiter trees and more frequent deadlocks. The enlarged lock queues in turn inflate session counts, context switches, and deadlock detection scans, which further consume CPU. Overall, users observe escalating commit latency, growing lock-wait and log-sync wait events, spikes in CPU run-queue length, widespread statement slow-downs, connection-pool exhaustion, and flurries of deadlock-victim or lock-timeout errors.

Causally, a saturated transaction-log path extends the duration of every commit, lengthening the time locks are held and sharply raising the probability of lock contention. The ensuing blocking and deadlock resolution workload drives additional CPU demand (lock-manager bookkeeping, deadlock graph construction, rollback processing). This extra CPU load competes with the log writer and archiver threads, slowing log flushes even more and creating a feedback loop that amplifies both the log bottleneck and lock contention. The mutually reinforcing pressures can push the system into a state where throughput collapses and recovery actions (forced rollbacks, failovers, or manual session kills) become necessary.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo as fast as the primary generates it, leading to widening log-position gaps and replay lag.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk data or index pages become physically or logically corrupted, breaking checksums, key order, or page links and making structures untrustworthy.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport or connection-handling resources between clients/peers and the database are saturated or unreliable, causing retransmissions, timeouts, or refusal of new sessions.

When all three conditions co-exist, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: replicas show rapidly growing write/flush/replay lag while simultaneously logging page-checksum or index-consistency errors during apply; replication workers disconnect or time out because of packet loss or listener backlog exhaustion, and repeatedly restart just to hit the same corrupted page, creating flapping apply states. Primary-side WAL archives accumulate because neither standbys nor downstream consumers can keep up, swelling disk usage and threatening outage-triggering disk-full scenarios. Client traffic may also suffer from elevated connection failures and erratic query results—some replicas return stale or incomplete data due to skipped or corrupted pages, while others are unavailable due to connectivity exhaustion. Monitoring views become noisy and ambiguous, mixing network wait spikes, replication slot bloat, and corruption alarms, complicating diagnosis.

Causally, network congestion or socket exhaustion first throttles WAL shipping, stretching replica lag. The prolonged retention of un-replayed log segments on standbys increases the time window during which any latent page or index corruption can surface; once a corrupted block is encountered, the apply process aborts and retries, further amplifying synchronization delay. Each retry re-reads the same bad page and retransmits the same WAL across an already constrained network, compounding bandwidth pressure and connection churn. Conversely, corruption on the primary can generate invalid WAL that stalls apply; the standbys repeatedly disconnect and reconnect over an overloaded network, intensifying listener and socket pressure. The intertwined feedback loops—corruption-induced replay failures and network-induced transport stalls—mutually reinforce, accelerating replica divergence, exhausting storage with retained WAL, and degrading both HA posture and client-facing performance.

Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same objects, forming blocking chains or deadlocks that stall commit progress and inflate lock-wait time.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standbys or downstream replicas are unable to receive or apply log records as fast as the primary generates them, causing growing log-position lag and retention of old log segments.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume nearly all available CPU cycles, driving run-queue growth and broad latency spikes across the workload.

When all three root causes arise together the database exhibits a blended failure pattern: application sessions pile up in lock-wait queues while overall query and transaction latency lengthens; at the same time replica apply and replay lag widens sharply, with relay logs or retained WAL segments ballooning on both primary and replicas. Monitoring views show surging lock-wait counters, escalating CPU utilization on primary and replica nodes, frequent deadlock victim errors, and replication delay alerts all at once. Because commit completion is blocked, primary log generation becomes bursty—alternating between idle periods and spikes—while replicas, already CPU-bound, struggle to catch up, leading to stale read-only traffic, compromised failover objectives, and disk pressure from unrecycled logs.

Causally, intense lock contention forces transactions to hold locks and keep their redo in the primary’s log for longer, inflating the volume of WAL that must eventually stream to replicas in a short time window. These bursts drive higher CPU demand for log shipping, decompression, and apply logic on both sides of the replication channel. Simultaneously, the CPU Resource Anomaly slows lock-manager arbitration and deadlock detection on the primary, prolonging blocking chains and further delaying commits. On replicas, CPU saturation throttles redo apply rates, which increases replication lag and prevents the primary from discarding old log segments, amplifying storage pressure and background housekeeping work that itself consumes more CPU. The feedback loop between lock-induced commit stalls, replication backlog, and compute exhaustion deepens end-to-end latency and threatens both transactional throughput and high-availability objectives.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from (1) a physical data-model and indexing layout that does not fit the workload, (2) an over-accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions that background cleaners cannot reclaim in time, and (3) saturation of the underlying storage subsystem’s throughput or IOPS budget. Together these three root causes create a self-reinforcing performance collapse that affects all foreground operations.

Combined observable phenomena: Queries that should be selective are forced into full scans because of missing or non-covering indexes; those scans traverse bloated tables and indexes swollen by unreclaimed row versions, causing many more pages to be read. Update- and delete-heavy transactions generate large amounts of new versions while every write waits on busy storage queues, inflating commit latency. Autovacuum / purge workers run continuously yet make little progress because their own I/O is throttled; monitoring shows high I/O wait time, deep device queues, rising table and index sizes, misestimated row counts, escalating buffer churn, and sudden spikes in response-time variance. Application sessions may experience both read latency (from scan expansion and I/O stalls) and write latency (from version logging and log-flush bottlenecks), with dead-tuple ratios and storage-level alerts increasing in parallel.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and index design forces the engine to touch far more pages per statement, multiplying physical reads and writes. The extra I/O load accelerates MVCC version churn, because non-covering updates and unnecessary full-row rewrites generate additional row versions and index entries. As obsolete versions pile up, cleanup workers must process larger heaps and indexes; however, their work is throttled by the same saturated storage layer, allowing bloat to grow unchecked. The expanding data footprint further degrades cache efficiency and amplifies I/O demand, pushing the storage subsystem deeper into saturation. This vicious cycle—design inefficiencies → excess version generation → storage bloat → I/O overload → slower cleanup → further bloat—causes a compounded degradation in throughput and latency that is far more severe than any single anomaly would produce in isolation.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer persistently picks sub-optimal execution plans despite reasonably accurate statistics, causing excessive I/O, CPU, or wrong join and access strategies.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Database memory regions (buffer/cache, work areas, plan cache, etc.) grow beyond safe limits, triggering OS memory pressure, paging, or OOM events.
