3. Space failures trigger rollbacks that generate additional undo/redo, amplifying both anomalies. The mutually reinforcing loop quickly degrades throughput, raises error rates, and can culminate in complete service outage unless both statistics and space issues are remediated together.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch far more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, or partition design is mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even for well-written queries.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are internally corrupted or inconsistent with logical row contents, making access paths unreliable.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, the database executes bloated or chatty SQL against ill-suited physical structures whose very pages or index chains may be corrupt. Operators observe extreme and erratic statement latencies, frequent plan oscillations from targeted index lookups to emergency full-table scans, sudden surges in I/O and lock contention, and intermittent wrong-result or duplicate-row anomalies. Slow-query logs fill with the same heavyweight statements; integrity-check utilities intermittently flag corruption; index rebuilds or ANALYZE operations run longer yet fail to stabilize performance; application retries increase, and replication or backup processes report checksum or page-verification errors.

Causally, inefficient SQL magnifies row counts and touch patterns, stressing the deficient schema and overworked indexes; the absence or misconfiguration of covering and selective indexes further pushes the optimizer toward full scans that traverse broader swaths of storage. These heavier scans repeatedly hit corrupt pages or disordered index leaves, triggering error handling, plan fallbacks, or silent result inconsistencies. Conversely, corruption inside indexes can hide existing keys, making the optimizer believe selectivity is lower than reality, thereby reinforcing poor plan choices already induced by weak schema design and chatty SQL. The feedback loop—bad logic driving excessive access, bad design preventing efficient paths, and corruption breaking the remaining paths—culminates in a system where performance degradation, data inconsistency risks, and operational instability are all mutually amplified.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback data accumulate faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and enlarging on-disk structures.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Total in-process memory for caches, work areas, and background structures outgrows physical limits, provoking OS-level pressure, paging, and OOM terminations.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : Log generation and flushing lag behind workload demand or archiving throughput, driving up commit latency and stalling writes.

When these three root causes strike together, the database simultaneously shows runaway memory usage, ballooning version stores and tables, and a saturated redo/commit path. Symptoms include: rapidly expanding data and log files, escalating checkpoint and log-flush waits, degraded cache hit ratios from eviction or swap, long-running VACUUM/cleanup workers perpetually behind, soaring commit times that induce application timeouts, and periodic instance restarts when memory or log space is exhausted. Performance diagnostics may reveal intertwined waits—sessions stuck on log syncs while also incurring excessive memory and I/O to scan bloated heaps—making isolation of any single culprit difficult.

Causally, high update/delete churn inflates both the MVCC version store and the volume of redo records, driving up memory demand and log throughput concurrently. Memory overcommitment reduces effective buffer cache and can force dirty pages to be flushed more aggressively, increasing log write frequency. Log back-pressure slows commit completion, leaving transactions open longer; these lingering snapshots prevent garbage collection, which in turn enlarges the version store, further consuming memory and I/O. The expanding memory footprint competes with log buffers and background workers for resources, slowing log archiving and cleanup tasks, creating a self-reinforcing loop that degrades throughput and risks crash or data-loss scenarios if not addressed promptly.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database allocates aggregate buffer, work-area, cache, and background-process memory beyond the safe physical or swap capacity of the host, driving paging, OOM kills, and cache churn.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database or its child processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, address space, or cgroup quotas, independent of the engine’s own configuration.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Listener, socket, authentication, or transport resources become saturated, producing connection refusals, long hand-shakes, stalled I/O, and elevated retransmissions.

When these three root causes co-exist the system exhibits a tangled failure pattern: memory pressure inflates process RSS and swap-in/out latency, while simultaneous kernel limit exhaustion returns intermittent ENOMEM, EMFILE, or EAGAIN errors for new threads, shared memory, and sockets. Clients see sporadic login failures, TLS hand-shake timeouts, and abrupt disconnects; surviving sessions suffer elevated client-read/client-write waits as network queues back up. Surge-driven connection storms inflate the number of backend processes and file handles, aggravating both kernel limit exhaustion and memory overcommit. The host may thrash, evict pages needed for socket buffers, and emit kernel warnings; the database may partially hang, unable to spawn workers, allocate work memory, or accept further connections even though some internal metrics appear normal.

Causally, excessive per-session memory allocations inflate each backend’s footprint, accelerating consumption of virtual memory, address space, and locked memory quotas. As processes bloat, they open more temporary files and sockets, quickly reaching per-process file-handle and thread limits. Failed spawns and resource denials lead to application-layer retries that flood the listener, saturating socket queues and exhausting connection slots, which in turn lengthens transaction latency and keeps active backends idle while holding their large memory heaps. The feedback loop—memory overuse → OS limit breaches → connection failures → retry storms → additional socket and process pressure—drives the system into a compounded degradation that is harder to diagnose because symptoms of each anomaly mask and magnify the others.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys or downstream consumers cannot ingest, persist, or apply primary-generated log records at the pace they are produced.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space for data, logs, archives, temp areas, or backups is exhausted or approaching hard limits.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Transport links, listeners, sockets, or connection slots are saturated, unstable, or otherwise unable to carry the required traffic between clients or database nodes.

When these three root causes co-exist, symptoms overlap and compound: replication lag grows rapidly while network round-trip times, retransmissions, and connection errors spike. Retained primary WAL/redo segments and expanding replica relay logs accumulate until disk groups, archive destinations, or temp areas hit 100 % usage, triggering space-allocation failures, halted check-pointing, and automatic safety shutdowns. Clients may see a mixture of slow queries, stale read-replicas, authentication timeouts, and "disk full" or "cannot allocate X" errors. Failover readiness degrades because replicas fall far behind and may themselves run out of space or lose connections, making recovery impossible if the primary crashes.

Causal interaction: (1) Intermittent or congested network paths throttle log shipping and inflate replication lag. (2) The lag forces the primary to retain old log segments and the replicas to buffer large relay logs, driving up disk consumption on both sides. (3) As storage fills, log archiving and auto-extension stall, which in turn blocks new transactions, further backs up replication, and amplifies network retransmissions due to repeated retries and larger bursts when connectivity resumes. The space pressure can also disrupt listener and logging subsystems, exacerbating connection churn. Conversely, once data-file or log volumes reach capacity, replication and client connections may be forcibly closed, triggering additional reconnect storms that worsen network saturation. The feedback loop between slow/unstable networks, replication backlog, and space exhaustion intensifies each anomaly, quickly destabilising the entire database estate.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design that forces the engine to read, change, or hold on to more data and for longer than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses or reuses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to excessive resource use.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The write-ahead log generation, flushing, or archival path cannot keep pace with the redo volume, making commit processing a throughput limiter.

Composite definition – This composite anomaly represents an OLTP workload in which (1) the application issues over-broad or poorly structured SQL and long-running transactions, (2) the optimizer compounds the problem by selecting inefficient execution plans for those very statements, and (3) the resulting surge in redo activity saturates the transaction-log subsystem, so both execution time and commit latency deteriorate simultaneously.

Combined anomalous phenomena – Operators observe erratic but generally rising statement and transaction latency, with some executions stalling specifically at COMMIT or during log-flush waits. Slow-query logs show the same SQL alternating between different, sometimes dramatically slower plans. Monitoring dashboards report spikes in logical I/O, buffer gets, and row versions together with sustained log write/sync wait events, frequent log-file switches, and backlog in archiving or replication shipping. Application tiers show a mix of CPU saturation (from bad plans), lock contention (from long transactions), and timeout-driven retries that further inflate redo generation and heap usage.

Causal chain – Verbose or chatty workload logic first inflates data touched per transaction; when the optimizer then mis-estimates costs or reuses a non-optimal cached plan, scans and join explosions amplify the physical and logical I/O as well as the amount of undo/redo produced. The multiplied redo volume quickly pushes the log buffer to its limits, triggering more frequent flushes and log-file switches. As the log device or archiver falls behind, commits stall, prolonging transaction lifetimes and keeping locks and latches held longer. These delays increase concurrency pressure, raising the likelihood of further plan invalidations and causing the application to retry, feeding back into even higher write and redo rates. The intertwined effects of bloated workload semantics, poor plan choices, and a saturated log path create a reinforcing loop that degrades overall OLTP performance and stability far more severely than any of the individual anomalies would in isolation.

Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions and index entries pile up faster than background cleanup can reclaim them, inflating the version store and slowing visibility checks.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Critical engine settings (memory, checkpointing, parallelism, worker limits, etc.) are poorly tuned for the hardware and workload, causing secondary resource-management pathologies.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes saturate CPU cores, producing run-queue buildup, context-switch pressure, and widespread latency once compute headroom is exhausted.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a compounded failure pattern: version stores and table sizes balloon while CPU usage remains pegged near 100 %, yet I/O or memory may appear under-utilised. Queries that touch bloated tables show steeply rising latency; planner estimates diverge from reality, leading to sub-optimal parallel or serial plans. Autovacuum/cleaner workers run constantly but make little headway, and their activity further taxes already saturated CPUs. Checkpoint or flush storms may appear irregularly as mis-set thresholds collide with the surging volume of dirty pages produced by long-running clean-up and re-scans. Wait-event views show a mix of CPU-spin and background-writer/vacuum delays, and administrators observe rapid growth in transaction-ID or undo/rollback segments alongside an overloaded scheduler.

Causally, poorly chosen configuration parameters (e.g., undersized maintenance work memory, conservative autovacuum cost limits, excessive parallel-worker counts, or aggressive checkpoint intervals) slow version garbage collection and simultaneously drive up CPU demand. As MVCC debris accumulates, each query’s visibility checks and table/index scans become more CPU-intensive, pushing the system toward compute saturation. The resulting CPU Resource Anomaly starves background workers of CPU slices, which impedes cleanup further, letting bloat expand unchecked. This feedback loop amplifies both the MVCC maintenance backlog and the CPU bottleneck, while the misconfiguration remains the root enabler that prevents the system from rebalancing resources, yielding a severe, self-reinforcing degradation of OLTP performance.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch more rows, more columns, or hold locks longer than the business case requires.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count, histogram, or correlation metadata is stale or incomplete, leading the optimizer to mis-estimate cardinalities.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer’s decision logic or plan-reuse policy picks a plan that is far from optimal even when acceptable alternatives exist.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from inefficient SQL semantics, inaccurate optimizer statistics, and a poor plan choice. Together they create a feedback loop in which the workload asks for too much work, the optimizer sees the data incorrectly, and then chooses an even worse way to execute it.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Extreme and highly variable statement latencies that defy normal tuning; 2) Identical queries alternating between different bad plans, with some executions exploding into full table scans, hash or nested-loop storms, massive temp-space spills, or runaway parallelism; 3) Sudden performance collapses after data loads or schema changes, followed by prolonged lock holds and blocking chains because long-running, over-wide transactions collide; 4) Chronic appearance of the same SQL in slow-query logs even after index tuning, and persistent discrepancies between estimated and actual rows in execution plans; 5) Frequent plan recompiles, memory-grant overallocations, and exhausted CPU/IO capacity leading to application timeouts and retries.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient application SQL increases data volume scanned and accentuates any small cardinality errors. The resulting large data modifications quickly render existing statistics obsolete, widening the estimate–actual gap. Stale or missing statistics, in turn, mislead the optimizer, which may already be prone to volatile or skew-sensitive plan selection. The optimizer therefore locks onto or oscillates between sub-optimal plans that amplify the workload’s excess data access, driving up resource consumption. The heavier execution footprint further delays automatic statistics refresh and enlarges plan-cache churn, reinforcing both the statistics and plan-selection problems. The intertwined effects create a self-perpetuating degradation cycle that is harder to diagnose because each individual anomaly masks and exacerbates the others.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to process or retain far more data and rows than business logic requires.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas or subscribers fall behind because they cannot receive or apply primary-generated log records at the production rate.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Allocated physical or logical storage for data, logs, or temporary areas reaches exhaustion, impeding normal allocation and recycling.

When all three exist concurrently, the system exhibits extreme and widening replica lag, growing on-disk log backlogs, and escalating disk-space consumption on both primary and replicas. Long-running or chatty transactions produced by inefficient SQL inflate the volume of redo, generate oversized result sets that spill to temp space, and keep locks open longer. Replicas struggling to apply these bloated change batches accumulate ever larger relay or archive logs; the primary cannot purge its own logs, and free space plummets. Users observe increasing statement latency, frequent timeouts, stalled or cancelled writes when log destinations fill, stale read-only traffic on replicas, and emergency auto-extend or out-of-space errors in data, temp, or log areas.

Causally, sub-optimal workload logic produces excessive data modifications and prolonged transactions, which directly amplifies the replication stream. The overwhelmed replication path slows, causing unapplied logs to pile up. Because those retained logs occupy the same filesystems or object stores as data, they accelerate space consumption and can eventually exhaust capacity. Imminent space exhaustion further degrades replica apply throughput (due to I/O contention and pause-on-error behavior) and can halt primary DML when log writes or temp allocations fail. Thus, each anomaly reinforces the others in a feedback loop: inefficient SQL inflates log volume, replication delay prevents log recycling, accumulated logs and temporary spill exceed storage limits, and storage pressure in turn magnifies both latency and replication backlog, culminating in a compound performance and availability crisis.

Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standbys, read replicas, or downstream consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo records as fast as the primary emits them, causing widening log-position gaps and replication lag.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical volumes that host data, log, temp, or backup files are saturated for bandwidth, IOPS, or latency, inflating I/O wait times and slowing every component that depends on disk access.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, AIO contexts, shared memory, semaphores, or process/thread counts block the database from opening more files, issuing I/O, or spawning workers, even though engine-level limits have not been reached.

When all three anomalies emerge concurrently, the database exhibits a mixture of symptoms that mask one another: replication lag grows rapidly while primary-side WAL files and replica relay logs pile up because slow, back-pressured storage and blocked I/O contexts prevent both the primary from recycling logs and the replicas from reading or replaying them. Data-file, log-file, and buffer-I/O waits dominate wait profiles, yet administrators also observe sporadic engine errors about "too many open files," "cannot allocate shared memory," "AIO context limit reached," or inability to start new replication workers. CPU utilization appears moderate, but end-user transactions and analytical queries stall on commit confirmation, stale replica reads, or buffer latch acquisition. Failover readiness deteriorates as replicas become hours behind, and disk-space alarms trigger due to retained WAL segments.

Causally, storage throughput saturation slows both the primary’s WAL flushes and the replicas’ read/replay pipelines. The longer each operation waits on disk, the more worker threads, file handles, AIO slots, and shared-memory objects remain in use. This steadily drives the database toward OS-level resource ceilings. Once those limits are hit, new I/O submissions fail or queue lengths collapse, further degrading storage performance and intensifying replication lag. Conversely, the escalating backlog of unapplied WAL produced by the replication anomaly forces more concurrent I/O and open files, accelerating consumption of kernel resources and aggravating the storage bottleneck. The feedback loop among slow storage, exhausted kernel resources, and widening replication gaps can rapidly push the system into a cascading performance and availability crisis.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statement or transaction design that processes or returns more data than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: Optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Physical or logical free space in data, temp, or log areas is exhausted or near exhaustion, blocking further allocations.

When these three root causes strike together, the system executes needlessly heavy statements with inefficient plans that materialize excessive intermediate results, generate bloated logs, and sustain long transactions exactly when the underlying storage pools are already at – or racing toward – capacity limits. Observable effects include dramatic and erratic query slowdowns, bursts of temporary‐segment growth, sudden switches to full table scans that flood I/O, rapid log or tablespace filling, allocation failures during sorts or hash joins, transaction rollbacks due to "out of space" errors, prolonged lock holding, application timeouts, and oscillating plan shapes as the optimizer reacts to space-induced feedback such as disabled parallelism or spilled hash areas.

Causally, inefficient workload logic feeds large row sets and long-running transactions to the optimizer. A poor plan choice magnifies that volume through full scans, wide hash joins, and repeated re-executions, inflating temp usage and redo/undo generation. The resulting surge in data, temp, and log consumption accelerates space depletion; once critical thresholds are crossed, auto-extension stops or file growth stalls, causing further plan instability (e.g., fallback to disk-heavy plans when memory spills cannot allocate space) and forcing the application to keep transactions open longer while retrying, which in turn continues enlarging logs and temp segments. Thus each anomaly amplifies the others, forming a feedback loop that degrades performance, increases failure rates, and complicates diagnosis.

Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Sustained physical read and write demand overruns the available throughput, IOPS, or latency capacity of the underlying storage volumes, making the disk subsystem the primary bottleneck.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly: Network transport, listener, authentication, or socket-handling resources are unable to service incoming connections and data transfers at the required rate, producing client-side timeouts, retransmissions, and connection refusals.

When both conditions coexist, the database experiences a multilayer performance collapse. Disk queues, read/write latencies, and durability flush waits soar while, in parallel, connection-establishment times lengthen, sockets pile up in wait states, and application pools flood the listener with retries. End-users observe highly variable query response times, periodic stalls, and sporadic disconnects. Server metrics show moderate CPU, but extreme I/O wait, swollen session counts, backlog and accept queue saturation, increased network round-trip times, and surges of aborted transactions. Because slow storage elongates statement execution and commit phases, each session holds its network resources longer, further exhausting socket and process limits, while network retransmissions and throttling delay log shipping, replication, or backup traffic, worsening storage congestion.

Causally, saturated storage inflates I/O waits, extending transaction and result-set lifetimes; this keeps connections open, grows the active session population, and drives the listener toward exhaustion. Simultaneously, network slowdowns or connection churn force the server to buffer more result data and maintain idle backends, increasing memory pressure and dirty-page accumulation that must eventually be flushed to already overtaxed disks. The feedback loop between elongated disk operations and protracted network interactions amplifies latency at both layers, obscuring which tier is primary and pushing the database into a compounded resource starvation state.

Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The database is simultaneously suffering from (1) mis-tuned engine parameters that misalign memory, checkpoint, logging, worker, or connection limits with actual workload and hardware characteristics; (2) intense buffer-cache and latch contention that serializes page access inside the buffer manager; and (3) saturation or instability in the network / connection-handling layer that throttles session establishment and data transfer. The overlap of these three root causes creates a multi-layer bottleneck in which configuration errors, internal synchronization stalls, and external connectivity pressure reinforce each other. 

Combined Observable Phenomena: • Highly variable response times where some calls time out at the client side while others hang inside the engine on buffer_busy or page-latch waits. • Low overall throughput despite modest CPU, memory, or storage utilization, accompanied by spikes in log-write or checkpoint waits. • Surges of refused or aborted connections, large pools of sessions stuck in client-read/write wait events, and operating-system socket queues filling. • Periodic storms of dirty-page flushes and redo generation triggered by aggressive or mis-set checkpoint parameters, coinciding with latch hotspots on index root or sequence pages. • CPU spin-loops in backend processes holding latches while simultaneously being slow to release them because outbound network buffers are blocked, making traditional single-layer diagnostics misleading.

Causal Interaction: Undersized or overly aggressive configuration parameters (small buffer pool, low shared memory per backend, or tight checkpoint intervals) force frequent page evictions and checkpoint activity, driving up latch acquisition and buffer churn. The resulting latch contention prolongs critical sections, keeping backends active longer and inflating their connection lifetimes. As session counts rise and data packets stall on an already congested or under-provisioned network/listener stack, authentication and I/O paths slow further, causing more client-read/write waits. These prolonged waits keep latches and buffer pins held, which in turn amplifies buffer contention and magnifies the impact of the misconfiguration. Conversely, network-induced back pressure masks true hardware capacity, leading administrators to mis-tune memory and checkpoint parameters even further, completing a feedback loop that degrades both throughput and latency across the entire system.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical data-model and indexing choices misaligned with workload, forcing inefficient access paths irrespective of statistics or plan selection.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages contain logical or physical corruption, making stored structures unreliable and causing inconsistent results.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores are saturated by database processes, leaving inadequate compute capacity for timely query execution.

When these three root causes co-exist, the database exhibits an intertwined symptom set: queries that already rely on sub-optimal or missing indexes are driven to perform full scans; corruption within the scanned pages or index trees forces the optimizer or execution engine to retry, fall back to heap scans, or invoke internal consistency checks, further inflating CPU consumption. Applications observe erratic response times, sudden spikes of CPU utilization, surges in context switches, and intermittent logical errors such as row count mismatches or duplicate key violations. Integrity-check utilities may report corruption while performance tools simultaneously show both index-related inefficiencies and CPU bottlenecks, making single-factor diagnosis misleading.

Causally, poor schema and index design expands I/O and CPU demand because queries traverse more pages and perform additional lookups. The heightened page churn increases the chance of touching corrupted blocks, which in turn triggers error handling, page retries, or forced full-table scans—multiplying CPU work and elongating execution time. The sustained CPU saturation masks the presence of underlying corruption by attributing slowdowns to resource pressure, while corruption-induced scan fallbacks exacerbate the CPU anomaly. Meanwhile, failed or partial index rebuilds caused by corruption can remove valuable indexes, further deepening the design mismatch. The feedback loop among design inefficiency, structural corruption, and CPU exhaustion accelerates performance deterioration and elevates the risk of widespread data inconsistency.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer persistently picks or reuses a sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to excessive I/O, CPU, or memory work per statement.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database components (buffer cache, work areas, plan cache, parallel worker buffers, etc.) collectively grow beyond the safe physical-memory envelope of the host, provoking paging, swapping, or OOM events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced quotas on handles, shared memory, threads, or address space are exhausted, preventing the database from allocating additional OS resources.

When these three root causes coexist, the workload can oscillate between slow but still-running and partial or complete outages. Sub-optimal plans trigger unexpectedly large hash joins, sorts, or full scans, inflating per-query memory demand and filling buffer and work pools. Escalating memory pressure induces paging, RSS bloat, and frequent eviction of useful cache pages; concurrently, kernel limits on shared memory segments, file descriptors, or thread counts are reached as the engine attempts to create more work areas, temporary files, or workers to compensate. Symptoms therefore include: erratic response-time spikes, sudden plan changes followed by memory spikes, frequent "cannot allocate memory / shared memory / file descriptor" errors, aborted parallel starts, background-process deaths, and intermittent connection failures even while existing sessions hang in memory-stall states.

Causal chain: a bad plan (1) dramatically increases memory consumption; the bloated buffers and work areas (2) drive the engine into aggressive allocation behavior that surpasses configured or implicit OS quotas; once kernel limits are hit (3) the database can no longer obtain additional shared memory, threads, or temp files, causing further plan invalidations, forced serial execution, or outright failures that feedback into the optimizer and connection pool. Conversely, prior exhaustion of OS resources can suppress parallelism or temp-space availability, nudging the optimizer toward still worse plans that consume yet more memory. The intertwined feedback loops among poor plan choice, runaway memory growth, and hard OS ceilings amplify each other, rapidly degrading throughput and stability across both OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Unbounded growth of buffer caches, plan caches, work areas, and other heaps drives the database process beyond the host’s safe physical-memory envelope.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space in data, log, and temporary areas falls to zero, triggering allocation failures and write stalls.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes saturate available CPU cycles, creating sustained high run-queue pressure and system-wide latency.

Composite anomaly definition: The database simultaneously overruns memory, storage, and CPU resources, so that each critical resource reaches or exceeds its capacity while the workload is executing.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Administrators observe relentless growth of resident memory alongside escalating swap activity; swap I/O floods the storage layer whose free space is already near exhaustion due to bloated data, logs, and oversized temp segments created by memory spills. At the same time, CPU utilization pins near 100 %, with long OS run queues and frequent context switches. Queries that spill from RAM to temp slow dramatically, increasing statement runtimes, amplifying CPU demand, and generating even more temporary and log files that quickly consume the last gigabytes of disk. As space runs out, data-file extensions, sort operations, and log archiving begin to fail, producing allocation errors, checkpoint stalls, and in clustered systems, node fencing or crash-recovery cycles. Monitoring shows simultaneous alerts for memory pressure, disk-full conditions, and CPU saturation, making single-symptom troubleshooting unreliable.

Causal chain and interaction: Excessive memory allocation pushes the OS into paging; paging traffic inflates I/O, which both consumes CPU (kernel time) and writes swap and temp data to disk, accelerating storage exhaustion. As free space disappears, the database is forced to spill active work sets to ever-shrinking temp areas and to retain unrecycled transaction logs, further intensifying disk usage. The additional I/O wait magnifies CPU demand through context switching and spin-waiting, keeping cores saturated and slowing foreground tasks and maintenance jobs that would normally release memory or reclaim space. The throttled CPU in turn delays memory reclamation threads and background checkpoints, perpetuating high memory residency and swelling on-disk footprints. This feedback loop rapidly degrades throughput and can culminate in out-of-memory kills, disk-full aborts, or complete node failure.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to unnecessary work, poor join methods, or non-selective access paths.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The physical storage layer is saturated, so read/write latency, IOPS queues, and device wait times all climb well above design limits.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Kernel-enforced caps on file handles, async-I/O contexts, threads, shared memory, or similar resources are reached, blocking further allocations by the database processes.

When these three root causes strike simultaneously, symptoms compound: a suddenly degraded plan may switch from index probes to full table scans, inflating I/O volume precisely when the storage subsystem is already at or beyond throughput capacity. The bloated I/O demand lengthens device queues and elevates buffer-I/O and log-file waits; meanwhile, the database tries to open more files, spawn extra parallel or I/O helper threads, or allocate larger async-I/O queues to cope, but the operating system refuses additional resources. End-users see erratic execution times, timeouts, and partial outages where existing sessions hang on I/O waits while new sessions, parallel workers, or background check-pointers fail to start, sometimes emitting kernel "too many open files", "cannot create thread", or "AIO context limit reached" errors. Performance metrics show a puzzling mix of optimizer plan churn, soaring physical I/O latency, and sporadic OS-level allocation failures that mask one another and hinder straightforward diagnosis.

Causally, a poor plan acts as the initial amplifier, multiplying page reads and log writes. The excess demand pushes the storage layer into saturation, driving up latency and elongating the lifespan of every I/O request. Prolonged I/O times inflate the number of simultaneously active requests, which in turn drives the engine to request more kernel objects—file descriptors for every open segment, async-I/O control blocks, and worker threads. Once OS limits are hit, these new allocations are denied, causing additional plan invalidations, failed worker creation, and fallback to even less efficient serial plans. Each layer therefore feeds the next: sub-optimal planning → storage overload → OS resource exhaustion → further planning and execution degradation, creating a reinforcing spiral that dramatically worsens overall database throughput and availability.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-level statements or transaction boundaries are written so they touch more rows, columns, or time than the business case requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Tables, indexes, partitions, and data types are laid out in a way that cannot satisfy the workload’s access patterns efficiently.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes consume an abnormally large share of CPU, driving the host to sustained saturation.

Composite definition: The composite anomaly represents the simultaneous presence of inefficient workload logic, a schema/index design that cannot serve the requested access patterns, and resulting CPU saturation. Poorly written queries meet a mismatched physical design, and the combined demand overwhelms compute resources.

Combined anomalous phenomena: Slow-query logs fill with recurring statements that show full-table scans or non-covering index probes; execution plans display wide scans, repeated lookups, and lack of partition pruning; host CPU utilization hovers near 100 %, with long OS run queues and scheduler wait events; statement latency forms a long tail, application timeouts and retries spike, and even well-written queries suffer from queueing delays. Monitoring may show sharp drops in throughput whenever a batch job or peak traffic window coincides with these conditions, and adding indexes or rewriting queries in isolation yields only partial relief.

Causal chain and interaction: Inefficient workload logic forces the engine to touch large data ranges. Because the schema lacks selective or covering indexes, these requests devolve into full scans and row-by-row lookups, multiplying CPU instructions per statement. The elevated CPU demand saturates the host, extending run-queue times and slowing plan compilation and context switching. CPU starvation, in turn, prolongs each already-inefficient query, causing longer transaction lifetimes, more contention, and additional retries that feed back into still higher CPU usage. Thus, the three root causes reinforce one another, creating a self-amplifying performance spiral that is harder to diagnose than any single issue alone.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : The submitted SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, write, or lock far more data and for longer intervals than the business case requires.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path—log buffer, log files, archiver, or replication retention—cannot keep pace with redo generation, throttling commit throughput.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas prevent the database from allocating the resources it needs.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: application statements show extreme and highly variable response times; commit latency spikes and fluctuates as log flushes back up; slow-query logs fill with the same chatty or scan-heavy statements; background error logs reveal "unable to open file", "cannot allocate shared memory", or thread-creation failures; checkpoints and log-switch storms occur more frequently; sessions intermittently fail to start or hang during commit; and archival/replication lag balloons, causing retention directories to overflow. Performance degradations appear erratic because even minor workload surges exacerbate both log contention and operating-system denial events, while the bloated, long-running transactions keep locks and resources held, amplifying blocking chains.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL or over-long transactions inflate redo generation and hold resources for extended periods, driving the transaction log subsystem to its limits. As log buffers and files saturate, the database requests more file handles, I/O contexts, shared memory, and background threads to flush, switch, or archive logs. Simultaneously, OS-level limits on these kernel objects cap the database’s ability to relieve log pressure. The stalled log subsystem lengthens commit times, which further prolongs the already excessive transactions produced by the workload logic anomaly, creating larger bursts of redo and compounding lock contention. This feedback loop accelerates consumption of kernel resources until limits are hit, after which both new sessions and log-handling processes fail, precipitating a cascading slowdown or partial outage of the transactional workload.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Physical data-model or indexing choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans, wide lock footprints, and excess I/O regardless of optimizer decisions.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions demand incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, or metadata, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput and trigger rollbacks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions fight for hot buffer pages, page-latch structures, or flush slots inside the buffer manager, leading to wait events and CPU spin without progress.

When all three conditions exist together, the system exhibits compounded symptoms: frequent full-table or non-covering index scans inflate the number and size of locked and latched pages; simultaneous transactions pile up behind both user-level locks and low-level latches, producing mixed "lock wait" and "buffer latch" wait spikes, CPU burn, erratic query latencies, and degraded TPS. Deadlock detector logs intermingle with buffer busy statistics, while adding or modifying indexes unpredictably shifts the pressure between lock manager and buffer manager, making the root problems appear transient or workload-dependent.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and index design widens each statement’s physical footprint, touching many more rows and pages than necessary. The surplus page visits not only enlarge lock scopes—escalating row locks to page or table locks—but also drive up buffer-page churn, keeping hot root and leaf pages in constant reuse. These oversized critical pages become latch hotspots; the resulting latch waits extend statement execution time, which in turn prolongs lock hold time. Longer lock durations heighten the probability of conflicting lock requests, deepening blocking chains and deadlock frequency. Meanwhile, lock contention forces some sessions to wait, while others spin on latches for the same pages, amplifying CPU usage and eroding throughput. Thus, flawed physical design, elevated lock contention, and buffer/latch thrashing reinforce one another, producing a severe, self-sustaining performance collapse in write-intensive transactional workloads.

Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to read, join, sort, or hold more data and locks than business logic actually requires.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Database components (buffer/plan caches, work areas, parallel worker buffers, etc.) grow beyond the safe physical-memory envelope, driving paging or OOM events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, address space, or cgroup quotas are reached, blocking further allocations by the database process.

When these three conditions coincide, the workload’s chatty or scan-heavy statements inflate per-query work buffers and keep transactions open, quickly consuming buffer cache and work memory. The swollen memory footprint pushes the host into sustained pressure, provoking paging, swap storms, or kernel OOM killers while simultaneously exhausting kernel objects such as SHM segments, semaphores, or thread slots. End-user symptoms include extreme and erratic statement latencies, bursts of slow-query log entries, session creation failures, aborted parallel workers, sporadic "cannot allocate memory / file descriptor" errors, and possible database or node restarts. Performance metrics may show oscillating cache hit ratios, climbing resident-set size, kernel message-log complaints, and a backlog of long-running, partially completed transactions.

Causally, inefficient SQL amplifies memory demand by inflating work areas (sorts, hashes, large result sets) and prolonging transaction lifetimes; this accelerates buffer-pool growth and plan-cache bloat, triggering the Database Memory Allocation Anomaly. As the engine competes for scarce RAM, it requests additional pages, shared memory, and threads, which collide with fixed operating-system limits. Hitting these limits feeds back into the workload: failed thread or memory allocations force retries, which keep transactions open even longer, further swelling memory consumption. The resulting loop of poor SQL logic → memory overcommit → kernel limit exhaustion causes a cascading degradation that is harder to diagnose because symptoms surface alternately at the SQL layer (slow queries), the database engine (memory pressure warnings), and the OS (resource-exhaustion errors).

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot or churn-heavy buffer pages, latches, or page-pin slots, spending CPU cycles on spin loops or waiting on buffer-busy / page-latch events.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table or index pages are physically or logically corrupt, causing mismatched keys, broken links, or checksum failures that render storage structures unreliable.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database engine hits kernel-enforced ceilings on file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or AIO contexts, blocking new I/O or background tasks even though database-level resources remain.

When these three root causes strike at once, the workload encounters a tangled failure signature: 1) queries intermittently stall on buffer-busy and latch waits that grow longer as corrupted pages force repeated rereads, retries, or full-table scans; 2) integrity check errors, checksum failures, or sudden plan shifts to full scans appear in logs, yet attempts to rebuild or validate objects are throttled by OS resource denials; 3) background writers, checkpointers, and recovery or validation workers fail to obtain kernel handles or shared-memory slots, leaving dirty or suspect pages in cache longer, which in turn amplifies latch contention and elevates CPU spin; 4) sessions already holding scarce latches may be unable to spawn helper threads, so foreground statement latency spikes and throughput collapses in both transactional and analytical paths while the instance remains partially alive.

Causally, physical corruption (Data Block and Index Integrity) triggers extra I/O and page replacement as the engine retries reads or forces page eviction, concentrating demand on specific buffer frames. This magnifies Buffer Cache and Latch Contention, extending latch-hold times and multiplying concurrent waiters. Prolonged contention keeps pages and I/O slots occupied, inflating the number of open file handles, AIO requests, and background tasks. These surges drive the system past Operating System Resource Limits, which then block new buffers, threads, or I/O contexts, preventing timely page flushes and integrity-repair operations. The OS denials further lengthen latch hold durations and impede corrective actions, while unresolved corruption perpetuates reaccess of the same hot pages—creating a feedback loop that steadily degrades performance, increases error rates, and risks a cascading partial outage or crash recovery failure.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Stale, missing, or insufficient optimizer statistics cause systematic cardinality misestimation and mis-costed execution plans.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, forming long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions vie for hot buffer pages, latches, or I/O slots, forcing serialization and CPU spin even when logical memory is sufficient.

When these three root causes coincide, the database exhibits compounded instability: poorly costed plans may favor full-table scans, unordered index usage, or lock-escalating access paths that touch far more rows and pages than necessary. The inflated footprint magnifies both row/table lock conflicts and the number of buffer pages and latches each transaction must pin. As blocking lengthens, pages stay latched and dirty longer, amplifying buffer-busy, page-latch, and lock-wait events, while deadlock detectors and application timeouts trigger frequent rollbacks and retries. Execution plans show severe row-count misestimates alongside bloated lock and latch wait statistics, checkpoint stalls, and oscillating CPU utilization.

Causally, inaccurate statistics misguide the optimizer into choosing plans that create wide lock scopes (e.g., table scans, range locks) and concentrate traffic on a few hot pages. The resulting lock contention prolongs transaction lifetimes, causing threads to hold latches and buffer pins for extended periods. Extended latch holds throttle page circulation, forcing more sessions to spin or sleep on latch acquisition, which in turn slows data access and keeps locks active even longer. The protracted blocking suppresses or delays statistics refresh operations, allowing data drift to grow and further degrading plan quality—forming a reinforcing loop that steadily degrades throughput and inflates latency in write-heavy transactional workloads.

Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The primary instance’s local write-ahead logging path cannot generate, flush, switch, or archive log segments at the rate demanded by the workload.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Downstream replicas or change-data consumers cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, causing growing replication lag and retention of old log segments.

Composite definition: Both bottlenecks are present at the same time— the primary’s log subsystem is saturated while the replication pipeline is simultaneously stalled—creating a feedback loop in which neither side can progress at the required throughput.

Combined observable phenomena: Commit latency, log-flush and log-sync waits rise sharply; checkpoints and log-file switches occur more frequently yet still leave log directories expanding. Replication monitoring shows widening send, receive, and replay lags; relay logs or retained primary segments mushroom, and replicas deliver increasingly stale reads or fall out of failover eligibility. The primary may throttle or stall new writes when log space cannot be recycled, while replicas may exhibit backpressure, single-threaded apply saturation, or network congestion. Because both paths are impaired, administrators see mixed symptoms—storage alerts on the primary, network or apply lag warnings on replicas, and cascading slowdowns of foreground user transactions.

Causal interaction: A slow local log subsystem inflates commit durations and extends the time each transaction’s log records occupy active segments, reducing the headroom available for replication retention; concurrently, replication lag prevents those segments from being recycled, further lengthening the primary’s log queue and intensifying the local I/O hotspot. Conversely, replication backpressure keeps log segments pinned, forcing the primary to switch to new segments more rapidly and increasing the write-amplification on an already over-stressed log device. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other—local log saturation starves the replication feed, and replication lag starves log-space reuse—leading to a vicious cycle that can culminate in full disks, suspended commits, and replica divergence.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model—including tables, partitions, indexes, and data types—and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient scans and excessive row touches even when SQL is well-written.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit path is throttled by log-buffer, log-file, or archive constraints so that generating, flushing, or retaining redo becomes the dominant bottleneck during write activity.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Underlying disks, flash, or shared storage cannot sustain the aggregate read/write bandwidth or IOPS demanded by data, temp, and log files, driving up latency and queue depth.

When these three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode: poorly indexed OLTP statements trigger large full-table scans, non-covering index lookups, and row-by-row updates that inflate redo generation while inflating random and sequential I/O. The swollen redo stream collides with an undersized or mis-placed transaction log that is already slow to flush, producing surging commit latency, frequent log-write and log-sync waits, prolonged checkpoint or log-switch stalls, and replication/archival backlogs. Meanwhile the same saturated storage layer must service both the inefficient data accesses and the frantic log writes, so device queue depths remain maxed, read latency for lookup queries spikes, and foreground sessions pile up on both I/O and log-related waits. Application symptoms range from sluggish queries and time-outs to lock contention and failed commits during peak periods.

Causally, the sub-optimal schema and index design multiplies the volume of physical page accesses and redo records per transaction. This heightened I/O demand strikes a storage subsystem already at its throughput limits, amplifying latency for every read and write. The bloated redo stream intensifies pressure on the transaction-log subsystem; slow log flushes extend commit duration, keeping locks and latches held longer and lengthening transaction runtimes—which in turn hold resources, increase contention, and compound I/O demand. As the log subsystem stalls, background checkpoints and archivers issue more aggressive I/O, further congesting the storage path that is simultaneously handling inefficient data scans. The feedback loop between design-induced I/O amplification, log-flush throttling, and device saturation produces a severe, self-reinforcing degradation that is difficult to diagnose if each layer is observed in isolation.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Costing metadata is stale, incomplete, or missing, so the optimizer systematically mis-estimates cardinalities and chooses sub-optimal execution plans.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes fall behind because they cannot receive or apply primary redo fast enough, causing widening log-position gaps and retention of log segments on the primary.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database or replica processes drive host CPU usage to sustained saturation, starving other work and inflating run-queue and scheduler waits.

When all three anomalies coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: poorly estimated queries on the primary choose CPU-intensive plans (e.g., full table scans or over-parallelized joins) that generate excess I/O and larger-than-normal redo streams. The primary’s CPU saturation slows foreground transactions, while the ballooning write-ahead log cannot be recycled because replicas are lagging. On the replicas, limited CPU capacity and inefficient apply paths struggle with the higher-volume, more complex redo, further lengthening replication lag. Monitoring shows simultaneous spikes in CPU wait events, soaring statement latencies, dramatic discrepancies between estimated and actual row counts, and ever-increasing replica delay and retained log volume. Failover readiness degrades, and storage pressure mounts on both primary (due to unrecycled logs) and replicas (due to growing relay logs).

Causally, stale or missing statistics trigger mis-estimated plans that inflate CPU consumption and redo generation. The resulting CPU Resource Anomaly on the primary slows transaction processing and log shipping threads, while the same or separate CPU pressure on replicas limits their apply throughput. Increased redo volume coupled with diminished processing capacity intensifies the Replication Synchronization Anomaly, which in turn prevents log truncation, forcing the primary to handle more log I/O and background cleanup work—further taxing CPU. This feedback loop between poor statistics, CPU saturation, and replication backlog amplifies each symptom, driving the entire database environment into a degraded and self-reinforcing state.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : The database engine and its sessions consume more physical or virtual memory than the host can safely supply, provoking paging, OOM events, and cache-churn. 
Replication Synchronization Anomaly : Standby, replica, or downstream consumers fall behind the primary because they cannot receive or apply log records at the production rate, widening log-position gaps and retaining log files. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space for data, log, temp, or backup areas falls to—or reaches—hard limits, producing allocation failures and preventing further growth or recycling.

When these three root causes coincide, the system exhibits a tangled symptom set: sustained OS memory pressure and swap storms slow both primary and replica processes; replication lag grows rapidly, causing ever-larger piles of unrecycled WAL/redo or relay logs; the ballooning log archives, combined with already constrained data, temp, and backup areas, drive the platform toward disk-full conditions. As space dwindles, checkpoints, autovacuum/clean-up jobs, temporary-object creation, and even normal DML may stall or error. Simultaneously, memory exhaustion can trigger process restarts that reset replication connections, further enlarging the backlog, while replicas under memory stress replay logs even more slowly, compounding lag metrics. Operations teams may see erratic query latency, intermittent OOM terminations, mounting replication delays, and cascading "out of space" or "cannot allocate" errors across primary and secondary nodes.

Causal chain: excessive memory allocation on the primary (and potentially replicas) reduces CPU throughput and elevates checkpoint frequency as dirty buffers are flushed under pressure. The slower checkpoint and apply throughput make replicas lag, which forces the primary to retain additional WAL segments. These retained logs, together with memory-induced delays in maintenance tasks (vacuum, purge, backup copy/move), accelerate consumption of storage capacity. As disk space nears exhaustion, background writers and archivers stall, which in turn increases in-memory pressure because buffers cannot be flushed or freed promptly. The interlocking feedback—memory overcommitment slowing replication, replication backlog inflating disk usage, and disk saturation inhibiting memory relief—drives the database into a critical state that threatens availability and data protection.

Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly : Excessive growth of buffer caches, work areas, session heaps, or other in-memory regions pushes the database process and operating system beyond safe physical or virtual memory limits.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space for data files, logs, temp segments, backups, or diagnostic areas is exhausted, causing allocation failures and write stalls.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Listener, socket, or network-path limitations prevent timely creation and servicing of client connections and data transfer.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a multilayer resource crisis: memory pressure triggers aggressive paging and swap I/O that rapidly depletes disk space; simultaneous log, temp, or swap growth collides with already scarce storage capacity, producing "out of space" errors, stalled checkpoints, and frozen DML. As space and memory related stalls lengthen response times, client sessions linger, connection pools retry, and partially opened or slow-draining sockets accumulate, overwhelming listener backlogs and exhausting server process slots. Administrators may observe a vicious cycle of rising resident-set size, skyrocketing swap usage, temp-space allocation failures, exploding archive/log volumes, surging connection timeouts, and cascading instance restarts or cluster failovers.

Causally, unbounded memory allocations provoke paging; paging writes inflate swap and temp files, accelerating storage consumption. Once disks fill, swap expansion and log growth halt, amplifying memory faults and forcing abrupt process terminations that leave orphaned TCP sessions. The mounting queue of stuck or retried clients sustains high connection counts, each reserving additional memory and socket buffers, further tightening the memory squeeze. Conversely, network slowdowns prolong transaction and bulk-load durations, keeping large result sets, work areas, and temp segments alive and growing, which hastens both memory and space exhaustion. The intertwined feedback loops among memory, storage, and connectivity thus reinforce each other, rapidly degrading overall database availability and making root-cause isolation difficult.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Optimizer input metadata (row counts, histograms, correlation data) is stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and sub-optimal plan choices.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is saturated or degraded, so read/write latency, IOPS, or throughput no longer meet the database engine’s demand.

When these two root causes coexist, the database may select plans that are already inefficient because of bad statistics (e.g., full table scans, merge joins, large hash spills) and then execute them on an I/O subsystem that cannot deliver the required bandwidth. Observable symptoms therefore include extreme divergence between estimated and actual rows, frequent plan re-compilations, bloated temp-space usage, AND prolonged wait events for data-file, log-file, and temp-I/O. CPU may stay low while wall-clock runtimes spike; batch windows overrun; ad-hoc queries oscillate between quick and pathological runtimes depending on cache warm-ness; emergency stats updates or index hints yield only partial relief because storage waits remain dominant.

Causally, stale or missing statistics drive the optimizer toward data-hungry execution strategies that issue far more physical reads and writes than necessary. This amplifies load on an already constrained storage subsystem, quickly pushing it past its throughput or latency limits. Conversely, high I/O latency causes many plans to complete slowly, delaying automatic statistics refresh thresholds and making statistics staleness more likely. The two conditions thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop: poor statistics cause I/O-intensive plans, I/O saturation prolongs execution and data-change windows, which further postpones statistics collection and exacerbates misestimation, resulting in a compounded degradation of overall database performance.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Sessions serialize on hot buffer-cache pages and the latches protecting them, producing buffer-busy/page-latch waits and spin loops inside the buffer manager.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume nearly all available CPU cycles, pushing system-wide utilization and run-queue lengths to saturation levels.

When both root causes strike simultaneously, the database experiences a feedback loop in which excessive CPU spin and context switching from latch contention coexist with, and intensify, host CPU saturation. Observable symptoms include: sustained 90-100 % CPU usage alongside a high fraction of CPU time spent in spin-wait; explosive run-queue growth paired with elevated buffer-busy, latch free, and scheduler wait events; steep, wide-ranging latency spikes where even simple statements stall behind both CPU scarcity and latch acquisition; and uneven throughput as hot pages intermittently freeze large parts of the workload while other sessions starve for CPU.

Causally, hot-page contention forces foreground processes to enter tight spin loops, burning CPU while waiting for latches; this self-generates the CPU Resource Anomaly. Conversely, a pre-existing CPU bottleneck lengthens critical sections inside the buffer manager because latch holders are scheduled less frequently, inflating the hold times seen by other sessions and deepening buffer contention. The two anomalies therefore reinforce each other: latch spin escalates CPU pressure, while CPU starvation magnifies latch hold durations, propagating stalls across the workload and driving the database into a mutually amplifying spiral of compute exhaustion and buffer-cache serialization.

Name: Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
Description:
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions serialize on hot buffer pages, latches, or page-pin slots inside the buffer manager, leading to CPU spin or waits while pages are being read, written, or flushed.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer is unable to sustain the read/write volume demanded by the engine, causing backlog, high latency, and prolonged I/O waits.

When both issues surface simultaneously, the database exhibits a compounded symptom set: severe and erratic response-time spikes, high buffer-busy and page-latch waits co-existing with swollen read/write wait times, CPU cores oscillating between spin-loops and idleness, log-write stalls, and checkpoint or bulk-load operations overrunning their windows. Buffer pages grow scarce because they take longer to be written back; sessions then thrash on the remaining hot pages, intensifying latch contention. Wait-event histograms show interleaved latch-related and I/O-related waits, making isolation of a single culprit difficult.

Causally, saturated storage slows page flushes and read-ins, lengthening the residency of dirty pages and inflating buffer churn. The reduced recycling rate leaves fewer clean frames, forcing more sessions to compete for the same hot pages and their protecting latches. In turn, the heavier latch contention stalls user work, producing bursty I/O patterns (e.g., massed retry reads or redo flush surges) that further overload the storage subsystem. The feedback loop between slow physical I/O and in-memory latch bottlenecks amplifies both anomalies, degrading throughput and stability across OLTP and analytical workloads.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
Description:
Composite Definition: The system simultaneously suffers from (1) the optimizer choosing markedly sub-optimal execution plans, (2) latent corruption or structural inconsistency inside data and index pages, and (3) exhaustion or instability of network/connection resources. The workload therefore executes with bad plans against unreliable storage structures while clients communicate through a congested or faulty network layer.

Compound Phenomena: Operators may see the same statement alternate between index scans, full table scans, and nested-loop explosions; some executions unexpectedly return wrong, missing, or duplicated rows because corrupted index pages mis-direct look-ups. The optimizer’s reactive plan changes trigger bursts of I/O that surface additional page-checksum or logical-consistency errors, causing retries or error messages. Concurrently, connection establishment slows, sockets pile up in TIME_WAIT or SYN_RECV, and clients experience intermittent timeouts or SSL-handshake failures. Long-running mis-planned queries stream enlarged result sets that clog already constrained network bandwidth, while aborted or retried sessions further inflate backend counts and plan-cache churn. Overall throughput becomes jagged, latency unpredictable, and data correctness suspect, making diagnosis difficult because each symptom can mask or mimic the others.

Causal Interaction: Page or index corruption distorts the optimizer’s cardinality feedback, leading it to misjudge access costs and select inefficient plans; when these plans downgrade to full scans or generate massively skewed join orders, they issue large I/O bursts that read additional damaged pages, escalating corruption errors. The heavier I/O and longer runtimes inflate result-set sizes and hold server processes busy, lengthening network streaming windows and aggravating existing network congestion. Network slowdowns, in turn, prolong compile times, increase plan cache eviction pressure, and provoke client-side retries that multiply connection attempts, amplifying listener and authentication stress. The compounded load heightens the probability of abrupt disconnects, which can interrupt in-flight writes and leave indexes half-rebuilt, feeding back into structural corruption. Thus each root cause not only adds its own failures but also reinforces the others, driving the database into a spiraling state of poor performance, data inconsistency, and connectivity instability.

Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between the data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and workload access patterns forces sub-optimal access paths independent of optimizer statistics.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages or index structures makes stored rows or keys unreliable, causing incorrect or unstable access results.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Imminent or actual exhaustion of data, log, temp, or backup space prevents new allocations and halts normal database operations.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode in which inefficient schema design drives excessive full scans, large sorts, and frequent page splits that rapidly consume the dwindling free space, while underlying corruption causes the optimizer to discard damaged indexes or return wrong results. Symptoms include: frequent plan shifts from index seeks to full scans, exploding temp-space and log usage followed by allocation-failed errors, inconsistent row counts between index and table scans, checksum or page-level I/O errors, aborted DML/DDL due to out-of-space or corruption detection, and severe performance degradation accompanied by data-quality incidents.

Causally, poor schema and missing/inefficient indexes inflate I/O volumes and fragment structures, accelerating space consumption and triggering emergency auto-extension or allocation failures. Near-full disks, in turn, restrict the engine’s ability to split pages cleanly or rebuild indexes, increasing the likelihood of partial writes and structural corruption. Emerging block or index damage leads the optimizer to ignore or drop indexes, which amplifies the impact of the original design flaws by forcing even heavier scans that further exhaust space. Attempts to repair corruption or add corrective indexes fail due to space shortages, creating a vicious cycle where design inefficiency, structural corruption, and capacity exhaustion continuously reinforce each other and degrade both performance and data integrity across all workload types.

Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly
Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer repeatedly selects a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are acceptable and no single plan should be reused.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Obsolete row versions and rollback records accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them, inflating the physical size of tables and indexes and adding visibility-check overhead.

Composite anomaly definition: The database concurrently suffers from plan-selection errors and runaway MVCC version buildup. While the workload is running, every statement is exposed both to bloated storage structures and to an execution plan that is not well adapted to the real cost landscape, creating a feedback loop that degrades throughput and latency.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) Plans flip between index probes and full scans or choose inefficient join orders; at the same time, table and index sizes grow rapidly, causing I/O and buffer-pool pressure. 2) Execution-time skew increases dramatically—some executions are trapped in long sequential scans over dead rows, others fail early due to timeout. 3) Autovacuum or cleanup workers show sustained backlog, yet long-running queries with bad plans keep old snapshots open, preventing garbage collection. 4) The optimizer’s estimated costs diverge even further from reality because the bloated heap increases page counts, but the cost model picks plans that are optimal only for the leaner structure assumed at compile time. 5) Administrators observe both plan cache churn and high version-store utilization without obvious blocking locks.

Causal chain and reinforcement: MVCC bloat inflates relation size and alters physical access costs; however, the optimizer’s plan selection anomaly fails to adapt, locking in plans that underweight the I/O penalty of scanning the expanded data. These inefficient plans run longer, holding snapshots and transaction IDs open for extended periods, which in turn delays vacuum/garbage collection and accelerates version accumulation. The growing version store further distorts cost dynamics, increasing the likelihood that the optimizer will mis-rank candidates on subsequent compilations, amplifying plan instability and continuing the vicious cycle. Without intervention—such as forced plan baselines plus aggressive vacuum tuning—both anomalies feed each other, driving the system into severe performance and storage crisis.

Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Stale, incomplete, or low-quality statistics cause the optimizer to misestimate cardinalities and choose inefficient execution plans.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Dead rows and old row versions accumulate because background cleaners cannot keep pace, inflating table and index size and adding visibility-check work.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Data, log, or temporary areas run short of free space, leading to allocation failures, auto-extend stalls, or write errors.

When all three root causes appear together, the system exhibits a blend of misestimated plans, rapidly growing on-disk structures, and mounting space-exhaustion warnings. Execution plans may swing from index probes to full scans against bloated tables, spilling large hash or sort operations into already constrained temp space. Vacuum/cleanup workers run continuously yet fall further behind, and their own I/O or temp needs trigger "no space left" errors that abort or defer maintenance. Catalog views show diverging row-count estimates from reality, while tablespaces, WAL/archive areas, and temp segments fill at an accelerating rate.
